title: 2.5 Convolution and mollifiers
text:
Mollification, that is, convolution with a smooth kernel of small support, is our basic tool for approximating functions and distributions by smooth functions. The convolution of two functions $f$ and $g$ on $\mathbb R^ d$ is \[  (f*g)(x)=\int _{\mathbb R^ d}f(y)g(x-y)\, \mathrm dy,  \] defined at every point $x$ at which the integral exists. As kernel we take \[  ho (x)= egin{cases} c\exp (-(1-|x|^2)^{-1}),& |x|<1,\ 0,& |x|\geq 1,\end{cases} \qquad \int _{\mathbb R^ d}ho \, \mathrm d x=1,  \] where the constant $c>0$ normalizes the integral. Inside the unit ball, each partial derivative of $ho $ is a polynomial in $x$ and $(1-|x|^2)^{-1}$ times $\exp (-(1-|x|^2)^{-1})$, and hence tends to zero at the unit sphere, because $t^ k\mathrm e^{-t}	o 0$ as $t	o \infty $. Since a coordinate line meets the sphere in at most two points, the mean value theorem on coordinate segments shows inductively that all partial derivatives of $ho $ exist on $\mathbb R^ d$, vanish on the sphere and are continuous. Thus $ho $ is a nonnegative function in $C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$; it is radial, that is, $ho (x)$ depends only on $|x|$, and in particular it is even. We write $B(x,r)=\{ y\in \mathbb R^ d:|y-x|<r\} $ for the open ball with center $x$ and radius $r>0$; its closure $\overline{B(x,r)}=\{ y\in \mathbb R^ d:|y-x|\leq r\} $ is the closed ball. For $\varepsilon >0$ the function $ho _\varepsilon (x)=\varepsilon ^{-d}ho (x/\varepsilon )$ is radial, has integral $1$ and is supported in $\overline{B(0,\varepsilon )}$. We call $ho $ and the functions $ho _\varepsilon $ mollifiers. Put \[  \Omega _\varepsilon =\{ x\in \Omega :\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb R^ d\setminus \Omega )>\varepsilon \} .  \] For $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, extended by zero outside $\Omega $, the mollification of $u$ is \[  u_\varepsilon (x)=(u*ho _\varepsilon )(x)=\int _\Omega u(y)ho _\varepsilon (x-y)\, \mathrm d y,\qquad x\in \Omega _\varepsilon .  \] The mollification $u_\varepsilon $ is smooth on $\Omega _\varepsilon $. To see this, let $\psi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$ be supported in $\overline{B(0,\varepsilon )}$, fix $x\in \Omega _\varepsilon $, and let $L\subset \Omega _\varepsilon $ be a closed ball about $x$. For $x'\in L$, only points $y$ of the compact set $L'=\{ y:\operatorname {dist}(y,L)\leq \varepsilon \} $ contribute to $(u*\psi )(x')$. Every point of $L'$ lies within distance $\varepsilon $ of a point of $L$, so $L'\subset \Omega $, and $u$ is integrable on $L'$. Hence $|(u*\psi )(x')-(u*\psi )(x)|\leq \sup _ y|\psi (x'-y)-\psi (x-y)|\int _{L'}|u|\, \mathrm dy$ for $x'\in L$, so $u*\psi $ is continuous at $x$ by the uniform continuity of $\psi $. Moreover, if $e_ j$ denotes the $j$th coordinate unit vector, the mean value theorem and the uniform continuity of $\partial _ j\psi $ show that $t^{-1}(\psi (x+te_ j-y)-\psi (x-y))	o \partial _ j\psi (x-y)$ uniformly in $y$ as $t	o 0$. Integrating against $u$ over $L'$, we obtain $\partial _ j(u*\psi )(x)=(u*\partial _ j\psi )(x)$. Applying this to $\psi =\partial ^\alpha ho _\varepsilon $, we find by induction on $|\alpha |$ that $u_\varepsilon \in C^\infty (\Omega _\varepsilon )$ and $\partial ^\alpha u_\varepsilon =u*\partial ^\alpha ho _\varepsilon $. Lemma 2.5.1 . 3C40E6BD1222 In the following assertions, limits are taken as $\varepsilon 	o 0$. If $u\in C(\Omega )$, then $u_\varepsilon 	o u$ uniformly on every compact subset of $\Omega $. Let $1\leq p<\infty $. Translation is continuous in $L^ p(\mathbb R^ d)$: if $v\in L^ p(\mathbb R^ d)$, then $\| v(\cdot -h)-v\| _ p	o 0$ as $h	o 0$. If $u\in L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, then $u_\varepsilon 	o u$ in $L^ p(K)$ for every compact set $K\subset \Omega $. If $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$ is extended by zero to $\mathbb R^ d$, then for small $\varepsilon $ the functions $\chi *ho _\varepsilon $ are supported in a fixed compact subset of $\Omega $, and $\partial ^\alpha (\chi *ho _\varepsilon )	o \partial ^\alpha \chi $ uniformly for every multi-index $\alpha $. If $K\subset U\subset \Omega $ with $K$ compact and $U$ open, there is a smooth cutoff function for $K$ in $U$ which equals $1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. If $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$ is extended by zero to $\mathbb R^ d$, then for small $\varepsilon $ the functions $f*ho _\varepsilon $ are test functions supported in a fixed compact subset of $\Omega $, and they converge uniformly to $f$. Consequently, $C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$ is dense in $L^ p(\mu )$ for every Radon measure $\mu $ on $\Omega $ and every $1\leq p<\infty $. Proof. (1) Since $\int ho _\varepsilon =1$, we have for $x\in \Omega _\varepsilon $ \[  |u_\varepsilon (x)-u(x)|\leq \int |u(x-h)-u(x)|ho _\varepsilon (h)\, \mathrm dh\leq \sup _{|h|\leq \varepsilon }|u(x-h)-u(x)|.  \] If $K\subset \Omega $ is compact, choose $\delta >0$ with $K'=\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)\leq \delta \} \subset \Omega $. For $\varepsilon <\delta $ we have $K\subset \Omega _\varepsilon $, because the closed ball of radius $\delta $ about each point of $K$ lies in $\Omega $, and the bound tends to zero uniformly on $K$ by the uniform continuity of $u$ on the compact set $K'$. (2) We first prove the continuity of translation. For $v\in C_ c(\mathbb R^ d)$ it follows from uniform continuity, since the functions $v(\cdot -h)$, $|h|\leq 1$, are supported in a fixed compact set; the general case follows by approximating $v$ in $L^ p$ by such functions (proposition 2.3.5 for Lebesgue measure), since translation preserves the $L^ p$ norm. Since $\int ho _\varepsilon =1$, we have $v*ho _\varepsilon (x)-v(x)=\int (v(x-h)-v(x))ho _\varepsilon (h)\, \mathrm dh$. Hence, by the triangle inequality and Jensen's inequality (lemma 2.2.4 ) for the convex function $t\mapsto |t|^ p$ on $\mathbb R$, applied to the function $h\mapsto |v(x-h)-v(x)|$, which is integrable for the probability measure $ho _\varepsilon (h)\, \mathrm dh$ because $|v|\leq 1+|v|^ p$, we obtain \[  |v*ho _\varepsilon (x)-v(x)|^ p\leq \int |v(x-h)-v(x)|^ pho _\varepsilon (h)\, \mathrm dh\qquad 	ext{for every }x.  \] We may take $v$ to be a Borel function, so that the integrand is a Borel function of $(x,h)$. Integrating in $x$ and using Tonelli's theorem, we obtain \[  \| v*ho _\varepsilon -v\| _ p^ p \leq \int ho _\varepsilon (h)\| v(\cdot -h)-v\| _ p^ p\, \mathrm d h\leq \sup _{|h|\leq \varepsilon }\| v(\cdot -h)-v\| _ p^ p	o 0.  \] Now let $u\in L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ and $K\subset \Omega $ compact, choose $\delta >0$ with $\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)\leq 2\delta \} \subset \Omega $, and let $v\in L^ p(\mathbb R^ d)$ equal $u$ on $W=\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)<2\delta \} $ and $0$ elsewhere. For $\varepsilon <\delta $, the values of $u_\varepsilon $ on $K$ only involve $u$ on $W$, so $\| u_\varepsilon -u\| _{L^ p(K)}\leq \| v*ho _\varepsilon -v\| _ p	o 0$. (3) The function $\chi *ho _\varepsilon $ vanishes outside the set of points at distance at most $\varepsilon $ from $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, which is a compact subset of $\Omega $ for small $\varepsilon $. Differentiation under the integral sign gives $\partial ^\alpha (\chi *ho _\varepsilon )=(\partial ^\alpha \chi )*ho _\varepsilon $, and the bound displayed in (1), applied on $\mathbb R^ d$ to the uniformly continuous function $\partial ^\alpha \chi $ in place of $u$, proves uniform convergence. (4) Choose $\delta >0$ with $3\delta <\operatorname {dist}(K,\mathbb R^ d\setminus U)$, and let $\eta $ be a cutoff function for $\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)\leq 2\delta \} $ in $\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)<3\delta \} $. If $\varepsilon <\delta $ is smaller than the distance from $\operatorname{Supp}\eta $ to $\mathbb R^ d\setminus U$, then $\eta *ho _\varepsilon $ is smooth with values in $[0,1]$ and compact support in $U$, and it equals $1$ on $\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)<\delta \} $, where the average only involves points at which $\eta =1$. (5) The support statement is proved as in (3), the functions $f*ho _\varepsilon $ are smooth by differentiation under the integral sign, and uniform convergence follows from (1) applied on $\mathbb R^ d$, since all these functions vanish outside a fixed compact set. If $g\in L^ p(\mu )$, choose $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$ close to $g$ in $L^ p(\mu )$ by proposition 2.3.5 . If all $f*ho _\varepsilon $ are supported in the compact set $L$, then so is their uniform limit $f$, and $\| f*ho _\varepsilon -f\| _{L^ p(\mu )}\leq \sup |f*ho _\varepsilon -f|\, \mu (L)^{1/p}	o 0$. $\square$ Smooth cutoff functions yield partitions of unity, which localize test functions and distributions. Lemma 2.5.2 . 677586F8712C Let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, and let $U_1,\ldots ,U_ n\subset \Omega $ be open sets covering $K$. Then there are smooth functions $\eta _ j\colon \Omega 	o [0,1]$ with compact support in $U_ j$, $1\leq j\leq n$, such that $\sum _ j\eta _ j\leq 1$ on $\Omega $ and $\sum _ j\eta _ j=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Consequently, every test function $\chi $ with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset U_1\cup \cdots \cup U_ n$ is the sum of the test functions $\chi \eta _ j$, which are supported in $U_ j$ and are nonnegative if $\chi $ is nonnegative. In particular, a distribution on $\Omega $ that vanishes on each member of a family of open subsets of $\Omega $ vanishes on their union. Proof. For every $x\in K$ choose an index $j(x)$ with $x\in U_{j(x)}$ and a radius $r_ x>0$ with $\overline{B(x,r_ x)}\subset U_{j(x)}$. Finitely many of the balls $B(x,r_ x)$ cover $K$; let $L_ j$ be the union of the closures of those among them with $j(x)=j$. Then $L_ j$ is a compact, possibly empty, subset of $U_ j$, and $K\subset L_1\cup \cdots \cup L_ n$. By lemma 2.5.1 (4), there are smooth cutoff functions $\psi _ j$ for $L_ j$ in $U_ j$ which equal $1$ on neighborhoods $V_ j$ of $L_ j$. Put $\eta _1=\psi _1$ and $\eta _ j=\psi _ j(1-\psi _1)\cdots (1-\psi _{j-1})$ for $2\leq j\leq n$. These functions are smooth with values in $[0,1]$, and $\operatorname{Supp}\eta _ j\subset \operatorname{Supp}\psi _ j$ is a compact subset of $U_ j$. By induction on $n$, \[  \sum _{j=1}^ n\eta _ j=1-\prod _{j=1}^ n(1-\psi _ j),  \] which takes values in $[0,1]$ and equals $1$ on the neighborhood $V_1\cup \cdots \cup V_ n$ of $K$. If $\chi $ is a test function with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset U_1\cup \cdots \cup U_ n$, we apply this to $K=\operatorname{Supp}\chi $; then $\chi =\sum _ j\chi \eta _ j$, and $\operatorname{Supp}(\chi \eta _ j)\subset \operatorname{Supp}\eta _ j$ is a compact subset of $U_ j$. Finally, let a distribution $T$ vanish on each member of a family of open subsets of $\Omega $, and let $\chi $ be a test function supported in their union. The compact set $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ is covered by finitely many members $U_1,\ldots ,U_ n$ of the family, and the decomposition $\chi =\sum _ j\chi \eta _ j$ just obtained gives $\langle T,\chi angle =\sum _ j\langle T,\chi \eta _ jangle =0$. $\square$ By the last assertion of lemma 2.5.2 , every distribution $T$ vanishes on $\Omega \setminus \operatorname{Supp}T$. A distribution is mollified by letting it act on the translated kernel. Let $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$, let $s>0$, and let $\phi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$ be supported in $\overline{B(0,s)}$. If $x\in \Omega _ s$, then $\phi (x-\cdot )$ is a test function on $\Omega $, supported in $\overline{B(x,s)}$, and we put \[  (T*\phi )(x)=\langle T,\phi (x-\cdot )angle ,\qquad x\in \Omega _ s.  \] For $T$ given by $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, this is the convolution $u*\phi $ of $u$, extended by zero, with $\phi $. The function $T_\varepsilon =T*ho _\varepsilon $ is called the mollification of $T$; for $T$ given by $u$, it is the mollification $u_\varepsilon $ of $u$. Proposition 2.5.3 . 0CB24AD25DC3 Let $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$ and $\varepsilon >0$, and let $T_\varepsilon (x)=\langle T,ho _\varepsilon (x-\cdot )angle $ for $x\in \Omega _\varepsilon $. If $s>0$ and $\phi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$ is supported in $\overline{B(0,s)}$, then $T*\phi $ is smooth on $\Omega _ s$, and $\partial ^\alpha (T*\phi )=T*\partial ^\alpha \phi =(\partial ^\alpha T)*\phi $ for every multi-index $\alpha $. In particular, $T_\varepsilon $ is smooth on $\Omega _\varepsilon $, and $\partial ^\alpha T_\varepsilon =(\partial ^\alpha T)_\varepsilon $. For every test function $\chi $, $\int T_\varepsilon \chi \, \mathrm d x	o \langle T,\chi angle $ as $\varepsilon 	o 0$; the integral is defined once $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset \Omega _\varepsilon $. If $T$ is positive, then $T_\varepsilon \geq 0$. A locally integrable function on $\Omega $ is determined by its distribution up to equality almost everywhere, and a Radon measure on $\Omega $ is determined by its distribution. Proof. (1) Fix $x\in \Omega _ s$ and $\delta >0$ with $\overline{B(x,\delta )}\subset \Omega _ s$. For $|x'-x|\leq \delta $, the test functions $\phi (x'-\cdot )$ are supported in the compact set $K=\overline{B(x,\delta +s)}$, which lies in $\Omega $ because $\overline{B(x',s)}\subset \Omega $ for every such $x'$. Taylor's formula, applied to all derivatives of $\phi $, shows that the difference quotients $t^{-1}(\phi (x+te_ j-\cdot )-\phi (x-\cdot ))$, where $e_ j$ is a coordinate unit vector, converge to $(\partial _ j\phi )(x-\cdot )$ in every seminorm $p_{K,m}$ as $t	o 0$; similarly, $\phi (x'-\cdot )	o \phi (x-\cdot )$ in every $p_{K,m}$ as $x'	o x$. By the estimate of definition 2.4.1 on $\mathcal D_ K(\Omega )$, $T*\phi $ is continuous at $x$ and $\partial _ j(T*\phi )(x)=\langle T,(\partial _ j\phi )(x-\cdot )angle =(T*\partial _ j\phi )(x)$. Applying the same argument to the derivatives of $\phi $, which are also supported in $\overline{B(0,s)}$, we find by induction that $T*\phi $ is smooth and $\partial ^\alpha (T*\phi )=T*\partial ^\alpha \phi $. Since $\partial _ y^\alpha [\phi (x-y)]=(-1)^{|\alpha |}(\partial ^\alpha \phi )(x-y)$, we have $((\partial ^\alpha T)*\phi )(x)=(-1)^{|\alpha |}\langle T,\partial _ y^\alpha [\phi (x-y)]angle =(T*\partial ^\alpha \phi )(x)$. The case $\phi =ho _\varepsilon $, $s=\varepsilon $, gives the assertions about $T_\varepsilon $. (2) Let $\chi $ be a test function with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset \Omega _\varepsilon $. We first prove that 3AA3C6A6F513 2.5.4  egin{equation}  \int T_\varepsilon (x)\chi (x)\, \mathrm d x =\langle T,\chi *ho _\varepsilon angle . \end{equation} Since $ho $ is even, $(\chi *ho _\varepsilon )(y)=\int \chi (x)ho _\varepsilon (x-y)\, \mathrm dx$, and $\chi *ho _\varepsilon $ is supported in the compact set $K\subset \Omega $ of points at distance at most $\varepsilon $ from $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $. Divide a closed cube containing $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ into $N^ d$ congruent subcubes $Q_ l$ with centers $c_ l$, and put $S_ N(y)=\sum _ l\chi (c_ l)ho _\varepsilon (c_ l-y)|Q_ l|$. Only centers $c_ l\in \operatorname{Supp}\chi $ contribute, so $S_ N\in \mathcal D_ K(\Omega )$ and $\langle T,S_ Nangle =\sum _ l\chi (c_ l)T_\varepsilon (c_ l)|Q_ l|$, a Riemann sum for the continuous function $T_\varepsilon \chi $, extended by zero; it tends to $\int T_\varepsilon \chi \, \mathrm dx$. On the other hand, each derivative $\partial ^ eta S_ N(y)$ is a Riemann sum for the integral over the cube of $x\mapsto \chi (x)\partial ^ eta _ y[ho _\varepsilon (x-y)]$, and this integral is $\partial ^ eta (\chi *ho _\varepsilon )(y)$ by differentiation under the integral sign. The integrand is uniformly continuous in $(x,y)$, so the difference between the Riemann sum and the integral is at most the volume of the cube times the largest oscillation of the integrand in $x$ over a subcube, which tends to zero uniformly in $y$. Hence $S_ N	o \chi *ho _\varepsilon $ in every seminorm $p_{K,m}$, and the estimate for $T$ on $\mathcal D_ K(\Omega )$ gives $\langle T,S_ Nangle 	o \langle T,\chi *ho _\varepsilon angle $. This proves ( 2.5.4 ). By lemma 2.5.1 (3), the functions $\chi *ho _\varepsilon $ are supported in a fixed compact set for small $\varepsilon $ and converge to $\chi $ with all derivatives uniformly, so $\langle T,\chi *ho _\varepsilon angle 	o \langle T,\chi angle $. (3) If $T$ is positive, then $T_\varepsilon (x)\geq 0$ because $ho _\varepsilon (x-\cdot )$ is a nonnegative test function. (4) If $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ defines the zero distribution, then $u_\varepsilon =T_\varepsilon =0$ for every $\varepsilon $, and $u_\varepsilon 	o u$ in $L^1(K)$ for every compact $K$ by lemma 2.5.1 (2); hence $u=0$ almost everywhere. If two Radon measures $\mu $ and $
u $ define the same distribution, then $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu =\int f\, \mathrm d
u $ for every $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$, because $f$ is the uniform limit of test functions supported in a fixed compact set (lemma 2.5.1 (5)). The uniqueness in theorem 2.3.3 gives $\mu =
u $. $\square$ Corollary 2.5.5 . DF54B49EC7D4 Let $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$ satisfy $\partial _ jT=0$ for $1\leq j\leq d$. Then $T$ is given by a locally constant function on $\Omega $. If $\Omega $ is connected, $T$ is a constant function. Proof. Let $B$ be an open ball with $\overline B\subset \Omega $, and fix $	heta \in C_ c^\infty (B)$ with $\int 	heta \, \mathrm dx=1$, for instance a translate of $ho _ s$ with $s>0$ small. Since $\overline B$ is compact, $\overline B\subset \Omega _\varepsilon $ for all small $\varepsilon $. By proposition 2.5.3 (1), the smooth function $T_\varepsilon $ has gradient $((\partial _ jT)_\varepsilon )_ j=0$ on $\Omega _\varepsilon $, so it is equal to a constant $c_\varepsilon $ on the convex set $B$. By proposition 2.5.3 (2), $c_\varepsilon =\int T_\varepsilon 	heta \, \mathrm dx	o \langle T,	heta angle =:c_ B$, and therefore, for every $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (B)$, \[  \langle T,\chi angle =\lim _{\varepsilon 	o 0}\int T_\varepsilon \chi \, \mathrm dx=\lim _{\varepsilon 	o 0}c_\varepsilon \int \chi \, \mathrm dx=c_ B\int \chi \, \mathrm dx.  \] If two such balls $B$ and $B'$ intersect, testing with a nonnegative function $\chi 
eq 0$ in $C_ c^\infty (B\cap B')$ gives $c_ B=c_{B'}$. Any two such balls containing a point $x\in \Omega $ intersect, so $c(x)=c_ B$, for any such ball $B$ containing $x$, is a well-defined function on $\Omega $; it is locally constant, since $c=c_ B$ on $B$. Every test function $\chi $ has compact support covered by finitely many such balls $B_ l$, and by lemma 2.5.2 it is a sum of test functions $\chi _ l$ supported in $B_ l$. Hence $\langle T,\chi angle =\sum _ lc_{B_ l}\int \chi _ l\, \mathrm dx=\int c\chi \, \mathrm dx$. Finally, if $\Omega $ is connected, the locally constant function $c$ is constant, because for each value $a$ the set $\{ c=a\} $ is open and so is its complement. $\square$ Theorem 2.5.6 . 6A928E70A605 Let $T$ be a positive distribution on $\Omega $. Then there is a unique Radon measure $\mu $ on $\Omega $ such that $\langle T,\chi angle =\int \chi \, \mathrm d\mu $ for every test function $\chi $. Conversely, every Radon measure defines a positive distribution in this way. Proof. Let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact and let $\eta $ be a smooth cutoff function for $K$ in $\Omega $ (lemma 2.5.1 (4)). For a real test function $\chi $ with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset K$, the test functions $\| \chi \| _\infty \eta \pm \chi $ are nonnegative, so positivity gives, as in ( 2.3.1 ), \[  |\langle T,\chi angle |\leq \langle T,\eta angle \| \chi \| _\infty .  \] We use this bound to extend $T$ to $C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$. If $f\in C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$, the real test functions $f*ho _\varepsilon $ are supported in a fixed compact set for small $\varepsilon $ and converge uniformly to $f$ (lemma 2.5.1 (5)). By the displayed estimate, $\langle T,f*ho _\varepsilon angle $ converges as $\varepsilon 	o 0$, and its limit $\Lambda (f)$ is also the limit of $\langle T,\chi _ kangle $ for any real test functions $\chi _ k$ supported in a common compact set and converging uniformly to $f$. Approximating two functions of $C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$ by test functions with a common compact support, we see that $\Lambda $ is linear. If $f\geq 0$, then $f*ho _\varepsilon \geq 0$, so $\Lambda (f)\geq 0$. By theorem 2.3.3 , there is a Radon measure $\mu $ with $\Lambda (f)=\int f\, \mathrm d\mu $. For a real test function $\chi $, the constant sequence $\chi _ k=\chi $ shows that $\Lambda (\chi )=\langle T,\chi angle $; applying this to $\operatorname{Re}\chi $ and $\operatorname{Im}\chi $ gives $\langle T,\chi angle =\int \chi \, \mathrm d\mu $ for all test functions. The measure $\mu $ is unique by proposition 2.5.3 (4). Conversely, if $\mu $ is a Radon measure, then $|\int \chi \, \mathrm d\mu |\leq (1+\mu (K))p_{K,0}(\chi )$ for $\chi \in \mathcal D_ K(\Omega )$, so integration against $\mu $ is a distribution, and it is positive. $\square$

title: Lemma 2.5.1
text: Lemma 2.5.1 . 3C40E6BD1222 In the following assertions, limits are taken as $\varepsilon \to 0$. If $u\in C(\Omega )$, then $u_\varepsilon \to u$ uniformly on every compact subset of $\Omega $. Let $1\leq p<\infty $. Translation is continuous in $L^ p(\mathbb R^ d)$: if $v\in L^ p(\mathbb R^ d)$, then $\| v(\cdot -h)-v\| _ p\to 0$ as $h\to 0$. If $u\in L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, then $u_\varepsilon \to u$ in $L^ p(K)$ for every compact set $K\subset \Omega $. If $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$ is extended by zero to $\mathbb R^ d$, then for small $\varepsilon $ the functions $\chi *\rho _\varepsilon $ are supported in a fixed compact subset of $\Omega $, and $\partial ^\alpha (\chi *\rho _\varepsilon )\to \partial ^\alpha \chi $ uniformly for every multi-index $\alpha $. If $K\subset U\subset \Omega $ with $K$ compact and $U$ open, there is a smooth cutoff function for $K$ in $U$ which equals $1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. If $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$ is extended by zero to $\mathbb R^ d$, then for small $\varepsilon $ the functions $f*\rho _\varepsilon $ are test functions supported in a fixed compact subset of $\Omega $, and they converge uniformly to $f$. Consequently, $C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$ is dense in $L^ p(\mu )$ for every Radon measure $\mu $ on $\Omega $ and every $1\leq p<\infty $. Proof. (1) Since $\int \rho _\varepsilon =1$, we have for $x\in \Omega _\varepsilon $ \[  |u_\varepsilon (x)-u(x)|\leq \int |u(x-h)-u(x)|\rho _\varepsilon (h)\, \mathrm dh\leq \sup _{|h|\leq \varepsilon }|u(x-h)-u(x)|.  \] If $K\subset \Omega $ is compact, choose $\delta >0$ with $K'=\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)\leq \delta \} \subset \Omega $. For $\varepsilon <\delta $ we have $K\subset \Omega _\varepsilon $, because the closed ball of radius $\delta $ about each point of $K$ lies in $\Omega $, and the bound tends to zero uniformly on $K$ by the uniform continuity of $u$ on the compact set $K'$. (2) We first prove the continuity of translation. For $v\in C_ c(\mathbb R^ d)$ it follows from uniform continuity, since the functions $v(\cdot -h)$, $|h|\leq 1$, are supported in a fixed compact set; the general case follows by approximating $v$ in $L^ p$ by such functions (proposition 2.3.5 for Lebesgue measure), since translation preserves the $L^ p$ norm. Since $\int \rho _\varepsilon =1$, we have $v*\rho _\varepsilon (x)-v(x)=\int (v(x-h)-v(x))\rho _\varepsilon (h)\, \mathrm dh$. Hence, by the triangle inequality and Jensen's inequality (lemma 2.2.4 ) for the convex function $t\mapsto |t|^ p$ on $\mathbb R$, applied to the function $h\mapsto |v(x-h)-v(x)|$, which is integrable for the probability measure $\rho _\varepsilon (h)\, \mathrm dh$ because $|v|\leq 1+|v|^ p$, we obtain \[  |v*\rho _\varepsilon (x)-v(x)|^ p\leq \int |v(x-h)-v(x)|^ p\rho _\varepsilon (h)\, \mathrm dh\qquad \text{for every }x.  \] We may take $v$ to be a Borel function, so that the integrand is a Borel function of $(x,h)$. Integrating in $x$ and using Tonelli's theorem, we obtain \[  \| v*\rho _\varepsilon -v\| _ p^ p \leq \int \rho _\varepsilon (h)\| v(\cdot -h)-v\| _ p^ p\, \mathrm d h\leq \sup _{|h|\leq \varepsilon }\| v(\cdot -h)-v\| _ p^ p\to 0.  \] Now let $u\in L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ and $K\subset \Omega $ compact, choose $\delta >0$ with $\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)\leq 2\delta \} \subset \Omega $, and let $v\in L^ p(\mathbb R^ d)$ equal $u$ on $W=\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)<2\delta \} $ and $0$ elsewhere. For $\varepsilon <\delta $, the values of $u_\varepsilon $ on $K$ only involve $u$ on $W$, so $\| u_\varepsilon -u\| _{L^ p(K)}\leq \| v*\rho _\varepsilon -v\| _ p\to 0$. (3) The function $\chi *\rho _\varepsilon $ vanishes outside the set of points at distance at most $\varepsilon $ from $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, which is a compact subset of $\Omega $ for small $\varepsilon $. Differentiation under the integral sign gives $\partial ^\alpha (\chi *\rho _\varepsilon )=(\partial ^\alpha \chi )*\rho _\varepsilon $, and the bound displayed in (1), applied on $\mathbb R^ d$ to the uniformly continuous function $\partial ^\alpha \chi $ in place of $u$, proves uniform convergence. (4) Choose $\delta >0$ with $3\delta <\operatorname {dist}(K,\mathbb R^ d\setminus U)$, and let $\eta $ be a cutoff function for $\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)\leq 2\delta \} $ in $\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)<3\delta \} $. If $\varepsilon <\delta $ is smaller than the distance from $\operatorname{Supp}\eta $ to $\mathbb R^ d\setminus U$, then $\eta *\rho _\varepsilon $ is smooth with values in $[0,1]$ and compact support in $U$, and it equals $1$ on $\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)<\delta \} $, where the average only involves points at which $\eta =1$. (5) The support statement is proved as in (3), the functions $f*\rho _\varepsilon $ are smooth by differentiation under the integral sign, and uniform convergence follows from (1) applied on $\mathbb R^ d$, since all these functions vanish outside a fixed compact set. If $g\in L^ p(\mu )$, choose $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$ close to $g$ in $L^ p(\mu )$ by proposition 2.3.5 . If all $f*\rho _\varepsilon $ are supported in the compact set $L$, then so is their uniform limit $f$, and $\| f*\rho _\varepsilon -f\| _{L^ p(\mu )}\leq \sup |f*\rho _\varepsilon -f|\, \mu (L)^{1/p}\to 0$. $\square$

title: Lemma 2.5.2
text: Lemma 2.5.2 . 677586F8712C Let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact, and let $U_1,\ldots ,U_ n\subset \Omega $ be open sets covering $K$. Then there are smooth functions $\eta _ j\colon \Omega \to [0,1]$ with compact support in $U_ j$, $1\leq j\leq n$, such that $\sum _ j\eta _ j\leq 1$ on $\Omega $ and $\sum _ j\eta _ j=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Consequently, every test function $\chi $ with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset U_1\cup \cdots \cup U_ n$ is the sum of the test functions $\chi \eta _ j$, which are supported in $U_ j$ and are nonnegative if $\chi $ is nonnegative. In particular, a distribution on $\Omega $ that vanishes on each member of a family of open subsets of $\Omega $ vanishes on their union. Proof. For every $x\in K$ choose an index $j(x)$ with $x\in U_{j(x)}$ and a radius $r_ x>0$ with $\overline{B(x,r_ x)}\subset U_{j(x)}$. Finitely many of the balls $B(x,r_ x)$ cover $K$; let $L_ j$ be the union of the closures of those among them with $j(x)=j$. Then $L_ j$ is a compact, possibly empty, subset of $U_ j$, and $K\subset L_1\cup \cdots \cup L_ n$. By lemma 2.5.1 (4), there are smooth cutoff functions $\psi _ j$ for $L_ j$ in $U_ j$ which equal $1$ on neighborhoods $V_ j$ of $L_ j$. Put $\eta _1=\psi _1$ and $\eta _ j=\psi _ j(1-\psi _1)\cdots (1-\psi _{j-1})$ for $2\leq j\leq n$. These functions are smooth with values in $[0,1]$, and $\operatorname{Supp}\eta _ j\subset \operatorname{Supp}\psi _ j$ is a compact subset of $U_ j$. By induction on $n$, \[  \sum _{j=1}^ n\eta _ j=1-\prod _{j=1}^ n(1-\psi _ j),  \] which takes values in $[0,1]$ and equals $1$ on the neighborhood $V_1\cup \cdots \cup V_ n$ of $K$. If $\chi $ is a test function with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset U_1\cup \cdots \cup U_ n$, we apply this to $K=\operatorname{Supp}\chi $; then $\chi =\sum _ j\chi \eta _ j$, and $\operatorname{Supp}(\chi \eta _ j)\subset \operatorname{Supp}\eta _ j$ is a compact subset of $U_ j$. Finally, let a distribution $T$ vanish on each member of a family of open subsets of $\Omega $, and let $\chi $ be a test function supported in their union. The compact set $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ is covered by finitely many members $U_1,\ldots ,U_ n$ of the family, and the decomposition $\chi =\sum _ j\chi \eta _ j$ just obtained gives $\langle T,\chi \rangle =\sum _ j\langle T,\chi \eta _ j\rangle =0$. $\square$

title: Proposition 2.5.3
text:
Proposition 2.5.3 . 0CB24AD25DC3 Let $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$ and $\varepsilon >0$, and let $T_\varepsilon (x)=\langle T,ho _\varepsilon (x-\cdot )angle $ for $x\in \Omega _\varepsilon $. If $s>0$ and $\phi \in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$ is supported in $\overline{B(0,s)}$, then $T*\phi $ is smooth on $\Omega _ s$, and $\partial ^\alpha (T*\phi )=T*\partial ^\alpha \phi =(\partial ^\alpha T)*\phi $ for every multi-index $\alpha $. In particular, $T_\varepsilon $ is smooth on $\Omega _\varepsilon $, and $\partial ^\alpha T_\varepsilon =(\partial ^\alpha T)_\varepsilon $. For every test function $\chi $, $\int T_\varepsilon \chi \, \mathrm d x	o \langle T,\chi angle $ as $\varepsilon 	o 0$; the integral is defined once $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset \Omega _\varepsilon $. If $T$ is positive, then $T_\varepsilon \geq 0$. A locally integrable function on $\Omega $ is determined by its distribution up to equality almost everywhere, and a Radon measure on $\Omega $ is determined by its distribution. Proof. (1) Fix $x\in \Omega _ s$ and $\delta >0$ with $\overline{B(x,\delta )}\subset \Omega _ s$. For $|x'-x|\leq \delta $, the test functions $\phi (x'-\cdot )$ are supported in the compact set $K=\overline{B(x,\delta +s)}$, which lies in $\Omega $ because $\overline{B(x',s)}\subset \Omega $ for every such $x'$. Taylor's formula, applied to all derivatives of $\phi $, shows that the difference quotients $t^{-1}(\phi (x+te_ j-\cdot )-\phi (x-\cdot ))$, where $e_ j$ is a coordinate unit vector, converge to $(\partial _ j\phi )(x-\cdot )$ in every seminorm $p_{K,m}$ as $t	o 0$; similarly, $\phi (x'-\cdot )	o \phi (x-\cdot )$ in every $p_{K,m}$ as $x'	o x$. By the estimate of definition 2.4.1 on $\mathcal D_ K(\Omega )$, $T*\phi $ is continuous at $x$ and $\partial _ j(T*\phi )(x)=\langle T,(\partial _ j\phi )(x-\cdot )angle =(T*\partial _ j\phi )(x)$. Applying the same argument to the derivatives of $\phi $, which are also supported in $\overline{B(0,s)}$, we find by induction that $T*\phi $ is smooth and $\partial ^\alpha (T*\phi )=T*\partial ^\alpha \phi $. Since $\partial _ y^\alpha [\phi (x-y)]=(-1)^{|\alpha |}(\partial ^\alpha \phi )(x-y)$, we have $((\partial ^\alpha T)*\phi )(x)=(-1)^{|\alpha |}\langle T,\partial _ y^\alpha [\phi (x-y)]angle =(T*\partial ^\alpha \phi )(x)$. The case $\phi =ho _\varepsilon $, $s=\varepsilon $, gives the assertions about $T_\varepsilon $. (2) Let $\chi $ be a test function with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset \Omega _\varepsilon $. We first prove that 3AA3C6A6F513 2.5.4  egin{equation}  \int T_\varepsilon (x)\chi (x)\, \mathrm d x =\langle T,\chi *ho _\varepsilon angle . \end{equation} Since $ho $ is even, $(\chi *ho _\varepsilon )(y)=\int \chi (x)ho _\varepsilon (x-y)\, \mathrm dx$, and $\chi *ho _\varepsilon $ is supported in the compact set $K\subset \Omega $ of points at distance at most $\varepsilon $ from $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $. Divide a closed cube containing $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ into $N^ d$ congruent subcubes $Q_ l$ with centers $c_ l$, and put $S_ N(y)=\sum _ l\chi (c_ l)ho _\varepsilon (c_ l-y)|Q_ l|$. Only centers $c_ l\in \operatorname{Supp}\chi $ contribute, so $S_ N\in \mathcal D_ K(\Omega )$ and $\langle T,S_ Nangle =\sum _ l\chi (c_ l)T_\varepsilon (c_ l)|Q_ l|$, a Riemann sum for the continuous function $T_\varepsilon \chi $, extended by zero; it tends to $\int T_\varepsilon \chi \, \mathrm dx$. On the other hand, each derivative $\partial ^ eta S_ N(y)$ is a Riemann sum for the integral over the cube of $x\mapsto \chi (x)\partial ^ eta _ y[ho _\varepsilon (x-y)]$, and this integral is $\partial ^ eta (\chi *ho _\varepsilon )(y)$ by differentiation under the integral sign. The integrand is uniformly continuous in $(x,y)$, so the difference between the Riemann sum and the integral is at most the volume of the cube times the largest oscillation of the integrand in $x$ over a subcube, which tends to zero uniformly in $y$. Hence $S_ N	o \chi *ho _\varepsilon $ in every seminorm $p_{K,m}$, and the estimate for $T$ on $\mathcal D_ K(\Omega )$ gives $\langle T,S_ Nangle 	o \langle T,\chi *ho _\varepsilon angle $. This proves ( 2.5.4 ). By lemma 2.5.1 (3), the functions $\chi *ho _\varepsilon $ are supported in a fixed compact set for small $\varepsilon $ and converge to $\chi $ with all derivatives uniformly, so $\langle T,\chi *ho _\varepsilon angle 	o \langle T,\chi angle $. (3) If $T$ is positive, then $T_\varepsilon (x)\geq 0$ because $ho _\varepsilon (x-\cdot )$ is a nonnegative test function. (4) If $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ defines the zero distribution, then $u_\varepsilon =T_\varepsilon =0$ for every $\varepsilon $, and $u_\varepsilon 	o u$ in $L^1(K)$ for every compact $K$ by lemma 2.5.1 (2); hence $u=0$ almost everywhere. If two Radon measures $\mu $ and $
u $ define the same distribution, then $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu =\int f\, \mathrm d
u $ for every $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$, because $f$ is the uniform limit of test functions supported in a fixed compact set (lemma 2.5.1 (5)). The uniqueness in theorem 2.3.3 gives $\mu =
u $. $\square$

title: Corollary 2.5.5
text: Corollary 2.5.5 . DF54B49EC7D4 Let $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$ satisfy $\partial _ jT=0$ for $1\leq j\leq d$. Then $T$ is given by a locally constant function on $\Omega $. If $\Omega $ is connected, $T$ is a constant function. Proof. Let $B$ be an open ball with $\overline B\subset \Omega $, and fix $\theta \in C_ c^\infty (B)$ with $\int \theta \, \mathrm dx=1$, for instance a translate of $\rho _ s$ with $s>0$ small. Since $\overline B$ is compact, $\overline B\subset \Omega _\varepsilon $ for all small $\varepsilon $. By proposition 2.5.3 (1), the smooth function $T_\varepsilon $ has gradient $((\partial _ jT)_\varepsilon )_ j=0$ on $\Omega _\varepsilon $, so it is equal to a constant $c_\varepsilon $ on the convex set $B$. By proposition 2.5.3 (2), $c_\varepsilon =\int T_\varepsilon \theta \, \mathrm dx\to \langle T,\theta \rangle =:c_ B$, and therefore, for every $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (B)$, \[  \langle T,\chi \rangle =\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0}\int T_\varepsilon \chi \, \mathrm dx=\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0}c_\varepsilon \int \chi \, \mathrm dx=c_ B\int \chi \, \mathrm dx.  \] If two such balls $B$ and $B'$ intersect, testing with a nonnegative function $\chi \neq 0$ in $C_ c^\infty (B\cap B')$ gives $c_ B=c_{B'}$. Any two such balls containing a point $x\in \Omega $ intersect, so $c(x)=c_ B$, for any such ball $B$ containing $x$, is a well-defined function on $\Omega $; it is locally constant, since $c=c_ B$ on $B$. Every test function $\chi $ has compact support covered by finitely many such balls $B_ l$, and by lemma 2.5.2 it is a sum of test functions $\chi _ l$ supported in $B_ l$. Hence $\langle T,\chi \rangle =\sum _ lc_{B_ l}\int \chi _ l\, \mathrm dx=\int c\chi \, \mathrm dx$. Finally, if $\Omega $ is connected, the locally constant function $c$ is constant, because for each value $a$ the set $\{ c=a\} $ is open and so is its complement. $\square$

title: Theorem 2.5.6
text: Theorem 2.5.6 . 6A928E70A605 Let $T$ be a positive distribution on $\Omega $. Then there is a unique Radon measure $\mu $ on $\Omega $ such that $\langle T,\chi \rangle =\int \chi \, \mathrm d\mu $ for every test function $\chi $. Conversely, every Radon measure defines a positive distribution in this way. Proof. Let $K\subset \Omega $ be compact and let $\eta $ be a smooth cutoff function for $K$ in $\Omega $ (lemma 2.5.1 (4)). For a real test function $\chi $ with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset K$, the test functions $\| \chi \| _\infty \eta \pm \chi $ are nonnegative, so positivity gives, as in ( 2.3.1 ), \[  |\langle T,\chi \rangle |\leq \langle T,\eta \rangle \| \chi \| _\infty .  \] We use this bound to extend $T$ to $C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$. If $f\in C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$, the real test functions $f*\rho _\varepsilon $ are supported in a fixed compact set for small $\varepsilon $ and converge uniformly to $f$ (lemma 2.5.1 (5)). By the displayed estimate, $\langle T,f*\rho _\varepsilon \rangle $ converges as $\varepsilon \to 0$, and its limit $\Lambda (f)$ is also the limit of $\langle T,\chi _ k\rangle $ for any real test functions $\chi _ k$ supported in a common compact set and converging uniformly to $f$. Approximating two functions of $C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$ by test functions with a common compact support, we see that $\Lambda $ is linear. If $f\geq 0$, then $f*\rho _\varepsilon \geq 0$, so $\Lambda (f)\geq 0$. By theorem 2.3.3 , there is a Radon measure $\mu $ with $\Lambda (f)=\int f\, \mathrm d\mu $. For a real test function $\chi $, the constant sequence $\chi _ k=\chi $ shows that $\Lambda (\chi )=\langle T,\chi \rangle $; applying this to $\operatorname{Re}\chi $ and $\operatorname{Im}\chi $ gives $\langle T,\chi \rangle =\int \chi \, \mathrm d\mu $ for all test functions. The measure $\mu $ is unique by proposition 2.5.3 (4). Conversely, if $\mu $ is a Radon measure, then $|\int \chi \, \mathrm d\mu |\leq (1+\mu (K))p_{K,0}(\chi )$ for $\chi \in \mathcal D_ K(\Omega )$, so integration against $\mu $ is a distribution, and it is positive. $\square$

title: 2.6 Weak convergence of measures
text: The families of measures whose limits we shall need are not always sequences, so we work with nets. A directed set is a nonempty set $I$ with a preorder $\leq $ in which every two elements have a common upper bound. A net $(x_ i)_{i\in I}$ in a topological space $X$ is a map $i\mapsto x_ i$ from a directed set $I$ to $X$; it converges to $x\in X$ if for every neighborhood $U$ of $x$ there is $i_0\in I$ with $x_ i\in U$ for all $i\geq i_0$. For a net $(a_ i)$ in $[-\infty ,\infty ]$, $\varliminf _ i a_ i=\sup _{i_0}\inf _{i\geq i_0}a_ i$ and $\varlimsup _ i a_ i=\inf _{i_0}\sup _{i\geq i_0}a_ i$. The weak topology on $\mathcal D'(\Omega )$ is the weakest topology for which all maps $T\mapsto \langle T,\chi \rangle $, $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$, are continuous. A set containing $T$ is a neighborhood of $T$ for this topology if and only if it contains a set $\{ S:|\langle S-T,\chi _ l\rangle |<r\text{ for }1\leq l\leq k\} $ with finitely many test functions $\chi _ l$ and $r>0$. Since the index set of a net is directed, it follows that a net $(T_ i)$ converges to $T$ exactly when $\langle T_ i,\chi \rangle \to \langle T,\chi \rangle $ for every test function $\chi $, and we then say that $T_ i\to T$ in the sense of distributions. Likewise, the vague topology on the set of Radon measures on $\Omega $ is the weakest topology for which all maps $\mu \mapsto \int f\, \mathrm d\mu $, $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$, are continuous. For the same reason, a net $(\mu _ i)$ converges to $\mu $ in this topology, and we say that $\mu _ i\to \mu $ vaguely, if and only if $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ i\to \int f\, \mathrm d\mu $ for every $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$. A net of finite Radon measures converges narrowly to a finite Radon measure $\mu $ if the same holds for every bounded continuous function $f$ on $\Omega $. Narrow convergence implies vague convergence, but the converse fails, because mass can escape to infinity or to the boundary of $\Omega $ (example 2.6.4 ). Proposition 2.6.1 . 4DFD880D9E4D Let $(T_ i)$ be a net of positive distributions on $\Omega $ converging in the sense of distributions to $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$. Then $T$ is positive, and the Radon measures associated with the $T_ i$ by theorem 2.5.6 converge vaguely to the Radon measure associated with $T$. Conversely, if a net of Radon measures converges vaguely, the associated distributions converge in the sense of distributions. Proof. For a nonnegative test function $\chi $, the numbers $\langle T_ i,\chi \rangle $ are nonnegative, hence so is their limit $\langle T,\chi \rangle $; likewise $\langle T,\chi \rangle $ is real for real $\chi $. Thus $T$ is positive, and $T$ and the $T_ i$ are given by Radon measures $\mu $ and $\mu _ i$. Let $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$. By lemma 2.5.1 (5), $f$ is the uniform limit of test functions supported in a fixed compact set $L$; in particular, $f$ vanishes outside $L$. If $\eta $ is a smooth cutoff function for $L$ in $\Omega $, then $\mu _ i(L)\leq \langle T_ i,\eta \rangle \to \langle T,\eta \rangle $. A convergent net of real numbers need not be bounded, but it is bounded from some index on; hence there is $i_0$ with $\mu _ i(L)\leq C=\langle T,\eta \rangle +1$ for $i\geq i_0$, and also $\mu (L)\leq \langle T,\eta \rangle <C$. For every test function $\chi $ supported in $L$ and every $i\geq i_0$, \[  \left|\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ i-\int f\, \mathrm d\mu \right|\leq 2C\| f-\chi \| _\infty +|\langle T_ i,\chi \rangle -\langle T,\chi \rangle |,  \] so $\varlimsup _ i|\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ i-\int f\, \mathrm d\mu |\leq 2C\| f-\chi \| _\infty $, which can be made arbitrarily small. Hence $\mu _ i\to \mu $ vaguely. The converse holds because test functions belong to $C_ c(\Omega )$. $\square$ Thus, by the uniqueness in theorem 2.5.6 , a net of Radon measures converges vaguely to a Radon measure if and only if it converges to it in the sense of distributions. In 2, where measures appear as currents of top degree, this mode of convergence is called weak convergence. Proposition 2.6.2 . 132090FCDF4A Let $(\mu _ i)$ be a net of Radon measures on $\Omega $ converging vaguely to a Radon measure $\mu $. Then for every open set $U\subset \Omega $ and every compact set $K\subset \Omega $, \[  \mu (U)\leq \varliminf _ i\mu _ i(U),\qquad \varlimsup _ i\mu _ i(K)\leq \mu (K).  \] Consequently, if $E\Subset \Omega $ is a Borel set with $\mu (\partial E)=0$, then $\mu _ i(E)\to \mu (E)$. Proof. If $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$, $0\leq f\leq 1$ and $\operatorname{Supp}f\subset U$, then $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu =\lim _ i\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ i\leq \varliminf _ i\mu _ i(U)$; taking the supremum over such $f$ and using ( 2.3.4 ) gives the first inequality. For the second, let $\varepsilon >0$, choose by outer regularity an open set $V\supset K$ with $\mu (V)<\mu (K)+\varepsilon $, and let $\eta $ be a cutoff function for $K$ in $V$. Then $\mu _ i(K)\leq \int \eta \, \mathrm d\mu _ i\to \int \eta \, \mathrm d\mu \leq \mu (V)$, so $\varlimsup _ i\mu _ i(K)\leq \mu (K)+\varepsilon $. Finally, for $E$ as in the last assertion, the closure $\overline E$ is a compact subset of $\Omega $, and $\overline E\setminus \operatorname{Int}E=\partial E$ is $\mu $-null, so $\mu (\operatorname{Int}E)=\mu (E)=\mu (\overline E)$. Since $\mu _ i(\operatorname{Int}E)\leq \mu _ i(E)\leq \mu _ i(\overline E)$, the two inequalities, applied to $\operatorname{Int}E$ and $\overline E$, give \[  \mu (E)=\mu (\operatorname{Int}E)\leq \varliminf _ i\mu _ i(E)\leq \varlimsup _ i\mu _ i(E)\leq \mu (\overline E)=\mu (E).  \] $\square$ Proposition 2.6.3 . 54258F39AC23 Let $(\mu _ i)$ be a net of finite Radon measures on $\Omega $ converging vaguely to $\mu $. Suppose that the net is eventually uniformly tight: for every $\varepsilon >0$ there are a compact set $K\subset \Omega $ and an index $i_0$ such that $\mu _ i(\Omega \setminus K)<\varepsilon $ for all $i\geq i_0$. Then $\mu $ is finite and $\mu _ i\to \mu $ narrowly. In particular, $\mu _ i(\Omega )\to \mu (\Omega )$. Proof. Let $\varepsilon >0$, and choose $K$ and $i_0$ as above. Since $\Omega \setminus K$ is open, proposition 2.6.2 gives $\mu (\Omega \setminus K)\leq \varepsilon $, and since $\mu (K)<\infty $, the measure $\mu $ is finite. Let $f$ be a bounded continuous function on $\Omega $ and $\eta $ a cutoff function for $K$ in $\Omega $. Then $f\eta \in C_ c(\Omega )$, so $\int f\eta \, \mathrm d\mu _ i\to \int f\eta \, \mathrm d\mu $, while $1-\eta $ takes values in $[0,1]$ and vanishes on $K$, so that for $i\geq i_0$ \[  \left|\int f(1-\eta )\, \mathrm d\mu _ i\right|\leq \| f\| _\infty \varepsilon , \qquad \left|\int f(1-\eta )\, \mathrm d\mu \right|\leq \| f\| _\infty \varepsilon .  \] Hence $\varlimsup _ i|\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ i-\int f\, \mathrm d\mu |\leq 2\| f\| _\infty \varepsilon $. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves narrow convergence, and $f=1$ gives the last assertion. $\square$ Example 2.6.4 . 81B4A3D092FF On $\mathbb R$, the Dirac measures $\delta _ j$, $j\geq 1$, converge vaguely to zero, since every $f\in C_ c(\mathbb R)$ vanishes at $j$ for large $j$; yet each has total mass one. On $\Omega =(0,1)$ the measures $\delta _{1/j}$, $j\geq 2$, behave in the same way, the mass escaping through the boundary point $0$, which does not belong to $\Omega $. Neither sequence is eventually uniformly tight: a compact subset of $\mathbb R$ does not contain $j$ for large $j$, and a compact subset of $(0,1)$ does not contain $1/j$ for large $j$, so the mass outside a fixed compact set is eventually equal to one. Theorem 2.6.5 . F9F4241C5BD2 Let $(\mu _ j)$ be a sequence of Radon measures on $\Omega $ such that $\sup _ j\mu _ j(K)<\infty $ for every compact set $K\subset \Omega $. Then $(\mu _ j)$ has a vaguely convergent subsequence. If, moreover, the $\mu _ j$ are finite and the sequence is eventually uniformly tight, then it has a narrowly convergent subsequence with a finite limit. Proof. Step 1: a countable dense family. Let $\varphi (t)=\max \{ 0,1-|t|\} $, so that $\sum _{n\in \mathbb Z}\varphi (t-n)=1$ for $t\in \mathbb R$. For $k\geq 1$ and $n\in \mathbb Z^ d$ put $\varphi _{k,n}(x)=\prod _{l=1}^ d\varphi (2^ kx_ l-n_ l)$. These are nonnegative continuous functions with $\sum _ n\varphi _{k,n}=1$, and $\varphi _{k,n}(x)\neq 0$ only if $|x-2^{-k}n|_\infty <2^{-k}$, where $|\cdot |_\infty $ is the maximum norm. Let $\mathcal F$ be the countable family of all finite sums $\sum _ nq_ n\varphi _{k,n}$, $k\geq 1$, with rational coefficients $q_ n$, whose support is a compact subset of $\Omega $. Given $f\in C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$, extended by zero to $\mathbb R^ d$, choose rational numbers $q_{k,n}$ with $|q_{k,n}-f(2^{-k}n)|\leq 2^{-k}$ and $q_{k,n}=0$ if $f(2^{-k}n)=0$, and put $f_ k=\sum _ nq_{k,n}\varphi _{k,n}$. Then \[  |f_ k(x)-f(x)|\leq \sum _ n|q_{k,n}-f(x)|\varphi _{k,n}(x)\leq 2^{-k}+\sup \{ |f(y)-f(x)|:|y-x|_\infty <2^{-k}\} ,  \] which tends to zero uniformly in $x$ because $f$ is uniformly continuous. Moreover, $f_ k$ vanishes at points of $|\cdot |_\infty $-distance more than $2^{-k}$ from $\operatorname{Supp}f$, so for large $k$ all the $f_ k$ belong to $\mathcal F$ and are supported in a fixed compact set $L\subset \Omega $. Step 2: diagonal extraction. Enumerate $\mathcal F=\{ g_1,g_2,\ldots \} $. For each $l$, the numbers $\int g_ l\, \mathrm d\mu _ j$ are bounded by $\| g_ l\| _\infty \sup _ j\mu _ j(\operatorname{Supp}g_ l)$. Choosing successively convergent subsequences for $g_1,g_2,\ldots $ and passing to the diagonal subsequence, we find $(\mu _{j_ k})$ such that $\int g_ l\, \mathrm d\mu _{j_ k}$ converges for every $l$. If $f\in C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$ and $L$, $f_ m$ are as in Step 1, then with $C_ L=\sup _ j\mu _ j(L)$, \[  \left|\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _{j_ k}-\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _{j_{k'}}\right|\leq 2C_ L\| f-f_ m\| _\infty +\left|\int f_ m\, \mathrm d\mu _{j_ k}-\int f_ m\, \mathrm d\mu _{j_{k'}}\right|,  \] so $(\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _{j_ k})_ k$ is a Cauchy sequence. Its limit is a positive linear functional of $f$, hence integration against a Radon measure $\mu $ by theorem 2.3.3 , and $\mu _{j_ k}\to \mu $ vaguely; complex $f$ are handled by linearity. If the sequence is eventually uniformly tight, so is every subsequence, and proposition 2.6.3 gives the last assertion. $\square$

title: Proposition 2.6.1
text: Proposition 2.6.1 . 4DFD880D9E4D Let $(T_ i)$ be a net of positive distributions on $\Omega $ converging in the sense of distributions to $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$. Then $T$ is positive, and the Radon measures associated with the $T_ i$ by theorem 2.5.6 converge vaguely to the Radon measure associated with $T$. Conversely, if a net of Radon measures converges vaguely, the associated distributions converge in the sense of distributions. Proof. For a nonnegative test function $\chi $, the numbers $\langle T_ i,\chi \rangle $ are nonnegative, hence so is their limit $\langle T,\chi \rangle $; likewise $\langle T,\chi \rangle $ is real for real $\chi $. Thus $T$ is positive, and $T$ and the $T_ i$ are given by Radon measures $\mu $ and $\mu _ i$. Let $f\in C_ c(\Omega )$. By lemma 2.5.1 (5), $f$ is the uniform limit of test functions supported in a fixed compact set $L$; in particular, $f$ vanishes outside $L$. If $\eta $ is a smooth cutoff function for $L$ in $\Omega $, then $\mu _ i(L)\leq \langle T_ i,\eta \rangle \to \langle T,\eta \rangle $. A convergent net of real numbers need not be bounded, but it is bounded from some index on; hence there is $i_0$ with $\mu _ i(L)\leq C=\langle T,\eta \rangle +1$ for $i\geq i_0$, and also $\mu (L)\leq \langle T,\eta \rangle <C$. For every test function $\chi $ supported in $L$ and every $i\geq i_0$, \[  \left|\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ i-\int f\, \mathrm d\mu \right|\leq 2C\| f-\chi \| _\infty +|\langle T_ i,\chi \rangle -\langle T,\chi \rangle |,  \] so $\varlimsup _ i|\int f\, \mathrm d\mu _ i-\int f\, \mathrm d\mu |\leq 2C\| f-\chi \| _\infty $, which can be made arbitrarily small. Hence $\mu _ i\to \mu $ vaguely. The converse holds because test functions belong to $C_ c(\Omega )$. $\square$

title: 2.7 Nets and compactness
text:
In a general topological space, compactness cannot be tested with sequences alone. For instance, the product $[0,1]^{[0,1]}$ of copies of $[0,1]$, whose points are the functions $[0,1]	o [0,1]$, is compact by Tychonoff's theorem (lemma 2.7.2 below), and convergence of a sequence in it is pointwise convergence. Let $f_ n(t)=\lfloor 2^ ntfloor -2\lfloor 2^{n-1}tfloor $ be the $n$th binary digit of $t$. Given $n_1<n_2<\cdots $, the number $t=\sum _{k	ext{ even}}2^{-n_ k}$ has a binary expansion with infinitely many zeros, whose digit at the place $n_ k$ is $1$ for even $k$ and $0$ for odd $k$. Hence $f_{n_ k}(t)$ alternates between $1$ and $0$, and no subsequence of $(f_ n)$ converges. For nets, subnets take the place of subsequences. Recall from the Conventions that subnets are Willard subnets: if $(x_ i)_{i\in I}$ is a net and $h\colon J	o I$ is an increasing map from a directed set $J$ which is final, meaning that for every $i_0\in I$ there is $j_0\in J$ with $h(j)\geq i_0$ for all $j\geq j_0$, then $(x_{h(j)})_{j\in J}$ is a subnet of $(x_ i)$. Every subnet of a net converging to $x$ converges to $x$: given a neighborhood $U$ of $x$, choose $i_0$ with $x_ i\in U$ for $i\geq i_0$, and then $j_0$ as in the definition of finality. Proposition 2.7.1 . 4603E36ECC71 A topological space $X$ is compact if and only if every net in $X$ has a convergent Willard subnet. Proof. Suppose that $X$ is compact, and let $(x_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a net in $X$. The closures $T_{i_0}$ of the tails $\{ x_ i:i\geq i_0\} $ have the finite intersection property, since finitely many of them contain the tail of a common upper bound of their indices. As $X$ is compact, they have a common point $x$; otherwise their complements would form an open cover without a finite subcover. Thus every neighborhood of $x$ meets every tail of the net. We now construct a subnet converging to $x$. Let $J$ be the set of triples $(i,U,k)$ with $i,k\in I$, $k\geq i$, $U$ an open neighborhood of $x$ and $x_ k\in U$, preordered by \[  (i,U,k)\leq (i',U',k')\quad 	ext{if }i\leq i',\  U'\subset U,\  k\leq k'.  \] It contains $(i,X,i)$ for every $i$, and it is directed: given two triples $(i_1,U_1,k_1)$ and $(i_2,U_2,k_2)$, choose $i\geq i_1,i_2,k_1,k_2$, put $U=U_1\cap U_2$, and choose $k\geq i$ with $x_ k\in U$, which is possible because $U$ meets the tail of $i$; then $(i,U,k)$ dominates both triples. The map $h(i,U,k)=k$ is increasing, and it is final because $(i,U,k)\geq (i_0,X,i_0)$ implies $k\geq i_0$. The subnet $(x_{h(j)})_{j\in J}$ converges to $x$: if $V$ is a neighborhood of $x$, choose an open neighborhood $U\subset V$ of $x$ and a triple $(i,U,k)\in J$; then $x_{k'}\in U'\subset V$ for every $(i',U',k')\geq (i,U,k)$. Conversely, suppose that $X$ is not compact, and let $\mathcal U$ be an open cover without a finite subcover. The finite subfamilies $F\subset \mathcal U$, ordered by inclusion, form a directed set, and we may choose points $x_ F
otin  igcup F$. If a subnet $(x_{h(j)})_{j\in J}$ converged to a point $x$, let $U\in \mathcal U$ contain $x$. Then $x_{h(j)}\in U$ for all large $j$, while finality gives $h(j)\supset \{ U\} $, and hence $x_{h(j)}
otin U$, for all large $j$. Since $J$ is directed, some $j$ satisfies both conditions, a contradiction. $\square$ Lemma 2.7.2 . 8734A1486521 A product of compact topological spaces is compact in the product topology. Proof. This is Tychonoff's theorem; we prove it with ultrafilters, using the axiom of choice in the form of Zorn's lemma. A filter on a set $Z$ is a family $\mathcal F$ of subsets of $Z$ such that $Z\in \mathcal F$, $\varnothing 
otin \mathcal F$, and $\mathcal F$ is closed under finite intersections and under passing to supersets. An ultrafilter is a filter which is maximal for inclusion. Since the union of a chain of filters containing a given filter is again a filter, Zorn's lemma shows that every filter is contained in an ultrafilter. A filter $\mathcal U$ on $Z$ is an ultrafilter if and only if, for every $A\subset Z$, either $A\in \mathcal U$ or $Z\setminus A\in \mathcal U$. Indeed, let $\mathcal U$ be an ultrafilter and $A\subset Z$. If $A$ meets every member of $\mathcal U$, the sets containing some $U\cap A$ with $U\in \mathcal U$ form a filter containing $\mathcal U$ and $A$, so $A\in \mathcal U$ by maximality; otherwise some $U\in \mathcal U$ is disjoint from $A$, and $Z\setminus A\supset U$ belongs to $\mathcal U$. Conversely, if $\mathcal U$ has this property, a strictly larger filter would contain some $A
otin \mathcal U$ together with $Z\setminus A$, hence $\varnothing $. A filter on a topological space $Z$ converges to $z$ if every neighborhood of $z$ belongs to it. We show that $Z$ is compact if and only if every ultrafilter on $Z$ converges. If $Z$ is compact and $\mathcal U$ is an ultrafilter, the closures of the members of $\mathcal U$ have the finite intersection property and hence a common point $z$. If an open neighborhood $N$ of $z$ were not in $\mathcal U$, the closed set $Z\setminus N$ would belong to $\mathcal U$. Since $z$ lies in the closure of every member of $\mathcal U$, this would give $z\in Z\setminus N$, which is absurd. Hence $\mathcal U$ converges to $z$. Conversely, suppose that every ultrafilter converges, and let $\mathcal C$ be a family of closed sets with the finite intersection property. The sets containing a finite intersection of members of $\mathcal C$ form a filter, which lies in an ultrafilter $\mathcal U$ converging to some $z$. If $z
otin C$ for some $C\in \mathcal C$, then both $C$ and its complement, a neighborhood of $z$, would belong to $\mathcal U$. Hence $z$ lies in every member of $\mathcal C$, and $Z$ is compact. Now let $Z=\prod _\alpha X_\alpha $ with compact factors and projections $p_\alpha $; if some $X_\alpha $ is empty, so is $Z$, and there is nothing to prove. Let $\mathcal U$ be an ultrafilter on $Z$. For each $\alpha $, the family $\{ A\subset X_\alpha :p_\alpha ^{-1}(A)\in \mathcal U\} $ is a filter with the property characterizing ultrafilters, hence an ultrafilter, and since $X_\alpha $ is compact it converges to some $z_\alpha \in X_\alpha $. Put $z=(z_\alpha )$. A basic neighborhood $ igcap _{l=1}^ np_{\alpha _ l}^{-1}(V_ l)$ of $z$, with $V_ l$ a neighborhood of $z_{\alpha _ l}$, is a finite intersection of members of $\mathcal U$, so every neighborhood of $z$ belongs to $\mathcal U$. Thus every ultrafilter on $Z$ converges, and $Z$ is compact. $\square$ Theorem 2.7.3 . DF30CEF15D17 Let $(K_ r)_{r\geq 1}$ be a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $. For each $r$, let $\chi _ r\in C_ c(\Omega )$ be a nonnegative function equal to $1$ on $K_ r$, and let $0\leq M_ r<\infty $. Then \[  \mathcal M=\left\{ \mu 	ext{ Radon measure on }\Omega :\int \chi _ r\, \mathrm d\mu \leq M_ r	ext{ for every }right\}   \] is compact in the vague topology. In particular, every net in $\mathcal M$ has a Willard subnet converging vaguely to an element of $\mathcal M$. Proof. We embed $\mathcal M$ homeomorphically onto a closed subset of a product of compact intervals. For $f\in C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$, choose $r(f)$ with $\operatorname{Supp}f\subset K_{r(f)}$; this is possible because $\operatorname{Supp}f$ is compact and the open sets $\operatorname{Int}K_ r$ increase to $\Omega $. For $\mu \in \mathcal M$ we have $|f|\leq \| f\| _\infty \chi _{r(f)}$, so $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu $ lies in $I_ f=[-M_{r(f)}\| f\| _\infty ,M_{r(f)}\| f\| _\infty ]$. The product $P=\prod _ fI_ f$ over all $f\in C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$ is compact by lemma 2.7.2 . The map $\Phi \colon \mathcal M	o P$, $\Phi (\mu )=(\int f\, \mathrm d\mu )_ f$, is injective by the uniqueness in theorem 2.3.3 , and it is a homeomorphism onto its image. Indeed, since $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu =\int \operatorname{Re}f\, \mathrm d\mu +\mathrm i\int \operatorname{Im}f\, \mathrm d\mu $, the vague topology on $\mathcal M$ is the weakest topology for which the maps $\mu \mapsto \int f\, \mathrm d\mu $ with real $f$ are continuous. The subspace topology of $\Phi (\mathcal M)$ is the weakest topology for which the restrictions of the coordinate projections are continuous, and $\Phi $ intertwines these two families of maps. The image consists of the points $(a_ f)\in P$ such that $a_{sf+tg}=sa_ f+ta_ g$ for all $f,g$ and real $s,t$, $a_ f\geq 0$ whenever $f\geq 0$, and $a_{\chi _ r}\leq M_ r$ for every $r$: a point satisfying these conditions defines a positive linear functional on $C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$, which by theorem 2.3.3 is integration against a Radon measure belonging to $\mathcal M$. Each condition involves finitely many coordinates and is closed, so $\Phi (\mathcal M)$ is closed in $P$ and hence compact. Therefore $\mathcal M$ is vaguely compact, and the assertion about nets follows from proposition 2.7.1 . $\square$ Proposition 2.7.4 (Arzelà–Ascoli) . 2963E35FB0D3 Let $K$ be a compact metric space, and let $\mathcal F\subset C(K)$ be equicontinuous and pointwise bounded, that is, $\sup _{f\in \mathcal F}|f(x)|<\infty $ for every $x\in K$. Then $\mathcal F$ is relatively compact for the uniform topology. In particular, every sequence in $\mathcal F$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence. Proof. We may assume that $K
eq \varnothing $. Let $\varepsilon >0$. By equicontinuity, every $x\in K$ is the center of an open ball on which $|f-f(x)|<\varepsilon $ for all $f\in \mathcal F$; by compactness, $K$ is covered by finitely many such balls $B_ l$ with centers $x_ l$, $1\leq l\leq N$. Then every $f\in \mathcal F$ is bounded on $K$ by $M=\varepsilon +\max _ l\sup _{g\in \mathcal F}|g(x_ l)|$, which is finite by pointwise boundedness. Let $G$ be a finite set of scalars such that every scalar of absolute value at most $M$ lies at distance less than $\varepsilon $ from some element of $G$. For each map $\gamma \colon \{ 1,\ldots ,N\} 	o G$, the functions $f\in \mathcal F$ with $|f(x_ l)-\gamma (l)|<\varepsilon $ for all $l$ form a set $\mathcal F_\gamma $, and these finitely many sets cover $\mathcal F$. If $f,g\in \mathcal F_\gamma $ and $y\in B_ l$, then \[  |f(y)-g(y)|\leq |f(y)-f(x_ l)|+|f(x_ l)-g(x_ l)|+|g(x_ l)-g(y)|<4\varepsilon .  \] Choosing one function in each nonempty $\mathcal F_\gamma $, we obtain a finite set within uniform distance $4\varepsilon $ of $\mathcal F$, and hence within $5\varepsilon $ of its closure $\overline{\mathcal F}$ in $C(K)$. Thus $\overline{\mathcal F}$ is totally bounded. It is also complete, because $C(K)$ is complete for the uniform metric: a uniform Cauchy sequence converges pointwise, and the limit is continuous since the convergence is uniform. A complete and totally bounded metric space $Y$ is sequentially compact and compact. Given a sequence in $Y$, cover $Y$ by finitely many sets of diameter less than $1$ and keep one containing infinitely many terms. Cover it by finitely many sets of diameter less than $1/2$, keep one containing infinitely many of those terms, and so on. A diagonal choice gives a Cauchy subsequence, which converges because $Y$ is complete. Suppose now that an open cover of $Y$ had no finite subcover, and put $S_0=Y$. Covering $S_{n-1}$ by finitely many subsets of diameter less than $1/n$, we see that one of them, $S_ n$, is not covered by finitely many members of the cover, since otherwise $S_{n-1}$ would be. This gives nested nonempty sets $S_1\supset S_2\supset \cdots $ with $\operatorname {diam}S_ n<1/n$, none of which is covered by finitely many members of the cover. Points $y_ n\in S_ n$ form a Cauchy sequence with a limit $y$. If the open ball of radius $s$ about $y$ in $Y$ lies in a member $U$ of the cover, then $S_ n$ lies in this ball, and hence in $U$, as soon as $1/n+\operatorname {dist}(y_ n,y)<s$, a contradiction. Hence $\overline{\mathcal F}$ is compact, and every sequence in $\mathcal F$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence. $\square$

title: Proposition 2.7.1
text: Proposition 2.7.1 . 4603E36ECC71 A topological space $X$ is compact if and only if every net in $X$ has a convergent Willard subnet. Proof. Suppose that $X$ is compact, and let $(x_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a net in $X$. The closures $T_{i_0}$ of the tails $\{ x_ i:i\geq i_0\} $ have the finite intersection property, since finitely many of them contain the tail of a common upper bound of their indices. As $X$ is compact, they have a common point $x$; otherwise their complements would form an open cover without a finite subcover. Thus every neighborhood of $x$ meets every tail of the net. We now construct a subnet converging to $x$. Let $J$ be the set of triples $(i,U,k)$ with $i,k\in I$, $k\geq i$, $U$ an open neighborhood of $x$ and $x_ k\in U$, preordered by \[  (i,U,k)\leq (i',U',k')\quad \text{if }i\leq i',\  U'\subset U,\  k\leq k'.  \] It contains $(i,X,i)$ for every $i$, and it is directed: given two triples $(i_1,U_1,k_1)$ and $(i_2,U_2,k_2)$, choose $i\geq i_1,i_2,k_1,k_2$, put $U=U_1\cap U_2$, and choose $k\geq i$ with $x_ k\in U$, which is possible because $U$ meets the tail of $i$; then $(i,U,k)$ dominates both triples. The map $h(i,U,k)=k$ is increasing, and it is final because $(i,U,k)\geq (i_0,X,i_0)$ implies $k\geq i_0$. The subnet $(x_{h(j)})_{j\in J}$ converges to $x$: if $V$ is a neighborhood of $x$, choose an open neighborhood $U\subset V$ of $x$ and a triple $(i,U,k)\in J$; then $x_{k'}\in U'\subset V$ for every $(i',U',k')\geq (i,U,k)$. Conversely, suppose that $X$ is not compact, and let $\mathcal U$ be an open cover without a finite subcover. The finite subfamilies $F\subset \mathcal U$, ordered by inclusion, form a directed set, and we may choose points $x_ F\notin \bigcup F$. If a subnet $(x_{h(j)})_{j\in J}$ converged to a point $x$, let $U\in \mathcal U$ contain $x$. Then $x_{h(j)}\in U$ for all large $j$, while finality gives $h(j)\supset \{ U\} $, and hence $x_{h(j)}\notin U$, for all large $j$. Since $J$ is directed, some $j$ satisfies both conditions, a contradiction. $\square$

title: Lemma 2.7.2
text:
Lemma 2.7.2 . 8734A1486521 A product of compact topological spaces is compact in the product topology. Proof. This is Tychonoff's theorem; we prove it with ultrafilters, using the axiom of choice in the form of Zorn's lemma. A filter on a set $Z$ is a family $\mathcal F$ of subsets of $Z$ such that $Z\in \mathcal F$, $\varnothing 
otin \mathcal F$, and $\mathcal F$ is closed under finite intersections and under passing to supersets. An ultrafilter is a filter which is maximal for inclusion. Since the union of a chain of filters containing a given filter is again a filter, Zorn's lemma shows that every filter is contained in an ultrafilter. A filter $\mathcal U$ on $Z$ is an ultrafilter if and only if, for every $A\subset Z$, either $A\in \mathcal U$ or $Z\setminus A\in \mathcal U$. Indeed, let $\mathcal U$ be an ultrafilter and $A\subset Z$. If $A$ meets every member of $\mathcal U$, the sets containing some $U\cap A$ with $U\in \mathcal U$ form a filter containing $\mathcal U$ and $A$, so $A\in \mathcal U$ by maximality; otherwise some $U\in \mathcal U$ is disjoint from $A$, and $Z\setminus A\supset U$ belongs to $\mathcal U$. Conversely, if $\mathcal U$ has this property, a strictly larger filter would contain some $A
otin \mathcal U$ together with $Z\setminus A$, hence $\varnothing $. A filter on a topological space $Z$ converges to $z$ if every neighborhood of $z$ belongs to it. We show that $Z$ is compact if and only if every ultrafilter on $Z$ converges. If $Z$ is compact and $\mathcal U$ is an ultrafilter, the closures of the members of $\mathcal U$ have the finite intersection property and hence a common point $z$. If an open neighborhood $N$ of $z$ were not in $\mathcal U$, the closed set $Z\setminus N$ would belong to $\mathcal U$. Since $z$ lies in the closure of every member of $\mathcal U$, this would give $z\in Z\setminus N$, which is absurd. Hence $\mathcal U$ converges to $z$. Conversely, suppose that every ultrafilter converges, and let $\mathcal C$ be a family of closed sets with the finite intersection property. The sets containing a finite intersection of members of $\mathcal C$ form a filter, which lies in an ultrafilter $\mathcal U$ converging to some $z$. If $z
otin C$ for some $C\in \mathcal C$, then both $C$ and its complement, a neighborhood of $z$, would belong to $\mathcal U$. Hence $z$ lies in every member of $\mathcal C$, and $Z$ is compact. Now let $Z=\prod _\alpha X_\alpha $ with compact factors and projections $p_\alpha $; if some $X_\alpha $ is empty, so is $Z$, and there is nothing to prove. Let $\mathcal U$ be an ultrafilter on $Z$. For each $\alpha $, the family $\{ A\subset X_\alpha :p_\alpha ^{-1}(A)\in \mathcal U\} $ is a filter with the property characterizing ultrafilters, hence an ultrafilter, and since $X_\alpha $ is compact it converges to some $z_\alpha \in X_\alpha $. Put $z=(z_\alpha )$. A basic neighborhood $ igcap _{l=1}^ np_{\alpha _ l}^{-1}(V_ l)$ of $z$, with $V_ l$ a neighborhood of $z_{\alpha _ l}$, is a finite intersection of members of $\mathcal U$, so every neighborhood of $z$ belongs to $\mathcal U$. Thus every ultrafilter on $Z$ converges, and $Z$ is compact. $\square$

title: Theorem 2.7.3
text: Theorem 2.7.3 . DF30CEF15D17 Let $(K_ r)_{r\geq 1}$ be a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $. For each $r$, let $\chi _ r\in C_ c(\Omega )$ be a nonnegative function equal to $1$ on $K_ r$, and let $0\leq M_ r<\infty $. Then \[  \mathcal M=\left\{ \mu \text{ Radon measure on }\Omega :\int \chi _ r\, \mathrm d\mu \leq M_ r\text{ for every }r\right\}   \] is compact in the vague topology. In particular, every net in $\mathcal M$ has a Willard subnet converging vaguely to an element of $\mathcal M$. Proof. We embed $\mathcal M$ homeomorphically onto a closed subset of a product of compact intervals. For $f\in C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$, choose $r(f)$ with $\operatorname{Supp}f\subset K_{r(f)}$; this is possible because $\operatorname{Supp}f$ is compact and the open sets $\operatorname{Int}K_ r$ increase to $\Omega $. For $\mu \in \mathcal M$ we have $|f|\leq \| f\| _\infty \chi _{r(f)}$, so $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu $ lies in $I_ f=[-M_{r(f)}\| f\| _\infty ,M_{r(f)}\| f\| _\infty ]$. The product $P=\prod _ fI_ f$ over all $f\in C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$ is compact by lemma 2.7.2 . The map $\Phi \colon \mathcal M\to P$, $\Phi (\mu )=(\int f\, \mathrm d\mu )_ f$, is injective by the uniqueness in theorem 2.3.3 , and it is a homeomorphism onto its image. Indeed, since $\int f\, \mathrm d\mu =\int \operatorname{Re}f\, \mathrm d\mu +\mathrm i\int \operatorname{Im}f\, \mathrm d\mu $, the vague topology on $\mathcal M$ is the weakest topology for which the maps $\mu \mapsto \int f\, \mathrm d\mu $ with real $f$ are continuous. The subspace topology of $\Phi (\mathcal M)$ is the weakest topology for which the restrictions of the coordinate projections are continuous, and $\Phi $ intertwines these two families of maps. The image consists of the points $(a_ f)\in P$ such that $a_{sf+tg}=sa_ f+ta_ g$ for all $f,g$ and real $s,t$, $a_ f\geq 0$ whenever $f\geq 0$, and $a_{\chi _ r}\leq M_ r$ for every $r$: a point satisfying these conditions defines a positive linear functional on $C_ c(\Omega ,\mathbb R)$, which by theorem 2.3.3 is integration against a Radon measure belonging to $\mathcal M$. Each condition involves finitely many coordinates and is closed, so $\Phi (\mathcal M)$ is closed in $P$ and hence compact. Therefore $\mathcal M$ is vaguely compact, and the assertion about nets follows from proposition 2.7.1 . $\square$

title: Proposition 2.7.4 (Arzelà–Ascoli)
text: Proposition 2.7.4 (Arzelà–Ascoli) . 2963E35FB0D3 Let $K$ be a compact metric space, and let $\mathcal F\subset C(K)$ be equicontinuous and pointwise bounded, that is, $\sup _{f\in \mathcal F}|f(x)|<\infty $ for every $x\in K$. Then $\mathcal F$ is relatively compact for the uniform topology. In particular, every sequence in $\mathcal F$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence. Proof. We may assume that $K\neq \varnothing $. Then every $f\in \mathcal F$ is bounded on $K$ by $M=\varepsilon +\max _ l\sup _{g\in \mathcal F}|g(x_ l)|$, which is finite by pointwise boundedness. Let $G$ be a finite set of scalars such that every scalar of absolute value at most $M$ lies at distance less than $\varepsilon $ from some element of $G$. For each map $\gamma \colon \{ 1,\ldots ,N\} \to G$, the functions $f\in \mathcal F$ with $|f(x_ l)-\gamma (l)|<\varepsilon $ for all $l$ form a set $\mathcal F_\gamma $, and these finitely many sets cover $\mathcal F$. If $f,g\in \mathcal F_\gamma $ and $y\in B_ l$, then \[  |f(y)-g(y)|\leq |f(y)-f(x_ l)|+|f(x_ l)-g(x_ l)|+|g(x_ l)-g(y)|<4\varepsilon .  \] Choosing one function in each nonempty $\mathcal F_\gamma $, we obtain a finite set within uniform distance $4\varepsilon $ of $\mathcal F$, and hence within $5\varepsilon $ of its closure $\overline{\mathcal F}$ in $C(K)$. Thus $\overline{\mathcal F}$ is totally bounded. It is also complete, because $C(K)$ is complete for the uniform metric: a uniform Cauchy sequence converges pointwise, and the limit is continuous since the convergence is uniform. A complete and totally bounded metric space $Y$ is sequentially compact and compact. Given a sequence in $Y$, cover $Y$ by finitely many sets of diameter less than $1$ and keep one containing infinitely many terms. Cover it by finitely many sets of diameter less than $1/2$, keep one containing infinitely many of those terms, and so on. A diagonal choice gives a Cauchy subsequence, which converges because $Y$ is complete. Suppose now that an open cover of $Y$ had no finite subcover, and put $S_0=Y$. Covering $S_{n-1}$ by finitely many subsets of diameter less than $1/n$, we see that one of them, $S_ n$, is not covered by finitely many members of the cover, since otherwise $S_{n-1}$ would be. This gives nested nonempty sets $S_1\supset S_2\supset \cdots $ with $\operatorname {diam}S_ n<1/n$, none of which is covered by finitely many members of the cover. Points $y_ n\in S_ n$ form a Cauchy sequence with a limit $y$. If the open ball of radius $s$ about $y$ in $Y$ lies in a member $U$ of the cover, then $S_ n$ lies in this ball, and hence in $U$, as soon as $1/n+\operatorname {dist}(y_ n,y)<s$, a contradiction. Hence $\overline{\mathcal F}$ is compact, and every sequence in $\mathcal F$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence. $\square$

title: 2.8 Densities and differentiation of integrals
text:
If a measure $\mu $ is dominated by a constant multiple of a measure $
u $, then $\mu $ has a bounded density with respect to $
u $. We construct it directly from averages over dyadic cubes and deduce the same for real distributions dominated by a multiple of $
u $. When $
u $ is Lebesgue measure, the Lebesgue differentiation theorem recovers a density at almost every point from its averages over small cubes. Together with a Poincaré inequality on cubes, these results relate a distributional Hessian to a pointwise second-order expansion (proposition 2.8.5 ), and they will later describe the coefficients of positive currents. For a Radon measure $
u $ on $\Omega $ and a Borel function $g\geq 0$, we write $g
u $ for the measure $E\mapsto \int _ Eg\, \mathrm d
u $ on Borel sets, and $g\, \mathrm dx$ when $
u $ is Lebesgue measure. Lemma 2.8.1 . 9790D3B21542 Let $
u $ be a Radon measure and $\mu $ a Borel measure on $\Omega $. If there is a constant $C\in [0,\infty )$ with $\mu (E)\leq C
u (E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset \Omega $, then $\mu =g
u $ for a Borel function $g$ with values in $[0,C]$. If every relatively compact open set $U\subset \Omega $ admits a constant $C_ U\in [0,\infty )$ with $\mu (E)\leq C_ U
u (E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset U$, then $\mu =g
u $ for a nonnegative Borel function $g$ such that $g\leq C_ U$ $
u $-almost everywhere on $U$ for every such $U$; in particular, $g$ is locally essentially bounded with respect to $

We first construct the density on a half-open cube as an $L^2$ limit of averages of $\mu $ over dyadic subcubes. Let $Q=\prod _{i=1}^ d[a_ i,a_ i+s)$ be a half-open cube whose closure lies in $\Omega $, so that $
u (Q)<\infty $, and suppose that $\mu (E)\leq C
u (E)$ for Borel sets $E\subset Q$; in particular, $\mu (Q)\leq C

u (Q')$ if $

u (Q)$, so $(g_ k)$ is a Cauchy sequence in $L^2(Q,
u )$. Choose $k_1<k_2<\cdots $ with $\| g_{k_{j+1}}-g_{k_ j}\| _2\leq 2^{-j}$. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, $\int _ Q|g_{k_{j+1}}-g_{k_ j}|\, \mathrm d

u (Q)^{1/2}2^{-j}$, so by monotone convergence $\sum _ j|g_{k_{j+1}}-g_{k_ j}|$ has finite integral; hence it is finite, and $(g_{k_ j})$ converges, $

If $U$ is open, every point of $U\cap Q$ lies in arbitrarily small dyadic subcubes, hence in one contained in $U$, so $U\cap Q$ is a countable union of dyadic subcubes. Thus these cubes generate the Borel $\sigma $-algebra of $Q$, and lemma 2.2.6 (2) shows that the finite measures $\mu $ and $g
u $, which agree on all dyadic subcubes including $Q$, agree on every Borel subset of $Q$. For uniqueness, let $g,h\geq 0$ be Borel functions with $g

u (A)=0$; by symmetry, $g=h$ $

u $-null sets. To construct the density on $\Omega $ in case (1), cover $\Omega $ by countably many half-open cubes $Q_1,Q_2,\ldots $ with closures in $\Omega $, for instance all half-open dyadic cubes with this property, let $g^{(k)}$ be the density on $Q_ k$ just constructed, and put $g=g^{(k)}$ on $P_ k=Q_ k\setminus  igcup _{l<k}Q_ l$. For every Borel set $E\subset \Omega $, \[  \mu (E)=\sum _ k\mu (E\cap P_ k)=\sum _ k\int _{E\cap P_ k}g^{(k)}\, \mathrm d
u =\int _ Eg\, \mathrm d
u ,  \] so $\mu =g
u $ with $0\leq g\leq C$. In case (2), every cube $Q$ with closure in $\Omega $ lies in a relatively compact open set $U\subset \Omega $, for instance a set of points at distance less than $\delta $ from $\overline Q$ with $\delta $ small, and $\mu \leq C_ U
u $ on Borel subsets of $Q$; the same construction gives $\mu =g
u $ with $g\geq 0$ Borel. If $U\subset \Omega $ is relatively compact and open, the sets $A_ j=U\cap \{ g>C_ U+1/j\} $ satisfy $(C_ U+1/j)
u (A_ j)\leq \mu (A_ j)\leq C_ U
u (A_ j)$ and $
u (A_ j)<\infty $, so $
u (A_ j)=0$; thus $g\leq C_ U$ $
u $-almost everywhere on $U$. The final assertion is case (1) for Lebesgue measure, which is a Radon measure by proposition 2.2.2 . $\square$ Distributions bounded by a multiple of a measure are themselves given by bounded densities. Corollary 2.8.2 . D30ED2659FC7 Let $
u $ be a Radon measure on $\Omega $, and let $T$ be a real distribution on $\Omega $. If there is a constant $C\geq 0$ with $|\langle T,\chi angle |\leq C\int \chi \, \mathrm d
u $ for every nonnegative test function $\chi $, then there is a Borel function $g$ with values in $[-C,C]$ such that $\langle T,\chi angle =\int \chi g\, \mathrm d

u $ for every nonnegative test function $\chi $ supported in $U$. Then there is a real Borel function $g$ such that $|g|\leq C_ U$ $

u $-null sets among the real Borel functions that are locally integrable with respect to $

u $ the positive distribution defined by integration against the Radon measure $C
u $. For every nonnegative test function $\chi $ we have $\langle C
u \pm T,\chi angle =C\int \chi \, \mathrm d
u \pm \langle T,\chi angle \geq 0$, so the real distributions $C
u \pm T$ are positive, and by theorem 2.5.6 they are given by Radon measures $\lambda _+$ and $\lambda _-$. The Radon measures $\lambda _++\lambda _-$ and $2C
u $ define the same distribution, so they are equal by proposition 2.5.3 (4). In particular, $\lambda _+(E)\leq 2C
u (E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset \Omega $, and lemma 2.8.1 (1) gives $\lambda _+=h
u $ for a Borel function $h$ with values in $[0,2C]$. Hence $\langle T,\chi angle =\int \chi \, \mathrm d\lambda _+-C\int \chi \, \mathrm d
u =\int \chi (h-C)\, \mathrm d
u $ for every test function $\chi $, and $g=h-C$ has the required properties. Uniqueness. Let $g$ and $g'$ be real Borel functions, locally integrable with respect to $
u $, with $\int \chi g\, \mathrm d
u =\int \chi g'\, \mathrm d
u $ for every test function $\chi $, and put $w=g-g'$. The Borel measures $w^+

u =0$, so that $
u (\{ w>0\} )=0$. Similarly $

u $-almost everywhere. (2) Let $\mathcal U$ be the family of the open sets $U$ in the hypothesis. Each set of a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $ is covered by finitely many members of $\mathcal U$, so countably many members $U_1,U_2,\ldots $ of $\mathcal U$ cover $\Omega $. Let $U\in \mathcal U$. The restriction of $
u $ to the Borel subsets of $U$ is a Radon measure on $U$ by proposition 2.2.2 , and test functions on $U$, extended by zero, are test functions on $\Omega $. Hence (1), applied on $U$, gives a Borel function $g_ U$ on $U$ with values in $[-C_ U,C_ U]$ which represents $T$ on $U$. By the uniqueness assertion, applied on the open sets $U_ k\cap U_ l$, we have $g_{U_ k}=g_{U_ l}$ $
u $-almost everywhere on $U_ k\cap U_ l$. Define $g=g_{U_ k}$ on $P_ k=U_ k\setminus  igcup _{l<k}U_ l$. Since $P_ l\cap U_ k=\varnothing $ for $l>k$, we have $g=g_{U_ k}$ $
