u $ for every test function $\chi $ supported in some $U_ k$; by lemma 2.5.2 , this holds for every test function. Finally, for every $U\in \mathcal U$, the uniqueness assertion on $U$ gives $g=g_ U$ $
u $-almost everywhere on $U$, so $|g|\leq C_ U$ $
u $-almost everywhere on $U$. $\square$ Theorem 2.8.3 (Lebesgue differentiation) . CF98893DE93E Let $f$ be a locally integrable function on $\Omega $. Then almost every $x\in \Omega $ is a Lebesgue point of $f$, that is, $f(x)$ is finite and \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac1{|Q(x,r)|} \int _{Q(x,r)}|f(y)-f(x)|\, \mathrm dy=0, \qquad Q(x,r)=x+(-r,r)^ d.  \] At every Lebesgue point $x$ of $f$, the mollifications satisfy $f_\varepsilon (x)	o f(x)$ as $\varepsilon 	o 0$. Proof. We prove a maximal inequality on $\mathbb R^ d$, deduce the theorem for integrable functions by approximation with continuous ones, and then localize. The set $N$ where $f$ is infinite is a null set. Changing $f$ to $0$ on $N$ changes neither the averages in the statement nor the values $f(x)$ for $x
otin N$, so the modified function has the same Lebesgue points outside $N$ and the same mollifications. We may therefore assume that $f$ is finite everywhere. Consider first $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^ d)$, and define its maximal function $Mf(x)$ as the supremum over $r>0$ of the averages of $|f|$ over $Q(x,r)$. For fixed $r$, the average of $|f|$ over $Q(x,r)$ depends continuously on $x$, because $\int _{Q(x,r)}|f|$ and $\int _{Q(x',r)}|f|$ differ by at most $\| f(\cdot +x-x')-f\| _1$, which tends to zero as $x'	o x$ by the continuity of translation in $L^1$ (lemma 2.5.1 (2)). As a supremum of continuous functions, $Mf$ is lower semicontinuous, so $\{ Mf>t\} $ is open. We claim the maximal inequality \[  |\{ Mf>t\} |\le  rac{3^ d}{t}\| f\| _1,\qquad t>0.  \] By inner regularity of Lebesgue measure, it suffices to bound $|L|$ for compact $L\subset \{ Mf>t\} $. Each point of $L$ is the center of an open cube over which the average of $|f|$ exceeds $t$, and finitely many of these cubes cover $L$. Select one of largest side length, discard all cubes meeting it, and repeat with the remaining ones. The selected cubes are disjoint, and each discarded cube meets a selected cube of at least the same side length, so it lies in the concentric cube with three times that side length. These enlarged cubes cover $L$, and therefore $|L|$ is at most $3^ d$ times the total volume of the selected cubes, which is less than $t^{-1}\| f\| _1$. Now let $g\in C_ c(\mathbb R^ d)$. For every $x$ and $r$, \[   egin{split}   rac1{|Q(x,r)|}\int _{Q(x,r)}|f(y)-f(x)|\, \mathrm dy\leq {}& M(f-g)(x)+|g(x)-f(x)|\ & + rac1{|Q(x,r)|}\int _{Q(x,r)}|g(y)-g(x)|\, \mathrm dy, \end{split}  \] and the last term tends to zero as $r\downarrow 0$ because $g$ is continuous at $x$. Corollary 2.8.2 . D30ED2659FC7 Let $

u $ for every nonnegative test function $\chi $, then there is a Borel function $g$ with values in $[-C,C]$ such that $\langle T,\chi angle =\int \chi g\, \mathrm d

u $ for every test function $\chi $. In both cases, $g$ is unique up to $
u $-null sets among the real Borel functions that are locally integrable with respect to $
u $. Proof. (1) Denote also by $C
u $ the positive distribution defined by integration against the Radon measure $C
u $. For every nonnegative test function $\chi $ we have $\langle C

u $ define the same distribution, so they are equal by proposition 2.5.3 (4). In particular, $\lambda _+(E)\leq 2C
u (E)$ for every Borel set $E\subset \Omega $, and lemma 2.8.1 (1) gives $\lambda _+=h
u $ for a Borel function $h$ with values in $[0,2C]$. Hence $\langle T,\chi angle =\int \chi \, \mathrm d\lambda _+-C\int \chi \, \mathrm d
u =\int \chi (h-C)\, \mathrm d
u $ for every test function $\chi $, and $g=h-C$ has the required properties. Uniqueness. Let $g$ and $g'$ be real Borel functions, locally integrable with respect to $
u $, with $\int \chi g\, \mathrm d
u =\int \chi g'\, \mathrm d
u $ for every test function $\chi $, and put $w=g-g'$. The Borel measures $w^+
u $ and $w^-

u (\{ w>0\} )=0$. Similarly $

Each set of a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $ is covered by finitely many members of $\mathcal U$, so countably many members $U_1,U_2,\ldots $ of $\mathcal U$ cover $\Omega $. Let $U\in \mathcal U$. Hence (1), applied on $U$, gives a Borel function $g_ U$ on $U$ with values in $[-C_ U,C_ U]$ which represents $T$ on $U$. By the uniqueness assertion, applied on the open sets $U_ k\cap U_ l$, we have $g_{U_ k}=g_{U_ l}$ $

title: Theorem 2.8.3 (Lebesgue differentiation)
text: Theorem 2.8.3 (Lebesgue differentiation) . CF98893DE93E Let $f$ be a locally integrable function on $\Omega $. Then almost every $x\in \Omega $ is a Lebesgue point of $f$, that is, $f(x)$ is finite and \[  \lim _{r\downarrow 0}\frac1{|Q(x,r)|} \int _{Q(x,r)}|f(y)-f(x)|\, \mathrm dy=0, \qquad Q(x,r)=x+(-r,r)^ d.  \] At every Lebesgue point $x$ of $f$, the mollifications satisfy $f_\varepsilon (x)\to f(x)$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Proof. We prove a maximal inequality on $\mathbb R^ d$, deduce the theorem for integrable functions by approximation with continuous ones, and then localize. The set $N$ where $f$ is infinite is a null set. Changing $f$ to $0$ on $N$ changes neither the averages in the statement nor the values $f(x)$ for $x\notin N$, so the modified function has the same Lebesgue points outside $N$ and the same mollifications. We may therefore assume that $f$ is finite everywhere. Consider first $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^ d)$, and define its maximal function $Mf(x)$ as the supremum over $r>0$ of the averages of $|f|$ over $Q(x,r)$. For fixed $r$, the average of $|f|$ over $Q(x,r)$ depends continuously on $x$, because $\int _{Q(x,r)}|f|$ and $\int _{Q(x',r)}|f|$ differ by at most $\| f(\cdot +x-x')-f\| _1$, which tends to zero as $x'\to x$ by the continuity of translation in $L^1$ (lemma 2.5.1 (2)). As a supremum of continuous functions, $Mf$ is lower semicontinuous, so $\{ Mf>t\} $ is open. We claim the maximal inequality \[  |\{ Mf>t\} |\le \frac{3^ d}{t}\| f\| _1,\qquad t>0.  \] By inner regularity of Lebesgue measure, it suffices to bound $|L|$ for compact $L\subset \{ Mf>t\} $. Each point of $L$ is the center of an open cube over which the average of $|f|$ exceeds $t$, and finitely many of these cubes cover $L$. Select one of largest side length, discard all cubes meeting it, and repeat with the remaining ones. The selected cubes are disjoint, and each discarded cube meets a selected cube of at least the same side length, so it lies in the concentric cube with three times that side length. These enlarged cubes cover $L$, and therefore $|L|$ is at most $3^ d$ times the total volume of the selected cubes, which is less than $t^{-1}\| f\| _1$. Now let $g\in C_ c(\mathbb R^ d)$. For every $x$ and $r$, \[  \begin{split}  \frac1{|Q(x,r)|}\int _{Q(x,r)}|f(y)-f(x)|\, \mathrm dy\leq {}& M(f-g)(x)+|g(x)-f(x)|\\ & +\frac1{|Q(x,r)|}\int _{Q(x,r)}|g(y)-g(x)|\, \mathrm dy, \end{split}  \] and the last term tends to zero as $r\downarrow 0$ because $g$ is continuous at $x$. Hence the upper limit $\Lambda f(x)$ of the left side satisfies $\Lambda f\leq M(f-g)+|f-g|$, and for $t>0$ the set $\{ \Lambda f>2t\} $ is contained in $\{ M(f-g)>t\} \cup \{ |f-g|>t\} $, whose measure is at most $(3^ d+1)t^{-1}\| f-g\| _1$ by the maximal inequality and Chebyshev's inequality. By proposition 2.3.5 , $\| f-g\| _1$ can be made arbitrarily small, so $\{ \Lambda f>2t\} $ is contained in measurable sets of arbitrarily small measure and is therefore a null set. Letting $t$ run through the positive rationals shows that $\Lambda f=0$ almost everywhere. Next, let $f$ be locally integrable on $\Omega $, and let $(K_ j)$ be a compact exhaustion of $\Omega $. The function equal to $f$ on $\operatorname{Int}K_{j+1}$ and to $0$ elsewhere belongs to $L^1(\mathbb R^ d)$, and for $x\in \operatorname{Int}K_ j$ and small $r$ the averages in the statement are the same for $f$ and for this function. Hence almost every point of each $\operatorname{Int}K_ j$, and therefore of $\Omega $, is a Lebesgue point of $f$. Finally, let $x$ be a Lebesgue point of $f$ and let $\varepsilon >0$ be so small that $x\in \Omega _\varepsilon $. The function $\rho _\varepsilon (x-\cdot )$ is bounded by $\varepsilon ^{-d}\sup \rho =2^ d\sup \rho /|Q(x,\varepsilon )|$ and vanishes outside $B(x,\varepsilon )\subset Q(x,\varepsilon )$. Since $\int \rho _\varepsilon =1$, \[  \begin{split}  |f_\varepsilon (x)-f(x)|& =\left|\int (f(y)-f(x))\rho _\varepsilon (x-y)\, \mathrm dy\right|\\ & \leq \frac{2^ d\sup \rho }{|Q(x,\varepsilon )|}\int _{Q(x,\varepsilon )}|f(y)-f(x)|\, \mathrm dy, \end{split}  \] which tends to zero as $\varepsilon \to 0$. $\square$

title: Lemma 2.8.4
text: Lemma 2.8.4 . CAAD90CD1576 Let $Q\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be a closed cube of side length $l$, and let $F$ be a locally integrable function on an open neighborhood $V$ of $Q$ whose distributional first derivatives $\partial _ kF$ on $V$ are locally integrable. Put $F_ Q=|Q|^{-1}\int _ QF\, \mathrm dx$. Then \[  \int _ Q|F-F_ Q|\, \mathrm dx\le l\sum _{k=1}^ d\int _ Q|\partial _ kF|\, \mathrm dx.  \] The same assertion holds componentwise for vector-valued $F$. Proof. Suppose first that $F$ is continuously differentiable near $Q$. For $x,y\in Q$, the points $z^{(k)}=(y_1,\ldots ,y_ k,x_{k+1},\ldots ,x_ d)$, $0\leq k\leq d$, lead from $x$ to $y$ by changing one coordinate at a time. If $I_ k$ is the $k$th side interval of $Q$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives \[  |F(y)-F(x)|\leq \sum _{k=1}^ d\int _{I_ k}|\partial _ kF(y_1,\ldots ,y_{k-1},t,x_{k+1},\ldots ,x_ d)|\, \mathrm dt.  \] Integrate over $(x,y)\in Q\times Q$. The $k$th term does not depend on the $d+1$ coordinates $x_1,\ldots ,x_ k,y_ k,\ldots ,y_ d$, which contribute a factor $l^{d+1}$, and integration over the remaining coordinates and $t$ gives $\int _ Q|\partial _ kF|\, \mathrm dx$. Since $|F(x)-F_ Q|\leq |Q|^{-1}\int _ Q|F(x)-F(y)|\, \mathrm dy$ and $|Q|=l^ d$, the inequality follows. In general, the mollifications $F_\varepsilon $ are smooth on $V_\varepsilon =\{ x\in V:\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb R^ d\setminus V)>\varepsilon \} $, which is a neighborhood of $Q$ for small $\varepsilon $. By lemma 2.5.1 (2) and proposition 2.5.3 (1), $F_\varepsilon \to F$ and $\partial _ kF_\varepsilon =(\partial _ kF)_\varepsilon \to \partial _ kF$ in $L^1(Q)$. Since $|(F_\varepsilon )_ Q-F_ Q|\leq |Q|^{-1}\| F_\varepsilon -F\| _{L^1(Q)}$, the left sides of the inequality for $F_\varepsilon $ and for $F$ differ by at most $2\| F_\varepsilon -F\| _{L^1(Q)}$, and the inequality for $F_\varepsilon $ passes to the limit. $\square$

title: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
search_title: Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Harmonic functions are the solutions of the Laplace equation $\Delta h=0$. In potential theory they play the role that affine functions play for convex functions: the subharmonic functions of section 3.4 are studied by comparison with them, and the fundamental solution of the Laplacian, together with the Green functions obtained from it by harmonic corrections, defines the potentials and energies of section 4.1 , section 4.2 . Unless stated otherwise, $\Omega $ denotes an open subset of $\mathbb R^ d$, where $d\geq 1$. We begin with mean values. After introducing surface measure, polar coordinates and the divergence theorem on balls, we show that a continuous function is harmonic exactly when its value at the center of every closed ball in its domain equals its mean over the boundary sphere (theorem 3.1.7 ). Averaging against a mollifier then shows that harmonic functions are smooth, with interior estimates for all their derivatives. A distribution in the sense of section 2.1 need not have pointwise values; nevertheless, Weyl's lemma (theorem 3.1.11 ) shows that a distribution with vanishing Laplacian is a smooth harmonic function. The fundamental solution of the Laplacian (proposition 3.1.13 ) fixes the sign conventions for all later potentials. The Dirichlet problem asks for a harmonic function with prescribed continuous boundary values. On a ball it is solved explicitly by the Poisson integral (theorem 3.1.18 ), whose kernel also yields the Harnack inequalities and the compactness of families of nonnegative harmonic functions. On a general bounded open set there is no such formula, and we use Perron's method instead. The candidate solution is the pointwise supremum of all continuous subsolutions whose boundary values do not exceed the data; replacing a subsolution on a small ball by the Poisson integral of its values shows that this envelope is harmonic (theorem 3.1.25 ). The envelope also depends linearly on the data (theorem 3.1.27 ). A boundary point is regular if the envelope attains the prescribed value there for all data. Regularity is decided by the existence of a barrier, which need only be constructed near the point (theorem 3.1.29 , proposition 3.1.30 ); for $d\geq 2$, regularity fails at the center of a punctured ball. When every boundary point is regular, the solution operator is integration against harmonic measure, and correcting the fundamental solution by the harmonic function with the same boundary values gives the Green function (theorem 3.1.34 ). Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in subsection 25.1.2 .

Recall from section 2.5 that $B(x,r)$ is the open ball with center $x$ and radius $r>0$; its closure $\overline{B(x,r)}$ is the closed ball. We write $S^{d-1}=\{ y\in \mathbb R^ d:|y|=1\} $ for the unit sphere. The Laplacian is $\Delta =\sum _{j=1}^ d\partial _{x_ j}^2$. A real function $h\in C^2(\Omega )$ is harmonic if $\Delta h=0$, and a complex function is harmonic if its real and imaginary parts are harmonic. In dimension one the harmonic functions are the functions that are affine on each component interval of $\Omega $, because $h''=0$ on an interval forces $h'$ to be constant there. We define surface measure on the unit sphere through the Lebesgue measure of cones: for a Borel set $A\subset S^{d-1}$ put \[  S(A)=d\,  igl |\{ t\omega :0<t<1,\  \omega \in A\}  igr |.  \] The cone over $A$ is the inverse image of $A$ under the continuous map $y\mapsto y/|y|$ on $B(0,1)\setminus \{ 0\} $, so it is a Borel set; moreover, the cone over a countable union is the union of the cones, and cones over disjoint sets are disjoint. Hence $S$ is a finite Borel measure on $S^{d-1}$, the surface measure . It is invariant under every orthogonal transformation $Q$ of $\mathbb R^ d$: the cone over $QA$ is the image under $Q$ of the cone over $A$, and Lebesgue measure is invariant under orthogonal transformations. By linearity and monotone convergence (proposition 2.2.3 ), it follows that $\int _{S^{d-1}}g\circ Q\, \mathrm dS=\int _{S^{d-1}}g\, \mathrm dS$ for every nonnegative or integrable Borel function $g$. We write $s_{d-1}=S(S^{d-1})$ for the area of the unit sphere, so that the unit ball has volume $s_{d-1}/d$. For instance, $s_0=2$, because $S$ is counting measure on $S^0=\{ \pm 1\} $, and $s_1=2\pi $, because the unit disc has area $\pi $. On a sphere $\partial B(x,r)$ we use the measure obtained by translation and dilation, again denoted $\mathrm dS$: \[  \int _{\partial B(x,r)}g\, \mathrm dS=r^{d-1}\int _{S^{d-1}}g(x+r\omega )\, \mathrm dS(\omega ).  \] Next we express Lebesgue measure in polar coordinates. Let $0\leq a<b$ and let $A\subset S^{d-1}$ be a Borel set. By dilation, the cone $\{ t\omega :0<t<b,\  \omega \in A\} $ has Lebesgue measure $b^ dS(A)/d$. The set $\{ t\omega :0<t\leq a,\  \omega \in A\} $ is the intersection of the decreasing cones $\{ t\omega :0<t<a+1/n,\  \omega \in A\} $, so its measure is $\lim _ n(a+1/n)^ dS(A)/d=a^ dS(A)/d$. Subtracting and translating, we find that for every $x\in \mathbb R^ d$ the annular sector $\{ x+t\omega :a<t<b,\  \omega \in A\} $ has Lebesgue measure \[   rac{(b^ d-a^ d)S(A)}{d}=S(A)\int _ a^ bt^{d-1}\, \mathrm dt.  \] Now fix $x\in \mathbb R^ d$ and $R>0$, let $\lambda $ be the measure $t^{d-1}\, \mathrm dt$ on the Borel sets of $(0,R)$, and let $\Phi (t,\omega )=x+t\omega $. The map $\Phi $ is a homeomorphism from $(0,R)	imes S^{d-1}$ onto $Z=B(x,R)\setminus \{ x\} $, with inverse $y\mapsto (|y-x|,(y-x)/|y-x|)$, and the annular sectors with center $x$ contained in $Z$ are the images under $\Phi $ of the rectangles $(a,b)	imes A$ with $b\leq R$. These sectors generate the Borel $\sigma $-algebra of $Z$. Indeed, the sets $(a,b)	imes (S^{d-1}\cap B(\omega ,q))$, where $0<a<b<R$ are rational, $\omega $ runs through a countable dense subset of $S^{d-1}$ and $q$ through the positive rationals, form a countable base of the topology of $(0,R)	imes S^{d-1}$. Hence every open subset of $Z$ is a countable union of their images, which are sectors. The sets $E\subset Z$ for which $\Phi ^{-1}(E)$ belongs to the product $\sigma $-algebra form a $\sigma $-algebra containing the sectors, and hence all Borel subsets of $Z$. Consequently $\mu (E)=(\lambda 	imes S)(\Phi ^{-1}(E))$ defines a finite Borel measure $\mu $ on $Z$, and $\mu $ agrees with Lebesgue measure on the sectors. The sectors are closed under finite intersections, and $Z$ itself is a sector, so the two finite measures agree on every Borel subset of $Z$ by part (2) of lemma 2.2.6 . Applying it to the positive and negative parts of $\operatorname{Re}f$ and $\operatorname{Im}f$ and using Fubini's theorem, we obtain ( 3.1.2 ) for every Borel function $f$ which is integrable on $B(x,R)$. Letting $R	o \infty $ and using monotone convergence, we see that ( 3.1.2 ) also holds with $R=\infty $, where $B(x,\infty )=\mathbb R^ d$. Conversely, harmonic functions have the sphere mean-value property by proposition 3.1.5 ; in particular they are smooth, and they satisfy $h=h_\varepsilon =h*\rho _\varepsilon $ on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ by the first part of the proof. Now let $h$ be harmonic and $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $. Then $x$ lies in the open set $\Omega _ r$, and $h=h_ r$ on $\Omega _ r$ by the first part of the proof. By the differentiation formula $\partial ^\alpha h_ r=h*\partial ^\alpha \rho _ r$ of section 2.5 , and since $\partial ^\alpha \rho _ r$ vanishes outside $B(0,r)$, we get \[  \partial ^\alpha h(x)=\int _{B(x,r)} h(y)\, (\partial ^\alpha \rho _ r)(x-y)\, \mathrm d y.  \] Since $\partial ^\alpha \rho _ r(z)=r^{-d-|\alpha |}(\partial ^\alpha \rho )(z/r)$, this proves ( 3.1.8 ) with $C_{d,\alpha }=\sup |\partial ^\alpha \rho |$, where $\rho $ is the mollifier on $\mathbb R^ d$ fixed in section 2.5 . $\square$

title: Proposition 3.1.10
section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Proposition 3.1.10 . B304785CC98D Let $h$ be a real harmonic function on an open set $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$. If $D$ is connected and $h$ attains its maximum or its minimum over $D$ at a point of $D$, then $h$ is constant. If $D$ is bounded and $\varlimsup _{D\ni x\to \zeta }h(x)\leq 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial D$, then $h\leq 0$ on $D$. Consequently, a harmonic function on a bounded open set which is continuous on its closure is determined by its boundary values. Proof. For the first assertion, suppose that $h$ attains its maximum $m$ at a point of $D$, and let $E=\{ x\in D:h(x)=m\} $. This set is nonempty and closed in $D$. If $x\in E$ and $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset D$, the ball mean-value property gives $\int _{B(x,r)}(m-h)\, \mathrm dy=0$. The integrand is continuous and nonnegative, so it vanishes on $B(x,r)$. Thus $E$ is open, and $E=D$ by connectedness. For the minimum, apply this to $-h$. For the second assertion, let $\varepsilon >0$, and suppose that $h>\varepsilon $ somewhere in $D$; we derive a contradiction. Each $\zeta \in \partial D$ has a ball $B(\zeta ,r_\zeta )$ such that $h<\varepsilon $ on $D\cap B(\zeta ,r_\zeta )$. Since $D$ is bounded, $\partial D$ is compact, and finitely many of these balls cover it; let $W$ be their union. Then $K=\overline D\setminus W=D\setminus W$ is compact. Since $h<\varepsilon $ on $D\setminus K=D\cap W$, the set $K$ is nonempty. The maximum of $h$ over $K$ is attained at some point $x_0$, and $h(x_0)>\varepsilon $; hence $h(x_0)$ is also the maximum of $h$ over $D$. Let $D_0$ be the component of $D$ containing $x_0$; it is open, because every point of $D$ lies in a ball contained in $D$, and balls are connected. By the first assertion, $h=h(x_0)$ on $D_0$. Since $\mathbb R^ d$ is connected and $D_0$ is a nonempty, bounded, open subset, $D_0$ is not closed, so it has a boundary point $\zeta $. This point does not lie in $D$: otherwise the component of $D$ containing $\zeta $ would be an open neighborhood of $\zeta $, so it would meet $D_0$ and hence equal $D_0$, which does not contain its boundary point $\zeta $. Thus $\zeta \in \partial D$ and $\varlimsup _{D\ni x\to \zeta }h(x)\geq h(x_0)>0$, contradicting the hypothesis. Hence $h\leq \varepsilon $ on $D$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $h\leq 0$. Finally, if two harmonic functions on a bounded open set are continuous on its closure and agree on its boundary, apply the second assertion to the real and imaginary parts of their difference and of its negative. $\square$

title: Theorem 3.1.11 (Weyl's lemma)
section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Theorem 3.1.11 (Weyl's lemma) . C9127FBA9AE8 Let $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$ satisfy $\Delta T=0$. Then there is a unique smooth harmonic function $h$ on $\Omega $ such that $\langle T,\chi \rangle =\int _\Omega h\chi \, \mathrm dx$ for every $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$. In particular, a locally integrable function whose distributional Laplacian vanishes agrees almost everywhere with a harmonic function. Proof. Recall from section 2.5 that $(T*\phi )(y)=\langle T,\phi (y-\cdot )\rangle $ for a test function $\phi $ on $\mathbb R^ d$ supported in $\overline{B(0,s)}$ and $y\in \Omega _ s$, and that $T_\varepsilon =T*\rho _\varepsilon $. By part (1) of proposition 2.5.3 , $T*\phi $ is smooth on $\Omega _ s$ and $\partial ^\alpha (T*\phi )=T*\partial ^\alpha \phi $; moreover $\Delta T_\varepsilon =(\Delta T)_\varepsilon =0$, so $T_\varepsilon $ is a smooth harmonic function on $\Omega _\varepsilon $. We show that $T_\varepsilon $ converges to the required $h$, locally uniformly with all derivatives, by writing $T_\varepsilon =T*(\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r)$ near each point for a fixed $r>0$. Fix $x\in \Omega $ and $r>0$ with $\overline{B(x,3r)}\subset \Omega $, and let $0<\varepsilon <r$. Since $\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb R^ d\setminus \Omega )>3r$, every point of $B(x,2r)$ has distance greater than $r$ from $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \Omega $, and every point of $B(x,r)$ has distance greater than $2r$; thus $B(x,2r)\subset \Omega _\varepsilon $ and $B(x,r)\subset \Omega _{2r}$. Let $y\in B(x,r)$. The closed ball $\overline{B(y,r)}$ lies in $B(x,2r)$, where $T_\varepsilon $ is harmonic, so the last assertion of theorem 3.1.7 , applied to $T_\varepsilon $ on $B(x,2r)$, gives $T_\varepsilon (y)=\int T_\varepsilon (z)\rho _ r(y-z)\, \mathrm dz$. The test function $\chi =\rho _ r(y-\cdot )$ is supported in $\overline{B(y,r)}\subset \Omega _\varepsilon $, so ( 2.5.4 ) gives $T_\varepsilon (y)=\langle T,\chi *\rho _\varepsilon \rangle $. Substituting $z=w+v$ and using that $\rho _\varepsilon $ is even, we find \begin{align*}  (\chi *\rho _\varepsilon )(w)& =\int \rho _ r(y-z)\rho _\varepsilon (w-z)\, \mathrm dz\\ & =\int \rho _\varepsilon (v)\rho _ r(y-w-v)\, \mathrm dv=(\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r)(y-w). \end{align*} The function $\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r$ is a test function supported in $\overline{B(0,\varepsilon +r)}\subset \overline{B(0,2r)}$, so we have shown that \[  T_\varepsilon =T*(\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r)\qquad \text{on }B(x,r).  \] Since $\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r=\rho _ r*\rho _\varepsilon $, part (3) of lemma 2.5.1 , applied on $\mathbb R^ d$ to $\rho _ r$, shows that $\partial ^\alpha (\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r)\to \partial ^\alpha \rho _ r$ uniformly for every multi-index $\alpha $ as $\varepsilon \to 0$. Let $C$ and $m$ be the constants of definition 2.4.1 for $T$ and the compact set $\overline{B(x,3r)}$, which contains the supports of $(\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r)(y-\cdot )$ and $\rho _ r(y-\cdot )$ for $y\in B(x,r)$. For $y\in B(x,r)$ and a multi-index $\alpha $, the difference $\partial ^\alpha T_\varepsilon (y)-\partial ^\alpha (T*\rho _ r)(y)$ is the pairing of $T$ with $w\mapsto \psi (y-w)$, where $\psi =\partial ^\alpha (\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r-\rho _ r)$, and the derivatives of order $\beta $ of this test function are $\pm (\partial ^\beta \psi )(y-w)$. Hence \[  \sup _{y\in B(x,r)}\bigl |\partial ^\alpha T_\varepsilon (y)-\partial ^\alpha (T*\rho _ r)(y)\bigr | \leq C\max _{|\beta |\leq m}\sup \bigl |\partial ^{\alpha +\beta }(\rho _\varepsilon *\rho _ r-\rho _ r)\bigr |,  \] which tends to zero. Thus $T_\varepsilon \to T*\rho _ r$ on $B(x,r)$, uniformly with all derivatives. Every point of $\Omega $ is the center of such a ball. Therefore $h(y)=\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0}T_\varepsilon (y)$ exists for every $y\in \Omega $, and on each ball $B(x,r)$ as above it equals $T*\rho _ r$ and is the limit of $T_\varepsilon $ uniformly with all derivatives. Thus $h$ is smooth and $\Delta h=\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0}\Delta T_\varepsilon =0$. Every compact subset of $\Omega $ is covered by finitely many of these balls, so $T_\varepsilon \to h$ uniformly on compact sets, and part (2) of proposition 2.5.3 gives $\int h\chi \, \mathrm dx=\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0}\int T_\varepsilon \chi \, \mathrm dx=\langle T,\chi \rangle $ for every test function $\chi $. If two continuous functions define the same distribution, they agree almost everywhere by part (4) of proposition 2.5.3 , and hence everywhere, since nonempty open sets have positive measure. This proves uniqueness. Finally, if $T$ is given by a locally integrable function $u$, then $u$ and $h$ define the same distribution, so $u=h$ almost everywhere by the same proposition. $\square$

title: 3.1.16 Poisson kernels and Harnack inequalities
section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text:
Let $D\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be a bounded open set. The Dirichlet problem on $D$ asks, for a given $f\in C(\partial D)$, for a function $h$ which is harmonic on $D$ and continuous on $\overline D$ with $h=f$ on $\partial D$. By proposition 3.1.10 it has at most one solution. On a ball $B=B(c,R)$ the solution is given by an explicit integral formula: for $x\in B$ and $\zeta \in \partial B$ put 1AF0CC9EF476 3.1.17  egin{equation}  P_ B(x,\zeta )= rac{R^2-|x-c|^2}{s_{d-1}R|x-\zeta |^ d}. \end{equation} This is the Poisson kernel of $B$. Indeed, if $B(a,2t)\subset D$ and $y\in B(a,t)$, then $r=|y-a|<t$, and the left inequality in ( 3.1.20 ) on $B(a,2t)$ gives $h(y)\geq (2t)^{d-2}(2t-r)(2t+r)^{1-d}h(a)\geq c_0h(a)$ with $c_0=2^{d-2}3^{1-d}$. Cover $K$ by finitely many balls $B(a_ k,t_ k)$ with $B(a_ k,2t_ k)\subset D$. Proposition 3.1.19 (3), applied to the compact set $\{ x_0\} $ and the base point $a_ k$, gives $h(x_0)\leq C_ kh(a_ k)$. Hence $h\geq (c_0/\max _ kC_ k)h(x_0)$ on $K$. Now let $(h_ j)$ be increasing and fix $x_0\in D$. The functions $h_ j-h_1$ are nonnegative and harmonic. If $h_ j(x_0)$ is bounded, the first assertion applies to every subsequence of $(h_ j-h_1)$. Since the sequence increases and, by proposition 3.1.19 (3), is bounded on compact sets, it has a finite pointwise limit, and every subsequence has a further subsequence converging in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets to this limit. Hence the whole sequence converges in $C^\infty $ on compact subsets, and the limit is a finite harmonic function. If $h_ j(x_0)\to +\infty $, the lower Harnack bound gives $h_ j-h_1\geq c(h_ j(x_0)-h_1(x_0))$ on each compact $K$, and since $h_1$ is bounded on $K$, $h_ j\to +\infty $ uniformly on $K$. For a decreasing sequence, apply this to $(-h_ j)$. $\square$

title: Corollary 3.1.22
section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Corollary 3.1.22 . F898AC76FE42 A real harmonic function on $\mathbb R^ d$ which is bounded above or bounded below is constant. Proof. After changing the sign and adding a constant, we may assume that the function $h$ is nonnegative. Fix $x\in \mathbb R^ d$ and put $r=|x|$. For $R>r$, ( 3.1.20 ) on $B(0,R)$ gives $c_ Rh(0)\leq h(x)\leq C_ Rh(0)$, where the coefficients $c_ R$ and $C_ R$ of ( 3.1.20 ) tend to one as $R\to \infty $. Letting $R\to \infty $ gives $h(x)=h(0)$. Hence $h$ is constant. $\square$

title: 3.1.23 Perron envelopes and boundary barriers
section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text:
We now solve the Dirichlet problem on a general bounded open set by Perron's method, and we characterize by barriers the boundary points at which the solution attains the prescribed values. Throughout this section $\Omega $ is a nonempty bounded open set, and all functions and boundary data are real-valued. The boundary $\partial \Omega $ is compact, and it is nonempty: otherwise $\Omega $ would be a nonempty proper subset of the connected space $\mathbb R^ d$ which is both open and closed. Let $D$ be an open set. A continuous subsolution on $D$ is a continuous function $v\colon D	o \mathbb R$ such that $v\leq H_ B(v|_{\partial B})$ on $B$ for every ball $B$ with $\overline B\subset D$. A function $w$ is a continuous supersolution if $-w$ is a continuous subsolution. Harmonic functions are both, by the Poisson representation in theorem 3.1.18 . At the center $c$ of $B=B(c,r)$ the Poisson kernel equals $(s_{d-1}r^{d-1})^{-1}$, so a continuous subsolution satisfies the sphere submean inequality $v(c)\leq M_ v(c,r)$ whenever $\overline{B(c,r)}\subset D$. Conversely, a continuous function $v$ on $D$ such that every $c\in D$ satisfies $v(c)\leq M_ v(c,r)$ for all sufficiently small $r>0$ is a continuous subsolution. The proof rests on the identity $M_{|\cdot |^2}(c,r)=|c|^2+r^2$ for the mean of $|y|^2$ over the sphere $\partial B(c,r)$, which holds because $|c+r\omega |^2=|c|^2+2r\, c\cdot \omega +r^2$ and $\int _{S^{d-1}}\omega \, \mathrm dS(\omega )=0$, by the invariance of $S$ under $\omega \mapsto -\omega $. To prove the claim, let $B$ be a ball with $\overline B\subset D$, let $H$ be the Poisson integral of $v|_{\partial B}$, regarded as a continuous function on $\overline B$, and for $\varepsilon >0$ put $w(y)=v(y)-H(y)+\varepsilon |y|^2$. Since $M_ H(c,r)=H(c)$ whenever $\overline{B(c,r)}\subset B$ (proposition 3.1.5 ), we obtain $w(c)\leq M_ w(c,r)-\varepsilon r^2$ for every $c\in B$ and all small $r>0$. Hence the continuous function $w$ cannot attain its maximum over the compact set $\overline B$ at a point $c\in B$, for we would then have $M_ w(c,r)\leq w(c)$ for all small $r$. The maximum is therefore attained on $\partial B$, where $H=v$ and hence $w(y)=\varepsilon |y|^2$. Thus $v-H\leq \varepsilon \max _{\overline B}|y|^2$ on $B$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $v\leq H$. In particular, being a continuous subsolution is a local property: if every point of $D$ has an open neighborhood on which $v$ is a continuous subsolution, then $v$ is a continuous subsolution on $D$. Moreover, a real-valued continuous function is subharmonic in the sense of definition 3.4.2 exactly when every point $c$ satisfies $v(c)\leq M_ v(c,r)$ for all small $r>0$, so the continuous subsolutions are exactly the real-valued continuous subharmonic functions. These functions are stable under the usual operations. If $v_1$ and $v_2$ are continuous subsolutions, then so is $\max \{ v_1,v_2\} $, because $H_ B$ preserves order, so that $v_ i\leq H_ B(v_ i|_{\partial B})\leq H_ B(\max \{ v_1,v_2\} |_{\partial B})$. Sums and multiples by nonnegative constants of continuous subsolutions are continuous subsolutions, by linearity of $H_ B$, and so is $v-h$ for every harmonic $h$, because $h=H_ B(h|_{\partial B})$ on $B$. Correspondingly, the minimum of two continuous supersolutions is a continuous supersolution. Finally, a real function $v\in C^2(D)$ with $\Delta v\geq 0$ is a continuous subsolution. Indeed, if $\overline{B(c,R)}\subset D$, then by ( 3.1.6 ) the mean $M_ v(c,r)$ is nondecreasing in $r\in (0,R)$, and it tends to $v(c)$ as $r\downarrow 0$ because $v$ is continuous at $c$; hence $v(c)\leq M_ v(c,r)$ for $0<r<R$, and the converse statement above applies. Lemma 3.1.24 . 3F83842AEB11 Let $D$ be a bounded open set and $v$ a continuous subsolution on $D$. If $\varlimsup _{D
i x	o \zeta }v(x)\leq 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial D$, then $v\leq 0$ on $D$. Moreover, if $B$ is a ball with $\overline B\subset D$, then the function $v^ B$ which equals $H_ B(v|_{\partial B})$ on $B$ and $v$ on $D\setminus B$ is a continuous subsolution on $D$ with $v^ B\geq v$. Proof. For the first assertion we may assume that $D
eq \varnothing $. Let $\varepsilon >0$, and put $w(y)=v(y)+\varepsilon |y|^2$ for $y\in D$. If $\overline{B(c,r)}\subset D$, then $v(c)\leq M_ v(c,r)$, and the identity $M_{|\cdot |^2}(c,r)=|c|^2+r^2$ gives $w(c)\leq M_ w(c,r)-\varepsilon r^2$. Consequently $w$ does not attain its supremum over $D$ at any point $c\in D$, for we would then have $M_ w(c,r)\leq w(c)$ for small $r$. Choose $x_ k\in D$ with $w(x_ k)	o \sup _ Dw$. Since $D$ is bounded, we may assume, after passing to a subsequence, that $x_ k$ converges to a point $p\in \overline D$. If $p$ were in $D$, the continuity of $w$ would give $w(p)=\sup _ Dw$, which we have excluded. Hence $p\in \partial D$. Since $\sup _ Dw=\lim _ k igl (v(x_ k)+\varepsilon |x_ k|^2 igr )$, the hypothesis gives $\sup _ Dw\leq \varlimsup _{D
i x	o p}v(x)+\varepsilon |p|^2\leq \varepsilon \max _{\overline D}|y|^2$. Thus $v\leq w\leq \varepsilon \max _{\overline D}|y|^2$ on $D$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $v\leq 0$. For the second assertion, $v^ B$ is harmonic on $B$ and equals $v$ on $D\setminus B$; it is continuous at the points of $\partial B$ because $H_ B(v|_{\partial B})$ extends continuously to $v$ on $\partial B$ (theorem 3.1.18 ). Moreover $v^ B\geq v$, because $v\leq H_ B(v|_{\partial B})$ on $B$. To verify the subsolution inequality, let $A$ be a ball with $\overline A\subset D$, and let $H=H_ A(v^ B|_{\partial A})$, regarded as a continuous function on $\overline A$. Since $v\leq v^ B$ and $H_ A$ preserves order, $v\leq H_ A(v|_{\partial A})\leq H$ on $A$; the same inequality holds on $\partial A$, where $H=v^ B\geq v$. On the open set $A\cap B$, the function $v^ B-H$ is harmonic, and it is continuous on the closure of $A\cap B$. A boundary point $\zeta $ of $A\cap B$ lies either on $\partial A$, where $v^ B(\zeta )=H(\zeta )$, or in $A\cap \partial B$, where $v^ B(\zeta )=v(\zeta )\leq H(\zeta )$. By part (2) of proposition 3.1.10 , applied to $v^ B-H$ on the bounded open set $A\cap B$, we get $v^ B\leq H$ on $A\cap B$. On $A\setminus B$ we have $v^ B=v\leq H$. Hence $v^ B\leq H_ A(v^ B|_{\partial A})$ on $A$, which is the subsolution inequality for $v^ B$ on $A$. $\square$ We call $v^ B$ the harmonic lifting of $v$ on $B$. For $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$, let $\mathcal S_ f$ be the set of continuous subsolutions $v$ on $\Omega $ such that $\varlimsup _{\Omega 
i x	o \zeta }v(x)\leq f(\zeta )$ for every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $. The lower Perron envelope of $f$ is \[  U_ f(x)=\sup _{v\in \mathcal S_ f}v(x),\qquad x\in \Omega .  \] The constant $\min _{\partial \Omega }f$ belongs to $\mathcal S_ f$, and every $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ satisfies $v\leq \max _{\partial \Omega }f$, by lemma 3.1.24 applied to $v-\max _{\partial \Omega }f$. Theorem 3.1.25 . 537ACE84788C Let $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$. Then $U_ f$ is harmonic on $\Omega $ and $\min _{\partial \Omega }f\leq U_ f\leq \max _{\partial \Omega }f$. If a harmonic function on $\Omega $ extends continuously to $\overline\Omega $ with boundary values $f$, then it equals $U_ f$. Proof. The bounds for $U_ f$ were proved above. To prove harmonicity, fix a ball $B$ with $\overline B\subset \Omega $ and a point $x_0\in B$; we show that $U_ f$ agrees on $B$ with a harmonic function. If $v\in \mathcal S_ f$, its harmonic lifting $v^ B$ on $B$ is a continuous subsolution by lemma 3.1.24 , and it coincides with $v$ near $\partial \Omega $ because $\overline B$ is a compact subset of $\Omega $; hence $v^ B\in \mathcal S_ f$. Choose $v_ j\in \mathcal S_ f$ with $v_ j(x_0)	o U_ f(x_0)$, and put $w_ j=\max \{ v_1,\ldots ,v_ j,\min _{\partial \Omega }f\} $. Then $(w_ j)$ is an increasing sequence in $\mathcal S_ f$ with values in $[\min _{\partial \Omega }f,\max _{\partial \Omega }f]$, and $w_ j(x_0)	o U_ f(x_0)$ because $v_ j\leq w_ j\leq U_ f$. The liftings $w_ j^ B$ belong to $\mathcal S_ f$ and satisfy $w_ j\leq w_ j^ B\leq U_ f$. On $B$ they are harmonic, increase with $j$ because $H_ B$ preserves order, and are bounded by $\max _{\partial \Omega }f$. By part (2) of corollary 3.1.21 , applied on the domain $B$ to this sequence, which is bounded above, they converge on $B$ to a harmonic function $h$, and $h\leq U_ f$ on $B$, while $h(x_0)=U_ f(x_0)$. Now let $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ be arbitrary. The same argument applied to the increasing sequence $\max \{ w_ j,v\} \in \mathcal S_ f$ shows that the liftings $(\max \{ w_ j,v\} )^ B$ increase on $B$ to a harmonic function $k$. Since these liftings dominate $w_ j^ B$ and $v$ and lie in $\mathcal S_ f$, we have $h\leq k\leq U_ f$ and $k\geq v$ on $B$. In particular $k(x_0)\leq U_ f(x_0)=h(x_0)$, so the nonnegative harmonic function $k-h$ on $B$ vanishes at $x_0$ and therefore vanishes identically, by proposition 3.1.19 (2). Hence $v\leq h$ on $B$. Taking the supremum over $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ gives $U_ f\leq h$, so $U_ f=h$ on $B$. Since $B$ was arbitrary, $U_ f$ is harmonic on $\Omega $. Finally, let $H$ be harmonic on $\Omega $ and continuous on $\overline\Omega $ with $H=f$ on $\partial \Omega $. Then $H\in \mathcal S_ f$, so $H\leq U_ f$. Conversely, for $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ the function $v-H$ is a continuous subsolution with $\varlimsup _{x	o \zeta }(v-H)(x)\leq 0$ at every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $, so $v\leq H$ by lemma 3.1.24 . Hence $U_ f=H$. $\square$ The upper Perron envelope is $V_ f=-U_{-f}$. Equivalently, $V_ f$ is the pointwise infimum of the set $-\mathcal S_{-f}$, which consists of the continuous supersolutions $w$ on $\Omega $ with $\varliminf _{\Omega 
i x	o \zeta }w(x)\geq f(\zeta )$ for every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $. If $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ and $w\in -\mathcal S_{-f}$, then $v-w$ is a continuous subsolution with $\varlimsup _{x	o \zeta }(v-w)(x)\leq f(\zeta )-f(\zeta )=0$ at every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $, so $v\leq w$ by lemma 3.1.24 . Hence $U_ f\leq V_ f$. To prove equality, we first treat data that extend smoothly to a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega $ and then approximate, using the following lemma. Lemma 3.1.26 . 23975478AEBA Let $K\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be compact and $f\in C(K)$. Then $f$ is the uniform limit on $K$ of restrictions to $K$ of functions in $C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$, which can be taken real-valued if $f$ is real-valued. Proof. We may assume that $K
eq \varnothing $. Let $\delta >0$. By compactness there are points $\zeta _1,\ldots ,\zeta _ N\in K$ with $K\subset  igcup _ iB(\zeta _ i,\delta )$. Put $\chi _ i(x)=ho ((x-\zeta _ i)/(2\delta ))$, where $ho $ is the mollifier of section 2.5 ; this function is smooth, positive on $B(\zeta _ i,2\delta )$ and zero outside it. The function $\sigma =\sum _ i\chi _ i$ is positive on the open set $W= igcup _ iB(\zeta _ i,2\delta )\supset K$. The resulting map $f\mapsto U_ f$ from $C(\partial \Omega )$ to harmonic functions on $\Omega $ is linear and positive, and it is a contraction for the supremum norm: $\sup _\Omega |U_ f|\leq \max _{\partial \Omega }|f|$. We show that $\mathcal R$ is a closed linear subspace of $C(\partial \Omega )$ containing a dense subset. Step 1: $\mathcal R$ is a closed linear subspace, and $f\mapsto U_ f$ is linear on it. If $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ and $w\in \mathcal S_ g$, then $v+w\in \mathcal S_{f+g}$; taking suprema over $v$ and $w$ at a fixed point gives $U_ f+U_ g\leq U_{f+g}$. Applying this to $-f$ and $-g$ and changing signs gives $V_{f+g}\leq V_ f+V_ g$. Together with the inequality $U_{f+g}\leq V_{f+g}$ proved above, we obtain \[  U_ f+U_ g\leq U_{f+g}\leq V_{f+g}\leq V_ f+V_ g.  \] Moreover $\mathcal S_{tf}=t\, \mathcal S_ f$ for $t>0$, so $U_{tf}=tU_ f$ and $V_{tf}=tV_ f$, while $U_{-f}=-V_ f$ and $V_{-f}=-U_ f$ by definition. Consequently, if $f,g\in \mathcal R$, the display forces $U_{f+g}=V_{f+g}=U_ f+U_ g$, and $tf\in \mathcal R$ for every real $t$. We claim that, for every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $, \[  \varlimsup _{x	o \zeta } igl (f(\xi )-\varepsilon -Cb(x) igr )\leq f(\zeta )\leq \varliminf _{x	o \zeta } igl (f(\xi )+\varepsilon +Cb(x) igr ).  \] If $|\zeta -\xi |<2\delta $, this holds because $b>0$ and $f(\xi )-\varepsilon <f(\zeta )<f(\xi )+\varepsilon $. Hence the continuous subsolution $f(\xi )-\varepsilon -Cb$ belongs to $\mathcal S_ f$, and the continuous supersolution $f(\xi )+\varepsilon +Cb$ belongs to $-\mathcal S_{-f}$, so that it dominates every member of $\mathcal S_ f$, as shown after theorem 3.1.25 . Therefore $|U_ f-f(\xi )|\leq \varepsilon +Cb$ on $\Omega $. Letting $x	o \xi $ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ shows that $U_ f(x)	o f(\xi )$. Thus $\xi $ is regular. The smooth function $v(x)=|x-\xi |^2/\operatorname {diam}\Omega $ satisfies $\Delta v\geq 0$, and $v\leq f$ on $\partial \Omega $ because $|\zeta -\xi |\leq \operatorname {diam}\overline\Omega =\operatorname {diam}\Omega $ for $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $; hence $v\in \mathcal S_ f$. Then $U_ f$ is harmonic on $\Omega $ by theorem 3.1.25 . By regularity and the continuity of $f$ on $\partial \Omega $, the function equal to $U_ f$ on $\Omega $ and to $f$ on $\partial \Omega $ is continuous on $\overline\Omega $. Uniqueness follows from proposition 3.1.10 . Finally, suppose that $\overline{B(a,r)}\cap \overline\Omega =\{ \xi \} $. Then $|\xi -a|=r$, since otherwise the open ball $B(a,r)$ would be a neighborhood of $\xi $ and would therefore contain points of $\Omega $, which differ from $\xi

Hence $b(x)	o 0$ as $x	o \xi $, and if $N$ is a neighborhood of $\xi $ with $\Omega \setminus N

Thus $b$ is a barrier at $\xi $. $\square$ It is often easier to construct a barrier only near $\xi $; the next proposition shows that this suffices. Proposition 3.1.30 . DBDE3CC0301D Let $\xi \in \partial \Omega $ and let $W$ be an open neighborhood of $\xi $. Suppose that $b$ is a positive continuous supersolution on $\Omega \cap W$ which extends continuously to $\overline\Omega \cap W$, and that the extension vanishes at $\xi $ but nowhere else on $\overline\Omega \cap W$. Then $\xi $ is regular. Proof. Choose $r>0$ with $\overline{B(\xi ,2r)}\subset W$ and $0<t<r$. The set $L=\overline\Omega \cap \{ r-t\leq |x-\xi |\leq r+t\} $ is compact, and $b$ is positive and continuous on it, so there is $c>0$ with $b\geq 2c$ on $L$ (if $L$ is empty, any $c>0$ will do). Define $	ilde b=\min \{ b,c\} $ on $\Omega \cap B(\xi ,r)$ and $	ilde b=c$ on $\Omega \setminus B(\xi ,r)$. Since $b\geq 2c$ on $L$, we have $	ilde b=\min \{ b,c\} $ on $\Omega \cap B(\xi ,r+t)$ and $	ilde b=c$ on $\Omega \setminus \overline{B(\xi ,r)}$. These two open sets cover $\Omega $, and on each of them $	ilde b$ is a continuous supersolution, being a minimum of two continuous supersolutions or a constant. By the locality of the subsolution property, noted after the definition of continuous subsolutions, $	ilde b$ is a continuous supersolution on $\Omega $. The function $	ilde b$ is positive, and it tends to zero at $\xi $, because $0<	ilde b\leq b$ on $\Omega \cap B(\xi ,r)$ and the extension of $b$ vanishes at $\xi $. If $N$ is a neighborhood of $\xi $, then $	ilde b\geq c$ on $\Omega \setminus B(\xi ,r)$, while on $(\Omega \cap B(\xi ,r))\setminus N$ it is at least the minimum of $c$ and of $b$ over the compact set $(\overline\Omega \cap \overline{B(\xi ,r)})\setminus \operatorname{Int}N$, on which $b$ is positive. Hence $	ilde b$ is a barrier at $\xi $, and theorem 3.1.29 shows that $\xi $ is regular. $\square$ Example 3.1.31 . 8C85C3D68394 Let $d\geq 2$. The punctured ball $\Omega =B(0,1)\setminus \{ 0\} $ is a bounded domain with boundary $S^{d-1}\cup \{ 0\} $, and the origin is an irregular boundary point, that is, a boundary point that is not regular. The punctured ball is connected, because it is the image of $(0,1)	imes S^{d-1}$ under the continuous map $(t,\omega )\mapsto t\omega $ and the sphere $S^{d-1}$ is path-connected when $d\geq 2$. Indeed, two points $\omega ,\omega '$ with $\omega '
eq -\omega $ are joined by the path $s\mapsto ((1-s)\omega +s\omega ')/|(1-s)\omega +s\omega '|$, $0\leq s\leq 1$, whose denominator does not vanish, and two antipodal points can be joined through a unit vector orthogonal to them, which exists because $d\geq 2$. To see that the origin is irregular, let $f$ equal one at the origin and zero on $S^{d-1}$; it is continuous on $\partial \Omega $ because the origin is an isolated point of $\partial \Omega $. Let $g(x)=\Gamma _ d(x)-\Gamma _ d(e_1)$, that is, $g(x)=(2\pi )^{-1}\log (1/|x|)$ if $d=2$ and $g(x)=((d-2)s_{d-1})^{-1}(|x|^{2-d}-1)$ if $d\geq 3$. This function is harmonic on $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \{ 0\} $ by proposition 3.1.13 , it vanishes on $S^{d-1}$, and it tends to $+\infty $ at the origin. Let $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ and $\varepsilon >0$; recall that $v\leq \max _{\partial \Omega }f=1$. For every sufficiently small $\delta \in (0,1)$ we have $\varepsilon g\geq 1$ on the sphere $|x|=\delta $. On the annulus $D=\{ \delta <|x|<1\} $, the function $v-\varepsilon g$ is a continuous subsolution; it is continuous and nonpositive on the inner sphere $|x|=\delta $, and its upper limit at every point of $S^{d-1}$ is at most $f=0$, because $g$ is continuous with value $0$ there. By lemma 3.1.24 , $v\leq \varepsilon g$ on $D$. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $v\leq 0$ on $\Omega $. Since $0\in \mathcal S_ f$, the Perron envelope $U_ f$ vanishes identically, so it does not tend to $f(0)=1$ at the origin. In dimension one the situation is different: the bounded open set $(-1,0)\cup (0,1)$ has boundary $\{ -1,0,1\} $. If $f$ is a function on this boundary, the function which is affine on each of the two intervals with the boundary values given by $f$ is harmonic and extends continuously to $[-1,1]$ with boundary values $f$, so it equals $U_ f$ by theorem 3.1.25 . Hence the origin is a regular boundary point of $(-1,0)\cup (0,1)$.

title: Lemma 3.1.24
section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text:
Lemma 3.1.24 . 3F83842AEB11 Let $D$ be a bounded open set and $v$ a continuous subsolution on $D$. If $\varlimsup _{D
i x	o \zeta }v(x)\leq 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial D$, then $v\leq 0$ on $D$. Moreover, if $B$ is a ball with $\overline B\subset D$, then the function $v^ B$ which equals $H_ B(v|_{\partial B})$ on $B$ and $v$ on $D\setminus B$ is a continuous subsolution on $D$ with $v^ B\geq v$. Proof. For the first assertion we may assume that $D
eq \varnothing $. Let $\varepsilon >0$, and put $w(y)=v(y)+\varepsilon |y|^2$ for $y\in D$. If $\overline{B(c,r)}\subset D$, then $v(c)\leq M_ v(c,r)$, and the identity $M_{|\cdot |^2}(c,r)=|c|^2+r^2$ gives $w(c)\leq M_ w(c,r)-\varepsilon r^2$. Consequently $w$ does not attain its supremum over $D$ at any point $c\in D$, for we would then have $M_ w(c,r)\leq w(c)$ for small $r$. Choose $x_ k\in D$ with $w(x_ k)	o \sup _ Dw$. Since $D$ is bounded, we may assume, after passing to a subsequence, that $x_ k$ converges to a point $p\in \overline D$. If $p$ were in $D$, the continuity of $w$ would give $w(p)=\sup _ Dw$, which we have excluded. Hence $p\in \partial D$. Since $\sup _ Dw=\lim _ k igl (v(x_ k)+\varepsilon |x_ k|^2 igr )$, the hypothesis gives $\sup _ Dw\leq \varlimsup _{D
i x	o p}v(x)+\varepsilon |p|^2\leq \varepsilon \max _{\overline D}|y|^2$. Thus $v\leq w\leq \varepsilon \max _{\overline D}|y|^2$ on $D$, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives $v\leq 0$. For the second assertion, $v^ B$ is harmonic on $B$ and equals $v$ on $D\setminus B$; it is continuous at the points of $\partial B$ because $H_ B(v|_{\partial B})$ extends continuously to $v$ on $\partial B$ (theorem 3.1.18 ). Moreover $v^ B\geq v$, because $v\leq H_ B(v|_{\partial B})$ on $B$. To verify the subsolution inequality, let $A$ be a ball with $\overline A\subset D$, and let $H=H_ A(v^ B|_{\partial A})$, regarded as a continuous function on $\overline A$. Since $v\leq v^ B$ and $H_ A$ preserves order, $v\leq H_ A(v|_{\partial A})\leq H$ on $A$; the same inequality holds on $\partial A$, where $H=v^ B\geq v$. On the open set $A\cap B$, the function $v^ B-H$ is harmonic, and it is continuous on the closure of $A\cap B$. A boundary point $\zeta $ of $A\cap B$ lies either on $\partial A$, where $v^ B(\zeta )=H(\zeta )$, or in $A\cap \partial B$, where $v^ B(\zeta )=v(\zeta )\leq H(\zeta )$. By part (2) of proposition 3.1.10 , applied to $v^ B-H$ on the bounded open set $A\cap B$, we get $v^ B\leq H$ on $A\cap B$. On $A\setminus B$ we have $v^ B=v\leq H$. Hence $v^ B\leq H_ A(v^ B|_{\partial A})$ on $A$, which is the subsolution inequality for $v^ B$ on $A$. $\square$

title: Theorem 3.1.25
section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Theorem 3.1.25 . 537ACE84788C Let $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$. Then $U_ f$ is harmonic on $\Omega $ and $\min _{\partial \Omega }f\leq U_ f\leq \max _{\partial \Omega }f$. If a harmonic function on $\Omega $ extends continuously to $\overline\Omega $ with boundary values $f$, then it equals $U_ f$. Proof. The bounds for $U_ f$ were proved above. To prove harmonicity, fix a ball $B$ with $\overline B\subset \Omega $ and a point $x_0\in B$; we show that $U_ f$ agrees on $B$ with a harmonic function. If $v\in \mathcal S_ f$, its harmonic lifting $v^ B$ on $B$ is a continuous subsolution by lemma 3.1.24 , and it coincides with $v$ near $\partial \Omega $ because $\overline B$ is a compact subset of $\Omega $; hence $v^ B\in \mathcal S_ f$. Choose $v_ j\in \mathcal S_ f$ with $v_ j(x_0)\to U_ f(x_0)$, and put $w_ j=\max \{ v_1,\ldots ,v_ j,\min _{\partial \Omega }f\} $. Then $(w_ j)$ is an increasing sequence in $\mathcal S_ f$ with values in $[\min _{\partial \Omega }f,\max _{\partial \Omega }f]$, and $w_ j(x_0)\to U_ f(x_0)$ because $v_ j\leq w_ j\leq U_ f$. The liftings $w_ j^ B$ belong to $\mathcal S_ f$ and satisfy $w_ j\leq w_ j^ B\leq U_ f$. On $B$ they are harmonic, increase with $j$ because $H_ B$ preserves order, and are bounded by $\max _{\partial \Omega }f$. By part (2) of corollary 3.1.21 , applied on the domain $B$ to this sequence, which is bounded above, they converge on $B$ to a harmonic function $h$, and $h\leq U_ f$ on $B$, while $h(x_0)=U_ f(x_0)$. Now let $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ be arbitrary. The same argument applied to the increasing sequence $\max \{ w_ j,v\} \in \mathcal S_ f$ shows that the liftings $(\max \{ w_ j,v\} )^ B$ increase on $B$ to a harmonic function $k$. Since these liftings dominate $w_ j^ B$ and $v$ and lie in $\mathcal S_ f$, we have $h\leq k\leq U_ f$ and $k\geq v$ on $B$. In particular $k(x_0)\leq U_ f(x_0)=h(x_0)$, so the nonnegative harmonic function $k-h$ on $B$ vanishes at $x_0$ and therefore vanishes identically, by proposition 3.1.19 (2). Hence $v\leq h$ on $B$. Taking the supremum over $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ gives $U_ f\leq h$, so $U_ f=h$ on $B$. Since $B$ was arbitrary, $U_ f$ is harmonic on $\Omega $. Finally, let $H$ be harmonic on $\Omega $ and continuous on $\overline\Omega $ with $H=f$ on $\partial \Omega $. Then $H\in \mathcal S_ f$, so $H\leq U_ f$. Conversely, for $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ the function $v-H$ is a continuous subsolution with $\varlimsup _{x\to \zeta }(v-H)(x)\leq 0$ at every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $, so $v\leq H$ by lemma 3.1.24 . Hence $U_ f=H$. $\square$

title: Lemma 3.1.26
section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Lemma 3.1.26 . 23975478AEBA Let $K\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be compact and $f\in C(K)$. Then $f$ is the uniform limit on $K$ of restrictions to $K$ of functions in $C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$, which can be taken real-valued if $f$ is real-valued. Proof. We may assume that $K\neq \varnothing $. Let $\delta >0$. By compactness there are points $\zeta _1,\ldots ,\zeta _ N\in K$ with $K\subset \bigcup _ iB(\zeta _ i,\delta )$. Put $\chi _ i(x)=\rho ((x-\zeta _ i)/(2\delta ))$, where $\rho $ is the mollifier of section 2.5 ; this function is smooth, positive on $B(\zeta _ i,2\delta )$ and zero outside it. The function $\sigma =\sum _ i\chi _ i$ is positive on the open set $W=\bigcup _ iB(\zeta _ i,2\delta )\supset K$. Choose a smooth function $\eta $ with compact support in $W$ which equals one near $K$ (lemma 2.5.1 (4)), and put \[  F=\eta \, \frac{\sum _ if(\zeta _ i)\chi _ i}{\sigma },  \] extended by zero outside $W$. This is a smooth function with compact support on $\mathbb R^ d$, because it is smooth on $W$, where $\sigma >0$, and vanishes on the open set $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \operatorname{Supp}\eta $; it is real-valued if $f$ is. For $\zeta \in K$ we have $\eta (\zeta )=1$, so $F(\zeta )$ is a convex combination of values $f(\zeta _ i)$ with $|\zeta _ i-\zeta |<2\delta $, and therefore $|F(\zeta )-f(\zeta )|\leq \sup \{ |f(y)-f(y')|:y,y'\in K,\  |y-y'|<2\delta \} $. By the uniform continuity of $f$ on the compact set $K$, this bound tends to zero as $\delta \to 0$. $\square$

title: Theorem 3.1.27
section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Theorem 3.1.27 . 8FE1B604CDA2 For every $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$ we have $U_ f=V_ f$. The resulting map $f\mapsto U_ f$ from $C(\partial \Omega )$ to harmonic functions on $\Omega $ is linear and positive, and it is a contraction for the supremum norm: $\sup _\Omega |U_ f|\leq \max _{\partial \Omega }|f|$. Proof. Write $\| f\| =\max _{\partial \Omega }|f|$, and let $\mathcal R$ be the set of $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$ with $U_ f=V_ f$. We show that $\mathcal R$ is a closed linear subspace of $C(\partial \Omega )$ containing a dense subset. Step 1: $\mathcal R$ is a closed linear subspace, and $f\mapsto U_ f$ is linear on it. If $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ and $w\in \mathcal S_ g$, then $v+w\in \mathcal S_{f+g}$; taking suprema over $v$ and $w$ at a fixed point gives $U_ f+U_ g\leq U_{f+g}$. Applying this to $-f$ and $-g$ and changing signs gives $V_{f+g}\leq V_ f+V_ g$. Together with the inequality $U_{f+g}\leq V_{f+g}$ proved above, we obtain \[  U_ f+U_ g\leq U_{f+g}\leq V_{f+g}\leq V_ f+V_ g.  \] Moreover $\mathcal S_{tf}=t\, \mathcal S_ f$ for $t>0$, so $U_{tf}=tU_ f$ and $V_{tf}=tV_ f$, while $U_{-f}=-V_ f$ and $V_{-f}=-U_ f$ by definition. Also $U_0=0$, because $0\in \mathcal S_0$ and every member of $\mathcal S_0$ is nonpositive by lemma 3.1.24 ; hence $V_0=-U_0=0$ and $0\in \mathcal R$. Consequently, if $f,g\in \mathcal R$, the display forces $U_{f+g}=V_{f+g}=U_ f+U_ g$, and $tf\in \mathcal R$ for every real $t$. Thus $\mathcal R$ is a linear subspace, and $f\mapsto U_ f$ is linear on it. To see that $\mathcal R$ is closed, we first show that $U_ f$ and $V_ f$ depend $1$-Lipschitz continuously on $f$ for the supremum norm. If $f\leq g$, then $\mathcal S_ f\subset \mathcal S_ g$ and hence $U_ f\leq U_ g$; and $\mathcal S_{f+t}=\mathcal S_ f+t$ for constants $t$, so $U_{f+t}=U_ f+t$. Since $f\leq g+\| f-g\| $, we get $U_ f\leq U_ g+\| f-g\| $, and by symmetry $|U_ f-U_ g|\leq \| f-g\| $; as $V_ f=-U_{-f}$ and $V_ g=-U_{-g}$, also $|V_ f-V_ g|\leq \| f-g\| $. If $f_ n\in \mathcal R$ converge uniformly to $f$, then $0\leq V_ f-U_ f\leq |V_ f-V_{f_ n}|+|U_{f_ n}-U_ f|\leq 2\| f-f_ n\| \to 0$, so $f\in \mathcal R$. Hence $\mathcal R$ is closed. Step 2: $\mathcal R$ contains the restriction to $\partial \Omega $ of every real smooth function on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega $. Suppose first that $F$ is a real smooth function on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega $ with $\Delta F\geq 0$ there. Then $F$ is a continuous subsolution on $\Omega $, and $F(x)\to F(\zeta )$ as $\Omega \ni x\to \zeta \in \partial \Omega $, so $F\in \mathcal S_{F|_{\partial \Omega }}$ and $U_{F|_{\partial \Omega }}\geq F$. Consequently the harmonic function $U_{F|_{\partial \Omega }}$ satisfies $\varliminf _{x\to \zeta }U_{F|_{\partial \Omega }}(x)\geq F(\zeta )$ at every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $, so it belongs to $-\mathcal S_{-F|_{\partial \Omega }}$ and $V_{F|_{\partial \Omega }}\leq U_{F|_{\partial \Omega }}$. Thus $F|_{\partial \Omega }\in \mathcal R$. Now let $F$ be an arbitrary real smooth function on an open neighborhood $W$ of $\overline\Omega $, and choose $\delta >0$ such that the compact set $L=\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,\overline\Omega )\leq \delta \} $ lies in $W$. Since $\Delta F$ is continuous, hence bounded below, on $L$, there is a constant $A\geq 0$ with $\Delta F+2dA\geq 0$ on $L$. As $\Delta (A|x|^2)=2dA$, both $F+A|x|^2$ and $A|x|^2$ are smooth with nonnegative Laplacian on the open neighborhood $\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,\overline\Omega )<\delta \} $ of $\overline\Omega $. By the first case their restrictions to $\partial \Omega $ lie in $\mathcal R$, and by Step 1 so does the restriction of their difference $F$. Step 3: these restrictions are dense in $C(\partial \Omega )$. This is lemma 3.1.26 , applied to real-valued functions on the compact set $\partial \Omega $. By Steps 1–3, $\mathcal R=C(\partial \Omega )$, and $f\mapsto U_ f$ is linear. By Step 1 it preserves order and satisfies $|U_ f-U_ g|\leq \| f-g\| $. Since $U_0=0$, it follows that $U_ f\geq 0$ whenever $f\geq 0$, and that $|U_ f|\leq \| f\| $. $\square$

title: Definition 3.1.28
section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Definition 3.1.28 . 31D179000C4D A boundary point $\xi \in \partial \Omega $ is regular if $U_ f(x)\to f(\xi )$ as $\Omega \ni x\to \xi $, for every $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$. A barrier at $\xi $ is a positive continuous supersolution $b$ on $\Omega $ such that $b(x)\to 0$ as $x\to \xi $ and, for every neighborhood $N$ of $\xi $ with $\Omega \setminus N\neq \varnothing $, \[  \inf _{\Omega \setminus N}b>0.  \]

title: Theorem 3.1.29
section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text:
Theorem 3.1.29 . C1B72E118338 A boundary point of $\Omega $ is regular if and only if it has a barrier. If every boundary point of $\Omega $ is regular, then for every $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$ the Perron envelope $U_ f$ is the unique harmonic function on $\Omega $ which extends continuously to $\overline\Omega $ with boundary values $f$. If $\xi \in \partial \Omega $ and there is a ball $B(a,r)$ with $\overline{B(a,r)}\cap \overline\Omega =\{ \xi \} $, then $\xi $ has a barrier. Proof. Suppose that $b$ is a barrier at $\xi $, and let $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$ and $\varepsilon >0$. We show that $|U_ f-f(\xi )|\leq \varepsilon +Cb$ on $\Omega $ for a suitable constant $C$. Choose $\delta >0$ such that $|f(\zeta )-f(\xi )|<\varepsilon $ for all $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $ with $|\zeta -\xi |<2\delta $, and put $c=\inf _{\Omega \setminus B(\xi ,\delta )}b>0$; if $\Omega \subset B(\xi ,\delta )$, then $|\zeta -\xi |\leq \delta $ for every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $, and we put $c=1$. If $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $ and $|\zeta -\xi |\geq 2\delta $, then $\Omega \cap B(\zeta ,\delta )$ lies outside $B(\xi ,\delta )$, so $\varliminf _{x	o \zeta }b(x)\geq c$. Let $M=\max _{\partial \Omega }|f|$ and fix $C\geq 2M/c$, which depends on $f$, $\varepsilon $ and $b$. We claim that, for every $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $, \[  \varlimsup _{x	o \zeta } igl (f(\xi )-\varepsilon -Cb(x) igr )\leq f(\zeta )\leq \varliminf _{x	o \zeta } igl (f(\xi )+\varepsilon +Cb(x) igr ).  \] If $|\zeta -\xi |<2\delta $, this holds because $b>0$ and $f(\xi )-\varepsilon <f(\zeta )<f(\xi )+\varepsilon $. If $|\zeta -\xi |\geq 2\delta $, it holds because $f(\xi )-Cc\leq M-2M\leq f(\zeta )$ and $f(\xi )+Cc\geq -M+2M\geq f(\zeta )$. Hence the continuous subsolution $f(\xi )-\varepsilon -Cb$ belongs to $\mathcal S_ f$, and the continuous supersolution $f(\xi )+\varepsilon +Cb$ belongs to $-\mathcal S_{-f}$, so that it dominates every member of $\mathcal S_ f$, as shown after theorem 3.1.25 . Therefore $|U_ f-f(\xi )|\leq \varepsilon +Cb$ on $\Omega $. Letting $x	o \xi $ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ shows that $U_ f(x)	o f(\xi )$. Thus $\xi $ is regular. Conversely, let $\xi $ be regular, and take the boundary function $f(\zeta )=|\zeta -\xi |$. The smooth function $v(x)=|x-\xi |^2/\operatorname {diam}\Omega $ satisfies $\Delta v\geq 0$, and $v\leq f$ on $\partial \Omega $ because $|\zeta -\xi |\leq \operatorname {diam}\overline\Omega =\operatorname {diam}\Omega $ for $\zeta \in \partial \Omega $; hence $v\in \mathcal S_ f$. Thus $b=U_ f$ is harmonic by theorem 3.1.25 , and hence a continuous supersolution, with $b\geq |x-\xi |^2/\operatorname {diam}\Omega $. In particular $b$ is positive on $\Omega $, and if $N$ is a neighborhood of $\xi $ containing a ball $B(\xi ,t)$, then $\inf _{\Omega \setminus N}b\geq t^2/\operatorname {diam}\Omega >0$. By regularity, $b(x)	o f(\xi )=0$ as $x	o \xi $. Hence $b$ is a barrier. Now suppose that every boundary point is regular, and let $f\in C(\partial \Omega )$. Then $U_ f$ is harmonic on $\Omega $ by theorem 3.1.25 . By regularity and the continuity of $f$ on $\partial \Omega $, the function equal to $U_ f$ on $\Omega $ and to $f$ on $\partial \Omega $ is continuous on $\overline\Omega $. Uniqueness follows from proposition 3.1.10 . Finally, suppose that $\overline{B(a,r)}\cap \overline\Omega =\{ \xi \} $. Then $|\xi -a|=r$, since otherwise the open ball $B(a,r)$ would be a neighborhood of $\xi $ and would therefore contain points of $\Omega $, which differ from $\xi 
otin \Omega $. In particular $a
otin \overline\Omega $, and every point of $\overline\Omega \setminus \{ \xi \} $ satisfies $|x-a|>r$. Put \[  b(x)= egin{cases}  |x-a|-r,& d=1,\  \log (|x-a|/r),& d=2,\  r^{2-d}-|x-a|^{2-d},& d\geq 3. \end{cases}  \] For $d\geq 2$ this is harmonic on $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \{ a\} $ by proposition 3.1.13 , being a positive multiple of $E_ d(x-a)$ plus a constant. In dimension one, each component of $\Omega $ is an open interval disjoint from $[a-r,a+r]$, so it lies on one side of this interval; hence $|x-a|$ is affine on each component, and $b$ is harmonic on $\Omega $ as well. In all dimensions $b$ is an increasing function of $|x-a|$ which vanishes when $|x-a|=r$, so it is continuous on the compact set $\overline\Omega $, positive on $\overline\Omega \setminus \{ \xi \} $ and zero at $\xi $. Hence $b(x)	o 0$ as $x	o \xi $, and if $N$ is a neighborhood of $\xi $ with $\Omega \setminus N
eq \varnothing $, the infimum of $b$ over the nonempty compact set $\overline\Omega \setminus \operatorname{Int}N$ is attained and positive. Thus $b$ is a barrier at $\xi $. $\square$

title: Proposition 3.1.30
section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Proposition 3.1.30 . DBDE3CC0301D Let $\xi \in \partial \Omega $ and let $W$ be an open neighborhood of $\xi $. Suppose that $b$ is a positive continuous supersolution on $\Omega \cap W$ which extends continuously to $\overline\Omega \cap W$, and that the extension vanishes at $\xi $ but nowhere else on $\overline\Omega \cap W$. Then $\xi $ is regular. Proof. Choose $r>0$ with $\overline{B(\xi ,2r)}\subset W$ and $0<t<r$. The set $L=\overline\Omega \cap \{ r-t\leq |x-\xi |\leq r+t\} $ is compact, and $b$ is positive and continuous on it, so there is $c>0$ with $b\geq 2c$ on $L$ (if $L$ is empty, any $c>0$ will do). Define $\tilde b=\min \{ b,c\} $ on $\Omega \cap B(\xi ,r)$ and $\tilde b=c$ on $\Omega \setminus B(\xi ,r)$. Since $b\geq 2c$ on $L$, we have $\tilde b=\min \{ b,c\} $ on $\Omega \cap B(\xi ,r+t)$ and $\tilde b=c$ on $\Omega \setminus \overline{B(\xi ,r)}$. These two open sets cover $\Omega $, and on each of them $\tilde b$ is a continuous supersolution, being a minimum of two continuous supersolutions or a constant. By the locality of the subsolution property, noted after the definition of continuous subsolutions, $\tilde b$ is a continuous supersolution on $\Omega $. The function $\tilde b$ is positive, and it tends to zero at $\xi $, because $0<\tilde b\leq b$ on $\Omega \cap B(\xi ,r)$ and the extension of $b$ vanishes at $\xi $. If $N$ is a neighborhood of $\xi $, then $\tilde b\geq c$ on $\Omega \setminus B(\xi ,r)$, while on $(\Omega \cap B(\xi ,r))\setminus N$ it is at least the minimum of $c$ and of $b$ over the compact set $(\overline\Omega \cap \overline{B(\xi ,r)})\setminus \operatorname{Int}N$, on which $b$ is positive. Hence $\tilde b$ is a barrier at $\xi $, and theorem 3.1.29 shows that $\xi $ is regular. $\square$

title: Example 3.1.31
section: 3.1 Harmonic functions and the Dirichlet problem
text: Example 3.1.31 . 8C85C3D68394 Let $d\geq 2$. The punctured ball $\Omega =B(0,1)\setminus \{ 0\} $ is a bounded domain with boundary $S^{d-1}\cup \{ 0\} $, and the origin is an irregular boundary point, that is, a boundary point that is not regular. The punctured ball is connected, because it is the image of $(0,1)\times S^{d-1}$ under the continuous map $(t,\omega )\mapsto t\omega $ and the sphere $S^{d-1}$ is path-connected when $d\geq 2$. Indeed, two points $\omega ,\omega '$ with $\omega '\neq -\omega $ are joined by the path $s\mapsto ((1-s)\omega +s\omega ')/|(1-s)\omega +s\omega '|$, $0\leq s\leq 1$, whose denominator does not vanish, and two antipodal points can be joined through a unit vector orthogonal to them, which exists because $d\geq 2$. To see that the origin is irregular, let $f$ equal one at the origin and zero on $S^{d-1}$; it is continuous on $\partial \Omega $ because the origin is an isolated point of $\partial \Omega $. Let $g(x)=\Gamma _ d(x)-\Gamma _ d(e_1)$, that is, $g(x)=(2\pi )^{-1}\log (1/|x|)$ if $d=2$ and $g(x)=((d-2)s_{d-1})^{-1}(|x|^{2-d}-1)$ if $d\geq 3$. This function is harmonic on $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \{ 0\} $ by proposition 3.1.13 , it vanishes on $S^{d-1}$, and it tends to $+\infty $ at the origin. Let $v\in \mathcal S_ f$ and $\varepsilon >0$; recall that $v\leq \max _{\partial \Omega }f=1$. For every sufficiently small $\delta \in (0,1)$ we have $\varepsilon g\geq 1$ on the sphere $|x|=\delta $. A nonempty bounded open set is called regular if all its boundary points are regular in the sense of definition 3.1.28 .
