title: Theorem 3.4.19
text: Theorem 3.4.19 . F159A5A96A98 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open, and let $(u_ j)$ be a sequence in $\mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$ that is uniformly bounded above on every compact subset of $\Omega $. If $\Omega $ is connected, then either $u_ j\to -\infty $ uniformly on compact subsets of $\Omega $, or a subsequence of $(u_ j)$ converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ to a locally integrable subharmonic function. If every $u_ j$ is locally integrable and $(u_ j)$ converges in the sense of distributions to some $T\in \mathcal D'(\Omega )$, then $T$ is real, $\Delta T\geq 0$, and $u_ j\to u$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, where $u$ is the canonical representative of $T$. Proof. We prove (2) first, because (1) reduces to it. As observed after theorem 3.4.12 , $T$ is real, $\Delta T\geq 0$, and $T$ has a canonical representative $u$. We begin by showing that $(u_ j)$ is bounded in $L^1(L)$ for every compact set $L\subset \Omega $. Fix such a set $L$, let $\chi $ be a nonnegative test function equal to one near $L$, and let $M\geq 0$ bound all $u_ j$ from above on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $. Then $|u_ j|\leq 2M-u_ j$ on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, so \[  \int _ L|u_ j|\, \mathrm d x\leq 2M\int \chi \, \mathrm d x-\int u_ j\chi \, \mathrm d x,  \] which is bounded because $\int u_ j\chi \, \mathrm d x$ converges. Next we show that the mollifications $u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon $ converge locally uniformly. Fix $\varepsilon >0$. For $x\in \Omega _\varepsilon $, the function $\rho _\varepsilon (x-\cdot )$ is a test function, so $u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon (x)\to \langle T,\rho _\varepsilon (x-\cdot )\rangle =u*\rho _\varepsilon (x)$. Let $L\subset \Omega _\varepsilon $ be compact; then $L'=\{ y:\operatorname {dist}(y,L)\leq \varepsilon \} $ is a compact subset of $\Omega $, and the mean value theorem, applied to $\rho _\varepsilon $, gives \[  |u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon (x)-u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon (x')|\leq \sup |\nabla \rho _\varepsilon |\cdot |x-x'|\int _{L'}|u_ j|\, \mathrm d y,\qquad x,x'\in L.  \] Thus the functions $u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon $ are $A$-Lipschitz on $L$, where $A=\sup |\nabla \rho _\varepsilon |\cdot \sup _ j\int _{L'}|u_ j|\, \mathrm dy$, and so is their pointwise limit $u*\rho _\varepsilon $. Given $\tau >0$, cover $L$ by finitely many balls $B(x_ i,\tau /(3A+1))$ with $x_ i\in L$, and choose $j_0$ such that $|u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon (x_ i)-u*\rho _\varepsilon (x_ i)|<\tau /3$ for all $i$ and all $j\geq j_0$. Then $|u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon -u*\rho _\varepsilon |<\tau $ on $L$ for $j\geq j_0$, so the convergence is uniform on $L$. Now let $\chi $ be a nonnegative test function, choose $\varepsilon $ so small that $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset \Omega _\varepsilon $, let $\delta >0$, and put $g=u*\rho _\varepsilon +\delta $. By ( 3.4.13 ), $u_ j\leq u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon $ and $u\leq u*\rho _\varepsilon $ on $\Omega _\varepsilon $. By the uniform convergence just proved, $u_ j\leq g$ on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ for all large $j$; also $u\leq g$. Hence $|u_ j-u|\leq (g-u_ j)+(g-u)$ almost everywhere on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, and since $\int u_ j\chi \, \mathrm d x\to \int u\chi \, \mathrm d x$, \[  \begin{aligned}  \varlimsup _ j\int |u_ j-u|\chi \, \mathrm d x & \leq \lim _ j\int (g-u_ j)\chi \, \mathrm d x+\int (g-u)\chi \, \mathrm d x\\ & =2\int (u*\rho _\varepsilon +\delta -u)\chi \, \mathrm d x. \end{aligned}  \] Let $\delta \downarrow 0$, and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; since $u*\rho _\varepsilon \to u$ in $L^1$ on $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ (lemma 2.5.1 ), the right-hand side tends to zero. Choosing $\chi $ equal to one on a prescribed compact set proves $L^1$ convergence on that set. This proves (2). (1) Suppose that $u_ j$ does not tend to $-\infty $ uniformly on compact subsets. Then there are a compact set $K\subset \Omega $, a constant $C_0$ and infinitely many indices $j$ with $\sup _ Ku_ j>-C_0$, and for these $j$ we can choose $x_ j\in K$ with $u_ j(x_ j)>-C_0$. By lemma 3.4.17 , a subsequence, which we again denote by $(u_ j)$, is bounded in $L^1(L)$ for every compact set $L\subset \Omega $; in particular, every $u_ j$ is locally integrable. By (2), it suffices to show that a further subsequence converges in the sense of distributions. Choose open sets $U_ m\Subset \Omega $ increasing to $\Omega $, for instance the interiors of the sets of a compact exhaustion (section 2.2 ), and constants $M_ m\geq 0$ with $u_ j\leq M_ m$ on $\overline{U_ m}$ for all $j$. On $U_ m$, the Borel measures $(M_ m-u_ j)\, \mathrm d x$ are positive, and their masses on a compact set $L\subset U_ m$ are at most $M_ m|L|+\sup _ j\int _ L|u_ j|\, \mathrm dx$, uniformly in $j$; in particular, they are Radon measures by proposition 2.2.2 . By theorem 2.6.5 and a diagonal extraction over $m$, we may assume that for each $m$ these measures converge vaguely on $U_ m$. Every $\chi \in C_ c(\Omega )$ has its support in some $U_ m$, so \[  \int u_ j\chi \, \mathrm d x=M_ m\int \chi \, \mathrm d x-\int (M_ m-u_ j)\chi \, \mathrm d x  \] converges. Let $T(\chi )$ denote the limit when $\chi $ is a test function. If $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset L$ with $L$ compact, then $|T(\chi )|\leq \sup _ j\int _ L|u_ j|\, \mathrm d x\cdot \sup |\chi |$. Hence $T$ is a distribution of order zero, and $u_ j\to T$ in the sense of distributions. $\square$

title: Theorem 3.4.20 (Hartogs' lemma)
text: Theorem 3.4.20 (Hartogs' lemma) . 5784B80133BF Let $(u_ j)$ be a sequence of locally integrable subharmonic functions on $\Omega $ converging in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ to a function $v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$. Then $\Delta v\geq 0$ in the sense of distributions. Let $u$ be the canonical representative of $v$, that is, the locally integrable subharmonic function equal to $v$ almost everywhere. Then, for every $x\in \Omega $ and every sequence $x_ j\to x$ in $\Omega $, \[  \varlimsup _ j u_ j(x_ j)\leq u(x).  \] For every compact set $K\subset \Omega $ and every lower semicontinuous function $f\colon K\to \mathbb R$, for instance every real continuous function on $K$, \[  \varlimsup _ j\sup _ K(u_ j-f)\leq \sup _ K(u-f).  \] In particular, if $f\colon K\to \mathbb R$ is lower semicontinuous and $u<f$ on $K$, then $u_ j<f$ on $K$ for all sufficiently large $j$. Proof. Convergence in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ implies convergence in the sense of distributions, because $|\int (u_ j-v)\chi \, \mathrm dx|\leq \sup |\chi |\int _{\operatorname{Supp}\chi }|u_ j-v|\, \mathrm dx$. Hence, as observed after theorem 3.4.12 , the distribution defined by $v$ is real, has positive Laplacian and has a canonical representative $u$. Let $x_ j\to x$, and choose $\varepsilon >0$ with $\overline{B(x,2\varepsilon )}\subset \Omega $. For $y\in B(x,\varepsilon )$ we have \[  |u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon (y)-u*\rho _\varepsilon (y)|\leq \sup \rho _\varepsilon \int _{B(x,2\varepsilon )}|u_ j-v|\, \mathrm d z,  \] so $u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon \to u*\rho _\varepsilon $ uniformly on $B(x,\varepsilon )$. For large $j$ we have $x_ j\in B(x,\varepsilon )$. Since $u_ j\leq u_ j*\rho _\varepsilon $ by ( 3.4.13 ) and $u*\rho _\varepsilon $ is continuous, we obtain \[  \varlimsup _ j u_ j(x_ j)\leq \varlimsup _ ju_ j*\rho _\varepsilon (x_ j)=u*\rho _\varepsilon (x).  \] Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and using ( 3.4.13 ) again proves the first assertion. For the second assertion we may assume $K\neq \varnothing $. Since $u$ and $-f$ are upper semicontinuous on the compact set $K$, they are bounded above there, so $s=\sup _ K(u-f)$ lies in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. Suppose that $\varlimsup _ j\sup _ K(u_ j-f)>c>s$ for some real $c$. Then $\sup _ K(u_ j-f)>c$ for infinitely many $j$, so along a subsequence there are points $x_ j\in K$ with $u_ j(x_ j)-f(x_ j)>c$, and after passing to a further subsequence we may assume $x_ j\to x\in K$. Since $\varliminf _ jf(x_ j)\geq f(x)$ by lower semicontinuity, the first assertion, applied to this subsequence, gives \[  c\leq \varlimsup _ j\bigl (u_ j(x_ j)-f(x_ j)\bigr )\leq \varlimsup _ ju_ j(x_ j)-\varliminf _ jf(x_ j)\leq u(x)-f(x)\leq s<c,  \] a contradiction. Finally, if $u<f$ on $K$, then the upper semicontinuous function $u-f$ attains a negative maximum on $K$, so $\sup _ K(u-f)<0$, and the second assertion gives $\sup _ K(u_ j-f)<0$ for all large $j$. $\square$

title: 3.4.21 Upper envelopes and countable selection
text:
The pointwise supremum of a family of subharmonic functions need not be upper semicontinuous (example 3.4.24 ), so we regularize it. Let $F\colon \Omega 	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ be locally bounded above, that is, bounded above on a neighborhood of each point. Its upper semicontinuous regularization is \[  F^*(x)=\inf _{r>0}\sup _{B(x,r)\cap \Omega }F.  \] Since $x\in B(x,r)$, we have $F^*\geq F$. The function $F^*$ is upper semicontinuous: if $F^*(x)<c$, then $\sup _{B(x,r)\cap \Omega }F<c$ for some $r>0$, and hence $F^*<c$ on $B(x,r)\cap \Omega $. It is the smallest upper semicontinuous function that dominates $F$: if $G$ is such a function and $c>G(x)$, then $G<c$ on some ball $B(x,r)$, so $\sup _{B(x,r)}F\leq c$ and $F^*(x)\leq c$. We take the supremum of an empty family of functions to be the constant $-\infty $. A family of functions on $\Omega $ is locally uniformly bounded above if every point of $\Omega $ has a neighborhood on which all members of the family are bounded above by one constant. The following lemma reduces such families to countable subfamilies. Lemma 3.4.22 (Choquet's lemma) . B37EED9280E3 Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty family of functions $\Omega 	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ that is locally uniformly bounded above, and let $F=\sup _{w\in \mathcal F}w$. Then there is a countable subfamily $\{ v_ j\} _{j\geq 1}\subset \mathcal F$ such that $v=\sup _ jv_ j$ satisfies $v^*=F^*$. Proof. Call $B(q,s)$ a rational ball if $q\in \mathbb Q^ d$ and $s$ is a positive rational number. Enumerate the rational balls $B$ with $\overline B\subset \Omega $ as $B_1,B_2,\ldots $, in such a way that each of them occurs infinitely often. Since $F$ is bounded above on the compact set $\overline{B_ j}$, we have $\sup _{B_ j}F<\infty $. If $\sup _{B_ j}F>-\infty $, choose $v_ j\in \mathcal F$ with $\sup _{B_ j}v_ j>\sup _{B_ j}F-1/j$; otherwise let $v_ j$ be any member of $\mathcal F$. Put $v=\sup _ jv_ j\leq F$. If $B$ is a rational ball with $\overline B\subset \Omega $, then $B=B_ j$ for infinitely many $j$, so $\sup _ Bv=\sup _ BF$. Every ball $B(x,r)$ contains a rational ball that contains $x$: choose $q\in \mathbb Q^ d$ with $|q-x|<r/3$ and a rational number $s\in (r/3,2r/3)$; then $x\in B(q,s)\subset B(x,r)$. Conversely, a rational ball $B(q,s)$ containing $x$ contains $B(x,s-|q-x|)$. Hence $F^*(x)$ is the infimum of $\sup _ BF$ over the rational balls $B
i x$ with $\overline B\subset \Omega $, and similarly for $v^*(x)$. Therefore $v^*=F^*$. $\square$ Theorem 3.4.23 . 1C986491E366 Let $\{ u_ t\} _{t\in I}$ be a family in $\mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$ that is uniformly bounded above on every compact subset of $\Omega $, and let $F=\sup _ tu_ t$. Then $F^*$ is subharmonic. Moreover, $F$ is Lebesgue measurable and $F=F^*$ almost everywhere. The functions $F$ and $F^*$ need not coincide everywhere (example 3.4.24 ). Proof. If the family is empty, then $F=F^*=-\infty $. Otherwise, we replace the family by an increasing sequence, using Choquet's lemma, and identify the regularized limit of this sequence with a canonical representative. For each $j$ we have $v_ j\leq v$, so $v_ j*ho _\varepsilon \leq v*ho _\varepsilon =w*ho _\varepsilon $, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ in ( 3.4.13 ) gives $v_ j\leq w$ everywhere. Hence $v\leq w$, and $v^*\leq w$ because $w$ is upper semicontinuous. Letting $r\downarrow 0$ gives $w(x)\leq v^*(x)$. Thus $F^*=v^*=w$ is subharmonic on $\Omega '$. Finally, $v\leq F\leq F^*=w$ on $\Omega '$, and $v=w$ almost everywhere. eq F^*$ is contained in the Borel null set $\{ v
eq w\} $. Since Lebesgue measure is complete, $F$ is Lebesgue measurable and $F=F^*$ almost everywhere. $\square$ Example 3.4.24 . 4B0199B64A0D Let $d\geq 2$. The fundamental solution $E_ d$ is negative on $B(0,1)$ and equals $-\infty $ at the origin. The functions $u_ j=\max \{ -1,E_ d/j\} $, $j\geq 1$, are subharmonic on $B(0,1)$, take values in $[-1,0)$ and increase with $j$. title: Lemma 3.4.22 (Choquet's lemma)
text: Lemma 3.4.22 (Choquet's lemma) . B37EED9280E3 Let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty family of functions $\Omega \to [-\infty ,\infty )$ that is locally uniformly bounded above, and let $F=\sup _{w\in \mathcal F}w$. Then there is a countable subfamily $\{ v_ j\} _{j\geq 1}\subset \mathcal F$ such that $v=\sup _ jv_ j$ satisfies $v^*=F^*$. Proof. Call $B(q,s)$ a rational ball if $q\in \mathbb Q^ d$ and $s$ is a positive rational number. Enumerate the rational balls $B$ with $\overline B\subset \Omega $ as $B_1,B_2,\ldots $, in such a way that each of them occurs infinitely often. Since $F$ is bounded above on the compact set $\overline{B_ j}$, we have $\sup _{B_ j}F<\infty $. If $\sup _{B_ j}F>-\infty $, choose $v_ j\in \mathcal F$ with $\sup _{B_ j}v_ j>\sup _{B_ j}F-1/j$; otherwise let $v_ j$ be any member of $\mathcal F$. Put $v=\sup _ jv_ j\leq F$. If $B$ is a rational ball with $\overline B\subset \Omega $, then $B=B_ j$ for infinitely many $j$, so $\sup _ Bv=\sup _ BF$. Every ball $B(x,r)$ contains a rational ball that contains $x$: choose $q\in \mathbb Q^ d$ with $|q-x|<r/3$ and a rational number $s\in (r/3,2r/3)$; then $x\in B(q,s)\subset B(x,r)$. Conversely, a rational ball $B(q,s)$ containing $x$ contains $B(x,s-|q-x|)$. Hence $F^*(x)$ is the infimum of $\sup _ BF$ over the rational balls $B\ni x$ with $\overline B\subset \Omega $, and similarly for $v^*(x)$. Therefore $v^*=F^*$. $\square$

title: 3.4.25 Polar sets and removable singularities
text:
The exceptional sets of potential theory are the sets that lie locally in the pole set of a nontrivial subharmonic function. They are Lebesgue null, and relatively closed ones are removable for subharmonic functions that are bounded above near them. Definition 3.4.26 . 03DCBB9E3633 A set $A\subset \Omega $ is polar if every point of $A$ has a connected open neighborhood $V\subset \Omega $ on which there is a nontrivial $\psi \in \mathrm{SH}(V)$ with $A\cap V\subset \{ \psi =-\infty \} $. Every polar set $A$ has Lebesgue measure zero. Indeed, since $\mathbb R^ d$ has a countable base, $A$ is covered by countably many of the neighborhoods $V$ in the definition, and each $A\cap V$ lies in a pole set $\{ \psi =-\infty \} $, which is null by proposition 3.4.8 . Subsets of polar sets are polar. If $d\geq 2$, every one-point set $\{ a\} \subset \Omega $ is polar, since $E_ d(\cdot -a)$ is a nontrivial subharmonic function with a pole at $a$. If $d=1$, the only polar set is the empty set, because nontrivial subharmonic functions on intervals are finite (example 3.4.15 ). In particular, a Lebesgue null set need not be polar. Polar sets are the natural exceptional sets of the limit theorems above: for $d\geq 2$, theorem 4.1.26 in the next chapter shows that the set where $F
eq F^*$ in theorem 3.4.23 is not only Lebesgue null but polar. Theorem 3.4.27 . 8B711E470600 Let $A\subset \Omega $ be a relatively closed polar set, and let $u\in \mathrm{SH}(\Omega \setminus A)$ be bounded above on $K\setminus A$ for every compact set $K\subset \Omega $. Then $u$ has a unique subharmonic extension $\widetilde u$ to $\Omega $; it is given on $A$ by \[  \widetilde u(x)=\varlimsup _{\Omega \setminus A
i y	o x}u(y).  \] If $\Omega $ is a domain, then $\Omega \setminus A$ is connected. Proof. Put $\widetilde u=u$ on $\Omega \setminus A$, and define $\widetilde u$ on $A$ by the displayed formula. Since $A$ has Lebesgue measure zero, it has no interior points, so every point of $A$ is a limit of points of $\Omega \setminus A$; together with the local upper bound for $u$, this shows that $\widetilde u(x)\in [-\infty ,\infty )$ is well defined for $x\in A$. We first show that $\widetilde u$ is upper semicontinuous and locally bounded above. On the open set $\Omega \setminus A$ both properties hold because $\widetilde u=u$ there. Let $x\in A$ and $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $. For $y\in A\cap B(x,r)$, the definition gives $\widetilde u(y)\leq \sup _{B(x,r)\setminus A}u$, hence \[  \sup _{B(x,r)}\widetilde u=\sup _{B(x,r)\setminus A}u.  \] The right-hand side is bounded above by hypothesis and tends to $\widetilde u(x)$ as $r\downarrow 0$, which proves both claims at $x$. Next we show that $\widetilde u$ is subharmonic near each point $x\in A$; near points of $\Omega \setminus A$ this holds because $\widetilde u=u$. The idea is to approximate $u$ from below by functions $u+\varepsilon \psi $ that tend to $-\infty $ at $A$. Let $V$ and $\psi $ be as in definition 3.4.26 . By proposition 3.4.8 , $\psi $ is locally integrable on the connected set $V$, so it is not identically $-\infty $ on any ball in $V$, and its pole set $\{ \psi =-\infty \} $ is a null set. Replacing $V$ by a ball centered at $x$ whose closure lies in $V$, and $\psi $ by $\psi $ minus an upper bound on that ball, we may therefore assume that $V$ is a ball, that $\psi \leq 0$ on $V$, and that $\psi $ is nontrivial on $V$. For $\varepsilon >0$ define $v_\varepsilon =u+\varepsilon \psi $ on $V\setminus A$ and $v_\varepsilon =-\infty $ on $A\cap V$. On the open set $V\setminus A$, $v_\varepsilon $ is subharmonic. At a point $y\in A\cap V$, $u$ is bounded above near $y$, and $\psi (z)	o -\infty $ as $z	o y$ because $\psi $ is upper semicontinuous with $\psi (y)=-\infty $; hence $v_\varepsilon (z)	o -\infty $ as $z	o y$. So $v_\varepsilon $ is upper semicontinuous at $y$, and the submean inequality at $y$ holds because $v_\varepsilon (y)=-\infty $. Thus $v_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{SH}(V)$. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the functions $v_\varepsilon $ increase because $\psi \leq 0$, and they are bounded above by $u$ on $V\setminus A$, hence uniformly bounded above on compact subsets of $V$. By theorem 3.4.23 , the regularized supremum $w=(\sup _{\varepsilon >0}v_\varepsilon )^*$ is subharmonic on $V$ and equals $\sup _{\varepsilon >0}v_\varepsilon $ almost everywhere. This supremum equals $u$ on $V\setminus (A\cup \{ \psi =-\infty \} )$, so $w=u$ almost everywhere on $V\setminus A$. Since $w$ and $u$ are subharmonic on the open set $V\setminus A$, they agree everywhere there by theorem 3.4.12 (2). It remains to show that $w=\widetilde u$ on $A\cap V$. Let $y\in A\cap V$. Since $w$ is upper semicontinuous and $w=u$ on $V\setminus A$, we have $w(y)\geq \varlimsup _{V\setminus A
i z	o y}u(z)=\widetilde u(y)$. Conversely, by ( 3.4.13 ), $w(y)$ is the limit of the averages of $w$ over $B(y,r)$. Since $A$ is null and $w=u$ off $A$, these averages are at most $\sup _{B(y,r)\setminus A}u$, which tends to $\widetilde u(y)$ as $r\downarrow 0$. Hence $\widetilde u=w$ on $V$, and $\widetilde u$ is subharmonic on $V$. This proves that $\widetilde u\in \mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$. For uniqueness, let $u'\in \mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$ agree with $u$ on $\Omega \setminus A$. Since $A$ is null, $u'=\widetilde u$ almost everywhere on $\Omega $, and hence everywhere by theorem 3.4.12 (2). Finally, let $\Omega $ be a domain, and suppose that $\Omega \setminus A$ is the union of two disjoint nonempty open sets $W_0$ and $W_1$. The function $g$ equal to $0$ on $W_0$ and to $1$ on $W_1$ is harmonic, hence subharmonic, and bounded on $\Omega \setminus A$. Its subharmonic extension $\widetilde g$ to $\Omega $ takes values in $[0,1]$ and equals $1$ on $W_1$, so it attains the finite maximum $1$. By proposition 3.4.7 , $\widetilde g$ is identically $1$ on $\Omega $, contradicting $\widetilde g=0$ on $W_0$. $\square$

title: Theorem 3.4.27

So $v_\varepsilon $ is upper semicontinuous at $y$, and the submean inequality at $y$ holds because $v_\varepsilon (y)=-\infty $. Thus $v_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{SH}(V)$. title: 4.1 Potentials, energy and capacity
text: Polar sets were introduced in subsection 3.4.25 as the sets that lie locally in the pole set of a nontrivial subharmonic function. Every polar set has Lebesgue measure zero, but the converse fails: a sphere is a Lebesgue null set, yet its normalized surface measure has a bounded potential (example 4.1.21 ), and we shall see that this prevents the sphere from being polar. In this chapter we introduce two quantities adapted to the Laplacian, the energy of a measure and the capacity of a set. They characterize the polar sets, and they show that the exceptional sets of the limit theorems of section 3.4 are polar. The energy of a positive measure is the integral of its potential against the measure itself. The Newtonian kernel, and the logarithmic kernel on measures of total mass zero, define positive definite energies, and minimizing the energy over the probability measures on a compact set gives its equilibrium measure. Measures with finite continuous potentials give no mass to polar sets, and by the continuity principle (theorem 4.1.10 ) every compactly supported measure whose potential is finite almost everywhere with respect to the measure itself is a countable sum of such measures. We also construct a polar Cantor set carrying an atom-free probability measure (proposition 4.1.12 ); this measure reappears in example 13.4.11 . Capacity is defined by an extremal problem for subharmonic functions. For a compact set $K$ in a ball $B$, let $u_ K$ be the upper semicontinuous regularization of the supremum of all nonpositive subharmonic functions on $B$ that are at most $-1$ on $K$. The relative capacity $C_ B(K)$ is the total mass of the Riesz measure of $u_ K$. A compact set is nonpolar if and only if it carries a nonzero measure of finite energy, if and only if its relative capacity is positive (theorem 4.1.17 ). With Choquet's capacitability theorem this extends to arbitrary sets with compact closure in $B$: such a set is polar if and only if its outer capacity vanishes (corollary 4.1.24 ). The main application, theorem 4.1.26 , has two parts. If subharmonic functions $v_ j$ converge to $v$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$, then the inequality $\varlimsup _ jv_ j\leq v$ of Hartogs' lemma (theorem 3.4.20 ) is an equality outside a polar set. Moreover, the upper envelope of a family of subharmonic functions that is locally uniformly bounded above agrees with its upper semicontinuous regularization outside a polar set, which sharpens theorem 3.4.23 . The chapter closes with the Dirichlet energy of Green potentials and the quasi-continuity of subharmonic functions. Throughout this chapter $d\geq 2$; in dimension one the empty set is the only polar set (subsection 3.4.25 ). Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in subsection 25.1.4 .

title: 4.1.1 Kernel energies and equilibrium measures
text:

Its discriminant is therefore nonpositive, which is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $I(\sigma ,	au )^2\leq I(\sigma )I(	au )$. $\square$

Then there is a unique probability measure $\mu _ K$ on $K$ of minimal energy, the equilibrium measure of $K$. Put $V(K)=I(\mu _ K)$, and $V_ D(K)=I_ D(\mu _ K)$ when $d=2$. title: 4.1.8 Continuous potentials and polar sets

To relate energy to polarity we need measures whose fundamental potentials $E_ d*\mu $, or equivalently whose potentials $U^\mu $, are finite and continuous. We show that such measures are plentiful: every compactly supported measure whose potential is finite almost everywhere with respect to the measure itself is a countable sum of them. We begin with a version of Lusin's theorem. Lemma 4.1.9 . 468BD94D4D83 Let $\mu $ be a finite Radon measure on $\mathbb R^ d$, and let $f$ be a Borel function with values in $[-\infty ,\infty ]$ that is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere. Then for every $\varepsilon >0$ there is a compact set $L$ with $\mu (\mathbb R^ d\setminus L)<\varepsilon $ such that $f$ is finite on $L$ and the restriction $f|_ L$ is continuous. Proof. The sets $\{ |f|>N\} $ decrease to the $\mu $-null set $\{ |f|=\infty \} $ as $N	o \infty $, and $\mu $ is finite, so we can choose $N$ with $\mu (\{ |f|>N\} )<\varepsilon /3$. The truncation $f_ N=\max \{ -N,\min \{ f,N\} \} $ is bounded, hence belongs to $L^1(\mu )$. By proposition 2.3.5 there are continuous functions $g_ j$, $j\geq 1$, with $\int |g_ j-f_ N|\, \mathrm d\mu <\varepsilon 2^{-2j}/3$. By Chebyshev's inequality, the set $E_ j=\{ |g_ j-f_ N|>2^{-j}\} $ satisfies $\mu (E_ j)<\varepsilon 2^{-j}/3$, so $\mu ( igcup _ jE_ j)<\varepsilon /3$. On the Borel set $F=\mathbb R^ d\setminus (\{ |f|>N\} \cup  igcup _ jE_ j)$ we have $f=f_ N$ and $|g_ j-f|\leq 2^{-j}$ for every $j$, so $g_ j	o f$ uniformly on $F$. Since $\mu (\mathbb R^ d\setminus F)<2\varepsilon /3$, inner regularity gives a compact set $L\subset F$ with $\mu (F\setminus L)<\varepsilon /3$. Then $\mu (\mathbb R^ d\setminus L)<\varepsilon $, and $f|_ L$ is finite and continuous as a uniform limit of continuous functions. $\square$ Theorem 4.1.10 . 872A6887585B Let $K\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be compact, let $\mu $ be a finite positive measure on $\mathbb R^ d$ with $\operatorname{Supp}\mu \subset K$, and put $p=E_ d*\mu $. Indeed, if $\psi $ is a nontrivial subharmonic function on a connected open set $V$, as in definition 3.4.26 , then its restriction to every ball contained in $V$ is nontrivial, because $\psi $ is locally integrable on $V$ (proposition 3.4.8 ). The next result shows that a bounded polar set lies in the pole set of a single potential. Proposition 4.1.11 . 64A94A9EE9E3 If $A\subset \mathbb R^ d$ is polar and has compact closure, there is a finite positive measure $

By definition 3.4.26 , after shrinking the neighborhood as explained above, there are an open ball $V\subset W$ centered at $a$ and a nontrivial function $\psi \in \mathrm{SH}(V)$ with $A\cap V\subset \{ \psi =-\infty \} $; by proposition 3.4.8 , $\psi $ is locally integrable. Choose an open ball $B_ a$ centered at $a$ with $\overline{B_ a}\subset V$, and a cutoff $\eta \in C_ c^\infty (V)$ with $0\leq \eta \leq 1$ and $\eta =1$ near $\overline{B_ a}$. By the Riesz decomposition (theorem 3.4.14 ), $\psi =E_ d*(\eta \mu _\psi )+h$ on $B_ a$, where $\mu _\psi $ is the Riesz measure of $\psi $ and $h$ is harmonic, hence finite; therefore $E_ d*(\eta \mu _\psi )=-\infty $ on $A\cap B_ a$. The measure $\eta \mu _\psi $ is finite, positive and supported in $\overline W$. Since $\mathbb R^ d$ has a countable base, countably many of the balls $B_ a$ cover $A$. Let $

The next proposition constructs a polar Cantor set carrying an atom-free probability measure whose fundamental potential equals $-\infty $ at every point of the set. Proposition 4.1.12 . EBEA4A14BCD2 There are a compact Cantor set $K\subset [0,1/10]\subset \mathbb C$ and an atom-free probability measure $\mu $ supported on $K$ such that \[  p(z)=\int _ K\log |z-a|^2\, \mathrm d\mu (a)  \] is locally integrable and subharmonic on $\mathbb C$, finite and harmonic on $\mathbb C\setminus K$, and equal to $-\infty $ at every point of $K$. In particular, $K$ is polar and $\mu $ has infinite logarithmic energy. Proof. The set. Put $a_ j=\mathrm e^{-4^ j}$ for $j\geq 1$, and let $K$ be the set of all sums $\sum _{j\geq 1}\varepsilon _ ja_ j$ with $\varepsilon _ j\in \{ 0,1\} $. Since $a_{j+1}/a_ j=\mathrm e^{-3\cdot 4^ j}\leq \mathrm e^{-12}<1/2$, the tails $R_ k=\sum _{j>k}a_ j$ satisfy \[  R_ k\leq a_{k+1}\sum _{i\geq 0}2^{-i}=2a_{k+1}\quad (k\geq 0),\qquad 2a_{k+1}<a_ k\quad (k\geq 1).  \] In particular $K\subset [0,R_0]\subset [0,2\mathrm e^{-4}]\subset [0,1/10]$. Let $\mathcal S=\prod _{j\geq 1}\{ 0,1\} $ carry the product topology, and let $c\colon \mathcal S	o \mathbb R$ be the coding map $c(\varepsilon )=\sum _ j\varepsilon _ ja_ j$. If $\varepsilon $ and $\varepsilon '$ agree in their first $k$ digits, then $|c(\varepsilon )-c(\varepsilon ')|\leq R_ k$; hence $c$ is continuous, and $K=c(\mathcal S)$ is compact by lemma 2.7.2 . If $\varepsilon $ and $\varepsilon '$ first differ at the $k$-th digit, say $\varepsilon _ k=1$ and $\varepsilon '_ k=0$, then $c(\varepsilon )-c(\varepsilon ')\geq a_ k-R_ k>0$; hence $c$ is injective. For a word $\sigma \in \{ 0,1\} ^ k$, let $K_\sigma $ be the image of the sequences beginning with $\sigma $. The $2^ k$ sets $K_\sigma $ are compact, pairwise disjoint by injectivity, cover $K$, and have diameter at most $R_ k$. Consequently each $K_\sigma $ is open and closed in $K$, and two distinct points of $K$ lie in different sets $K_\sigma $ once $k$ is large; thus $K$ is totally disconnected. Changing the $k$-th digit of $\varepsilon $ produces a point of $K$ different from $c(\varepsilon )$ at distance $a_ k$, so $K$ has no isolated points. Hence $K$ is a Cantor set: a nonempty compact metric space that is totally disconnected and has no isolated points. The measure. For $t\in [0,1)$ let $\varepsilon _ j(t)$ be its binary digits, using the terminating expansion at dyadic rationals, and put $\Phi (t)=\sum _ j\varepsilon _ j(t)a_ j$. It is a probability measure carried by the compact set $K$, and it is a Radon measure by proposition 2.2.2 . For $\sigma \in \{ 0,1\} ^ k$, injectivity of $c$ shows that $\Phi (t)\in K_\sigma $ if and only if the first $k$ binary digits of $t$ form the word $\sigma $, and this happens exactly on a dyadic interval of length $2^{-k}$. Since $\log |z-a|^2=4\pi E_2(z-a)$, we have $p=4\pi E_2*\mu $, which is subharmonic and locally integrable on $\mathbb C$ by proposition 3.4.11 . Let $z_0
otin K$ and $\delta = rac12\operatorname {dist}(z_0,K)$. For $|z-z_0|<\delta $ and $a\in K$, the kernel and all its derivatives in $z$ are bounded uniformly, so differentiation under the integral sign shows that $p$ is smooth on $B(z_0,\delta )$ with $\Delta p(z)=\int \Delta _ z\log |z-a|^2\, \mathrm d\mu (a)=0$. Thus $p$ is finite and harmonic on $\mathbb C\setminus K$. Polarity. Let $x\in K$ and $k\geq 1$, and let $K_\sigma $, with $\sigma $ of length $k$, be the piece containing $x$. Since $\operatorname {diam}K\leq R_0<1$, every term $\log |x-a|^2$ with $a\in K$ is nonpositive, and for $a\in K_\sigma $ we have $|x-a|\leq R_ k\leq 2a_{k+1}$. Consequently \[  p(x)\leq \int _{K_\sigma }\log |x-a|^2\, \mathrm d\mu (a)\leq \mu (K_\sigma )\log  igl (4a_{k+1}^2 igr ) =2^{-k} igl (\log 4-2\cdot 4^{k+1} igr ).  \] The right side tends to $-\infty $ as $k	o \infty $, so $p(x)=-\infty $. Since $p$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb C$ and not identically $-\infty $, the set $K$ is polar. For $D>\operatorname {diam}K$, the logarithmic potential of the probability measure $\mu $ is $U^\mu =(2\pi )^{-1}\log D-p/(4\pi )$, which equals $+\infty $ on $K$. Since $\mu $ is carried by $K$, Tonelli's theorem gives $I_ D(\mu )=\int U^\mu \, \mathrm d\mu =+\infty $. $\square$

title: Lemma 4.1.9
text: Lemma 4.1.9 . 468BD94D4D83 Let $\mu $ be a finite Radon measure on $\mathbb R^ d$, and let $f$ be a Borel function with values in $[-\infty ,\infty ]$ that is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere. Then for every $\varepsilon >0$ there is a compact set $L$ with $\mu (\mathbb R^ d\setminus L)<\varepsilon $ such that $f$ is finite on $L$ and the restriction $f|_ L$ is continuous. Proof. The sets $\{ |f|>N\} $ decrease to the $\mu $-null set $\{ |f|=\infty \} $ as $N\to \infty $, and $\mu $ is finite, so we can choose $N$ with $\mu (\{ |f|>N\} )<\varepsilon /3$. The truncation $f_ N=\max \{ -N,\min \{ f,N\} \} $ is bounded, hence belongs to $L^1(\mu )$. By proposition 2.3.5 there are continuous functions $g_ j$, $j\geq 1$, with $\int |g_ j-f_ N|\, \mathrm d\mu <\varepsilon 2^{-2j}/3$. By Chebyshev's inequality, the set $E_ j=\{ |g_ j-f_ N|>2^{-j}\} $ satisfies $\mu (E_ j)<\varepsilon 2^{-j}/3$, so $\mu (\bigcup _ jE_ j)<\varepsilon /3$. On the Borel set $F=\mathbb R^ d\setminus (\{ |f|>N\} \cup \bigcup _ jE_ j)$ we have $f=f_ N$ and $|g_ j-f|\leq 2^{-j}$ for every $j$, so $g_ j\to f$ uniformly on $F$. Since $\mu (\mathbb R^ d\setminus F)<2\varepsilon /3$, inner regularity gives a compact set $L\subset F$ with $\mu (F\setminus L)<\varepsilon /3$. Then $\mu (\mathbb R^ d\setminus L)<\varepsilon $, and $f|_ L$ is finite and continuous as a uniform limit of continuous functions. $\square$

text:
Theorem 4.1.10 . 872A6887585B Let $K\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be compact, let $\mu $ be a finite positive measure on $\mathbb R^ d$ with $\operatorname{Supp}\mu \subset K$, and put $p=E_ d*\mu $. If $x\in K$ and the restriction $p|_ K$ is continuous at $x$, then $p$ is continuous at $x$ as a function on $\mathbb R^ d$ with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. If $p$ is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere, then $\mu =\sum _ j\mu _ j$, where the $\mu _ j$ are the restrictions of $\mu $ to pairwise disjoint compact sets and every $E_ d*\mu _ j$ is finite and continuous on $\mathbb R^ d$. Assume that $p(x)$ is finite; we must show that $\varliminf _{z	o x}p(z)\geq p(x)$. For $z\in \mathbb R^ d$ choose a point $z'\in K$ closest to $z$. Then $|z'-x|\leq |z'-z|+|z-x|\leq 2|z-x|$, so $z'	o x$ as $z	o x$, and $|z'-y|\leq |z'-z|+|z-y|\leq 2|z-y|$ for every $y\in K$. Consequently, for $y\in K$, \[  E_ d(z-y)\geq 2^{d-2}E_ d(z'-y)\quad (d\geq 3),\qquad E_2(z-y)\geq E_2(z'-y)- rac{\log 2}{2\pi }\quad (d=2).  \] Fix $\delta >0$ and split $p=p'_\delta +p''_\delta $, where $p'_\delta (w)=\int _{B(x,\delta )}E_ d(w-y)\, \mathrm d\mu (y)$ is the near part and $p''_\delta $ the far part. Proposition 4.1.11 . 64A94A9EE9E3 If $A\subset \mathbb R^ d$ is polar and has compact closure, there is a finite positive measure $

title: Proposition 4.1.12
text: Proposition 4.1.12 . EBEA4A14BCD2 There are a compact Cantor set $K\subset [0,1/10]\subset \mathbb C$ and an atom-free probability measure $\mu $ supported on $K$ such that \[  p(z)=\int _ K\log |z-a|^2\, \mathrm d\mu (a)  \] is locally integrable and subharmonic on $\mathbb C$, finite and harmonic on $\mathbb C\setminus K$, and equal to $-\infty $ at every point of $K$. In particular, $K$ is polar and $\mu $ has infinite logarithmic energy. Proof. The set. Put $a_ j=\mathrm e^{-4^ j}$ for $j\geq 1$, and let $K$ be the set of all sums $\sum _{j\geq 1}\varepsilon _ ja_ j$ with $\varepsilon _ j\in \{ 0,1\} $. Since $a_{j+1}/a_ j=\mathrm e^{-3\cdot 4^ j}\leq \mathrm e^{-12}<1/2$, the tails $R_ k=\sum _{j>k}a_ j$ satisfy \[  R_ k\leq a_{k+1}\sum _{i\geq 0}2^{-i}=2a_{k+1}\quad (k\geq 0),\qquad 2a_{k+1}<a_ k\quad (k\geq 1).  \] In particular $K\subset [0,R_0]\subset [0,2\mathrm e^{-4}]\subset [0,1/10]$. Let $\mathcal S=\prod _{j\geq 1}\{ 0,1\} $ carry the product topology, and let $c\colon \mathcal S\to \mathbb R$ be the coding map $c(\varepsilon )=\sum _ j\varepsilon _ ja_ j$. If $\varepsilon $ and $\varepsilon '$ agree in their first $k$ digits, then $|c(\varepsilon )-c(\varepsilon ')|\leq R_ k$; hence $c$ is continuous, and $K=c(\mathcal S)$ is compact by lemma 2.7.2 . If $\varepsilon $ and $\varepsilon '$ first differ at the $k$-th digit, say $\varepsilon _ k=1$ and $\varepsilon '_ k=0$, then $c(\varepsilon )-c(\varepsilon ')\geq a_ k-R_ k>0$; hence $c$ is injective. For a word $\sigma \in \{ 0,1\} ^ k$, let $K_\sigma $ be the image of the sequences beginning with $\sigma $. The $2^ k$ sets $K_\sigma $ are compact, pairwise disjoint by injectivity, cover $K$, and have diameter at most $R_ k$. Consequently each $K_\sigma $ is open and closed in $K$, and two distinct points of $K$ lie in different sets $K_\sigma $ once $k$ is large; thus $K$ is totally disconnected. Changing the $k$-th digit of $\varepsilon $ produces a point of $K$ different from $c(\varepsilon )$ at distance $a_ k$, so $K$ has no isolated points. Hence $K$ is a Cantor set: a nonempty compact metric space that is totally disconnected and has no isolated points. The measure. For $t\in [0,1)$ let $\varepsilon _ j(t)$ be its binary digits, using the terminating expansion at dyadic rationals, and put $\Phi (t)=\sum _ j\varepsilon _ j(t)a_ j$. Each $\varepsilon _ j$ is a Borel step function, so $\Phi $ is Borel as a uniform limit of Borel functions. Let $\mu $ be the image of Lebesgue measure on $[0,1)$ under $\Phi $. It is a probability measure carried by the compact set $K$, and it is a Radon measure by proposition 2.2.2 . For $\sigma \in \{ 0,1\} ^ k$, injectivity of $c$ shows that $\Phi (t)\in K_\sigma $ if and only if the first $k$ binary digits of $t$ form the word $\sigma $, and this happens exactly on a dyadic interval of length $2^{-k}$. Hence $\mu (K_\sigma )=2^{-k}$. Every $x\in K$ lies in one of the sets $K_\sigma $ with $\sigma $ of length $k$, so $\mu (\{ x\} )\leq 2^{-k}$ for every $k$; thus $\mu $ has no atoms. The potential. Since $\log |z-a|^2=4\pi E_2(z-a)$, we have $p=4\pi E_2*\mu $, which is subharmonic and locally integrable on $\mathbb C$ by proposition 3.4.11 . Let $z_0\notin K$ and $\delta =\frac12\operatorname {dist}(z_0,K)$. For $|z-z_0|<\delta $ and $a\in K$, the kernel and all its derivatives in $z$ are bounded uniformly, so differentiation under the integral sign shows that $p$ is smooth on $B(z_0,\delta )$ with $\Delta p(z)=\int \Delta _ z\log |z-a|^2\, \mathrm d\mu (a)=0$. Thus $p$ is finite and harmonic on $\mathbb C\setminus K$. Polarity. Let $x\in K$ and $k\geq 1$, and let $K_\sigma $, with $\sigma $ of length $k$, be the piece containing $x$. Since $\operatorname {diam}K\leq R_0<1$, every term $\log |x-a|^2$ with $a\in K$ is nonpositive, and for $a\in K_\sigma $ we have $|x-a|\leq R_ k\leq 2a_{k+1}$. Consequently \[  p(x)\leq \int _{K_\sigma }\log |x-a|^2\, \mathrm d\mu (a)\leq \mu (K_\sigma )\log \bigl (4a_{k+1}^2\bigr ) =2^{-k}\bigl (\log 4-2\cdot 4^{k+1}\bigr ).  \] The right side tends to $-\infty $ as $k\to \infty $, so $p(x)=-\infty $. Since $p$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb C$ and not identically $-\infty $, the set $K$ is polar. For $D>\operatorname {diam}K$, the logarithmic potential of the probability measure $\mu $ is $U^\mu =(2\pi )^{-1}\log D-p/(4\pi )$, which equals $+\infty $ on $K$. Since $\mu $ is carried by $K$, Tonelli's theorem gives $I_ D(\mu )=\int U^\mu \, \mathrm d\mu =+\infty $. $\square$

title: 4.1.13 Relative extremal functions and capacity
text:
The Newtonian and logarithmic capacities of subsection 4.1.1 , which we call kernel capacities, are defined by minimizing energy over measures. We now define a second capacity by maximizing over subharmonic functions. Its values depend on a surrounding ball, but it is increasing, continuous along decreasing sequences and strongly subadditive (proposition 4.1.18 ). These properties allow us to extend it to arbitrary sets (theorem 4.1.19 ), and we shall show that its null sets are exactly the polar sets. From now on, $B=B(0,R)$ is an open ball centered at the origin; the results hold for every radius $R>0$, and in some proofs we take $R$ large. For a set $A\Subset B$, we say that a function $v$ is admissible for $A$ if $v\in \mathrm{SH}(B)$, $v\leq 0$ on $B$ and $v\leq -1$ on $A$. The relative extremal function of $A$ and its regularization are \[  f_ A=\sup \{ v:v	ext{ is admissible for }A\} ,\qquad u_ A=f_ A^*.  \] The constant $-1$ is admissible, so $-1\leq f_ A\leq u_ A\leq 0$, and $u_ A$ is subharmonic by theorem 3.4.23 . The condition $v\leq -1$ is imposed at every point of $A$, but the regularization $u_ A$ may exceed $-1$ at some points of $A$. For instance, let $A=\{ 0\} $. Since $E_ d$ is a radial function that increases with $|x|$, the function $\varepsilon (E_ d-c_ R)$, where $c_ R$ is the value of $E_ d$ on $\partial B$, is nonpositive on $B$ for every $\varepsilon >0$. It is subharmonic by proposition 3.4.11 and equals $-\infty $ at the origin, so it is admissible for $A$. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we obtain $f_ A=0$ on $B\setminus \{ 0\} $, and therefore $u_ A(0)=0$. Extremal functions will be represented as Green potentials. On a ball, the Green function $G_ B$ of theorem 3.1.34 is given by an explicit formula, from which we read off its symmetry and its smoothness near $\partial B$. Lemma 4.1.14 . D17D3298467B The Green function of $B$ is symmetric: $G_ B(x,y)=G_ B(y,x)$ for $x,y\in B$. For $x,y\in B$ with $y
eq 0$, put $y^*=R^2y/|y|^2$. Then for $d\geq 3$, \[  G_ B(x,y)=\Gamma _ d(x-y)-\left( rac R{|y|}ight)^{d-2}\Gamma _ d(x-y^*),  \] and for $d=2$, \[  G_ B(x,y)= rac1{2\pi }\log  rac{|y|\, |x-y^*|}{R|x-y|}.  \] For $y=0$, $G_ B(x,0)=\Gamma _ d(x)-\Gamma _ d(Re_1)$ if $d\geq 3$ and $G_ B(x,0)=(2\pi )^{-1}\log (R/|x|)$ if $d=2$; here $e_1$ is the first coordinate unit vector. Moreover, for $0<r<R$, these formulas extend the difference $G_ B(x,y)-\Gamma _ d(x-y)$ to a smooth function of $(x,y)$ on the set where $|y|\leq r$ and $|x|<R^2/r$; this range of $x$ contains a neighborhood of $\overline B$. Proof. Fix $y\in B\setminus \{ 0\} $. Since $|y^*|=R^2/|y|>R$, the function $x\mapsto \Gamma _ d(x-y^*)$ is harmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B$. Expanding the square gives B44D46472BE9 4.1.15  egin{equation}  |y|^2|x-y^*|^2=R^4-2R^2x\mathbin {\cdot }y+|x|^2|y|^2, \end{equation} and therefore $|y|^2|x-y^*|^2-R^2|x-y|^2=(R^2-|x|^2)(R^2-|y|^2)$. Each displayed expression, as a function of $x$, is the sum of $\Gamma _ d(x-y)$ and a function harmonic near $\overline B$. By proposition 3.1.13 , it is therefore harmonic on $B\setminus \{ y\} $ and locally integrable on $B$, with distributional Laplacian $-\delta _ y$ on $B$. Moreover, the last identity shows that $|y|\, |x-y^*|>R|x-y|$ on $B$, with equality on $\partial B$. Hence the expression is positive on $B\setminus \{ y\} $ and tends to zero at every point of $\partial B$. The ball is a regular domain by theorem 3.1.29 , and the uniqueness assertion of theorem 3.1.34 identifies the displayed expression with $G_ B(y,x)$ for $x
eq y$. The same argument applies to $y=0$, where the stated expressions differ from $\Gamma _ d(x)$ by constants. Let $Q(x,y)$ denote the right side of ( 4.1.15 ); it is symmetric in $x$ and $y$, and $Q(x,0)=R^4$. The formulas just proved can be written, for all $x,y\in B$ including $y=0$, as \[   egin{aligned}  G_ B(y,x)& =\Gamma _ d(x-y)- rac{R^{d-2}Q(x,y)^{(2-d)/2}}{(d-2)s_{d-1}}& & (d\geq 3),\  G_ B(y,x)& =\Gamma _2(x-y)+ rac1{4\pi }\log  rac{Q(x,y)}{R^2}& & (d=2). \end{aligned}  \] Both right sides are symmetric in $x$ and $y$, so $G_ B(y,x)=G_ B(x,y)$; this also proves the formulas in the order stated. Finally, $Q(x,y)\geq (R^2-|x||y|)^2>0$ when $|y|\leq r$ and $|x|<R^2/r$, so the correction terms $G_ B(x,y)-\Gamma _ d(x-y)$ in the last display are smooth functions of $(x,y)$ there. $\square$ For a finite positive measure $\lambda $ with compact support in $B$, its Green potential is \[  G_ B\lambda (x)=\int G_ B(x,y)\, \mathrm d\lambda (y),\qquad x\in B.  \] Proposition 4.1.16 . 4A7451727417 Let $K\subset B$ be compact. The function $f_ K$ is the supremum of the continuous admissible functions for $K$; it is lower semicontinuous, equals $-1$ on $K$, and equals $u_ K$ on $B\setminus K$. The function $u_ K$ is harmonic on $B\setminus K$ and tends to zero at $\partial B$. Let $\lambda $ be a finite positive measure with compact support in $B$, and put $u=-G_ B\lambda $. Then $u=E_ d*\lambda -H_ B igl ((E_ d*\lambda )|_{\partial B} igr )$ on $B$, where $H_ B$ is the Poisson integral of theorem 3.1.18 ; in particular, $u$ is subharmonic on $B$ with Riesz measure $\lambda $. If $\operatorname{Supp}\lambda \subset B(0,r)$ with $0<r<R$, then the restriction of $u$ to the annulus $r<|x|<R$ extends to a harmonic function on the annulus $r<|x|<R^2/r$ that vanishes on $\partial B$. Moreover, \[  \lambda (B)=\int _{\partial B}\partial _ nu\, \mathrm d S,  \] where $\partial _ n$ is the derivative along the outward unit normal of $\partial B$. If $\lambda '$ is another such measure and $-G_ B\lambda \leq -G_ B\lambda '$ on $B$, then $\lambda (B)\geq \lambda '(B)$. Conversely, if $v$ is a locally integrable subharmonic function on $B$ whose Riesz measure $\lambda $ has compact support in $B$, and if $v(x)	o 0$ as $x$ tends to any point of $\partial B$, then $v=-G_ B\lambda $. The Riesz measure $\lambda _ K=\Delta u_ K$ is a finite positive measure supported on $K$, and $u_ K=-G_ B\lambda _ K$. The number $C_ B(K)=\lambda _ K(K)$ is called the relative capacity of $K$ with respect to $B$; by (2) and (3), $C_ B(K)=\int _{\partial B}\partial _ nu_ K\, \mathrm dS$. Proof. (1) Since $K$ is a compact subset of $B$, there is $c>0$ such that $q(x)=c(|x|^2-R^2)\leq -1$ on $K$. The function $q$ is smooth and subharmonic, since $\Delta q=2dc>0$, and it is nonpositive on $B$; hence it is admissible, and $q\leq f_ K\leq u_ K\leq 0$. In particular $f_ K$ and $u_ K$ tend to zero at $\partial B$. We show that $f_ K$ is the supremum of the continuous admissible functions. Let $v$ be admissible. We first extend $\max \{ v,q\} $ to a subharmonic function on $\mathbb R^ d$: put $w=\max \{ v,q\} $ on $B$ and $w=q$ on $\mathbb R^ d\setminus B$. At $\zeta \in \partial B$ we have $w(\zeta )=0$ and $\varlimsup _{x	o \zeta }w(x)\leq 0$, because $v\leq 0$ on $B$ and $q$ is continuous with $q(\zeta )=0$; so $w$ is upper semicontinuous. We verify the comparison principle of theorem 3.4.5 for $w$ on an arbitrary ball $D$. Let $h$ be harmonic on $D$ and continuous on $\overline D$, with $\varlimsup _{D
i x	o \zeta }w(x)\leq h(\zeta )$ for $\zeta \in \partial D$. Since $w\geq q$ and $q$ is continuous, $q\leq h$ on $\partial D$, hence on $D$ by the comparison principle for $q$; in particular $w=q\leq h$ on $D\setminus B$. On the bounded open set $D\cap B$, the function $v-h$ has nonpositive boundary upper limits: at points of $\partial D\cap B$ because $v\leq w$, and at points of $\partial B$ because $\varlimsup v\leq 0=q\leq h$ there. By the comparison principle on bounded open sets (the remark after theorem 3.4.5 ), $v\leq h$ on $D\cap B$. Thus $w\leq h$ on $D$, and the converse part of theorem 3.4.5 shows that $w$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb R^ d$. Since $w\geq q$, it is locally integrable. Its mollifications $w*ho _\varepsilon $ are smooth and satisfy $\Delta (w*ho _\varepsilon )=(\Delta w)*ho _\varepsilon \geq 0$, so they are subharmonic, and they decrease to $w$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ by ( 3.4.13 ). Fix $\delta >0$. On $B$ we have $w*ho _\varepsilon \leq \sup _{B(0,R+\varepsilon )}w\leq c((R+\varepsilon )^2-R^2)$, because $w\leq 0$ on $B$ and $w=q$ outside $B$; hence $w*ho _\varepsilon -\delta \leq 0$ on $B$ for small $\varepsilon $. On $K$ we have $w\leq -1$. Since the continuous functions $w*ho _\varepsilon $ decrease to $w$, the open sets $\{ w*ho _\varepsilon <-1+\delta \} $ increase and cover the compact set $K$, so $w*ho _\varepsilon <-1+\delta $ on $K$ for small $\varepsilon $. For such $\varepsilon $ the function $w*ho _\varepsilon -\delta $ is continuous and admissible, and it is at least $w-\delta \geq v-\delta $. Since $v$ and $\delta $ are arbitrary, $f_ K$ is the supremum of the continuous admissible functions; in particular $f_ K$ is lower semicontinuous. Every admissible function is at most $-1$ on $K$, so $f_ K=-1$ on $K$. Let $D$ be an open ball with $\overline D\subset B\setminus K$; we show that $f_ K=u_ K$ on $D$ and that $u_ K$ is harmonic there. For a continuous admissible function $v$, let $v^ D$ be its harmonic lifting on $D$, which equals the Poisson integral of $v|_{\partial D}$ on $D$ and $v$ elsewhere. As noted in subsection 3.1.23 , the continuous subsolutions defined there are exactly the real-valued continuous subharmonic functions. Hence lemma 3.1.24 shows that $v^ D$ is continuous and subharmonic and that $v^ D\geq v$. It is admissible: $v^ D\leq 0$ because the Poisson integral preserves order, and $v^ D=v$ on $K$. Apply Choquet's lemma (lemma 3.4.22 ) to the family of continuous admissible functions, whose supremum is $f_ K$: there are continuous admissible functions $v_1,v_2,\ldots $ with $(\sup _ jv_ j)^*=u_ K$. The functions $w_ j=\max \{ -1,v_1,\ldots ,v_ j\} $ are continuous, admissible and increasing, and so are the functions $w_ j^ D$. On $D$, the harmonic functions $w_ j^ D$ take values in $[-1,0]$ and increase, so by corollary 3.1.21 they converge locally uniformly to a harmonic function $H$. On the one hand, each $w_ j^ D$ is admissible, so $H\leq f_ K\leq u_ K$ on $D$. On the other hand, $H\geq \sup _ jw_ j$. The upper semicontinuous regularization of $\sup _ jw_ j=\max \{ -1,\sup _ jv_ j\} $ is $\max \{ -1,u_ K\} =u_ K$, so $\sup _ jw_ j=u_ K$ almost everywhere by theorem 3.4.23 . Hence $H=u_ K$ almost everywhere on $D$; since both functions are subharmonic and locally integrable, $H=u_ K$ on $D$ by theorem 3.4.12 . Therefore $f_ K=u_ K=H$ on $D$. As $D$ is arbitrary, $f_ K=u_ K$ on $B\setminus K$, and $u_ K$ is harmonic there. (2) Fix $0<r<R$ with $\operatorname{Supp}\lambda \subset B(0,r)$. By the definition of $G_ B$ in theorem 3.1.34 and the symmetry in lemma 4.1.14 , \[  u(x)=-\int G_ B(y,x)\, \mathrm d\lambda (y)=E_ d*\lambda (x)-\int H_ B igl (E_ d(\cdot -y)|_{\partial B} igr )(x)\, \mathrm d\lambda (y).  \] By Fubini's theorem the last integral is the Poisson integral of the continuous function $\zeta \mapsto E_ d*\lambda (\zeta )$ on $\partial B$, so it is harmonic on $B$. Hence $u$ is subharmonic with Riesz measure $\lambda $, by proposition 3.4.11 . By lemma 4.1.14 , for $y\in \operatorname{Supp}\lambda $ the formula given there for $G_ B(x,y)$ defines a harmonic function of $x$ on the annulus $r<|x|<R^2/r$, which vanishes for $|x|=R$. Since this function is jointly smooth in $(x,y)$, its derivatives in $x$ are bounded uniformly in $y\in \operatorname{Supp}\lambda $ on compact subsets of the annulus. Differentiating under the integral sign, we see that $-\int G_ B(x,y)\, \mathrm d\lambda (y)$ defines a harmonic function on this annulus that extends $u$ across $\partial B$ and vanishes on $\partial B$; we denote the extension again by $u$. Choose $r<r'<R$ and $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (B)$ with $\chi =1$ on a neighborhood of $\overline{B(0,r')}$. Then $\lambda (B)=\int \chi \, \mathrm d\lambda =\int _ Bu\Delta \chi \, \mathrm d x$. The integrand vanishes outside the annulus $r'<|x|<R$, near whose closure $u$ is smooth and harmonic. The divergence identity ( 3.1.4 ) on this annulus, applied to the field $u
abla \chi -\chi 
abla u$, whose divergence there is $u\Delta \chi $, gives \[  \int _ Bu\Delta \chi \, \mathrm d x=\int _{|x|=r'}\partial _ ru\, \mathrm d S,  \] because $\chi $ and its derivatives vanish near $|x|=R$, while $\chi =1$ near $|x|=r'$; here $\partial _ r$ is the radial derivative. Applying the divergence identity on the same annulus to $
abla u$, whose divergence vanishes there, we see that this integral equals $\int _{\partial B}\partial _ nu\, \mathrm dS$. This proves the flux identity. For the comparison of masses, let $u'=-G_ B\lambda '$ be a second function as above with $u\leq u'$ on $B$. text: Lemma 4.1.14 . D17D3298467B The Green function of $B$ is symmetric: $G_ B(x,y)=G_ B(y,x)$ for $x,y\in B$. For $x,y\in B$ with $y\neq 0$, put $y^*=R^2y/|y|^2$. Then for $d\geq 3$, \[  G_ B(x,y)=\Gamma _ d(x-y)-\left(\frac R{|y|}\right)^{d-2}\Gamma _ d(x-y^*),  \] and for $d=2$, \[  G_ B(x,y)=\frac1{2\pi }\log \frac{|y|\, |x-y^*|}{R|x-y|}.  \] For $y=0$, $G_ B(x,0)=\Gamma _ d(x)-\Gamma _ d(Re_1)$ if $d\geq 3$ and $G_ B(x,0)=(2\pi )^{-1}\log (R/|x|)$ if $d=2$; here $e_1$ is the first coordinate unit vector. Moreover, for $0<r<R$, these formulas extend the difference $G_ B(x,y)-\Gamma _ d(x-y)$ to a smooth function of $(x,y)$ on the set where $|y|\leq r$ and $|x|<R^2/r$; this range of $x$ contains a neighborhood of $\overline B$. Proof. Fix $y\in B\setminus \{ 0\} $. Since $|y^*|=R^2/|y|>R$, the function $x\mapsto \Gamma _ d(x-y^*)$ is harmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B$. Expanding the square gives B44D46472BE9 4.1.15 \begin{equation}  |y|^2|x-y^*|^2=R^4-2R^2x\mathbin {\cdot }y+|x|^2|y|^2, \end{equation} and therefore $|y|^2|x-y^*|^2-R^2|x-y|^2=(R^2-|x|^2)(R^2-|y|^2)$. Each displayed expression, as a function of $x$, is the sum of $\Gamma _ d(x-y)$ and a function harmonic near $\overline B$. By proposition 3.1.13 , it is therefore harmonic on $B\setminus \{ y\} $ and locally integrable on $B$, with distributional Laplacian $-\delta _ y$ on $B$. Moreover, the last identity shows that $|y|\, |x-y^*|>R|x-y|$ on $B$, with equality on $\partial B$. Hence the expression is positive on $B\setminus \{ y\} $ and tends to zero at every point of $\partial B$. The ball is a regular domain by theorem 3.1.29 , and the uniqueness assertion of theorem 3.1.34 identifies the displayed expression with $G_ B(y,x)$ for $x\neq y$. The same argument applies to $y=0$, where the stated expressions differ from $\Gamma _ d(x)$ by constants. Let $Q(x,y)$ denote the right side of ( 4.1.15 ); it is symmetric in $x$ and $y$, and $Q(x,0)=R^4$. The formulas just proved can be written, for all $x,y\in B$ including $y=0$, as \[  \begin{aligned}  G_ B(y,x)& =\Gamma _ d(x-y)-\frac{R^{d-2}Q(x,y)^{(2-d)/2}}{(d-2)s_{d-1}}& & (d\geq 3),\\  G_ B(y,x)& =\Gamma _2(x-y)+\frac1{4\pi }\log \frac{Q(x,y)}{R^2}& & (d=2). \end{aligned}  \] Both right sides are symmetric in $x$ and $y$, so $G_ B(y,x)=G_ B(x,y)$; this also proves the formulas in the order stated. Finally, $Q(x,y)\geq (R^2-|x||y|)^2>0$ when $|y|\leq r$ and $|x|<R^2/r$, so the correction terms $G_ B(x,y)-\Gamma _ d(x-y)$ in the last display are smooth functions of $(x,y)$ there. $\square$

title: Proposition 4.1.16
text:
Proposition 4.1.16 . 4A7451727417 Let $K\subset B$ be compact. The function $f_ K$ is the supremum of the continuous admissible functions for $K$; it is lower semicontinuous, equals $-1$ on $K$, and equals $u_ K$ on $B\setminus K$. The function $u_ K$ is harmonic on $B\setminus K$ and tends to zero at $\partial B$. Let $\lambda $ be a finite positive measure with compact support in $B$, and put $u=-G_ B\lambda $. Then $u=E_ d*\lambda -H_ B igl ((E_ d*\lambda )|_{\partial B} igr )$ on $B$, where $H_ B$ is the Poisson integral of theorem 3.1.18 ; in particular, $u$ is subharmonic on $B$ with Riesz measure $\lambda $. If $\operatorname{Supp}\lambda \subset B(0,r)$ with $0<r<R$, then the restriction of $u$ to the annulus $r<|x|<R$ extends to a harmonic function on the annulus $r<|x|<R^2/r$ that vanishes on $\partial B$. Moreover, \[  \lambda (B)=\int _{\partial B}\partial _ nu\, \mathrm d S,  \] where $\partial _ n$ is the derivative along the outward unit normal of $\partial B$. If $\lambda '$ is another such measure and $-G_ B\lambda \leq -G_ B\lambda '$ on $B$, then $\lambda (B)\geq \lambda '(B)$. Conversely, if $v$ is a locally integrable subharmonic function on $B$ whose Riesz measure $\lambda $ has compact support in $B$, and if $v(x)	o 0$ as $x$ tends to any point of $\partial B$, then $v=-G_ B\lambda $. The Riesz measure $\lambda _ K=\Delta u_ K$ is a finite positive measure supported on $K$, and $u_ K=-G_ B\lambda _ K$. The number $C_ B(K)=\lambda _ K(K)$ is called the relative capacity of $K$ with respect to $B$; by (2) and (3), $C_ B(K)=\int _{\partial B}\partial _ nu_ K\, \mathrm dS$. Proof. (1) Since $K$ is a compact subset of $B$, there is $c>0$ such that $q(x)=c(|x|^2-R^2)\leq -1$ on $K$. The function $q$ is smooth and subharmonic, since $\Delta q=2dc>0$, and it is nonpositive on $B$; hence it is admissible, and $q\leq f_ K\leq u_ K\leq 0$. In particular $f_ K$ and $u_ K$ tend to zero at $\partial B$. We show that $f_ K$ is the supremum of the continuous admissible functions. Let $v$ be admissible. We first extend $\max \{ v,q\} $ to a subharmonic function on $\mathbb R^ d$: put $w=\max \{ v,q\} $ on $B$ and $w=q$ on $\mathbb R^ d\setminus B$. At $\zeta \in \partial B$ we have $w(\zeta )=0$ and $\varlimsup _{x	o \zeta }w(x)\leq 0$, because $v\leq 0$ on $B$ and $q$ is continuous with $q(\zeta )=0$; so $w$ is upper semicontinuous. We verify the comparison principle of theorem 3.4.5 for $w$ on an arbitrary ball $D$. Let $h$ be harmonic on $D$ and continuous on $\overline D$, with $\varlimsup _{D
i x	o \zeta }w(x)\leq h(\zeta )$ for $\zeta \in \partial D$. Since $w\geq q$ and $q$ is continuous, $q\leq h$ on $\partial D$, hence on $D$ by the comparison principle for $q$; in particular $w=q\leq h$ on $D\setminus B$. On the bounded open set $D\cap B$, the function $v-h$ has nonpositive boundary upper limits: at points of $\partial D\cap B$ because $v\leq w$, and at points of $\partial B$ because $\varlimsup v\leq 0=q\leq h$ there. By the comparison principle on bounded open sets (the remark after theorem 3.4.5 ), $v\leq h$ on $D\cap B$. Thus $w\leq h$ on $D$, and the converse part of theorem 3.4.5 shows that $w$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb R^ d$. Since $w\geq q$, it is locally integrable. Its mollifications $w*ho _\varepsilon $ are smooth and satisfy $\Delta (w*ho _\varepsilon )=(\Delta w)*ho _\varepsilon \geq 0$, so they are subharmonic, and they decrease to $w$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ by ( 3.4.13 ). Fix $\delta >0$. On $B$ we have $w*ho _\varepsilon \leq \sup _{B(0,R+\varepsilon )}w\leq c((R+\varepsilon )^2-R^2)$, because $w\leq 0$ on $B$ and $w=q$ outside $B$; hence $w*ho _\varepsilon -\delta \leq 0$ on $B$ for small $\varepsilon $. On $K$ we have $w\leq -1$. Since the continuous functions $w*ho _\varepsilon $ decrease to $w$, the open sets $\{ w*ho _\varepsilon <-1+\delta \} $ increase and cover the compact set $K$, so $w*ho _\varepsilon <-1+\delta $ on $K$ for small $\varepsilon $. For such $\varepsilon $ the function $w*ho _\varepsilon -\delta $ is continuous and admissible, and it is at least $w-\delta \geq v-\delta $. Since $v$ and $\delta $ are arbitrary, $f_ K$ is the supremum of the continuous admissible functions; in particular $f_ K$ is lower semicontinuous. Every admissible function is at most $-1$ on $K$, so $f_ K=-1$ on $K$. Let $D$ be an open ball with $\overline D\subset B\setminus K$; we show that $f_ K=u_ K$ on $D$ and that $u_ K$ is harmonic there. For a continuous admissible function $v$, let $v^ D$ be its harmonic lifting on $D$, which equals the Poisson integral of $v|_{\partial D}$ on $D$ and $v$ elsewhere. As noted in subsection 3.1.23 , the continuous subsolutions defined there are exactly the real-valued continuous subharmonic functions. Hence lemma 3.1.24 shows that $v^ D$ is continuous and subharmonic and that $v^ D\geq v$. It is admissible: $v^ D\leq 0$ because the Poisson integral preserves order, and $v^ D=v$ on $K$. Apply Choquet's lemma (lemma 3.4.22 ) to the family of continuous admissible functions, whose supremum is $f_ K$: there are continuous admissible functions $v_1,v_2,\ldots $ with $(\sup _ jv_ j)^*=u_ K$. The functions $w_ j=\max \{ -1,v_1,\ldots ,v_ j\} $ are continuous, admissible and increasing, and so are the functions $w_ j^ D$. On $D$, the harmonic functions $w_ j^ D$ take values in $[-1,0]$ and increase, so by corollary 3.1.21 they converge locally uniformly to a harmonic function $H$. On the one hand, each $w_ j^ D$ is admissible, so $H\leq f_ K\leq u_ K$ on $D$. On the other hand, $H\geq \sup _ jw_ j$. The upper semicontinuous regularization of $\sup _ jw_ j=\max \{ -1,\sup _ jv_ j\} $ is $\max \{ -1,u_ K\} =u_ K$, so $\sup _ jw_ j=u_ K$ almost everywhere by theorem 3.4.23 . Hence $H=u_ K$ almost everywhere on $D$; since both functions are subharmonic and locally integrable, $H=u_ K$ on $D$ by theorem 3.4.12 . Therefore $f_ K=u_ K=H$ on $D$. As $D$ is arbitrary, $f_ K=u_ K$ on $B\setminus K$, and $u_ K$ is harmonic there. (2) Fix $0<r<R$ with $\operatorname{Supp}\lambda \subset B(0,r)$. By the definition of $G_ B$ in theorem 3.1.34 and the symmetry in lemma 4.1.14 , \[  u(x)=-\int G_ B(y,x)\, \mathrm d\lambda (y)=E_ d*\lambda (x)-\int H_ B igl (E_ d(\cdot -y)|_{\partial B} igr )(x)\, \mathrm d\lambda (y).  \] By Fubini's theorem the last integral is the Poisson integral of the continuous function $\zeta \mapsto E_ d*\lambda (\zeta )$ on $\partial B$, so it is harmonic on $B$. Hence $u$ is subharmonic with Riesz measure $\lambda $, by proposition 3.4.11 . By lemma 4.1.14 , for $y\in \operatorname{Supp}\lambda $ the formula given there for $G_ B(x,y)$ defines a harmonic function of $x$ on the annulus $r<|x|<R^2/r$, which vanishes for $|x|=R$. Since this function is jointly smooth in $(x,y)$, its derivatives in $x$ are bounded uniformly in $y\in \operatorname{Supp}\lambda $ on compact subsets of the annulus. Differentiating under the integral sign, we see that $-\int G_ B(x,y)\, \mathrm d\lambda (y)$ defines a harmonic function on this annulus that extends $u$ across $\partial B$ and vanishes on $\partial B$; we denote the extension again by $u$. Choose $r<r'<R$ and $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (B)$ with $\chi =1$ on a neighborhood of $\overline{B(0,r')}$. Then $\lambda (B)=\int \chi \, \mathrm d\lambda =\int _ Bu\Delta \chi \, \mathrm d x$. The integrand vanishes outside the annulus $r'<|x|<R$, near whose closure $u$ is smooth and harmonic. The divergence identity ( 3.1.4 ) on this annulus, applied to the field $u
abla \chi -\chi 
abla u$, whose divergence there is $u\Delta \chi $, gives \[  \int _ Bu\Delta \chi \, \mathrm d x=\int _{|x|=r'}\partial _ ru\, \mathrm d S,  \] because $\chi $ and its derivatives vanish near $|x|=R$, while $\chi =1$ near $|x|=r'$; here $\partial _ r$ is the radial derivative. Applying the divergence identity on the same annulus to $
abla u$, whose divergence vanishes there, we see that this integral equals $\int _{\partial B}\partial _ nu\, \mathrm dS$. This proves the flux identity. For the comparison of masses, let $u'=-G_ B\lambda '$ be a second function as above with $u\leq u'$ on $B$. Then $u-u'\leq 0$ on $B$ and $u-u'=0$ on $\partial B$, and since $u-u'$ is smooth near $\partial B$, its derivative at a point of $\partial B$ along the outward normal is the limit of difference quotients $((u-u')(\zeta -sn)-0)/(-s)\geq 0$ as $s\downarrow 0$. Hence $\partial _ nu\geq \partial _ nu'$ on $\partial B$, and integration gives $\lambda (B)\geq \lambda '(B)$. For the converse, let $v$ and $\lambda $ be as stated, extend $\lambda $ by zero to $\mathbb R^ d$, and put $p=E_ d*\lambda $. By proposition 3.4.11 , $\Delta (v-p)=0$ on $B$ in the sense of distributions, so by theorem 3.1.11 the locally integrable function $v-p$ agrees almost everywhere on $B$ with a harmonic function $h$. Then $p+h$ is a locally integrable subharmonic function on $B$ that agrees with $v$ almost everywhere, hence everywhere by theorem 3.4.12 . The function $p$ is finite and continuous on the neighborhood $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \operatorname{Supp}\lambda $ of $\partial B$: if $x
otin \operatorname{Supp}\lambda $, then $E_ d(w-y)	o E_ d(x-y)$ uniformly in $y\in \operatorname{Supp}\lambda $ as $w	o x$, because $E_ d$ is uniformly continuous on compact subsets of $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \{ 0\} $. As $v$ tends to zero at $\partial B$, the harmonic function $h=v-p$ extends continuously to $\overline B$ with boundary values $-p|_{\partial B}$, and the uniqueness in theorem 3.1.18 gives $h=-H_ B(p|_{\partial B})$. By the formula for $-G_ B\lambda $ proved at the beginning of (2), $v=p-H_ B(p|_{\partial B})=-G_ B\lambda $. (3) By (1), $u_ K$ is harmonic on $B\setminus K$, so its Riesz measure $\lambda _ K$, a positive Radon measure on $B$ by theorem 3.4.12 , is supported on the compact set $K$; in particular it is finite. Moreover $-1\leq u_ K\leq 0$, so $u_ K$ is locally integrable, and $u_ K$ tends to zero at $\partial B$ by (1). The converse in (2) therefore gives $u_ K=-G_ B\lambda _ K$. The flux formula for $C_ B(K)$ is now (2) with $\lambda =\lambda _ K$. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.1.17
text:
Theorem 4.1.17 . 5B4ACD7E054D For a compact set $K\subset \mathbb R^ d$, the following conditions are equivalent: $K$ is not polar; $K$ carries a nonzero positive measure with finite energy; $K$ carries a nonzero positive measure $\mu $ such that $E_ d*\mu $ is finite and continuous on $\mathbb R^ d$. If $K\subset B$, they are also equivalent to $C_ B(K)>0$. Moreover, every finite positive measure with compact support and finite energy gives zero mass to polar sets: every polar set is contained in a Borel set of measure zero. Proof. Conditions (1)–(3) do not involve $B$, so for their equivalence we may enlarge $R$ and assume that $K\subset B$. We first show, for every ball $B=B(0,R)$ containing $K$, that $K$ is polar if and only if $C_ B(K)=0$. Since $u_ K=-G_ B\lambda _ K$ and $C_ B(K)=\lambda _ K(K)$ (proposition 4.1.16 ), we have $C_ B(K)=0$ if and only if $u_ K=0$. Suppose $u_ K=0$. Then $f_ K=0$ almost everywhere by theorem 3.4.23 . Choose a point $x\in B$ with $f_ K(x)=0$ and admissible functions $v_ j$ with $v_ j(x)>-2^{-j}$. The partial sums $\sum _{j\leq N}v_ j$ are subharmonic and decrease with $N$, and their values at $x$ stay above $-1$. By theorem 3.4.9 , the limit $\sum _ jv_ j$ is subharmonic on $B$ and not identically $-\infty $. It equals $-\infty $ on $K$, since every $v_ j$ is at most $-1$ there. Thus $K$ is polar. Conversely, if $K$ is polar, proposition 4.1.11 gives a function $E_ d*
u $, not identically $-\infty $, that equals $-\infty $ on $K$; subtracting a constant, we may assume it is negative on $B$. All its positive multiples are then admissible, so $f_ K=0$ wherever $E_ d*
u >-\infty $, that is, almost everywhere. Hence $u_ K=0$ almost everywhere, and therefore everywhere by theorem 3.4.12 . Suppose that $K$ is not polar, so that $\lambda _ K
eq 0$. By parts (2) and (3) of proposition 4.1.16 , $u_ K=E_ d*\lambda _ K+h$ with the harmonic function $h=-H_ B igl ((E_ d*\lambda _ K)|_{\partial B} igr )$ on $B$. Since $u_ K\geq -1$, it follows that $E_ d*\lambda _ K\geq -1-h>-\infty $ on $K$. Theorem 4.1.10 writes $\lambda _ K$ as a sum of measures with finite continuous potentials, and one of them, $\mu $, is nonzero; so (3) holds. A measure $\mu $ as in (3) has finite energy, because its potential $U^\mu $ is bounded on the compact support of $\mu $; so (3) implies (2). Next, let $\mu $ be a finite positive measure with compact support such that $E_ d*\mu $ is finite and continuous, and let $
u $ be any finite positive measure with compact support. We show that $\mu $ gives measure zero to the Borel set $\{ E_ d*
u =-\infty \} $; by proposition 4.1.11 , every bounded polar set lies in a set of this form. By the reciprocity law ( 4.1.2 ), $\int (E_ d*
u )\, \mathrm d\mu =\int (E_ d*\mu )\, \mathrm d
u $. The right side is finite because $E_ d*\mu $ is continuous, hence so is the left side, and therefore $E_ d*
u >-\infty $ $\mu $-almost everywhere. Now let $\mu $ be a finite positive measure with compact support and finite energy. Then $U^\mu <\infty $ $\mu $-almost everywhere, that is, $E_ d*\mu $ is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere, and theorem 4.1.10 writes $\mu $ as a sum of measures with finite continuous potentials. If $A$ is a bounded polar set and $
u $ is chosen for $A$ as in proposition 4.1.11 , the previous paragraph shows that each of these measures, and hence $\mu $, gives measure zero to the Borel set $\{ E_ d*
u =-\infty \} $, which contains $A$. An arbitrary polar set is a countable union of bounded polar sets, so it is contained in a countable union of Borel sets of $\mu $-measure zero; this proves the final assertion. In particular, a nonzero measure with finite energy cannot be carried by a polar compact set, so (2) implies (1). $\square$

title: Proposition 4.1.18
text: Proposition 4.1.18 . 3CC68CCFAF3A The relative capacity of compact subsets of $B$ has the following properties. It is increasing: $C_ B(K)\leq C_ B(L)$ for compact sets $K\subset L\subset B$. It is continuous along decreasing sequences: if compact sets $K_ j\subset B$ decrease to $K$, then $C_ B(K_ j)\to C_ B(K)$. It is strongly subadditive: for compact sets $K,L\subset B$, \[  C_ B(K\cup L)+C_ B(K\cap L)\leq C_ B(K)+C_ B(L).  \] Proof. If $K\subset L$, every function admissible for $L$ is admissible for $K$, so $u_ L\leq u_ K$. By proposition 4.1.16 , $u_ L=-G_ B\lambda _ L$ and $u_ K=-G_ B\lambda _ K$, and part (2) of that proposition gives $C_ B(L)\geq C_ B(K)$. Let $K_ j$ be compact sets decreasing to $K$. Their extremal functions increase with $j$ and are bounded above by $f_ K$. Let $v$ be admissible for $K$ and $\varepsilon >0$. The function $v+\varepsilon (|x|^2-R^2)$ is less than $-1$ on $K$, so by upper semicontinuity it is less than $-1$ on an open neighborhood $U$ of $K$. The compact sets $K_ j\setminus U$ decrease and have empty intersection, so one of them is empty; thus $K_ j\subset U$ for all large $j$. Hence $v+\varepsilon (|x|^2-R^2)$ is admissible for $K_ j$, and therefore at most $f_{K_ j}$, when $j$ is large. Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and taking the supremum over $v$, we obtain $f_{K_ j}\to f_ K$ pointwise. Since $f_{K_ j}=u_{K_ j}$ and $f_ K=u_ K$ almost everywhere (theorem 3.4.23 ) and all these functions take values in $[-1,0]$, bounded convergence gives $u_{K_ j}\to u_ K$ in $L^1(B)$. Choose $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (B)$ equal to one near $K_1$. Since all the Riesz measures are supported in $K_1$, \[  C_ B(K_ j)=\int \chi \, \mathrm d\lambda _{K_ j}=\int u_{K_ j}\Delta \chi \, \mathrm d x\longrightarrow \int u_ K\Delta \chi \, \mathrm d x=C_ B(K).  \] For strong subadditivity we first prove that $F=f_{K\cup L}+f_{K\cap L}$ satisfies $F\geq f_ K+f_ L$. At a point of $K$ we have $f_{K\cup L}=-1=f_ K$, and $f_{K\cap L}\geq f_ L$ because $K\cap L\subset L$; the case of a point of $L$ is symmetric. So the inequality holds on $K\cup L$. By proposition 4.1.16 , $F$ is harmonic on the open set $U=B\setminus (K\cup L)$, lower semicontinuous on $B$, and tends to zero at $\partial B$. Let $v$ and $w$ be continuous admissible functions for $K$ and $L$. At a boundary point $\zeta $ of $U$ in $B$, which lies in $K\cup L$, we have \[  \begin{aligned}  \varlimsup _{U\ni x\to \zeta }(v+w)(x)& =v(\zeta )+w(\zeta )\leq f_ K(\zeta )+f_ L(\zeta )\\ & \leq F(\zeta )\leq \varliminf _{U\ni x\to \zeta }F(x), \end{aligned}  \] and at points of $\partial B$ the upper limits of $v+w$ are nonpositive while $F$ tends to zero. By proposition 3.4.7 , applied to the subharmonic function $v+w-F$ on the bounded open set $U$, we get $v+w\leq F$ on $U$. Taking the supremum over $v$ and $w$, which by proposition 4.1.16 gives $f_ K$ and $f_ L$, proves the inequality on $U$, hence on $B$. Since each $f$ equals the corresponding $u$ almost everywhere, we obtain $u_{K\cup L}+u_{K\cap L}\geq u_ K+u_ L$ almost everywhere; taking ball averages and letting the radius tend to zero, ( 3.4.13 ) gives this inequality everywhere. The two sides are the negatives of the Green potentials of $\lambda _{K\cup L}+\lambda _{K\cap L}$ and of $\lambda _ K+\lambda _ L$, so part (2) of proposition 4.1.16 gives the asserted inequality of masses. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.1.19
text:
Theorem 4.1.19 . AEE550586C10 The outer relative capacity has the following properties. $C_ B^*(K)=C_ B(K)$ for every compact set $K\subset B$. It is increasing and countably subadditive: $C_ B^*( igcup _ jA_ j)\leq \sum _ jC_ B^*(A_ j)$ whenever $ igcup _ jA_ j\Subset B$. If $A_1\subset A_2\subset \cdots $ and $A= igcup _ jA_ j\Subset B$, then $C_ B^*(A_ j)	o C_ B^*(A)$. If $C_ B^*(A)=0$, then $A$ is polar. Proof. (1) Let $K\subset B$ be compact; we may assume that $K
eq \varnothing $, since $C_ B^*(\varnothing )=0=C_ B(\varnothing )$. For $0<\delta <\operatorname {dist}(K,\mathbb R^ d\setminus B)$, the compact sets $K_ j=\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)\leq \delta /j\} $ are neighborhoods of $K$ in $B$ that decrease to $K$; let $O_ j$ be their interiors. Every open set containing $K$ has capacity at least $C_ B(K)$, so by proposition 4.1.18 \[  C_ B(K)\leq C_ B^*(K)\leq C_ B(O_ j)\leq C_ B(K_ j)\longrightarrow C_ B(K).  \] Strong subadditivity. Parts (2) and (3) rest on two inequalities for $C_ B^*$, the first of which is $C_ B^*(A\cup A')+C_ B^*(A\cap A')\leq C_ B^*(A)+C_ B^*(A')$ for $A,A'\Subset B$. Consider first open sets $O,O'\Subset B$, and let $K\subset O\cup O'$ and $L\subset O\cap O'$ be compact. Cover $K$ by finitely many closed balls, each contained in $O$ or in $O'$, and let $K'$ and $K''$ be the intersections of $K$ with the union of those contained in $O$ and in $O'$, respectively. Then $K'\cup L\subset O$ and $K''\cup L\subset O'$ are compact, their union contains $K$ and their intersection contains $L$. By monotonicity and proposition 4.1.18 , \[   egin{aligned}  C_ B(K)+C_ B(L)& \leq C_ B igl ((K'\cup L)\cup (K''\cup L) igr )+C_ B igl ((K'\cup L)\cap (K''\cup L) igr )\ & \leq C_ B(K'\cup L)+C_ B(K''\cup L)\leq C_ B(O)+C_ B(O'). \end{aligned}  \] Taking the supremum over $K$ and $L$ proves the inequality for open sets. For arbitrary $A,A'\Subset B$, apply it to open sets $O\supset A$ and $O'\supset A'$ with compact closures in $B$, and take the infimum. An excess inequality. Let $A_ j\subset E_ j$ be sets with $E_1\cup E_2\Subset B$. All the capacities involved are finite. Strong subadditivity applied to $E_1$ and $A_1\cup E_2$, and to $A_1\cup A_2$ and $E_2$, gives \[   egin{aligned}  C_ B^*(E_1\cup E_2)+C_ B^*(A_1)& \leq C_ B^*(E_1)+C_ B^*(A_1\cup E_2),\  C_ B^*(A_1\cup E_2)+C_ B^*(A_2)& \leq C_ B^*(A_1\cup A_2)+C_ B^*(E_2), \end{aligned}  \] where we have used monotonicity to bound the capacities of the intersections from below. Adding these inequalities and cancelling $C_ B^*(A_1\cup E_2)$ gives the case $N=2$ of 0A0CA0153B81 4.1.20  egin{equation}  C_ B^*\left( igcup _{j=1}^ NE_ jight)-C_ B^*\left( igcup _{j=1}^ NA_ jight) \leq \sum _{j=1}^ N igl (C_ B^*(E_ j)-C_ B^*(A_ j) igr ), \end{equation} valid whenever $A_ j\subset E_ j$ and $ igcup _ jE_ j\Subset B$. Induction on $N$, applied to the pairs $ igcup _{j<N}A_ j\subset  igcup _{j<N}E_ j$ and $A_ N\subset E_ N$, proves ( 4.1.20 ) in general. (2) and (3). If $O_ j$ are open sets increasing to an open set $O\Subset B$, every compact subset of $O$ lies in some $O_ j$, so $C_ B(O_ j)	o C_ B(O)$. Now let $A_ j$ be arbitrary sets with $A= igcup _ jA_ j\Subset B$, fix an open set $W$ with $\overline A\subset W\Subset B$, and let $\varepsilon >0$. Intersecting almost optimal open sets in the definition of $C_ B^*(A_ j)$ with $W$, we find open sets $E_ j$ with $A_ j\subset E_ j\subset W$ and $C_ B(E_ j)<C_ B^*(A_ j)+\varepsilon 2^{-j}$. By ( 4.1.20 ) and the result for open sets, \[  C_ B^*\left( igcup _ j A_ jight)\leq C_ B\left( igcup _ j E_ jight)=\lim _{N	o \infty }C_ B\left( igcup _{j=1}^ NE_ jight) \leq \lim _{N	o \infty }C_ B^*\left( igcup _{j=1}^ N A_ jight)+\varepsilon .  \] Let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. If the $A_ j$ increase, the right side is $\lim _ NC_ B^*(A_ N)\leq C_ B^*(A)$, which proves (3). In general, strong subadditivity gives finite subadditivity, and the displayed inequality extends it to countable subadditivity, which proves (2). (4) Suppose $C_ B^*(A)=0$. We construct subharmonic functions $v_ j$ on $B$ that equal $-1$ on $A$ and whose Riesz measures have mass less than $2^{-j}$. Their sum will be a nontrivial subharmonic function equal to $-\infty $ on $A$. Fix an open set $W$ with $\overline A\subset W\Subset B$, and choose open sets $O_ j$ with $A\subset O_ j\subset W$ and $C_ B(O_ j)<2^{-j}$. Exhaust $O_ j$ by compact sets $L_{j,m}$, increasing in $m$, whose interiors cover $O_ j$. Choose $c>0$ with $q(x)=c(|x|^2-R^2)\leq -1$ on $\overline W$; then $q$ is admissible for every $L_{j,m}$, so $u_{L_{j,m}}\geq q$. The functions $u_{L_{j,m}}$ decrease as $m$ increases, and their limit $v_ j$ is subharmonic by theorem 3.4.9 , lies between $q$ and $0$, and hence tends to zero at $\partial B$. Moreover, $v_ j=-1$ on $O_ j$, since $f_{L_{j,m}}$ and hence $u_{L_{j,m}}$ equal $-1$ on the interior of $L_{j,m}$. The functions $u_{L_{j,m}}$ converge to $v_ j$ in $L^1(B)$ by bounded convergence, so their Riesz measures, which are supported in $\overline W$, converge in the sense of distributions on $B$, and hence vaguely by proposition 2.6.1 , to the Riesz measure $\lambda _ j$ of $v_ j$. By proposition 2.6.2 , applied to the open set $B\setminus \overline W$, the measure $\lambda _ j$ is supported in $\overline W$. Testing against a function in $C_ c^\infty (B)$ equal to one near $\overline W$ gives $\lambda _ j(B)=\lim _ mC_ B(L_{j,m})=C_ B(O_ j)$, since every compact subset of $O_ j$ lies in some $L_{j,m}$. The function $v_ j$ is bounded, hence locally integrable, tends to zero at $\partial B$, and has a Riesz measure with compact support in $B$; by the converse in part (2) of proposition 4.1.16 , $v_ j=-G_ B\lambda _ j$. The measure $
u =\sum _ j\lambda _ j$ is finite, since $\lambda _ j(B)=C_ B(O_ j)<2^{-j}$, and it is supported in $\overline W$. By Tonelli's theorem for the nonnegative kernel $G_ B$, we have $\sum _ jv_ j=-G_ B
u $. By part (2) of proposition 4.1.16 , $-G_ B
u $ is subharmonic on $B$ with Riesz measure $
u $, so it is locally integrable and not identically $-\infty $. Since every $v_ j$ equals $-1$ on $A$, the sum $\sum _ jv_ j$ equals $-\infty $ on $A$. Hence $A$ is polar. $\square$
