title: Example 4.1.21
text:
Example 4.1.21 . FC1E9D9B42F0 Let $0<r<R$ and $K=\overline{B(0,r)}$. The function $x\mapsto G_ B(x,0)$ is radial and decreasing in $|x|$ by lemma 4.1.14 . We claim that $u_ K=f_ K=w$, where \[  w=\max \left\{ -1,- rac{G_ B(\cdot ,0)}{G_ B(re_1,0)}ight\} .  \] The function $w$ equals $-1$ on $K$ and $-G_ B(x,0)/G_ B(re_1,0)$ on the annulus $r<|x|<R$. It is subharmonic, because $-G_ B(\cdot ,0)/G_ B(re_1,0)$ is a positive multiple of $E_ d$ plus a constant on $B$, and it is nonpositive; hence it is admissible and $w\leq f_ K$. Conversely, let $v$ be admissible. On the annulus, $w$ is harmonic and continuous up to the boundary, with boundary values $-1$ on $|x|=r$ and $0$ on $|x|=R$. Since $v\leq -1$ on the inner sphere and $v\leq 0$ on $B$, upper semicontinuity shows that the boundary upper limits of $v$ are at most these values. The comparison principle (theorem 3.4.5 ) on the annulus gives $v\leq w$ there, and $v\leq -1=w$ on $K$. Hence $f_ K=w$, and since $w$ is continuous, $u_ K=w$. Near $\partial B$, $u_ K$ is $-1/G_ B(re_1,0)$ times $G_ B(\cdot ,0)$, whose outward normal derivative on $\partial B$ is $-(s_{d-1}R^{d-1})^{-1}$. Therefore the flux formula of proposition 4.1.16 gives \[  C_ B(\overline{B(0,r)})= rac{1}{G_ B(re_1,0)}=  egin{cases}  2\pi /\log (R/r),& d=2,\  (d-2)s_{d-1}/(r^{2-d}-R^{2-d}),& d\geq 3. \end{cases}  \] These are relative capacities. To compute the kernel capacities of the same ball, let $\sigma _ r$ be the normalized surface measure on the sphere $|x|=r$ and $p=E_ d*\sigma _ r$. If $|x|>r$, then $p(x)$ is the spherical mean over $\partial B(0,r)$ of the function $y\mapsto E_ d(x-y)$, which is harmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline{B(0,r)}$; hence $p(x)=E_ d(x)$ by the mean-value property (theorem 3.1.7 ). Surface measure is invariant under orthogonal transformations (subsection 3.1.1 ), which act transitively on spheres centered at the origin, so $p$ is radial. On the ball $|x|<r$, the function $p$ is harmonic: by proposition 3.4.11 and theorem 3.1.11 it agrees almost everywhere with a harmonic function there, hence everywhere by theorem 3.4.12 . Since $p$ is radial, for $0<|x|<r$ the value $p(x)$ is the spherical mean of $p$ over $\partial B(0,|x|)$, which equals $p(0)$ by the mean-value property; moreover, $p(0)=E_ d(re_1)$ because $E_ d$ is radial. Finally, $p$ is constant on the sphere $|x|=r$, which is the support of $\sigma _ r$, so part (1) of theorem 4.1.10 shows that $p$ is continuous at the points of the sphere. Hence $p=E_ d(re_1)$ on $K$. Consequently the Newtonian potential of $\sigma _ r$ equals $\Gamma _ d(re_1)$ on $K$ and $\Gamma _ d(x)$ for $|x|>r$, and the logarithmic potential with a scale $D>2r$ equals $(2\pi )^{-1}\log (D/r)$ on $K$ and $(2\pi )^{-1}\log (D/|x|)$ for $|x|>r$. In particular $\sigma _ r$ has finite energy, and its potential $U^{\sigma _ r}$ has a constant value $V$ on $K$. Since $\sigma _ r$ is a nonzero measure with finite energy carried by the sphere $|x|=r$, theorem 4.1.17 shows that this sphere is not polar, although it has Lebesgue measure zero: for $0<\varepsilon <r$ it is contained in $B(0,r+\varepsilon )\setminus B(0,r-\varepsilon )$, whose measure $s_{d-1} igl ((r+\varepsilon )^ d-(r-\varepsilon )^ d igr )/d$ tends to zero as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Let $
u $ be a probability measure on $K$ with finite energy. Then $
u -\sigma _ r$ has total mass zero, and its positive and negative parts are dominated by $
u $ and $\sigma _ r$, so they have finite energy because the kernel is nonnegative on $K	imes K$. Moreover, $\int U^{\sigma _ r}\, \mathrm d(
u -\sigma _ r)=V-V=0$. Hence proposition 4.1.5 gives \[  I(
u )=I(\sigma _ r)+2\int U^{\sigma _ r}\, \mathrm d(
u -\sigma _ r)+I(
u -\sigma _ r)\geq I(\sigma _ r).  \] Thus $\sigma _ r$ is the equilibrium measure of $K$, the Newtonian capacity of $K$ is $(d-2)s_{d-1}r^{d-2}$ if $d\geq 3$, and its logarithmic capacity is $r$ if $d=2$. A probability measure on a compact set is also one on every larger compact set, so the kernel capacities are increasing; when $d=2$, we compute both logarithmic capacities with a scale exceeding the diameter of the larger set, as theorem 4.1.7 allows. Letting $r\downarrow 0$, we recover the fact that a point has kernel capacity zero.

title: 4.1.22 Capacitability and exceptional sets
text:
Theorem 4.1.17 characterizes the polar compact sets. To extend this characterization to Borel sets, in particular to the exceptional sets of limits of subharmonic functions, we approximate sets from inside by compact sets. A set $A\Subset B$ is capacitable if \[  C_ B^*(A)=\sup \{ C_ B(K):K\subset A	ext{ compact}\} .  \] Open sets are capacitable by definition, and compact sets by theorem 4.1.19 . So is every set of the form $A= igcup _ jK_ j\Subset B$ with compact sets $K_ j$: the compact sets $K_1\cup \cdots \cup K_ j$ increase to $A$, so part (3) of theorem 4.1.19 gives $C_ B^*(A)=\lim _ jC_ B(K_1\cup \cdots \cup K_ j)$. The exceptional sets $\{ \varlimsup _ jv_ j<v\} $ that we meet below are Borel sets, but a Borel set need not be a countable union of closed sets. For instance, let $0<s<R$ and consider the Borel set $A=\{ te_1:0\leq t\leq s,\  t
otin \mathbb Q\} $, a segment with countably many points removed. Suppose that $A= igcup _ nF_ n$ with closed sets $F_ n$. The closed sets $\{ t\in [0,s]:te_1\in F_ n\} $ and the one-point sets $\{ q\} $ with $q\in \mathbb Q\cap [0,s]$ form a sequence $D_1,D_2,\ldots $ of closed sets covering $[0,s]$, none of which contains an interval of positive length, since the former consist of irrational numbers. Put $J_0=[0,s]$, and choose closed intervals $J_ k\subset J_{k-1}$ of positive length with $J_ k\cap D_ k=\varnothing $: the interior of $J_{k-1}$ contains a point outside $D_ k$, and since $D_ k$ is closed, a short closed interval around this point lies in $J_{k-1}$ and misses $D_ k$. The nested compact intervals $J_ k$ have a common point, which lies in no $D_ k$; this is a contradiction. Choquet's theorem shows that, nevertheless, every Borel set is capacitable. Theorem 4.1.23 . 62C826EB1B48 Let $L\subset B$ be compact. Every Borel set $A\subset L$ is capacitable. More generally, let $X$ be a compact Hausdorff space, $f\colon X	o L$ a continuous map, and $\widetilde A= igcap _{i\geq 1} igcup _{k\geq 1}K_{ik}$ with compact sets $K_{ik}\subset X$; then $f(\widetilde A)$ is capacitable. In particular, every Borel set $A\subset L$ contains an increasing sequence of compact sets whose capacities increase to $C_ B^*(A)$. Proof. Capacitability of $f(\widetilde A)$. Replacing $K_{ik}$ by $K_{i1}\cup \cdots \cup K_{ik}$, we may assume that $K_{ik}$ increases with $k$. Put $A=f(\widetilde A)$ and fix $\varepsilon >0$. We choose integers $h_1,h_2,\ldots $ inductively. Put $\widetilde A_0=\widetilde A$, and suppose $\widetilde A_{p-1}$ has been defined. Since $\widetilde A_{p-1}\subset  igcup _ kK_{pk}$, the sets $\widetilde A_{p-1}\cap K_{ph}$ increase with $h$ and have union $\widetilde A_{p-1}$, so their images under $f$ increase to $f(\widetilde A_{p-1})\subset L$. By part (3) of theorem 4.1.19 , we can choose $h_ p$ such that $\widetilde A_ p=\widetilde A_{p-1}\cap K_{p,h_ p}$ satisfies \[  C_ B^* igl (f(\widetilde A_ p) igr )>C_ B^* igl (f(\widetilde A_{p-1}) igr )-\varepsilon 2^{-p}.  \] Hence $C_ B^*(f(\widetilde A_ p))>C_ B^*(A)-\varepsilon $ for every $p$. The sets $L_ p=K_{1,h_1}\cap \cdots \cap K_{p,h_ p}$ are compact, because compact subsets of the Hausdorff space $X$ are closed; they decrease and contain $\widetilde A_ p$, so the compact sets $f(L_ p)\subset L$ decrease and, by part (1) of theorem 4.1.19 and the monotonicity of $C_ B^*$, satisfy $C_ B(f(L_ p))=C_ B^*(f(L_ p))\geq C_ B^*(f(\widetilde A_ p))>C_ B^*(A)-\varepsilon $. Moreover $ igcap _ pf(L_ p)=f( igcap _ pL_ p)$: if $y\in f(L_ p)$ for every $p$, the sets $f^{-1}(y)\cap L_ p$ form a decreasing sequence of nonempty compact sets, since $f^{-1}(y)$ is closed, and hence have a common point. Since $ igcap _ pL_ p= igcap _ iK_{i,h_ i}\subset \widetilde A$, the compact set $ igcap _ pf(L_ p)$ is contained in $A$, and by proposition 4.1.18 its capacity is $\lim _ pC_ B(f(L_ p))\geq C_ B^*(A)-\varepsilon $. As $\varepsilon $ is arbitrary, $A$ is capacitable. Borel sets. If $L=\varnothing $ there is nothing to prove, so let $L
eq \varnothing $. Call a subset of $L$ analytic if it has the form $f(\widetilde A)$ considered above; this is the notion of descriptive set theory and is unrelated to complex analytic sets. In such a representation we may assume that $X$ is nonempty, since the empty set is the image of the empty subset of a one-point space under a constant map. We may also assume that $X=Y	imes L$ for a nonempty compact Hausdorff space $Y$ and that $f$ is the projection onto $L$. Indeed, put $Y=X$. The map $g\colon X	o Y	imes L$, $g(x)=(x,f(x))$, is continuous and injective, so $g(\widetilde A)= igcap _ i igcup _ kg(K_{ik})$ with compact sets $g(K_{ik})$, and the projection of $g(\widetilde A)$ onto $L$ is $f(\widetilde A)$. Analytic sets are closed under countable intersections and countable unions. To see this, let $A_ j=\pi (\widetilde A_ j)$, $j\geq 1$, be analytic, with $\widetilde A_ j\subset Y_ j	imes L$ as above and $\pi $ denoting projections onto $L$. The space $X=(\prod _ jY_ j)	imes L$ is compact by lemma 2.7.2 and Hausdorff, as a product of Hausdorff spaces. Let $\widehat A_ j\subset X$ be the inverse image of $\widetilde A_ j$ under the continuous map $\pi _ j\colon (y,z)\mapsto (y_ j,z)$. If $\widetilde A_ j= igcap _ i igcup _ kK^{(j)}_{ik}$ with compact sets $K^{(j)}_{ik}\subset Y_ j	imes L$, then $\widehat A_ j= igcap _ i igcup _ k\pi _ j^{-1}(K^{(j)}_{ik})$. Each $K^{(j)}_{ik}$ is closed, being a compact subset of a Hausdorff space, so $\pi _ j^{-1}(K^{(j)}_{ik})$ is a closed and hence compact subset of $X$. Thus each $\widehat A_ j$, and therefore also $ igcap _ j\widehat A_ j$, is a countable intersection of countable unions of compact subsets of $X$. A point $z\in L$ lies in $ igcap _ jA_ j$ if and only if for every $j$ there is $y_ j\in Y_ j$ with $(y_ j,z)\in \widetilde A_ j$, that is, if and only if $(y,z)\in  igcap _ j\widehat A_ j$ for some $y=(y_ j)_ j\in \prod _ jY_ j$. Hence the projection of $ igcap _ j\widehat A_ j$ onto $L$ is $ igcap _ jA_ j$, and countable intersections of analytic sets are analytic. Since every $Y_ i$ is nonempty, the same reasoning shows that the projection of each $\widehat A_ j$ onto $L$ is $A_ j$. For unions, write $\widehat A_ j= igcap _ n igcup _ kH_{jnk}$ with compact $H_{jnk}\subset X$, and consider, in the product of $X$ with the one-point compactification $\{ 1,2,\ldots \} \cup \{ \infty \} $ of the positive integers (a compact Hausdorff space, homeomorphic to $\{ 1/j:j\geq 1\} \cup \{ 0\} \subset \mathbb R$), the set \[   igcap _ n igcup _{j,k} igl (H_{jnk}	imes \{ j\}  igr ).  \] A point $(x,j)$ belongs to it if and only if $j
eq \infty $ and $x\in \widehat A_ j$, so its projection onto $L$ is $ igcup _ jA_ j$. Each $H_{jnk}	imes \{ j\} $ is compact, so countable unions of analytic sets are analytic. Closed subsets of the compact metric space $L$ are compact, hence analytic, and an open set $U\subset L$ is the union of the compact sets $\{ z\in L:\operatorname {dist}(z,L\setminus U)\geq 1/n\} $, hence analytic. The family of sets $E\subset L$ such that both $E$ and $L\setminus E$ are analytic is closed under complements, and under countable unions, because the complement of a countable union is the countable intersection of the complements. It is therefore a $\sigma $-algebra containing all open subsets of $L$, so every Borel subset of $L$ is analytic and hence capacitable. Increasing compact sets. Let $A\subset L$ be Borel. Since $A$ is capacitable, there are compact sets $K_ j\subset A$ with $C_ B(K_ j)	o C_ B^*(A)$. The compact sets $K_1\cup \cdots \cup K_ j\subset A$ increase, and by monotonicity their capacities increase to $C_ B^*(A)$. $\square$ Corollary 4.1.24 . 098882E3CBEB Let $A\Subset B$. Then $A$ is polar if and only if $C_ B^*(A)=0$. A compact set has Newtonian or logarithmic capacity zero if and only if it is polar. Proof. By theorem 4.1.19 , it remains to show that a polar set has outer capacity zero. By proposition 4.1.11 , $A$ is contained in the pole set of a function $E_ d*
u $ with $
u $ finite, positive and compactly supported. Let $N$ be a compact neighborhood of $\overline A$ in $B$. The set $P=N\cap \{ E_ d*
u =-\infty \} $ is Borel, being the intersection of $N$ with the open sets $\{ E_ d*
u <-n\} $, $n\geq 1$. Every compact subset of $P$ is polar and therefore has capacity zero by theorem 4.1.17 . By theorem 4.1.23 , $C_ B^*(P)=0$, and monotonicity gives $C_ B^*(A)=0$. For the kernel capacities, a compact set has capacity zero if and only if it carries no probability measure of finite energy (theorem 4.1.7 ), that is, no nonzero positive measure of finite energy; by theorem 4.1.17 this happens if and only if it is polar. $\square$ The main step towards the polarity of exceptional sets is the following lemma, which tests $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ convergence of subharmonic functions against measures with continuous potentials. Lemma 4.1.25 . 59F83B6EAAB7 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open, and let $v_ j$ and $v$ be locally integrable subharmonic functions on $\Omega $ with $v_ j	o v$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$. If $\sigma $ is a finite positive measure with compact support in $\Omega $ such that $E_ d*\sigma $ is finite and continuous, then \[  \int v_ j\, \mathrm d\sigma \longrightarrow \int v\, \mathrm d\sigma > -\infty , \qquad \varlimsup _ jv_ j=v\quad \sigma 	ext{-almost everywhere}.  \] Proof. Choose a cutoff $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$ with $0\leq \chi \leq 1$ and $\chi =1$ on an open neighborhood $V$ of $\operatorname{Supp}\sigma $, and put $

u +h$ on $V$, with $h_ j$ and $h$ harmonic. We show that $h_ j	o h$ uniformly on compact subsets of $V$. For a test function $\varphi $, Fubini's theorem gives $\int (E_ d*

u _ j$: if $Q\subset V$ is compact and $s>0$ is such that $Q-\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset B(0,s)$, then Tonelli's theorem gives \[  \int _ Q|E_ d*

Moreover, $h_ j	o h$ pointwise on $V$. Indeed, if $x\in V$ and $\varepsilon >0$ is less than the distance from $x$ to $\mathbb R^ d\setminus V$, then $h_ j(x)=(h_ j*ho _\varepsilon )(x)$ and $h(x)=(h*ho _\varepsilon )(x)$ by the last assertion of theorem 3.1.7 , and $(h_ j*ho _\varepsilon )(x)	o (h*ho _\varepsilon )(x)$ by distributional convergence. To upgrade this to uniform convergence, let $Q\subset V$ be compact and $	heta >0$. By equicontinuity, every point of $Q$ has a neighborhood on which each $h_ j$, and also the continuous function $h$, varies by less than $	heta $. Finitely many of these neighborhoods, centered at points $x_1,\ldots ,x_ N$, cover $Q$, and for all large $j$ we have $|h_ j(x_ i)-h(x_ i)|<	heta $ for every $i$; hence $|h_ j-h|<3	heta $ on $Q$. Adding the integrals of $h_ j$, which converge to $\int h\, \mathrm d\sigma $, proves that $\int v_ j\, \mathrm d\sigma 	o \int v\, \mathrm d\sigma >-\infty $. By Hartogs' lemma (theorem 3.4.20 ), $\varlimsup _ jv_ j\leq v$ everywhere, and the $v_ j$ are bounded above on $\operatorname{Supp}\sigma $ by a common constant for large $j$. Reverse Fatou's lemma therefore gives \[  \int \varlimsup _ jv_ j\, \mathrm d\sigma \geq \lim _ j\int v_ j\, \mathrm d\sigma =\int v\, \mathrm d\sigma .  \] Since $v-\varlimsup _ jv_ j\geq 0$ and $\int v\, \mathrm d\sigma $ is finite, it follows that $\varlimsup _ jv_ j=v$ $\sigma $-almost everywhere. $\square$ Theorem 4.1.26 . E54414B74C32 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open. If $v_ j$ and $v$ are locally integrable subharmonic functions on $\Omega $ with $v_ j	o v$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, then the set $\{ \varlimsup _ jv_ j<v\} $ is polar. Let $\{ u_ t\} $ be a family of subharmonic functions on $\Omega $ with a common upper bound on every compact subset, and let $F=\sup _ tu_ t$. Then the set $\{ F<F^*\} $, where the supremum differs from its upper semicontinuous regularization, is polar. Proof. (1) Let $N\subset \Omega $ be compact, and take $R$ so large that $N\subset B$. The set $E=\{ x\in N:\varlimsup _ jv_ j(x)<v(x)\} $ is the union, over rational numbers $a<b$ and integers $J\geq 1$, of the Borel sets \[  N\cap \{ v\geq b\} \cap  igcap _{j\geq J}\{ v_ j\leq a\} ,  \] so it is Borel. Suppose some compact subset $S$ of $E$ were not polar. By theorem 4.1.17 , $S$ would carry a nonzero positive measure $\sigma $ with $E_ d*\sigma $ finite and continuous, and lemma 4.1.25 would give $\varlimsup _ jv_ j=v$ $\sigma $-almost everywhere on $S$, which is impossible. Hence every compact subset of $E$ is polar and has capacity zero. By theorem 4.1.23 and corollary 4.1.24 , $E$ is polar. Since countably many compact sets $N$ cover $\Omega $, proposition 4.1.11 completes the proof. (2) If the family is empty, or if all its members are identically $-\infty $ on a component of $\Omega $, then $F=F^*=-\infty $ there. Let $\Omega '$ be a component on which some member $u_{t_0}$ is not identically $-\infty $; by proposition 3.4.8 , $u_{t_0}$ is locally integrable on $\Omega '$. By lemma 3.4.22 , applied on $\Omega '$, there are members $u_{t_1},u_{t_2},\ldots $ of the family with $(\sup _{k\geq 1}u_{t_ k})^*=F^*$ on $\Omega '$. Put $w_ j=\max \{ u_{t_0},\ldots ,u_{t_ j}\} $ and $w=\sup _ jw_ j$. Since $\sup _{k\geq 1}u_{t_ k}\leq w\leq F$, we have $w^*=F^*$ on $\Omega '$, and theorem 3.4.23 , applied to the family $(w_ j)$, shows that $F^*$ is subharmonic on $\Omega '$ and that $w=F^*$ almost everywhere on $\Omega '$. We show next that $w_ j	o F^*$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega ')$. As $u_{t_0}\leq w_ j\leq F^*$, the functions $w_ j$ and $F^*$ are locally integrable on $\Omega '$. If $Q\subset \Omega '$ is compact and $M$ is a common upper bound of the $w_ j$ on $Q$, then $0\leq M-w_ j\leq M-u_{t_0}$ on $Q$ and $M-w_ j$ decreases to $M-w$, so dominated convergence gives $w_ j	o w=F^*$ in $L^1(Q)$. Since $\varlimsup _ jw_ j=w$, part (1) shows that $\{ w<F^*\} \cap \Omega '$ is polar, and $\{ F<F^*\} \cap \Omega '$ is contained in it because $w\leq F$. The components of $\Omega $ are pairwise disjoint nonempty open sets, hence of positive Lebesgue measure, so there are at most countably many of them (lemma 2.2.5 ), and the union over them is polar by proposition 4.1.11 . $\square$ Capacitability also gives Frostman's description of the potential of the equilibrium measure. Proposition 4.1.27 . CA3187A3AD4F Let $K$ be a compact set carrying a probability measure of finite energy, and let $\mu _ K$ be its equilibrium measure (theorem 4.1.7 ). When $d=2$, $U^{\mu _ K}$ and $V(K)$ stand for the potential and the minimal energy with respect to a fixed scale $D>\operatorname {diam}K$. Then $U^{\mu _ K}\geq V(K)$ on $K$ outside a polar set, $U^{\mu _ K}=V(K)$ almost everywhere with respect to $\mu _ K$, and $U^{\mu _ K}\leq V(K)$ on all of $\mathbb R^ d$. Proof. Take $R$ so large that $K\subset B$. Let $\varepsilon >0$, and consider the set $E_\varepsilon =\{ x\in K:U^{\mu _ K}(x)<V(K)-\varepsilon \} $, which is Borel since $U^{\mu _ K}$ is lower semicontinuous. If $C_ B^*(E_\varepsilon )>0$, then by theorem 4.1.23 $E_\varepsilon $ contains a compact set of positive capacity, which is not polar by theorem 4.1.17 ; that theorem provides a probability measure $
u $ on this compact set with finite continuous potential, hence with finite energy. Then $I(\mu _ K,
u )=\int U^{\mu _ K}\, \mathrm d
u \leq V(K)-\varepsilon $, contradicting theorem 4.1.7 . Thus $C_ B^*(E_\varepsilon )=0$ for every $\varepsilon >0$, and countable subadditivity (theorem 4.1.19 ) and corollary 4.1.24 show that $\{ x\in K:U^{\mu _ K}(x)<V(K)\} $ is polar. The finite-energy measure $\mu _ K$ gives zero mass to this set (theorem 4.1.17 ), so $U^{\mu _ K}\geq V(K)$ $\mu _ K$-almost everywhere. Since $\int U^{\mu _ K}\, \mathrm d\mu _ K=V(K)$, it follows that $U^{\mu _ K}=V(K)$ $\mu _ K$-almost everywhere. Let $x\in \operatorname{Supp}\mu _ K$. Every neighborhood of $x$ has positive $\mu _ K$-measure and therefore contains points where $U^{\mu _ K}=V(K)$; by lower semicontinuity, $U^{\mu _ K}(x)\leq V(K)$. To extend this bound to $\mathbb R^ d$, decompose $\mu _ K=\sum _ j\mu _ j$ by theorem 4.1.10 , which applies because $E_ d*\mu _ K$ is finite $\mu _ K$-almost everywhere, and let $\pi _ N=\sum _{j\leq N}\mu _ j$. The potential $U^{\pi _ N}$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^ d$ and, by differentiation under the integral sign, harmonic off the compact set $S_ N=\operatorname{Supp}\pi _ N\subset \operatorname{Supp}\mu _ K$. Since the kernel is nonnegative on $K	imes K$, we have $U^{\pi _ N}\leq U^{\mu _ K}\leq V(K)$ on $S_ N$. We claim that $U^{\pi _ N}\leq V(K)$ on $\mathbb R^ d$. If $\pi _ N=0$, this holds because $V(K)\geq 0$, so let $\pi _ N
eq 0$. As $|x|	o \infty $, the Newtonian potential $U^{\pi _ N}(x)$ tends to $0<V(K)$, and the logarithmic potential tends to $-\infty $. Applying the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.10 ) to $U^{\pi _ N}$ on the bounded open sets $B(0,ho )\setminus S_ N$ with $ho $ large, we obtain the claim. Finally, fix $x\in \mathbb R^ d$. The kernel $k(x,\cdot )$ is bounded below on $K$ by a constant $-c_ x$ (with $c_ x=0$ in the Newtonian case), and monotone convergence applied to $k(x,\cdot )+c_ x$ gives $U^{\pi _ N}(x)	o U^{\mu _ K}(x)$. Hence $U^{\mu _ K}(x)\leq V(K)$. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.1.23
text: Theorem 4.1.23 . 62C826EB1B48 Let $L\subset B$ be compact. Every Borel set $A\subset L$ is capacitable. More generally, let $X$ be a compact Hausdorff space, $f\colon X\to L$ a continuous map, and $\widetilde A=\bigcap _{i\geq 1}\bigcup _{k\geq 1}K_{ik}$ with compact sets $K_{ik}\subset X$; then $f(\widetilde A)$ is capacitable. In particular, every Borel set $A\subset L$ contains an increasing sequence of compact sets whose capacities increase to $C_ B^*(A)$. Proof. Capacitability of $f(\widetilde A)$. Replacing $K_{ik}$ by $K_{i1}\cup \cdots \cup K_{ik}$, we may assume that $K_{ik}$ increases with $k$. Put $A=f(\widetilde A)$ and fix $\varepsilon >0$. We choose integers $h_1,h_2,\ldots $ inductively. Put $\widetilde A_0=\widetilde A$, and suppose $\widetilde A_{p-1}$ has been defined. Since $\widetilde A_{p-1}\subset \bigcup _ kK_{pk}$, the sets $\widetilde A_{p-1}\cap K_{ph}$ increase with $h$ and have union $\widetilde A_{p-1}$, so their images under $f$ increase to $f(\widetilde A_{p-1})\subset L$. By part (3) of theorem 4.1.19 , we can choose $h_ p$ such that $\widetilde A_ p=\widetilde A_{p-1}\cap K_{p,h_ p}$ satisfies \[  C_ B^*\bigl (f(\widetilde A_ p)\bigr )>C_ B^*\bigl (f(\widetilde A_{p-1})\bigr )-\varepsilon 2^{-p}.  \] Hence $C_ B^*(f(\widetilde A_ p))>C_ B^*(A)-\varepsilon $ for every $p$. The sets $L_ p=K_{1,h_1}\cap \cdots \cap K_{p,h_ p}$ are compact, because compact subsets of the Hausdorff space $X$ are closed; they decrease and contain $\widetilde A_ p$, so the compact sets $f(L_ p)\subset L$ decrease and, by part (1) of theorem 4.1.19 and the monotonicity of $C_ B^*$, satisfy $C_ B(f(L_ p))=C_ B^*(f(L_ p))\geq C_ B^*(f(\widetilde A_ p))>C_ B^*(A)-\varepsilon $. Moreover $\bigcap _ pf(L_ p)=f(\bigcap _ pL_ p)$: if $y\in f(L_ p)$ for every $p$, the sets $f^{-1}(y)\cap L_ p$ form a decreasing sequence of nonempty compact sets, since $f^{-1}(y)$ is closed, and hence have a common point. Since $\bigcap _ pL_ p=\bigcap _ iK_{i,h_ i}\subset \widetilde A$, the compact set $\bigcap _ pf(L_ p)$ is contained in $A$, and by proposition 4.1.18 its capacity is $\lim _ pC_ B(f(L_ p))\geq C_ B^*(A)-\varepsilon $. As $\varepsilon $ is arbitrary, $A$ is capacitable. Borel sets. If $L=\varnothing $ there is nothing to prove, so let $L\neq \varnothing $. Call a subset of $L$ analytic if it has the form $f(\widetilde A)$ considered above; this is the notion of descriptive set theory and is unrelated to complex analytic sets. In such a representation we may assume that $X$ is nonempty, since the empty set is the image of the empty subset of a one-point space under a constant map. We may also assume that $X=Y\times L$ for a nonempty compact Hausdorff space $Y$ and that $f$ is the projection onto $L$. Indeed, put $Y=X$. The map $g\colon X\to Y\times L$, $g(x)=(x,f(x))$, is continuous and injective, so $g(\widetilde A)=\bigcap _ i\bigcup _ kg(K_{ik})$ with compact sets $g(K_{ik})$, and the projection of $g(\widetilde A)$ onto $L$ is $f(\widetilde A)$. Analytic sets are closed under countable intersections and countable unions. To see this, let $A_ j=\pi (\widetilde A_ j)$, $j\geq 1$, be analytic, with $\widetilde A_ j\subset Y_ j\times L$ as above and $\pi $ denoting projections onto $L$. The space $X=(\prod _ jY_ j)\times L$ is compact by lemma 2.7.2 and Hausdorff, as a product of Hausdorff spaces. Let $\widehat A_ j\subset X$ be the inverse image of $\widetilde A_ j$ under the continuous map $\pi _ j\colon (y,z)\mapsto (y_ j,z)$. If $\widetilde A_ j=\bigcap _ i\bigcup _ kK^{(j)}_{ik}$ with compact sets $K^{(j)}_{ik}\subset Y_ j\times L$, then $\widehat A_ j=\bigcap _ i\bigcup _ k\pi _ j^{-1}(K^{(j)}_{ik})$. Each $K^{(j)}_{ik}$ is closed, being a compact subset of a Hausdorff space, so $\pi _ j^{-1}(K^{(j)}_{ik})$ is a closed and hence compact subset of $X$. Thus each $\widehat A_ j$, and therefore also $\bigcap _ j\widehat A_ j$, is a countable intersection of countable unions of compact subsets of $X$. A point $z\in L$ lies in $\bigcap _ jA_ j$ if and only if for every $j$ there is $y_ j\in Y_ j$ with $(y_ j,z)\in \widetilde A_ j$, that is, if and only if $(y,z)\in \bigcap _ j\widehat A_ j$ for some $y=(y_ j)_ j\in \prod _ jY_ j$. Hence the projection of $\bigcap _ j\widehat A_ j$ onto $L$ is $\bigcap _ jA_ j$, and countable intersections of analytic sets are analytic. Since every $Y_ i$ is nonempty, the same reasoning shows that the projection of each $\widehat A_ j$ onto $L$ is $A_ j$. For unions, write $\widehat A_ j=\bigcap _ n\bigcup _ kH_{jnk}$ with compact $H_{jnk}\subset X$, and consider, in the product of $X$ with the one-point compactification $\{ 1,2,\ldots \} \cup \{ \infty \} $ of the positive integers (a compact Hausdorff space, homeomorphic to $\{ 1/j:j\geq 1\} \cup \{ 0\} \subset \mathbb R$), the set \[  \bigcap _ n\bigcup _{j,k}\bigl (H_{jnk}\times \{ j\} \bigr ).  \] A point $(x,j)$ belongs to it if and only if $j\neq \infty $ and $x\in \widehat A_ j$, so its projection onto $L$ is $\bigcup _ jA_ j$. Each $H_{jnk}\times \{ j\} $ is compact, so countable unions of analytic sets are analytic. Closed subsets of the compact metric space $L$ are compact, hence analytic, and an open set $U\subset L$ is the union of the compact sets $\{ z\in L:\operatorname {dist}(z,L\setminus U)\geq 1/n\} $, hence analytic. The family of sets $E\subset L$ such that both $E$ and $L\setminus E$ are analytic is closed under complements, and under countable unions, because the complement of a countable union is the countable intersection of the complements. It is therefore a $\sigma $-algebra containing all open subsets of $L$, so every Borel subset of $L$ is analytic and hence capacitable. Increasing compact sets. Let $A\subset L$ be Borel. Since $A$ is capacitable, there are compact sets $K_ j\subset A$ with $C_ B(K_ j)\to C_ B^*(A)$. The compact sets $K_1\cup \cdots \cup K_ j\subset A$ increase, and by monotonicity their capacities increase to $C_ B^*(A)$. $\square$

title: Corollary 4.1.24
text:
Corollary 4.1.24 . 098882E3CBEB Let $A\Subset B$. Then $A$ is polar if and only if $C_ B^*(A)=0$. A compact set has Newtonian or logarithmic capacity zero if and only if it is polar. Proof. By theorem 4.1.19 , it remains to show that a polar set has outer capacity zero. By proposition 4.1.11 , $A$ is contained in the pole set of a function $E_ d*
u $ with $
u $ finite, positive and compactly supported. Let $N$ be a compact neighborhood of $\overline A$ in $B$. The set $P=N\cap \{ E_ d*
u =-\infty \} $ is Borel, being the intersection of $N$ with the open sets $\{ E_ d*
u <-n\} $, $n\geq 1$. Every compact subset of $P$ is polar and therefore has capacity zero by theorem 4.1.17 . By theorem 4.1.23 , $C_ B^*(P)=0$, and monotonicity gives $C_ B^*(A)=0$. For the kernel capacities, a compact set has capacity zero if and only if it carries no probability measure of finite energy (theorem 4.1.7 ), that is, no nonzero positive measure of finite energy; by theorem 4.1.17 this happens if and only if it is polar. $\square$

title: Theorem 4.1.26
text: Theorem 4.1.26 . E54414B74C32 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open. If $v_ j$ and $v$ are locally integrable subharmonic functions on $\Omega $ with $v_ j\to v$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, then the set $\{ \varlimsup _ jv_ j<v\} $ is polar. Let $\{ u_ t\} $ be a family of subharmonic functions on $\Omega $ with a common upper bound on every compact subset, and let $F=\sup _ tu_ t$. Then the set $\{ F<F^*\} $, where the supremum differs from its upper semicontinuous regularization, is polar. Proof. (1) Let $N\subset \Omega $ be compact, and take $R$ so large that $N\subset B$. The set $E=\{ x\in N:\varlimsup _ jv_ j(x)<v(x)\} $ is the union, over rational numbers $a<b$ and integers $J\geq 1$, of the Borel sets \[  N\cap \{ v\geq b\} \cap \bigcap _{j\geq J}\{ v_ j\leq a\} ,  \] so it is Borel. Suppose some compact subset $S$ of $E$ were not polar. By theorem 4.1.17 , $S$ would carry a nonzero positive measure $\sigma $ with $E_ d*\sigma $ finite and continuous, and lemma 4.1.25 would give $\varlimsup _ jv_ j=v$ $\sigma $-almost everywhere on $S$, which is impossible. Hence every compact subset of $E$ is polar and has capacity zero. By theorem 4.1.23 and corollary 4.1.24 , $E$ is polar. Since countably many compact sets $N$ cover $\Omega $, proposition 4.1.11 completes the proof. (2) If the family is empty, or if all its members are identically $-\infty $ on a component of $\Omega $, then $F=F^*=-\infty $ there. Let $\Omega '$ be a component on which some member $u_{t_0}$ is not identically $-\infty $; by proposition 3.4.8 , $u_{t_0}$ is locally integrable on $\Omega '$. By lemma 3.4.22 , applied on $\Omega '$, there are members $u_{t_1},u_{t_2},\ldots $ of the family with $(\sup _{k\geq 1}u_{t_ k})^*=F^*$ on $\Omega '$. Put $w_ j=\max \{ u_{t_0},\ldots ,u_{t_ j}\} $ and $w=\sup _ jw_ j$. Since $\sup _{k\geq 1}u_{t_ k}\leq w\leq F$, we have $w^*=F^*$ on $\Omega '$, and theorem 3.4.23 , applied to the family $(w_ j)$, shows that $F^*$ is subharmonic on $\Omega '$ and that $w=F^*$ almost everywhere on $\Omega '$. We show next that $w_ j\to F^*$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega ')$. As $u_{t_0}\leq w_ j\leq F^*$, the functions $w_ j$ and $F^*$ are locally integrable on $\Omega '$. If $Q\subset \Omega '$ is compact and $M$ is a common upper bound of the $w_ j$ on $Q$, then $0\leq M-w_ j\leq M-u_{t_0}$ on $Q$ and $M-w_ j$ decreases to $M-w$, so dominated convergence gives $w_ j\to w=F^*$ in $L^1(Q)$. Since $\varlimsup _ jw_ j=w$, part (1) shows that $\{ w<F^*\} \cap \Omega '$ is polar, and $\{ F<F^*\} \cap \Omega '$ is contained in it because $w\leq F$. The components of $\Omega $ are pairwise disjoint nonempty open sets, hence of positive Lebesgue measure, so there are at most countably many of them (lemma 2.2.5 ), and the union over them is polar by proposition 4.1.11 . $\square$

title: Proposition 4.1.27
text:
Proposition 4.1.27 . CA3187A3AD4F Let $K$ be a compact set carrying a probability measure of finite energy, and let $\mu _ K$ be its equilibrium measure (theorem 4.1.7 ). When $d=2$, $U^{\mu _ K}$ and $V(K)$ stand for the potential and the minimal energy with respect to a fixed scale $D>\operatorname {diam}K$. Then $U^{\mu _ K}\geq V(K)$ on $K$ outside a polar set, $U^{\mu _ K}=V(K)$ almost everywhere with respect to $\mu _ K$, and $U^{\mu _ K}\leq V(K)$ on all of $\mathbb R^ d$. Proof. Take $R$ so large that $K\subset B$. Let $\varepsilon >0$, and consider the set $E_\varepsilon =\{ x\in K:U^{\mu _ K}(x)<V(K)-\varepsilon \} $, which is Borel since $U^{\mu _ K}$ is lower semicontinuous. If $C_ B^*(E_\varepsilon )>0$, then by theorem 4.1.23 $E_\varepsilon $ contains a compact set of positive capacity, which is not polar by theorem 4.1.17 ; that theorem provides a probability measure $
u $ on this compact set with finite continuous potential, hence with finite energy. Then $I(\mu _ K,
u )=\int U^{\mu _ K}\, \mathrm d
u \leq V(K)-\varepsilon $, contradicting theorem 4.1.7 . Thus $C_ B^*(E_\varepsilon )=0$ for every $\varepsilon >0$, and countable subadditivity (theorem 4.1.19 ) and corollary 4.1.24 show that $\{ x\in K:U^{\mu _ K}(x)<V(K)\} $ is polar. The finite-energy measure $\mu _ K$ gives zero mass to this set (theorem 4.1.17 ), so $U^{\mu _ K}\geq V(K)$ $\mu _ K$-almost everywhere. Since $\int U^{\mu _ K}\, \mathrm d\mu _ K=V(K)$, it follows that $U^{\mu _ K}=V(K)$ $\mu _ K$-almost everywhere. Let $x\in \operatorname{Supp}\mu _ K$. Every neighborhood of $x$ has positive $\mu _ K$-measure and therefore contains points where $U^{\mu _ K}=V(K)$; by lower semicontinuity, $U^{\mu _ K}(x)\leq V(K)$. To extend this bound to $\mathbb R^ d$, decompose $\mu _ K=\sum _ j\mu _ j$ by theorem 4.1.10 , which applies because $E_ d*\mu _ K$ is finite $\mu _ K$-almost everywhere, and let $\pi _ N=\sum _{j\leq N}\mu _ j$. The potential $U^{\pi _ N}$ is continuous on $\mathbb R^ d$ and, by differentiation under the integral sign, harmonic off the compact set $S_ N=\operatorname{Supp}\pi _ N\subset \operatorname{Supp}\mu _ K$. Since the kernel is nonnegative on $K	imes K$, we have $U^{\pi _ N}\leq U^{\mu _ K}\leq V(K)$ on $S_ N$. We claim that $U^{\pi _ N}\leq V(K)$ on $\mathbb R^ d$. If $\pi _ N=0$, this holds because $V(K)\geq 0$, so let $\pi _ N
eq 0$. As $|x|	o \infty $, the Newtonian potential $U^{\pi _ N}(x)$ tends to $0<V(K)$, and the logarithmic potential tends to $-\infty $. Applying the maximum principle (proposition 3.1.10 ) to $U^{\pi _ N}$ on the bounded open sets $B(0,ho )\setminus S_ N$ with $ho $ large, we obtain the claim. Finally, fix $x\in \mathbb R^ d$. The kernel $k(x,\cdot )$ is bounded below on $K$ by a constant $-c_ x$ (with $c_ x=0$ in the Newtonian case), and monotone convergence applied to $k(x,\cdot )+c_ x$ gives $U^{\pi _ N}(x)	o U^{\mu _ K}(x)$. Hence $U^{\mu _ K}(x)\leq V(K)$. $\square$

title: 4.1.28 Dirichlet energy and quasi-continuity
text:
The Green energy of a finite positive measure $\mu $ with compact support in $B$ is the integral $\int G_ B\mu \, \mathrm d\mu $ of its Green potential against the measure itself. The mutual Green energy of two such measures $\mu $ and $
u $ is $\iint G_ B(x,y)\, \mathrm d\mu (x)\, \mathrm d
u (y)$. Both lie in $[0,\infty ]$ because $G_ B>0$. When the Green potentials are bounded, these energies are Dirichlet integrals of the potentials. This identity allows us to bound capacities by $L^2$ norms of gradients, and it leads to the quasi-continuity of subharmonic functions. u $. Choose $0<r<R$ with $\operatorname{Supp}\mu \subset B(0,r)$, and put $R'=R^2/r$. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in $L^2(B)$ now gives the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the Green energy. Finally, $u_ K$ satisfies the hypotheses by proposition 4.1.16 , and since $u_ K\geq -1$ and $\lambda _ K$ has total mass $C_ B(K)$, we get $\| 
abla u_ K\| _2^2=-\int u_ K\, \mathrm d\lambda _ K\leq C_ B(K)$. $\square$ Theorem 4.1.30 . 6B0925DDDD3A Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ be an open set with $\overline B\subset \Omega $, and let $u\in \mathrm{SH}(\Omega )$ be not identically $-\infty $ on $B$. Then $u$ is quasi-continuous: for every compact set $L\subset B$ and every $\eta >0$ there is an open set $O\Subset B$ with $C_ B(O)<\eta $ such that the restriction of $u$ to $L\setminus O$ is finite and continuous. Proof. The case of a bounded Green potential. Suppose first that $u$ is a bounded subharmonic function on $B$ that tends to zero at $\partial B$ and whose Riesz measure $\mu $ has compact support in $B$. Let $Q\subset B$ and $u_\varepsilon $ be the compact set and the regularizations given by the last assertion of proposition 4.1.29 . These regularizations are continuous on $\overline B$, decrease to $u$, equal $u$ on $B\setminus Q$, and $
abla u_\varepsilon 	o 
abla u$ in $L^2(B)$. For $\delta >0$, the set $O_{\delta ,\varepsilon }=\{ u_\varepsilon -u>\delta \} $ is open, because $u_\varepsilon -u$ is lower semicontinuous, and it is contained in $Q$, so it has compact closure in $B$. Let $K\subset O_{\delta ,\varepsilon }$ be compact. title: 4.2 Fine topology and balayage
text:
Throughout this chapter $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ d$ is open and $d\geq 2$. Subharmonic functions are upper semicontinuous but in general not continuous. For instance, let $e_1$ be the first coordinate unit vector, and let $u=E_ d*
u $ be the fundamental potential of the probability measure $
u =\sum _{j\geq 1}2^{-j}\delta _{e_1/j}$, which is supported on the compact set $\{ 0\} \cup \{ e_1/j:j\geq 1\} $. By proposition 3.4.11 , $u$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb R^ d$. At each atom we have $u(e_1/j)=-\infty $, because the integrand $E_ d(e_1/j-\cdot )$ is bounded above on the support of $
u $ and equals $-\infty $ at $e_1/j$. On the other hand, $u(0)=\sum _ j2^{-j}E_ d(e_1/j)$ is finite, since $|E_ d(e_1/j)|$ equals $(2\pi )^{-1}\log j$ if $d=2$ and a constant multiple of $j^{d-2}$ if $d\geq 3$. Hence $u$ is not continuous at $0$. By theorem 4.1.30 , the discontinuities of subharmonic functions are nevertheless controlled by capacity: on a compact subset of a ball, a nontrivial subharmonic function becomes continuous once an open set of arbitrarily small capacity has been removed. In this chapter we study two further constructions, the fine topology and balayage, in which the polar sets of section 3.4 , section 4.1 appear as exceptional sets. Both have counterparts in the pluripotential theory of 2. The fine topology is the coarsest topology that contains the Euclidean topology and makes every subharmonic function continuous. In this topology, thinness of a set at a point becomes an ordinary neighborhood condition (proposition 4.2.4 ). Polar sets are finely closed, and the fine topology induces the discrete topology on them (proposition 4.2.6 ). Since there are uncountable compact polar sets, the fine topology is neither Lindelöf nor second countable (example 4.2.8 ). Up to polar sets, however, it has the Lindelöf property: by Choquet's lemma and theorem 4.1.26 , every union of finely open sets agrees with a countable subunion outside a polar set (theorem 4.2.22 ). Consequently finely open sets are measurable, and together with quasi-continuity this shows that they are open up to sets of small capacity (proposition 4.2.23 ). Balayage is based on reduction. For a nonnegative superharmonic function $s$ and a set $A$, the reduction $R_ s^ A$ of $s$ on $A$ is the infimum of all nonnegative superharmonic functions that majorize $s$ on $A$: it keeps the values of $s$ on $A$ and removes as much of $s$ elsewhere as superharmonicity permits. Its lower semicontinuous regularization $\widehat R_ s^ A$ is superharmonic and agrees with $R_ s^ A$ outside a polar set. On a ball, when $A$ is compact and $s$ is the Green potential of a measure $\mu $ whose potential is bounded on $A$ or whose Green energy is finite, $\widehat R_ s^ A$ is the Green potential of a measure $\mu ^ A$ carried by $A$, the balayage of $\mu $ onto $A$. We characterize $\mu ^ A$ by an orthogonality relation for the Green energy, which is a positive definite quadratic form on signed measures of finite energy (proposition 4.2.11 , theorem 4.2.16 , theorem 4.2.18 ), and express the balayage of a Dirac mass through harmonic measure (example 4.2.20 ). Finally, we compare the fine topology of $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ with the topology generated by the functions that are subharmonic on complex lines, which becomes the plurifine topology of section 5.47 ; for $n\geq 2$ the two topologies differ (proposition 4.2.25 ). Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in subsection 25.1.5 .

title: 4.2.1 Fine neighborhoods and thinness
text:
A subharmonic function $u$ is upper semicontinuous, so its sublevel sets $\{ u<a\} $ are open. It is continuous exactly when its superlevel sets $\{ u>a\} $ are open as well. The fine topology is obtained by declaring all these superlevel sets open. Definition 4.2.2 . C067468FA3F0 The classical fine topology on $\Omega $ is the coarsest topology on $\Omega $ that contains the Euclidean topology and makes every subharmonic function $u\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$, on every Euclidean open set $V\subset \Omega $, continuous as a map from $V$ with the induced topology to $[-\infty ,\infty )$. A set is finely open if it is open in this topology, and a fine neighborhood of a point is a neighborhood of it in this topology. Since the sublevel sets of upper semicontinuous functions are Euclidean open, a subbasis of the fine topology consists of the Euclidean open sets and the sets $\{ x\in V:u(x)>a\} $, where $V\subset \Omega $ is Euclidean open, $u\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$ and $a\in \mathbb R$. Restricting finitely many such functions to the intersection of their domains, we see that the sets \[  V\cap \{ u_1>a_1\} \cap \dots \cap \{ u_ m>a_ m\} ,\qquad m\geq 0,\quad u_ i\in \mathrm{SH}(V),\quad a_ i\in \mathbb R,  \] with $V\subset \Omega $ Euclidean open, form a basis of the fine topology. Superharmonic functions, being negatives of subharmonic functions, are finely continuous as well. The fine topology depends on the pointwise values of subharmonic functions. These values are determined by the almost-everywhere class: by theorem 3.4.12 , a locally integrable subharmonic function is the canonical representative ( 3.4.13 ) of its distribution class. A function that merely agrees almost everywhere with a subharmonic function need not be finely continuous. For instance, the indicator function $\mathbf1_{\{ x_0\} }$ of a point $x_0\in \Omega $ agrees almost everywhere with the zero function, but $\{ \mathbf1_{\{ x_0\} }>1/2\} =\{ x_0\} $ is not finely open by proposition 4.2.5 below. In dimension one every subharmonic function is continuous, since on each component interval of its domain it is either identically $-\infty $ or finite, continuous and convex (example 3.4.15 ). The fine topology is then the Euclidean topology, and this is why we assume $d\geq 2$. Definition 4.2.3 . 2B94F86FC31D A set $A\subset \Omega $ is thin at a point $x\in \Omega $ if either $x$ does not belong to the Euclidean closure of $A\setminus \{ x\} $, or there is a subharmonic function $u$ on a Euclidean open neighborhood of $x$ such that \[  u(x)>\varlimsup _{\substack {y	o x\ y\in A\setminus \{ x\} }}u(y).  \] Proposition 4.2.4 . CAAD6BABA60C Let $A\subset \Omega $ and $x\in \Omega $. Then $A$ is thin at $x$ if and only if some fine neighborhood of $x$ does not meet $A\setminus \{ x\} $. Moreover, every fine neighborhood of $x$ contains a set $\{ y\in V:u(y)>a\} $, where $V$ is a Euclidean open neighborhood of $x$, $u\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$, $a\in \mathbb R$ and $u(x)>a$. Proof. Suppose first that $A$ is thin at $x$. If $x$ does not belong to the Euclidean closure of $A\setminus \{ x\} $, some Euclidean neighborhood of $x$ does not meet $A\setminus \{ x\} $. Otherwise let $u$ be a subharmonic function on a Euclidean open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ as in definition 4.2.3 , and choose $a\in \mathbb R$ strictly between the upper limit in that definition and $u(x)$. By the definition of the upper limit, after shrinking $V$ we have $u<a$ on $(A\setminus \{ x\} )\cap V$. Hence $\{ y\in V:u(y)>a\} $ is a fine neighborhood of $x$ that does not meet $A\setminus \{ x\} $. Conversely, let $N$ be a fine neighborhood of $x$. By the description of the basis above, $N$ contains a set \[  N_0=V\cap  igcap _{i=1}^ m\{ u_ i>a_ i\} ,\qquad u_ i\in \mathrm{SH}(V),\quad u_ i(x)>a_ i,  \] where $V$ is a Euclidean open neighborhood of $x$; adding the function $0$ with the constant $-1$ if necessary, we may assume that $m\geq 1$. Each $u_ i(x)$ is finite, since $u_ i(x)>a_ i$. Put $b_ i=u_ i(x)-a_ i>0$ and \[  v=\sum _{i=1}^ m rac{u_ i-u_ i(x)}{b_ i}\in \mathrm{SH}(V).  \] Then $v(x)=0$. We claim that \[  \varlimsup _{\substack {y	o x\ y\in V\setminus N_0}}v(y)\leq -1.  \] There is nothing to prove if $x$ is not an accumulation point of $V\setminus N_0$. Otherwise let $y_ k	o x$ be a sequence in $V\setminus N_0$ along which $v(y_ k)$ converges to the upper limit. For each $k$ some index $i$ satisfies $u_ i(y_ k)\leq a_ i$, that is, $(u_ i(y_ k)-u_ i(x))/b_ i\leq -1$; passing to a subsequence, we may assume that this index $i$ is the same for all $k$. For every other index $j$, upper semicontinuity of $u_ j$ at $x$ gives $\varlimsup _ k(u_ j(y_ k)-u_ j(x))/b_ j\leq 0$. Hence $\lim _ kv(y_ k)\leq -1$, which proves the claim. If $N$ does not meet $A\setminus \{ x\} $, then $(A\setminus \{ x\} )\cap V\subset V\setminus N_0$, and the claim shows that either $x$ is not in the Euclidean closure of $A\setminus \{ x\} $ or the upper limit of $v$ along $A\setminus \{ x\} $ is at most $-1<v(x)$. In both cases $A$ is thin at $x$. For the last assertion, the claim provides a Euclidean open neighborhood $V'\subset V$ of $x$ such that $v<-1/2$ on $V'\setminus N_0$. Thus $\{ y\in V':v(y)>-1/2\} \subset N_0\subset N$, and $v(x)=0>-1/2$. $\square$ Proposition 4.2.5 . 9E787ECDB068 Let $N$ be a fine neighborhood of a point $x\in \Omega $. Then every Euclidean ball centered at $x$ contains a Borel subset of $N$ of positive Lebesgue measure. In particular, the fine topology has no isolated points. Proof. By proposition 4.2.4 , $N$ contains a set $\{ y\in V:u(y)>a\} $ with $u\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$ and $u(x)>a$. It suffices to consider balls $B(x,r)$ with $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset V$. The set $E=\{ y\in B(x,r):u(y)>a\} $ is a Borel subset of $N$, because $u$ is Borel measurable. Let $M$ be a finite upper bound for $u$ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$; then $M\geq u(x)>a$. Since $u\leq M$ on $E$ and $u\leq a$ on $B(x,r)\setminus E$, the ball submean inequality of theorem 3.4.5 gives \[  u(x)\leq  rac{1}{|B(x,r)|}\int _{B(x,r)}u(y)\, \mathrm d y\leq a+(M-a) rac{|E|}{|B(x,r)|}.  \] Hence $|E|\geq |B(x,r)|\, (u(x)-a)/(M-a)>0$. As a singleton has Lebesgue measure zero, it is not a fine neighborhood of its point. $\square$ Proposition 4.2.6 . 498B2C3E2413 Let $A\subset \Omega $ be polar. For every $x\in \Omega $ there is a fine neighborhood $N$ of $x$ such that $N\cap A\subset \{ x\} $. Consequently, $A$ is finely closed, and the topology induced on $A$ by the fine topology is discrete. Proof. We construct a subharmonic function on $\mathbb R^ d$ that is finite at $x$ and equals $-\infty $ on $A\setminus \{ x\} $ near $x$. Fix $x\in \Omega $ and $ho >0$ with $\overline{B(x,ho )}\subset \Omega $. For $k\geq 0$ put $r_ k=2^{-k}ho $, let $S_ k=\{ y:r_{k+1}\leq |y-x|\leq r_ k\} $ be the closed annulus, and let $A_ k=A\cap S_ k$; these sets cover $A\cap \overline{B(x,ho )}\setminus \{ x\} $. Each $A_ k$ is polar and has compact closure, so proposition 4.1.11 provides a finite positive measure $
u _ k'$ of compact support with $E_ d*
u _ k'=-\infty $ on $A_ k$. We restrict it to the open set $U_ k=\{ y:r_{k+2}<|y-x|<2ho \} $, which contains $S_ k$, and put $
u _ k=
u _ k'|_{U_ k}$. For $y\in A_ k$ and $z\in \operatorname{Supp}
u _ k'\setminus U_ k$ we have $|y-z|\geq \operatorname {dist}(S_ k,\mathbb R^ d\setminus U_ k)>0$, so $E_ d(y-z)$ is bounded on this set of pairs and \[  E_ d*
u _ k(y)=E_ d*
u _ k'(y)-\int _{\mathbb R^ d\setminus U_ k}E_ d(y-z)\, \mathrm d
u _ k'(z)=-\infty ,\qquad y\in A_ k.  \] Moreover, $

u _ k(\mathbb R^ d) igr ),  \] where every term on the right is nonpositive. Hence $p(x)$ is finite, and $p=-\infty $ on $A\cap \overline{B(x,ho )}\setminus \{ x\} $, because there one term equals $-\infty $. Since $p$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb R^ d$ (proposition 3.4.11 ), the set \[  N=\{ y\in B(x,ho ):p(y)>p(x)-1\}   \] is a fine neighborhood of $x$, and $N\cap A\subset \{ x\} $. If $x

If $x\in A$, it shows that $\{ x\} $ is relatively open in $A$ for the fine topology. $\square$ Singletons are polar since $d\geq 2$, and countable unions of polar sets are polar by proposition 4.1.11 ; hence every countable set is polar. In particular, if $\Omega 
eq \varnothing $, the set $\Omega \cap \mathbb Q^ d$ is finely closed but Euclidean dense in $\Omega $, so the fine topology is strictly finer than the Euclidean topology. As we show in example 4.2.8 below, the fine topology is not even Lindelöf; this is why the countability theorem of subsection 4.2.21 must allow a polar exceptional set. To produce uncountable compact polar sets in every dimension, we use the following observation: a subharmonic function of some of the variables is subharmonic in all of them. Lemma 4.2.7 . A1CB0D81584C Let $1\leq k<d$, write $x=(z,y)\in \mathbb R^ k	imes \mathbb R^{d-k}$, let $V\subset \mathbb R^ k$ be open, and let $g\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$. Then the function $G(z,y)=g(z)$ is subharmonic on $V	imes \mathbb R^{d-k}$. Proof. The function $G$ is upper semicontinuous, because $\{ G<a\} =\{ g<a\} 	imes \mathbb R^{d-k}$ for every real $a$. Since subharmonicity is a local property, it suffices to show that $G$ is subharmonic on $D	imes \mathbb R^{d-k}$ for every open ball $D=B(z_0,s)\subset \mathbb R^ k$ with $\overline{B(z_0,2s)}\subset V$. If $g$ is identically $-\infty $ on $B(z_0,2s)$, then so is $G$ on $B(z_0,2s)	imes \mathbb R^{d-k}$, and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise $g$ is locally integrable on the ball $B(z_0,2s)$ by proposition 3.4.8 . For $0<\varepsilon <s$, the $k$-dimensional mollification $g_\varepsilon =g*ho _\varepsilon $ is smooth on $D$ and satisfies $\Delta _ zg_\varepsilon =(\Delta g)*ho _\varepsilon \geq 0$ there, by part (1) of theorem 3.4.12 and parts (1) and (3) of proposition 2.5.3 ; moreover, $g_\varepsilon $ decreases to $g$ on $D$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, by ( 3.4.13 ). The function $G_\varepsilon (z,y)=g_\varepsilon (z)$ is smooth on $D	imes \mathbb R^{d-k}$, with $\Delta _ xG_\varepsilon (z,y)=\Delta _ zg_\varepsilon (z)\geq 0$. By ( 3.1.6 ), its sphere means in $\mathbb R^ d$ increase with the radius, and they tend to its value at the center as the radius tends to zero, because $G_\varepsilon $ is continuous. Hence $G_\varepsilon $ satisfies the submean inequality and is subharmonic on $D	imes \mathbb R^{d-k}$. Along the sequence $\varepsilon _ j=s/(j+1)$, the functions $G_{\varepsilon _ j}$ decrease to $G$, which is therefore subharmonic on $D	imes \mathbb R^{d-k}$ by theorem 3.4.9 . $\square$ Example 4.2.8 . 4D234E8193AC Every Euclidean ball in $\mathbb R^ d$ contains an uncountable compact polar set. Consequently, if $\Omega $ is nonempty, the fine topology on $\Omega $ is neither Lindelöf nor second countable. Proof. A similarity $x\mapsto a+tx$ with $t>0$ preserves upper semicontinuity and sphere means, and hence maps polar sets to polar sets. It therefore suffices to find one uncountable compact polar subset of $\mathbb R^ d$. For $d=2$ we take the Cantor set $K$ of proposition 4.1.12 . It is compact and polar, and it is uncountable because it carries an atom-free probability measure. For $d>2$, write $x=(z,y)\in \mathbb R^2	imes \mathbb R^{d-2}$. By lemma 4.2.7 , applied with $k=2$ to the subharmonic function $p$ of proposition 4.1.12 , the function $P(x)=p(z)$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb R^ d$. It is finite when $z
otin K$ and equals $-\infty $ on $K	imes \mathbb R^{d-2}$. Hence $K	imes \{ 0\} $ is an uncountable compact polar subset of $\mathbb R^ d$. Now let $\Omega 
eq \varnothing $, and let $K'\subset \Omega $ be an uncountable compact polar set. By proposition 4.2.6 , $K'$ is finely closed, and its induced fine topology is discrete. A closed subspace $F$ of a Lindelöf space $X$ is Lindelöf: extend the members of an open cover of $F$ to open subsets of $X$, add $X\setminus F$, and pass to a countable subcover. On the other hand, the cover of an uncountable discrete space by its singletons has no countable subcover. Hence the fine topology on $\Omega $ is not Lindelöf. Nor is it second countable, because a second countable space is Lindelöf: given an open cover and a countable basis, choose, for each basis element contained in some member of the cover, one such member; these countably many members cover the space. $\square$

title: Definition 4.2.2
text: Definition 4.2.2 . C067468FA3F0 The classical fine topology on $\Omega $ is the coarsest topology on $\Omega $ that contains the Euclidean topology and makes every subharmonic function $u\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$, on every Euclidean open set $V\subset \Omega $, continuous as a map from $V$ with the induced topology to $[-\infty ,\infty )$. A set is finely open if it is open in this topology, and a fine neighborhood of a point is a neighborhood of it in this topology.

title: Definition 4.2.3
text: Definition 4.2.3 . 2B94F86FC31D A set $A\subset \Omega $ is thin at a point $x\in \Omega $ if either $x$ does not belong to the Euclidean closure of $A\setminus \{ x\} $, or there is a subharmonic function $u$ on a Euclidean open neighborhood of $x$ such that \[  u(x)>\varlimsup _{\substack {y\to x\\ y\in A\setminus \{ x\} }}u(y).  \]

title: Proposition 4.2.4
text: Proposition 4.2.4 . CAAD6BABA60C Let $A\subset \Omega $ and $x\in \Omega $. Then $A$ is thin at $x$ if and only if some fine neighborhood of $x$ does not meet $A\setminus \{ x\} $. Moreover, every fine neighborhood of $x$ contains a set $\{ y\in V:u(y)>a\} $, where $V$ is a Euclidean open neighborhood of $x$, $u\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$, $a\in \mathbb R$ and $u(x)>a$. Proof. Suppose first that $A$ is thin at $x$. If $x$ does not belong to the Euclidean closure of $A\setminus \{ x\} $, some Euclidean neighborhood of $x$ does not meet $A\setminus \{ x\} $. Otherwise let $u$ be a subharmonic function on a Euclidean open neighborhood $V$ of $x$ as in definition 4.2.3 , and choose $a\in \mathbb R$ strictly between the upper limit in that definition and $u(x)$. By the definition of the upper limit, after shrinking $V$ we have $u<a$ on $(A\setminus \{ x\} )\cap V$. Hence $\{ y\in V:u(y)>a\} $ is a fine neighborhood of $x$ that does not meet $A\setminus \{ x\} $. Conversely, let $N$ be a fine neighborhood of $x$. By the description of the basis above, $N$ contains a set \[  N_0=V\cap \bigcap _{i=1}^ m\{ u_ i>a_ i\} ,\qquad u_ i\in \mathrm{SH}(V),\quad u_ i(x)>a_ i,  \] where $V$ is a Euclidean open neighborhood of $x$; adding the function $0$ with the constant $-1$ if necessary, we may assume that $m\geq 1$. Each $u_ i(x)$ is finite, since $u_ i(x)>a_ i$. Put $b_ i=u_ i(x)-a_ i>0$ and \[  v=\sum _{i=1}^ m\frac{u_ i-u_ i(x)}{b_ i}\in \mathrm{SH}(V).  \] Then $v(x)=0$. We claim that \[  \varlimsup _{\substack {y\to x\\ y\in V\setminus N_0}}v(y)\leq -1.  \] There is nothing to prove if $x$ is not an accumulation point of $V\setminus N_0$. Otherwise let $y_ k\to x$ be a sequence in $V\setminus N_0$ along which $v(y_ k)$ converges to the upper limit. For each $k$ some index $i$ satisfies $u_ i(y_ k)\leq a_ i$, that is, $(u_ i(y_ k)-u_ i(x))/b_ i\leq -1$; passing to a subsequence, we may assume that this index $i$ is the same for all $k$. For every other index $j$, upper semicontinuity of $u_ j$ at $x$ gives $\varlimsup _ k(u_ j(y_ k)-u_ j(x))/b_ j\leq 0$. Hence $\lim _ kv(y_ k)\leq -1$, which proves the claim. If $N$ does not meet $A\setminus \{ x\} $, then $(A\setminus \{ x\} )\cap V\subset V\setminus N_0$, and the claim shows that either $x$ is not in the Euclidean closure of $A\setminus \{ x\} $ or the upper limit of $v$ along $A\setminus \{ x\} $ is at most $-1<v(x)$. In both cases $A$ is thin at $x$. For the last assertion, the claim provides a Euclidean open neighborhood $V'\subset V$ of $x$ such that $v<-1/2$ on $V'\setminus N_0$. Thus $\{ y\in V':v(y)>-1/2\} \subset N_0\subset N$, and $v(x)=0>-1/2$. $\square$

title: Proposition 4.2.5
text: Proposition 4.2.5 . 9E787ECDB068 Let $N$ be a fine neighborhood of a point $x\in \Omega $. Then every Euclidean ball centered at $x$ contains a Borel subset of $N$ of positive Lebesgue measure. In particular, the fine topology has no isolated points. Proof. By proposition 4.2.4 , $N$ contains a set $\{ y\in V:u(y)>a\} $ with $u\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$ and $u(x)>a$. It suffices to consider balls $B(x,r)$ with $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset V$. The set $E=\{ y\in B(x,r):u(y)>a\} $ is a Borel subset of $N$, because $u$ is Borel measurable. Let $M$ be a finite upper bound for $u$ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$; then $M\geq u(x)>a$. Since $u\leq M$ on $E$ and $u\leq a$ on $B(x,r)\setminus E$, the ball submean inequality of theorem 3.4.5 gives \[  u(x)\leq \frac{1}{|B(x,r)|}\int _{B(x,r)}u(y)\, \mathrm d y\leq a+(M-a)\frac{|E|}{|B(x,r)|}.  \] Hence $|E|\geq |B(x,r)|\, (u(x)-a)/(M-a)>0$. As a singleton has Lebesgue measure zero, it is not a fine neighborhood of its point. $\square$

title: Lemma 4.2.7
text: Lemma 4.2.7 . A1CB0D81584C Let $1\leq k<d$, write $x=(z,y)\in \mathbb R^ k\times \mathbb R^{d-k}$, let $V\subset \mathbb R^ k$ be open, and let $g\in \mathrm{SH}(V)$. Then the function $G(z,y)=g(z)$ is subharmonic on $V\times \mathbb R^{d-k}$. Proof. The function $G$ is upper semicontinuous, because $\{ G<a\} =\{ g<a\} \times \mathbb R^{d-k}$ for every real $a$. Since subharmonicity is a local property, it suffices to show that $G$ is subharmonic on $D\times \mathbb R^{d-k}$ for every open ball $D=B(z_0,s)\subset \mathbb R^ k$ with $\overline{B(z_0,2s)}\subset V$. If $g$ is identically $-\infty $ on $B(z_0,2s)$, then so is $G$ on $B(z_0,2s)\times \mathbb R^{d-k}$, and there is nothing to prove. Otherwise $g$ is locally integrable on the ball $B(z_0,2s)$ by proposition 3.4.8 . For $0<\varepsilon <s$, the $k$-dimensional mollification $g_\varepsilon =g*\rho _\varepsilon $ is smooth on $D$ and satisfies $\Delta _ zg_\varepsilon =(\Delta g)*\rho _\varepsilon \geq 0$ there, by part (1) of theorem 3.4.12 and parts (1) and (3) of proposition 2.5.3 ; moreover, $g_\varepsilon $ decreases to $g$ on $D$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, by ( 3.4.13 ). The function $G_\varepsilon (z,y)=g_\varepsilon (z)$ is smooth on $D\times \mathbb R^{d-k}$, with $\Delta _ xG_\varepsilon (z,y)=\Delta _ zg_\varepsilon (z)\geq 0$. By ( 3.1.6 ), its sphere means in $\mathbb R^ d$ increase with the radius, and they tend to its value at the center as the radius tends to zero, because $G_\varepsilon $ is continuous. Hence $G_\varepsilon $ satisfies the submean inequality and is subharmonic on $D\times \mathbb R^{d-k}$. Along the sequence $\varepsilon _ j=s/(j+1)$, the functions $G_{\varepsilon _ j}$ decrease to $G$, which is therefore subharmonic on $D\times \mathbb R^{d-k}$ by theorem 3.4.9 . $\square$

title: Example 4.2.8
text: Example 4.2.8 . 4D234E8193AC Every Euclidean ball in $\mathbb R^ d$ contains an uncountable compact polar set. Consequently, if $\Omega $ is nonempty, the fine topology on $\Omega $ is neither Lindelöf nor second countable. Proof. A similarity $x\mapsto a+tx$ with $t>0$ preserves upper semicontinuity and sphere means, and hence maps polar sets to polar sets. It therefore suffices to find one uncountable compact polar subset of $\mathbb R^ d$. For $d=2$ we take the Cantor set $K$ of proposition 4.1.12 . It is compact and polar, and it is uncountable because it carries an atom-free probability measure. For $d>2$, write $x=(z,y)\in \mathbb R^2\times \mathbb R^{d-2}$. By lemma 4.2.7 , applied with $k=2$ to the subharmonic function $p$ of proposition 4.1.12 , the function $P(x)=p(z)$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb R^ d$. It is finite when $z\notin K$ and equals $-\infty $ on $K\times \mathbb R^{d-2}$. Hence $K\times \{ 0\} $ is an uncountable compact polar subset of $\mathbb R^ d$. Now let $\Omega \neq \varnothing $, and let $K'\subset \Omega $ be an uncountable compact polar set. By proposition 4.2.6 , $K'$ is finely closed, and its induced fine topology is discrete. A closed subspace $F$ of a Lindelöf space $X$ is Lindelöf: extend the members of an open cover of $F$ to open subsets of $X$, add $X\setminus F$, and pass to a countable subcover. On the other hand, the cover of an uncountable discrete space by its singletons has no countable subcover. Hence the fine topology on $\Omega $ is not Lindelöf. Nor is it second countable, because a second countable space is Lindelöf: given an open cover and a countable basis, choose, for each basis element contained in some member of the cover, one such member; these countably many members cover the space. $\square$

title: 4.2.9 Green energy and compact reduction
text:
This section prepares balayage: the Green energy is a positive definite quadratic form on signed measures of finite energy (proposition 4.2.11 ), and a regularized reduction on a compact set is the Green potential of a measure carried by that set (theorem 4.2.14 ). Fix an open ball $B\subset \mathbb R^ d$ and let $G_ B$ be its Green function (theorem 3.1.34 ); it is nonnegative and symmetric (lemma 4.1.14 ). The results of section 4.1 about balls are stated for balls centered at the origin; we apply them to $B$ after a translation. In this section and the next, unless signed measures are explicitly mentioned, a measure means a finite positive Borel measure with compact support in $B$. Recall from subsection 4.1.13 that the Green potential of a measure $\mu $ is $G_ B\mu (x)=\int G_ B(x,y)\, \mathrm d\mu (y)$. We denote the mutual Green energy of measures $\mu $ and $
u $ and the Green energy of $\mu $ (subsection 4.1.28 ) by \[  I_ B(\mu ,
u )=\iint G_ B(x,y)\, \mathrm d\mu (x)\, \mathrm d
u (y),\qquad I_ B(\mu )=I_ B(\mu ,\mu ).  \] By lemma 4.1.14 , $G_ B(x,y)-\Gamma _ d(x-y)$ is continuous on $B	imes B$, so $G_ B$ is a continuous function on $B	imes B$ with values in $[0,\infty ]$, and these integrals are defined in $[0,\infty ]$ by Tonelli's theorem. For finite signed measures we use the same formulas whenever $G_ B$ is integrable for the product of the total variations. Let $\mu $ be supported in a compact set $K\subset B$. By the definition of $G_ B$ in theorem 3.1.34 and by theorem 3.1.18 , the harmonic correction $G_ B(x,y)-\Gamma _ d(x-y)=-H_ B(\Gamma _ d(\cdot -x)|_{\partial B})(y)$ has absolute value at most $\max _{\zeta \in \partial B}|\Gamma _ d(\zeta -x)|$, which is bounded for $x\in K$ because $K$ has positive distance from $\partial B$. Hence, on $K	imes K$, the Green function differs by a bounded function from the kernel $k$ of subsection 4.1.1 if $d\geq 3$, and from the kernel $k_ D$ with $D>\operatorname {diam}K$ if $d=2$, because $k(x,y)=\Gamma _ d(x-y)$ and $k_ D(x,y)-\Gamma _2(x-y)$ is constant. Consequently $\mu $ has finite Green energy if and only if it has finite energy in the sense of subsection 4.1.1 . In particular, by theorem 4.1.17 , a measure $\mu $ of finite Green energy does not charge polar sets: every polar set is contained in a Borel set of $\mu $-measure zero. Definition 4.2.10 . CD643C4C40FF A property holds quasi-everywhere on a set $E\subset \mathbb R^ d$ if it holds at every point of $E$ outside a polar set. Thus a property that holds quasi-everywhere on a compact set $K\subset B$ holds $\mu $-almost everywhere for every measure $\mu $ on $K$ with finite Green energy. In 2 the exceptional sets are pluripolar, and quasi-everywhere will mean outside a pluripolar set (definition 5.47.2 ). Proposition 4.2.11 . 2BC493B5F349 Let $\mu $ and $
u $ be measures with finite Green energy. Then the distributional gradients $

u $ belong to $L^2(B)$, the mutual energy $I_ B(\mu ,

u )=\int _ B

On such signed measures, $I_ B$ is a positive definite quadratic form, that is, $I_ B(\sigma )\geq 0$ with equality only for $\sigma =0$, and it satisfies the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $I_ B(\sigma ,	au )^2\leq I_ B(\sigma )I_ B(	au )$. Moreover, every measure $\mu $ with finite Green energy is the sum of its restrictions $\mu ^{(1)},\mu ^{(2)},\ldots $ to countably many pairwise disjoint compact sets, and for every $n$ the Green potential of $\mu ^{(1)}+\cdots +\mu ^{(n)}$ is finite, continuous and bounded on $B$. Proof. We first prove the gradient identity for the partial sums of a decomposition of $\mu $ and $
u $ into pieces with bounded Green potentials, to which proposition 4.1.29 applies, and then pass to the limit. Translating, we may assume that $B=B(0,R)$ for some $R>0$, and we choose $r<R$ such that the supports of $\mu $ and $
u $ lie in $B(0,r)$. By lemma 4.1.14 , the function $\kappa (x,y)=G_ B(x,y)-\Gamma _ d(x-y)$ extends to a continuous function on the compact set $\overline B	imes \overline{B(0,r)}$; let $C$ be a bound for $|\kappa |$ there. Since $\Gamma _ d=-E_ d$, every finite positive measure $\lambda $ supported in $B(0,r)$ satisfies \[  G_ B\lambda (x)=-E_ d*\lambda (x)+\int \kappa (x,y)\, \mathrm d\lambda (y),\qquad x\in B,  \] and the last integral is a continuous function of $x\in \overline B$ bounded by $C\lambda (B)$. Step 1: decomposition. Since $\int G_ B\mu \, \mathrm d\mu =I_ B(\mu )<\infty $, the Green potential $G_ B\mu $ is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere, and by the display so is $E_ d*\mu $. By part (2) of theorem 4.1.10 , $\mu $ is therefore the sum of its restrictions to countably many disjoint compact sets, each of which has a finite and continuous fundamental potential. Let $\mu _ n$ be the sum of the first $n$ of these restrictions. Since $E_ d*\mu _ n$ is finite and continuous, the display shows that $G_ B\mu _ n$ is finite, continuous and bounded on $B$; this proves the last assertion of the proposition. By part (2) of proposition 4.1.16 , $-G_ B\mu _ n$ is a subharmonic function on $B$ with Riesz measure $\mu _ n$, which extends harmonically across $\partial B$ and vanishes on $\partial B$; in particular, it tends to zero at $\partial B$. The measure $\mu -\mu _ n$ is the restriction of $\mu $ to a decreasing sequence of sets whose intersection is $\mu $-null. Since $G_ B$ is nonnegative and integrable for $\mu \otimes \mu $, dominated convergence gives $I_ B(\mu -\mu _ n)	o 0$. Thus $(

Hence $G_ B\mu _ n	o G_ B\mu $ in $L^1(B)$ by monotone convergence. abla G_ B\sigma \| _2^2\geq 0$. Suppose that $I_ B(\sigma )=0$, so that $
abla G_ B\sigma =0$ as a distribution on $B$. Since $B$ is connected, corollary 2.5.5 shows that the distribution defined by $G_ B\sigma $ is a constant. On the other hand, $-\Delta G_ B\sigma =\sigma $ in the sense of distributions, by part (2) of proposition 4.1.16 . Hence $\sigma ^+$ and $\sigma ^-$, which are Radon measures by proposition 2.2.2 , define the same distribution, so $\sigma ^+=\sigma ^-$ by part (4) of proposition 2.5.3 , that is, $\sigma =0$. Finally, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for $I_ B$ follows from the gradient identity and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in $L^2(B)$. $\square$ Recall from subsection 4.1.13 the relative extremal function $u_ K$ of a compact set $K\subset B$, its Riesz measure $\lambda _ K=\Delta u_ K$, the relative capacity $C_ B(K)=\lambda _ K(K)$, and the outer capacity $C_ B^*$. Proposition 4.2.12 . AF6AC1F168D7 Let $K\subset B$ be compact. Then \[  C_ B(K)=\left(\inf _{\substack {	au \geq 0,\  \operatorname{Supp}	au \subset K\ 	au (K)=1}} I_ B(	au )ight)^{-1},  \] with the conventions that the infimum of an empty family is $+\infty $ and that $1/(+\infty )=0$. If $C_ B(K)>0$, then $\lambda _ K/C_ B(K)$ is the unique probability measure on $K$ minimizing $I_ B$. Moreover, if $D\subset B$ are open balls and $A\Subset D$, then $C_ B^*(A)\leq C_ D^*(A)$. Proof. By part (3) of proposition 4.1.16 , the function $w_ K=-u_ K$ is the Green potential $G_ B\lambda _ K$, and $0\leq w_ K\leq 1$ because $-1\leq u_ K\leq 0$. Since $u_ K$ is the upper semicontinuous regularization of the envelope $f_ K$, which equals $-1$ on $K$, part (2) of theorem 4.1.26 shows that $w_ K=1$ quasi-everywhere on $K$. In particular $I_ B(\lambda _ K)=\int w_ K\, \mathrm d\lambda _ K\leq \lambda _ K(K)$, so $\lambda _ K$ has finite Green energy. As measures of finite Green energy do not charge polar sets, we obtain, with $m=C_ B(K)$, \[  I_ B(\lambda _ K)=\int _ Kw_ K\, \mathrm d\lambda _ K=m,\qquad I_ B(\lambda _ K,	au )=\int _ Kw_ K\, \mathrm d	au =1  \] for every probability measure $	au $ on $K$ with finite Green energy; in the second identity we used the symmetry of $G_ B$. Suppose that $m>0$, and let $	au $ be a probability measure on $K$. If $I_ B(	au )<\infty $, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality of proposition 4.2.11 gives $1=I_ B(\lambda _ K,	au )^2\leq mI_ B(	au )$; thus $I_ B(	au )\geq 1/m$ in all cases. Equality holds for $	au =\lambda _ K/m$, whose energy is $m/m^2=1/m$. Hence the infimum equals $1/m$, which proves the formula. If $	au _1
eq 	au _2$ were two minimizers, their midpoint would again be a probability measure on $K$, and by positive definiteness \[  I_ B\Bigl ( rac{	au _1+	au _2}{2}\Bigr )= rac{I_ B(	au _1)+I_ B(	au _2)}{2}- rac{I_ B(	au _1-	au _2)}{4}< rac1m,  \] a contradiction. For the last assertion, recall that balls are regular domains (theorem 3.1.29 ). The monotonicity of Green functions in the domain (theorem 3.1.34 ) gives $G_ D\leq G_ B$ on $D	imes D$. Hence $I_ B(	au )\geq I_ D(	au )$ for every measure $	au $ supported on a compact set $K\subset D$, and the variational formula, applied in $B$ and in $D$, gives $C_ B(K)\leq C_ D(K)$. Taking suprema over compact subsets, we obtain $C_ B(O)\leq C_ D(O)$ for every open $O\Subset D$. Every such $O$ containing $A$ is also allowed in the infimum defining $C_ B^*(A)$, so $C_ B^*(A)\leq C_ D^*(A)$. $\square$ We now turn to reduction. Let $U$ be an open set, $s$ a nonnegative superharmonic function on $U$, and $A\subset U$ an arbitrary subset. The reduction of $s$ on $A$, also called the réduite, and the regularized reduction are \[  R_ s^ A=\inf \{ h:h\geq 0	ext{ is superharmonic on }U,\  h\geq s	ext{ on }A\} , \qquad \widehat R_ s^ A=(R_ s^ A)_*.  \] Here $F_*=-(-F)^*$, with $(-F)^*$ the upper semicontinuous regularization of subsection 3.4.21 , is the lower semicontinuous regularization of a function $F$ that is locally bounded below; explicitly, $F_*(x)=\sup _{r>0}\inf _{B(x,r)\cap U}F$. We call the functions $h$ in this infimum admissible for $R_ s^ A$; the inequality $h\geq s$ is required at every point of $A$. If $U=B$, $s=1$ and $A\Subset B$, the admissible functions are exactly the negatives of the functions admissible for $A$ in the sense of subsection 4.1.13 , so that $R_1^ A=-f_ A$ and $\widehat R_1^ A=-u_ A$. Since $s$ itself is admissible, $0\leq R_ s^ A\leq s$, and $R_ s^ A=s$ on all of $A$. The negatives of the admissible functions form a family of subharmonic functions bounded above by zero, whose supremum is $-R_ s^ A$. Since $(-R_ s^ A)^*=-\widehat R_ s^ A$, theorem 3.4.23 shows that $\widehat R_ s^ A$ is superharmonic, and part (2) of theorem 4.1.26 shows that $R_ s^ A=\widehat R_ s^ A$ outside a polar set. The ball-average formula ( 3.4.13 ) holds for every subharmonic function, integrable or not. Applied to $-w$, it shows that every superharmonic function $w$ on an open set satisfies \[  w(x)=\lim _{r\downarrow 0} rac{1}{|B(x,r)|}\int _{B(x,r)}w(y)\, \mathrm d y  \] at every point $x$ of that set. Consequently, two superharmonic functions satisfying an inequality almost everywhere satisfy it everywhere. Proposition 4.2.13 . Then \[  R_ s^ A\leq R_ s^{A'},\qquad R_{cs}^ A=cR_ s^ A,\qquad R_{s+t}^ A\leq R_ s^ A+R_ t^ A,  \] and $R_ s^ A\leq R_ t^ A$ if $s\leq t$. For $c>0$, multiplication by $c$ is a bijection between the admissible functions for $s$ and those for $cs$; for $c=0$, both sides vanish (with $0\cdot \infty =0$), since the zero function is admissible. If $h_1$ and $h_2$ are admissible for $s$ and $t$ respectively, then $h_1+h_2$ is admissible for $s+t$, so $R_{s+t}^ A\leq R_ s^ A+R_ t^ A$. For subadditivity, recall that each reduction agrees with its regularization outside a polar set, hence almost everywhere. Therefore $\widehat R_{s+t}^ A\leq \widehat R_ s^ A+\widehat R_ t^ A$ almost everywhere. Both sides are superharmonic, so the inequality holds everywhere by the ball-average formula above. u $ of compact support with $E_ d*

i y	o \zeta }H(y)\geq h(\zeta ),\qquad \zeta \in \partial D.  \] Define $h^ D=H$ on $D$ and $h^ D=h$ on $B\setminus D$. text: Proposition 4.2.12 . AF6AC1F168D7 Let $K\subset B$ be compact. Then \[  C_ B(K)=\left(\inf _{\substack {\tau \geq 0,\  \operatorname{Supp}\tau \subset K\\ \tau (K)=1}} I_ B(\tau )\right)^{-1},  \] with the conventions that the infimum of an empty family is $+\infty $ and that $1/(+\infty )=0$. If $C_ B(K)>0$, then $\lambda _ K/C_ B(K)$ is the unique probability measure on $K$ minimizing $I_ B$. Moreover, if $D\subset B$ are open balls and $A\Subset D$, then $C_ B^*(A)\leq C_ D^*(A)$. Proof. By part (3) of proposition 4.1.16 , the function $w_ K=-u_ K$ is the Green potential $G_ B\lambda _ K$, and $0\leq w_ K\leq 1$ because $-1\leq u_ K\leq 0$. Since $u_ K$ is the upper semicontinuous regularization of the envelope $f_ K$, which equals $-1$ on $K$, part (2) of theorem 4.1.26 shows that $w_ K=1$ quasi-everywhere on $K$. In particular $I_ B(\lambda _ K)=\int w_ K\, \mathrm d\lambda _ K\leq \lambda _ K(K)$, so $\lambda _ K$ has finite Green energy. As measures of finite Green energy do not charge polar sets, we obtain, with $m=C_ B(K)$, \[  I_ B(\lambda _ K)=\int _ Kw_ K\, \mathrm d\lambda _ K=m,\qquad I_ B(\lambda _ K,\tau )=\int _ Kw_ K\, \mathrm d\tau =1  \] for every probability measure $\tau $ on $K$ with finite Green energy; in the second identity we used the symmetry of $G_ B$. Suppose that $m>0$, and let $\tau $ be a probability measure on $K$. If $I_ B(\tau )<\infty $, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality of proposition 4.2.11 gives $1=I_ B(\lambda _ K,\tau )^2\leq mI_ B(\tau )$; thus $I_ B(\tau )\geq 1/m$ in all cases. Equality holds for $\tau =\lambda _ K/m$, whose energy is $m/m^2=1/m$. Hence the infimum equals $1/m$, which proves the formula. If $\tau _1\neq \tau _2$ were two minimizers, their midpoint would again be a probability measure on $K$, and by positive definiteness \[  I_ B\Bigl (\frac{\tau _1+\tau _2}{2}\Bigr )=\frac{I_ B(\tau _1)+I_ B(\tau _2)}{2}-\frac{I_ B(\tau _1-\tau _2)}{4}<\frac1m,  \] a contradiction. Suppose next that $m=0$. Then $K$ is polar by theorem 4.1.17 , so it carries no probability measure of finite energy, and the infimum is $+\infty $ (if $K=\varnothing $, the family is empty). For the last assertion, recall that balls are regular domains (theorem 3.1.29 ). The monotonicity of Green functions in the domain (theorem 3.1.34 ) gives $G_ D\leq G_ B$ on $D\times D$. Hence $I_ B(\tau )\geq I_ D(\tau )$ for every measure $\tau $ supported on a compact set $K\subset D$, and the variational formula, applied in $B$ and in $D$, gives $C_ B(K)\leq C_ D(K)$. Taking suprema over compact subsets, we obtain $C_ B(O)\leq C_ D(O)$ for every open $O\Subset D$. Every such $O$ containing $A$ is also allowed in the infimum defining $C_ B^*(A)$, so $C_ B^*(A)\leq C_ D^*(A)$. $\square$
