Summing over $i$ and $j$ then gives \[  \sum _ j\| (\eta _ jv)\circ \psi _ j^{-1}\| _{W^{k,p}(\psi _ j(V_ j))}\leq C\| v\| _{W^{k,p}(X)},  \] and by symmetry the two norms are equivalent. To prove the claim about $(\eta _ j\chi _ iv)\circ \psi _ j^{-1}$, fix $i$ and $j$. The compact set $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ i\cap \operatorname{Supp}\eta _ j$ lies in $U_ i\cap V_ j$, so by lemma 2.5.1 (4) in the chart $\varphi _ i$ there is a smooth function $\vartheta $ on $X$, with compact support in $U_ i\cap V_ j$, that equals $1$ on a neighborhood of it. Then $\eta _ j\chi _ iv=(\vartheta \eta _ j)\chi _ iv$, and $(\vartheta \eta _ j)\circ \varphi _ i^{-1}$ is smooth with compact support in $\varphi _ i(U_ i\cap V_ j)$. By lemma 2.9.14 (1), the function $w=(\eta _ j\chi _ iv)\circ \varphi _ i^{-1}$ belongs to $W^{k,p}(\varphi _ i(U_ i))$, vanishes outside the compact set $\varphi _ i(\operatorname{Supp}\vartheta )$, and satisfies $\| w\| _{W^{k,p}(\varphi _ i(U_ i))}\leq C\| (\chi _ iv)\circ \varphi _ i^{-1}\| _{W^{k,p}(\varphi _ i(U_ i))}$. We now change charts. By lemma 2.9.14 (2), applied to the restriction of $w$ to $\varphi _ i(U_ i\cap V_ j)$ and to the diffeomorphism $\Phi =\varphi _ i\circ \psi _ j^{-1}$ from $\psi _ j(U_ i\cap V_ j)$ onto $\varphi _ i(U_ i\cap V_ j)$, the function $(\eta _ j\chi _ iv)\circ \psi _ j^{-1}=w\circ \Phi $ belongs to $W^{k,p}(\psi _ j(U_ i\cap V_ j))$, with norm at most $C\| w\| _{W^{k,p}(\varphi _ i(U_ i))}$, and vanishes outside the compact set $\psi _ j(\operatorname{Supp}\vartheta )$. By lemma 2.9.14 (1), applied with a smooth cutoff function equal to $1$ near this set, its extension by zero belongs to $W^{k,p}(\psi _ j(V_ j))$, with norm at most a constant multiple of the previous one. Lemma 2.9.15 . 06216156055D Let $1\leq p<\infty $ and $\varepsilon >0$. There is a constant $C_{d,\varepsilon }$, depending only on $d$ and $\varepsilon $, such that \[  \| 
abla v\| _ p\leq \varepsilon \| D^2v\| _ p+C_{d,\varepsilon }\| v\| _ p, \qquad v\in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d).  \] Proof. Let $e_ a$ be the $a$th coordinate vector and $h>0$. Taylor's formula with integral remainder gives \[  h\partial _ av(x)=v(x+he_ a)-v(x) -\int _0^ h(h-t)\partial _ a^2v(x+te_ a)\, \mathrm d t.  \] The $L^ p$ norm is invariant under translation. Moreover, $\omega (t)\, \mathrm d t=2h^{-2}(h-t)\, \mathrm d t$ is a probability measure on $[0,h]$, so Hölder's inequality gives $|\int _0^ hg\, \omega \, \mathrm d t|^ p\leq \int _0^ h|g|^ p\omega \, \mathrm d t$ for every measurable function $g$ on $[0,h]$. Applying this to $g(t)=\partial _ a^2v(x+te_ a)$, integrating in $x$ and using Tonelli's theorem, we obtain \[  \Bigl \| \int _0^ h(h-t)\partial _ a^2v(\cdot +te_ a)\, \mathrm d t\Bigr \| _ p\leq  rac{h^2}2\Bigl (\int _0^ h\| \partial _ a^2v(\cdot +te_ a)\| _ p^ p\, \omega (t)\, \mathrm d t\Bigr )^{1/p}= rac{h^2}2\| \partial _ a^2v\| _ p.  \] Hence $h\| \partial _ av\| _ p\leq 2\| v\| _ p+(h^2/2)\| \partial _ a^2v\| _ p$. Since $|
abla v|\leq \sum _ a|\partial _ av|$ and $|\partial _ a^2v|\leq |D^2v|$, summing over $a$ yields $\| 
abla v\| _ p\leq 2dh^{-1}\| v\| _ p+(dh/2)\| D^2v\| _ p$. The choice $h=2\varepsilon /d$ proves the lemma with $C_{d,\varepsilon }=d^2/\varepsilon $. $\square$ For a compact set $F\subset \mathbb R^ d$ and $0<\alpha \leq 1$, the Hölder norm of a function $v$ on $F$ is \[  \| v\| _{C^{0,\alpha }(F)}=\sup _ F|v|+\sup _{x,y\in F,\  x
eq y} rac{|v(x)-v(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha }.  \] A continuously differentiable function on an open set $U$ is of class $C^{1,\alpha }$ on a compact set $F\subset U$ if its first derivatives have finite $C^{0,\alpha }(F)$ norm, and it belongs to $C^{1,\alpha }_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ if it is of class $C^{1,\alpha }$ on every compact subset of $U$. Lemma 2.9.16 (Morrey's inequality) . DE7722E667E2 Let $d<p<\infty $, put $\alpha =1-d/p$, and let $B'\Subset B$ be Euclidean balls in $\mathbb R^ d$. Every $v\in W^{1,p}(B)$ has a representative that is continuous on $B$ and satisfies \[  \| v\| _{C^{0,\alpha }(\overline{B'})}\leq C\| v\| _{W^{1,p}(B)},  \] where $C$ depends only on $d,p,B',B$. Consequently, for an open set $U\subset \mathbb R^ d$, every function in $W^{2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ has a representative in $C^{1,\alpha }_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Proof. We prove the estimate for smooth $v$, pass to general $v$ by mollification, and then apply the result to first derivatives. Assume first that $v$ is smooth on $B$. Let $Q\subset B$ be a ball of radius $r$, let $v_ Q=|Q|^{-1}\int _ Qv$ be the average of $v$ over $Q$, and let $x\in Q$. We claim that \[  |v(x)-v_ Q|\leq C_ d\int _ Q|
abla v(z)|\, |x-z|^{1-d}\, \mathrm d z.  \] For $z\in Q$, write $z=x+s	heta $ with $s=|z-x|$ and $	heta \in S^{d-1}$; then $|v(z)-v(x)|\leq \int _0^ s|
abla v(x+t	heta )|\, \mathrm d t$, and $|v(x)-v_ Q|$ is at most the average over $z\in Q$ of these segment integrals. Since $Q$ is convex and open and contains $x$, for each $	heta $ the radii $s>0$ with $x+s	heta \in Q$ form an interval $0<s<R(	heta )$, and $R(	heta )\leq 2r$. In polar coordinates about $x$ (( 3.1.2 ) on $B(x,2r)\supset Q$), the average of the segment integrals is \[   rac1{|Q|}\int _{S^{d-1}}\int _0^{R(	heta )}s^{d-1}\int _0^ s|
abla v(x+t	heta )|\, \mathrm d t\, \mathrm d s\, \mathrm d S(	heta ).  \] Interchanging the integrals in $s$ and $t$ produces the factor $|Q|^{-1}\int _ t^{R(	heta )}s^{d-1}\, \mathrm d s$, which is at most $(2r)^ d/(d|Q|)$ and hence bounded by a constant depending only on $d$. The remaining integral $\int _{S^{d-1}}\int _0^{R(	heta )}|
abla v(x+t	heta )|\, \mathrm d t\, \mathrm d S(	heta )$ is the integral on the right side of the claim, written in polar coordinates. This proves the claim. By Hölder's inequality with $p'=p/(p-1)$, the right side of the claim is at most $C_{d,p}r^{1-d/p}\| 
abla v\| _{L^ p(Q)}$, because \[  \int _ Q|x-z|^{(1-d)p'}\, \mathrm d z\leq \int _{B(x,2r)}|x-z|^{(1-d)p'}\, \mathrm d z=C_{d,p}r^{(1-d)p'+d},  \] and this integral is finite exactly when $(1-d)p'>-d$, that is, when $p>d$. (For $d=1$ the exponent $(1-d)p'$ is zero.) Let $\delta >0$ be the distance from $B'$ to $\mathbb R^ d\setminus B$. If $x,y\in B'$ and $0<|x-y|<\delta /2$, the ball $Q=B(x,2|x-y|)$ lies in $B$ and contains $x$ and $y$. Applying the preceding bound at both points gives \[  |v(x)-v(y)|\leq C_{d,p}|x-y|^{1-d/p}\| 
abla v\| _{L^ p(B)}.  \] For $x\in B'$, the same bound on the ball $Q=B(x,\delta /2)\subset B$, together with the estimate $|v_ Q|\leq |Q|^{-1/p}\| v\| _{L^ p(B)}$ from Hölder's inequality, gives $\sup _{B'}|v|\leq C\| v\| _{W^{1,p}(B)}$ with $C$ depending on $d,p,\delta $. If $|x-y|\geq \delta /2$, then $|v(x)-v(y)|/|x-y|^\alpha \leq 2(\delta /2)^{-\alpha }\sup _{B'}|v|$. These bounds prove the estimate for smooth $v$ on $B'$, and hence on $\overline{B'}$, since $v$ is continuous on $B\supset \overline{B'}$. For general $v\in W^{1,p}(B)$, choose a ball $B''$, depending only on $B'$ and $B$, with $B'\Subset B''\Subset B$, and let $v_\varepsilon =v*ho _\varepsilon $, which is smooth on $B''$ for small $\varepsilon $. By the remark preceding lemma 2.9.14 , $\partial _ av_\varepsilon =(\partial _ av)_\varepsilon $, and $v_\varepsilon 	o v$ and $\partial _ av_\varepsilon 	o \partial _ av$ in $L^ p(B'')$. The estimate for smooth functions, applied on $B'\Subset B''$ to the differences of the $v_\varepsilon $, shows that they form a Cauchy family in the norm of $C^{0,\alpha }(\overline{B'})$. Their uniform limit is continuous on $\overline{B'}$, agrees almost everywhere with $v$, and satisfies the asserted estimate, because $\| v\| _{W^{1,p}(B'')}\leq \| v\| _{W^{1,p}(B)}$. Two continuous functions that agree almost everywhere on an open set agree everywhere on it. Hence the continuous representatives obtained from different balls $B'\Subset B$ agree on their overlaps and define a single continuous representative on $B$. Finally, let $v\in W^{2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. On every ball $B\Subset U$, both $v$ and its first derivatives $\partial _ av$ belong to $W^{1,p}(B)$. By the preceding paragraph, on each smaller ball $B'\Subset B$ the mollifications $v_\varepsilon $ and $\partial _ av_\varepsilon =(\partial _ av)_\varepsilon $ converge uniformly to the continuous representatives $	ilde v$ of $v$ and $	ilde w_ a$ of $\partial _ av$. Passing to the limit in \[  v_\varepsilon (x+he_ a)-v_\varepsilon (x)=\int _0^ h\partial _ av_\varepsilon (x+te_ a)\, \mathrm d t  \] shows that $	ilde v$ has the continuous partial derivatives $\partial _ a	ilde v=	ilde w_ a$. Hence $	ilde v$ is continuously differentiable, and by the first part its first derivatives are Hölder continuous with exponent $\alpha $ on each $\overline{B'}$. Every compact subset of $U$ is covered by finitely many such balls $B'$; pairs of points closer than a Lebesgue number of this cover lie in a common ball, and for the remaining pairs the supremum bound suffices. Hence $	ilde v\in C^{1,\alpha }_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. $\square$

title: Lemma 2.9.10
section: 2.9 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text:
Lemma 2.9.10 . 0821A7B52A3B Let $1\leq a,b\leq d$, and define an operator $T_{ab}$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^ d)$ by \[  \widehat{T_{ab}f}(\xi )=- rac{\xi _ a\xi _ b}{|\xi |^2}\widehat f(\xi ), \qquad \xi 
eq 0,  \] the multiplier being zero at the origin. Then $T_{ab}$ is self-adjoint and has norm at most one. Moreover: There is a smooth real function $K_{ab}$ on $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \{ 0\} $ such that \[  |K_{ab}(z)|\leq C_ d|z|^{-d},\qquad |
abla K_{ab}(z)|\leq C_ d|z|^{-d-1}.  \] If $f\in L^2(\mathbb R^ d)$ vanishes almost everywhere outside a compact set $F$, then $f$ is integrable, and for almost every $x\in \mathbb R^ d\setminus F$, \[  T_{ab}f(x)=\int K_{ab}(x-y)f(y)\, \mathrm d y.  \] For $v\in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d)$ we have $\partial _ a\partial _ bv=T_{ab}(-\Delta v)$. Proof. The multiplier is real and bounded by one in absolute value, so Plancherel's theorem shows that $T_{ab}$ is self-adjoint with norm at most one. For $v\in C_ c^\infty $, the first rule in ( 2.9.3 ) (lemma 2.9.2 ), applied twice, gives $\widehat{-\Delta v}(\xi )=4\pi ^2|\xi |^2\widehat v(\xi )$ and $\widehat{\partial _ a\partial _ bv}(\xi )=-4\pi ^2\xi _ a\xi _ b\widehat v(\xi )$. Multiplying the first identity by the multiplier of $T_{ab}$ gives the second, which proves (3). To construct the kernel we use the heat kernel $H_ t(z)=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\mathrm e^{-|z|^2/(4t)}$, $t>0$. By lemma 2.9.2 , $\widehat H_ t(\xi )=\mathrm e^{-4\pi ^2t|\xi |^2}$, and hence $\widehat{\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t}(\xi )=-4\pi ^2\xi _ a\xi _ b\mathrm e^{-4\pi ^2t|\xi |^2}$. For $0<\varepsilon <R<\infty $ put \[  k_{\varepsilon ,R}=\int _\varepsilon ^ R\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t\, \mathrm d t.  \] Since $\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t(z)= igl (z_ az_ b/(4t^2)-\delta _{ab}/(2t) igr )H_ t(z)$, where $\delta _{ab}$ is the Kronecker symbol, we have \[  |\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t(z)|\leq C_ dt^{-d/2-1}(1+|z|^2/t)\mathrm e^{-|z|^2/(4t)}.  \] Hence $\sup _ z|\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t(z)|\leq C_ dt^{-d/2-1}$, and the substitution $z=\sqrt t\, w$ gives $\int |\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t(z)|\, \mathrm d z\leq C_ dt^{-1}$. Therefore the kernel $k_{\varepsilon ,R}$ is bounded and integrable, and Fubini's theorem, applied with the integrable majorant $|\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t(z)|$ on $\mathbb R^ d	imes [\varepsilon ,R]$, gives its Fourier transform: \[  \widehat{k_{\varepsilon ,R}}(\xi )=- rac{\xi _ a\xi _ b}{|\xi |^2}  igl (\mathrm e^{-4\pi ^2\varepsilon |\xi |^2} -\mathrm e^{-4\pi ^2R|\xi |^2} igr ),\qquad \xi 
eq 0.  \] Let $f\in L^1\cap L^2$. Then $k_{\varepsilon ,R}*f$ is bounded and integrable, hence in $L^2$, and by Fubini's theorem and the last assertion of theorem 2.9.4 its Fourier transform is $\widehat{k_{\varepsilon ,R}}\widehat f$. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and $R\uparrow \infty $, these multipliers are bounded by one and converge to $-\xi _ a\xi _ b/|\xi |^2$ for $\xi 
eq 0$. By dominated convergence on the Fourier side and Plancherel's theorem, $k_{\varepsilon ,R}*f	o T_{ab}f$ in $L^2$. For $z
eq 0$ define \[  K_{ab}(z)=\int _0^\infty \partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t(z)\, \mathrm d t.  \] Since $H_ t(z)=t^{-d/2}H_1(z/\sqrt t)$, every derivative satisfies \[  \partial ^\gamma H_ t(z)=t^{-(d+|\gamma |)/2}(\partial ^\gamma H_1)(z/\sqrt t),  \] and induction on $|\gamma |$ shows that $\partial ^\gamma H_1(w)=P_\gamma (w)\mathrm e^{-|w|^2/4}$ for a polynomial $P_\gamma $, of degree $m_\gamma $ say. Fix $0<c\leq c'$, and let $c\leq |z|\leq c'$ and $|\gamma |\geq 2$. Since $|P_\gamma (w)|\leq C_\gamma (1+|w|)^{m_\gamma }$ and $\mathrm e^{-|z|^2/(4t)}\leq \mathrm e^{-c^2/(4t)}$, we obtain $|\partial ^\gamma H_ t(z)|\leq g_\gamma (t)$, where \[  g_\gamma (t)= egin{cases}  C_\gamma t^{-(d+|\gamma |)/2}(1+c't^{-1/2})^{m_\gamma }\mathrm e^{-c^2/(4t)}, &  0<t\leq 1,\  C_\gamma (1+c')^{m_\gamma }t^{-(d+|\gamma |)/2}, &  t\geq 1. \end{cases}  \] This function is integrable on $(0,\infty )$ and does not depend on $z$: near $t=0$ the factor $\mathrm e^{-c^2/(4t)}$ dominates every power of $t^{-1}$, and for $t\geq 1$ the exponent satisfies $(d+|\gamma |)/2\geq 3/2>1$. By the mean value theorem and dominated convergence, we may therefore differentiate under the integral sign any number of times. Hence $K_{ab}$ is smooth on $\mathbb R^ d\setminus \{ 0\} $, and its derivatives are the integrals of the corresponding derivatives of $\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t$. Moreover, the integrals $\int _0^\varepsilon $ and $\int _ R^\infty $ of $|\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t(z)|$ tend to zero as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ and $R\uparrow \infty $, uniformly for $c\leq |z|\leq c'$. Differentiating the identity $H_{r^2s}(rz)=r^{-d}H_ s(z)$ twice in $z$ and substituting $t=r^2s$, we find that $K_{ab}(rz)=r^{-d}K_{ab}(z)$ for $r>0$. Thus $K_{ab}$ is homogeneous of degree $-d$ and $
abla K_{ab}$ is homogeneous of degree $-d-1$, and the bounds in (1) follow from the boundedness of the continuous functions $K_{ab}$ and $
abla K_{ab}$ on the unit sphere. The same scaling shows that the function $z\mapsto \int _0^\infty |\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t(z)|\, \mathrm d t$ is homogeneous of degree $-d$; it is bounded on the unit sphere by $\int _0^\infty g_\gamma (t)\, \mathrm d t$, where $\partial ^\gamma =\partial _ a\partial _ b$ and $c=c'=1$, so it is at most $C_ d|z|^{-d}$. To prove (2), let $f$ and $F$ be as there. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality on $F$, the function $f$ is integrable, so $f\in L^1\cap L^2$. Let $L$ be a compact set disjoint from $F$. For $x\in L$, \[  k_{\varepsilon ,R}*f(x)=\int f(y)\int _\varepsilon ^ R\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t(x-y)\, \mathrm d t\, \mathrm d y,  \] where the outer integral may be taken over $F$. The differences $x-y$, with $x\in L$ and $y\in F$, form a compact set not containing the origin, on which $c\leq |x-y|\leq c'$ for some $0<c\leq c'$. By the uniform estimates just proved, the inner integral converges to $K_{ab}(x-y)$ uniformly on this set, and it is bounded by $\int _0^\infty |\partial _ a\partial _ bH_ t(x-y)|\, \mathrm d t\leq C_ dc^{-d}$. Hence, since $f$ is integrable, $k_{\varepsilon ,R}*f$ converges uniformly on $L$ to $\int K_{ab}(x-y)f(y)\, \mathrm d y$. Since it also converges to $T_{ab}f$ in $L^2$, a subsequence converges almost everywhere to $T_{ab}f$, and the two limits agree almost everywhere on $L$. Covering the open set $\mathbb R^ d\setminus F$ by countably many such compact sets proves (2). For $d=1$ the kernel vanishes, in accordance with $T_{11}=-1$: a direct differentiation gives $\partial _ z^2H_ t= igl (z^2/(4t^2)-1/(2t) igr )H_ t=\partial _ tH_ t$, so $K_{11}(z)=\lim _{t\uparrow \infty }H_ t(z)-\lim _{t\downarrow 0}H_ t(z)=0$ for $z
eq 0$. $\square$

title: Lemma 2.9.11
section: 2.9 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text:
Lemma 2.9.11 . 780F1882B8A5 Let $T_{ab}$ be the operator of lemma 2.9.10 , let $f\in L^1(\mathbb R^ d)\cap L^2(\mathbb R^ d)$ and let $\lambda >0$. Then \[  |\{ x:|T_{ab}f(x)|>\lambda \} |\leq  rac{C_ d}{\lambda }\| f\| _1.  \] Proof. We use the Calderón–Zygmund decomposition of $f$ at height $\lambda $ into a bounded part $g$, handled by the $L^2$ bound for $T_{ab}$, and parts $b_ Q$ of mean zero on disjoint cubes $Q$, handled by lemma 2.9.10 . The dyadic cubes are the cubes $2^ k(m+[0,1)^ d)$ with $k\in \mathbb Z$ and $m\in \mathbb Z^ d$. Two dyadic cubes are either disjoint or nested, and each dyadic cube $Q$ lies in a unique dyadic cube of twice its side length, its parent, which has volume $2^ d|Q|$. Call a dyadic cube $Q$ selected if the average of $|f|$ over $Q$ exceeds $\lambda $, while the average over every strictly larger dyadic cube containing $Q$ does not. Every dyadic cube on which the average of $|f|$ exceeds $\lambda $ is contained in a selected cube, because the averages over its successive ancestors are at most $\| f\| _1$ divided by their volumes and therefore tend to zero. The selected cubes are pairwise disjoint. For each of them, the average over its parent is at most $\lambda $, and hence \[  \lambda < rac1{|Q|}\int _ Q|f|\leq 2^ d\lambda ,\qquad \sum _ Q|Q|\leq  rac1\lambda \sum _ Q\int _ Q|f|\leq  rac1\lambda \| f\| _1.  \] Moreover, $|f|\leq \lambda $ almost everywhere outside the union of the selected cubes. Indeed, let $x$ be a point outside this union at which the conclusion of theorem 2.8.3 holds. Every dyadic cube containing $x$ has average of $|f|$ at most $\lambda $, since otherwise it would lie in a selected cube. The dyadic cube of side $2^ k$ containing $x$ lies in the cube $x+(-2^ k,2^ k)^ d$, whose volume is $2^ d$ times larger. Hence the average of $|f-f(x)|$ over it tends to zero as $k	o -\infty $, so its average of $|f|$ tends to $|f(x)|$, and therefore $|f(x)|\leq \lambda $. For a selected cube $Q$, let $f_ Q=|Q|^{-1}\int _ Qf$ be the average of $f$. Define $g=f$ outside the selected cubes and $g=f_ Q$ on each selected cube $Q$, and put $b_ Q=(f-f_ Q)\mathbf1_ Q$. Each $b_ Q$ has integral zero, and \[  \| g\| _1\leq \| f\| _1,\quad \| g\| _\infty \leq 2^ d\lambda , \quad \| g\| _2^2\leq 2^ d\lambda \| f\| _1, \qquad \sum _ Q\| b_ Q\| _1\leq 2\| f\| _1.  \] By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, $|Q||f_ Q|^2\leq \int _ Q|f|^2$, so $\| b_ Q\| _2\leq 2\| f\mathbf1_ Q\| _2$. Since the $b_ Q$ have disjoint supports, the series $\sum _ Qb_ Q$ converges to $f-g$ in $L^2$. Let $c_ Q$ be the center of $Q$, and let $Q^*$ be the cube with center $c_ Q$ and $4\sqrt d$ times the side length of $Q$. If $x
otin Q^*$ and $y\in Q$, then $|x-c_ Q|\geq 2\operatorname {diam}Q$ and $|y-c_ Q|\leq \operatorname {diam}Q/2$, so every point of the segment from $x-c_ Q$ to $x-y$ has norm at least $|x-c_ Q|/2$. The function $b_ Q\in L^2$ vanishes outside the compact set $\overline Q$, which does not meet $\mathbb R^ d\setminus Q^*$, and it has integral zero. Therefore parts (1) and (2) of lemma 2.9.10 and the mean value theorem give, for almost every $x
otin Q^*$, \[   egin{aligned}  |T_{ab}b_ Q(x)| & =\left|\int _ Q igl (K_{ab}(x-y)-K_{ab}(x-c_ Q) igr )b_ Q(y)\, \mathrm d yight|\ & \leq C_ d rac{\operatorname {diam}Q}{|x-c_ Q|^{d+1}}\| b_ Q\| _1. \end{aligned}  \] Integrating in polar coordinates about $c_ Q$ over the region $|x-c_ Q|\geq 2\operatorname {diam}Q$, which contains $\mathbb R^ d\setminus Q^*$, we obtain \[  \int _{\mathbb R^ d\setminus Q^*}|T_{ab}b_ Q|\leq C_ d\| b_ Q\| _1.  \] Put $B^*= igcup _ QQ^*$. Then $|B^*|\leq (4\sqrt d)^ d\sum _ Q|Q|\leq C_ d\lambda ^{-1}\| f\| _1$. Enumerate the selected cubes, and let $S_ N$ be the partial sums of $\sum _ Qb_ Q$. Since $S_ N	o f-g$ in $L^2$, also $T_{ab}S_ N	o T_{ab}(f-g)$ in $L^2$, and a subsequence converges almost everywhere. Moreover $\int _{\mathbb R^ d\setminus B^*}|T_{ab}S_ N|\leq \sum _ Q\int _{\mathbb R^ d\setminus Q^*}|T_{ab}b_ Q|\leq C_ d\| f\| _1$, so Fatou's lemma gives \[  \int _{\mathbb R^ d\setminus B^*}|T_{ab}(f-g)|\leq C_ d\| f\| _1.  \] Finally, $T_{ab}f=T_{ab}g+T_{ab}(f-g)$, and the set where $|T_{ab}f|>\lambda $ is contained in the union of $B^*$, the set where $|T_{ab}g|>\lambda /2$, and the set of $x
otin B^*$ with $|T_{ab}(f-g)(x)|>\lambda /2$. By Chebyshev's inequality and the $L^2$ bound for $T_{ab}$, the second set has measure at most $4\lambda ^{-2}\| g\| _2^2\leq 2^{d+2}\lambda ^{-1}\| f\| _1$, and the third has measure at most $2\lambda ^{-1}\int _{\mathbb R^ d\setminus B^*}|T_{ab}(f-g)|\leq C_ d\lambda ^{-1}\| f\| _1$. Together with the bound for $|B^*|$, this proves the lemma. $\square$

title: Theorem 2.9.12
section: 2.9 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text: Theorem 2.9.12 . CAB0E7754072 Let $1<p<\infty $, and let $T_{ab}$ be the operators of lemma 2.9.10 . There is a constant $C_{d,p}$ such that $\| T_{ab}f\| _ p\leq C_{d,p}\| f\| _ p$ for all $a,b$ and all $f\in L^ p\cap L^2$; consequently each $T_{ab}$ extends uniquely to a bounded operator on $L^ p(\mathbb R^ d)$. In particular 61BC1B5115B3 2.9.13 \begin{equation}  \| D^2v\| _ p\leq C_{d,p}\| \Delta v\| _ p, \qquad v\in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d). \end{equation} Proof. Assume first that $1<p<2$, and let $f\in L^ p\cap L^2$. Fix $\lambda >0$ and split $f=f_1+f_2$ with $f_1=f\mathbf1_{\{ |f|>\lambda \} }$ and $f_2=f\mathbf1_{\{ |f|\leq \lambda \} }$. Since $|f_1|\leq \lambda ^{1-p}|f|^ p$, we have $f_1\in L^1\cap L^2$, and $f_2\in L^2$. Apply lemma 2.9.11 to $f_1$, and Chebyshev's inequality with the $L^2$ bound to $f_2$, both with threshold $\lambda /2$. This gives \[  |\{ |T_{ab}f|>\lambda \} | \leq \frac{C_ d}{\lambda }\int _{\{ |f|>\lambda \} }|f| +\frac{C_ d}{\lambda ^2}\int _{\{ |f|\leq \lambda \} }|f|^2.  \] For a measurable function $h$, Tonelli's theorem applied to $|h(x)|^ p=\int _0^{|h(x)|}p\lambda ^{p-1}\, \mathrm d\lambda $ expresses $\| h\| _ p^ p$ as the integral of $p\lambda ^{p-1}$ times the distribution function $\lambda \mapsto |\{ |h|>\lambda \} |$, also when the norm is infinite. We apply this to $h=T_{ab}f$: multiply the last inequality by $p\lambda ^{p-1}$ and integrate in $\lambda $. By Tonelli's theorem again, the first term on the right contributes $C_ d\int |f|\int _0^{|f|}p\lambda ^{p-2}\, \mathrm d\lambda \, \mathrm d x=C_ dp\| f\| _ p^ p/(p-1)$, and the second contributes $C_ d\int |f|^2\int _{|f|}^\infty p\lambda ^{p-3}\, \mathrm d\lambda \, \mathrm d x=C_ dp\| f\| _ p^ p/(2-p)$; the inner integrals converge precisely because $p>1$ and $p<2$. Therefore \[  \| T_{ab}f\| _ p^ p \leq C_ dp\left(\frac1{p-1}+\frac1{2-p}\right)\| f\| _ p^ p.  \] For $p=2$ the bound is Plancherel's theorem. Now let $2<p<\infty $, put $p'=p/(p-1)\in (1,2)$, let $f\in L^ p\cap L^2$, and write $h=T_{ab}f\in L^2$. For integers $N\geq 1$, put $E_ N=B(0,N)\cap \{ |h|\leq N\} $ and $g_ N=\mathbf1_{E_ N}h|h|^{p-2}$. Then $|g_ N|\leq N^{p-1}\mathbf1_{E_ N}$, so $g_ N\in L^2\cap L^{p'}$, and $|g_ N|^{p'}=\mathbf1_{E_ N}|h|^ p$. Since $T_{ab}$ is self-adjoint on $L^2$, the case $p'$ already proved and Hölder's inequality give \[  \int _{E_ N}|h|^ p=\int h\overline{g_ N} =\int f\overline{T_{ab}g_ N} \leq C_{d,p'}\| f\| _ p\left(\int _{E_ N}|h|^ p\right)^{1/p'}.  \] The integral on the left is finite. If it is nonzero, dividing by its $(1/p')$th power gives $(\int _{E_ N}|h|^ p)^{1/p}\leq C_{d,p'}\| f\| _ p$; if it is zero, this bound is trivial. The sets $E_ N$ increase to $\{ |h|<\infty \} $, which has full measure since $h\in L^2$, so monotone convergence gives $\| T_{ab}f\| _ p\leq C_{d,p'}\| f\| _ p$. By lemma 2.5.1 (5), $C_ c^\infty \subset L^ p\cap L^2$ is dense in $L^ p$, and $L^ p$ is complete, so $T_{ab}$ has a unique bounded extension from $L^ p\cap L^2$ to $L^ p$. Finally, for $v\in C_ c^\infty $, lemma 2.9.10 (3) gives $\| \partial _ a\partial _ bv\| _ p=\| T_{ab}\Delta v\| _ p\leq C_{d,p}\| \Delta v\| _ p$, and summing over $a$ and $b$ proves ( 2.9.13 ). $\square$

title: Lemma 2.9.14
section: 2.9 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text: Lemma 2.9.14 . 534938A78D42 Let $k\geq 0$ and $1\leq p<\infty $, let $U,V\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open, and let $v\in W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. If $\chi \in C^\infty (U)$, then $\chi v\in W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, and $\partial ^\alpha (\chi v)=\sum _{\beta \leq \alpha }\binom \alpha \beta \partial ^{\alpha -\beta }\chi \, \partial ^\beta v$ for $|\alpha |\leq k$. If moreover $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ is a compact subset of $U$, then $\chi v$, extended by zero, belongs to $W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^ d)$, its derivatives are given by the same formula extended by zero, and $\| \chi v\| _{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^ d)}\leq C\| v\| _{W^{k,p}(W)}$ for every open set $W$ with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset W\subset U$, where $C$ depends only on $d$, $k$ and $\chi $. If $\Phi \colon V\to U$ is a $C^\infty $ diffeomorphism, then $v\circ \Phi \in W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(V)$. If moreover $v$ vanishes almost everywhere outside a compact set $K\subset U$, then $v\circ \Phi $ vanishes almost everywhere outside the compact set $\Phi ^{-1}(K)$, and $\| v\circ \Phi \| _{W^{k,p}(V)}\leq C\| v\| _{W^{k,p}(U)}$, where $C$ depends only on $k$, $p$, $\Phi $ and $K$. Proof. (1) For $k=0$ the first assertion holds because $\chi $ is bounded on compact sets. Let $k\geq 1$ and $1\leq j\leq d$. For a test function $\phi $ on $U$, the function $\chi \phi $ is a test function with $\partial _ j(\chi \phi )=\chi \partial _ j\phi +\phi \partial _ j\chi $, so \[  \int \chi v\, \partial _ j\phi \, \mathrm d x=\int v\, \partial _ j(\chi \phi )\, \mathrm d x-\int v\, \partial _ j\chi \, \phi \, \mathrm d x=-\int \bigl (\chi \partial _ jv+v\partial _ j\chi \bigr )\phi \, \mathrm d x.  \] Thus $\partial _ j(\chi v)=\chi \partial _ jv+(\partial _ j\chi )v$. The functions $\partial _ jv$ and $v$ belong to $W^{k-1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, so by induction on $k$ both terms belong to $W^{k-1,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$; hence $\chi v\in W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, and iterating the formula for first derivatives gives the Leibniz formula, exactly as for smooth functions. Now let $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ be a compact subset of $U$, and let $W$ be as in the statement. By the Leibniz formula, $\chi v$ and its derivatives of order at most $k$ vanish almost everywhere outside $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, and there they are bounded by $C\sum _{|\beta |\leq k}|\partial ^\beta v|$, where $C$ depends on $d$, $k$ and the derivatives of $\chi $ of order at most $k$. Hence their $L^ p$ norms are at most $C\| v\| _{W^{k,p}(W)}$, which is finite when $W\Subset U$. To identify the derivatives of the extension by zero, let $\phi $ be a test function on $\mathbb R^ d$, and choose a smooth cutoff function $\zeta $ for $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ in $U$ which equals $1$ on a neighborhood $N$ of $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ (lemma 2.5.1 (4)). Then $\zeta \phi $ is a test function on $U$, and $\partial ^\alpha (\zeta \phi )=\partial ^\alpha \phi $ on $N$. Since $\chi v$ and $\partial ^\alpha (\chi v)$ vanish almost everywhere outside $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, \[  \begin{split}  \int \chi v\, \partial ^\alpha \phi \, \mathrm d x& =\int \chi v\, \partial ^\alpha (\zeta \phi )\, \mathrm d x\\ & =(-1)^{|\alpha |}\int \partial ^\alpha (\chi v)\, \zeta \phi \, \mathrm d x=(-1)^{|\alpha |}\int \partial ^\alpha (\chi v)\, \phi \, \mathrm d x. \end{split}  \] This proves (1). (2) The composite $v\circ \Phi $ is defined almost everywhere: if $Z\subset U$ is a Borel null set, the change of variables formula for the diffeomorphism $\Phi ^{-1}$ gives $|\Phi ^{-1}(Z)|=\int _ Z|\det D\Phi ^{-1}(x)|\, \mathrm d x=0$. For a smooth function $w$ on $U$ and $1\leq |\alpha |\leq k$, the classical chain rule gives \[  \partial ^\alpha (w\circ \Phi )=\sum _{1\leq |\beta |\leq |\alpha |}c_{\alpha \beta }\, (\partial ^\beta w)\circ \Phi \qquad \text{on }V,  \] with smooth functions $c_{\alpha \beta }$ on $V$ that depend only on $\Phi $: for $|\alpha |=1$ this is $\partial _ j(w\circ \Phi )=\sum _ i\partial _ j\Phi _ i\, (\partial _ iw)\circ \Phi $, and differentiating the formula once more, with the product rule and the chain rule applied to each $(\partial ^\beta w)\circ \Phi $, gives the induction step. Assume first that $v$ vanishes almost everywhere outside the compact set $K$. By (1), applied with a smooth cutoff function equal to $1$ near $K$, the extension of $v$ by zero belongs to $W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^ d)$. Its derivatives of order at most $k$ vanish almost everywhere outside $K$, because $v$ vanishes almost everywhere on the open set $\mathbb R^ d\setminus K$ and hence so do its distributional derivatives. Choose $\delta >0$ such that the compact set $K'=\{ x:\operatorname {dist}(x,K)\leq \delta \} $ lies in $U$. For $\varepsilon <\delta $, the mollification $v_\varepsilon =v*\rho _\varepsilon $ is smooth and vanishes outside $K'$, and $\partial ^\beta v_\varepsilon =(\partial ^\beta v)*\rho _\varepsilon \to \partial ^\beta v$ in $L^ p(\mathbb R^ d)$ for $|\beta |\leq k$, by the remark preceding the lemma, applied on $\mathbb R^ d$ to a bounded open set containing $K'$, outside of which both sides vanish. Let $J$ be the maximum of $|\det D\Phi ^{-1}|$ on $K'$, and let $M\geq 1$ bound the functions $|c_{\alpha \beta }|$ on the compact set $\Phi ^{-1}(K')$. By the change of variables formula, \[  \int _ V|g\circ \Phi |^ p\, \mathrm d y=\int _ U|g(x)|^ p|\det D\Phi ^{-1}(x)|\, \mathrm d x\leq J\| g\| _ p^ p  \] for every measurable function $g$ on $U$ that vanishes outside $K'$. The smooth functions $w_\varepsilon =v_\varepsilon \circ \Phi $ vanish outside $\Phi ^{-1}(K')$. Applying this inequality to $v_\varepsilon -v$ and its derivatives, we find that $w_\varepsilon \to v\circ \Phi $ and, for $1\leq |\alpha |\leq k$, \[  \partial ^\alpha w_\varepsilon \to G_\alpha =\sum _{1\leq |\beta |\leq |\alpha |}c_{\alpha \beta }\, (\partial ^\beta v)\circ \Phi \qquad \text{in }L^ p(V),  \] with $\| G_\alpha \| _ p\leq MJ^{1/p}\sum _{1\leq |\beta |\leq |\alpha |}\| \partial ^\beta v\| _ p$. For a test function $\phi $ on $V$, we obtain \[  \begin{split}  \int (v\circ \Phi )\, \partial ^\alpha \phi \, \mathrm d y& =\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0}\int w_\varepsilon \, \partial ^\alpha \phi \, \mathrm d y\\ & =(-1)^{|\alpha |}\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0}\int \partial ^\alpha w_\varepsilon \, \phi \, \mathrm d y=(-1)^{|\alpha |}\int G_\alpha \phi \, \mathrm d y. \end{split}  \] Hence $\partial ^\alpha (v\circ \Phi )=G_\alpha \in L^ p(V)$. These functions, and $v\circ \Phi $, vanish almost everywhere outside $\Phi ^{-1}(K)$, and summing the bounds over $|\alpha |\leq k$ gives $\| v\circ \Phi \| _{W^{k,p}(V)}\leq C\| v\| _{W^{k,p}(U)}$, with $C$ depending only on $k$, $p$, $J$ and $M$, that is, on $k$, $p$, $\Phi $ and $K$ once $\delta $ has been fixed in terms of $K$ and $U$. In general, let $V'\Subset V$ be open. Choose a smooth cutoff function $\chi $ for the compact set $\Phi (\overline{V'})$ in $U$ (lemma 2.5.1 (4)). By (1), $\chi v\in W^{k,p}(U)$, and it vanishes outside $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $; by the case just treated, $(\chi v)\circ \Phi \in W^{k,p}(V)$. Since $(\chi v)\circ \Phi =v\circ \Phi $ on $V'$, we obtain $v\circ \Phi \in W^{k,p}(V')$. Hence $v\circ \Phi \in W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(V)$. $\square$

title: Lemma 2.9.15
section: 2.9 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text:
Lemma 2.9.15 . 06216156055D Let $1\leq p<\infty $ and $\varepsilon >0$. There is a constant $C_{d,\varepsilon }$, depending only on $d$ and $\varepsilon $, such that \[  \| 
abla v\| _ p\leq \varepsilon \| D^2v\| _ p+C_{d,\varepsilon }\| v\| _ p, \qquad v\in C_ c^\infty (\mathbb R^ d).  \] Proof. Let $e_ a$ be the $a$th coordinate vector and $h>0$. Taylor's formula with integral remainder gives \[  h\partial _ av(x)=v(x+he_ a)-v(x) -\int _0^ h(h-t)\partial _ a^2v(x+te_ a)\, \mathrm d t.  \] The $L^ p$ norm is invariant under translation. Moreover, $\omega (t)\, \mathrm d t=2h^{-2}(h-t)\, \mathrm d t$ is a probability measure on $[0,h]$, so Hölder's inequality gives $|\int _0^ hg\, \omega \, \mathrm d t|^ p\leq \int _0^ h|g|^ p\omega \, \mathrm d t$ for every measurable function $g$ on $[0,h]$. Applying this to $g(t)=\partial _ a^2v(x+te_ a)$, integrating in $x$ and using Tonelli's theorem, we obtain \[  \Bigl \| \int _0^ h(h-t)\partial _ a^2v(\cdot +te_ a)\, \mathrm d t\Bigr \| _ p\leq  rac{h^2}2\Bigl (\int _0^ h\| \partial _ a^2v(\cdot +te_ a)\| _ p^ p\, \omega (t)\, \mathrm d t\Bigr )^{1/p}= rac{h^2}2\| \partial _ a^2v\| _ p.  \] Hence $h\| \partial _ av\| _ p\leq 2\| v\| _ p+(h^2/2)\| \partial _ a^2v\| _ p$. Since $|
abla v|\leq \sum _ a|\partial _ av|$ and $|\partial _ a^2v|\leq |D^2v|$, summing over $a$ yields $\| 
abla v\| _ p\leq 2dh^{-1}\| v\| _ p+(dh/2)\| D^2v\| _ p$. The choice $h=2\varepsilon /d$ proves the lemma with $C_{d,\varepsilon }=d^2/\varepsilon $. $\square$

title: Lemma 2.9.16 (Morrey's inequality)
section: 2.9 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text:
Lemma 2.9.16 (Morrey's inequality) . DE7722E667E2 Let $d<p<\infty $, put $\alpha =1-d/p$, and let $B'\Subset B$ be Euclidean balls in $\mathbb R^ d$. Every $v\in W^{1,p}(B)$ has a representative that is continuous on $B$ and satisfies \[  \| v\| _{C^{0,\alpha }(\overline{B'})}\leq C\| v\| _{W^{1,p}(B)},  \] where $C$ depends only on $d,p,B',B$. Consequently, for an open set $U\subset \mathbb R^ d$, every function in $W^{2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ has a representative in $C^{1,\alpha }_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. Proof. We prove the estimate for smooth $v$, pass to general $v$ by mollification, and then apply the result to first derivatives. Assume first that $v$ is smooth on $B$. Let $Q\subset B$ be a ball of radius $r$, let $v_ Q=|Q|^{-1}\int _ Qv$ be the average of $v$ over $Q$, and let $x\in Q$. We claim that \[  |v(x)-v_ Q|\leq C_ d\int _ Q|
abla v(z)|\, |x-z|^{1-d}\, \mathrm d z.  \] For $z\in Q$, write $z=x+s	heta $ with $s=|z-x|$ and $	heta \in S^{d-1}$; then $|v(z)-v(x)|\leq \int _0^ s|
abla v(x+t	heta )|\, \mathrm d t$, and $|v(x)-v_ Q|$ is at most the average over $z\in Q$ of these segment integrals. Since $Q$ is convex and open and contains $x$, for each $	heta $ the radii $s>0$ with $x+s	heta \in Q$ form an interval $0<s<R(	heta )$, and $R(	heta )\leq 2r$. In polar coordinates about $x$ (( 3.1.2 ) on $B(x,2r)\supset Q$), the average of the segment integrals is \[   rac1{|Q|}\int _{S^{d-1}}\int _0^{R(	heta )}s^{d-1}\int _0^ s|
abla v(x+t	heta )|\, \mathrm d t\, \mathrm d s\, \mathrm d S(	heta ).  \] Interchanging the integrals in $s$ and $t$ produces the factor $|Q|^{-1}\int _ t^{R(	heta )}s^{d-1}\, \mathrm d s$, which is at most $(2r)^ d/(d|Q|)$ and hence bounded by a constant depending only on $d$. The remaining integral $\int _{S^{d-1}}\int _0^{R(	heta )}|
abla v(x+t	heta )|\, \mathrm d t\, \mathrm d S(	heta )$ is the integral on the right side of the claim, written in polar coordinates. This proves the claim. By Hölder's inequality with $p'=p/(p-1)$, the right side of the claim is at most $C_{d,p}r^{1-d/p}\| 
abla v\| _{L^ p(Q)}$, because \[  \int _ Q|x-z|^{(1-d)p'}\, \mathrm d z\leq \int _{B(x,2r)}|x-z|^{(1-d)p'}\, \mathrm d z=C_{d,p}r^{(1-d)p'+d},  \] and this integral is finite exactly when $(1-d)p'>-d$, that is, when $p>d$. (For $d=1$ the exponent $(1-d)p'$ is zero.) Let $\delta >0$ be the distance from $B'$ to $\mathbb R^ d\setminus B$. If $x,y\in B'$ and $0<|x-y|<\delta /2$, the ball $Q=B(x,2|x-y|)$ lies in $B$ and contains $x$ and $y$. Applying the preceding bound at both points gives \[  |v(x)-v(y)|\leq C_{d,p}|x-y|^{1-d/p}\| 
abla v\| _{L^ p(B)}.  \] For $x\in B'$, the same bound on the ball $Q=B(x,\delta /2)\subset B$, together with the estimate $|v_ Q|\leq |Q|^{-1/p}\| v\| _{L^ p(B)}$ from Hölder's inequality, gives $\sup _{B'}|v|\leq C\| v\| _{W^{1,p}(B)}$ with $C$ depending on $d,p,\delta $. If $|x-y|\geq \delta /2$, then $|v(x)-v(y)|/|x-y|^\alpha \leq 2(\delta /2)^{-\alpha }\sup _{B'}|v|$. These bounds prove the estimate for smooth $v$ on $B'$, and hence on $\overline{B'}$, since $v$ is continuous on $B\supset \overline{B'}$. For general $v\in W^{1,p}(B)$, choose a ball $B''$, depending only on $B'$ and $B$, with $B'\Subset B''\Subset B$, and let $v_\varepsilon =v*ho _\varepsilon $, which is smooth on $B''$ for small $\varepsilon $. By the remark preceding lemma 2.9.14 , $\partial _ av_\varepsilon =(\partial _ av)_\varepsilon $, and $v_\varepsilon 	o v$ and $\partial _ av_\varepsilon 	o \partial _ av$ in $L^ p(B'')$. The estimate for smooth functions, applied on $B'\Subset B''$ to the differences of the $v_\varepsilon $, shows that they form a Cauchy family in the norm of $C^{0,\alpha }(\overline{B'})$. Their uniform limit is continuous on $\overline{B'}$, agrees almost everywhere with $v$, and satisfies the asserted estimate, because $\| v\| _{W^{1,p}(B'')}\leq \| v\| _{W^{1,p}(B)}$. Two continuous functions that agree almost everywhere on an open set agree everywhere on it. Hence the continuous representatives obtained from different balls $B'\Subset B$ agree on their overlaps and define a single continuous representative on $B$. Finally, let $v\in W^{2,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. On every ball $B\Subset U$, both $v$ and its first derivatives $\partial _ av$ belong to $W^{1,p}(B)$. By the preceding paragraph, on each smaller ball $B'\Subset B$ the mollifications $v_\varepsilon $ and $\partial _ av_\varepsilon =(\partial _ av)_\varepsilon $ converge uniformly to the continuous representatives $	ilde v$ of $v$ and $	ilde w_ a$ of $\partial _ av$. Passing to the limit in \[  v_\varepsilon (x+he_ a)-v_\varepsilon (x)=\int _0^ h\partial _ av_\varepsilon (x+te_ a)\, \mathrm d t  \] shows that $	ilde v$ has the continuous partial derivatives $\partial _ a	ilde v=	ilde w_ a$. Hence $	ilde v$ is continuously differentiable, and by the first part its first derivatives are Hölder continuous with exponent $\alpha $ on each $\overline{B'}$. Every compact subset of $U$ is covered by finitely many such balls $B'$; pairs of points closer than a Lebesgue number of this cover lie in a common ball, and for the remaining pairs the supremum bound suffices. Hence $	ilde v\in C^{1,\alpha }_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$. $\square$

title: 2.9.17 Unitarily invariant measures
section: 2.9 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text:
The incidence argument outlined at the beginning of the chapter averages over complex directions and over complex hyperplanes, so we need invariant probability measures on complex projective space and on the Grassmannian of hyperplanes. We construct them from the Gaussian measure on matrices, compute the measure of small balls in projective space, and introduce orthonormal frames on hyperplanes that depend on the hyperplane in a Borel way. We identify $\mathbb C^ n$ with $\mathbb R^{2n}$ and write $\langle z,wangle =\sum _ jz_ j\overline{w_ j}$ for the Hermitian inner product, so that the Euclidean inner product is $\operatorname{Re}\langle z,wangle $. The unitary group $\mathrm U(n)$ consists of the complex $n	imes n$ matrices $U$ with $U^*U=1$, where $U^*$ is the conjugate transpose; it is compact, being closed and bounded in the space of matrices. Proposition 2.9.18 . D01DFDB6AE9A There is a Borel probability measure $\eta $ on $\mathrm U(n)$ that is invariant under left and right multiplication by elements of $\mathrm U(n)$. Let $Y$ be a nonempty metric space on which $\mathrm U(n)$ acts continuously and transitively. Then $Y$ is compact, and it carries a unique $\mathrm U(n)$-invariant Borel probability measure; for every $y_0\in Y$, this measure is the image of $\eta $ under the map $g\mapsto gy_0$. In particular, the unit sphere of $\mathbb C^ n$ and the complex Grassmannians described below carry unique unitarily invariant probability measures. Proof. Identify the space of complex $n	imes n$ matrices with $\mathbb R^{2n^2}$ through the real and imaginary parts of the entries, and let $\gamma $ be the measure on it with density $\mathrm e^{-\pi \operatorname {tr}(X^*X)}$ with respect to Lebesgue measure. Since $\operatorname {tr}(X^*X)=\sum _{j,k}|X_{jk}|^2$, this density is the Gaussian $\mathrm e^{-\pi |x|^2}$ on $\mathbb R^{2n^2}$, so $\gamma $ is a probability measure by lemma 2.9.2 (with $\xi =0$ and $t=1$). The singular matrices form a $\gamma $-null set: they are the zero set of the real polynomial $|\det X|^2$, which is not identically zero since $\det 1=1$, and the zero set of such a polynomial is Lebesgue null. To prove the last fact, let $P$ be a real polynomial in $m\geq 1$ variables that is not identically zero; we argue by induction on $m$. If $m=1$, the zero set is finite. If $m\geq 2$, write $P=\sum _ kc_ k(x')x_ m^ k$ as a polynomial in the last variable, with coefficients $c_ k$ that are polynomials in $x'=(x_1,\ldots ,x_{m-1})$. Some $c_ k$ is not identically zero, so by induction the common zero set $Z'$ of the coefficients is null in $\mathbb R^{m-1}$. For $x'
otin Z'$, the polynomial $P(x',\cdot )$ is not identically zero and has finitely many zeros. By Tonelli's theorem applied to the indicator function of the closed set $\{ P=0\} $, this set is null. For invertible $X$ define \[  Q(X)=X(X^*X)^{-1/2},  \] where $(X^*X)^{1/2}$ is the positive square root of the positive definite matrix $X^*X$. By the spectral theorem for Hermitian matrices, this square root exists and is unique. It depends continuously on the matrix. Indeed, let $A_ k	o A$ be positive definite matrices. The square roots $A_ k^{1/2}$ are bounded, since $\operatorname {tr}(A_ k^{1/2}A_ k^{1/2})=\operatorname {tr}A_ k$. Every convergent subsequence of them has a positive semidefinite limit $S$ with $S^2=A$; then $S$ is invertible, hence positive definite, and $S=A^{1/2}$ by uniqueness. A bounded sequence of matrices all of whose convergent subsequences have the same limit converges to it, so $A_ k^{1/2}	o A^{1/2}$. Since inversion is continuous on invertible matrices, $Q$ is continuous on the open set of invertible matrices, and $Q(X)^*Q(X)=(X^*X)^{-1/2}X^*X(X^*X)^{-1/2}=1$. Let $\eta $ be the image under $Q$ of the restriction of $\gamma $ to the invertible matrices; it is a Borel probability measure on $\mathrm U(n)$. Fix $U,V\in \mathrm U(n)$. The map $X\mapsto UXV$ is real linear and preserves $\operatorname {tr}(X^*X)$, so it is orthogonal on $\mathbb R^{2n^2}$ and preserves $\gamma $. By uniqueness of positive square roots, $(V^*X^*XV)^{1/2}=V^*(X^*X)^{1/2}V$, and therefore $Q(UXV)=UQ(X)V$. Consequently the image of $\eta $ under $g\mapsto UgV$ is the image of $\gamma $ under $X\mapsto Q(UXV)$, which is $\eta $ because $X\mapsto UXV$ preserves $\gamma $. This proves the invariance of $\eta $ on both sides. Now let $Y$ be as in the statement and fix $y_0\in Y$. By transitivity, $Y$ is the image of the compact space $\mathrm U(n)$ under the continuous map $g\mapsto gy_0$, so $Y$ is compact, and hence separable. Let $\sigma $ be the image of $\eta $ under $g\mapsto gy_0$. For $h\in \mathrm U(n)$, the image of $\sigma $ under $h$ is the image of $\eta $ under $g\mapsto hgy_0$, which is $\sigma $ by left invariance; thus $\sigma $ is invariant. Let $f$ be continuous on $Y$. Every $y\in Y$ has the form $hy_0$, by transitivity, and right invariance gives \[  \int f(gy)\, \mathrm d\eta (g)=\int f(ghy_0)\, \mathrm d\eta (g)=\int f\, \mathrm d\sigma .  \] Let $	au $ be any invariant Borel probability measure on $Y$. We integrate the last identity against $	au $ and apply Fubini's theorem to the bounded continuous function $(g,y)\mapsto f(gy)$ on $\mathrm U(n)	imes Y$, which is product-measurable by lemma 2.2.8 because $\mathrm U(n)$ and $Y$ are separable metric spaces. We obtain \[  \int f\, \mathrm d\sigma =\int _{\mathrm U(n)}\int _ Yf(gy)\, \mathrm d	au (y)\, \mathrm d\eta (g)=\int f\, \mathrm d	au .  \] Thus $\sigma $ and $	au $ agree on continuous functions. For a nonempty closed set $F\subset Y$, the continuous functions $\max \{ 0,1-j\operatorname {dist}(y,F)\} $ decrease to $\mathbf1_ F$, so dominated convergence gives $\sigma (F)=	au (F)$. The closed sets are stable under finite intersections and generate the Borel $\sigma $-algebra, so lemma 2.2.6 (2) gives $\sigma =	au $. In particular $\sigma $ does not depend on $y_0$. Finally, $\mathrm U(n)$ acts continuously on the unit sphere of $\mathbb C^ n$, and transitively: every unit vector is the first column of a unitary matrix, obtained by completing it to an orthonormal basis with the Gram–Schmidt process. For the Grassmannians, these properties are verified below, where they are introduced. $\square$ For an integer $0\leq k\leq n$, we realize the complex Grassmannian $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(k,n)$ of $k$-dimensional complex subspaces of $\mathbb C^ n$ as the set of Hermitian matrices $P$ with $P^2=P$ and $\operatorname {tr}P=k$. By the spectral theorem, such a matrix has the eigenvalues $0$ and $1$ only, so it is the orthogonal projection onto its image, which has dimension $\operatorname {tr}P=k$; conversely, the orthogonal projection onto a $k$-dimensional subspace is such a matrix. The set $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(k,n)$ is closed and bounded, since $\operatorname {tr}(P^*P)=\operatorname {tr}P=k$, and hence compact. The unitary group acts continuously by $P\mapsto UPU^*$, which replaces the image of $P$ by its image under $U$. The action is transitive: given two $k$-dimensional subspaces, choose orthonormal bases of $\mathbb C^ n$ whose first $k$ vectors span them; the unitary matrix carrying one basis to the other maps one subspace onto the other. Complex projective space $\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ is the case $k=1$. For $\xi \in \mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ we write $P_\xi $ for the corresponding rank-one projection, and we denote the invariant probability measure on $\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ by $\sigma $. The Hopf map $q\colon S^{2n-1}	o \mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ sends a unit vector $e$ to the complex line it spans, that is, to the projection $ee^*$. For $\xi ,\xi '\in \mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ with unit representatives $e,e'$, set \[  d(\xi ,\xi ')=\arccos |\langle e,e'angle |\in [0,\pi /2];  \] this does not depend on the choice of representatives. We claim that $d$ is a metric inducing the topology of $\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$. Let $\delta (e,e')=\arccos \operatorname{Re}\langle e,e'angle \in [0,\pi ]$ be the angle between two unit vectors, that is, their great-circle distance on $S^{2n-1}$. Since the maximum of $\operatorname{Re}\langle \mathrm e^{\mathrm i	heta }e,e'angle $ over $	heta $ is $|\langle e,e'angle |$ and $\arccos $ is decreasing, the number $d(\xi ,\xi ')$ is the minimum of $\delta $ over the unit representatives of $\xi $ and $\xi '$. The angle $\delta $ satisfies the triangle inequality. Indeed, let $e,e',e''$ be unit vectors, put $a=\delta (e,e')$ and $b=\delta (e',e'')$, and write $e=\cos a\, e'+\sin a\, u$ and $e''=\cos b\, e'+\sin b\, w$ with unit vectors $u,w$ orthogonal to $e'$ for the Euclidean inner product. Then $\operatorname{Re}\langle e,e''angle =\cos a\cos b+\sin a\sin b\operatorname{Re}\langle u,wangle \geq \cos (a+b)$ by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality. Hence $\delta (e,e'')\leq a+b$ when $a+b\leq \pi $, and this inequality is trivial when $a+b>\pi $. To deduce the triangle inequality for $d$, fix a unit representative $e'$ of $\xi '$, and choose the representatives $e$ of $\xi $ and $e''$ of $\xi ''$ such that $\delta (e,e')=d(\xi ,\xi ')$ and $\delta (e',e'')=d(\xi ',\xi '')$. Then \[  d(\xi ,\xi '')\leq \delta (e,e'')\leq d(\xi ,\xi ')+d(\xi ',\xi '').  \] The function $d$ is symmetric, and $d(\xi ,\xi ')=0$ forces equality in the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality $|\langle e,e'angle |\leq 1$, hence $\xi =\xi '$. Finally, $\cos ^2d(\xi ,\xi ')=|\langle e,e'angle |^2=\operatorname {tr}(P_\xi P_{\xi '})$ depends continuously on the two projections. Therefore the identity map from $\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$, with its compact matrix topology, to the metric space $(\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C),d)$ is a continuous bijection onto a Hausdorff space, hence a homeomorphism. Since $q$ is a continuous surjection from a compact space onto a Hausdorff space, this topology is also the quotient topology of the Hopf map. Lemma 2.9.19 . 80451E036222 Let $n\geq 1$, $0<a\leq \pi /2$ and $\xi _0\in \mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$. Then \[  \sigma \{ \xi :d(\xi ,\xi _0)<a\} =(\sin a)^{2n-2}.  \] In particular, this ball has $\sigma $-measure at most $a^{2n-2}$. Proof. If $n=1$, then $\mathbb P^0(\mathbb C)$ is a single point, and both sides equal $1$; so let $n\geq 2$. Let $\gamma $ be the probability measure on $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ with density $\mathrm e^{-\pi |z|^2}$. Unitary maps are orthogonal on $\mathbb R^{2n}$, so they preserve Lebesgue measure and $|z|$; hence $\gamma $ is unitarily invariant. Moreover $\gamma (\{ 0\} )=0$. The map $z\mapsto \mathbb Cz$ from $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $ to $\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$, that is, $z\mapsto zz^*/|z|^2$, is continuous and commutes with the action of $\mathrm U(n)$. Hence the image of $\gamma $ under this map is a unitarily invariant Borel probability measure, and by the uniqueness in proposition 2.9.18 it is $\sigma $. The metric $d$ is unitarily invariant, because unitary matrices preserve $\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle $. Since $\sigma $ is invariant and the unitary group acts transitively, we may therefore take $\xi _0=\mathbb Ce_1$, the first coordinate line. Write $z=(z_1,z')$ with $z'\in \mathbb C^{n-1}$. For the line $\xi =\mathbb Cz$, the condition $d(\xi ,\xi _0)<a$ means $|z_1|>\cos a\, |z|$, because $\arccos $ is strictly decreasing; that is, $|z_1|^2\sin ^2a>\cos ^2a\, |z'|^2$, or $|z_1|^2>\cot ^2a\, |z'|^2$, where $\cot (\pi /2)=0$. Thus the preimage of the ball under $z\mapsto \mathbb Cz$ is the set of $z
eq 0$ with $|z_1|^2>\cot ^2a\, |z'|^2$. We compute its $\gamma $-measure by Fubini's theorem, integrating first in $z_1$. For $c\geq 0$, polar coordinates in $\mathbb C$ give \[  \int _{\{ w\in \mathbb C:|w|^2>c\} }\mathrm e^{-\pi |w|^2}\, \mathrm d w=2\pi \int _{\sqrt c}^\infty r\mathrm e^{-\pi r^2}\, \mathrm d r=\mathrm e^{-\pi c},  \] and we apply this with $c=\cot ^2a\, |z'|^2$. Using lemma 2.9.2 in $\mathbb C^{n-1}=\mathbb R^{2n-2}$ with $\xi =0$ and $t=1+\cot ^2a$, we obtain \[  \sigma \{ \xi :d(\xi ,\xi _0)<a\} =\int _{\mathbb C^{n-1}}\mathrm e^{-\pi (1+\cot ^2a)|z'|^2}\, \mathrm d z'=(1+\cot ^2a)^{-(n-1)}=(\sin a)^{2n-2}.  \] The last assertion follows from $\sin a\leq a$. $\square$ We write $\mathcal H=\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(n-1,n)$ for the space of complex hyperplanes through the origin in $\mathbb C^ n$, and $
u $ for its invariant probability measure. For $H\in \mathcal H$, the orthogonal projection $P_ H$ onto $H$ is the matrix representing $H$, and the orthogonal complement $H^\perp $ is a complex line. Let $m_ H$ be the Lebesgue measure of $H$, that is, the image of Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb C^{n-1}=\mathbb R^{2n-2}$ under any complex linear isometry $\mathbb C^{n-1}	o H$. To integrate functions that depend on $H$, we use orthonormal frames of $H$ that depend on $H$ in a Borel way. Let $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$ be the standard basis of $\mathbb C^ n$, and order the $(n-1)$-element subsets $I$ of $\{ 1,\ldots ,n\} $. For each $I$, let $W_ I$ be the set of hyperplanes $H$ for which the vectors $P_ He_ i$, $i\in I$, are linearly independent. Since $\langle P_ He_ i,P_ He_ jangle =\langle P_ He_ i,e_ jangle $, the Gram determinant of these vectors is the principal minor of $P_ H$ with indices in $I$, so $W_ I$ is open. These sets cover $\mathcal H$, because the $n$ vectors $P_ He_1,\ldots ,P_ He_ n$ span the $(n-1)$-dimensional space $H$, so that $n-1$ of them form a basis. Let $W_ I'$ be the Borel set of hyperplanes $H$ for which $I$ is the first index with $H\in W_ I$; these finitely many sets partition $\mathcal H$. For $H\in W_ I'$, the Gram–Schmidt process applied to $(P_ He_ i)_{i\in I}$ gives an orthonormal basis of $H$, and hence a complex linear isometry $T_ H\colon \mathbb C^{n-1}	o H$. The Gram–Schmidt process depends continuously on linearly independent families, so the map $(H,w)\mapsto T_ Hw$ is continuous on each set $W_ I'	imes \mathbb C^{n-1}$. Hence the preimage of an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$ under this map is a finite union of relatively open subsets of these Borel sets, and $(H,w)\mapsto T_ Hw$ is a Borel map from $\mathcal H	imes \mathbb C^{n-1}$ to $\mathbb C^ n$. A map into a product of two separable metric spaces whose components are Borel is Borel, because the preimage of a product of Borel sets is Borel and these products generate the Borel sets of the product (lemma 2.2.8 ). In particular, $(H,w)\mapsto (H,T_ Hw)$ is a Borel map into $\mathcal H	imes \mathbb C^ n$. Consequently, for every nonnegative Borel function $f$ on the closed set $\{ (H,c)\in \mathcal H	imes \mathbb C^ n:c\in H\} $, the function \[  H\longmapsto \int _ Hf(H,c)\, \mathrm d m_ H(c)=\int _{\mathbb C^{n-1}}f(H,T_ Hw)\, \mathrm d w  \] is Borel, by Tonelli's theorem (proposition 2.2.7 ), applied with respect to $
u $ and Lebesgue measure to the Borel function $(H,w)\mapsto f(H,T_ Hw)$, which is product-measurable by lemma 2.2.8 , since $\mathcal H$ and $\mathbb C^{n-1}$ are separable metric spaces. The value of the integral does not depend on the frame, because a change of orthonormal frame preserves Lebesgue measure.

title: Proposition 2.9.18
section: 2.9 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text: Proposition 2.9.18 . D01DFDB6AE9A There is a Borel probability measure $\eta $ on $\mathrm U(n)$ that is invariant under left and right multiplication by elements of $\mathrm U(n)$. Let $Y$ be a nonempty metric space on which $\mathrm U(n)$ acts continuously and transitively. Then $Y$ is compact, and it carries a unique $\mathrm U(n)$-invariant Borel probability measure; for every $y_0\in Y$, this measure is the image of $\eta $ under the map $g\mapsto gy_0$. In particular, the unit sphere of $\mathbb C^ n$ and the complex Grassmannians described below carry unique unitarily invariant probability measures. Proof. Identify the space of complex $n\times n$ matrices with $\mathbb R^{2n^2}$ through the real and imaginary parts of the entries, and let $\gamma $ be the measure on it with density $\mathrm e^{-\pi \operatorname {tr}(X^*X)}$ with respect to Lebesgue measure. Since $\operatorname {tr}(X^*X)=\sum _{j,k}|X_{jk}|^2$, this density is the Gaussian $\mathrm e^{-\pi |x|^2}$ on $\mathbb R^{2n^2}$, so $\gamma $ is a probability measure by lemma 2.9.2 (with $\xi =0$ and $t=1$). The singular matrices form a $\gamma $-null set: they are the zero set of the real polynomial $|\det X|^2$, which is not identically zero since $\det 1=1$, and the zero set of such a polynomial is Lebesgue null. To prove the last fact, let $P$ be a real polynomial in $m\geq 1$ variables that is not identically zero; we argue by induction on $m$. If $m=1$, the zero set is finite. If $m\geq 2$, write $P=\sum _ kc_ k(x')x_ m^ k$ as a polynomial in the last variable, with coefficients $c_ k$ that are polynomials in $x'=(x_1,\ldots ,x_{m-1})$. Some $c_ k$ is not identically zero, so by induction the common zero set $Z'$ of the coefficients is null in $\mathbb R^{m-1}$. For $x'\notin Z'$, the polynomial $P(x',\cdot )$ is not identically zero and has finitely many zeros. By Tonelli's theorem applied to the indicator function of the closed set $\{ P=0\} $, this set is null. For invertible $X$ define \[  Q(X)=X(X^*X)^{-1/2},  \] where $(X^*X)^{1/2}$ is the positive square root of the positive definite matrix $X^*X$. By the spectral theorem for Hermitian matrices, this square root exists and is unique. It depends continuously on the matrix. Indeed, let $A_ k\to A$ be positive definite matrices. The square roots $A_ k^{1/2}$ are bounded, since $\operatorname {tr}(A_ k^{1/2}A_ k^{1/2})=\operatorname {tr}A_ k$. Every convergent subsequence of them has a positive semidefinite limit $S$ with $S^2=A$; then $S$ is invertible, hence positive definite, and $S=A^{1/2}$ by uniqueness. A bounded sequence of matrices all of whose convergent subsequences have the same limit converges to it, so $A_ k^{1/2}\to A^{1/2}$. Since inversion is continuous on invertible matrices, $Q$ is continuous on the open set of invertible matrices, and $Q(X)^*Q(X)=(X^*X)^{-1/2}X^*X(X^*X)^{-1/2}=1$. Let $\eta $ be the image under $Q$ of the restriction of $\gamma $ to the invertible matrices; it is a Borel probability measure on $\mathrm U(n)$. Fix $U,V\in \mathrm U(n)$. The map $X\mapsto UXV$ is real linear and preserves $\operatorname {tr}(X^*X)$, so it is orthogonal on $\mathbb R^{2n^2}$ and preserves $\gamma $. By uniqueness of positive square roots, $(V^*X^*XV)^{1/2}=V^*(X^*X)^{1/2}V$, and therefore $Q(UXV)=UQ(X)V$. Consequently the image of $\eta $ under $g\mapsto UgV$ is the image of $\gamma $ under $X\mapsto Q(UXV)$, which is $\eta $ because $X\mapsto UXV$ preserves $\gamma $. This proves the invariance of $\eta $ on both sides. Now let $Y$ be as in the statement and fix $y_0\in Y$. By transitivity, $Y$ is the image of the compact space $\mathrm U(n)$ under the continuous map $g\mapsto gy_0$, so $Y$ is compact, and hence separable. Let $\sigma $ be the image of $\eta $ under $g\mapsto gy_0$. For $h\in \mathrm U(n)$, the image of $\sigma $ under $h$ is the image of $\eta $ under $g\mapsto hgy_0$, which is $\sigma $ by left invariance; thus $\sigma $ is invariant. Let $f$ be continuous on $Y$. Every $y\in Y$ has the form $hy_0$, by transitivity, and right invariance gives \[  \int f(gy)\, \mathrm d\eta (g)=\int f(ghy_0)\, \mathrm d\eta (g)=\int f\, \mathrm d\sigma .  \] Let $\tau $ be any invariant Borel probability measure on $Y$. We integrate the last identity against $\tau $ and apply Fubini's theorem to the bounded continuous function $(g,y)\mapsto f(gy)$ on $\mathrm U(n)\times Y$, which is product-measurable by lemma 2.2.8 because $\mathrm U(n)$ and $Y$ are separable metric spaces. We obtain \[  \int f\, \mathrm d\sigma =\int _{\mathrm U(n)}\int _ Yf(gy)\, \mathrm d\tau (y)\, \mathrm d\eta (g)=\int f\, \mathrm d\tau .  \] Thus $\sigma $ and $\tau $ agree on continuous functions. For a nonempty closed set $F\subset Y$, the continuous functions $\max \{ 0,1-j\operatorname {dist}(y,F)\} $ decrease to $\mathbf1_ F$, so dominated convergence gives $\sigma (F)=\tau (F)$. The closed sets are stable under finite intersections and generate the Borel $\sigma $-algebra, so lemma 2.2.6 (2) gives $\sigma =\tau $. In particular $\sigma $ does not depend on $y_0$. Finally, $\mathrm U(n)$ acts continuously on the unit sphere of $\mathbb C^ n$, and transitively: every unit vector is the first column of a unitary matrix, obtained by completing it to an orthonormal basis with the Gram–Schmidt process. For the Grassmannians, these properties are verified below, where they are introduced. $\square$

title: 2.9.20 Circle selection and high-value sets
section: 2.9 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text: An affine complex line in $\mathbb C^ n$ is a set $L=a+\mathbb Cb$ with $a\in \mathbb C^ n$ and $b\in \mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $. For an open set $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$, we identify the section $D\cap L$ with the open set $\{ \zeta \in \mathbb C:a+\zeta b\in D\} $, and we call a function on a connected component of $D\cap L$ subharmonic if its composite with $\zeta \mapsto a+\zeta b$ is subharmonic in the sense of definition 3.4.2 . In the plane, the spherical means of ( 3.4.3 ) are averages with respect to arc length: the surface measure $S$ on the unit circle (subsection 3.1.1 ) is the image of Lebesgue measure on $[0,2\pi )$ under $\theta \mapsto \mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }$. Indeed, by the change of variables formula for $(t,\theta )\mapsto t\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }$, whose Jacobian determinant is $t$, the cone over an arc $\{ \mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }:\theta _1\leq \theta <\theta _2\} $ with $0\leq \theta _1\leq \theta _2\leq 2\pi $ has area $(\theta _2-\theta _1)/2$, so the arc has $S$-measure $\theta _2-\theta _1$. These arcs are closed under finite intersections, and every open subset of the circle is a countable union of them, so they generate the Borel sets of the circle. Since the whole circle is such an arc, lemma 2.2.6 (2) identifies the two finite measures. Hence \[  M_ w(\zeta ,r)=\frac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }w(\zeta +r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta })\, \mathrm d\theta  \] for an upper semicontinuous function $w$ on an open subset of $\mathbb C$ containing $\overline{B(\zeta ,r)}$. Consequently, subharmonicity on $D\cap L$ does not depend on the parametrization. Two parametrizations differ by a map $\psi (\zeta )=\alpha \zeta +\beta $ with $\alpha \neq 0$, which is a homeomorphism and maps the circle of radius $r$ about $\zeta $ onto the circle of radius $|\alpha |r$ about $\psi (\zeta )$. Since $\psi (\zeta +r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta })=\psi (\zeta )+|\alpha |r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i(\theta +\arg \alpha )}$ and Lebesgue measure on the circle is invariant under rotations, the arc-length formula gives $M_{w\circ \psi }(\zeta ,r)=M_ w(\psi (\zeta ),|\alpha |r)$. In the proof of theorem 2.9.22 we must choose, measurably in the circle, a point of each circle at which a given function is large. The sets of admissible points will be closed and have positive length, and for such sets the arc-length median provides an explicit Borel choice. Lemma 2.9.21 . DC992DBF55C7 Let $T$ be a separable metric space, and let $F\subset T\times [0,2\pi ]$ be a Borel set whose sections $F_ t=\{ \theta :(t,\theta )\in F\} $ are closed and have positive Lebesgue measure for every $t\in T$. Then there is a Borel map $a\colon T\to [0,2\pi ]$ such that $a(t)\in F_ t$ for every $t\in T$. Proof. Write $|\cdot |$ for Lebesgue measure on $[0,2\pi ]$, and put $\ell (t)=|F_ t|$ and $A_ t(b)=|F_ t\cap [0,b]|$ for $b\in [0,2\pi ]$. We first show that, for fixed $b$, the function $t\mapsto A_ t(b)$ is Borel; with $b=2\pi $, so is $\ell $. Since $T$ and $[0,2\pi ]$ are separable metric spaces, the Borel sets of $T\times [0,2\pi ]$ form the $\sigma $-algebra generated by the products of Borel sets (lemma 2.2.8 ). Hence the sections $G_ t$ of a Borel set $G$ are Borel, because the sets all of whose sections are Borel form a $\sigma $-algebra containing these products. The class of Borel sets $G\subset T\times [0,2\pi ]$ for which $t\mapsto |G_ t\cap [0,b]|$ is Borel contains the products $B_1\times B_2$ of Borel sets, for which this function is $\mathbf1_{B_1}(t)|B_2\cap [0,b]|$. It is closed under complements, since the complement of $G$ gives $b-|G_ t\cap [0,b]|$, and under countable disjoint unions, which give sums. Since the products of Borel sets are closed under finite intersections, lemma 2.2.6 (1) shows that the class contains every Borel set. For fixed $t$, the function $A_ t$ is nondecreasing and $1$-Lipschitz, with $A_ t(0)=0$ and $A_ t(2\pi )=\ell (t)>0$. Define \[  a(t)=\inf \{ b\in \mathbb Q\cap [0,2\pi ]:A_ t(b)\geq \ell (t)/2\} .  \] Because $A_ t$ is continuous and nondecreasing and $0<\ell (t)/2<\ell (t)$, the set of all $b\in [0,2\pi ]$ with $A_ t(b)\geq \ell (t)/2$ is an interval $[b_ t,2\pi ]$ with $0<b_ t<2\pi $ and $A_ t(b_ t)=\ell (t)/2$. The rational numbers are dense in this interval, so $a(t)=b_ t$ and $A_ t(a(t))=\ell (t)/2$. The map $a$ is Borel, since for every $c\in (0,2\pi ]$ \[  \{ t:a(t)<c\} =\bigcup _{b\in \mathbb Q\cap [0,c)}\{ t:A_ t(b)\geq \ell (t)/2\} .  \] Finally, suppose that $a(t)\notin F_ t$. Since $F_ t$ is closed and $a(t)>0$, some interval $[a(t)-\varepsilon ,a(t)]$ with $\varepsilon >0$ misses $F_ t$, and $A_ t$ is constant on it. A rational number $b$ in this interval with $b<a(t)$ then satisfies $A_ t(b)=\ell (t)/2$, contradicting the definition of $a(t)$. Hence $a(t)\in F_ t$. $\square$ Theorem 2.9.22 . 2C0F0197F3BF Let $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, with $n\geq 2$, and let $x\in D$ and $R>0$ satisfy $\overline{B(x,R)}\subset D$. Let $u\colon D\to [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a Borel function such that, for every complex line $L$ through $x$, the restriction of $u$ to the connected component of $D\cap L$ containing $x$ is subharmonic, and put $A=u(x)$. Then there is a Borel probability measure $\mu $ carried by the Borel set \[  E=\{ y\in \mathbb C^ n:R/2\leq |y-x|\leq R,\  u(y)\geq A\}   \] such that $I_{2n-2}(\mu )\leq C_ nR^{-(2n-2)}$, where the constant $C_ n$ depends only on $n$. Proof. We obtain $\mu $ by choosing, in a Borel way, a point of $E$ on each circle of radius $r\in [R/2,R]$ centered at $x$ in a complex line through $x$, and then we estimate its energy. For $\xi \in \mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ we first choose a unit vector $e_0(\xi )\in \xi $ in a Borel way: if $j$ is the first index with $(P_\xi )_{jj}>0$, put $e_0(\xi )=P_\xi e_ j/\sqrt{(P_\xi )_{jj}}$. Since $|P_\xi e_ j|^2=\langle P_\xi e_ j,e_ j\rangle =(P_\xi )_{jj}$, this is a unit vector in $\xi $. The set of $\xi $ with a given first index $j$ is Borel, and $e_0$ is continuous on it. Let $r\in [R/2,R]$ and $\xi \in \mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$. The circle $\theta \mapsto x+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }e_0(\xi )$ lies in the closed disc $\{ x+\zeta e_0(\xi ):|\zeta |\leq r\} $, which is connected, contains $x$ and is contained in $D$; hence it lies in the connected component containing $x$ of the section of $D$ by the line $x+\xi $. On this component $u$ is subharmonic; in particular it is upper semicontinuous and bounded above on the circle, and by theorem 3.4.5 (2) and the arc-length formula for circle means at the beginning of this section, it satisfies the submean inequality \[  A=u(x)\leq \frac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }u(x+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }e_0(\xi ))\, \mathrm d\theta .  \] Let \[  F_{r,\xi }=\{ \theta \in [0,2\pi ]:u(x+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }e_0(\xi ))\geq A\} .  \] This set is closed by upper semicontinuity, and it has positive length. If $A=-\infty $, it is the whole interval $[0,2\pi ]$. If $A$ is finite and $F_{r,\xi }$ were a null set, then $A-u$ would be positive almost everywhere on the circle, so the circle mean of $u$ would be strictly less than $A$, contradicting the submean inequality. The set of $(r,\xi ,\theta )$ with $\theta \in F_{r,\xi }$ is Borel, because $u$ is Borel and the map $(r,\xi ,\theta )\mapsto x+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }e_0(\xi )$ into $\overline{B(x,R)}$ is Borel, being continuous on each of the finitely many Borel sets on which $e_0$ is continuous. Since $[R/2,R]\times \mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ is a compact, hence separable, metric space, lemma 2.9.21 gives a Borel map $(r,\xi )\mapsto \alpha (r,\xi )$ with $\alpha (r,\xi )\in F_{r,\xi }$. Put $e(r,\xi )=\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\alpha (r,\xi )}e_0(\xi )$ and $\Psi (r,\xi )=x+re(r,\xi )$. Then $\Psi $ is Borel, hence product-measurable (lemma 2.2.8 ), and it takes its values in $E$. Let $\mu $ be the image under $\Psi $ of the product of normalized Lebesgue measure on $[R/2,R]$ and $\sigma $. It is a Borel probability measure carried by $E$. It remains to estimate the energy; the estimate does not depend on the choice of the phases $\alpha (r,\xi )$. For $r,r'\in [R/2,R]$ and unit vectors $e,e'$ spanning $\xi ,\xi '$, \[  |re-r'e'|^2=(r-r')^2+rr'|e-e'|^2 \geq (r-r')^2+\frac{R^2}{4}\bigl (2-2|\langle e,e'\rangle |\bigr ),  \] where the identity follows by expanding both sides with $|e|=|e'|=1$ and $|e-e'|^2=2-2\operatorname{Re}\langle e,e'\rangle $, and the inequality holds since $rr'\geq R^2/4$ and $\operatorname{Re}\langle e,e'\rangle \leq |\langle e,e'\rangle |$. With $a=d(\xi ,\xi ')\in [0,\pi /2]$, we have $2-2|\langle e,e'\rangle |=4\sin ^2(a/2)\geq 4a^2/\pi ^2$, because $\sin y\geq 2y/\pi $ for $0\leq y\leq \pi /2$ by concavity of the sine on this interval. Hence $|re-r'e'|^2\geq (r-r')^2+R^2a^2/\pi ^2$. Write $r=Rt$ with $t\in [1/2,1]$. Equip $[1/2,1]\times \mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ with the metric $\rho $ defined by $\rho ((t,\xi ),(t',\xi '))^2=(t-t')^2+d(\xi ,\xi ')^2$, and with the product probability $m$ of normalized Lebesgue measure and $\sigma $, which is defined on all Borel sets of this separable metric space by lemma 2.2.8 . Then $\mu $ is the image of $m$ under $(t,\xi )\mapsto \Psi (Rt,\xi )$, and the lower bound for $|re-r'e'|^2$, together with $\pi >1$, gives \[  |\Psi (Rt,\xi )-\Psi (Rt',\xi ')|\geq \frac R\pi \, \rho ((t,\xi ),(t',\xi ')).  \] A $\rho $-ball of radius $s\leq 1$ is contained in the product of an interval of length $2s$, whose normalized measure is at most $4s$, and a ball of radius $s$ for the metric $d$. Since $s\leq 1<\pi /2$, lemma 2.9.19 shows that its $m$-measure is at most $4s^{2n-1}$. In particular $m$ has no atoms, so the diagonal, a closed and hence product-measurable set (lemma 2.2.8 ), is null for $m\times m$ by Tonelli's theorem. Fix $z\in [1/2,1]\times \mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$. Splitting the integral into the set where $\rho (z,z')\geq 1$ and the shells where $2^{-k-1}\leq \rho (z,z')<2^{-k}$, $k\geq 0$, we obtain \[  \int \rho (z,z')^{-(2n-2)}\, \mathrm d m(z') \leq 1+\sum _{k=0}^\infty 2^{(k+1)(2n-2)}\cdot 4\cdot 2^{-k(2n-1)}=1+2^{2n+1}.  \] Since $\mu $ is the image of $m$, the product $\mu \times \mu $ is the image of $m\times m$ under the product map, because both measures agree on rectangles (proposition 2.2.7 ). Therefore the lower bound for $|\Psi (Rt,\xi )-\Psi (Rt',\xi ')|$, valid off the $m\times m$-null diagonal, and an integration in $z$ give \[  I_{2n-2}(\mu )\leq \Bigl (\frac\pi R\Bigr )^{2n-2}\iint \rho (z,z')^{-(2n-2)}\, \mathrm d m(z')\, \mathrm d m(z)\leq \pi ^{2n-2}(1+2^{2n+1})R^{-(2n-2)}.  \] This is the assertion, with $C_ n=\pi ^{2n-2}(1+2^{2n+1})$. $\square$

title: Lemma 2.9.21
section: 2.9 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text: Lemma 2.9.21 . DC992DBF55C7 Let $T$ be a separable metric space, and let $F\subset T\times [0,2\pi ]$ be a Borel set whose sections $F_ t=\{ \theta :(t,\theta )\in F\} $ are closed and have positive Lebesgue measure for every $t\in T$. Then there is a Borel map $a\colon T\to [0,2\pi ]$ such that $a(t)\in F_ t$ for every $t\in T$. Proof. Write $|\cdot |$ for Lebesgue measure on $[0,2\pi ]$, and put $\ell (t)=|F_ t|$ and $A_ t(b)=|F_ t\cap [0,b]|$ for $b\in [0,2\pi ]$. We first show that, for fixed $b$, the function $t\mapsto A_ t(b)$ is Borel; with $b=2\pi $, so is $\ell $. Since $T$ and $[0,2\pi ]$ are separable metric spaces, the Borel sets of $T\times [0,2\pi ]$ form the $\sigma $-algebra generated by the products of Borel sets (lemma 2.2.8 ). Hence the sections $G_ t$ of a Borel set $G$ are Borel, because the sets all of whose sections are Borel form a $\sigma $-algebra containing these products. The class of Borel sets $G\subset T\times [0,2\pi ]$ for which $t\mapsto |G_ t\cap [0,b]|$ is Borel contains the products $B_1\times B_2$ of Borel sets, for which this function is $\mathbf1_{B_1}(t)|B_2\cap [0,b]|$. It is closed under complements, since the complement of $G$ gives $b-|G_ t\cap [0,b]|$, and under countable disjoint unions, which give sums. Since the products of Borel sets are closed under finite intersections, lemma 2.2.6 (1) shows that the class contains every Borel set. For fixed $t$, the function $A_ t$ is nondecreasing and $1$-Lipschitz, with $A_ t(0)=0$ and $A_ t(2\pi )=\ell (t)>0$. Define \[  a(t)=\inf \{ b\in \mathbb Q\cap [0,2\pi ]:A_ t(b)\geq \ell (t)/2\} .  \] Because $A_ t$ is continuous and nondecreasing and $0<\ell (t)/2<\ell (t)$, the set of all $b\in [0,2\pi ]$ with $A_ t(b)\geq \ell (t)/2$ is an interval $[b_ t,2\pi ]$ with $0<b_ t<2\pi $ and $A_ t(b_ t)=\ell (t)/2$. The rational numbers are dense in this interval, so $a(t)=b_ t$ and $A_ t(a(t))=\ell (t)/2$. The map $a$ is Borel, since for every $c\in (0,2\pi ]$ \[  \{ t:a(t)<c\} =\bigcup _{b\in \mathbb Q\cap [0,c)}\{ t:A_ t(b)\geq \ell (t)/2\} .  \] Finally, suppose that $a(t)\notin F_ t$. Since $F_ t$ is closed and $a(t)>0$, some interval $[a(t)-\varepsilon ,a(t)]$ with $\varepsilon >0$ misses $F_ t$, and $A_ t$ is constant on it. A rational number $b$ in this interval with $b<a(t)$ then satisfies $A_ t(b)=\ell (t)/2$, contradicting the definition of $a(t)$. Hence $a(t)\in F_ t$. $\square$

text: Theorem 2.9.22 . 2C0F0197F3BF Let $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, with $n\geq 2$, and let $x\in D$ and $R>0$ satisfy $\overline{B(x,R)}\subset D$. Then there is a Borel probability measure $\mu $ carried by the Borel set \[  E=\{ y\in \mathbb C^ n:R/2\leq |y-x|\leq R,\  u(y)\geq A\}   \] such that $I_{2n-2}(\mu )\leq C_ nR^{-(2n-2)}$, where the constant $C_ n$ depends only on $n$. Let $r\in [R/2,R]$ and $\xi \in \mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$.
