The set of $(r,\xi ,\theta )$ with $\theta \in F_{r,\xi }$ is Borel, because $u$ is Borel and the map $(r,\xi ,\theta )\mapsto x+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }e_0(\xi )$ into $\overline{B(x,R)}$ is Borel, being continuous on each of the finitely many Borel sets on which $e_0$ is continuous. Since $[R/2,R]\times \mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ is a compact, hence separable, metric space, lemma 2.9.21 gives a Borel map $(r,\xi )\mapsto \alpha (r,\xi )$ with $\alpha (r,\xi )\in F_{r,\xi }$. Put $e(r,\xi )=\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\alpha (r,\xi )}e_0(\xi )$ and $\Psi (r,\xi )=x+re(r,\xi )$. Then $\Psi $ is Borel, hence product-measurable (lemma 2.2.8 ), and it takes its values in $E$. Let $\mu $ be the image under $\Psi $ of the product of normalized Lebesgue measure on $[R/2,R]$ and $\sigma $. It is a Borel probability measure carried by $E$. It remains to estimate the energy; the estimate does not depend on the choice of the phases $\alpha (r,\xi )$. For $r,r'\in [R/2,R]$ and unit vectors $e,e'$ spanning $\xi ,\xi '$, \[  |re-r'e'|^2=(r-r')^2+rr'|e-e'|^2 \geq (r-r')^2+\frac{R^2}{4}\bigl (2-2|\langle e,e'\rangle |\bigr ),  \] where the identity follows by expanding both sides with $|e|=|e'|=1$ and $|e-e'|^2=2-2\operatorname{Re}\langle e,e'\rangle $, and the inequality holds since $rr'\geq R^2/4$ and $\operatorname{Re}\langle e,e'\rangle \leq |\langle e,e'\rangle |$. With $a=d(\xi ,\xi ')\in [0,\pi /2]$, we have $2-2|\langle e,e'\rangle |=4\sin ^2(a/2)\geq 4a^2/\pi ^2$, because $\sin y\geq 2y/\pi $ for $0\leq y\leq \pi /2$ by concavity of the sine on this interval. Hence $|re-r'e'|^2\geq (r-r')^2+R^2a^2/\pi ^2$. Write $r=Rt$ with $t\in [1/2,1]$. Equip $[1/2,1]\times \mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ with the metric $\rho $ defined by $\rho ((t,\xi ),(t',\xi '))^2=(t-t')^2+d(\xi ,\xi ')^2$, and with the product probability $m$ of normalized Lebesgue measure and $\sigma $, which is defined on all Borel sets of this separable metric space by lemma 2.2.8 . Then $\mu $ is the image of $m$ under $(t,\xi )\mapsto \Psi (Rt,\xi )$, and the lower bound for $|re-r'e'|^2$, together with $\pi >1$, gives \[  |\Psi (Rt,\xi )-\Psi (Rt',\xi ')|\geq \frac R\pi \, \rho ((t,\xi ),(t',\xi ')).  \] A $\rho $-ball of radius $s\leq 1$ is contained in the product of an interval of length $2s$, whose normalized measure is at most $4s$, and a ball of radius $s$ for the metric $d$. Since $s\leq 1<\pi /2$, lemma 2.9.19 shows that its $m$-measure is at most $4s^{2n-1}$. In particular $m$ has no atoms, so the diagonal, a closed and hence product-measurable set (lemma 2.2.8 ), is null for $m\times m$ by Tonelli's theorem. Fix $z\in [1/2,1]\times \mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$. Splitting the integral into the set where $\rho (z,z')\geq 1$ and the shells where $2^{-k-1}\leq \rho (z,z')<2^{-k}$, $k\geq 0$, we obtain \[  \int \rho (z,z')^{-(2n-2)}\, \mathrm d m(z') \leq 1+\sum _{k=0}^\infty 2^{(k+1)(2n-2)}\cdot 4\cdot 2^{-k(2n-1)}=1+2^{2n+1}.  \] Since $\mu $ is the image of $m$, the product $\mu \times \mu $ is the image of $m\times m$ under the product map, because both measures agree on rectangles (proposition 2.2.7 ). Therefore the lower bound for $|\Psi (Rt,\xi )-\Psi (Rt',\xi ')|$, valid off the $m\times m$-null diagonal, and an integration in $z$ give \[  I_{2n-2}(\mu )\leq \Bigl (\frac\pi R\Bigr )^{2n-2}\iint \rho (z,z')^{-(2n-2)}\, \mathrm d m(z')\, \mathrm d m(z)\leq \pi ^{2n-2}(1+2^{2n+1})R^{-(2n-2)}.  \] This is the assertion, with $C_ n=\pi ^{2n-2}(1+2^{2n+1})$. $\square$

title: 2.9.23 Projection densities and incidence
section: 2.9 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text:
We now show that a measure of finite Riesz $(2n-2)$-energy on $\mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 2$, projects onto almost every complex hyperplane with a square-integrable density, and we deduce the incidence theorem. The first step expresses averages over hyperplanes as a weighted integral over $\mathbb C^ n$. Lemma 2.9.24 . 7D4E3784406E Let $n\geq 2$. For every nonnegative Borel function $f$ on $\mathbb C^ n$, \[  \int _{\mathcal H}\int _ H f(\xi )\, \mathrm d m_ H(\xi )\, \mathrm d
u (H) =a_ n\int _{\mathbb C^ n}f(\xi )|\xi |^{-2}\, \mathrm d\xi , \qquad a_ n= rac{s_{2n-3}}{s_{2n-1}}.  \] Proof. We write the inner integral in polar coordinates on $H$ and show that the normalized surface measures of the unit spheres of the hyperplanes $H$ average to the normalized surface measure of $S^{2n-1}$. For $H\in \mathcal H$, let $S_ H$ be the unit sphere of $H$, and let $	au _ H$ be the image under $T_ H$ of the normalized surface measure $\mathrm dS/s_{2n-3}$ of the unit sphere $S^{2n-3}$ of $\mathbb C^{n-1}=\mathbb R^{2n-2}$. We regard $	au _ H$ as a Borel probability measure on $S^{2n-1}$ carried by $S_ H$; it does not depend on the frame, since surface measure is invariant under orthogonal transformations (subsection 3.1.1 ). Polar coordinates ( 3.1.2 ) on all of $\mathbb C^{n-1}$, transported to $H$ by $T_ H$, give \[  \int _ Hf\, \mathrm d m_ H=s_{2n-3}\int _0^\infty r^{2n-3}\int f(r	heta )\, \mathrm d	au _ H(	heta )\, \mathrm d r.  \] Measurability. Let $h$ be a nonnegative Borel function on $(0,\infty )	imes S^{2n-1}$. By the definition of $	au _ H$, 115E6AD9CC4F 2.9.25  egin{equation}  \int h(r,	heta )\, \mathrm d	au _ H(	heta )= rac1{s_{2n-3}}\int _{S^{2n-3}}h(r,T_ H\omega )\, \mathrm dS(\omega ). \end{equation} The map $(H,r,\omega )\mapsto (r,T_ H\omega )$ is Borel by the frame construction of subsection 2.9.17 , since its two components are Borel. Hence $(H,r,\omega )\mapsto h(r,T_ H\omega )$ is a nonnegative Borel function on the product of the separable metric spaces $\mathcal H	imes (0,\infty )$ and $S^{2n-3}$, and by lemma 2.2.8 and Tonelli's theorem the right side of ( 2.9.25 ) is a Borel function of $(H,r)$. In particular, taking $h(r,	heta )=g(	heta )$, we see that $H\mapsto \int g\, \mathrm d	au _ H$ is Borel for every nonnegative Borel function $g$ on $S^{2n-1}$; for instance, $H\mapsto 	au _ H(B)$ is Borel for every Borel set $B\subset S^{2n-1}$. Averaging. For a Borel set $B\subset S^{2n-1}$ put $	au (B)=\int 	au _ H(B)\, \mathrm d
u (H)$. By monotone convergence, $	au $ is countably additive, so it is a Borel probability measure on $S^{2n-1}$. For a unitary matrix $U$, the map $UT_ H$ is a complex linear isometry from $\mathbb C^{n-1}$ onto $UH$, so $U$ maps $	au _ H$ to $	au _{UH}$, that is, $	au _ H(U^{-1}B)=	au _{UH}(B)$. Since $
u $ is invariant, it follows that $	au (U^{-1}B)=\int 	au _{UH}(B)\, \mathrm d
u (H)=	au (B)$, so $	au $ is unitarily invariant. The normalized surface measure $\mathrm dS/s_{2n-1}$ of $S^{2n-1}$ is also unitarily invariant, because unitary matrices are orthogonal transformations of $\mathbb R^{2n}$. By the uniqueness in proposition 2.9.18 , $	au =\mathrm dS/s_{2n-1}$. By the definition of $	au $ for indicator functions, by linearity for simple functions, and by monotone convergence in general, $\int _{\mathcal H}\int g\, \mathrm d	au _ H\, \mathrm d
u (H)=\int g\, \mathrm d	au $ for every nonnegative Borel function $g$ on $S^{2n-1}$. Conclusion. Integrate the polar-coordinate identity over $H$ with respect to $
u $. The function $(r,	heta )\mapsto f(r	heta )$ is Borel on $(0,\infty )	imes S^{2n-1}$, so by the measurability step $(H,r)\mapsto r^{2n-3}\int f(r	heta )\, \mathrm d	au _ H(	heta )$ is a nonnegative Borel function on $\mathcal H	imes (0,\infty )$, which is product-measurable by lemma 2.2.8 . Tonelli's theorem therefore allows us to integrate first over $H$, and the averaging identity with $g(	heta )=f(r	heta )$ shows that the left side of the lemma equals \[  s_{2n-3}\int _0^\infty r^{2n-3}\int _{S^{2n-1}}f(r	heta )\,  rac{\mathrm d S(	heta )}{s_{2n-1}}\, \mathrm d r.  \] In polar coordinates $\xi =r	heta $ on all of $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$, ( 3.1.2 ) gives $|\xi |^{-2}\, \mathrm d\xi =r^{2n-3}\, \mathrm d r\, \mathrm dS(	heta )$, so this is the right side. All integrals may be infinite. $\square$ Theorem 2.9.26 . 03F670D5FB5A Let $n\geq 2$, and let $\mu $ be a finite positive Borel measure on $\mathbb C^ n$ with $I_{2n-2}(\mu )<\infty $. Then for $
u $-almost every $H\in \mathcal H$, the projected measure $(P_ H)_*\mu $ has a density $g_ H\in L^2(H,m_ H)$ with respect to $m_ H$, and \[  \int _{\mathcal H}\| g_ H\| _2^2\, \mathrm d
u (H)= eta _ n I_{2n-2}(\mu ), \qquad  eta _ n= rac{a_ n}{b_{2n,2n-2}}= rac{\Gamma (n)}{\pi ^{n-1}}>0.  \] Proof. On $H$ we use the Fourier transform defined by the Euclidean inner product $\operatorname{Re}\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle $ and the measure $m_ H$; in an orthonormal frame it is the transform of subsection 2.9.1 on $\mathbb R^{2n-2}$. For $y\in \mathbb C^ n$ and $\xi \in H$ we have $\operatorname{Re}\langle P_ Hy,\xi angle =\operatorname{Re}\langle y,\xi angle $, because $y-P_ Hy$ is orthogonal to $H$. Hence the Fourier transform of $(P_ H)_*\mu $ at $\xi \in H$ is $\int \mathrm e^{-2\pi \mathrm i\operatorname{Re}\langle P_ Hy,\xi angle }\, \mathrm d\mu (y)=\widehat\mu (\xi )$; that is, it is the restriction of $\widehat\mu $ to $H$. Apply lemma 2.9.24 to the continuous function $|\widehat\mu |^2$, and then theorem 2.9.6 with $d=2n$ and $s=2n-2$, for which $|\xi |^{s-d}=|\xi |^{-2}$. We obtain \[  \int _{\mathcal H}\int _ H|\widehat\mu (\xi )|^2\, \mathrm d m_ H(\xi )\, \mathrm d
u (H) =a_ n\int _{\mathbb C^ n}|\widehat\mu (\xi )|^2|\xi |^{-2}\, \mathrm d\xi = eta _ n I_{2n-2}(\mu )<\infty .  \] The inner integral is a Borel function of $H$, by the frame construction in subsection 2.9.17 ; hence it is finite for $
u $-almost every $H$. For each such $H$, we apply proposition 2.9.5 on $\mathbb C^{n-1}=\mathbb R^{2n-2}$ to the image of $\mu $ under $T_ H^{-1}P_ H$. Since $T_ H$ preserves $\operatorname{Re}\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle $, the Fourier transform of this image is $w\mapsto \widehat\mu (T_ Hw)$, whose squared $L^2$ norm is $\int _ H|\widehat\mu |^2\, \mathrm d m_ H<\infty $. Hence the image has a density in $L^1\cap L^2$, and composing it with $T_ H^{-1}$ we obtain a density $g_ H$ of $(P_ H)_*\mu $ with respect to $m_ H$, with $\| g_ H\| _2^2=\int _ H|\widehat\mu |^2\, \mathrm d m_ H$. In particular, $H\mapsto \| g_ H\| _2^2$ is Borel, being equal to this Fourier integral, so no measurable choice of the densities themselves is needed. Integrating over $H$ proves the identity. To compute $ eta _ n$, recall from ( 2.9.8 ) that $s_{k-1}=2\pi ^{k/2}/\Gamma (k/2)$ for every $k\geq 1$. Hence $a_ n=\Gamma (n)/(\pi \Gamma (n-1))$, while $b_{2n,2n-2}=\pi ^{n-2}/\Gamma (n-1)$, and therefore $ eta _ n=\Gamma (n)/\pi ^{n-1}$. $\square$ Theorem 2.9.27 . AF10D8C2B9D9 Let $n\geq 2$, let $K\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be bounded, and let $E_ j\subset K$, $j\geq 1$, be Borel sets. Suppose that there are Borel probability measures $\mu _ j$ on $\mathbb C^ n$ such that $\mu _ j(E_ j)=1$ and $I_{2n-2}(\mu _ j)\leq C$ for a constant $C<\infty $ independent of $j$. Then some affine complex line meets $E_ j$ for infinitely many $j$. Proof. We parametrize the affine complex lines that can meet $K$ by a compact set carrying a finite measure $\lambda $, and bound from below, independently of $j$, the $\lambda $-measure of a set of lines meeting $E_ j$. Choose $M>0$ with $K\subset B(0,M)$. Every affine complex line can be written as $c+H^\perp $ with $H\in \mathcal H$ and $c\in H$, and $c=P_ Hy$ for every point $y$ of the line. Indeed, if the line is $a+\mathbb Cb$, let $H$ be the hyperplane orthogonal to $b$, so that $H^\perp =\mathbb Cb$, and put $c=P_ Ha$; then $P_ H(a+\zeta b)=c$ for every $\zeta \in \mathbb C$. If the line meets $K$ at a point $y$, then $|c|=|P_ Hy|\leq |y|<M$. Hence the lines that can meet $K$ are parametrized by the set \[  \mathcal L_ M=\{ (H,c):H\in \mathcal H,\  c\in H,\  |c|\leq M\} ,  \] which is compact, being closed in $\mathcal H	imes \overline{B(0,M)}$ because $c\in H$ means $P_ Hc=c$. We equip $\mathcal L_ M$ with the finite measure $\lambda $ defined by \[  \int h\, \mathrm d\lambda =\int _{\mathcal H}\int _{H\cap \overline{B(0,M)}}h(H,c)\, \mathrm d m_ H(c)\, \mathrm d
u (H)  \] for nonnegative Borel functions $h$. In the frames of subsection 2.9.17 , $\lambda $ is the image of the product of $
u $ and Lebesgue measure on the closed ball of radius $M$ in $\mathbb C^{n-1}$. Thus it is a Borel measure, and its total mass is the volume of a ball of radius $M$ in $\mathbb R^{2n-2}$. By inner regularity (proposition 2.2.2 ), choose compact sets $F_ j\subset E_ j$ with $\mu _ j(F_ j)\geq 1/2$. The set \[  J_ j=\{ (H,c):H\in \mathcal H,\  c\in P_ HF_ j\} \subset \mathcal L_ M  \] parametrizes the lines meeting $F_ j$. It is compact, as the image of $\mathcal H	imes F_ j$ under the continuous map $(H,y)\mapsto (H,P_ Hy)$. Its section over $H$ is $P_ HF_ j$, so $\lambda (J_ j)=\int m_ H(P_ HF_ j)\, \mathrm d
u (H)$. Let $g_{j,H}$ be the densities given by theorem 2.9.26 for $\mu _ j$. Since $F_ j\subset P_ H^{-1}(P_ HF_ j)$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives, for $
u $-almost every $H$, \[   rac12\leq \mu _ j(F_ j)\leq (P_ H)_*\mu _ j(P_ HF_ j)=\int _{P_ HF_ j}g_{j,H}\, \mathrm d m_ H \leq \| g_{j,H}\| _2\, m_ H(P_ HF_ j)^{1/2}.  \] Integrate this inequality over $H$ with respect to the probability measure $
u $, and apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality once more. Squaring the result and using theorem 2.9.26 , we obtain \[   rac14\leq \lambda (J_ j)\int _{\mathcal H}\| g_{j,H}\| _2^2\, \mathrm d
u (H) \leq \lambda (J_ j) eta _ n C.  \] In particular $C>0$, and $\lambda (J_ j)\geq \delta =1/(4 eta _ n C)$ for every $j$. The sets $ igcup _{j\geq m}J_ j$ decrease in $m$ and have measure at least $\delta $. Since $\lambda $ is finite, continuity from above gives \[  \lambda \left( igcap _ m igcup _{j\geq m}J_ jight)\geq \delta >0,  \] so this set is nonempty. If $(H,c)$ belongs to it, then $c\in P_ HF_ j$ for infinitely many $j$. For each such $j$ there is $y\in F_ j$ with $c=P_ Hy$, so $y\in c+H^\perp $. Hence the line $c+H^\perp $ meets $F_ j$, and therefore $E_ j$, for infinitely many $j$. $\square$ Corollary 2.9.28 . 644CAD92A580 Let $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, with $n\geq 1$, and let $u\colon D	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a Borel function whose restriction to every connected component of every affine complex-line section of $D$ is subharmonic. Then $u$ is locally bounded above on $D$. Proof. If $n=1$, the only affine complex line is $\mathbb C$ itself. Thus $u$ is subharmonic on every component of $D$, hence upper semicontinuous and locally bounded above. Let $n\geq 2$, and suppose that $u$ is not bounded above on any neighborhood of some point $p\in D$. Then there are points $x_ j	o p$ with $A_ j=u(x_ j)	o \infty $. Choose $R>0$ with $\overline{B(p,2R)}\subset D$; discarding finitely many terms, we may assume that $|x_ j-p|<R$ for all $j$. Then $\overline{B(x_ j,R)}\subset B(p,2R)\subset D$, and theorem 2.9.22 gives Borel probability measures $\mu _ j$ carried by the sets \[  E_ j=\{ y\in \mathbb C^ n:R/2\leq |y-x_ j|\leq R,\  u(y)\geq A_ j\} ,  \] with $I_{2n-2}(\mu _ j)\leq C_ nR^{-(2n-2)}$ for every $j$. All the sets $E_ j$ lie in the bounded set $B(p,2R)$. By theorem 2.9.27 , some affine complex line $L$ meets $E_ j$ for all $j$ in an infinite set $J$. Choose $y_ j\in L\cap E_ j$ for $j\in J$. Passing to a subsequence, we may assume that $y_ j	o y\in L\cap \overline{B(p,2R)}\subset D$. A small closed disc in $L$ centered at $y$ lies in $D$, so for large $j$ the points $y_ j$ lie in the same connected component of $D\cap L$ as $y$. On this component $u$ is subharmonic, hence upper semicontinuous, and therefore $\varlimsup _ ju(y_ j)\leq u(y)<\infty $. This contradicts $u(y_ j)\geq A_ j	o \infty $. $\square$ Borel measurability enters this argument through the construction of the measures in theorem 2.9.22 . In the proof of theorem 5.8.4 , measurability is first derived from the line hypothesis, and only then is corollary 2.9.28 applied.

title: Lemma 2.9.24
section: 2.9 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text:
Lemma 2.9.24 . 7D4E3784406E Let $n\geq 2$. For every nonnegative Borel function $f$ on $\mathbb C^ n$, \[  \int _{\mathcal H}\int _ H f(\xi )\, \mathrm d m_ H(\xi )\, \mathrm d
u (H) =a_ n\int _{\mathbb C^ n}f(\xi )|\xi |^{-2}\, \mathrm d\xi , \qquad a_ n= rac{s_{2n-3}}{s_{2n-1}}.  \] Proof. We write the inner integral in polar coordinates on $H$ and show that the normalized surface measures of the unit spheres of the hyperplanes $H$ average to the normalized surface measure of $S^{2n-1}$. For $H\in \mathcal H$, let $S_ H$ be the unit sphere of $H$, and let $	au _ H$ be the image under $T_ H$ of the normalized surface measure $\mathrm dS/s_{2n-3}$ of the unit sphere $S^{2n-3}$ of $\mathbb C^{n-1}=\mathbb R^{2n-2}$. We regard $	au _ H$ as a Borel probability measure on $S^{2n-1}$ carried by $S_ H$; it does not depend on the frame, since surface measure is invariant under orthogonal transformations (subsection 3.1.1 ). Polar coordinates ( 3.1.2 ) on all of $\mathbb C^{n-1}$, transported to $H$ by $T_ H$, give \[  \int _ Hf\, \mathrm d m_ H=s_{2n-3}\int _0^\infty r^{2n-3}\int f(r	heta )\, \mathrm d	au _ H(	heta )\, \mathrm d r.  \] Measurability. Let $h$ be a nonnegative Borel function on $(0,\infty )	imes S^{2n-1}$. By the definition of $	au _ H$, 115E6AD9CC4F 2.9.25  egin{equation}  \int h(r,	heta )\, \mathrm d	au _ H(	heta )= rac1{s_{2n-3}}\int _{S^{2n-3}}h(r,T_ H\omega )\, \mathrm dS(\omega ). \end{equation} The map $(H,r,\omega )\mapsto (r,T_ H\omega )$ is Borel by the frame construction of subsection 2.9.17 , since its two components are Borel. Hence $(H,r,\omega )\mapsto h(r,T_ H\omega )$ is a nonnegative Borel function on the product of the separable metric spaces $\mathcal H	imes (0,\infty )$ and $S^{2n-3}$, and by lemma 2.2.8 and Tonelli's theorem the right side of ( 2.9.25 ) is a Borel function of $(H,r)$. In particular, taking $h(r,	heta )=g(	heta )$, we see that $H\mapsto \int g\, \mathrm d	au _ H$ is Borel for every nonnegative Borel function $g$ on $S^{2n-1}$; for instance, $H\mapsto 	au _ H(B)$ is Borel for every Borel set $B\subset S^{2n-1}$. Averaging. For a Borel set $B\subset S^{2n-1}$ put $	au (B)=\int 	au _ H(B)\, \mathrm d
u (H)$. By monotone convergence, $	au $ is countably additive, so it is a Borel probability measure on $S^{2n-1}$. For a unitary matrix $U$, the map $UT_ H$ is a complex linear isometry from $\mathbb C^{n-1}$ onto $UH$, so $U$ maps $	au _ H$ to $	au _{UH}$, that is, $	au _ H(U^{-1}B)=	au _{UH}(B)$. Since $
u $ is invariant, it follows that $	au (U^{-1}B)=\int 	au _{UH}(B)\, \mathrm d
u (H)=	au (B)$, so $	au $ is unitarily invariant. The normalized surface measure $\mathrm dS/s_{2n-1}$ of $S^{2n-1}$ is also unitarily invariant, because unitary matrices are orthogonal transformations of $\mathbb R^{2n}$. By the uniqueness in proposition 2.9.18 , $	au =\mathrm dS/s_{2n-1}$. By the definition of $	au $ for indicator functions, by linearity for simple functions, and by monotone convergence in general, $\int _{\mathcal H}\int g\, \mathrm d	au _ H\, \mathrm d
u (H)=\int g\, \mathrm d	au $ for every nonnegative Borel function $g$ on $S^{2n-1}$. Conclusion. Integrate the polar-coordinate identity over $H$ with respect to $
u $. The function $(r,	heta )\mapsto f(r	heta )$ is Borel on $(0,\infty )	imes S^{2n-1}$, so by the measurability step $(H,r)\mapsto r^{2n-3}\int f(r	heta )\, \mathrm d	au _ H(	heta )$ is a nonnegative Borel function on $\mathcal H	imes (0,\infty )$, which is product-measurable by lemma 2.2.8 . Tonelli's theorem therefore allows us to integrate first over $H$, and the averaging identity with $g(	heta )=f(r	heta )$ shows that the left side of the lemma equals \[  s_{2n-3}\int _0^\infty r^{2n-3}\int _{S^{2n-1}}f(r	heta )\,  rac{\mathrm d S(	heta )}{s_{2n-1}}\, \mathrm d r.  \] In polar coordinates $\xi =r	heta $ on all of $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$, ( 3.1.2 ) gives $|\xi |^{-2}\, \mathrm d\xi =r^{2n-3}\, \mathrm d r\, \mathrm dS(	heta )$, so this is the right side. All integrals may be infinite. $\square$

title: Theorem 2.9.26
section: 2.9 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text:
Theorem 2.9.26 . 03F670D5FB5A Let $n\geq 2$, and let $\mu $ be a finite positive Borel measure on $\mathbb C^ n$ with $I_{2n-2}(\mu )<\infty $. Then for $
u $-almost every $H\in \mathcal H$, the projected measure $(P_ H)_*\mu $ has a density $g_ H\in L^2(H,m_ H)$ with respect to $m_ H$, and \[  \int _{\mathcal H}\| g_ H\| _2^2\, \mathrm d
u (H)= eta _ n I_{2n-2}(\mu ), \qquad  eta _ n= rac{a_ n}{b_{2n,2n-2}}= rac{\Gamma (n)}{\pi ^{n-1}}>0.  \] Proof. On $H$ we use the Fourier transform defined by the Euclidean inner product $\operatorname{Re}\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle $ and the measure $m_ H$; in an orthonormal frame it is the transform of subsection 2.9.1 on $\mathbb R^{2n-2}$. For $y\in \mathbb C^ n$ and $\xi \in H$ we have $\operatorname{Re}\langle P_ Hy,\xi angle =\operatorname{Re}\langle y,\xi angle $, because $y-P_ Hy$ is orthogonal to $H$. Hence the Fourier transform of $(P_ H)_*\mu $ at $\xi \in H$ is $\int \mathrm e^{-2\pi \mathrm i\operatorname{Re}\langle P_ Hy,\xi angle }\, \mathrm d\mu (y)=\widehat\mu (\xi )$; that is, it is the restriction of $\widehat\mu $ to $H$. Apply lemma 2.9.24 to the continuous function $|\widehat\mu |^2$, and then theorem 2.9.6 with $d=2n$ and $s=2n-2$, for which $|\xi |^{s-d}=|\xi |^{-2}$. We obtain \[  \int _{\mathcal H}\int _ H|\widehat\mu (\xi )|^2\, \mathrm d m_ H(\xi )\, \mathrm d
u (H) =a_ n\int _{\mathbb C^ n}|\widehat\mu (\xi )|^2|\xi |^{-2}\, \mathrm d\xi = eta _ n I_{2n-2}(\mu )<\infty .  \] The inner integral is a Borel function of $H$, by the frame construction in subsection 2.9.17 ; hence it is finite for $
u $-almost every $H$. For each such $H$, we apply proposition 2.9.5 on $\mathbb C^{n-1}=\mathbb R^{2n-2}$ to the image of $\mu $ under $T_ H^{-1}P_ H$. Since $T_ H$ preserves $\operatorname{Re}\langle \cdot ,\cdot angle $, the Fourier transform of this image is $w\mapsto \widehat\mu (T_ Hw)$, whose squared $L^2$ norm is $\int _ H|\widehat\mu |^2\, \mathrm d m_ H<\infty $. Hence the image has a density in $L^1\cap L^2$, and composing it with $T_ H^{-1}$ we obtain a density $g_ H$ of $(P_ H)_*\mu $ with respect to $m_ H$, with $\| g_ H\| _2^2=\int _ H|\widehat\mu |^2\, \mathrm d m_ H$. In particular, $H\mapsto \| g_ H\| _2^2$ is Borel, being equal to this Fourier integral, so no measurable choice of the densities themselves is needed. Integrating over $H$ proves the identity. To compute $ eta _ n$, recall from ( 2.9.8 ) that $s_{k-1}=2\pi ^{k/2}/\Gamma (k/2)$ for every $k\geq 1$. Hence $a_ n=\Gamma (n)/(\pi \Gamma (n-1))$, while $b_{2n,2n-2}=\pi ^{n-2}/\Gamma (n-1)$, and therefore $ eta _ n=\Gamma (n)/\pi ^{n-1}$. $\square$

title: Theorem 2.9.27
section: 2.9 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text:
Theorem 2.9.27 . AF10D8C2B9D9 Let $n\geq 2$, let $K\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be bounded, and let $E_ j\subset K$, $j\geq 1$, be Borel sets. Suppose that there are Borel probability measures $\mu _ j$ on $\mathbb C^ n$ such that $\mu _ j(E_ j)=1$ and $I_{2n-2}(\mu _ j)\leq C$ for a constant $C<\infty $ independent of $j$. Then some affine complex line meets $E_ j$ for infinitely many $j$. Proof. We parametrize the affine complex lines that can meet $K$ by a compact set carrying a finite measure $\lambda $, and bound from below, independently of $j$, the $\lambda $-measure of a set of lines meeting $E_ j$. Choose $M>0$ with $K\subset B(0,M)$. Every affine complex line can be written as $c+H^\perp $ with $H\in \mathcal H$ and $c\in H$, and $c=P_ Hy$ for every point $y$ of the line. Indeed, if the line is $a+\mathbb Cb$, let $H$ be the hyperplane orthogonal to $b$, so that $H^\perp =\mathbb Cb$, and put $c=P_ Ha$; then $P_ H(a+\zeta b)=c$ for every $\zeta \in \mathbb C$. If the line meets $K$ at a point $y$, then $|c|=|P_ Hy|\leq |y|<M$. Hence the lines that can meet $K$ are parametrized by the set \[  \mathcal L_ M=\{ (H,c):H\in \mathcal H,\  c\in H,\  |c|\leq M\} ,  \] which is compact, being closed in $\mathcal H	imes \overline{B(0,M)}$ because $c\in H$ means $P_ Hc=c$. We equip $\mathcal L_ M$ with the finite measure $\lambda $ defined by \[  \int h\, \mathrm d\lambda =\int _{\mathcal H}\int _{H\cap \overline{B(0,M)}}h(H,c)\, \mathrm d m_ H(c)\, \mathrm d
u (H)  \] for nonnegative Borel functions $h$. In the frames of subsection 2.9.17 , $\lambda $ is the image of the product of $
u $ and Lebesgue measure on the closed ball of radius $M$ in $\mathbb C^{n-1}$. Thus it is a Borel measure, and its total mass is the volume of a ball of radius $M$ in $\mathbb R^{2n-2}$. By inner regularity (proposition 2.2.2 ), choose compact sets $F_ j\subset E_ j$ with $\mu _ j(F_ j)\geq 1/2$. The set \[  J_ j=\{ (H,c):H\in \mathcal H,\  c\in P_ HF_ j\} \subset \mathcal L_ M  \] parametrizes the lines meeting $F_ j$. It is compact, as the image of $\mathcal H	imes F_ j$ under the continuous map $(H,y)\mapsto (H,P_ Hy)$. Its section over $H$ is $P_ HF_ j$, so $\lambda (J_ j)=\int m_ H(P_ HF_ j)\, \mathrm d
u (H)$. Let $g_{j,H}$ be the densities given by theorem 2.9.26 for $\mu _ j$. Since $F_ j\subset P_ H^{-1}(P_ HF_ j)$, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives, for $
u $-almost every $H$, \[   rac12\leq \mu _ j(F_ j)\leq (P_ H)_*\mu _ j(P_ HF_ j)=\int _{P_ HF_ j}g_{j,H}\, \mathrm d m_ H \leq \| g_{j,H}\| _2\, m_ H(P_ HF_ j)^{1/2}.  \] Integrate this inequality over $H$ with respect to the probability measure $
u $, and apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality once more. Squaring the result and using theorem 2.9.26 , we obtain \[   rac14\leq \lambda (J_ j)\int _{\mathcal H}\| g_{j,H}\| _2^2\, \mathrm d
u (H) \leq \lambda (J_ j) eta _ n C.  \] In particular $C>0$, and $\lambda (J_ j)\geq \delta =1/(4 eta _ n C)$ for every $j$. The sets $ igcup _{j\geq m}J_ j$ decrease in $m$ and have measure at least $\delta $. Since $\lambda $ is finite, continuity from above gives \[  \lambda \left( igcap _ m igcup _{j\geq m}J_ jight)\geq \delta >0,  \] so this set is nonempty. If $(H,c)$ belongs to it, then $c\in P_ HF_ j$ for infinitely many $j$. For each such $j$ there is $y\in F_ j$ with $c=P_ Hy$, so $y\in c+H^\perp $. Hence the line $c+H^\perp $ meets $F_ j$, and therefore $E_ j$, for infinitely many $j$. $\square$

title: Corollary 2.9.28
section: 2.9 Fourier analysis and incidence of complex lines
text: Corollary 2.9.28 . 644CAD92A580 Let $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, with $n\geq 1$, and let $u\colon D\to [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a Borel function whose restriction to every connected component of every affine complex-line section of $D$ is subharmonic. Then $u$ is locally bounded above on $D$. Proof. If $n=1$, the only affine complex line is $\mathbb C$ itself. Thus $u$ is subharmonic on every component of $D$, hence upper semicontinuous and locally bounded above. Let $n\geq 2$, and suppose that $u$ is not bounded above on any neighborhood of some point $p\in D$. Then there are points $x_ j\to p$ with $A_ j=u(x_ j)\to \infty $. Choose $R>0$ with $\overline{B(p,2R)}\subset D$; discarding finitely many terms, we may assume that $|x_ j-p|<R$ for all $j$. Then $\overline{B(x_ j,R)}\subset B(p,2R)\subset D$, and theorem 2.9.22 gives Borel probability measures $\mu _ j$ carried by the sets \[  E_ j=\{ y\in \mathbb C^ n:R/2\leq |y-x_ j|\leq R,\  u(y)\geq A_ j\} ,  \] with $I_{2n-2}(\mu _ j)\leq C_ nR^{-(2n-2)}$ for every $j$. All the sets $E_ j$ lie in the bounded set $B(p,2R)$. By theorem 2.9.27 , some affine complex line $L$ meets $E_ j$ for all $j$ in an infinite set $J$. Choose $y_ j\in L\cap E_ j$ for $j\in J$. Passing to a subsequence, we may assume that $y_ j\to y\in L\cap \overline{B(p,2R)}\subset D$. A small closed disc in $L$ centered at $y$ lies in $D$, so for large $j$ the points $y_ j$ lie in the same connected component of $D\cap L$ as $y$. On this component $u$ is subharmonic, hence upper semicontinuous, and therefore $\varlimsup _ ju(y_ j)\leq u(y)<\infty $. This contradicts $u(y_ j)\geq A_ j\to \infty $. $\square$

title: 5.1 Complex differential forms and positive currents
search_title: Complex differential forms and positive currents
section: 5.1 Complex differential forms and positive currents
text: This chapter sets up the calculus on which Part II is built. The central object of the following chapters is the complex Hessian $(\partial ^2u/\partial z_ j\partial \bar z_ k)$ of a function $u$ on an open subset of $\mathbb {C}^ n$, or rather the $(1,1)$-form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ that it defines. Two features distinguish it from the Laplacian of Part I: its positivity is a condition in every complex direction, and it transforms naturally under holomorphic changes of coordinates. Complex differential forms express both features, and currents, that is, differential forms with distribution coefficients, allow us to apply $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ to locally integrable functions such as $\log |f|^2$ with $f$ holomorphic. We begin with the elementary calculus of holomorphic functions, complex manifolds and differential forms of type $(p,q)$. Positivity of a current is defined by duality from positivity of forms, which is a matter of linear algebra (section 5.3 ); along the way we prove a pointwise form of the Hodge index theorem for mixed discriminants (lemma 5.3.4 ). The basic analytic fact is theorem 5.3.7 : the coefficients of a positive current are measures, all dominated by a single positive measure, its trace measure. Consequently, on a manifold with a countable basis, every sequence of positive currents with locally bounded trace measures has a weakly convergent subsequence. A closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ is locally of the form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$, with $u$ unique up to pluriharmonic functions (theorem 5.4.3 ), and positivity of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ survives composition with holomorphic maps. The fundamental example is the Poincaré–Lelong formula $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2=[\operatorname{div}(f)]$ of theorem 5.5.6 , which identifies the complex Hessian of $\log |f|^2$ with the current of integration over the zero set of $f$, counted with multiplicities. The chapter closes with pushforward and pullback of currents and with Hermitian metrics, which give trace measures independent of coordinates. Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in subsection 25.1.7 .

title: 5.2 Complex manifolds and differential forms
text: Let $n\geq 0$ be an integer. On $\mathbb {C}^ n$ we write $z_ j=x_ j+\mathrm{i}y_ j$ for $1\leq j\leq n$, and we use the complex partial derivatives and differentials \[  \partial _{z_ j}=\tfrac 12(\partial _{x_ j}-\mathrm{i}\partial _{y_ j}),\qquad \partial _{\bar z_ j}=\tfrac 12(\partial _{x_ j}+\mathrm{i}\partial _{y_ j}),\qquad \mathrm{d}z_ j=\mathrm{d}x_ j+\mathrm{i}\mathrm{d}y_ j.  \] A smooth function $f$ on an open subset of $\mathbb {C}^ n$ is holomorphic if $\partial _{\bar z_ j}f=0$ for $1\leq j\leq n$. Substituting the definitions, we find $\mathrm df=\sum _ j(\partial _{z_ j}f\, \mathrm dz_ j+\partial _{\bar z_ j}f\, \mathrm d\bar z_ j)$ for every smooth $f$. On each tangent space the forms $\mathrm dz_ j$ are complex linear and the forms $\mathrm d\bar z_ j$ are conjugate linear, and a real-linear form which is both complex linear and conjugate linear vanishes; hence $f$ is holomorphic if and only if its real derivative is complex linear at every point. By the chain rule, compositions of holomorphic maps, that is, of maps with holomorphic components, are therefore holomorphic. A holomorphic function is holomorphic in each variable separately in the sense of one-variable theory, since it satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations in each variable, and its derivatives $\partial _{z_ j}f$ are again holomorphic, because partial derivatives of smooth functions commute. Let $n\geq 1$, and let $f$ be holomorphic on a neighborhood of the closed polydisc $\{ |z_ j-a_ j|\leq r,\  1\leq j\leq n\} $, where $a\in \mathbb C^ n$ and $r>0$. Applying the one-variable Cauchy formula in each variable in turn, we obtain the Cauchy formula on a polydisc: for $|z_ j-a_ j|<r$, \[  f(z)=\frac{1}{(2\pi \mathrm{i})^ n} \int _{|\zeta _1-a_1|=r}\cdots \int _{|\zeta _ n-a_ n|=r} \frac{f(\zeta )\, \mathrm{d}\zeta _1\cdots \mathrm{d}\zeta _ n}{\prod _ j(\zeta _ j-z_ j)}.  \] For $|z_ j-a_ j|\leq s<r$, the geometric series $(\zeta _ j-z_ j)^{-1}=\sum _{k\geq 0}(z_ j-a_ j)^ k(\zeta _ j-a_ j)^{-k-1}$ converge uniformly for $|\zeta _ j-a_ j|=r$. The product of these series is a multiple series which converges absolutely and uniformly on the torus $\{ |\zeta _ j-a_ j|=r\} $; integrating it term by term, we obtain the power series expansion E0E563B56BCE 5.2.1 \begin{equation}  f(z)=\sum _{\alpha \in \mathbb N^ n}c_\alpha (z-a)^\alpha ,\qquad |c_\alpha |\leq \frac{M}{r^{|\alpha |}}, \end{equation} with \[  c_\alpha =\frac{1}{(2\pi \mathrm{i})^ n}\int _{|\zeta _1-a_1|=r}\cdots \int _{|\zeta _ n-a_ n|=r}\frac{f(\zeta )\, \mathrm d\zeta _1\cdots \mathrm d\zeta _ n}{\prod _ j(\zeta _ j-a_ j)^{\alpha _ j+1}},  \] where $(z-a)^\alpha =\prod _ j(z_ j-a_ j)^{\alpha _ j}$, $|\alpha |=\alpha _1+\cdots +\alpha _ n$, and $M$ is the maximum of $|f|$ on the torus $\{ |\zeta _ j-a_ j|=r\} $. The series converges normally on every polydisc $\{ |z_ j-a_ j|\leq s\} $ with $s<r$, since $\sum _\alpha (s/r)^{|\alpha |}=(1-s/r)^{-n}$. Differentiating the Cauchy formula under the integral sign, we obtain integral formulas for all derivatives of $f$, and in particular $\partial _{z_1}^{\alpha _1}\cdots \partial _{z_ n}^{\alpha _ n}f(a)=\alpha _1!\cdots \alpha _ n!\, c_\alpha $. Grouping the terms of ( 5.2.1 ) by degree, we write $f(a+w)=\sum _{k\geq 0}P_ k(w)$ for $|w|<r$, where $P_ k$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $k$; this is the homogeneous expansion of $f$ at $a$. If $P_ k=0$ for all $k<m$, then 284A415465F7 5.2.2 \begin{equation}  |f(a+w)-P_ m(w)|\leq 2^{m+n+1}M\Big(\frac{|w|}r\Big)^{m+1}\qquad \text{for }|w|\leq \frac r2. \end{equation} Indeed, with $t=|w|/r\leq \frac12$ we have $|w^\alpha |\leq |w|^{|\alpha |}$ and $t^{|\alpha |}\leq t^{m+1}2^{m+1-|\alpha |}$ for $|\alpha |\geq m+1$, so the terms of degree at least $m+1$ contribute at most $Mt^{m+1}2^{m+1}\sum _\alpha 2^{-|\alpha |}=2^{m+n+1}Mt^{m+1}$. The expansion ( 5.2.1 ) also gives the identity theorem: a holomorphic function on a domain that vanishes on a nonempty open subset vanishes identically. Indeed, the set of points at which all derivatives $\partial _{z_1}^{\alpha _1}\cdots \partial _{z_ n}^{\alpha _ n}f$ vanish is nonempty, and it is closed because these derivatives are continuous. It is also open: at each of its points $a$ all coefficients $c_\alpha $ vanish, by the formula for the derivatives at $a$, so $f$ vanishes on a polydisc around $a$. Hence this set is the whole domain. Definition 5.2.3 . 42A02A1A5EFE A complex manifold of dimension $n$ is a paracompact Hausdorff space with an atlas of homeomorphisms onto open subsets of $\mathbb {C}^ n$, whose coordinate changes are holomorphic with holomorphic inverses. A map between complex manifolds is holomorphic if its coordinate expressions are holomorphic. A complex submanifold is a closed subset that is locally a coordinate plane in suitable holomorphic coordinates. The underlying real manifold has dimension $2n$. If $F=(F_1,\ldots ,F_ m)$ is a holomorphic map from an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$ to $\mathbb C^ m$, then $\mathrm dF_ j=\sum _ k\partial _{z_ k}F_ j\, \mathrm dz_ k$, so the real derivative of $F$ at a point $a$ is the complex-linear map given by the complex Jacobian matrix $(\partial _{z_ k}F_ j(a))_{j,k}$. Consequently the inverse function theorem has the following holomorphic version. Proposition 5.2.4 . A683A13C69D9 Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, let $F\colon U\to \mathbb C^ n$ be holomorphic, and let $a\in U$ be a point at which the complex Jacobian matrix $(\partial _{z_ k}F_ j(a))_{j,k}$ is invertible. Then there are open neighborhoods $U'\subset U$ of $a$ and $V'\subset \mathbb C^ n$ of $F(a)$ such that $F$ maps $U'$ bijectively onto $V'$ and the inverse map $V'\to U'$ is holomorphic. Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ m$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f_1,\ldots ,f_ r$, $0\le r\le m$, be holomorphic functions on $U$ whose complex Jacobian matrix $(\partial _{z_ k}f_ j(a))_{1\le j\le r,\, 1\le k\le m}$ at $a$ has rank $r$. Then there are indices $k_1<\cdots <k_{m-r}$ such that the map $(f_1,\ldots ,f_ r,z_{k_1},\ldots ,z_{k_{m-r}})$ is biholomorphic from an open neighborhood of $a$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb C^ m$. Thus $f_1,\ldots ,f_ r$ are the first $r$ coordinates of a holomorphic chart near $a$. Let $X$ be a complex manifold of dimension $m$, let $a\in X$, and let $f_1,\ldots ,f_ r$ be holomorphic functions on a neighborhood of $a$ whose complex Jacobian matrix at $a$, computed in a holomorphic chart, has rank $r$. Then $f_1,\ldots ,f_ r$ are the first $r$ coordinates of a holomorphic chart of $X$ near $a$. Proof. (1) The real derivative of $F$ at $a$ is the complex-linear map given by the invertible matrix $(\partial _{z_ k}F_ j(a))$, so it is invertible. By the real inverse function theorem there are open neighborhoods $U'$ of $a$ and $V'$ of $F(a)$ such that $F$ maps $U'$ bijectively onto $V'$, the inverse map $G\colon V'\to U'$ is smooth, and $\mathrm dG_ w=(\mathrm dF_{G(w)})^{-1}$ for $w\in V'$. Since $F$ is holomorphic, $\mathrm dF_{G(w)}$ is complex linear, and hence so is its inverse. Thus the real derivative of $G$ is complex linear at every point, that is, $G$ is holomorphic. (2) If $r=0$, the identity map has the required property. Otherwise some $r\times r$ minor of the matrix $(\partial _{z_ k}f_ j(a))$ is nonzero; let $k_1<\cdots <k_{m-r}$ be the indices of the columns not used by this minor. The map $\Phi =(f_1,\ldots ,f_ r,z_{k_1},\ldots ,z_{k_{m-r}})$ is holomorphic on $U$. The last $m-r$ rows of its complex Jacobian matrix at $a$ are the unit row vectors with entry $1$ in the columns $k_1,\ldots ,k_{m-r}$, so, expanding the determinant along these rows, we see that it equals the chosen minor up to sign; hence it is nonzero. By (1), $\Phi $ maps an open neighborhood of $a$ bijectively onto an open subset of $\mathbb C^ m$, with holomorphic inverse. (3) The rank of the complex Jacobian matrix does not depend on the chart, by the chain rule, since coordinate changes have invertible complex Jacobian matrices. Let $\kappa \colon U\to \kappa (U)\subset \mathbb C^ m$ be a holomorphic chart around $a$ on which the $f_ j$ are defined. By (2), applied to the functions $f_ j\circ \kappa ^{-1}$ at $\kappa (a)$, there is a map $\Phi $ from an open neighborhood $V\subset \kappa (U)$ of $\kappa (a)$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb C^ m$, biholomorphic and with first components $f_ j\circ \kappa ^{-1}$. Then $\Phi \circ \kappa $ is a homeomorphism of $\kappa ^{-1}(V)$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb C^ m$ whose first $r$ components are $f_1,\ldots ,f_ r$. For every chart $\lambda $ of the atlas, the coordinate changes $(\Phi \circ \kappa )\circ \lambda ^{-1}=\Phi \circ (\kappa \circ \lambda ^{-1})$ and $\lambda \circ (\Phi \circ \kappa )^{-1}=(\lambda \circ \kappa ^{-1})\circ \Phi ^{-1}$ are compositions of holomorphic maps, so $\Phi \circ \kappa $ is a holomorphic chart. $\square$ A complex submanifold $Z$ of a complex manifold $X$ that is locally a coordinate plane of dimension $r$ is itself a complex manifold of dimension $r$. Indeed, the restrictions to $Z$ of the charts in which $Z$ is a coordinate plane $\mathbb C^ r\times \{ 0\} $, followed by the projection to $\mathbb C^ r$, form an atlas of $Z$ whose coordinate changes are restrictions of holomorphic maps to coordinate planes. Moreover $Z$ is paracompact, that is, every open cover of $Z$ has a locally finite open refinement: given an open cover of $Z$ by sets $Z\cap O_ i$ with $O_ i$ open in $X$, a locally finite open refinement of the cover of $X$ by the $O_ i$ and by $X\setminus Z$ restricts to a locally finite open refinement on $Z$. Every connected component of a complex manifold $X$ is open, since manifolds are locally connected, and it has a countable basis of its topology. To see this, refine the cover of $X$ by all relatively compact coordinate balls to a locally finite open cover $(U_ a)$. Each $U_ a$ lies in a coordinate ball, hence in a single connected component, and its closure is compact, so it meets only finitely many members of the cover. Fix a member $U_{a_0}$, and call a member reachable if it is joined to $U_{a_0}$ by a finite chain of members, each meeting the next. By the finiteness just noted, there are only countably many reachable members. The union of the reachable members and the union of the remaining ones are disjoint open sets covering $X$. Hence the first union is open and closed; it contains the connected component $C$ of $U_{a_0}$, and it is contained in $C$ because each member lies in a single component. Thus $C$ is covered by countably many coordinate balls, and therefore has a countable basis. In particular, connected manifolds and compact manifolds have a countable basis, whereas a general complex manifold may have uncountably many components, for instance the product of $\mathbb C^ n$ with an uncountable discrete space. We state the countability of a basis as a hypothesis whenever a global subsequence or another countable selection requires it. A differential $k$-form is a smooth field of alternating $k$-linear forms on the real tangent spaces, with complex values. In a chart with real coordinates $t_1,\ldots ,t_ N$, where $N$ is the real dimension, every $k$-form is uniquely $\alpha =\sum _ J\alpha _ J\, \mathrm dt_ J$ with smooth coefficients $\alpha _ J$; here $J=(j_1<\cdots <j_ k)$ runs over the increasing multi-indices of length $k$, and $\mathrm dt_ J=\mathrm dt_{j_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dt_{j_ k}$. The pullback of $\alpha $ by a smooth map $F$ is defined pointwise by $(F^*\alpha )_ x(v_1,\ldots ,v_ k)=\alpha _{F(x)}(\mathrm dF_ xv_1,\ldots ,\mathrm dF_ xv_ k)$; it is multiplicative for the exterior product, and $F^*\mathrm dt_ j=\mathrm dF_ j$ for the components $F_ j=t_ j\circ F$. The exterior derivative is defined in coordinates by \[  \mathrm d\Big(\sum _ J\alpha _ J\, \mathrm dt_ J\Big)=\sum _ J\sum _ l\partial _{t_ l}\alpha _ J\, \mathrm dt_ l\wedge \mathrm dt_ J.  \] It satisfies B25865120DE7 5.2.5 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{d}(\alpha \wedge \gamma )=\mathrm{d}\alpha \wedge \gamma +(-1)^ k\alpha \wedge \mathrm{d}\gamma , \qquad \mathrm{d}^2=0,\qquad F^*\mathrm d\alpha =\mathrm dF^*\alpha \end{equation} for a $k$-form $\alpha $, every form $\gamma $ and every smooth map $F$ between open subsets of coordinate spaces. Indeed, the Leibniz rule follows from the product rule for the coefficients, the sign $(-1)^ k$ arising when $\mathrm dt_ l$ is moved past the $k$ factors of $\alpha $. Next, $\mathrm d^2(f\, \mathrm dt_ J)=\sum _{l,l'}\partial _{t_{l'}}\partial _{t_ l}f\, \mathrm dt_{l'}\wedge \mathrm dt_ l\wedge \mathrm dt_ J=0$, because the second derivatives of $f$ are symmetric in $l$ and $l'$, whereas $\mathrm dt_{l'}\wedge \mathrm dt_ l$ is antisymmetric. Finally, for a function $f$ the chain rule gives $\mathrm d(f\circ F)=\sum _ j(\partial _{t_ j}f\circ F)\, \mathrm dF_ j=F^*\mathrm df$. Since $\mathrm d(\mathrm dF_{j_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dF_{j_ k})=0$ by the Leibniz rule and $\mathrm d^2=0$, it follows that \[  \mathrm dF^*(f\, \mathrm dt_ J)=\mathrm d\big ((f\circ F)\, \mathrm dF_{j_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dF_{j_ k}\big )=F^*\mathrm df\wedge F^*\mathrm dt_ J=F^*\mathrm d(f\, \mathrm dt_ J).  \] Applied to coordinate changes, the last identity shows that the exterior derivative does not depend on the chart. Hence $\mathrm d$ is defined for forms on manifolds, and the rules ( 5.2.5 ) hold there, for smooth maps $F$ between manifolds. On a complex manifold of dimension $n$, in holomorphic coordinates $z_ j=x_ j+\mathrm iy_ j$, the $1$-forms $\mathrm dz_ j$ and $\mathrm d\bar z_ j$ form a basis of the complex-valued real-linear forms on each tangent space, so every $k$-form $\alpha $ decomposes uniquely as \[  \alpha =\sum _{p+q=k}\alpha ^{p,q},\qquad \alpha ^{p,q}=\sum _{|I|=p,\, |J|=q}\alpha _{I,J}\, \mathrm{d}z_ I\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ J,  \] where, for an increasing multi-index $I=(i_1<\cdots <i_ p)$, we write $\mathrm{d}z_ I=\mathrm{d}z_{i_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{d}z_{i_ p}$, and similarly $\mathrm{d}\bar z_ J$. The form $\alpha ^{p,q}$ is the component of bidegree, or type, $(p,q)$ of $\alpha $. A holomorphic change of coordinates $w=w(z)$ gives $\mathrm dw_ j=\sum _ k\partial _{z_ k}w_ j\, \mathrm dz_ k$ and $\mathrm d\bar w_ j=\sum _ k\overline{\partial _{z_ k}w_ j}\, \mathrm d\bar z_ k$, so it transforms the $\mathrm dz_ j$ among themselves and the $\mathrm d\bar z_ j$ among themselves. Hence this decomposition does not depend on the chart, and, for the same reason, pullback by holomorphic maps preserves bidegrees. Since $\mathrm d(\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J)=0$ and $\mathrm df=\sum _ l(\partial _{z_ l}f\, \mathrm dz_ l+\partial _{\bar z_ l}f\, \mathrm d\bar z_ l)$, we have $\mathrm d(f\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J)=\sum _ l(\partial _{z_ l}f\, \mathrm dz_ l+\partial _{\bar z_ l}f\, \mathrm d\bar z_ l)\wedge \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$. Thus, for a form $\alpha $ of type $(p,q)$, the form $\mathrm d\alpha $ is the sum of a form $\partial \alpha $ of type $(p+1,q)$ and a form $\bar\partial \alpha $ of type $(p,q+1)$. Extending $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $ linearly to all forms, we have $\mathrm{d}=\partial +\bar\partial $. Comparing types in $\mathrm d^2=0$ gives \[  \partial ^2=\bar\partial ^2=0,\qquad \partial \bar\partial =-\bar\partial \partial .  \] Complex conjugation exchanges the types $(p,q)$ and $(q,p)$, and a form is real if it equals its conjugate. We orient a complex manifold by the form $\mathrm{d}x_1\wedge \mathrm{d}y_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{d}x_ n\wedge \mathrm{d}y_ n$ in each holomorphic chart. These orientations agree on overlapping charts. Indeed, since $\frac{\mathrm i}2\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j=\mathrm dx_ j\wedge \mathrm dy_ j$ and $2$-forms commute with all forms, this form equals $c_ n\, \mathrm dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ n$ for a constant $c_ n\neq 0$ depending only on $n$. If $w$ is a second holomorphic chart, then $\mathrm dw_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dw_ n=\det (\partial _{z_ k}w_ j)\, \mathrm dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n$ by multilinearity and antisymmetry of the exterior product, and the conjugate identity holds for the $\mathrm d\bar w_ j$. Hence the form defined by $w$ is $|\det (\partial _{z_ k}w_ j)|^2>0$ times the form defined by $z$. Let $X$ be a complex manifold of dimension $n$, and let $\alpha $ be a $2n$-form on $X$ with compact support whose coefficients are locally integrable, that is, Lebesgue integrable on compact subsets of charts. If $\operatorname{Supp}\alpha $ lies in a holomorphic chart, in which $\alpha =g\, \mathrm dx_1\wedge \mathrm dy_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dx_ n\wedge \mathrm dy_ n$, we put $\int _ X\alpha =\int g\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$, the Lebesgue integral in the coordinates. This does not depend on the chart. Indeed, by the preceding paragraph, the coefficient $\tilde g$ of $\alpha $ in a second chart $w$ satisfies $g=(\tilde g\circ w)\, |\det (\partial _{z_ k}w_ j)|^2$, and $|\det (\partial _{z_ k}w_ j)|^2$ is the real Jacobian determinant of the coordinate change $z\mapsto w$, so the change of variables formula gives $\int g\, \mathrm dV_{2n}(z)=\int \tilde g\, \mathrm dV_{2n}(w)$. For general $\alpha $, we choose a partition of unity $(\chi _ a)$ subordinate to a cover of $X$ by charts (proposition 5.2.6 below). Only finitely many $\chi _ a$ are not identically zero on the compact set $\operatorname{Supp}\alpha $, and we put $\int _ X\alpha =\sum _ a\int _ X\chi _ a\alpha $. If $(\psi _ b)$ is a second such partition of unity, then, by the case of a single chart, \[  \sum _ a\int _ X\chi _ a\alpha =\sum _{a,b}\int _ X\chi _ a\psi _ b\alpha =\sum _ b\int _ X\psi _ b\alpha ,  \] so the integral is well defined. It is linear, and $\int _ X\alpha \geq 0$ if $\alpha $ is a nonnegative multiple of the volume form at every point. The same definition applies to complex submanifolds, which are complex manifolds with their own complex orientation. Proposition 5.2.6 . DAE61F3D77A3 Let $X$ be a complex manifold of dimension $n$. Then $X$ admits smooth partitions of unity subordinate to every open cover and consisting of functions with compact support. For every compact set $K\subset X$ and every open set $U\supset K$ there is a smooth function $\chi \colon X\to [0,1]$ with compact support in $U$ that equals one on a neighborhood of $K$. If $n\geq 1$ and $\alpha $ is a smooth $(2n-1)$-form with compact support on $X$, then $\int _ X\mathrm{d}\alpha =0$. Proof. Since the connected components of $X$ are open, it suffices to construct partitions of unity on each component; the union of the families so obtained is locally finite on $X$. So let $X$ be connected. By the preceding discussion, $X$ is covered by a sequence of coordinate balls $B_1,B_2,\ldots $ with compact closures. Put $K_1=\overline{B_1}$, and, once the compact set $K_ j$ is defined, cover it by finitely many of the balls $B_ i$ and let $K_{j+1}$ be the union of their closures and of $\overline{B_1},\ldots ,\overline{B_{j+1}}$. We obtain compact sets $K_1\subset \operatorname{Int}K_2\subset K_2\subset \operatorname{Int}K_3\subset \cdots $ with union $X$; put $K_ j=\varnothing $ for $j\leq 0$. Now let an open cover of $X$ be given. For $j\geq 1$, the compact set $K_ j\setminus \operatorname{Int}K_{j-1}$ lies in the open set $\operatorname{Int}K_{j+1}\setminus K_{j-2}$. Cover it by finitely many coordinate balls $B'$ whose concentric enlargements $B$ have compact closures contained in a member of the given cover and in $\operatorname{Int}K_{j+1}\setminus K_{j-2}$. For each such pair choose, in the chart, a smooth function with values in $[0,1]$ and compact support in $B$ that equals one on $B'$ (lemma 2.5.1 ), and extend it by zero to $X$. The resulting family is locally finite, since a point of $\operatorname{Int}K_ i$ has the neighborhood $\operatorname{Int}K_ i$, which meets the supports chosen at stage $j$ only if $j\leq i+1$. Its sum is therefore smooth, and it is positive, because the balls $B'$ cover $X$. Dividing each function by this sum gives the required partition of unity. For the cutoff function, cover $K$ by finitely many relatively compact coordinate balls with closures in $U$, and let $V$ be their union; thus $K\subset V$ and $\overline V$ is a compact subset of $U$. Let $(\chi _ a)$ be a partition of unity with compact supports subordinate to the cover $\{ V,X\setminus K\} $, and let $\chi $ be the sum of those $\chi _ a$ whose support is not contained in $X\setminus K$. Each of these has its support in $V$; by local finiteness, only finitely many supports meet the compact set $\overline V$, so $\chi $ is a finite sum, smooth, with values in $[0,1]$ and compact support in $\overline V\subset U$. The supports of the remaining $\chi _ a$ lie in $X\setminus K$, and their union $F$ is closed, as a locally finite union of closed sets. On the neighborhood $X\setminus F$ of $K$ we have $\chi =\sum _ a\chi _ a=1$. For the last assertion, consider first a compactly supported $(2n-1)$-form $\gamma $ in a single chart. Then $\mathrm{d}\gamma $ is a sum of terms $\pm \partial _{t_ l}g\, \mathrm dt_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dt_{2n}$, where $t_1,\ldots ,t_{2n}$ are the real coordinates $x_1,y_1,\ldots ,x_ n,y_ n$ and $g$ is smooth with compact support; the integral of each term vanishes by Fubini's theorem and the fundamental theorem of calculus on lines parallel to the $t_ l$-axis. Now let $(\chi _ a)$ be a partition of unity subordinate to a cover by charts. Only finitely many $\chi _ a$ are nonzero on the compact set $\operatorname{Supp}\alpha $, so $\alpha =\sum _ a\chi _ a\alpha $ is a finite sum of compactly supported forms in single charts, and $\int _ X\mathrm d\alpha =\sum _ a\int _ X\mathrm d(\chi _ a\alpha )=0$. $\square$ Cutoff functions also embed a compact manifold in a Euclidean space; later chapters use the resulting metric to measure distances to closed sets. Lemma 5.2.7 . 98494B0CCC31 Let $X$ be a compact complex manifold. Then there are an integer $N\ge 0$ and a smooth injective map $F\colon X\to \mathbb R^ N$ which is a homeomorphism of $X$ onto $F(X)$. Consequently, $d(x,y)=|F(x)-F(y)|$ is a metric on $X$ which induces the topology of $X$. Proof. If $X$ is empty, take $N=0$. Otherwise let $n$ be the dimension of $X$. For each $x\in X$ choose a holomorphic chart $\kappa _ x\colon U_ x\to \mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ with $x\in U_ x$. By proposition 5.2.6 , applied to the compact set $\{ x\} $ and the open set $U_ x$, there is a smooth function $\chi _ x\colon X\to [0,1]$ with compact support in $U_ x$ which equals one on an open neighborhood $W_ x$ of $x$. Since $X$ is compact, finitely many of the sets $W_ x$ cover $X$; we denote the corresponding charts, cutoff functions and neighborhoods by $\kappa _ i\colon U_ i\to \mathbb R^{2n}$, $\chi _ i$ and $W_ i$, $1\le i\le k$. The map $\chi _ i\kappa _ i$, defined as the product on $U_ i$ and as $0$ on $X\setminus U_ i$, is smooth: it is smooth on $U_ i$, it vanishes on $X\setminus \operatorname{Supp}\chi _ i$, which is open because the compact set $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ i$ is closed in the Hausdorff space $X$, and these two open sets cover $X$ because $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ i\subset U_ i$. Put $N=k+2nk$ and \[  F=(\chi _1,\ldots ,\chi _ k,\chi _1\kappa _1,\ldots ,\chi _ k\kappa _ k)\colon X\to \mathbb R^ N,  \] a smooth map. It is injective. Indeed, let $F(x)=F(y)$, and choose $i$ with $x\in W_ i$. Then $\chi _ i(y)=\chi _ i(x)=1$, so $y\in \operatorname{Supp}\chi _ i\subset U_ i$, and $\chi _ i\kappa _ i(x)=\chi _ i\kappa _ i(y)$ gives $\kappa _ i(x)=\kappa _ i(y)$; since $\kappa _ i$ is injective on $U_ i$, we obtain $x=y$. If $C\subset X$ is closed, then $C$ is compact, so $F(C)$ is compact and hence closed in $\mathbb R^ N$. Thus the continuous bijection $F\colon X\to F(X)$ maps closed sets to closed sets, so its inverse is continuous, and $F$ is a homeomorphism onto $F(X)$. Hence $d$, the Euclidean metric of $F(X)$ transported to $X$ by $F$, is a metric on $X$ that induces its topology. $\square$ For computations in $\mathbb {C}^ n$ we use the Euclidean Kähler form E58B935C99BA 5.2.8 \begin{equation}  \beta =\frac{\mathrm{i}}2\sum _{j=1}^ n\mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ j, \qquad \frac{\beta ^ n}{n!}=\mathrm{d}V_{2n}. \end{equation} Here $\mathrm dV_{2n}=\mathrm dx_1\wedge \mathrm dy_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dx_ n\wedge \mathrm dy_ n$ is the Euclidean volume form, which we identify with Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb {C}^ n=\mathbb {R}^{2n}$; for $n=0$, $\mathrm dV_0$ is the unit mass on the singleton $\mathbb C^0$. The second identity holds because $(\mathrm{i}/2)\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j=\mathrm dx_ j\wedge \mathrm dy_ j$ and these $2$-forms commute and have square zero, so that in the expansion of $\beta ^ n$ only the $n!$ products containing each of them once survive, each equal to $\mathrm dV_{2n}$. The operator $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ is normalized as in the Conventions: EFB1A41694DE 5.2.9 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\partial \bar\partial u =\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\sum _{j,k}u_{j\bar k}\, \mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ k, \qquad \Delta u=4\sum _ j u_{j\bar j}. \end{equation} Here $u_{j\bar k}=\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{\bar z_ k}u$, and $\Delta $ is the Laplacian of $\mathbb R^{2n}$; the matrix $(u_{j\bar k})$ is the complex Hessian of $u$. The same formulas define $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ for a distribution $u$ on an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$, with distributional derivatives $u_{j\bar k}$; then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is a current in the sense of the next section. We also use the real operator C44E7362B437 5.2.10 \begin{equation}  \mathrm d^{\mathrm c}=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{4\pi }(\bar\partial -\partial )=\frac{\partial -\bar\partial }{4\pi \mathrm{i}}, \qquad \text{so that}\qquad \mathrm d\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2\pi }\partial \bar\partial =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}. \end{equation} Indeed, since $\partial ^2=\bar\partial ^2=0$ and $\bar\partial \partial =-\partial \bar\partial $, we have $(\partial +\bar\partial )(\bar\partial -\partial )=\partial \bar\partial -\bar\partial \partial =2\partial \bar\partial $. Moreover $\overline{\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\alpha }=\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}\bar\alpha $, because conjugation exchanges $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $ and changes the sign of $\mathrm{i}$; hence $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}$ maps real forms to real forms.

title: Definition 5.2.3
text: Definition 5.2.3 . 42A02A1A5EFE A complex manifold of dimension $n$ is a paracompact Hausdorff space with an atlas of homeomorphisms onto open subsets of $\mathbb {C}^ n$, whose coordinate changes are holomorphic with holomorphic inverses. A map between complex manifolds is holomorphic if its coordinate expressions are holomorphic. A complex submanifold is a closed subset that is locally a coordinate plane in suitable holomorphic coordinates.

title: Proposition 5.2.4
text: Proposition 5.2.4 . A683A13C69D9 Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, let $F\colon U\to \mathbb C^ n$ be holomorphic, and let $a\in U$ be a point at which the complex Jacobian matrix $(\partial _{z_ k}F_ j(a))_{j,k}$ is invertible. Then there are open neighborhoods $U'\subset U$ of $a$ and $V'\subset \mathbb C^ n$ of $F(a)$ such that $F$ maps $U'$ bijectively onto $V'$ and the inverse map $V'\to U'$ is holomorphic. Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ m$ be open, let $a\in U$, and let $f_1,\ldots ,f_ r$, $0\le r\le m$, be holomorphic functions on $U$ whose complex Jacobian matrix $(\partial _{z_ k}f_ j(a))_{1\le j\le r,\, 1\le k\le m}$ at $a$ has rank $r$. Then there are indices $k_1<\cdots <k_{m-r}$ such that the map $(f_1,\ldots ,f_ r,z_{k_1},\ldots ,z_{k_{m-r}})$ is biholomorphic from an open neighborhood of $a$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb C^ m$. Thus $f_1,\ldots ,f_ r$ are the first $r$ coordinates of a holomorphic chart near $a$. Let $X$ be a complex manifold of dimension $m$, let $a\in X$, and let $f_1,\ldots ,f_ r$ be holomorphic functions on a neighborhood of $a$ whose complex Jacobian matrix at $a$, computed in a holomorphic chart, has rank $r$. Then $f_1,\ldots ,f_ r$ are the first $r$ coordinates of a holomorphic chart of $X$ near $a$. Proof. (1) The real derivative of $F$ at $a$ is the complex-linear map given by the invertible matrix $(\partial _{z_ k}F_ j(a))$, so it is invertible. By the real inverse function theorem there are open neighborhoods $U'$ of $a$ and $V'$ of $F(a)$ such that $F$ maps $U'$ bijectively onto $V'$, the inverse map $G\colon V'\to U'$ is smooth, and $\mathrm dG_ w=(\mathrm dF_{G(w)})^{-1}$ for $w\in V'$. Since $F$ is holomorphic, $\mathrm dF_{G(w)}$ is complex linear, and hence so is its inverse. Thus the real derivative of $G$ is complex linear at every point, that is, $G$ is holomorphic. (2) If $r=0$, the identity map has the required property. Otherwise some $r\times r$ minor of the matrix $(\partial _{z_ k}f_ j(a))$ is nonzero; let $k_1<\cdots <k_{m-r}$ be the indices of the columns not used by this minor. The map $\Phi =(f_1,\ldots ,f_ r,z_{k_1},\ldots ,z_{k_{m-r}})$ is holomorphic on $U$. The last $m-r$ rows of its complex Jacobian matrix at $a$ are the unit row vectors with entry $1$ in the columns $k_1,\ldots ,k_{m-r}$, so, expanding the determinant along these rows, we see that it equals the chosen minor up to sign; hence it is nonzero. By (1), $\Phi $ maps an open neighborhood of $a$ bijectively onto an open subset of $\mathbb C^ m$, with holomorphic inverse. (3) The rank of the complex Jacobian matrix does not depend on the chart, by the chain rule, since coordinate changes have invertible complex Jacobian matrices. Let $\kappa \colon U\to \kappa (U)\subset \mathbb C^ m$ be a holomorphic chart around $a$ on which the $f_ j$ are defined. By (2), applied to the functions $f_ j\circ \kappa ^{-1}$ at $\kappa (a)$, there is a map $\Phi $ from an open neighborhood $V\subset \kappa (U)$ of $\kappa (a)$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb C^ m$, biholomorphic and with first components $f_ j\circ \kappa ^{-1}$. Then $\Phi \circ \kappa $ is a homeomorphism of $\kappa ^{-1}(V)$ onto an open subset of $\mathbb C^ m$ whose first $r$ components are $f_1,\ldots ,f_ r$. For every chart $\lambda $ of the atlas, the coordinate changes $(\Phi \circ \kappa )\circ \lambda ^{-1}=\Phi \circ (\kappa \circ \lambda ^{-1})$ and $\lambda \circ (\Phi \circ \kappa )^{-1}=(\lambda \circ \kappa ^{-1})\circ \Phi ^{-1}$ are compositions of holomorphic maps, so $\Phi \circ \kappa $ is a holomorphic chart. $\square$

title: Equation 5.2.5
text: B25865120DE7 5.2.5 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{d}(\alpha \wedge \gamma )=\mathrm{d}\alpha \wedge \gamma +(-1)^ k\alpha \wedge \mathrm{d}\gamma , \qquad \mathrm{d}^2=0,\qquad F^*\mathrm d\alpha =\mathrm dF^*\alpha \end{equation}

title: Proposition 5.2.6
text: Proposition 5.2.6 . DAE61F3D77A3 Let $X$ be a complex manifold of dimension $n$. Then $X$ admits smooth partitions of unity subordinate to every open cover and consisting of functions with compact support. For every compact set $K\subset X$ and every open set $U\supset K$ there is a smooth function $\chi \colon X\to [0,1]$ with compact support in $U$ that equals one on a neighborhood of $K$. If $n\geq 1$ and $\alpha $ is a smooth $(2n-1)$-form with compact support on $X$, then $\int _ X\mathrm{d}\alpha =0$. Proof. Since the connected components of $X$ are open, it suffices to construct partitions of unity on each component; the union of the families so obtained is locally finite on $X$. So let $X$ be connected. By the preceding discussion, $X$ is covered by a sequence of coordinate balls $B_1,B_2,\ldots $ with compact closures. Put $K_1=\overline{B_1}$, and, once the compact set $K_ j$ is defined, cover it by finitely many of the balls $B_ i$ and let $K_{j+1}$ be the union of their closures and of $\overline{B_1},\ldots ,\overline{B_{j+1}}$. We obtain compact sets $K_1\subset \operatorname{Int}K_2\subset K_2\subset \operatorname{Int}K_3\subset \cdots $ with union $X$; put $K_ j=\varnothing $ for $j\leq 0$. Now let an open cover of $X$ be given. For $j\geq 1$, the compact set $K_ j\setminus \operatorname{Int}K_{j-1}$ lies in the open set $\operatorname{Int}K_{j+1}\setminus K_{j-2}$. Cover it by finitely many coordinate balls $B'$ whose concentric enlargements $B$ have compact closures contained in a member of the given cover and in $\operatorname{Int}K_{j+1}\setminus K_{j-2}$. For each such pair choose, in the chart, a smooth function with values in $[0,1]$ and compact support in $B$ that equals one on $B'$ (lemma 2.5.1 ), and extend it by zero to $X$. The resulting family is locally finite, since a point of $\operatorname{Int}K_ i$ has the neighborhood $\operatorname{Int}K_ i$, which meets the supports chosen at stage $j$ only if $j\leq i+1$. Its sum is therefore smooth, and it is positive, because the balls $B'$ cover $X$. Dividing each function by this sum gives the required partition of unity. For the cutoff function, cover $K$ by finitely many relatively compact coordinate balls with closures in $U$, and let $V$ be their union; thus $K\subset V$ and $\overline V$ is a compact subset of $U$. Let $(\chi _ a)$ be a partition of unity with compact supports subordinate to the cover $\{ V,X\setminus K\} $, and let $\chi $ be the sum of those $\chi _ a$ whose support is not contained in $X\setminus K$. Each of these has its support in $V$; by local finiteness, only finitely many supports meet the compact set $\overline V$, so $\chi $ is a finite sum, smooth, with values in $[0,1]$ and compact support in $\overline V\subset U$. The supports of the remaining $\chi _ a$ lie in $X\setminus K$, and their union $F$ is closed, as a locally finite union of closed sets. On the neighborhood $X\setminus F$ of $K$ we have $\chi =\sum _ a\chi _ a=1$. For the last assertion, consider first a compactly supported $(2n-1)$-form $\gamma $ in a single chart. Then $\mathrm{d}\gamma $ is a sum of terms $\pm \partial _{t_ l}g\, \mathrm dt_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dt_{2n}$, where $t_1,\ldots ,t_{2n}$ are the real coordinates $x_1,y_1,\ldots ,x_ n,y_ n$ and $g$ is smooth with compact support; the integral of each term vanishes by Fubini's theorem and the fundamental theorem of calculus on lines parallel to the $t_ l$-axis. Now let $(\chi _ a)$ be a partition of unity subordinate to a cover by charts. Only finitely many $\chi _ a$ are nonzero on the compact set $\operatorname{Supp}\alpha $, so $\alpha =\sum _ a\chi _ a\alpha $ is a finite sum of compactly supported forms in single charts, and $\int _ X\mathrm d\alpha =\sum _ a\int _ X\mathrm d(\chi _ a\alpha )=0$. $\square$

title: Lemma 5.2.7
text: Lemma 5.2.7 . 98494B0CCC31 Let $X$ be a compact complex manifold. Then there are an integer $N\ge 0$ and a smooth injective map $F\colon X\to \mathbb R^ N$ which is a homeomorphism of $X$ onto $F(X)$. Consequently, $d(x,y)=|F(x)-F(y)|$ is a metric on $X$ which induces the topology of $X$. Proof. If $X$ is empty, take $N=0$. Otherwise let $n$ be the dimension of $X$. For each $x\in X$ choose a holomorphic chart $\kappa _ x\colon U_ x\to \mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ with $x\in U_ x$. By proposition 5.2.6 , applied to the compact set $\{ x\} $ and the open set $U_ x$, there is a smooth function $\chi _ x\colon X\to [0,1]$ with compact support in $U_ x$ which equals one on an open neighborhood $W_ x$ of $x$. Since $X$ is compact, finitely many of the sets $W_ x$ cover $X$; we denote the corresponding charts, cutoff functions and neighborhoods by $\kappa _ i\colon U_ i\to \mathbb R^{2n}$, $\chi _ i$ and $W_ i$, $1\le i\le k$. The map $\chi _ i\kappa _ i$, defined as the product on $U_ i$ and as $0$ on $X\setminus U_ i$, is smooth: it is smooth on $U_ i$, it vanishes on $X\setminus \operatorname{Supp}\chi _ i$, which is open because the compact set $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ i$ is closed in the Hausdorff space $X$, and these two open sets cover $X$ because $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ i\subset U_ i$. Put $N=k+2nk$ and \[  F=(\chi _1,\ldots ,\chi _ k,\chi _1\kappa _1,\ldots ,\chi _ k\kappa _ k)\colon X\to \mathbb R^ N,  \] a smooth map. It is injective. Indeed, let $F(x)=F(y)$, and choose $i$ with $x\in W_ i$. Then $\chi _ i(y)=\chi _ i(x)=1$, so $y\in \operatorname{Supp}\chi _ i\subset U_ i$, and $\chi _ i\kappa _ i(x)=\chi _ i\kappa _ i(y)$ gives $\kappa _ i(x)=\kappa _ i(y)$; since $\kappa _ i$ is injective on $U_ i$, we obtain $x=y$. If $C\subset X$ is closed, then $C$ is compact, so $F(C)$ is compact and hence closed in $\mathbb R^ N$. Thus the continuous bijection $F\colon X\to F(X)$ maps closed sets to closed sets, so its inverse is continuous, and $F$ is a homeomorphism onto $F(X)$. Hence $d$, the Euclidean metric of $F(X)$ transported to $X$ by $F$, is a metric on $X$ that induces its topology. $\square$
