title: 5.3 Currents and positivity
text: Let $X$ be a complex manifold of dimension $n$. A test form on $X$ is a smooth complex differential form with compact support; the test forms of degree zero are the test functions. In a chart with real coordinates $t_1,\ldots ,t_{2n}$ we write test forms as $\varphi =\sum _ J\varphi _ J\, \mathrm dt_ J$ and measure them by the seminorms $p_{K,m}$ of section 2.4 applied to their coefficients. For an integer $0\leq k\leq 2n$, a current of degree $k$ on $X$ is a complex-linear functional $T$ on the test forms of degree $2n-k$ with the following continuity property: for every coordinate chart and every compact set $K$ in it, there are $C>0$ and $m\in \mathbb N$ such that $|T(\varphi )|\leq C\sum _ Jp_{K,m}(\varphi _ J)$ for all test forms $\varphi $ of degree $2n-k$ supported in $K$. Equivalently, in every chart and for every multi-index $J$ with $|J|=2n-k$, the functional $\chi \mapsto T(\chi \, \mathrm dt_ J)$ is a distribution. In a chart there are therefore unique distributions $T_ J$, $|J|=k$, such that \[  T(\varphi )=\sum _ J\langle T_ J,g_ J\rangle ,\qquad \text{where }\mathrm dt_ J\wedge \varphi =g_ J\, \mathrm dt_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dt_{2n},  \] for all test forms $\varphi $ supported in the chart. Namely, if $J'$ is the increasing multi-index complementary to $J$ and $\mathrm dt_ J\wedge \mathrm dt_{J'}=\varepsilon _ J\, \mathrm dt_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dt_{2n}$ with $\varepsilon _ J=\pm 1$, then $\langle T_ J,\chi \rangle =\varepsilon _ JT(\chi \, \mathrm dt_{J'})$, because $g_ J=\varepsilon _ J\varphi _{J'}$ for $\varphi =\sum _ L\varphi _ L\, \mathrm dt_ L$. We write $T=\sum _ JT_ J\, \mathrm dt_ J$ and call the $T_ J$ the coefficients of $T$; more generally, for multi-indices $M$ that are not increasing, $S\, \mathrm dt_ M$ denotes the current $\varphi \mapsto \langle S,g\rangle $, where $\mathrm dt_ M\wedge \varphi =g\, \mathrm dt_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dt_{2n}$. In holomorphic coordinates we use the basis $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ in the same way. Thus locally a current is a differential form with distribution coefficients. A locally integrable $k$-form $\alpha $, that is, a form with locally integrable coefficients, defines the current $T_\alpha (\varphi )=\int _ X\alpha \wedge \varphi $ of degree $k$, which we usually denote again by $\alpha $. A current of degree $k$ has bidegree $(p,q)$, where $p+q=k$, if it vanishes on all test forms of bidegree other than $(n-p,n-q)$; in holomorphic coordinates it is then $T=\sum _{|I|=p,|J|=q}T_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$. Its bidimension is $(n-p,n-q)$. Every current is the sum of its components of pure bidegree. Forms and currents of a degree or bidegree outside the admissible range are taken to be zero. The conjugate of a current $T$ is $\overline T(\varphi )=\overline{T(\bar\varphi )}$, and $T$ is real if $\overline T=T$, that is, $T(\bar\varphi )=\overline{T(\varphi )}$ for every test form $\varphi $. A sequence, or more generally a net, of currents $T_ i$ of degree $k$ converges weakly to $T$ if $T_ i(\varphi )\to T(\varphi )$ for every test form $\varphi $ of degree $2n-k$. For currents of degree $2n$ given by positive measures, weak convergence is the vague convergence of these measures; see the discussion following definition 5.3.5 . As for distributions (section 2.4 ), a current $T$ vanishes on an open set $W\subset X$ if $T(\varphi )=0$ for every test form $\varphi $ with $\operatorname{Supp}\varphi \subset W$, and the support $\operatorname{Supp}T$ of $T$ is the complement of the union of all open sets on which $T$ vanishes. If $T$ vanishes on each member of a family of open sets, it vanishes on their union, because a partition of unity subordinate to the cover formed by these sets and by $X\setminus \operatorname{Supp}\varphi $ (proposition 5.2.6 ) writes every test form $\varphi $ supported in the union as a finite sum of test forms supported in single members. Hence $X\setminus \operatorname{Supp}T$ is the largest open set on which $T$ vanishes, and $T(\varphi )=0$ whenever $\operatorname{Supp}\varphi \cap \operatorname{Supp}T=\varnothing $. Let $T$ be a current of degree $k$ and $\alpha $ a smooth form. We define \[  (\mathrm{d}T)(\varphi )=(-1)^{k+1}T(\mathrm{d}\varphi ),\qquad (T\wedge \alpha )(\varphi )=T(\alpha \wedge \varphi ),  \] and, in the same way, $(\partial T)(\varphi )=(-1)^{k+1}T(\partial \varphi )$ and $(\bar\partial T)(\varphi )=(-1)^{k+1}T(\bar\partial \varphi )$. These are currents, because $\mathrm d$, $\partial $, $\bar\partial $ and multiplication by $\alpha $ map test forms supported in a compact set $K$ of a chart to test forms supported in $K$, and the seminorms $p_{K,m}$ of the new coefficients are bounded by a constant times the seminorms $p_{K,m+1}$ of the old ones. For a smooth form $T$ these definitions agree with the exterior derivative and the exterior product: by the Leibniz rule and proposition 5.2.6 , $\int _ X\mathrm dT\wedge \varphi =(-1)^{k+1}\int _ XT\wedge \mathrm d\varphi $, and applying this identity to the components of pure bidegree of $T$ and $\varphi $, of which only the products of bidegree $(n,n)$ have nonzero integrals, we obtain the analogous identities for $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $. In a chart, these operations act on the distribution coefficients exactly as on the coefficients of smooth forms. Indeed, let $t=(x_1,y_1,\ldots ,x_ n,y_ n)$ be the real coordinates of a holomorphic chart, let $\varphi $ be a test form of degree $2n-k-1$ supported in the chart, and write $\mathrm dt_ l\wedge \mathrm dt_ J\wedge \varphi =g_{l,J}\, \mathrm dt_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dt_{2n}$ and $\mathrm dt_ J\wedge \mathrm d\varphi =h_ J\, \mathrm dt_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dt_{2n}$. For every smooth function $a$ on the chart, the identity just proved for the smooth form $a\, \mathrm dt_ J$ reads $\sum _ l\int \partial _{t_ l}a\, g_{l,J}\, \mathrm dV_{2n}=(-1)^{k+1}\int ah_ J\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$. Integrating by parts on the left, we find $(-1)^{k+1}h_ J=-\sum _ l\partial _{t_ l}g_{l,J}$. Hence, for a current $T=\sum _ JT_ J\, \mathrm dt_ J$, \[  (\mathrm dT)(\varphi )=(-1)^{k+1}\sum _ J\langle T_ J,h_ J\rangle =-\sum _{J,l}\langle T_ J,\partial _{t_ l}g_{l,J}\rangle =\sum _{J,l}\langle \partial _{t_ l}T_ J,g_{l,J}\rangle ,  \] that is, $\mathrm dT=\sum _{J,l}\partial _{t_ l}T_ J\, \mathrm dt_ l\wedge \mathrm dt_ J$ with distributional derivatives. The same computation applies to $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $ in the basis $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$, and directly from the definitions $T\wedge \alpha =\sum _{J,L}\alpha _ LT_ J\, \mathrm dt_ J\wedge \mathrm dt_ L$ for $\alpha =\sum _ L\alpha _ L\, \mathrm dt_ L$. If $\alpha $ has degree $r$, then, by the Leibniz rule for $\alpha \wedge \varphi $, \begin{align*}  (\mathrm dT\wedge \alpha )(\varphi )+(-1)^ k(T\wedge \mathrm d\alpha )(\varphi )& =(-1)^{k+1}T\big (\mathrm d(\alpha \wedge \varphi )\big )+(-1)^ kT(\mathrm d\alpha \wedge \varphi )\\ & =(-1)^{k+r+1}T(\alpha \wedge \mathrm d\varphi ), \end{align*} so that $\mathrm d(T\wedge \alpha )=\mathrm dT\wedge \alpha +(-1)^ kT\wedge \mathrm d\alpha $, and similarly for $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $. In general, the product of two currents is not defined. We put $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T=(\mathrm{i}/2\pi )\partial \bar\partial T$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}T=(\mathrm{i}/4\pi )(\bar\partial T-\partial T)$. Since $(\partial \bar\partial T)(\varphi )=(-1)^{k+2}(\bar\partial T)(\partial \varphi )=-T(\bar\partial \partial \varphi )=T(\partial \bar\partial \varphi )$, and since the identities $\mathrm d=\partial +\bar\partial $, $\partial ^2=\bar\partial ^2=0$ and $\bar\partial \partial =-\partial \bar\partial $ pass from test forms to currents by duality, we obtain \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T)(\varphi )=T(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi ),\qquad \mathrm d\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}T=\frac{\mathrm i}{4\pi }(\partial +\bar\partial )(\bar\partial -\partial )T=\frac{\mathrm i}{4\pi }(\partial \bar\partial T-\bar\partial \partial T)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T.  \] All these operations are continuous for weak convergence, directly from the definitions. A current $T$ is closed if $\mathrm{d}T=0$. For a current of pure bidegree this is equivalent to $\partial T=\bar\partial T=0$, since $\partial T$ and $\bar\partial T$ are the components of $\mathrm dT$ of two different bidegrees. We now turn to positivity of forms, which is a question of linear algebra. Let $V$ be a complex vector space of dimension $n$, identified with $\mathbb C^ n$ by linear coordinates $z_1,\ldots ,z_ n$, and let $\beta $ be the form ( 5.2.8 ) in these coordinates; the forms below are constant forms on $V$. For an integer $0\leq p\leq n$, a real $(p,p)$-form is strongly positive if it is a finite sum, with nonnegative coefficients, of the forms 976BD2929614 5.3.1 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{i}^{p^2}\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ p \wedge \bar\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \bar\theta _ p =\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p(\mathrm{i}\theta _ j\wedge \bar\theta _ j), \end{equation} where $\theta _1,\ldots ,\theta _ p\in V^*$ are complex-linear forms, that is, forms of type $(1,0)$. We call the forms ( 5.3.1 ) generators. The identity in ( 5.3.1 ) holds because rearranging the factors of the right-hand side produces the sign $(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}=\mathrm{i}^{p^2-p}$, and the generators are real because each factor $\mathrm i\theta _ j\wedge \bar\theta _ j$ is real. A real $(p,p)$-form is weakly positive if its exterior product with every strongly positive $(n-p,n-p)$-form is a nonnegative multiple of the volume form $\beta ^ n/n!$. In degree zero both notions mean a nonnegative real number. A form on a complex manifold is strongly or weakly positive if it is so at every point, as a form on the tangent space. Finally, the restriction of a $(p,p)$-form to a complex subspace $W$ of dimension $p$ is a form of top degree on $W$; we call it nonnegative if it is a nonnegative multiple of the volume form of $W$ in its complex orientation. Proposition 5.3.2 . E58104E974B0 Let $0\leq p\leq n$. The strongly positive $(p,p)$-forms on $V$ form a closed convex cone, which spans the real vector space of real $(p,p)$-forms and contains $\beta ^ p$ in its interior. A real $(p,p)$-form is weakly positive if and only if its restriction to every complex $p$-dimensional subspace of $V$ is nonnegative. Pullback by complex-linear maps, and hence by holomorphic maps between complex manifolds, preserves strong and weak positivity. The product of strongly positive forms is strongly positive, and the product of a weakly positive form with a strongly positive form is weakly positive when its bidegree is at most $(n,n)$. Moreover, strongly positive forms are weakly positive. Proof. We use the Hermitian inner product on $V^*$ for which $\mathrm dz_1,\ldots ,\mathrm dz_ n$ are orthonormal. The form $\beta $ is invariant under unitary changes of coordinates: if $\mathrm dw_ j=\sum _ kU_{jk}\, \mathrm dz_ k$ with a unitary matrix $U$, then $\sum _ j\mathrm dw_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar w_ j=\sum _{k,l}\big (\sum _ jU_{jk}\overline{U_{jl}}\big )\mathrm dz_ k\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ l=\sum _ k\mathrm dz_ k\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ k$. Let $\Lambda ^{p,0}V^*$ be the space of $(p,0)$-forms. For $\theta \in \Lambda ^{p,0}V^*$ put $g(\theta )=\mathrm i^{p^2}\theta \wedge \bar\theta $, so that $g(c\theta )=|c|^2g(\theta )$ and the generators are the forms $g(\theta )$ with $\theta $ decomposable. Closedness. Let $G$ be the set of the generators $g(e_1\wedge \cdots \wedge e_ p)$ with $e_1,\ldots ,e_ p$ orthonormal in $V^*$. It is the continuous image of the compact set of orthonormal $p$-tuples, so $G$ is compact. Every nonzero generator $g(\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ p)$ is a positive multiple of an element of $G$. Indeed, the $\theta _ j$ are linearly independent, and the Gram–Schmidt process gives an orthonormal family $e_1,\ldots ,e_ p$ such that each $\theta _ j$ is a linear combination of $e_1,\ldots ,e_ j$; hence $\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ p=c\, e_1\wedge \cdots \wedge e_ p$, where $c\neq 0$ is the product of the diagonal entries of the triangular transition matrix, and $g(\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ p)=|c|^2g(e_1\wedge \cdots \wedge e_ p)$. Define a linear functional $\tau $ on real $(p,p)$-forms by $u\wedge \beta ^{n-p}=\tau (u)\beta ^ n/n!$. If $e_1,\ldots ,e_ p$ is orthonormal, complete it to an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$ of $V^*$ and use the unitary coordinates $w_ j$ with $\mathrm dw_ j=e_ j$. Then $\beta =(\mathrm{i}/2)\sum _ j\mathrm dw_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar w_ j$, only one term of $\beta ^{n-p}$ contributes, and $\tau (g(e_1\wedge \cdots \wedge e_ p))=2^ p(n-p)!$. Thus $\tau $ is a positive constant $c_0$ on $G$. Let $H$ be the convex hull of $G$ in the real vector space of real $(p,p)$-forms, of dimension $N$ say. Then $H$ is compact, by Carathéodory's argument: if a point is a convex combination of more than $N+1$ points of $G$, these points are affinely dependent, and subtracting a suitable multiple of an affine dependence relation makes one coefficient zero while the others stay nonnegative. Repeating this, we see that $H$ is the continuous image of the compact set $G^{N+1}\times \Delta _ N$, where $\Delta _ N$ is the standard simplex of dimension $N$. Every strongly positive form can be written as $u=sh$ with $h\in H$ and $s=\tau (u)/c_0\geq 0$. If strongly positive forms $u_ k=s_ kh_ k$ converge to $u$, then $s_ k=\tau (u_ k)/c_0$ converges to some $s\geq 0$, and a subsequence of $(h_ k)$ converges to some $h\in H$; hence $u=sh$ is strongly positive. The cone is convex by definition. Spanning. Let $\lambda $ be a real-linear functional on the real $(p,p)$-forms that vanishes on all generators; we show that $\lambda =0$. Every $(p,p)$-form is uniquely $u+\mathrm iv$ with $u,v$ real, so $\lambda $ extends complex-linearly to all $(p,p)$-forms. The form $B(a,b)=\lambda (\mathrm i^{p^2}a\wedge \bar b)$ on $\Lambda ^{p,0}V^*$ is sesquilinear, and $B(a,a)=0$ for every decomposable $a$. We prove by induction on $r=0,\ldots ,p$ that $B(a_1\wedge \cdots \wedge a_ p,b_1\wedge \cdots \wedge b_ p)=0$ whenever $a_ j=b_ j$ for all $j>r$. For $r=0$ this is the hypothesis. Assume it for $r-1$, and fix all vectors except the $r$th ones. The resulting form $B_ r(x,y)=B(\cdots \wedge x\wedge \cdots ,\cdots \wedge y\wedge \cdots )$, with $x$ and $y$ in the $r$th slots, is sesquilinear and vanishes for $x=y$ by the induction hypothesis. By the polarization identity $B_ r(x,y)=\frac14\sum _{k=0}^3\mathrm{i}^ kB_ r(x+\mathrm{i}^ ky,x+\mathrm{i}^ ky)$, valid for every sesquilinear form, $B_ r$ vanishes identically. For $r=p$ we obtain $B=0$ on decomposable vectors, which span $\Lambda ^{p,0}V^*$, so $B=0$. Since the forms $a\wedge \bar b$ with $a,b\in \Lambda ^{p,0}V^*$ span all $(p,p)$-forms, $\lambda =0$. Hence the generators span the real $(p,p)$-forms over $\mathbb R$. Interior. Since the generators span the real $(p,p)$-forms and every nonzero generator is a positive multiple of an element of $G$, we can choose finitely many elements $q_1,\ldots ,q_ M$ of $G$ spanning the real $(p,p)$-forms. For a permutation $\sigma $ of $\{ 1,\ldots ,n\} $ and signs $\varepsilon \in \{ \pm 1\} ^ n$, consider the linear map $z\mapsto (\varepsilon _1z_{\sigma (1)},\ldots ,\varepsilon _ nz_{\sigma (n)})$; its pullback maps generators to generators. Let $\widehat q_ r$ be the average of the pullbacks of $q_ r$ under all these maps. To compute $\widehat q_ r$, write $q_ r=\mathrm i^{p^2}\sum _{I,J}c_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$. The sign changes multiply $c_{IJ}$ by $\prod _{i\in I}\varepsilon _ i\prod _{j\in J}\varepsilon _ j$, whose average over $\varepsilon $ vanishes unless $I=J$. A permutation maps $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ I$ to $\mathrm dz_{I'}\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_{I'}$, where $I'$ is the permuted index set in increasing order, because reordering the factors produces the same sign for $\mathrm dz_{I'}$ and for $\mathrm d\bar z_{I'}$; since every $p$-element set is mapped to every other one by the same number of permutations, the average makes all diagonal coefficients equal to $\binom np^{-1}\sum _ Ic_{II}$. Since $q_ r=g(\theta )$ with $\theta =\sum _ I\theta _ I\, \mathrm dz_ I\neq 0$, we have $c_{IJ}=\theta _ I\overline{\theta _ J}$ and $s_ r=\sum _ Ic_{II}=\sum _ I|\theta _ I|^2>0$. Therefore, by ( 5.3.1 ) and the expansion $\beta ^ p=p!\sum _{|I|=p}\bigwedge _{i\in I}(\frac{\mathrm i}2\mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ i)$, \[  \widehat q_ r=s_ r\binom np^{-1}\mathrm{i}^{p^2}\sum _{|I|=p}\mathrm{d}z_ I\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ I =\frac{2^ ps_ r}{p!\binom np}\beta ^ p.  \] Consequently $\beta ^ p$ is a positive multiple of $\sum _ r\widehat q_ r$, which is a combination of generators with strictly positive coefficients in which every $q_ r$ occurs. A real $(p,p)$-form $v$ of small norm can be written as $\sum _ rt_ r(v)q_ r$ with small coefficients depending linearly on $v$. Adding these coefficients to the positive coefficients of the $q_ r$ keeps all of them positive, so $\beta ^ p+v$ is strongly positive. Thus $\beta ^ p$ is an interior point. Restriction criterion. Let $W$ be a complex subspace of dimension $p$, and choose linear coordinates in which $W=\{ z_{p+1}=\cdots =z_ n=0\} $. For a real $(p,p)$-form $u$, the product $u\wedge \bigwedge _{j>p}(\mathrm{i}\mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ j)$ involves only the coefficient of $\mathrm dz_{(1,\ldots ,p)}\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_{(1,\ldots ,p)}$ in $u$, which is also the coefficient of the restriction $u|_ W$ in the coordinates $z_1,\ldots ,z_ p$ of $W$. Hence this product is a nonnegative multiple of the volume form if and only if $u|_ W$ is nonnegative. Conversely, every generator $\bigwedge _{j=1}^{n-p}(\mathrm{i}\theta _ j\wedge \bar\theta _ j)$ of bidegree $(n-p,n-p)$ is zero if the $\theta _ j$ are linearly dependent, and otherwise it is of the above form, with $z_{p+j}=\theta _ j$ and $W=\{ \theta _1=\cdots =\theta _{n-p}=0\} $. Since weak positivity need only be tested on generators, the restriction criterion follows. Pullbacks and products. Let $F\colon V'\to V$ be complex linear. The pullback of the generator $\bigwedge _ j(\mathrm i\theta _ j\wedge \bar\theta _ j)$ is the generator $\bigwedge _ j(\mathrm iF^*\theta _ j\wedge \overline{F^*\theta _ j})$, so $F^*$ preserves strong positivity. Let $u$ be weakly positive on $V$ and let $W'\subset V'$ be a complex subspace of dimension $p$. If $F|_{W'}$ is injective, it is a complex-linear isomorphism onto the $p$-dimensional subspace $F(W')$ and preserves the complex orientations, so $(F^*u)|_{W'}=(F|_{W'})^*(u|_{F(W')})$ is nonnegative. Otherwise $F(W')$ has dimension less than $p$, and $(F^*u)|_{W'}=0$ because it factors through the $(p,p)$-forms on $F(W')$. By the restriction criterion, $F^*u$ is weakly positive. For a holomorphic map, apply this to its derivative at each point. A product of generators is a generator, so products of strongly positive forms are strongly positive. If $u$ is a weakly positive $(p,p)$-form and $s$ a strongly positive $(r,r)$-form with $p+r\leq n$, then $s\wedge t$ is strongly positive for every strongly positive $(n-p-r,n-p-r)$-form $t$, so $u\wedge s\wedge t$ is a nonnegative multiple of the volume form; hence $u\wedge s$ is weakly positive. Finally, an $(n,n)$-generator equals $|\det (\theta _1,\ldots ,\theta _ n)|^2\bigwedge _ j(\mathrm i\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j)$, a nonnegative multiple of the volume form, so strongly positive forms are weakly positive. $\square$ In bidegree $(1,1)$ the two notions coincide. Write a real $(1,1)$-form as $u=\mathrm{i}\sum a_{j\bar k}\mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ k$, where reality means that the matrix $A=(a_{j\bar k})$ is Hermitian. The restriction of $u$ to the complex line spanned by a vector $\xi $ is $(\sum _{j,k}a_{j\bar k}\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k)\, \mathrm i\mathrm dt\wedge \mathrm d\bar t$ in the coordinate $t$ of the line $\{ t\xi :t\in \mathbb C\} $. Hence, by the restriction criterion of proposition 5.3.2 , $u$ is weakly positive if and only if $A$ is positive semidefinite. In that case a unitary diagonalization of $A$ writes $u$ as $\sum _ r\lambda _ r\mathrm{i}\theta _ r\wedge \bar\theta _ r$ with $\lambda _ r\geq 0$, a sum of generators. By duality, the two notions also coincide in bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$. Let $u$ be a real $(n-1,n-1)$-form. For $\theta ,\eta \in V^*$ define $B_ u(\theta ,\eta )\in \mathbb C$ by $u\wedge \mathrm i\theta \wedge \bar\eta =B_ u(\theta ,\eta )\, \beta ^ n/n!$. Then $B_ u$ is sesquilinear, and $B_ u(\eta ,\theta )=\overline{B_ u(\theta ,\eta )}$ because $u$ is real; thus $H_ u(\theta )=B_ u(\theta ,\theta )$ is a Hermitian quadratic form on $V^*$, and it depends linearly on $u$. Moreover, a distribution that agrees near every point with a complex Radon measure is a complex Radon measure. Indeed, take a partition of unity $(\chi _ a)$ subordinate to a cover by open sets on which the distribution agrees with complex Radon measures $\sigma _ a$. Then the distribution is the locally finite sum of the complex measures $\chi _ a\sigma _ a$. Each of these is a combination of four positive Radon measures with compact support, and the locally finite sums of such measures are Borel measures finite on compact sets, hence Radon by proposition 2.2.2 . Consequently, it suffices to check the condition of order zero in the charts of an atlas. A family $(T_ i)$ of currents of order zero has locally uniformly bounded total variation if the total variations of the coefficient measures of the $T_ i$ are uniformly bounded on every compact subset of every chart, and $T_ i\to T$ in total variation on compact sets if the total variations of the coefficient measures of $T_ i-T$ tend to zero on every such compact set. A current of order zero extends, by the formula $T(\varphi )=\sum _ J\int g_ J\, \mathrm dT_ J$ in charts and a partition of unity, to forms $\varphi $ with bounded Borel coefficients and compact support. The result does not depend on the choices: ( 5.3.6 ) persists for bounded Borel functions $h$ with compact support in $U\cap U'$, because both sides are integrals against complex Radon measures which agree on test functions, hence on $C_ c(U\cap U')$ by lemma 2.5.1 , hence as measures; and two partitions of unity give the same value by the computation used for integrals of forms. If $f$ is a locally bounded Borel function on $X$, multiplying all coefficient measures by $f$ defines a current $fT$ of order zero; this is compatible with coordinate changes. In particular $\mathbf1_ ET$ is defined for every Borel set $E\subset X$. We say that $T$ gives $E$ zero mass, or does not charge $E$, if $\mathbf1_ ET=0$, that is, if all coefficient measures of $T$ vanish on $E$ in every chart. Theorem 5.3.7 . 1C212E45A497 Let $T$ be a positive current of bidegree $(p,p)$ on a complex manifold $X$ of dimension $n$. Then $T$ is real and of order zero. More precisely, in every coordinate chart the coefficient measures of $T=\sum _{|I|=|J|=p}T_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ satisfy \[  |T_{IJ}|\leq C_{n,p}\, \mu _ T,  \] where $\mu _ T$ is the trace measure and $C_{n,p}$ depends only on $n$ and $p$. Moreover, suppose that $X$ has a countable basis, and let $(T_ j)$ be a sequence of positive currents of bidegree $(p,p)$ whose trace measures are locally uniformly bounded: $\sup _ j\mu _{T_ j}(K)<\infty $ for every compact subset $K$ of every chart. Then a subsequence converges weakly to a positive current, which is closed if all $T_ j$ are closed. Proof. Fix a chart and put $q=n-p$. By proposition 5.3.2 , $\beta ^ q$ is an interior point of the cone of strongly positive $(q,q)$-forms. Hence for every constant real $(q,q)$-form $\tau $ there is $C_\tau >0$ such that the forms $C_\tau \beta ^ q\pm \tau $ are strongly positive. For a nonnegative test function $\chi $, the forms $\chi (C_\tau \beta ^ q\pm \tau )$ are strongly positive test forms, so positivity of $T$ gives $T(\chi (C_\tau \beta ^ q\pm \tau ))\geq 0$. Therefore $T(\chi \tau )$ is real and \[  |T(\chi \tau )|\le C_\tau \mu _ T(\chi ).  \] The distributions $C_\tau \mu _ T\pm T(\, \cdot \, \tau )$ are nonnegative on nonnegative test functions, hence positive Radon measures by the remark after definition 5.3.5 and theorem 2.5.6 . Consequently $S_\tau =T(\, \cdot \, \tau )$ is a real signed Radon measure, the difference of the positive measures $(C_\tau \mu _ T\pm S_\tau )/2$, and $|S_\tau (A)|\leq C_\tau \mu _ T(A)$ for every relatively compact Borel set $A$, so that $|S_\tau |\leq C_\tau \mu _ T$. Choose real constant $(q,q)$-forms $\tau _1,\ldots ,\tau _ N$ forming a basis of the real $(q,q)$-forms; they also form a complex basis of all constant $(q,q)$-forms, and they can be chosen depending only on $n$ and $p$. Up to a constant factor depending only on $n$, $I$ and $J$, the coefficient $T_{IJ}$ is the distribution $\chi \mapsto T(\chi \, \mathrm dz_{I^ c}\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_{J^ c})$, where $I^ c$ and $J^ c$ are the complementary multi-indices. Expanding $\mathrm dz_{I^ c}\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_{J^ c}=\sum _ rc_ r\tau _ r$, we see that $T_{IJ}$ is a fixed complex linear combination of the measures $S_{\tau _ r}$, and the coefficient bound follows from $|S_{\tau _ r}|\leq C_{\tau _ r}\mu _ T$. To prove that $T$ is real, let $\varphi $ be a test form supported in the chart; only its $(q,q)$-component contributes, and we write it as $\sum _ rf_ r\tau _ r$ with complex test functions $f_ r$. Since $T(f\tau _ r)=\int f\, \mathrm dS_{\tau _ r}$ is real for real $f$, we obtain $T(\bar\varphi )=\overline{T(\varphi )}$, and a partition of unity extends this identity to all test forms. Now let $X$ have a countable basis, and let $(T_ j)$ be as in the statement. Then $X$ is covered by countably many charts $U_1,U_2,\ldots $: for each basic open set contained in some chart, choose one such chart. On $U_1$ the positive Radon measures $C_{\tau _ r}\mu _{T_ j}\pm S^ j_{\tau _ r}$, where $S^ j_\tau =T_ j(\, \cdot \, \tau )$, have mass at most $2C_{\tau _ r}\sup _ j\mu _{T_ j}(K)$ on every compact $K\subset U_1$. Applying theorem 2.6.5 successively to these finitely many sequences, we find a subsequence along which all of them converge vaguely on $U_1$; then each $S^ j_{\tau _ r}$ converges vaguely, and $T_ j(\varphi )$ converges for every test form $\varphi $ supported in $U_1$. Repeating the extraction for $U_2,U_3,\ldots $ and passing to the diagonal subsequence, we may assume that $T_ j(\varphi )$ converges for every test form $\varphi $ supported in some $U_ k$. A partition of unity subordinate to $(U_ k)$ writes every test form as a finite sum of such forms, so $T(\varphi )=\lim _ jT_ j(\varphi )$ exists for every test form $\varphi $. The functional $T$ is linear, and it is a current. Indeed, if $\varphi =\sum _ rf_ r\tau _ r$ is supported in a compact set $K\subset U_ k$, then $|T_ j(\varphi )|\leq \sum _ rC_{\tau _ r}\| f_ r\| _\infty \sup _ i\mu _{T_ i}(K)$ for all $j$, and this bound passes to the limit. On compact subsets of the intersection of two charts, the coefficients of a form in the two charts are related by a matrix of continuous functions. Hence, covering a compact subset of an arbitrary chart by finitely many $U_ k$ and using a partition of unity, we obtain the estimate in the definition of a current, with $m=0$. Thus $T_ j\to T$ weakly. If $\varphi $ is a strongly positive test form, then $T(\varphi )=\lim _ jT_ j(\varphi )\geq 0$; and if all $T_ j$ are closed, then $T(\mathrm d\psi )=\lim _ jT_ j(\mathrm d\psi )=0$ for every test form $\psi $. $\square$ Currents can be regularized in coordinates, and the regularization preserves positivity and closedness. Let $T$ be a current on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ with coefficients $T_{IJ}$, and let $\rho _\varepsilon $ and $\Omega _\varepsilon $ be as in section 2.5 . The smooth form $T_\varepsilon =\sum _{I,J}(T_{IJ})_\varepsilon \, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ satisfies $T_\varepsilon (\varphi )=T(\varphi *\rho _\varepsilon )$ for test forms $\varphi $ supported in $\Omega _\varepsilon $, where $\varphi *\rho _\varepsilon $ is obtained by mollifying the coefficients of $\varphi $; this is ( 2.5.4 ), applied to each coefficient. By proposition 2.5.3 , $T_\varepsilon \to T$ weakly as $\varepsilon \to 0$, in the sense that $T_\varepsilon (\varphi )\to T(\varphi )$ for every test form $\varphi $ on $\Omega $; here $T_\varepsilon (\varphi )$ is defined as soon as $\operatorname{Supp}\varphi \subset \Omega _\varepsilon $. If $T$ is positive, so is $T_\varepsilon $ on $\Omega _\varepsilon $. Indeed, let $\varphi $ be a strongly positive test form supported in $\Omega _\varepsilon $. Since the frame $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ is invariant under translations, the translates $x\mapsto \varphi (x-h)$ are strongly positive, and $(\varphi *\rho _\varepsilon )(x)=\int \rho _\varepsilon (h)\varphi (x-h)\, \mathrm dV_{2n}(h)$ is a limit of Riemann sums, which are nonnegative combinations of strongly positive forms; it is strongly positive because the cone is closed (proposition 5.3.2 ). Moreover, $\varphi *\rho _\varepsilon $ is a test form on $\Omega $, supported in the set of points at distance at most $\varepsilon $ from $\operatorname{Supp}\varphi $. Hence $T_\varepsilon (\varphi )=T(\varphi *\rho _\varepsilon )\geq 0$. Finally, if $T$ is closed, so is $T_\varepsilon $, since $\mathrm d$ acts on the coefficients by differentiation, and derivatives commute with mollification (proposition 2.5.3 ). If $T$ is positive of bidegree $(p,p)$ and $\alpha $ is a smooth strongly positive $(s,s)$-form with $p+s\leq n$, then $T\wedge \alpha $ is positive, because $\alpha \wedge \varphi $ is a strongly positive test form for every strongly positive test form $\varphi $ (proposition 5.3.2 ). The trace measure $T\wedge \beta ^{n-p}$ is an example. Currents on a complex manifold $X$ can be glued from local pieces; we use this in section 5.6 to define pullbacks of currents. For an open set $W\subset X$, the restriction of $T$ to $W$ is the current on $W$ given by the values of $T$ on test forms supported in $W$; two currents agree on $W$ if their restrictions to $W$ coincide. Lemma 5.3.8 . 376F5C171BED Let $(W_ a)_{a\in A}$ be an open cover of $X$, and for each $a$ let $T_ a$ be a current of degree $k$ on $W_ a$, such that $T_ a$ and $T_ b$ agree on $W_ a\cap W_ b$ for all $a,b\in A$. Then there is a unique current $T$ of degree $k$ on $X$ which agrees with $T_ a$ on $W_ a$ for every $a$. If all $T_ a$ have bidegree $(p,q)$, then so has $T$; if all $T_ a$ are closed, then so is $T$; and if $p=q$ and all $T_ a$ are positive, then so is $T$. Proof. If two currents on $X$ agree with $T_ a$ on $W_ a$ for every $a$, their difference vanishes on every $W_ a$, hence on $X$, since a current that vanishes on each member of a family of open sets vanishes on their union, as shown at the beginning of this section. For existence, choose a partition of unity $(\chi _ c)_{c\in C}$ with compact supports subordinate to the cover (proposition 5.2.6 ), and for each $c$ an index $a(c)$ with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ c\subset W_{a(c)}$. For a test form $\varphi $ of degree $2n-k$ on $X$, only finitely many $\chi _ c$ are not identically zero on the compact set $\operatorname{Supp}\varphi $, and $\chi _ c\varphi $ is a test form supported in $W_{a(c)}$; we put \[  T(\varphi )=\sum _ cT_{a(c)}(\chi _ c\varphi ).  \] This is a linear functional, and it is a current. Indeed, let $K$ be a compact subset of a chart domain $U$. Only finitely many indices $c_1,\ldots ,c_ N$ have $\chi _{c_ i}\not\equiv 0$ on $K$, and for test forms $\varphi $ supported in $K$ the form $\chi _{c_ i}\varphi $ is supported in the compact subset $K\cap \operatorname{Supp}\chi _{c_ i}$ of the chart domain $U\cap W_{a(c_ i)}$ of $W_{a(c_ i)}$. By the Leibniz rule, its seminorms $p_{K,m}$ are bounded by a constant times those of $\varphi $, so the estimates for the currents $T_{a(c_ i)}$ give the estimate in the definition of a current for $T$. If $\varphi $ is supported in some $W_ b$, then each $\chi _ c\varphi $ is supported in $W_{a(c)}\cap W_ b$, where $T_{a(c)}$ and $T_ b$ agree, so that $T(\varphi )=\sum _ cT_ b(\chi _ c\varphi )=T_ b(\varphi )$. Thus $T$ agrees with $T_ b$ on $W_ b$. Multiplication by $\chi _ c$ preserves bidegrees, and $\chi _ c\varphi $ is strongly positive at every point if $\varphi $ is, because $\chi _ c\geq 0$; so the assertions about bidegrees and positivity follow from the formula for $T(\varphi )$. Finally, if all $T_ a$ are closed and $\psi $ is a test form supported in $W_ a$, then so is $\mathrm d\psi $, and $(\mathrm dT)(\psi )=(-1)^{k+1}T(\mathrm d\psi )=(-1)^{k+1}T_ a(\mathrm d\psi )=(\mathrm dT_ a)(\psi )=0$; hence $\mathrm dT$ vanishes on every $W_ a$, and therefore $\mathrm dT=0$. $\square$ Example 5.3.9 . 1176DC9B7704 Let $Z$ be a complex submanifold of $X$ of dimension $r$, with its complex orientation. Then \[  [Z](\varphi )=\int _ Z\varphi |_ Z  \] defines a closed positive current of bidegree $(n-r,n-r)$ on $X$, the current of integration over $Z$. Since $Z$ is closed, $Z\cap \operatorname{Supp}\varphi $ is compact for every test form $\varphi $, so the integral is defined. In a chart in which $Z=\{ z_{r+1}=\cdots =z_ n=0\} $, the value $[Z](\varphi )$ is a constant times the integral over this coordinate plane of the coefficient of $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ I$ in $\varphi $, where $I=(1,\ldots ,r)$, because the pullbacks of $\mathrm dz_ j$ and $\mathrm d\bar z_ j$ to $Z$ vanish for $j>r$. Hence $[Z]$ is a current, and its coefficients in such a chart are constant multiples of Lebesgue measure on the plane. Since $[Z]$ vanishes on $X\setminus Z$, the charts of this kind and the charts contained in $X\setminus Z$ form an atlas in which $[Z]$ has measure coefficients, and $[Z]$ is a current of order zero. If $\varphi $ is strongly positive, so is its pullback $\varphi |_ Z$ to $Z$, which is therefore a nonnegative multiple of the volume form of $Z$ at each point (proposition 5.3.2 ); thus $[Z](\varphi )\geq 0$. Finally, since pullback commutes with $\mathrm d$ by ( 5.2.5 ), $[Z](\mathrm d\psi )=\int _ Z\mathrm d(\psi |_ Z)=0$ by proposition 5.2.6 applied on $Z$ when $r\geq 1$; when $r=0$ the current $[Z]$ has degree $2n$, and $\mathrm d[Z]=0$ because currents of degree $2n+1$ are zero.

title: Equation 5.3.1
text: 976BD2929614 5.3.1 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{i}^{p^2}\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ p \wedge \bar\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \bar\theta _ p =\bigwedge _{j=1}^ p(\mathrm{i}\theta _ j\wedge \bar\theta _ j), \end{equation}

title: Proposition 5.3.2
text: Proposition 5.3.2 . E58104E974B0 Let $0\leq p\leq n$. The strongly positive $(p,p)$-forms on $V$ form a closed convex cone, which spans the real vector space of real $(p,p)$-forms and contains $\beta ^ p$ in its interior. A real $(p,p)$-form is weakly positive if and only if its restriction to every complex $p$-dimensional subspace of $V$ is nonnegative. Pullback by complex-linear maps, and hence by holomorphic maps between complex manifolds, preserves strong and weak positivity. The product of strongly positive forms is strongly positive, and the product of a weakly positive form with a strongly positive form is weakly positive when its bidegree is at most $(n,n)$. Moreover, strongly positive forms are weakly positive. Proof. We use the Hermitian inner product on $V^*$ for which $\mathrm dz_1,\ldots ,\mathrm dz_ n$ are orthonormal. The form $\beta $ is invariant under unitary changes of coordinates: if $\mathrm dw_ j=\sum _ kU_{jk}\, \mathrm dz_ k$ with a unitary matrix $U$, then $\sum _ j\mathrm dw_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar w_ j=\sum _{k,l}\big (\sum _ jU_{jk}\overline{U_{jl}}\big )\mathrm dz_ k\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ l=\sum _ k\mathrm dz_ k\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ k$. Let $\Lambda ^{p,0}V^*$ be the space of $(p,0)$-forms. For $\theta \in \Lambda ^{p,0}V^*$ put $g(\theta )=\mathrm i^{p^2}\theta \wedge \bar\theta $, so that $g(c\theta )=|c|^2g(\theta )$ and the generators are the forms $g(\theta )$ with $\theta $ decomposable. Closedness. Let $G$ be the set of the generators $g(e_1\wedge \cdots \wedge e_ p)$ with $e_1,\ldots ,e_ p$ orthonormal in $V^*$. It is the continuous image of the compact set of orthonormal $p$-tuples, so $G$ is compact. Every nonzero generator $g(\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ p)$ is a positive multiple of an element of $G$. Indeed, the $\theta _ j$ are linearly independent, and the Gram–Schmidt process gives an orthonormal family $e_1,\ldots ,e_ p$ such that each $\theta _ j$ is a linear combination of $e_1,\ldots ,e_ j$; hence $\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ p=c\, e_1\wedge \cdots \wedge e_ p$, where $c\neq 0$ is the product of the diagonal entries of the triangular transition matrix, and $g(\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ p)=|c|^2g(e_1\wedge \cdots \wedge e_ p)$. Define a linear functional $\tau $ on real $(p,p)$-forms by $u\wedge \beta ^{n-p}=\tau (u)\beta ^ n/n!$. If $e_1,\ldots ,e_ p$ is orthonormal, complete it to an orthonormal basis $e_1,\ldots ,e_ n$ of $V^*$ and use the unitary coordinates $w_ j$ with $\mathrm dw_ j=e_ j$. Then $\beta =(\mathrm{i}/2)\sum _ j\mathrm dw_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar w_ j$, only one term of $\beta ^{n-p}$ contributes, and $\tau (g(e_1\wedge \cdots \wedge e_ p))=2^ p(n-p)!$. Thus $\tau $ is a positive constant $c_0$ on $G$. Let $H$ be the convex hull of $G$ in the real vector space of real $(p,p)$-forms, of dimension $N$ say. Then $H$ is compact, by Carathéodory's argument: if a point is a convex combination of more than $N+1$ points of $G$, these points are affinely dependent, and subtracting a suitable multiple of an affine dependence relation makes one coefficient zero while the others stay nonnegative. Repeating this, we see that $H$ is the continuous image of the compact set $G^{N+1}\times \Delta _ N$, where $\Delta _ N$ is the standard simplex of dimension $N$. Every strongly positive form can be written as $u=sh$ with $h\in H$ and $s=\tau (u)/c_0\geq 0$. If strongly positive forms $u_ k=s_ kh_ k$ converge to $u$, then $s_ k=\tau (u_ k)/c_0$ converges to some $s\geq 0$, and a subsequence of $(h_ k)$ converges to some $h\in H$; hence $u=sh$ is strongly positive. The cone is convex by definition. Spanning. Let $\lambda $ be a real-linear functional on the real $(p,p)$-forms that vanishes on all generators; we show that $\lambda =0$. Every $(p,p)$-form is uniquely $u+\mathrm iv$ with $u,v$ real, so $\lambda $ extends complex-linearly to all $(p,p)$-forms. The form $B(a,b)=\lambda (\mathrm i^{p^2}a\wedge \bar b)$ on $\Lambda ^{p,0}V^*$ is sesquilinear, and $B(a,a)=0$ for every decomposable $a$. We prove by induction on $r=0,\ldots ,p$ that $B(a_1\wedge \cdots \wedge a_ p,b_1\wedge \cdots \wedge b_ p)=0$ whenever $a_ j=b_ j$ for all $j>r$. For $r=0$ this is the hypothesis. Assume it for $r-1$, and fix all vectors except the $r$th ones. The resulting form $B_ r(x,y)=B(\cdots \wedge x\wedge \cdots ,\cdots \wedge y\wedge \cdots )$, with $x$ and $y$ in the $r$th slots, is sesquilinear and vanishes for $x=y$ by the induction hypothesis. By the polarization identity $B_ r(x,y)=\frac14\sum _{k=0}^3\mathrm{i}^ kB_ r(x+\mathrm{i}^ ky,x+\mathrm{i}^ ky)$, valid for every sesquilinear form, $B_ r$ vanishes identically. For $r=p$ we obtain $B=0$ on decomposable vectors, which span $\Lambda ^{p,0}V^*$, so $B=0$. Since the forms $a\wedge \bar b$ with $a,b\in \Lambda ^{p,0}V^*$ span all $(p,p)$-forms, $\lambda =0$. Hence the generators span the real $(p,p)$-forms over $\mathbb R$. Interior. Since the generators span the real $(p,p)$-forms and every nonzero generator is a positive multiple of an element of $G$, we can choose finitely many elements $q_1,\ldots ,q_ M$ of $G$ spanning the real $(p,p)$-forms. For a permutation $\sigma $ of $\{ 1,\ldots ,n\} $ and signs $\varepsilon \in \{ \pm 1\} ^ n$, consider the linear map $z\mapsto (\varepsilon _1z_{\sigma (1)},\ldots ,\varepsilon _ nz_{\sigma (n)})$; its pullback maps generators to generators. Let $\widehat q_ r$ be the average of the pullbacks of $q_ r$ under all these maps. To compute $\widehat q_ r$, write $q_ r=\mathrm i^{p^2}\sum _{I,J}c_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$. The sign changes multiply $c_{IJ}$ by $\prod _{i\in I}\varepsilon _ i\prod _{j\in J}\varepsilon _ j$, whose average over $\varepsilon $ vanishes unless $I=J$. A permutation maps $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ I$ to $\mathrm dz_{I'}\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_{I'}$, where $I'$ is the permuted index set in increasing order, because reordering the factors produces the same sign for $\mathrm dz_{I'}$ and for $\mathrm d\bar z_{I'}$; since every $p$-element set is mapped to every other one by the same number of permutations, the average makes all diagonal coefficients equal to $\binom np^{-1}\sum _ Ic_{II}$. Since $q_ r=g(\theta )$ with $\theta =\sum _ I\theta _ I\, \mathrm dz_ I\neq 0$, we have $c_{IJ}=\theta _ I\overline{\theta _ J}$ and $s_ r=\sum _ Ic_{II}=\sum _ I|\theta _ I|^2>0$. Therefore, by ( 5.3.1 ) and the expansion $\beta ^ p=p!\sum _{|I|=p}\bigwedge _{i\in I}(\frac{\mathrm i}2\mathrm dz_ i\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ i)$, \[  \widehat q_ r=s_ r\binom np^{-1}\mathrm{i}^{p^2}\sum _{|I|=p}\mathrm{d}z_ I\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ I =\frac{2^ ps_ r}{p!\binom np}\beta ^ p.  \] Consequently $\beta ^ p$ is a positive multiple of $\sum _ r\widehat q_ r$, which is a combination of generators with strictly positive coefficients in which every $q_ r$ occurs. A real $(p,p)$-form $v$ of small norm can be written as $\sum _ rt_ r(v)q_ r$ with small coefficients depending linearly on $v$. Adding these coefficients to the positive coefficients of the $q_ r$ keeps all of them positive, so $\beta ^ p+v$ is strongly positive. Thus $\beta ^ p$ is an interior point. Restriction criterion. Let $W$ be a complex subspace of dimension $p$, and choose linear coordinates in which $W=\{ z_{p+1}=\cdots =z_ n=0\} $. For a real $(p,p)$-form $u$, the product $u\wedge \bigwedge _{j>p}(\mathrm{i}\mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ j)$ involves only the coefficient of $\mathrm dz_{(1,\ldots ,p)}\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_{(1,\ldots ,p)}$ in $u$, which is also the coefficient of the restriction $u|_ W$ in the coordinates $z_1,\ldots ,z_ p$ of $W$. Hence this product is a nonnegative multiple of the volume form if and only if $u|_ W$ is nonnegative. Conversely, every generator $\bigwedge _{j=1}^{n-p}(\mathrm{i}\theta _ j\wedge \bar\theta _ j)$ of bidegree $(n-p,n-p)$ is zero if the $\theta _ j$ are linearly dependent, and otherwise it is of the above form, with $z_{p+j}=\theta _ j$ and $W=\{ \theta _1=\cdots =\theta _{n-p}=0\} $. Since weak positivity need only be tested on generators, the restriction criterion follows. Pullbacks and products. Let $F\colon V'\to V$ be complex linear. The pullback of the generator $\bigwedge _ j(\mathrm i\theta _ j\wedge \bar\theta _ j)$ is the generator $\bigwedge _ j(\mathrm iF^*\theta _ j\wedge \overline{F^*\theta _ j})$, so $F^*$ preserves strong positivity. Let $u$ be weakly positive on $V$ and let $W'\subset V'$ be a complex subspace of dimension $p$. If $F|_{W'}$ is injective, it is a complex-linear isomorphism onto the $p$-dimensional subspace $F(W')$ and preserves the complex orientations, so $(F^*u)|_{W'}=(F|_{W'})^*(u|_{F(W')})$ is nonnegative. Otherwise $F(W')$ has dimension less than $p$, and $(F^*u)|_{W'}=0$ because it factors through the $(p,p)$-forms on $F(W')$. By the restriction criterion, $F^*u$ is weakly positive. For a holomorphic map, apply this to its derivative at each point. A product of generators is a generator, so products of strongly positive forms are strongly positive. If $u$ is a weakly positive $(p,p)$-form and $s$ a strongly positive $(r,r)$-form with $p+r\leq n$, then $s\wedge t$ is strongly positive for every strongly positive $(n-p-r,n-p-r)$-form $t$, so $u\wedge s\wedge t$ is a nonnegative multiple of the volume form; hence $u\wedge s$ is weakly positive. Finally, an $(n,n)$-generator equals $|\det (\theta _1,\ldots ,\theta _ n)|^2\bigwedge _ j(\mathrm i\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j)$, a nonnegative multiple of the volume form, so strongly positive forms are weakly positive. $\square$

title: Lemma 5.3.3
text: Lemma 5.3.3 . 3D25BAD0C21E Let $n\geq 1$, and let $A,A_1,\ldots ,A_ n$ be Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices. The mixed discriminant is real, symmetric and real-multilinear in its arguments, and $D(A,\ldots ,A)=\det A$. More precisely, \[  n!\, D(A_1,\ldots ,A_ n)=\sum _\sigma \det \big (A_{\sigma (1)}e_1,\ldots ,A_{\sigma (n)}e_ n\big ),  \] the sum running over all permutations $\sigma $ of $\{ 1,\ldots ,n\} $, where $Ae_ l$ is the $l$th column of $A$. We have \[  \omega _ A^ n=\det A\, \omega _ I^ n,\qquad \omega _{A_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _{A_ n}=D(A_1,\ldots ,A_ n)\, \omega _ I^ n,  \] where $\omega _ I^ n=n!\bigwedge _ l(\mathrm i\mathrm dz_ l\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ l)=2^ n\beta ^ n$ is a positive multiple of the volume form. If $A_1,\ldots ,A_ n$ are positive semidefinite, then $D(A_1,\ldots ,A_ n)\geq 0$. If they are positive definite, then $D(A_1,\ldots ,A_ n)>0$. Proof. (1) The $l$th column of $\sum _ jt_ jA_ j$ is $\sum _ jt_ jA_ je_ l$. Expanding the determinant by multilinearity in its columns, we obtain \[  \det \Bigl (\sum _ jt_ jA_ j\Bigr )=\sum _\tau t_{\tau (1)}\cdots t_{\tau (n)}\det \big (A_{\tau (1)}e_1,\ldots ,A_{\tau (n)}e_ n\big ),  \] the sum running over all maps $\tau \colon \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} \to \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} $. The monomial $t_{\tau (1)}\cdots t_{\tau (n)}$ equals $t_1\cdots t_ n$ exactly when $\tau $ is a permutation, which gives the displayed formula. A permutation of $A_1,\ldots ,A_ n$ permutes the terms of this sum, so $D$ is symmetric. Each term is multilinear in $(A_1,\ldots ,A_ n)$, since each $A_ j$ occurs in exactly one column, so $D$ is multilinear. For $A_1=\cdots =A_ n=A$ all $n!$ terms equal $\det A$, so $D(A,\ldots ,A)=\det A$. Finally, $D$ is real: for real $t_ j$ the matrix $\sum _ jt_ jA_ j$ is Hermitian, so its determinant is real, being the product of its real eigenvalues; hence the polynomial $\det (\sum _ jt_ jA_ j)$ is real on $\mathbb R^ n$, and so are its coefficients, which are its partial derivatives at $t=0$ divided by factorials. (2) In the expansion of $\omega _ A^ n$, the products $\bigwedge _ l(\mathrm dz_{j_ l}\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_{k_ l})$ vanish unless $(j_1,\ldots ,j_ n)$ and $(k_1,\ldots ,k_ n)$ are permutations of $(1,\ldots ,n)$. Since the $2$-forms $\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ k$ commute, such a product equals $\bigwedge _ l(\mathrm dz_ l\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_{\pi (l)})$ for a permutation $\pi $, which arises from $n!$ ordered products, and $\bigwedge _ l(\mathrm dz_ l\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_{\pi (l)})=\operatorname {sign}(\pi )\bigwedge _ l(\mathrm dz_ l\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ l)$, because the two products differ by a permutation of the factors $\mathrm d\bar z_ k$. Therefore \[  \omega _ A^ n=n!\sum _\pi \operatorname {sign}(\pi )\prod _ lA_{l\overline{\pi (l)}}\bigwedge _ l(\mathrm i\mathrm dz_ l\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ l)=n!\det A\bigwedge _ l(\mathrm i\mathrm dz_ l\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ l)=\det A\, \omega _ I^ n,  \] where the last equality is the case $A=I$ of the preceding one. Since $\mathrm i\mathrm dz_ l\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ l=2\, \mathrm dx_ l\wedge \mathrm dy_ l$, we get $\omega _ I^ n=2^ nn!\, \mathrm dV_{2n}=2^ n\beta ^ n$ by ( 5.2.8 ). Now let $t_1,\ldots ,t_ n$ be real, and apply the first identity to the Hermitian matrix $\sum _ jt_ jA_ j$, for which $\omega _{\sum _ jt_ jA_ j}=\sum _ jt_ j\omega _{A_ j}$. Since $2$-forms commute, the coefficient of $t_1\cdots t_ n$ in $(\sum _ jt_ j\omega _{A_ j})^ n$ is $n!\, \omega _{A_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _{A_ n}$, while in $\det (\sum _ jt_ jA_ j)\, \omega _ I^ n$ it is $n!\, D(A_1,\ldots ,A_ n)\, \omega _ I^ n$. Two polynomials that agree on $\mathbb R^ n$ have the same coefficients, and we obtain the second identity. (3) A real $(1,1)$-form $\omega _ A$ with $A$ positive semidefinite is strongly positive, by the discussion following proposition 5.3.2 : a unitary diagonalization of $A$ writes it as a sum of generators with nonnegative coefficients. By proposition 5.3.2 , the product $\omega _{A_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \omega _{A_ n}$ is then strongly positive, hence weakly positive, that is, a nonnegative multiple of the volume form. By (2) and since $\omega _ I^ n$ is a positive multiple of the volume form, $D(A_1,\ldots ,A_ n)\geq 0$. If all $A_ j$ are positive definite, choose $\varepsilon >0$ smaller than the least eigenvalue of every $A_ j$, so that every $A_ j-\varepsilon I$ is positive semidefinite, and expand $D(A_1,\ldots ,A_ n)=D\bigl ((A_1-\varepsilon I)+\varepsilon I,\ldots ,(A_ n-\varepsilon I)+\varepsilon I\bigr )$ by multilinearity. Every term is the mixed discriminant of positive semidefinite matrices, hence nonnegative, and one of them is $D(\varepsilon I,\ldots ,\varepsilon I)=\varepsilon ^ n\det I=\varepsilon ^ n>0$. $\square$

title: Lemma 5.3.4
text: Lemma 5.3.4 . 8907196C3513 Let $n\geq 2$, and let $A_3,\ldots ,A_ n$ be positive definite Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices. The real symmetric bilinear form \[  q(M,N)=D(M,N,A_3,\ldots ,A_ n)  \] on the real vector space of Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices, which has dimension $n^2$, has signature $(1,n^2-1)$. For every positive definite $H$, the restriction of $q$ to the hyperplane $\{ M:q(M,H)=0\} $ is negative definite. Proof. We first show that, for a given tuple $A_3,\ldots ,A_ n$, the second assertion follows from the first. Let $H$ be positive definite. Then $q(H,H)>0$ by lemma 5.3.3 (3), so the space of Hermitian matrices is the $q$-orthogonal direct sum of $\mathbb RH$ and $H^\perp =\{ M:q(M,H)=0\} $. The restriction of $q$ to $H^\perp $ is nondegenerate, since a vector of $H^\perp $ orthogonal to $H^\perp $ would be orthogonal to the whole space. By Sylvester's law of inertia it has signature $(0,n^2-1)$; that is, it is negative definite. We prove the signature assertion by induction on $n$. For $n=2$ there are no fixed matrices, and expanding $\det (t_1M+t_2N)$ gives $q(M,N)=(\operatorname {tr}M\operatorname {tr}N-\operatorname {tr}(MN))/2$. The decomposition of a matrix into a scalar matrix and a trace-free matrix is $q$-orthogonal, $q(I,I)=1$, and $q(M,M)=-\operatorname {tr}(M^2)/2<0$ for a nonzero trace-free $M$, since $\operatorname {tr}(M^2)$ is the sum of the squares of the real eigenvalues of $M$. Hence the signature is $(1,3)$. Let $n\geq 3$, and assume both assertions in dimension $n-1$. We first show that $q$ is nondegenerate for every tuple of positive definite matrices. Replacing every matrix $X$ by $G^*XG$ multiplies $D$ by $|\det G|^2$, by the definition of $D$ through the determinant, and preserves positive definiteness; since $X\mapsto G^*XG$ is a linear automorphism of the Hermitian matrices, we may take $G=A_ n^{-1/2}$ and assume that $A_ n=I$. For a Hermitian matrix $X$, let $X^{(i)}$ be the $(n-1)\times (n-1)$ matrix obtained by deleting the $i$th row and column, and let $P_ i$ be the diagonal matrix with entry $1$ in position $(i,i)$ and zeros elsewhere. Expanding along the $i$th row, $\det (tP_ i+Y)=\det Y+t\det Y^{(i)}$; comparing coefficients of $t_1\cdots t_ n$ in $\det (t_1P_ i+\sum _{j\geq 2}t_ jB_ j)$ gives, for Hermitian matrices $B_2,\ldots ,B_ n$, \[  D(P_ i,B_2,\ldots ,B_ n)=\frac1nD_{n-1}(B_2^{(i)},\ldots ,B_ n^{(i)}),  \] where the factor $1/n=(n-1)!/n!$ comes from the normalizations of $D$ and of the mixed discriminant $D_{n-1}$ of size $n-1$. Put \[  q_ i(B,C)=D_{n-1}(B,C,A_3^{(i)},\ldots ,A_{n-1}^{(i)});  \] the matrices $A_ j^{(i)}$ and $I^{(i)}$ are positive definite, as principal submatrices of positive definite matrices. Using the last formula, and writing $I=\sum _ iP_ i$ in the last slot of $q(M,M)$, we obtain \[  q(M,P_ i)=\frac1nq_ i(M^{(i)},I^{(i)}),\qquad q(M,M)=\frac1n\sum _{i=1}^ nq_ i(M^{(i)},M^{(i)}).  \] Now let $M$ lie in the kernel of $q$. Then $q(M,P_ i)=0$, so $M^{(i)}$ lies in the hyperplane $\{ q_ i(\, \cdot \, ,I^{(i)})=0\} $, on which $q_ i$ is negative definite by the induction hypothesis. Since also $q(M,M)=0$, every term of the sum vanishes, and $M^{(i)}=0$ for every $i$. As $n\geq 3$, every entry of $M$ lies in some $M^{(i)}$, so $M=0$. Finally, the set of tuples $A=(A_3,\ldots ,A_ n)$ of positive definite matrices is convex, hence connected, and we write $q_ A$ for the corresponding form. By Sylvester's law of inertia, the number $k(A)$ of positive squares of $q_ A$ is the largest dimension of a subspace on which $q_ A$ is positive definite. We show that $k$ is locally constant. Fix a tuple $A^0$. Since $q_{A^0}$ is nondegenerate, the space of Hermitian matrices is a direct sum $E_+\oplus E_-$, where $q_{A^0}$ is positive definite on $E_+$, negative definite on $E_-$, and $\dim E_+=k(A^0)$. The function $(A,M)\mapsto q_ A(M,M)$ is continuous, and it is positive on $\{ A^0\} \times S_+$ and negative on $\{ A^0\} \times S_-$, where $S_\pm $ is the unit sphere of $E_\pm $ for some norm. These spheres are compact, so for all tuples $A$ near $A^0$ the form $q_ A$ is still positive definite on $E_+$ and negative definite on $E_-$. Then $k(A)\geq \dim E_+$, and $k(A)\leq \dim E_+$ because a subspace of larger dimension meets $E_-$ in a nonzero vector. Hence $k(A)=k(A^0)$ near $A^0$, and $k$ is constant on the connected set of tuples. It therefore suffices to compute the signature at $A_3=\cdots =A_ n=I$. With $s=t_3+\cdots +t_ n$, the coefficient of $s^{n-2}$ in $\det (t_1M+t_2N+sI)$ is the sum of the principal $2\times 2$ minors of $t_1M+t_2N$, that is, $((\operatorname {tr}X)^2-\operatorname {tr}(X^2))/2$ for $X=t_1M+t_2N$, in which $t_1t_2$ has the coefficient $\operatorname {tr}M\operatorname {tr}N-\operatorname {tr}(MN)$; moreover, the coefficient of $t_3\cdots t_ n$ in $s^{n-2}$ is $(n-2)!$. Hence \[  q(M,N)=\frac{\operatorname {tr}M\operatorname {tr}N-\operatorname {tr}(MN)}{n(n-1)},  \] and, as in the case $n=2$, the decomposition into scalar and trace-free matrices shows that the signature is $(1,n^2-1)$. $\square$

title: Definition 5.3.5
text: Definition 5.3.5 . A86EC2473CB6 Let $0\leq p\leq n$. A current $T$ of bidegree $(p,p)$ on $X$ is positive if $T(\varphi )\ge 0$ for every test form $\varphi $ of bidegree $(n-p,n-p)$ that is strongly positive at every point. We then write $T\geq 0$, and $T\geq S$ if $T-S\geq 0$. If $T$ is positive and $U$ is a coordinate chart, the trace measure of $T$ in $U$ is the positive Radon measure \[  \mu _ T=T\wedge \beta ^{n-p},\qquad \text{that is,}\qquad \mu _ T(\chi )=T(\chi \beta ^{n-p})\quad \text{for test functions }\chi \text{ on }U,  \] where $\beta $ is the form ( 5.2.8 ) in the coordinates of $U$.
