Proposition 5.5.3 . 37EEAF275A32 Let $f$ be holomorphic on a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, and not identically zero, and put $\log |f|^2=-\infty $ on the zero set of $f$. Then $\log |f|^2$ is locally integrable, it is the canonical subharmonic representative of its class, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2\geq 0$. Moreover, let $P\subset \Omega $ be a polydisc, let $1\leq j\leq n$, and write points of $P$ as $(z',z_ j)$, where $z'$ consists of the coordinates other than $z_ j$. Then for every test function $\varphi $ on $P$, FF48D92EEC58 5.5.4  egin{equation}   ig \langle (\log |f|^2)_{j ar j},\varphi  ig angle =\pi \int _{\mathbb {C}^{n-1}}\sum _{a:\, f(z',a)=0} m(z',a)\varphi (z',a)\, \mathrm{d}V_{2n-2}(z'), \end{equation} where the sum runs over the zeros $a$ of $z_ j\mapsto f(z',z_ j)$ in the fiber of $P$ over $z'$, and $m(z',a)$ is the order of that zero; the integrand is defined outside the null set of those $z'$ over which $f$ vanishes identically on the fiber. In particular, if $\pi _ j$ is the projection of $P$ omitting $z_ j$, the positive measure $(\log |f|^2)_{j ar j}$ gives zero mass to $\pi _ j^{-1}(N)$ for every Lebesgue null set $N$. Proof. Local integrability. Near a point where $f
eq 0$, the function $\log |f|^2$ is smooth. Let $a$ be a zero of $f$. After a translation and a complex-linear change of coordinates, which preserve local integrability, we may assume that $a=0$ and that $f(0,w)$ does not vanish identically in the last variable $w$ (lemma 5.5.1 ). Then $f(0,\cdot )$ has a zero of some order $m\geq 1$ at $0$, and by theorem 5.5.2 , $f=gW$ on a polydisc $P'	imes \{ |w|<ho \} $, where $g$ is a holomorphic unit and $W(z',w)=\prod _{l=1}^ m(w-\lambda _ l(z'))$ with all roots in $\{ |w|<ho _1\} $ for some $ho _1<ho $. Choose $r\in (ho _1,ho )$ and replace $P'$ by a smaller concentric polydisc with compact closure in $P'$; since $g$ is continuous and nowhere zero, $\log |g|^2$ is then bounded on $P'	imes \{ |w|<r\} $. For $|\lambda |\leq ho _1$ we have \[  \int _{|w|<r} ig |\log |w-\lambda | ig |\, \mathrm{d}V_2(w)\le C,  \] with $C$ independent of $\lambda $: the positive part of $\log |w-\lambda |$ is at most $\max \{ \log (r+ho _1),0\} $, and after the translation $\zeta =w-\lambda $ the integral of its negative part is at most $\int _{|\zeta |<1}(-\log |\zeta |)\, \mathrm dV_2(\zeta )$. Since $|\log |W(z',w)||\leq \sum _ l|\log |w-\lambda _ l(z')||$, it follows that $\int _{|w|<r}|\log |W(z',w)||\, \mathrm dV_2(w)\leq mC$ for every $z'\in P'$. (The estimate holds for each fiber separately, so we need not choose the roots as measurable functions of $z'$.) By Tonelli's theorem $\log |W|^2$, and hence $\log |f|^2$, is integrable on $P'	imes \{ |w|<r\} $, a neighborhood of $a=0$. The slice formula. For $n=1$, example 3.4.15 gives $\Delta \log |f|^2=4\pi \sum _ am(a)\delta _ a$ locally, that is, $(\log |f|^2)_{z ar z}=\pi \sum _ am(a)\delta _ a$; this is ( 5.5.4 ) with $\mathbb C^0$ a point. In general, write $P=P'	imes D$ with $D$ a disc in the variable $z_ j$. By lemma 5.5.1 , the set $N_0$ of points $z'\in P'$ over which $f$ vanishes identically on $D$ is null. By Fubini's theorem,  egin{align*}   ig \langle (\log |f|^2)_{j ar j},\varphi  ig angle & =\int _ P\log |f|^2\, \partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ j}\varphi \, \mathrm dV_{2n}\ & =\int _{P'}\Big(\int _ D\log |f(z',w)|^2\, \partial _ w\partial _{ ar w}\varphi (z',w)\, \mathrm dV_2(w)\Big)\mathrm dV_{2n-2}(z'), \end{align*} the inner integral being an integrable function of $z'$. For $z'
otin N_0$, the one-variable case applied to $f(z',\cdot )$ on $D$ shows that the inner integral equals $\pi \sum _ am(z',a)\varphi (z',a)$. This proves ( 5.5.4 ); the integrand on the right is measurable and integrable, being equal almost everywhere to the inner integral. Positivity. By ( 5.5.4 ), $(\log |f|^2)_{j ar j}$ is nonnegative on nonnegative test functions supported in polydiscs contained in $\Omega $, hence on all nonnegative test functions, which are finite sums of such functions by lemma 2.5.2 . This holds in every system of complex linear coordinates, since $f$ remains holomorphic after a linear change of coordinates. Applying this after a unitary change of coordinates, as in the matrix criterion of section 5.4 , we see that $\sum _{j,k}(\log |f|^2)_{j ar k}\xi _ j ar\xi _ k$ is a positive measure for every $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n$. By the matrix criterion, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2\geq 0$, and by theorem 5.3.7 its coefficients are measures. Null sets. Let $
u =(\log |f|^2)_{j ar j}$ on $P=P'	imes D$, and let $\eta \geq 0$ be a test function on $D$. By ( 5.5.4 ), for every nonnegative test function $\psi $ on $P'$, \[  \int _ P\psi (z')\eta (z_ j)\, \mathrm d
u =\int _{P'}\psi \, h_\eta \, \mathrm dV_{2n-2},\qquad h_\eta (z')=\pi \sum _ am(z',a)\eta (a)\geq 0.  \] Both sides define positive Radon measures on $P'$ in $\psi $, the function $h_\eta $ being locally integrable by the identity itself. By the uniqueness in theorem 2.5.6 , the image measure $A\mapsto \int _{\pi _ j^{-1}(A)}\eta \, \mathrm d
u $ of $\eta 
u $ under $\pi _ j$ is therefore $h_\eta \, \mathrm dV_{2n-2}$. Every null set is contained in a Borel null set, by outer regularity of Lebesgue measure, so we may assume that $N$ is a Borel set. Then $\int _{\pi _ j^{-1}(N)}\eta \, \mathrm d
u =\int _ Nh_\eta \, \mathrm dV_{2n-2}=0$. Letting $\eta $ increase to $1$ on $D$ along a sequence, we obtain $
u (\pi _ j^{-1}(N))=0$ by monotone convergence. The canonical representative. The trace of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2$ is positive, so by theorem 3.4.12 the class of $\log |f|^2$ has a canonical subharmonic representative $v$, given by the limits of ball averages in ( 3.4.13 ). At a point where $f
eq 0$, the function $\log |f|^2$ is continuous, so $v$ agrees with it there. At a zero $a$, there is $C$ with $|f(z)|\leq C|z-a|$ near $a$, since $f$ is smooth and $f(a)=0$; hence the average of $\log |f|^2$ over $B(a,r)$ is at most $\log C^2+2\log r$, which tends to $-\infty $ as $r	o 0$. Thus $v(a)=-\infty =\log |f(a)|^2$, and $v=\log |f|^2$ everywhere. $\square$

title: Lemma 5.5.5
section: 5.5 Holomorphic zeros and the Poincaré–Lelong formula
text:
Lemma 5.5.5 . 116B90FD9752 Let $f$ be as in proposition 5.5.3 , and let $z_0$ be a zero of $f$. There are complex linear coordinates centered at $z_0$ and a polydisc $P$ centered at $z_0$ such that, for every $j=1,\ldots ,n$, the projection $\pi _ j$ of $P$ omitting the coordinate $z_ j$ satisfies $S\cap P\subset \pi _ j^{-1}(N_ j)$ for a Lebesgue null set $N_ j$. Proof. Choose coordinates as in lemma 5.5.1 , so that $f$ does not vanish identically on any coordinate axis through $z_0=0$. Fix $j$, and write points as $(z',w)$ with $w=z_ j$. By theorem 5.5.2 in the variable $w$, there is a polydisc $P_ j=P'_ j	imes \{ |w|<ho \} $ in the domain of $f$ on which $f=gW$, where $g$ is a holomorphic unit and $W$ is a monic polynomial in $w$ of some degree $m\geq 1$ whose coefficients are holomorphic on $P'_ j$ and whose roots lie in $\{ |w|<ho _1\} $ for some $ho _1<ho $. We shall find a holomorphic function $h$ on $P'_ j$, not identically zero, such that every zero of $f$ in $P_ j$ lying over $\{ h
eq 0\} $ belongs to $V_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Then $S\cap P_ j\subset \pi _ j^{-1}(N_ j)$ with $N_ j=\{ h=0\} $, which is null by lemma 5.5.1 if $n\geq 2$, and empty if $n=1$, when $P'_ j$ is a point. Any polydisc $P$ centered at $0$ and contained in $P_1\cap \cdots \cap P_ n$ then has the required property. For $z'\in P'_ j$, let $\lambda _1(z'),\ldots ,\lambda _ m(z')$ be the roots of $W(z',\cdot )$, repeated according to multiplicity, and put $p_ k(z')=\sum _ l\lambda _ l(z')^ k$ for $k\geq 0$. By the residue theorem, \[  p_ k(z')= rac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|w|=ho '}w^ k rac{\partial _ wW(z',w)}{W(z',w)}\, \mathrm dw\qquad (ho _1<ho '<ho ),  \] so $p_ k$ is holomorphic on $P'_ j$, by differentiation under the integral sign. Let $s$ be the largest number of distinct roots of $W(z',\cdot )$ for $z'\in P'_ j$, and let $h$ be the determinant of the $s	imes s$ matrix $(p_{a+b})_{0\leq a,b\leq s-1}$; it is holomorphic on $P'_ j$. For fixed $z'$, this matrix is $A^{\mathsf T}A$, where $A$ is the $m	imes s$ matrix with entries $A_{la}=\lambda _ l^ a$. To compute $h(z')$, note that the $b$th column of $A^{\mathsf T}A$ is $\sum _ l\lambda _ l^ bv_ l$, where $v_ l=(\lambda _ l^0,\ldots ,\lambda _ l^{s-1})$ is the $l$th row of $A$. Expanding the determinant by multilinearity in the columns, discarding the terms in which some $v_ l$ occurs twice, and grouping the remaining terms according to the set $L$ of indices that occur, we find that each group contributes $(\det A_ L)^2$. Indeed, if $L=\{ l_1<\cdots <l_ s\} $, the terms of this group are indexed by the permutations $\pi $ of $\{ 1,\ldots ,s\} $, the term of $\pi $ taking $\lambda _{l_{\pi (b+1)}}^ bv_{l_{\pi (b+1)}}$ from the $b$th column. Reordering the columns multiplies the determinant by $\operatorname {sign}(\pi )$, so the group contributes $\det A_ L\sum _\pi \operatorname {sign}(\pi )\prod _{b=0}^{s-1}\lambda _{l_{\pi (b+1)}}^ b$, and this sum is the Leibniz expansion of $\det A_ L$. Thus we obtain the Cauchy–Binet formula \[  h(z')=\det (A^{\mathsf T}A)=\sum _ L(\det A_ L)^2=\sum _ L\prod _{l<l',\  l,l'\in L}(\lambda _ l-\lambda _{l'})^2,  \] where $L$ runs over the $s$-element subsets of $\{ 1,\ldots ,m\} $, $A_ L$ is the square matrix formed by the rows of $A$ with indices in $L$, and the last equality is the Vandermonde formula. If $W(z',\cdot )$ has fewer than $s$ distinct roots, every set $L$ contains two indices with equal roots, and $h(z')=0$. If $W(z',\cdot )$ has exactly $s$ distinct roots $\mu _1,\ldots ,\mu _ s$, of multiplicities $k_1,\ldots ,k_ s$, then the nonzero terms are those of the $k_1\cdots k_ s$ sets $L$ containing exactly one index of each root, and each of them equals $\prod _{c<c'}(\mu _ c-\mu _{c'})^2
eq 0$; hence $h(z')

Then $W(z'_0,w_0)=0$, since $g$ is a unit, and $W(z'_0,\cdot )$ has exactly $s$ distinct roots $\mu _1,\ldots ,\mu _ s$, of multiplicities $k_1,\ldots ,k_ s$; say $w_0=\mu _1$. Choose disjoint closed discs $E_ c$ centered at $\mu _ c$ in $\{ |w|<ho \} $, and a connected neighborhood $Y$ of $z'_0$ in $P'_ j$ such that $W(z',\cdot )$ has no zeros on the boundary circles $\partial E_ c$ for $z'\in Y$; this is possible because $W(z'_0,\cdot )$ has no zeros on these compact circles and $W$ is continuous. By the argument principle, the number of roots of $W(z',\cdot )$ in $E_ c$, counted with multiplicity, is $(2\pi \mathrm i)^{-1}\int _{\partial E_ c}\partial _ wW/W\, \mathrm dw$, a continuous integer-valued function on $Y$, hence equal to $k_ c$. Thus each $E_ c$ contains at least one root of $W(z',\cdot )$. Since $W(z',\cdot )$ has at most $s$ distinct roots, each $E_ c$ contains exactly one, $\mu _ c(z')$, of multiplicity $k_ c$, and since $k_1+\cdots +k_ s=m$, there are no other roots. By the residue theorem, \[  \mu _ c(z')= rac1{2\pi \mathrm ik_ c}\int _{\partial E_ c}w\,  rac{\partial _ wW(z',w)}{W(z',w)}\, \mathrm dw,  \] which is holomorphic on $Y$, and $W(z',w)=\prod _ c(w-\mu _ c(z'))^{k_ c}$ for $z'\in Y$, both sides being monic polynomials in $w$ with the same roots and multiplicities. Near $(z'_0,w_0)$ the function $U=\prod _{c\geq 2}(w-\mu _ c(z'))^{k_ c}$ does not vanish, so $f=(gU)(w-\mu _1(z'))^{k_1}$, where $gU$ is a holomorphic unit and $\mathrm d(w-\mu _1(z'))

title: Theorem 5.5.6 (Poincaré–Lelong)
section: 5.5 Holomorphic zeros and the Poincaré–Lelong formula
text: Theorem 5.5.6 (Poincaré–Lelong) . 8D4BA339507E Let $f$ be a holomorphic function on a complex manifold $X$ that is not identically zero on any connected component of $X$, and let $V$, $V_{\mathrm{reg}}$ and $S$ be as above. Then the current $m[V_{\mathrm{reg}}]$ on $X\setminus S$, the integration over $V_{\mathrm{reg}}$ weighted by the multiplicity $m$, has locally finite mass near $S$: its coefficient measures have finite total variation on $K\setminus S$ for every compact subset $K$ of a chart. Extending its coefficient measures by zero on $S$, we obtain a closed positive $(1,1)$-current $[\operatorname{div}(f)]$ on $X$, and 9E4726681500 5.5.7 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2=[\operatorname{div}(f)]. \end{equation} Proof. If $X$ has dimension zero, then $f$ has no zeros and both sides vanish. Let $X$ have dimension $n\geq 1$. The set of points near which $f$ vanishes identically is open, and it is closed by the identity theorem, applied in connected coordinate neighborhoods; since $f$ does not vanish identically on any component of $X$, this set is empty. Hence proposition 5.5.3 applies in every connected chart: the function $\log |f|^2$ is locally integrable, and $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2$, given by $T(\varphi )=\int _ X\log |f|^2\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\varphi $ independently of coordinates, is a positive current with measure coefficients. It is closed because $\mathrm d\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=\mathrm d\mathrm d\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}=0$. We show that $T$ gives zero mass to $S$ and agrees with $m[V_{\mathrm{reg}}]$ outside $S$. Step 1: $T$ gives $S$ zero mass. Let $x_0\in S$, and choose coordinates and a polydisc $P$ centered at $x_0$ as in lemma 5.5.5 . For each $j$, the last assertion of proposition 5.5.3 shows that the diagonal coefficient $(\log |f|^2)_{j\bar j}$ vanishes on $S\cap P\subset \pi _ j^{-1}(N_ j)$. By the computation of the trace measure in section 5.4 , the sum of these diagonal coefficients is a positive multiple of the trace measure of $T$ in these coordinates, which therefore vanishes on $S\cap P$; by theorem 5.3.7 so do all coefficient measures of $T$ in these coordinates. By ( 5.3.6 ), the vanishing of the coefficient measures on a Borel set does not depend on the chart. Every compact subset of $S\cap U$, for a chart $U$, is covered by finitely many such polydiscs $P$, so by inner regularity all coefficient measures of $T$ vanish on $S\cap U$. Step 2: $T=m[V_{\mathrm{reg}}]$ on $X\setminus S$. Since $T$ is defined without reference to coordinates, we may compute it in any holomorphic coordinates. Away from $V$ the function $\log |f|^2$ is pluriharmonic, so $T=0$ there. Near a point $p\in V_{\mathrm{reg}}$ write $f=g\, a^ m$ as above, and use holomorphic coordinates $(t,x')$ with $t=a$. Then $\log |f|^2=\log |g|^2+m\log |t|^2$, where $\log |g|^2$ is pluriharmonic. In one variable, $\partial _ t\partial _{\bar t}\log |t|^2=\pi \delta _0$ by example 3.4.15 . Since $\log |t|^2$ does not depend on $x'$, Fubini's theorem shows that its distributional derivatives involving $x'$ or $\bar x'$ vanish and that $\langle (\log |t|^2)_{t\bar t},\psi \rangle =\pi \int \psi (0,x')\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2}(x')$ for test functions $\psi $; thus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |t|^2=(\mathrm i/2\pi )(\log |t|^2)_{t\bar t}\, \mathrm dt\wedge \mathrm d\bar t$. Let $\varphi $ be a test form of bidegree $(n-1,n-1)$, and let $\varphi _0=c(t,x')\bigwedge _ l(\frac{\mathrm i}2\mathrm dx'_ l\wedge \mathrm d\bar x'_ l)$ be its component without $\mathrm dt$ and $\mathrm d\bar t$, the only one that contributes. Since $(\mathrm i/2\pi )\, \mathrm dt\wedge \mathrm d\bar t\wedge \varphi _0=\pi ^{-1}c\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$, we obtain \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |t|^2)(\varphi )=\int c(0,x')\, \mathrm dV_{2n-2}(x')=\int _{\{ t=0\} }\varphi |_{\{ t=0\} },  \] that is, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |t|^2=[\{ t=0\} ]$ in the sense of example 5.3.9 , the hypersurface carrying its complex orientation. Therefore $T=m[V_{\mathrm{reg}}]$ near $p$. Step 3: extension across $S$. Let $U$ be a chart and $K\subset U$ compact. By Step 2, the trace measure of the positive current $m[V_{\mathrm{reg}}]$ on $U\setminus S$ is the restriction of $\mu _ T$, so its mass on $K\setminus S$ is at most $\mu _ T(K)<\infty $. By the coefficient bound of theorem 5.3.7 , applied on $U\setminus S$, the coefficient measures of $m[V_{\mathrm{reg}}]$, a positive current of bidegree $(1,1)$, have total variation at most $C_{n,1}\mu _ T(K)$ on $K\setminus S$. Hence they extend by zero on $S$ to complex Radon measures on $U$. Indeed, each coefficient measure $\sigma $ is a complex combination of the positive and negative variations of $\operatorname{Re}\sigma $ and $\operatorname{Im}\sigma $, which are positive Radon measures on $U\setminus S$ bounded by $|\sigma |$; extended by zero on $S$, they become Borel measures on $U$ that are finite on compact sets, hence Radon by proposition 2.2.2 . By Step 2 the coefficient measures of $T$ agree with those of $m[V_{\mathrm{reg}}]$ on $U\setminus S$, and by Step 1 they vanish on $S$. Thus the extensions by zero are the coefficient measures of the current $T$ of order zero; we denote this current by $[\operatorname{div}(f)]$. This proves ( 5.5.7 ), and $[\operatorname{div}(f)]=T$ is positive and closed. $\square$

title: Example 5.5.8
section: 5.5 Holomorphic zeros and the Poincaré–Lelong formula
text: Example 5.5.8 . DB42A2BDBC5B Let $1\leq r\leq n$ and $f(z)=z_1^{a_1}\cdots z_ r^{a_ r}$ on $\mathbb C^ n$, with positive integers $a_ j$. Then $\log |f|^2=\sum _ ja_ j\log |z_ j|^2$ everywhere, both sides being $-\infty $ on the zero set, and theorem 5.5.6 applied to each $z_ j$ gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\log |f|^2=\sum _{j=1}^ r a_ j[\{ z_ j=0\} ]$ on all of $\mathbb C^ n$, including the intersections of the coordinate hyperplanes. More generally, let $g$ and $h$ be holomorphic and not identically zero on a connected coordinate neighborhood. The function $\log |g|^2-\log |h|^2$, defined outside the null set where $g$ or $h$ vanishes, is locally integrable, and its complex Hessian is $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\log |g|^2-\log |h|^2)=[\operatorname{div}(g)]-[\operatorname{div}(h)]$. This current depends only on the quotient $g/h$: if $g',h'$ is another such pair with $gh'=g'h$, the two logarithmic differences agree almost everywhere, hence as distributions. We regard the difference only as an element of $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$; in particular, it is assigned no values at the common zeros of $g$ and $h$.

title: 5.6 Maps of currents and local mass
search_title: Maps of currents and local mass
section: 5.6 Maps of currents and local mass
text: Let $F\colon X\to Y$ be a holomorphic map between complex manifolds, with $\dim _{\mathbb C}X=m$ and $\dim _{\mathbb C}Y=n$. Smooth forms on $Y$ can be pulled back to $X$ by means of the derivative of $F$; the pullback commutes with $\mathrm d$, by ( 5.2.5 ), and also with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, because pullback by a holomorphic map preserves types. By duality, currents on $X$ can be pushed forward to $Y$ when $F$ is proper on their support, and currents on $Y$ can be pulled back when $F$ is a submersion. Closed positive $(1,1)$-currents can also be pulled back through their local potentials, as long as these do not become identically $-\infty $. Proposition 5.6.1 . EB9FCD4819C3 Let $T$ be a current of bidegree $(p,q)$ on $X$, and assume that the restriction of $F$ to $\operatorname{Supp}T$ is proper, that is, $\operatorname{Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(L)$ is compact for every compact set $L\subset Y$. Then the pushforward $F_*T$ defined below is a current of bidegree $(p+n-m,q+n-m)$ on $Y$; it is the zero current if this bidegree lies outside the range $0,\ldots ,n$. The pushforward commutes with $\mathrm{d}$, $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, and if $p=q$ and $T$ is positive, then $F_*T$ is positive. Proof. Let $\varphi $ be a test form on $Y$. By properness, the set $\operatorname{Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(\operatorname{Supp}\varphi )$ is compact. Choose a smooth function $\chi \geq 0$ with compact support on $X$ that equals one on a neighborhood of this set (proposition 5.2.6 ), and define \[  (F_*T)(\varphi )=T(\chi F^*\varphi ).  \] The value does not depend on $\chi $: if $\chi '$ is another choice, then $(\chi -\chi ')F^*\varphi $ is a test form whose support is disjoint from $\operatorname{Supp}T$, since $\chi =\chi '$ near $\operatorname{Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(\operatorname{Supp}\varphi )$ and $F^*\varphi =0$ outside $F^{-1}(\operatorname{Supp}\varphi )$; so $T$ vanishes on this form. For all test forms supported in a fixed compact set $L\subset Y$ a single cutoff serves, namely one equal to one near the compact set $\operatorname{Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(L)$; in particular, $F_*T$ is linear. Now let $L$ lie in a chart of $Y$, fix such a cutoff $\chi $, cover $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ by finitely many charts of $X$ and choose a partition of unity subordinate to this cover near $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $. By the chain rule, the coefficients of the pieces of $\chi F^*\varphi $ in these charts, together with their derivatives of order at most $m'$, are bounded by a constant times $\sum _ Jp_{L,m'}(\varphi _ J)$, where the $\varphi _ J$ are the coefficients of $\varphi $ (at points mapped outside $\operatorname{Supp}\varphi $ they vanish). The estimates for $T$ in these charts therefore give the estimate in the definition of a current for $F_*T$. Pullback preserves bidegrees, and $T$ acts on test forms of bidegree $(m-p,m-q)$, so $F_*T$ has bidegree $(n-(m-p),n-(m-q))$. For differentiation, note that $\mathrm d(\chi F^*\varphi )=\chi F^*\mathrm d\varphi +\mathrm d\chi \wedge F^*\varphi $, and $T$ vanishes on the last term because its support is disjoint from $\operatorname{Supp}T$. Since the degrees of $T$ and $F_*T$ differ by the even integer $2(m-n)$, the signs in the definitions of $\mathrm dT$ and $\mathrm dF_*T$ agree, and $\mathrm d(F_*T)=F_*(\mathrm dT)$; the same argument applies to $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $. If $\varphi $ is strongly positive, so is $\chi F^*\varphi $ by proposition 5.3.2 , which proves the last assertion. $\square$ For example, the current $[Z]$ of example 5.3.9 is the pushforward of the constant function $1$, regarded as a current of degree zero on $Z$, under the inclusion $Z\hookrightarrow X$, which is proper. A current with compact support can be pushed forward by every holomorphic map. Proposition 5.6.2 . 36A2806D4E71 Assume that $F$ is a submersion, that is, its complex derivative has rank $n$ at every point of $X$. Then every current $T$ on $Y$ has a pullback $F^*T$, a current on $X$ of the same bidegree, which agrees with the pullback of forms when $T$ is smooth, and with the locally integrable function $a\circ F$ when $T$ is given by a locally integrable function $a$ on $Y$. The map $T\mapsto F^*T$ is continuous for weak convergence, commutes with $\mathrm d$, $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, and maps positive currents to positive currents. Proof. Local construction. Let $x\in X$, and choose holomorphic coordinates $z=(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)$ near $F(x)$. Since $F$ is a submersion, the complex Jacobian matrix at $x$ of the $n$ components of $z\circ F$ has rank $n$ in every chart around $x$. By proposition 5.2.4 (3), these components are the first $n$ coordinates of holomorphic coordinates $(z,w)\in \mathbb C^ n\times \mathbb C^{m-n}$ near $x$, in which $F$ is the projection $(z,w)\mapsto z$; shrinking, we may assume that the coordinate domain is a product $U\times W$. For a distribution $a$ on $U$, define the distribution $F^*a$ on $U\times W$ by \[  \langle F^*a,\psi \rangle =\left\langle a,\int _{W}\psi (\cdot ,w)\, \mathrm{d}V_{2m-2n}(w)\right\rangle .  \] Integration in $w$ maps test functions on $U\times W$ continuously to test functions on $U$: the $z$-derivatives of $\int _ W\psi (\cdot ,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2m-2n}(w)$ are the integrals of the $z$-derivatives of $\psi $, by differentiation under the integral sign, and its support lies in the projection of $\operatorname{Supp}\psi $. Hence $F^*a$ is a distribution, and if $a$ is locally integrable, then $F^*a$ is the function $(z,w)\mapsto a(z)$, by Fubini's theorem. For $T=\sum T_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ on $U$ put $F^*T=\sum F^*T_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$. This is a linear map from currents on $U$ to currents on $U\times W$ preserving bidegrees, continuous for weak convergence, and equal to the pullback of forms for smooth $T$. It commutes with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, since these act on the coefficients by differentiation, $\partial _{z_ l}F^*a=F^*\partial _{z_ l}a$, and $\partial _{w_ l}F^*a=0$ because $\int _ W\partial _{w_ l}\psi (\cdot ,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2m-2n}(w)=0$ by the fundamental theorem of calculus; similarly for the conjugate derivatives. Continuity for weak convergence holds because the coefficients of a current depend continuously on it, by their explicit description in section 5.3 . Independence and gluing. Two such local constructions near $x$ agree. Indeed, mollifying the coefficients of $T$ in a chart near $F(x)$, we obtain smooth forms $T_\varepsilon \to T$ weakly on a neighborhood of $F(x)$, as in the discussion following theorem 5.3.7 . Both constructions are weakly continuous and agree with the pullback of forms on each $T_\varepsilon $, so they agree on $T$ near $x$. Consequently the local pullbacks agree on the overlaps of their domains, and by lemma 5.3.8 they glue to a unique current $F^*T$ on $X$ that agrees with each local pullback on its domain. Explicitly, if $(\chi _ c)$ is a partition of unity with compact supports subordinate to the cover of $X$ by the domains of the local pullbacks, and $(F^*T)_ c$ denotes a local pullback whose domain contains $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ c$, then $(F^*T)(\varphi )=\sum _ c(F^*T)_ c(\chi _ c\varphi )$. The local pullbacks are linear, preserve bidegrees and commute with $\mathrm d$, $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $; they give the pullback of forms if $T$ is smooth, and the function $a\circ F$ if $T$ is given by a locally integrable function $a$. By the uniqueness in lemma 5.3.8 , $F^*T$ has the same properties. Continuity for weak convergence follows from the explicit formula, since each of the finitely many nonzero terms $(F^*T)_ c(\chi _ c\varphi )$ depends continuously on $T$. Positivity. If $T$ is positive, the forms $T_\varepsilon $ are positive near $F(x)$, hence weakly positive at every point. By proposition 5.3.2 their pullbacks are weakly positive at every point, hence positive currents, and positivity passes to the weak limit, the local pullback of $T$ near $x$. Hence $F^*T$ is positive, by lemma 5.3.8 . $\square$ On currents of order zero, the submersion pullback is described by product measures. Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ and $W\subset \mathbb C^ k$ be open, and let $\lambda _ W$ be Lebesgue measure $\mathrm dV_{2k}$ on $W$, which is the unit mass on the point $W=\mathbb C^0$ if $k=0$ and $W\neq \varnothing $. Every open subset of $U\times W$ is a countable union of products of open boxes, so the Borel sets of $U\times W$ form the $\sigma $-algebra generated by the products of Borel subsets of $U$ and of $W$. For a positive Radon measure $\sigma $ on $U$, which is $\sigma $-finite by proposition 2.2.2 , Tonelli's theorem therefore defines the product measure $\sigma \otimes \lambda _ W$ on the Borel sets of $U\times W$, and 56D4111AE674 5.6.3 \begin{equation}  \int _{U\times W}h\, \mathrm d(\sigma \otimes \lambda _ W)=\int _ U\Bigl (\int _ Wh(z,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2k}(w)\Bigr )\mathrm d\sigma (z) \end{equation} for every nonnegative Borel function $h$ on $U\times W$, the inner integral being a Borel function of $z$. A compact subset of $U\times W$ lies in the product of its two projections, which are compact, so $\sigma \otimes \lambda _ W$ is finite on compact sets and hence a positive Radon measure, by proposition 2.2.2 . For a complex Radon measure $\sigma =\sigma _1-\sigma _2+\mathrm i(\sigma _3-\sigma _4)$ on $U$ we put $\sigma \otimes \lambda _ W=\sigma _1\otimes \lambda _ W-\sigma _2\otimes \lambda _ W+\mathrm i(\sigma _3\otimes \lambda _ W-\sigma _4\otimes \lambda _ W)$. By linearity, ( 5.6.3 ) holds for every bounded Borel function $h$ with compact support. Its right-hand side is the integral against $\sigma $ of the bounded Borel function $\widehat h(z)=\int _ Wh(z,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2k}(w)$, which has compact support, so it does not depend on the decomposition of $\sigma $; neither does $\sigma \otimes \lambda _ W$, which is determined by its integrals of continuous functions with compact support. Corollary 5.6.4 . FFF97DDD2CF2 Let $F\colon X\to Y$ be a submersion, and let $T$ be a current of order zero on $Y$. Suppose that $X=U\times W$ and $Y=U$, where $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ and $W\subset \mathbb C^{m-n}$ are open, and that $F$ is the projection $(z,w)\mapsto z$. Write $T=\sum _{I,J}T_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$. Then, with the product measures $T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W$ defined above, \[  F^*T=\sum _{I,J}(T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W)\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J;  \] that is, in the coordinates $(z,w)$ the coefficient measure of $F^*T$ at $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ is $T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W$, and the coefficients at the basis forms containing some $\mathrm dw_ l$ or $\mathrm d\bar w_ l$ vanish. In general, $F^*T$ has order zero, and \[  F^*(fT)=(f\circ F)\, F^*T  \] for every locally bounded Borel function $f$ on $Y$. In particular, $F^*(\mathbf1_ ET)=\mathbf1_{F^{-1}(E)}F^*T$ for every Borel set $E\subset Y$. Proof. (1) The local construction in the proof of proposition 5.6.2 can be carried out with the coordinates $z$ on $U$ and $(z,w)$ on $U\times W$, and it is then defined on all of $U\times W$. By the independence of the local constructions shown in that proof, $F^*T$ agrees with it near every point, hence on $U\times W$. Thus the coefficients of $F^*T$ at the basis forms containing some $\mathrm dw_ l$ or $\mathrm d\bar w_ l$ vanish, and the coefficient at $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ is the distribution $\psi \mapsto \langle T_{IJ},\widehat\psi \rangle $, where $\widehat\psi (z)=\int _ W\psi (z,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2m-2n}(w)$ is a test function on $U$. Since $T_{IJ}$ is a complex Radon measure, ( 5.6.3 ) gives $\langle T_{IJ},\widehat\psi \rangle =\int _ U\widehat\psi \, \mathrm dT_{IJ}=\int \psi \, \mathrm d(T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W)$ for every test function $\psi $ on $U\times W$. Hence this coefficient is the complex Radon measure $T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W$. (2) Let $x\in X$. As in the proof of proposition 5.6.2 , there are holomorphic coordinates $z$ on a chart of $Y$ around $F(x)$ and holomorphic coordinates $(z,w)$ on a neighborhood $N$ of $x$, with coordinate domain a product $U\times W$, in which $F$ is the projection $(z,w)\mapsto z$. On $N$, the current $F^*T$ is the pullback of the restriction of $T$ to the open set $U$ by this projection. By (1), the coefficients of $F^*T$ in the chart $N$ are complex Radon measures. The charts $N$ obtained in this way form an atlas of $X$, so $F^*T$ has order zero, by the discussion following ( 5.3.6 ). Now let $f$ be a locally bounded Borel function on $Y$; then $f\circ F$ is a locally bounded Borel function on $X$, since $F$ is continuous. In the coordinates above, the coefficient measures of $fT$ are the measures $fT_{IJ}$, where $f$ is written in the coordinates $z$, so by (1) the coefficient measures of $F^*(fT)$ on $N$ are the measures $(fT_{IJ})\otimes \lambda _ W$, while those of $(f\circ F)F^*T$ are the measures $(f\circ F)(T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W)$; the coefficients at the basis forms containing some $\mathrm dw_ l$ or $\mathrm d\bar w_ l$ vanish for both currents. Let $g$ be a continuous function with compact support in $U\times W$. The function $g\cdot (f\circ F)$ is bounded, Borel and compactly supported, and $\widehat g(z)=\int _ Wg(z,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2m-2n}(w)$ is a bounded Borel function on $U$ with compact support. Applying ( 5.6.3 ) twice, we obtain \[  \int g\, (f\circ F)\, \mathrm d(T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W)=\int _ U\widehat g\, f\, \mathrm dT_{IJ}=\int _ U\widehat g\, \mathrm d(fT_{IJ})=\int g\, \mathrm d\bigl ((fT_{IJ})\otimes \lambda _ W\bigr ).  \] Hence the two currents have the same coefficient measures on $N$, and therefore agree on $N$. Since the sets $N$ cover $X$, the currents $F^*(fT)$ and $(f\circ F)F^*T$ coincide. The last assertion is the case $f=\mathbf1_ E$, since $\mathbf1_ E\circ F=\mathbf1_{F^{-1}(E)}$. $\square$ Proposition 5.6.5 . 6DAA1675792B Let $T$ be a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $Y$, and let $F\colon X\to Y$ be holomorphic. Suppose that every point of $X$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $F(W)$ lies in the domain of a canonical local potential $u$ of $T$ and $u\circ F$ is not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component of $W$. Then the currents $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)$ on these neighborhoods glue to a closed positive current \[  F^*T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)  \] on $X$, which does not depend on the chosen potentials. It agrees with the pullback of forms if $T$ is smooth, and with the pullback of proposition 5.6.2 if $F$ is a submersion. Proof. Canonical local potentials are defined on manifolds of positive dimension (theorem 5.4.3 ), so $Y$ has positive dimension. If $X$ has dimension zero, every $(1,1)$-current on $X$ vanishes, and $F^*T=0$. Assume that $X$ has positive dimension, let $W$ and $u$ be as in the hypothesis, and let $W_0$ be a connected component of $W$. Each point of $W_0$ has a connected neighborhood $W'\subset W_0$ in a chart of $X$ such that $F(W')$ lies in a chart of $Y$ contained in the domain of $u$. In that chart, $u$ is the canonical subharmonic representative of its class, by the remark following proposition 5.4.4 , so by that proposition $u\circ F$ is either identically $-\infty $ on $W'$, or locally integrable on $W'$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)\geq 0$. No point has neighborhoods $W'$ of both kinds, because a locally integrable function is finite almost everywhere. Hence the points of $W_0$ having a neighborhood of the first kind and those having one of the second kind form two disjoint open sets covering $W_0$. Since $W_0$ is connected and $u\circ F$ is not identically $-\infty $ on $W_0$, the first set is empty. Thus $u\circ F$ is locally integrable on $W$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)\geq 0$ there. Let $(\widetilde W,\widetilde u)$ be another pair as in the hypothesis. Near each point of the intersection of the domains of $u$ and $\widetilde u$ we have $\widetilde u=u+h$ with $h$ smooth and pluriharmonic, by theorem 5.4.3 and the remark following proposition 5.4.4 . Locally $h=\operatorname{Re}g$ with $g$ holomorphic, so $h\circ F=\operatorname{Re}(g\circ F)$ is smooth and pluriharmonic, and $\widetilde u\circ F=u\circ F+h\circ F$ near each point of $W\cap \widetilde W$. Consequently $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\widetilde u\circ F)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)$ near each point of $W\cap \widetilde W$, hence on $W\cap \widetilde W$, since a current that vanishes near each point vanishes. By lemma 5.3.8 , the local currents $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)$, which are positive and closed because $\mathrm d\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=0$, glue to a unique closed positive current $F^*T$ on $X$. It is independent of the choices: the currents obtained from two systems of choices agree near each point, by what we have just shown, and hence coincide by the uniqueness in lemma 5.3.8 . If $T$ is smooth, lemma 5.4.2 gives smooth real local potentials $v$ with $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$; they are subharmonic, by the matrix criterion and proposition 3.1.5 , hence their own canonical representatives, so we may use them as the potentials $u$. For a smooth potential $u$ the chain rule gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)=F^*\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=F^*T$. Now let $F$ be a submersion, and let $V$ be the domain of $u$. The restriction of $F$ to $F^{-1}(V)$ is a submersion to $V$, and its submersion pullback agrees on $F^{-1}(V)$ with that of $F$, since both are glued from the same local constructions. By proposition 5.6.2 , the locally integrable function $u\circ F$ represents the submersion pullback $F^*u$, and since this pullback commutes with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, we obtain $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F^*u=F^*\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=F^*T$ on $F^{-1}(V)$, in particular on $W$. $\square$ Example 5.6.6 . 5A6B397A8B30 On $\mathbb {C}^2$, the current $T=[\{ z_1=0\} ]$ has the canonical local potential $\log |z_1|^2$, by theorem 5.5.6 and proposition 5.5.3 . For $F(w)=(0,w)$, the composition $\log |z_1|^2\circ F$ is identically $-\infty $, and so is the composition of every canonical local potential, since these differ from $\log |z_1|^2$ by smooth functions; thus proposition 5.6.5 does not define $F^*T$. For $G(w)=(w,0)$, the composition is $\log |w|^2$, and $G^*T=[0]$ is the Dirac mass at the origin. Thus the current of integration over a line can be restricted to a transverse line, but not to the line itself. We finally compare trace measures in different charts by means of a Hermitian metric. A Hermitian metric on $X$ is a smooth field of positive definite Hermitian quadratic forms on its tangent spaces. In coordinates we write it as $h=\sum h_{j\bar k}\mathrm{d}z_ j\otimes \mathrm{d}\bar z_ k$, with $(h_{j\bar k})$ a positive definite Hermitian matrix at each point, and we associate with it the real $(1,1)$-form $\omega =(\mathrm{i}/2)\sum h_{j\bar k}\mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ k$; for the Euclidean metric $\sum _ j\mathrm dz_ j\otimes \mathrm d\bar z_ j$ we obtain $\omega =\beta $. Every complex manifold carries Hermitian metrics: a partition of unity combines the Euclidean metrics of charts into a locally finite convex combination, which is positive definite. By the matrix description of strict positivity in section 5.3 , the forms $\omega $ obtained in this way are exactly the smooth real $(1,1)$-forms that are strictly positive at every point; we call them Hermitian forms . A Hermitian form is a Kähler form if it is closed, and a complex manifold carrying a Kähler form is a Kähler manifold . For instance, $\beta $ is a Kähler form on $\mathbb C^ n$, but in general $\mathrm d\omega \neq 0$: on $\mathbb C^2$, the Hermitian form $\omega =\beta +\frac{\mathrm i}2|z_1|^2\mathrm dz_2\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_2$ has $\mathrm d\omega =\frac{\mathrm i}2(\bar z_1\mathrm dz_1+z_1\mathrm d\bar z_1)\wedge \mathrm dz_2\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_2\neq 0$. We usually denote Hermitian and Kähler forms by $\omega $; in 1 the same letter denoted other objects, such as points of the unit sphere and harmonic measures. For a positive current $T$ of bidegree $(p,p)$ on $X$, its trace measure with respect to $\omega $ is \[  \sigma _{T,\omega }=T\wedge \frac{\omega ^{n-p}}{(n-p)!}.  \] Since $\omega $ is positive, $\omega ^{n-p}$ is a smooth strongly positive form (proposition 5.3.2 ), so $T\wedge \omega ^{n-p}$ is a positive current of degree $2n$; hence $\sigma _{T,\omega }$ is a positive Radon measure on $X$, by the discussion following definition 5.3.5 , and unlike $\mu _ T$ it does not depend on a chart. It is comparable with the trace measures in charts. Let $K$ be a compact subset of a chart, choose a compact neighborhood $K'$ of $K$ in the chart, and let $0<c\leq C$ be lower and upper bounds for the eigenvalues of $(h_{j\bar k})$ on $K'$. At a point of $K'$, a unitary change of coordinates $w$ puts $\omega $ in the form $(\mathrm i/2)\sum _ j\lambda _ j\, \mathrm dw_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar w_ j$ with $c\leq \lambda _ j\leq C$, while $\beta $ keeps its form. Expanding, \[  \frac{\omega ^{n-p}}{(n-p)!}=\sum _{|L|=n-p}\Big(\prod _{l\in L}\lambda _ l\Big)\bigwedge _{l\in L}\Big(\frac{\mathrm i}2\mathrm dw_ l\wedge \mathrm d\bar w_ l\Big),  \] \[  \frac{\beta ^{n-p}}{(n-p)!}=\sum _{|L|=n-p}\bigwedge _{l\in L}\Big(\frac{\mathrm i}2\mathrm dw_ l\wedge \mathrm d\bar w_ l\Big).  \] Hence $\omega ^{n-p}-c^{n-p}\beta ^{n-p}$ and $C^{n-p}\beta ^{n-p}-\omega ^{n-p}$ are strongly positive at every point of $K'$, and positivity of $T$ gives \[  c^{n-p}\mu _ T\leq (n-p)!\, \sigma _{T,\omega }\leq C^{n-p}\mu _ T\qquad \text{on }\operatorname{Int}K'\supset K.  \] Consequently, for a family of positive currents, locally uniform bounds for the trace measures in charts, as in theorem 5.3.7 , are equivalent to uniform bounds for $\sigma _{T,\omega }(K)$ on every compact set $K\subset X$, for any Hermitian metric. For a complex submanifold $Z$ of $X$ of dimension $r$, the restriction of $\omega ^ r/r!$ to $Z$ is the volume form of the Riemannian metric $\operatorname{Re}h$ restricted to $Z$, that is, the $2r$-form on $Z$ that takes the value $1$ on positively oriented bases of the tangent spaces which are orthonormal for $\operatorname{Re}h$. Indeed, at a point of $Z$ choose a basis $e_1,\ldots ,e_ r$ of the complex tangent space of $Z$ that is orthonormal for $h$. Then $e_1,\mathrm ie_1,\ldots ,e_ r,\mathrm ie_ r$ is a positively oriented orthonormal basis for $\operatorname{Re}h$, and in the dual real coordinates the restriction of $\omega $ is $\sum _{j=1}^ r\mathrm{d}x_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}y_ j$, whose $r$th power divided by $r!$ is $\mathrm dx_1\wedge \mathrm dy_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dx_ r\wedge \mathrm dy_ r$. Consequently the trace measure $\sigma _{[Z],\omega }$, given by $\sigma _{[Z],\omega }(\chi )=\int _ Z\chi \, \omega ^ r/r!$, is the Riemannian volume measure of $Z$. Finally, in dimension zero all forms of positive degree and all $(1,1)$-currents vanish, and integration currents and currents of degree zero are sums over the discrete points of the manifold.

title: Proposition 5.6.1
section: 5.6 Maps of currents and local mass
text: Proposition 5.6.1 . EB9FCD4819C3 Let $T$ be a current of bidegree $(p,q)$ on $X$, and assume that the restriction of $F$ to $\operatorname{Supp}T$ is proper, that is, $\operatorname{Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(L)$ is compact for every compact set $L\subset Y$. Then the pushforward $F_*T$ defined below is a current of bidegree $(p+n-m,q+n-m)$ on $Y$; it is the zero current if this bidegree lies outside the range $0,\ldots ,n$. The pushforward commutes with $\mathrm{d}$, $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, and if $p=q$ and $T$ is positive, then $F_*T$ is positive. Proof. Let $\varphi $ be a test form on $Y$. By properness, the set $\operatorname{Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(\operatorname{Supp}\varphi )$ is compact. Choose a smooth function $\chi \geq 0$ with compact support on $X$ that equals one on a neighborhood of this set (proposition 5.2.6 ), and define \[  (F_*T)(\varphi )=T(\chi F^*\varphi ).  \] The value does not depend on $\chi $: if $\chi '$ is another choice, then $(\chi -\chi ')F^*\varphi $ is a test form whose support is disjoint from $\operatorname{Supp}T$, since $\chi =\chi '$ near $\operatorname{Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(\operatorname{Supp}\varphi )$ and $F^*\varphi =0$ outside $F^{-1}(\operatorname{Supp}\varphi )$; so $T$ vanishes on this form. For all test forms supported in a fixed compact set $L\subset Y$ a single cutoff serves, namely one equal to one near the compact set $\operatorname{Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(L)$; in particular, $F_*T$ is linear. Now let $L$ lie in a chart of $Y$, fix such a cutoff $\chi $, cover $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ by finitely many charts of $X$ and choose a partition of unity subordinate to this cover near $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $. By the chain rule, the coefficients of the pieces of $\chi F^*\varphi $ in these charts, together with their derivatives of order at most $m'$, are bounded by a constant times $\sum _ Jp_{L,m'}(\varphi _ J)$, where the $\varphi _ J$ are the coefficients of $\varphi $ (at points mapped outside $\operatorname{Supp}\varphi $ they vanish). The estimates for $T$ in these charts therefore give the estimate in the definition of a current for $F_*T$. Pullback preserves bidegrees, and $T$ acts on test forms of bidegree $(m-p,m-q)$, so $F_*T$ has bidegree $(n-(m-p),n-(m-q))$. For differentiation, note that $\mathrm d(\chi F^*\varphi )=\chi F^*\mathrm d\varphi +\mathrm d\chi \wedge F^*\varphi $, and $T$ vanishes on the last term because its support is disjoint from $\operatorname{Supp}T$. Since the degrees of $T$ and $F_*T$ differ by the even integer $2(m-n)$, the signs in the definitions of $\mathrm dT$ and $\mathrm dF_*T$ agree, and $\mathrm d(F_*T)=F_*(\mathrm dT)$; the same argument applies to $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $. If $\varphi $ is strongly positive, so is $\chi F^*\varphi $ by proposition 5.3.2 , which proves the last assertion. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.6.2
section: 5.6 Maps of currents and local mass
text: Proposition 5.6.2 . 36A2806D4E71 Assume that $F$ is a submersion, that is, its complex derivative has rank $n$ at every point of $X$. Then every current $T$ on $Y$ has a pullback $F^*T$, a current on $X$ of the same bidegree, which agrees with the pullback of forms when $T$ is smooth, and with the locally integrable function $a\circ F$ when $T$ is given by a locally integrable function $a$ on $Y$. The map $T\mapsto F^*T$ is continuous for weak convergence, commutes with $\mathrm d$, $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, and maps positive currents to positive currents. Proof. Local construction. Let $x\in X$, and choose holomorphic coordinates $z=(z_1,\ldots ,z_ n)$ near $F(x)$. Since $F$ is a submersion, the complex Jacobian matrix at $x$ of the $n$ components of $z\circ F$ has rank $n$ in every chart around $x$. By proposition 5.2.4 (3), these components are the first $n$ coordinates of holomorphic coordinates $(z,w)\in \mathbb C^ n\times \mathbb C^{m-n}$ near $x$, in which $F$ is the projection $(z,w)\mapsto z$; shrinking, we may assume that the coordinate domain is a product $U\times W$. For a distribution $a$ on $U$, define the distribution $F^*a$ on $U\times W$ by \[  \langle F^*a,\psi \rangle =\left\langle a,\int _{W}\psi (\cdot ,w)\, \mathrm{d}V_{2m-2n}(w)\right\rangle .  \] Integration in $w$ maps test functions on $U\times W$ continuously to test functions on $U$: the $z$-derivatives of $\int _ W\psi (\cdot ,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2m-2n}(w)$ are the integrals of the $z$-derivatives of $\psi $, by differentiation under the integral sign, and its support lies in the projection of $\operatorname{Supp}\psi $. Hence $F^*a$ is a distribution, and if $a$ is locally integrable, then $F^*a$ is the function $(z,w)\mapsto a(z)$, by Fubini's theorem. For $T=\sum T_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ on $U$ put $F^*T=\sum F^*T_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$. This is a linear map from currents on $U$ to currents on $U\times W$ preserving bidegrees, continuous for weak convergence, and equal to the pullback of forms for smooth $T$. It commutes with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, since these act on the coefficients by differentiation, $\partial _{z_ l}F^*a=F^*\partial _{z_ l}a$, and $\partial _{w_ l}F^*a=0$ because $\int _ W\partial _{w_ l}\psi (\cdot ,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2m-2n}(w)=0$ by the fundamental theorem of calculus; similarly for the conjugate derivatives. Continuity for weak convergence holds because the coefficients of a current depend continuously on it, by their explicit description in section 5.3 . Independence and gluing. Two such local constructions near $x$ agree. Indeed, mollifying the coefficients of $T$ in a chart near $F(x)$, we obtain smooth forms $T_\varepsilon \to T$ weakly on a neighborhood of $F(x)$, as in the discussion following theorem 5.3.7 . Both constructions are weakly continuous and agree with the pullback of forms on each $T_\varepsilon $, so they agree on $T$ near $x$. Consequently the local pullbacks agree on the overlaps of their domains, and by lemma 5.3.8 they glue to a unique current $F^*T$ on $X$ that agrees with each local pullback on its domain. Explicitly, if $(\chi _ c)$ is a partition of unity with compact supports subordinate to the cover of $X$ by the domains of the local pullbacks, and $(F^*T)_ c$ denotes a local pullback whose domain contains $\operatorname{Supp}\chi _ c$, then $(F^*T)(\varphi )=\sum _ c(F^*T)_ c(\chi _ c\varphi )$. The local pullbacks are linear, preserve bidegrees and commute with $\mathrm d$, $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $; they give the pullback of forms if $T$ is smooth, and the function $a\circ F$ if $T$ is given by a locally integrable function $a$. By the uniqueness in lemma 5.3.8 , $F^*T$ has the same properties. Continuity for weak convergence follows from the explicit formula, since each of the finitely many nonzero terms $(F^*T)_ c(\chi _ c\varphi )$ depends continuously on $T$. Positivity. If $T$ is positive, the forms $T_\varepsilon $ are positive near $F(x)$, hence weakly positive at every point. By proposition 5.3.2 their pullbacks are weakly positive at every point, hence positive currents, and positivity passes to the weak limit, the local pullback of $T$ near $x$. Hence $F^*T$ is positive, by lemma 5.3.8 . $\square$

title: Corollary 5.6.4
section: 5.6 Maps of currents and local mass
text: Corollary 5.6.4 . FFF97DDD2CF2 Let $F\colon X\to Y$ be a submersion, and let $T$ be a current of order zero on $Y$. Suppose that $X=U\times W$ and $Y=U$, where $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ and $W\subset \mathbb C^{m-n}$ are open, and that $F$ is the projection $(z,w)\mapsto z$. Write $T=\sum _{I,J}T_{IJ}\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$. Then, with the product measures $T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W$ defined above, \[  F^*T=\sum _{I,J}(T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W)\, \mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J;  \] that is, in the coordinates $(z,w)$ the coefficient measure of $F^*T$ at $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ is $T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W$, and the coefficients at the basis forms containing some $\mathrm dw_ l$ or $\mathrm d\bar w_ l$ vanish. In general, $F^*T$ has order zero, and \[  F^*(fT)=(f\circ F)\, F^*T  \] for every locally bounded Borel function $f$ on $Y$. In particular, $F^*(\mathbf1_ ET)=\mathbf1_{F^{-1}(E)}F^*T$ for every Borel set $E\subset Y$. Proof. (1) The local construction in the proof of proposition 5.6.2 can be carried out with the coordinates $z$ on $U$ and $(z,w)$ on $U\times W$, and it is then defined on all of $U\times W$. By the independence of the local constructions shown in that proof, $F^*T$ agrees with it near every point, hence on $U\times W$. Thus the coefficients of $F^*T$ at the basis forms containing some $\mathrm dw_ l$ or $\mathrm d\bar w_ l$ vanish, and the coefficient at $\mathrm dz_ I\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ J$ is the distribution $\psi \mapsto \langle T_{IJ},\widehat\psi \rangle $, where $\widehat\psi (z)=\int _ W\psi (z,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2m-2n}(w)$ is a test function on $U$. Since $T_{IJ}$ is a complex Radon measure, ( 5.6.3 ) gives $\langle T_{IJ},\widehat\psi \rangle =\int _ U\widehat\psi \, \mathrm dT_{IJ}=\int \psi \, \mathrm d(T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W)$ for every test function $\psi $ on $U\times W$. Hence this coefficient is the complex Radon measure $T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W$. (2) Let $x\in X$. As in the proof of proposition 5.6.2 , there are holomorphic coordinates $z$ on a chart of $Y$ around $F(x)$ and holomorphic coordinates $(z,w)$ on a neighborhood $N$ of $x$, with coordinate domain a product $U\times W$, in which $F$ is the projection $(z,w)\mapsto z$. On $N$, the current $F^*T$ is the pullback of the restriction of $T$ to the open set $U$ by this projection. By (1), the coefficients of $F^*T$ in the chart $N$ are complex Radon measures. The charts $N$ obtained in this way form an atlas of $X$, so $F^*T$ has order zero, by the discussion following ( 5.3.6 ). Now let $f$ be a locally bounded Borel function on $Y$; then $f\circ F$ is a locally bounded Borel function on $X$, since $F$ is continuous. In the coordinates above, the coefficient measures of $fT$ are the measures $fT_{IJ}$, where $f$ is written in the coordinates $z$, so by (1) the coefficient measures of $F^*(fT)$ on $N$ are the measures $(fT_{IJ})\otimes \lambda _ W$, while those of $(f\circ F)F^*T$ are the measures $(f\circ F)(T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W)$; the coefficients at the basis forms containing some $\mathrm dw_ l$ or $\mathrm d\bar w_ l$ vanish for both currents. Let $g$ be a continuous function with compact support in $U\times W$. The function $g\cdot (f\circ F)$ is bounded, Borel and compactly supported, and $\widehat g(z)=\int _ Wg(z,w)\, \mathrm dV_{2m-2n}(w)$ is a bounded Borel function on $U$ with compact support. Applying ( 5.6.3 ) twice, we obtain \[  \int g\, (f\circ F)\, \mathrm d(T_{IJ}\otimes \lambda _ W)=\int _ U\widehat g\, f\, \mathrm dT_{IJ}=\int _ U\widehat g\, \mathrm d(fT_{IJ})=\int g\, \mathrm d\bigl ((fT_{IJ})\otimes \lambda _ W\bigr ).  \] Hence the two currents have the same coefficient measures on $N$, and therefore agree on $N$. Since the sets $N$ cover $X$, the currents $F^*(fT)$ and $(f\circ F)F^*T$ coincide. The last assertion is the case $f=\mathbf1_ E$, since $\mathbf1_ E\circ F=\mathbf1_{F^{-1}(E)}$. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.6.5
section: 5.6 Maps of currents and local mass
text: Proposition 5.6.5 . 6DAA1675792B Let $T$ be a closed positive $(1,1)$-current on $Y$, and let $F\colon X\to Y$ be holomorphic. Suppose that every point of $X$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $F(W)$ lies in the domain of a canonical local potential $u$ of $T$ and $u\circ F$ is not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component of $W$. Then the currents $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)$ on these neighborhoods glue to a closed positive current \[  F^*T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)  \] on $X$, which does not depend on the chosen potentials. It agrees with the pullback of forms if $T$ is smooth, and with the pullback of proposition 5.6.2 if $F$ is a submersion. Proof. Canonical local potentials are defined on manifolds of positive dimension (theorem 5.4.3 ), so $Y$ has positive dimension. If $X$ has dimension zero, every $(1,1)$-current on $X$ vanishes, and $F^*T=0$. Assume that $X$ has positive dimension, let $W$ and $u$ be as in the hypothesis, and let $W_0$ be a connected component of $W$. Each point of $W_0$ has a connected neighborhood $W'\subset W_0$ in a chart of $X$ such that $F(W')$ lies in a chart of $Y$ contained in the domain of $u$. In that chart, $u$ is the canonical subharmonic representative of its class, by the remark following proposition 5.4.4 , so by that proposition $u\circ F$ is either identically $-\infty $ on $W'$, or locally integrable on $W'$ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)\geq 0$. No point has neighborhoods $W'$ of both kinds, because a locally integrable function is finite almost everywhere. Hence the points of $W_0$ having a neighborhood of the first kind and those having one of the second kind form two disjoint open sets covering $W_0$. Since $W_0$ is connected and $u\circ F$ is not identically $-\infty $ on $W_0$, the first set is empty. Thus $u\circ F$ is locally integrable on $W$, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)\geq 0$ there. Let $(\widetilde W,\widetilde u)$ be another pair as in the hypothesis. Near each point of the intersection of the domains of $u$ and $\widetilde u$ we have $\widetilde u=u+h$ with $h$ smooth and pluriharmonic, by theorem 5.4.3 and the remark following proposition 5.4.4 . Locally $h=\operatorname{Re}g$ with $g$ holomorphic, so $h\circ F=\operatorname{Re}(g\circ F)$ is smooth and pluriharmonic, and $\widetilde u\circ F=u\circ F+h\circ F$ near each point of $W\cap \widetilde W$. Consequently $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\widetilde u\circ F)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)$ near each point of $W\cap \widetilde W$, hence on $W\cap \widetilde W$, since a current that vanishes near each point vanishes. By lemma 5.3.8 , the local currents $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)$, which are positive and closed because $\mathrm d\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}=0$, glue to a unique closed positive current $F^*T$ on $X$. It is independent of the choices: the currents obtained from two systems of choices agree near each point, by what we have just shown, and hence coincide by the uniqueness in lemma 5.3.8 . If $T$ is smooth, lemma 5.4.2 gives smooth real local potentials $v$ with $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v$; they are subharmonic, by the matrix criterion and proposition 3.1.5 , hence their own canonical representatives, so we may use them as the potentials $u$. For a smooth potential $u$ the chain rule gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)=F^*\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=F^*T$. Now let $F$ be a submersion, and let $V$ be the domain of $u$. The restriction of $F$ to $F^{-1}(V)$ is a submersion to $V$, and its submersion pullback agrees on $F^{-1}(V)$ with that of $F$, since both are glued from the same local constructions. By proposition 5.6.2 , the locally integrable function $u\circ F$ represents the submersion pullback $F^*u$, and since this pullback commutes with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, we obtain $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u\circ F)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F^*u=F^*\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=F^*T$ on $F^{-1}(V)$, in particular on $W$. $\square$

For $F(w)=(0,w)$, the composition $\log |z_1|^2\circ F$ is identically $-\infty $, and so is the composition of every canonical local potential, since these differ from $\log |z_1|^2$ by smooth functions; thus proposition 5.6.5 does not define $F^*T$. title: 5.7 Plurisubharmonic functions
text: Plurisubharmonic functions are the basic objects of pluripotential theory. On a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$, a plurisubharmonic function is an upper semicontinuous function whose restriction to every complex line is subharmonic. By ( 5.2.9 ), the Laplacian of a function on $\Omega $, viewed as an open subset of $\mathbb R^{2n}$, is four times the trace of its complex Hessian, so subharmonicity controls only this trace. Subharmonicity on all complex lines is the pointwise counterpart of the positivity of the whole complex Hessian, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ determines $u$ only almost everywhere, the pointwise definition and the distributional condition must be kept apart. We first show that the upper semicontinuity required in the definition follows from the condition on complex lines (theorem 5.8.4 ); the proof combines the incidence estimate of section 2.9 with the distributional theory of section 3.4 . We then identify the plurisubharmonic functions with the canonical representatives, in the sense of theorem 3.4.12 , of the distributions with positive complex Hessian (theorem 5.9.1 ). This makes the potential theory of Part I available. A smooth function is plurisubharmonic exactly when its complex Hessian is positive semidefinite, and mollification approximates every plurisubharmonic function from above by smooth ones. Plurisubharmonicity is invariant under holomorphic maps, hence makes sense on complex manifolds, and it is preserved by decreasing limits, regularized upper envelopes and $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ limits. Moreover, plurisubharmonic functions belong to $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for every finite $p$, and near each point $\mathrm e^{-\alpha u}$ is integrable for small $\alpha >0$. In the last two sections we extend plurisubharmonic functions across closed sets that are locally contained in zero sets of holomorphic functions or are small in the sense of Hausdorff measure, and we prove Kiselman's minimum principle: although an infimum of plurisubharmonic functions is in general not plurisubharmonic, a partial infimum over real variables is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ under convexity assumptions, provided that the function does not depend on the corresponding imaginary parts. Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in subsection 25.1.8 . Plurisubharmonic functions are studied through their restrictions to complex lines, their positive complex Hessians, and their local integrability. The conventions and normalizations below also apply to quasi-plurisubharmonic functions and singular Hermitian metrics. The chapter begins with plurisubharmonic functions on domains in $\mathbb C^ n$ and on complex manifolds. We also include the $0$-dimensional case, which is occasionally convenient in inductive arguments. The basic permanence properties of plurisubharmonic functions are recalled: stability under upper envelopes and decreasing limits, Choquet's lemma, local integrability, gluing, extension across analytic subsets, and Kiselman's principle. The plurifine topology makes local plurisubharmonic functions continuous. Its neighborhood bases and local connectedness are used in arguments involving contact sets and non-pluripolar products. The next part of the chapter fixes our conventions for Lelong numbers and multiplier ideal sheaves. These conventions differ by harmless but important factors from some common references; the conversions are explained in 5.16.3 , 5.16.12 . We also recall Siu's semicontinuity theorem, the strong openness theorem of Guan–Zhou, the Ohsawa–Takegoshi extension theorem, and the valuative characterization of multiplier ideals. The remaining sections develop the global language used throughout these constructions. We introduce $\theta $-plurisubharmonic functions, quasi-plurisubharmonic functions, the preorder $\preceq $ of singularity types, and compactness properties in $L^1$. We then recall analytic singularities, log resolutions and quasi-equisingular approximation. Finally, we discuss closed positive $(1,1)$-currents, pseudo-effective and big classes, Kähler currents, Siu decomposition, non-Kähler and non-nef loci, modified nef classes, and singular Hermitian metrics on line bundles. Nets and subnets use the convention in 2.7 Nets and compactness . In particular, a subnet of a monotone net is monotone.

We identify $\mathbb {C}^ n$ with $\mathbb R^{2n}$ through $z_ j=x_ j+\mathrm{i}y_ j$, and we call a function on an open subset of $\mathbb {C}^ n$ subharmonic if it is subharmonic in the sense of definition 3.4.2 on the corresponding open subset of $\mathbb R^{2n}$. Recall from subsection 2.9.20 that an affine complex line is a set $L=\{ a+\zeta b:\zeta \in \mathbb {C}\} $ with $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ and $b\in \mathbb {C}^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $. For an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$, the section $L\cap \Omega $ is identified with the open set $\{ \zeta \in \mathbb {C}:a+\zeta b\in \Omega \} $, and a function on a connected component of $L\cap \Omega $ is called subharmonic if its composite with $\zeta \mapsto a+\zeta b$ is subharmonic; this does not depend on the parametrization of $L$. Accordingly, the restriction of a function $u$ on $\Omega $ to $L\cap \Omega $ is the function $\zeta \mapsto u(a+\zeta b)$. Definition 5.8.1 . 6070D2D83EC6 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain. If $n\ge 1$, a function $u\colon \Omega 	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ is plurisubharmonic if $u
ot\equiv -\infty $, $u$ is upper semicontinuous, and for every affine complex line $L$ the restriction of $u$ to each connected component of $L\cap \Omega $ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. The set of plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $ is denoted by $\mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. In dimension zero a domain is a single point, and the plurisubharmonic functions on it are the real-valued functions. We often abbreviate plurisubharmonic to psh . Since the constant $-\infty $ is subharmonic by definition 3.4.2 , the alternative “identically $-\infty $” in the line condition is stated only for emphasis; it occurs, for instance, for $\log |z_1|^2$ on the line $\{ z_1=0\} $. In dimension one the only affine complex line is $\mathbb {C}$ itself, so $\mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ is the set of nontrivial subharmonic functions on $\Omega $, that is, of those not identically $-\infty $. Whenever a limit of plurisubharmonic functions may degenerate to the function identically $-\infty $, we state this alternative explicitly. We keep upper semicontinuity in definition 5.8.1 , but it is redundant: theorem 5.8.4 below shows that it follows from the other two conditions. The proof of that theorem uses the following slicing lemma, which we apply again in theorem 5.9.1 , theorem 5.11.3 : for a locally integrable function, subharmonicity on the complex lines parallel to a fixed direction makes the second derivative in that direction a positive distribution. Hence $G_ N(z',w)=u(z',w)$ for all $N\geq M$, and $u=\lim _ NG_ N$ is Borel on $B'	imes B(w_0,ho )$. Countably many such product sets cover $\Omega $, so $u$ is Borel on $\Omega $. Write the points of $\mathbb {C}^ n$ as $v+ta$ with $v\in (\mathbb {C}a)^\perp $ and $t\in \mathbb {C}$, and put $K_ v=\{ t\in \mathbb {C}:v+ta\in \operatorname{Supp}\chi \} $. Assume that for almost every $v\in (\mathbb {C}a)^\perp $ there is an open set $G_ v\subset \{ t\in \mathbb {C}:v+ta\in \Omega \} $ containing $K_ v$ such that the restriction of $t\mapsto u(v+ta)$ to each connected component of $G_ v$ is subharmonic, possibly identically $-\infty $. Then \[  \Bigl \langle \sum _{j,k}a_ j\bar a_ ku_{j\bar k},\chi \Bigr \rangle \geq 0.  \] Consequently, if this hypothesis holds for every unit vector $a$ and every nonnegative $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. This is the case, in particular, if the restriction of $u$ to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is subharmonic. Proof. The map $(v,t)\mapsto v+ta$ is a unitary isomorphism of $(\mathbb {C}a)^\perp \times \mathbb {C}$ onto $\mathbb {C}^ n$, so it preserves Lebesgue measure, and by the chain rule $\partial _ t\partial _{\bar t}[\chi (v+ta)]=\sum _{j,k}a_ j\bar a_ k\chi _{j\bar k}(v+ta)$. We extend $u$ and $\chi $ by zero outside $\Omega $. Since $u$ is locally integrable and the derivatives of $\chi $ are bounded and supported in $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $, Fubini's theorem gives \[  \Bigl \langle \sum _{j,k}a_ j\bar a_ ku_{j\bar k},\chi \Bigr \rangle =\int _{(\mathbb {C}a)^\perp }I(v)\, \mathrm{d}V_{2n-2}(v),  \] where \[  I(v)=\int _{\mathbb {C}}u(v+ta)\, \partial _ t\partial _{\bar t}[\chi (v+ta)]\, \mathrm{d}V_2(t).  \] Applied to $|u|\mathbf1_{\operatorname{Supp}\chi }$, Fubini's theorem also shows that for almost every $v$ the function $t\mapsto u(v+ta)$ is integrable on $K_ v$. It therefore suffices to show that $I(v)\geq 0$ for every $v$ for which this integrability holds and an open set $G_ v$ as in the hypothesis exists. Fix such a $v$. The compact set $K_ v$ is covered by the disjoint open connected components of $G_ v$, so it meets only finitely many of them, say $U_1,\ldots ,U_ N$, and each set $K_ v\cap U_ i$ is compact, being the complement in $K_ v$ of the open set $K_ v\cap \bigcup _{l\neq i}U_ l$. Hence the function $\chi _ i(t)=\chi (v+ta)$, $t\in U_ i$, is a nonnegative test function on $U_ i$, and \[  I(v)=\sum _{i=1}^ N\int _{U_ i}u(v+ta)\, \partial _ t\partial _{\bar t}\chi _ i(t)\, \mathrm{d}V_2(t).  \] If $\chi _ i\equiv 0$, the $i$-th term vanishes. Thus the subharmonic function $w_ i(t)=u(v+ta)$ on the domain $U_ i$ is not identically $-\infty $, and it is locally integrable by proposition 3.4.8 . Since $\partial _ t\partial _{\bar t}=\frac14\Delta $, the $i$-th term equals $\frac14\langle \Delta w_ i,\chi _ i\rangle $, which is nonnegative by theorem 3.4.12 (1). Hence $I(v)\geq 0$. text: Theorem 5.8.4 . 1A391017E17A Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, $n\ge 1$, and let $u\colon \Omega \to [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a function that is not identically $-\infty $. For $n=1$ the only affine complex line is $\mathbb {C}$, so $u$ is subharmonic on $\Omega $ and in particular upper semicontinuous. Let $n\geq 2$, assume the assertion in dimension $n-1$, and let $u$ be as in the assertion. Write $z=(z',w)$ with $z'\in \mathbb {C}^{n-1}$ and $w\in \mathbb {C}$.
