By the induction hypothesis, $u(\, \cdot \, ,w)$ is therefore upper semicontinuous on this open set. For fixed $z'$, the function $u(z',\, \cdot \, )$ is subharmonic on each connected component of $\{ w:(z',w)\in \Omega \} $. Step 1: $u$ is Borel measurable. We need joint measurability of $u$ before we can integrate it. Fix a ball $B'\subset \mathbb {C}^{n-1}$, a point $w_0\in \mathbb {C}$ and $\rho >0$ with $B'\times B(w_0,2\rho )\subset \Omega $. For integers $N\ge 1$ put $u_ N=\min \{ u,N\} $, and for $0<r<\rho $ and $(z',w)\in B'\times B(w_0,\rho )$ define \[  F_ r^ N(z',w)=\frac{1}{\pi r^2}\int _{B(w,r)}u_ N(z',\eta )\, \mathrm{d}V_2(\eta ).  \] The integral exists, since $u(z',\, \cdot \, )$ is subharmonic, hence upper semicontinuous, on $B(w_0,2\rho )\supset B(w,r)$, so the integrand is a Borel function with values in $[0,N]$. For fixed $w$, the function $F_ r^ N(\, \cdot \, ,w)$ is upper semicontinuous: if $z'_ l\to z'$ in $B'$, the reverse Fatou lemma, applicable because $0\le u_ N\le N$, gives \[  \varlimsup _{l\to \infty }F_ r^ N(z'_ l,w) \le \frac{1}{\pi r^2}\int _{B(w,r)}\varlimsup _{l\to \infty }u_ N(z'_ l,\eta )\, \mathrm{d}V_2(\eta ) \le F_ r^ N(z',w),  \] where the last inequality holds because each $u_ N(\, \cdot \, ,\eta )$ is upper semicontinuous on $B'$. For fixed $z'$, the function $F_ r^ N(z',\, \cdot \, )$ is continuous: for $|w-v|\leq r$ the symmetric difference $B(w,r)\mathbin \triangle B(v,r)$ lies in the annulus $\{ r-|w-v|\leq |\eta -w|<r+|w-v|\} $, whose area is $4\pi r|w-v|$, so that $|F_ r^ N(z',w)-F_ r^ N(z',v)|\le 4N|w-v|/r$. A function on $B'\times B(w_0,\rho )$ that is Borel in $z'$ and continuous in $w$ is Borel; we check this for $F_ r^ N$. For $k\geq 1$ partition $B(w_0,\rho )$ into countably many Borel sets $E_{k,i}$ of diameter less than $1/k$, choose a point $w_{k,i}$ in each nonempty $E_{k,i}$, and put $F_ k(z',w)=F_ r^ N(z',w_{k,i})$ for $w\in E_{k,i}$. Each $F_ k$ is Borel, because each $F_ r^ N(\, \cdot \, ,w_{k,i})$ is upper semicontinuous, hence Borel, and $F_ k(z',w)\to F_ r^ N(z',w)$ for every $(z',w)$, because $F_ r^ N(z',\, \cdot \, )$ is continuous and the chosen points $w_{k,i}$ with $w\in E_{k,i}$ tend to $w$. Thus $F_ r^ N$ is Borel, and so is $G_ N=\varlimsup _{k\to \infty }F^ N_{\rho /(k+1)}$. Now fix $(z',w)\in B'\times B(w_0,\rho )$. The upper semicontinuous function $u(z',\, \cdot \, )$ is bounded above on the closed disc $\overline{B(w,\rho /2)}$ by some $M$. For $N\geq M$ the truncation does not change $u(z',\, \cdot \, )$ on this disc, so $F^ N_{\rho /(k+1)}(z',w)$ is the mean of $u(z',\, \cdot \, )$ over $B(w,\rho /(k+1))$. The function $u(z',\, \cdot \, )$ is subharmonic and finite on $B(w_0,2\rho )$, hence locally integrable there by proposition 3.4.8 , and by ( 3.4.13 ) its means over the discs $B(w,\rho /(k+1))$ converge to $u(z',w)$ as $k\to \infty $. Hence $G_ N(z',w)=u(z',w)$ for all $N\geq M$, and $u=\lim _ NG_ N$ is Borel on $B'\times B(w_0,\rho )$. Countably many such product sets cover $\Omega $, so $u$ is Borel on $\Omega $. Step 2: the canonical representative. By corollary 2.9.28 , the finite Borel function $u$ is locally bounded above. Since $u\geq 0$, it follows that $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$. Since the restriction of $u$ to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is subharmonic, lemma 5.8.2 gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. In particular $\Delta u=4\sum _ ju_{j\bar j}\geq 0$, so by theorem 3.4.12 $u$ has a canonical subharmonic representative $\widetilde u$, a locally integrable subharmonic function on $\Omega $ equal to $u$ almost everywhere. Its complex Hessian is the same positive current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$. Applying proposition 5.4.4 to the parametrizations of affine complex lines, we see that the restriction of $\widetilde u$ to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Since $\widetilde u$ is upper semicontinuous and agrees almost everywhere with the finite function $u$, we conclude that $\widetilde u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Step 3: $u=\widetilde u$ everywhere. Fix $x\in \Omega $ and $r>0$ with $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $. The set $Z=\{ u\ne \widetilde u\} $ is Borel, by Step 1, and Lebesgue null, so the left-hand side of ( 5.8.3 ) vanishes for $F=\mathbf1_ Z$. Since the weight $|t|^{2n-2}$ is positive for $t\neq 0$, for $\tau $-almost every $a$ the set $\{ t:|t|<r,\  x+ta\in Z\} $ has planar measure zero. Fix such an $a$. On the disc $\{ |t|<r\} $, the function $t\mapsto u(x+ta)$ is finite and subharmonic, while $t\mapsto \widetilde u(x+ta)$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $; the latter is impossible, because the two functions agree almost everywhere on the disc. By proposition 3.4.8 both are locally integrable subharmonic functions on the disc that agree almost everywhere, so they agree everywhere by theorem 3.4.12 . At $t=0$ this gives $u(x)=\widetilde u(x)$. As $x$ was arbitrary, $u=\widetilde u$ is upper semicontinuous. This completes the induction. Step 4: truncation. Let $u$ be as in the theorem, and for integers $m\geq 1$ put $u_ m=\max \{ u,-m\} +m$. This is a finite nonnegative function. Its restriction to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is subharmonic: if the restriction of $u$ is subharmonic, so is its maximum with the constant $-m$, and if the restriction of $u$ is identically $-\infty $, the restriction of $u_ m$ is the constant $0$. By the case already proved, each $u_ m$, and hence each $\max \{ u,-m\} $, is upper semicontinuous. For every real $c$ we have $\{ u<c\} =\bigcup _ m\{ \max \{ u,-m\} <c\} $, which is open. Thus $u$ is upper semicontinuous, and together with the hypotheses this gives $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. $\square$

title: 5.9 Positive Hessians and holomorphic maps
text:
We now compare plurisubharmonicity with the distributional condition $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$, where $(u_{j ar k})$ is the complex Hessian of ( 5.2.9 ). The next theorem shows that every almost-everywhere class satisfying this condition contains exactly one plurisubharmonic function, namely its canonical representative. We then treat smooth functions, regularization and holomorphic maps, and define plurisubharmonic functions on complex manifolds. Theorem 5.9.1 . 2A4F77263F48 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, $n\ge 1$. Every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ is subharmonic and locally integrable on $\Omega $, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. Conversely, a real distribution $T$ on $\Omega $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T\geq 0$ has a unique plurisubharmonic representative, that is, there is exactly one $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ with $\langle T,\chi angle =\int _\Omega u\chi \, \mathrm dV_{2n}$ for every test function $\chi $. This representative is the canonical subharmonic representative of $T$ given by theorem 3.4.12 , and it satisfies ( 3.4.13 ). Proof. Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Being upper semicontinuous, $u$ is bounded above on compact sets. Fix $x\in \Omega $ and $r>0$ with $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $, and let $M$ be an upper bound for $u$ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$. For every unit vector $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ the closed disc $\{ x+ta:|t|\leq r\} $ lies in $\Omega $, and the restriction $t\mapsto u(x+ta)$ is subharmonic, possibly identically $-\infty $, on a neighborhood of this disc. The monotonicity of circle means in theorem 3.4.5 therefore gives \[  u(x)\leq  rac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }u(x+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta }a)\, \mathrm d	heta .  \] With $	au $ as in ( 5.8.3 ), we integrate this inequality over $a\in S^{2n-1}$ with respect to $	au $; by Tonelli's theorem, applied to the nonnegative function $M-u$, and by the invariance of $	au $ under $a\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta }a$, the right-hand side becomes the sphere mean $\int _{S^{2n-1}}u(x+ra)\, \mathrm{d}	au (a)$. Thus $u$ satisfies the submean inequality of definition 3.4.2 at every point, so $u$ is subharmonic. Since $\Omega $ is connected and $u
ot\equiv -\infty $, proposition 3.4.8 shows that $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$. Since, moreover, the restriction of $u$ to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is subharmonic, possibly identically $-\infty $, lemma 5.8.2 gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\ge 0$. Conversely, let $T$ be a real distribution with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T\geq 0$. Then $\Delta T=4\sum _ jT_{j ar j}\geq 0$, so by theorem 3.4.12 $T$ has a canonical subharmonic representative $v$, which is locally integrable and satisfies ( 3.4.13 ). Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T\geq 0$, proposition 5.4.4 shows that the restriction of $v$ to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. As $v$ is upper semicontinuous and locally integrable, hence not identically $-\infty $, it is plurisubharmonic. If $w$ is another plurisubharmonic representative of $T$, then $w$ is a locally integrable subharmonic function by the first part, and $w=v$ almost everywhere; by the uniqueness in theorem 3.4.12 , $w=v$ everywhere. $\square$ The condition $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ depends only on the almost-everywhere class of $u$, whereas plurisubharmonicity is a pointwise property, and theorem 5.9.1 singles out one function in each class. For example, the function equal to $1$ at one point $x_0$ and to $0$ elsewhere is upper semicontinuous and has zero distributional complex Hessian, but it violates the submean inequality on complex lines at $x_0$; the plurisubharmonic representative of its class is the zero function. For smooth functions, plurisubharmonicity is a pointwise condition on the complex Hessian, and every plurisubharmonic function is, locally, the decreasing limit of smooth plurisubharmonic functions. In the next proposition, $ho _\varepsilon $ is the radial mollifier of section 2.5 and, as there, $\Omega _\varepsilon =\{ x\in \Omega :\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega )>\varepsilon \} $ for an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ and $\varepsilon >0$. Proposition 5.9.2 . 06C722B7D837 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be open, $n\geq 1$. A real function $u$ of class $C^2$ on $\Omega $ is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega $ if and only if the Hermitian matrix $(u_{j ar k}(z))$ is positive semidefinite at every point $z\in \Omega $. Let $u$ be a function on $\Omega $ which is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega $, and let $\varepsilon >0$. Then $u*ho _\varepsilon $ is smooth on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ and plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega _\varepsilon $, and $u*ho _\varepsilon (x)$ decreases to $u(x)$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, for every $x\in \Omega $. Proof. (1) Let $\Omega _0$ be a connected component of $\Omega $. We show that both conditions are equivalent to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ on $\Omega _0$. Since $u$ is of class $C^2$, integration by parts shows that its distributional derivatives $u_{j ar k}$ are the continuous functions $\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}u$, so for $\xi \in \mathbb {C}^ n$ the distribution $\sum _{j,k}u_{j ar k}\xi _ j ar\xi _ k$ is the continuous real function $z\mapsto \sum _{j,k}u_{j ar k}(z)\xi _ j ar\xi _ k$. A continuous real function is a positive distribution exactly when it is nonnegative: if it were negative at a point, it would be negative on a ball around that point, and its integral against a nonnegative test function supported in this ball and positive at its center would be negative. Hence, by the matrix criterion of section 5.4 , $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ on $\Omega _0$ if and only if $(u_{j ar k}(z))$ is positive semidefinite at every $z\in \Omega _0$. If $u$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega _0$, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ there by theorem 5.9.1 . Conversely, if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ on $\Omega _0$, then by theorem 5.9.1 the class of $u$ has a plurisubharmonic representative $v$ on $\Omega _0$ satisfying the ball-average formula in ( 3.4.13 ). Since $v=u$ almost everywhere and $u$ is continuous, $v(x)$ is the limit of the averages of $u$ over the balls $B(x,r)$ as $r	o 0$, that is, $v(x)=u(x)$. Hence $u=v$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega _0$. (2) By theorem 5.9.1 , applied on each connected component of $\Omega $, the function $u$ is subharmonic and locally integrable on $\Omega $, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. By proposition 2.5.3 (1), $u*ho _\varepsilon $ is smooth on $\Omega _\varepsilon $, and its derivatives are the mollifications of the distributional derivatives of $u$. Thus, for $\xi \in \mathbb {C}^ n$, the function $\sum _{j,k}(u*ho _\varepsilon )_{j ar k}\xi _ j ar\xi _ k$ is the mollification of the distribution $\sum _{j,k}u_{j ar k}\xi _ j ar\xi _ k$, which is positive by the matrix criterion; so it is nonnegative by proposition 2.5.3 (3). By (1), $u*ho _\varepsilon $ is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega _\varepsilon $. Finally, since $u$ is subharmonic on $\Omega $, theorem 3.4.12 (2) shows that $u*ho _\varepsilon (x)\downarrow u(x)$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, for every $x\in \Omega $. $\square$ Let $u$ be a smooth real function on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$. We call $u$ strictly plurisubharmonic if its complex Hessian matrix $(u_{j ar k})$ is positive definite everywhere. For a general $u$, strict plurisubharmonicity means that every point has a neighborhood on which $u-\varepsilon |z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic for some $\varepsilon >0$; on a complex manifold we require this in local holomorphic coordinates around each point, and $\varepsilon $ may depend on the point and the coordinates. For smooth $u$ the two definitions agree. Since $(|z|^2)_{j ar k}=\delta _{jk}$, the complex Hessian of $u-\varepsilon |z|^2$ is $(u_{j ar k})-\varepsilon I$. The smallest eigenvalue $\lambda (z)=\min _{|\xi |=1}\sum _{j,k}u_{j ar k}(z)\xi _ j ar\xi _ k$ of the matrix $(u_{j ar k}(z))$ is a continuous function of $z$, as the minimum over the compact unit sphere of a jointly continuous function of $(z,\xi )$. If the matrix is positive definite everywhere, then $\lambda $ is positive, hence bounded below by some $\varepsilon >0$ on a closed ball around each point, and on the open ball the smooth function $u-\varepsilon |z|^2$ has a positive semidefinite complex Hessian, so it is plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.2 (1). Conversely, the plurisubharmonicity of $u-\varepsilon |z|^2$ on a ball around a point gives $(u_{j ar k})\geq \varepsilon I$ there, by the same criterion. Proposition 5.9.3 . F6423BCE3BB1 Let $D\subset \mathbb {C}^ m$ and $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be domains, let $F\colon D	o \Omega $ be a holomorphic map, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Then $u\circ F$ is either identically $-\infty $ or plurisubharmonic on $D$. More generally, if $D\subset \mathbb {C}^ m$ is only assumed to be open, this alternative holds on each connected component of $D$. Proof. The statement for open $D$ follows by applying the statement for domains to each connected component of $D$. If $n=0$, then $\Omega $ is a point, $u$ is a real constant, and so is $u\circ F$. If $m=0$, then $D$ is a point and $u\circ F$ is a single value in $[-\infty ,\infty )$; it is either $-\infty $ or a real number, that is, a plurisubharmonic function on the point. Now let $m,n\geq 1$. By theorem 5.9.1 , $u$ is the canonical subharmonic representative of a locally integrable function with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$, so proposition 5.4.4 applies: $u\circ F$ is either identically $-\infty $, or locally integrable and subharmonic, in particular upper semicontinuous. In the second case, the restriction of $u\circ F$ to a connected component of an affine complex-line section of $D$ is the composition of $u$ with a holomorphic map from an open subset of $\mathbb {C}$, so it is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ by the same proposition. Hence $u\circ F$ is plurisubharmonic. $\square$ Let $X$ be a complex manifold. A function $u\colon X	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ is plurisubharmonic if its expression in every holomorphic chart with connected domain is plurisubharmonic in the sense of definition 5.8.1 ; we write $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ for the set of such functions. On a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, plurisubharmonicity is a local property: if every point of $\Omega $ has an open neighborhood on which $u$ is plurisubharmonic, then $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Indeed, upper semicontinuity is a local condition. Let $\Lambda $ be a connected component of an affine complex-line section of $\Omega $. Near each point of $\Lambda $, the restriction of $u$ to $\Lambda $ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $, hence subharmonic; since subharmonicity is a local property, the restriction of $u$ to $\Lambda $ is subharmonic. Finally, $u$ is locally integrable by theorem 5.9.1 , hence not identically $-\infty $. It follows that it suffices to check the condition on $X$ for the charts of one atlas with connected chart domains. Indeed, the transition maps are biholomorphic, so by proposition 5.9.3 the expression of $u$ in another chart with connected domain is, on a connected neighborhood of each point, plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. The second alternative would make the expression of $u$ in a chart of the atlas identically $-\infty $ on a nonempty open set, which is impossible because plurisubharmonic functions are locally integrable. Hence the expression of $u$ in the other chart is plurisubharmonic near each point, and therefore on its connected domain. Consequently plurisubharmonicity is also a local property on $X$: if every point of $X$ has a neighborhood on which $u$ is plurisubharmonic, then $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, because the expression of $u$ in a chart with connected domain is then plurisubharmonic near each point. Since a plurisubharmonic function on $X$ is locally integrable in charts, it is not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component of $X$. On an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, regarded as a complex manifold, a function is plurisubharmonic exactly when it is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega $: each component is a connected chart domain, and conversely the locality just proved applies. Limits of plurisubharmonic functions may degenerate to the constant $-\infty $. On a connected manifold, whether this happens can be decided locally. Lemma 5.9.4 . 598B886D700E Let $X$ be a connected complex manifold, and let $v\colon X	o [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a function such that every point of $X$ has an open neighborhood on which $v$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Then $v$ is plurisubharmonic on $X$ or identically $-\infty $ on $X$. Proof. Let $A$ be the set of points of $X$ having an open neighborhood on which $v\equiv -\infty $, and $B$ the set of points having an open neighborhood on which $v$ is plurisubharmonic. Both sets are open, and they cover $X$ by hypothesis. They are disjoint: if $x\in A\cap B$, with open neighborhoods $W_1$ on which $v\equiv -\infty $ and $W_2$ on which $v$ is plurisubharmonic, then the restriction of $v$ to the nonempty open set $W_1\cap W_2$ is plurisubharmonic and identically $-\infty $, which is impossible because plurisubharmonic functions are locally integrable. Since $X$ is connected, either $X=A$, and then $v\equiv -\infty $, or $X=B$, and then $v$ is plurisubharmonic near every point, hence on $X$, because plurisubharmonicity is a local property. $\square$ Every closed positive $(1,1)$-current $T$ on a complex manifold of positive dimension has local plurisubharmonic potentials: every point has a neighborhood on which $T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ for a plurisubharmonic function $u$. Indeed, on a coordinate ball inside the neighborhood given by theorem 5.4.3 , the canonical local potential is the canonical subharmonic representative of a class with positive complex Hessian, hence plurisubharmonic by theorem 5.9.1 . Proposition 5.9.5 . 7EBEE004A7FA Let $X$ be a complex manifold. Nonnegative multiples, finite sums and maxima of nonempty finite families of plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ are plurisubharmonic; here the zero multiple of a function is the zero function. Moreover, let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, let $D\subset X$ be open, and let $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(D)$. If \[  \varlimsup _{D
i y	o x}v(y)\le u(x)\qquad 	ext{for every }x\in \partial D,  \] where $\partial D$ is the boundary of $D$ in $X$, then the function equal to $\max \{ u,v\} $ on $D$ and to $u$ on $X\setminus D$ is plurisubharmonic on $X$. This boundary inequality holds in particular if \[  \varliminf _{\substack {D
i y	o x\ v(y)>-\infty }}(u(y)-v(y))\ge 0 \qquad 	ext{for every }x\in \partial D.  \] Proof. In local coordinates, upper semicontinuity and the submean inequality on complex lines are preserved by nonnegative multiples, sums and maxima; for sums we use that circle means are additive on functions with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. It remains to check that the resulting functions are not identically $-\infty $ on any component. For $cu$ with $c>0$ this holds because $cu=-\infty $ exactly where $u=-\infty $; a sum of plurisubharmonic functions is locally integrable by theorem 5.9.1 , and a maximum dominates each of its members. This proves the first assertion. Let $w$ denote the glued function. On $D$ it equals $\max \{ u,v\} $, which is plurisubharmonic by the first part, and on the open set $X\setminus \overline D$ it equals $u$. At $x\in \partial D$ we have $w(x)=u(x)$, and the upper semicontinuity of $u$ together with the boundary inequality gives \[  \varlimsup _{y	o x}w(y)\leq \max \Bigl \{ \varlimsup _{y	o x}u(y),\  \varlimsup _{D
i y	o x}v(y)\Bigr \} \leq u(x)=w(x).  \] Hence $w$ is upper semicontinuous. To verify the line condition, work in a chart and restrict $w$ to a connected component of an affine complex-line section. At points of $D$ and of $X\setminus \overline D$, the restriction satisfies the submean inequality on small circles, because $w$ is plurisubharmonic near such points. At a point $x\in \partial D$ we have $w\geq u$ everywhere and $w(x)=u(x)$, so each small circle mean of $w$ is at least the corresponding circle mean of $u$, which is at least $u(x)=w(x)$; if the restriction of $u$ is identically $-\infty $, then $w(x)=u(x)=-\infty $ and there is nothing to prove. Thus the restriction of $w$ is upper semicontinuous and satisfies the submean inequality on small circles at every point; that is, it is subharmonic. Finally $w\geq u$, so $w$ is not identically $-\infty $ in any chart, and $w$ is plurisubharmonic. For the sufficient condition, fix $x\in \partial D$ and $\varepsilon >0$. By hypothesis, $x$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $v(y)<u(y)+\varepsilon $ for all $y\in W\cap D$ with $v(y)>-\infty $. Hence $v\leq u+\varepsilon $ on $W\cap D$, the inequality being trivial where $v=-\infty $, and the upper semicontinuity of $u$ gives \[  \varlimsup _{D
i y	o x}v(y)\leq \varlimsup _{y	o x}u(y)+\varepsilon \leq u(x)+\varepsilon .  \] Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives the boundary inequality. $\square$

title: Theorem 5.9.1
text: Theorem 5.9.1 . 2A4F77263F48 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, $n\ge 1$. Every $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ is subharmonic and locally integrable on $\Omega $, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. Conversely, a real distribution $T$ on $\Omega $ with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T\geq 0$ has a unique plurisubharmonic representative, that is, there is exactly one $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ with $\langle T,\chi \rangle =\int _\Omega u\chi \, \mathrm dV_{2n}$ for every test function $\chi $. This representative is the canonical subharmonic representative of $T$ given by theorem 3.4.12 , and it satisfies ( 3.4.13 ). Proof. Let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Being upper semicontinuous, $u$ is bounded above on compact sets. Fix $x\in \Omega $ and $r>0$ with $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $, and let $M$ be an upper bound for $u$ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$. For every unit vector $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ the closed disc $\{ x+ta:|t|\leq r\} $ lies in $\Omega $, and the restriction $t\mapsto u(x+ta)$ is subharmonic, possibly identically $-\infty $, on a neighborhood of this disc. The monotonicity of circle means in theorem 3.4.5 therefore gives \[  u(x)\leq \frac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }u(x+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }a)\, \mathrm d\theta .  \] With $\tau $ as in ( 5.8.3 ), we integrate this inequality over $a\in S^{2n-1}$ with respect to $\tau $; by Tonelli's theorem, applied to the nonnegative function $M-u$, and by the invariance of $\tau $ under $a\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }a$, the right-hand side becomes the sphere mean $\int _{S^{2n-1}}u(x+ra)\, \mathrm{d}\tau (a)$. Thus $u$ satisfies the submean inequality of definition 3.4.2 at every point, so $u$ is subharmonic. Since $\Omega $ is connected and $u\not\equiv -\infty $, proposition 3.4.8 shows that $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$. Since, moreover, the restriction of $u$ to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is subharmonic, possibly identically $-\infty $, lemma 5.8.2 gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\ge 0$. Conversely, let $T$ be a real distribution with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T\geq 0$. Then $\Delta T=4\sum _ jT_{j\bar j}\geq 0$, so by theorem 3.4.12 $T$ has a canonical subharmonic representative $v$, which is locally integrable and satisfies ( 3.4.13 ). Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T\geq 0$, proposition 5.4.4 shows that the restriction of $v$ to each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $\Omega $ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. As $v$ is upper semicontinuous and locally integrable, hence not identically $-\infty $, it is plurisubharmonic. If $w$ is another plurisubharmonic representative of $T$, then $w$ is a locally integrable subharmonic function by the first part, and $w=v$ almost everywhere; by the uniqueness in theorem 3.4.12 , $w=v$ everywhere. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.9.2
text: Proposition 5.9.2 . 06C722B7D837 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be open, $n\geq 1$. A real function $u$ of class $C^2$ on $\Omega $ is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega $ if and only if the Hermitian matrix $(u_{j\bar k}(z))$ is positive semidefinite at every point $z\in \Omega $. Let $u$ be a function on $\Omega $ which is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega $, and let $\varepsilon >0$. Then $u*\rho _\varepsilon $ is smooth on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ and plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega _\varepsilon $, and $u*\rho _\varepsilon (x)$ decreases to $u(x)$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, for every $x\in \Omega $. Proof. (1) Let $\Omega _0$ be a connected component of $\Omega $. We show that both conditions are equivalent to $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ on $\Omega _0$. Since $u$ is of class $C^2$, integration by parts shows that its distributional derivatives $u_{j\bar k}$ are the continuous functions $\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{\bar z_ k}u$, so for $\xi \in \mathbb {C}^ n$ the distribution $\sum _{j,k}u_{j\bar k}\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$ is the continuous real function $z\mapsto \sum _{j,k}u_{j\bar k}(z)\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$. A continuous real function is a positive distribution exactly when it is nonnegative: if it were negative at a point, it would be negative on a ball around that point, and its integral against a nonnegative test function supported in this ball and positive at its center would be negative. Hence, by the matrix criterion of section 5.4 , $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ on $\Omega _0$ if and only if $(u_{j\bar k}(z))$ is positive semidefinite at every $z\in \Omega _0$. If $u$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega _0$, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ there by theorem 5.9.1 . Conversely, if $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$ on $\Omega _0$, then by theorem 5.9.1 the class of $u$ has a plurisubharmonic representative $v$ on $\Omega _0$ satisfying the ball-average formula in ( 3.4.13 ). Since $v=u$ almost everywhere and $u$ is continuous, $v(x)$ is the limit of the averages of $u$ over the balls $B(x,r)$ as $r\to 0$, that is, $v(x)=u(x)$. Hence $u=v$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega _0$. (2) By theorem 5.9.1 , applied on each connected component of $\Omega $, the function $u$ is subharmonic and locally integrable on $\Omega $, and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$. By proposition 2.5.3 (1), $u*\rho _\varepsilon $ is smooth on $\Omega _\varepsilon $, and its derivatives are the mollifications of the distributional derivatives of $u$. Thus, for $\xi \in \mathbb {C}^ n$, the function $\sum _{j,k}(u*\rho _\varepsilon )_{j\bar k}\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$ is the mollification of the distribution $\sum _{j,k}u_{j\bar k}\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k$, which is positive by the matrix criterion; so it is nonnegative by proposition 2.5.3 (3). By (1), $u*\rho _\varepsilon $ is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega _\varepsilon $. Finally, since $u$ is subharmonic on $\Omega $, theorem 3.4.12 (2) shows that $u*\rho _\varepsilon (x)\downarrow u(x)$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, for every $x\in \Omega $. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.9.3
text: Proposition 5.9.3 . F6423BCE3BB1 Let $D\subset \mathbb {C}^ m$ and $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be domains, let $F\colon D\to \Omega $ be a holomorphic map, and let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$. Then $u\circ F$ is either identically $-\infty $ or plurisubharmonic on $D$. More generally, if $D\subset \mathbb {C}^ m$ is only assumed to be open, this alternative holds on each connected component of $D$. Proof. The statement for open $D$ follows by applying the statement for domains to each connected component of $D$. If $n=0$, then $\Omega $ is a point, $u$ is a real constant, and so is $u\circ F$. If $m=0$, then $D$ is a point and $u\circ F$ is a single value in $[-\infty ,\infty )$; it is either $-\infty $ or a real number, that is, a plurisubharmonic function on the point. Now let $m,n\geq 1$. By theorem 5.9.1 , $u$ is the canonical subharmonic representative of a locally integrable function with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\geq 0$, so proposition 5.4.4 applies: $u\circ F$ is either identically $-\infty $, or locally integrable and subharmonic, in particular upper semicontinuous. In the second case, the restriction of $u\circ F$ to a connected component of an affine complex-line section of $D$ is the composition of $u$ with a holomorphic map from an open subset of $\mathbb {C}$, so it is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $ by the same proposition. Hence $u\circ F$ is plurisubharmonic. $\square$

title: Lemma 5.9.4
text: Lemma 5.9.4 . 598B886D700E Let $X$ be a connected complex manifold, and let $v\colon X\to [-\infty ,\infty )$ be a function such that every point of $X$ has an open neighborhood on which $v$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Then $v$ is plurisubharmonic on $X$ or identically $-\infty $ on $X$. Proof. Let $A$ be the set of points of $X$ having an open neighborhood on which $v\equiv -\infty $, and $B$ the set of points having an open neighborhood on which $v$ is plurisubharmonic. Both sets are open, and they cover $X$ by hypothesis. They are disjoint: if $x\in A\cap B$, with open neighborhoods $W_1$ on which $v\equiv -\infty $ and $W_2$ on which $v$ is plurisubharmonic, then the restriction of $v$ to the nonempty open set $W_1\cap W_2$ is plurisubharmonic and identically $-\infty $, which is impossible because plurisubharmonic functions are locally integrable. Since $X$ is connected, either $X=A$, and then $v\equiv -\infty $, or $X=B$, and then $v$ is plurisubharmonic near every point, hence on $X$, because plurisubharmonicity is a local property. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.9.5
text:
Proposition 5.9.5 . 7EBEE004A7FA Let $X$ be a complex manifold. Nonnegative multiples, finite sums and maxima of nonempty finite families of plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ are plurisubharmonic; here the zero multiple of a function is the zero function. Moreover, let $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(X)$, let $D\subset X$ be open, and let $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(D)$. If \[  \varlimsup _{D
i y	o x}v(y)\le u(x)\qquad 	ext{for every }x\in \partial D,  \] where $\partial D$ is the boundary of $D$ in $X$, then the function equal to $\max \{ u,v\} $ on $D$ and to $u$ on $X\setminus D$ is plurisubharmonic on $X$. This boundary inequality holds in particular if \[  \varliminf _{\substack {D
i y	o x\ v(y)>-\infty }}(u(y)-v(y))\ge 0 \qquad 	ext{for every }x\in \partial D.  \] Proof. In local coordinates, upper semicontinuity and the submean inequality on complex lines are preserved by nonnegative multiples, sums and maxima; for sums we use that circle means are additive on functions with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$. It remains to check that the resulting functions are not identically $-\infty $ on any component. For $cu$ with $c>0$ this holds because $cu=-\infty $ exactly where $u=-\infty $; a sum of plurisubharmonic functions is locally integrable by theorem 5.9.1 , and a maximum dominates each of its members. This proves the first assertion. Let $w$ denote the glued function. On $D$ it equals $\max \{ u,v\} $, which is plurisubharmonic by the first part, and on the open set $X\setminus \overline D$ it equals $u$. At $x\in \partial D$ we have $w(x)=u(x)$, and the upper semicontinuity of $u$ together with the boundary inequality gives \[  \varlimsup _{y	o x}w(y)\leq \max \Bigl \{ \varlimsup _{y	o x}u(y),\  \varlimsup _{D
i y	o x}v(y)\Bigr \} \leq u(x)=w(x).  \] Hence $w$ is upper semicontinuous. To verify the line condition, work in a chart and restrict $w$ to a connected component of an affine complex-line section. At points of $D$ and of $X\setminus \overline D$, the restriction satisfies the submean inequality on small circles, because $w$ is plurisubharmonic near such points. At a point $x\in \partial D$ we have $w\geq u$ everywhere and $w(x)=u(x)$, so each small circle mean of $w$ is at least the corresponding circle mean of $u$, which is at least $u(x)=w(x)$; if the restriction of $u$ is identically $-\infty $, then $w(x)=u(x)=-\infty $ and there is nothing to prove. Thus the restriction of $w$ is upper semicontinuous and satisfies the submean inequality on small circles at every point; that is, it is subharmonic. Finally $w\geq u$, so $w$ is not identically $-\infty $ in any chart, and $w$ is plurisubharmonic. For the sufficient condition, fix $x\in \partial D$ and $\varepsilon >0$. By hypothesis, $x$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $v(y)<u(y)+\varepsilon $ for all $y\in W\cap D$ with $v(y)>-\infty $. Hence $v\leq u+\varepsilon $ on $W\cap D$, the inequality being trivial where $v=-\infty $, and the upper semicontinuity of $u$ gives \[  \varlimsup _{D
i y	o x}v(y)\leq \varlimsup _{y	o x}u(y)+\varepsilon \leq u(x)+\varepsilon .  \] Letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ gives the boundary inequality. $\square$

title: 5.10 Limits, envelopes and local integrability
text:
This section treats limits and envelopes of plurisubharmonic functions and their local integrability. Throughout, $X$ is a complex manifold of positive dimension, except in theorem 5.10.10 , which also allows dimension zero. By theorem 5.9.1 , plurisubharmonic functions are locally integrable, and we regard each of them as the distinguished representative of its class. Local $L^ p$ norms on $X$ are computed with Euclidean volume in local coordinates, and “almost everywhere” refers to Lebesgue measure in charts. Any smooth positive volume form gives the same local $L^ p$ spaces and the same $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}$ convergence, since in coordinates its density is bounded above and below by positive constants on compact sets. By the discussion following definition 5.2.3 , each connected component of $X$ has a countable basis; $X$ itself need not have one, and we assume this explicitly when a global countable selection is needed. We call a subset of an open set in $\mathbb {C}^ n$ real polar if it is polar in the sense of definition 3.4.26 when $\mathbb {C}^ n$ is identified with $\mathbb R^{2n}$. The adjective distinguishes these sets from the pluripolar sets of section 5.47 . Real polar sets are Lebesgue null, by the remark following definition 3.4.26 . Theorem 5.10.1 . FE144A69076E Let $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$, that is, $u_ j\leq u_ i$ whenever $i\leq j$, and let $u=\lim _ iu_ i=\inf _ iu_ i$ be its pointwise limit. Then on each connected component $X_0$ of $X$, exactly one of the following holds: either $u$ is plurisubharmonic on $X_0$ and $u_ i	o u$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X_0)$, or $u\equiv -\infty $ on $X_0$ and $u_ i	o -\infty $ locally uniformly on $X_0$. Proof. The limit $u$ is upper semicontinuous, since $\{ u<c\} = igcup _ i\{ u_ i<c\} $ is open for every real $c$. Fix a connected component $X_0$ of $X$; it has a countable basis. Step 1: a decreasing sequence with the same limit. Let $i_0\in I$. We show that there are indices $i_0\leq i_1\leq i_2\leq \cdots $ such that $u_{i_ l}\downarrow u$ pointwise on $X_0$. Replacing $I$ by the cofinal directed set $\{ i\in I:i\geq i_0\} $, which does not change the limit, we only have to find indices $i_1\leq i_2\leq \cdots $. For each rational $c$, the open sets $\{ u_ i<c\} \cap X_0$ cover $\{ u<c\} \cap X_0$, and countably many of them suffice: for each basis element of $X_0$ contained in some set $\{ u_ i<c\} $, choose one such index $i$; every point of $\{ u<c\} \cap X_0$ lies in such a basis element. Let $k_1,k_2,\ldots $ be an enumeration, with repetitions allowed, of the indices chosen for all rational $c$. Since $I$ is directed, we can choose inductively $i_1\geq k_1$ and $i_{l+1}\geq i_ l,k_{l+1}$. The sequence $(u_{i_ l})$ is decreasing and bounded below by $u$. If $u(x)<c$ with $c$ rational and $x\in X_0$, then $u_{k_ l}(x)<c$ for some $l$, hence $u_{i_ l}(x)\leq u_{k_ l}(x)<c$. Therefore $u_{i_ l}\downarrow u$ on $X_0$. Step 2: the limit. Let $V\subset X_0$ be a connected coordinate neighborhood, identified with a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. On each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $V$, the restrictions of the $u_{i_ l}$ form a decreasing sequence of subharmonic functions, whose limit is subharmonic by theorem 3.4.9 . Since $u$ is upper semicontinuous, it is either plurisubharmonic on $V$ or identically $-\infty $ on $V$, by definition 5.8.1 . As $X_0$ is connected, lemma 5.9.4 shows that either $u$ is plurisubharmonic on $X_0$ or $u\equiv -\infty $ on $X_0$. Step 3: convergence. Suppose first that $u$ is plurisubharmonic on $X_0$. Fix $i_0\in I$, take the sequence of Step 1, and let $K$ be a compact subset of a coordinate neighborhood in $X_0$. Then $0\leq u_{i_ l}-u\leq u_{i_0}-u$ almost everywhere, namely wherever $u$ is finite, and $u_{i_0}-u$ is integrable on $K$. By dominated convergence, $\| u_{i_ l}-u\| _{L^1(K)}	o 0$. Given $\varepsilon >0$, choose $l$ with $\| u_{i_ l}-u\| _{L^1(K)}<\varepsilon $; for every $i\geq i_ l$ we have $0\leq u_ i-u\leq u_{i_ l}-u$ almost everywhere, hence $\| u_ i-u\| _{L^1(K)}<\varepsilon $. Thus the net converges to $u$ in $L^1(K)$, and covering an arbitrary compact subset of $X_0$ by finitely many such sets $K$ gives convergence in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X_0)$. Suppose now that $u\equiv -\infty $ on $X_0$, and let $K\subset X_0$ be compact and $A>0$. The open sets $\{ u_ i<-A\} $ cover $K$, so finitely many of them, say those with indices $j_1,\ldots ,j_ p$, already cover $K$. If $i\geq j_1,\ldots ,j_ p$, then $u_ i\leq u_{j_ q}$ for each $q$, and hence $u_ i<-A$ on $K$. This is locally uniform convergence to $-\infty $. $\square$ Recall that a function $F$ with values in $[-\infty ,\infty )$ that is locally bounded above has an upper semicontinuous regularization $F^*$, the smallest upper semicontinuous function that dominates $F$. On $X$ it is given by $F^*(x)=\inf _ W\sup _ WF$, where $W$ ranges over the neighborhoods of $x$, and in a chart it is the regularization of subsection 3.4.21 . Theorem 5.10.2 . D32A2FB94F6B Let $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a nonempty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ that is locally uniformly bounded above, and let $F=\sup _ iu_ i$ be its upper envelope. Then the upper semicontinuous regularization $F^*$ is plurisubharmonic, and $F=F^*$ almost everywhere; more precisely, in every coordinate chart the set $\{ F<F^*\} $ is real polar. If $X$ has a countable basis, there is a countable subset $J\subset I$ such that $(\sup _{i\in J}u_ i)^*=F^*$. Proof. Since $F^*$ is defined by a local formula and plurisubharmonicity is a local property, it suffices to prove that $F^*$ is plurisubharmonic on every connected coordinate neighborhood $V$, which we identify with a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. By theorem 3.4.23 , $F^*$ is subharmonic on $V$, and $F$ is Lebesgue measurable and equal to $F^*$ almost everywhere on $V$. By Choquet's lemma, lemma 3.4.22 , there is a countable set $J_ V\subset I$ with $(\sup _{i\in J_ V}u_ i)^*=F^*$ on $V$. We next show that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F^*\geq 0$ on $V$. Fix $i_0\in I$, enumerate $J_ V\cup \{ i_0\} $ as $i_0,i_1,i_2,\ldots $, with repetitions if this set is finite, and put $v_ j=\max \{ u_{i_0},\ldots ,u_{i_ j}\} $. The functions $v_ j$ are plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.5 , increase with $j$, are locally uniformly bounded above, and dominate the locally integrable function $u_{i_0}$. Their limit $G=\sup _ jv_ j$ lies between $\sup _{i\in J_ V}u_ i$ and $F$, so $G^*=F^*$, and hence $G=F^*$ almost everywhere by theorem 3.4.23 applied to the countable family. On a compact set $K\subset V$ on which every $u_ i$ is bounded above by $M$, we have $0\leq v_ j-u_{i_0}\leq M-u_{i_0}$, so dominated convergence gives $v_ j	o F^*$ in $L^1(K)$. Therefore $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F^*\geq 0$, as a limit of positive currents. Since $F^*$ is subharmonic and dominates the locally integrable function $u_{i_0}$, it is locally integrable and hence the canonical representative of its class, and theorem 5.9.1 shows that $F^*$ is plurisubharmonic on $V$. If $X$ has a countable basis, cover $X$ by countably many connected coordinate neighborhoods $V_1,V_2,\ldots $ and put $J= igcup _ mJ_{V_ m}$. On each $V_ m$ we have $F^*=(\sup _{i\in J_{V_ m}}u_ i)^*\leq (\sup _{i\in J}u_ i)^*\leq F^*$, and since the regularization is local, $(\sup _{i\in J}u_ i)^*=F^*$ on $X$. Finally, in each chart the functions $u_ i$ are subharmonic, so the second assertion of theorem 4.1.26 shows that $\{ F<F^*\} $ is polar in the corresponding open subset of $\mathbb R^{2n}$, that is, real polar. $\square$ Proposition 5.10.3 . 1A6F10A07BA5 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, $n\geq 1$, and let $g=(g_1,\ldots ,g_ r)$, $r\geq 1$, be a tuple of holomorphic functions on $\Omega $, not all identically zero. Then the function $\log \sum _ j|g_ j|^2$, with the value $-\infty $ at the common zeros of the $g_ j$, is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $. In particular, for every $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ the function $\log |z-a|^2$ is plurisubharmonic on $\mathbb {C}^ n$. Proof. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, with equality for $\lambda $ proportional to $(\overline{g_1(z)},\ldots ,\overline{g_ r(z)})$, we have \[  \log \sum _ j|g_ j(z)|^2 =\sup _{\sum _ j|\lambda _ j|^2=1}\log \left|\sum _ j\lambda _ jg_ j(z)ight|^2  \] for every $z\in \Omega $, both sides being $-\infty $ at a common zero. The supremum does not change if we omit the $\lambda $ for which $\sum _ j\lambda _ jg_ j$ vanishes identically: at a point $z$ that is not a common zero, the maximizing $\lambda $ gives $\sum _ j\lambda _ jg_ j(z)
eq 0$, and at a common zero all terms equal $-\infty $. Some $g_ j$ is not identically zero, so the remaining family is nonempty. Its members are plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.5.3 , theorem 5.9.1 , and they are locally uniformly bounded above by the left-hand side. Their supremum $\log \sum _ j|g_ j|^2$ is already upper semicontinuous: it is continuous as a map to $[-\infty ,\infty )$, because $\sum _ j|g_ j|^2$ is continuous and its logarithm tends to $-\infty $ at a common zero. Hence it equals its regularization, which is plurisubharmonic by theorem 5.10.2 . The particular case is the tuple $(z_1-a_1,\ldots ,z_ n-a_ n)$. $\square$ Theorem 5.10.4 . C2DB8DFE9E2C Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a domain, $n\geq 1$. Every sequence in $\mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ that is locally uniformly bounded above has a subsequence that either converges locally uniformly to $-\infty $ or converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ to a plurisubharmonic function. If a sequence $(u_ j)$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, then its limit has a plurisubharmonic representative $u$, and the following holds: for every compact set $K\subset \Omega $ and every lower semicontinuous function $f\colon K	o \mathbb R$ with $u<f$ on $K$, for instance every real continuous function on $K$, one has $u_ j<f$ on $K$ for all sufficiently large $j$. In particular $\varlimsup _ j u_ j(x)\le u(x)$ for every $x\in \Omega $. Proof. Plurisubharmonic functions are subharmonic by theorem 5.9.1 . Hence, by the compactness theorem (theorem 3.4.19 ), a sequence as in the first assertion either tends to $-\infty $ locally uniformly, or has a subsequence converging in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ to a locally integrable subharmonic function $v$. In the second case $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq 0$, as a distributional limit of positive currents, and $v$ is the canonical representative of its class; so $v$ is plurisubharmonic by theorem 5.9.1 . Now let $(u_ j)$ converge in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ to $T$. As above, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T\geq 0$, so $T$ has a plurisubharmonic representative $u$, namely its canonical subharmonic representative. The $u_ j$ are locally integrable subharmonic functions converging in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, and $u$ is the canonical representative of their limit, so the remaining assertions are Hartogs' lemma for subharmonic functions, theorem 3.4.20 , which requires no upper bound on the sequence; the last one is its first assertion with the constant sequence $x_ j=x$. $\square$ We next show that plurisubharmonic functions belong to $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for every finite $p$, and that $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ convergence of plurisubharmonic functions implies $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}$ convergence. We first treat a subharmonic function $v\leq 0$ on the unit disc. By the Riesz decomposition (theorem 3.4.14 ), $v$ is locally the sum of a harmonic function and the fundamental potential $E_2*\mu $ of a measure, and the kernel $E_2(z)=(2\pi )^{-1}\log |z|$ belongs locally to every $L^ p$ with $p<\infty $; this gives an $L^ p$ bound in terms of the value of $v$ at the center. Applying this bound in one complex variable at a time then gives the estimate for plurisubharmonic functions on polydiscs. We write $D(a,r)=\{ z\in \mathbb C:|z-a|<r\} $ and $D=D(0,1)$, and for $t>0$ we write $tD=D(0,t)$; thus $D^ n$ is the unit polydisc in $\mathbb C^ n$ and $(tD)^ n$ the polydisc of radius $t$ centered at $0$. Integrals over discs and polydiscs are taken with respect to Lebesgue measure $\mathrm dV$. Lemma 5.10.5 . 69CE23EA1637 There is a constant $C_0\geq 1$ with the following property. Let $v\leq 0$ be a subharmonic function on $D$ with $v(0)>-\infty $. Then there are a finite positive Borel measure $

Adding the estimates for $P$ and $h$ on $D(0,1/2)$, we obtain \[  \| v\| _{L^ p(D(0,1/2))}\leq \| P\| _{L^ p(D(0,4/5))}+(\pi /4)^{1/p}C_0|v(0)|\leq C'|v(0)|,  \] which proves the last assertion. $\square$ Proposition 5.10.8 . B979DF329B28 Let $n\geq 1$ and $1\leq p<\infty $. There are constants $C_{n,p},A_{n,p}>0$ such that every plurisubharmonic function $v\leq 0$ on the unit polydisc $D^ n$ satisfies \[  \| v\| _{L^ p((	frac 12D)^ n)}\leq C_{n,p}|v(0)| \quad 	ext{if }v(0)>-\infty ,  \] and 8326366018BB 5.10.9  egin{equation}  \| v\| _{L^ p((	frac 14D)^ n)}\leq A_{n,p}\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}. \end{equation} Here $\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}$ may be infinite, in which case there is nothing to prove. Proof. We prove the first estimate by induction on $n$. For $n=1$ it is lemma 5.10.5 . Let $n\geq 2$, write $z=(z_1,z')$ with $z'\in \mathbb C^{n-1}$, and let $v$ be as in the statement with $v(0)>-\infty $. The function $w(z')=v(0,z')$ is the composition of $v$ with the holomorphic map $z'\mapsto (0,z')$, so by proposition 5.9.3 it is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $D^{n-1}$. Since $w(0)=v(0)>-\infty $, it is plurisubharmonic, hence locally integrable and finite outside a Lebesgue null set $E\subset D^{n-1}$. For $z'\in D^{n-1}\setminus E$, the function $z_1\mapsto v(z_1,z')$ is subharmonic and nonpositive on $D$, with the finite value $w(z')$ at the center, so lemma 5.10.5 gives \[  \int _{ rac12D}|v(z_1,z')|^ p\, \mathrm dV(z_1) \leq C_ p^ p|w(z')|^ p.  \] We integrate over $z'\in (	frac 12D)^{n-1}$ using Tonelli's theorem; the null set $E$, on which the inner integral may be infinite, does not contribute. The induction hypothesis applied to $w$ then gives \[  \| v\| _{L^ p(( rac12D)^ n)}^ p\leq C_ p^ p\| w\| _{L^ p(( rac12D)^{n-1})}^ p\leq C_ p^ pC_{n-1,p}^ p|v(0)|^ p,  \] which is the first estimate with $C_{n,p}=C_ pC_{n-1,p}$. For the second estimate, let $Q=(	frac 1{10}D)^ n$ and $|Q|$ its volume. If $\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}=0$, then $v=0$ almost everywhere, hence $v\equiv 0$ by theorem 5.9.1 , and there is nothing to prove; we may also assume that $\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}<\infty $. Put $\lambda =2|Q|^{-1}\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}>0$. By Chebyshev's inequality, the set of points of $Q$ with $|v|>\lambda $ has measure at most $\lambda ^{-1}\int _ Q|v|\, \mathrm dV\leq |Q|/2$, so its complement in $Q$ has positive measure. Since $v$ is finite almost everywhere, there is a point $a\in Q$ with $v(a)>-\infty $ and \[  |v(a)|\leq 2|Q|^{-1}\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}.  \] The polydisc of radius $4/5$ centered at $a$ lies in $D^ n$, and the polydisc of radius $2/5$ centered at $a$ contains $(	frac 14D)^ n$, since $	frac 14+	frac 1{10}<	frac 25$. We apply the first estimate to the plurisubharmonic function $\zeta \mapsto v(a+	frac 45\zeta )\leq 0$ on $D^ n$ and change variables: \[  \| v\| _{L^ p(( rac14D)^ n)}\leq  igl (	frac 45 igr )^{2n/p}C_{n,p}|v(a)|\leq 2 igl (	frac 45 igr )^{2n/p}C_{n,p}|Q|^{-1}\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}.  \] This is ( 5.10.9 ). $\square$ Theorem 5.10.10 . F2A3CA649325 Let $X$ be a complex manifold and $1\leq p<\infty $. Every plurisubharmonic function on $X$ belongs to $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$. If a sequence of plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$, then it converges in $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$ to the same limit. Proof. If $X$ has dimension zero, every compact subset of $X$ is finite, plurisubharmonic functions are real-valued, and convergence in $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is pointwise convergence; so both assertions hold. Let $X$ have dimension $n\geq 1$. Every compact subset of $X$ is covered by finitely many coordinate polydiscs, so it suffices to work near a point $x\in X$ in a chart in which $x=0$ and the closed polydisc $\overline{(RD)^ n}$ lies in the chart, for some $R>0$. Let $v$ be plurisubharmonic. Being upper semicontinuous, $v$ is bounded above on $\overline{(RD)^ n}$ by some constant $A$. The function $\zeta \mapsto v(R\zeta )-A$ is plurisubharmonic and nonpositive on $D^ n$, and its $L^1$ norm on $D^ n$ is finite because $v$ is locally integrable. By ( 5.10.9 ), $v$ belongs to $L^ p$ on the polydisc $(	frac R4D)^ n$. This proves the first assertion. Now let $(u_ j)$ be a sequence of plurisubharmonic functions converging in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$. For $p=1$ there is nothing to prove, so let $p>1$. By theorem 5.10.4 applied in charts, together with the uniqueness in theorem 5.9.1 , the limit is represented by a plurisubharmonic function $u$. The norms $\| u_ j\| _{L^1((RD)^ n)}$ are bounded because the sequence converges. If $y\in (	frac R2D)^ n$, the ball $B(y,R/2)$ lies in $(RD)^ n$, so the ball submean inequality gives $u_ j(y)\leq |B(y,R/2)|^{-1}\| u_ j\| _{L^1((RD)^ n)}$. Hence there is a constant $M$, independent of $j$, with $u_ j\leq M$ and $u\leq M$ on $(	frac R2D)^ n$. Applying ( 5.10.9 ) to $\zeta \mapsto u_ j(	frac R2\zeta )-M$ and to $\zeta \mapsto u(	frac R2\zeta )-M$, whose $L^1$ norms on $D^ n$ are bounded independently of $j$, we obtain a bound for the $L^{2p}$ norms of $u_ j$ and $u$ on $(	frac R8D)^ n$ that is uniform in $j$. By a finite covering, for every compact set $K\subset X$ the norms $\| u_ j\| _{L^{2p}(K)}$ and $\| u\| _{L^{2p}(K)}$ are bounded independently of $j$. We interpolate between $L^1$ and $L^{2p}$. For a function $f$ on $K$, write $|f|^ p=|f|^{p/(2p-1)}\cdot |f|^{p(2p-2)/(2p-1)}$ and apply Hölder's inequality with the conjugate exponents $(2p-1)/p$ and $(2p-1)/(p-1)$; since $ rac{p(2p-2)}{2p-1}\cdot  rac{2p-1}{p-1}=2p$, this gives \[  \int _ K|f|^ p\, \mathrm dV\leq \Bigl (\int _ K|f|\, \mathrm dV\Bigr )^{p/(2p-1)}\Bigl (\int _ K|f|^{2p}\, \mathrm dV\Bigr )^{(p-1)/(2p-1)},  \] that is, $\| f\| _{L^ p(K)}\leq \| f\| _{L^1(K)}^{1/(2p-1)}\| f\| _{L^{2p}(K)}^{(2p-2)/(2p-1)}$. With $f=u_ j-u$, whose $L^{2p}(K)$ norms are bounded independently of $j$, we obtain \[  \| u_ j-u\| _{L^ p(K)} \leq \| u_ j-u\| _{L^1(K)}^{1/(2p-1)} \| u_ j-u\| _{L^{2p}(K)}^{(2p-2)/(2p-1)}\longrightarrow 0.  \] $\square$ The same Riesz decomposition gives exponential integrability: if $v\leq 0$ is plurisubharmonic on a ball, then $\mathrm e^{-\alpha v}$ is integrable on a smaller concentric ball for every sufficiently small $\alpha >0$, and the admissible $\alpha $ and the bound for the integral depend only on a bound for the $L^1$ norm of $v$. In one variable this follows from Jensen's inequality applied to the fundamental potential in the Riesz decomposition. In several variables we integrate the one-variable estimates over all complex lines through a suitable point. For $t>0$ we write $tB$ for the ball of radius $t$ centered at $0$ in $\mathbb C^ n$; thus $B$ is the unit ball. Lemma 5.10.11 . 03676DBFBA61 There are constants $ eta ,C>0$ such that every subharmonic function $v\leq 0$ on $D$ with $v(0)\geq -1$ satisfies \[  \int _{D(0,1/2)}\mathrm e^{- eta v}\, \mathrm dV\leq C.  \] Proof. Since $v(0)\geq -1>-\infty $, lemma 5.10.5 gives a finite positive measure $
u $ with support in $D(0,9/10)$ and a harmonic function $h$ on $D(0,4/5)$ such that \[  v=P+h,\qquad P(z)= rac1{2\pi }\int \log |z-\zeta |\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta )  \] at every point of $D(0,4/5)$. Since $|v(0)|\leq 1$, the bounds ( 5.10.6 ) give $M=
u (D)\leq C_0$ and $\sup _{D(0,1/2)}|h|\leq C_0$, where $C_0\geq 1$ is the universal constant of that lemma. Fix $ eta \in (0,1]$ with $ eta C_0\leq 2\pi $. We show that $\int _{D(0,1/2)}\mathrm e^{- eta P}\, \mathrm dV\leq 8\pi $. If $M=0$, then $P=0$, and this integral is $\pi /4$. Assume $M>0$ and put $b= eta M/(2\pi )\in (0,1]$. Fix $z\in D(0,1/2)$. For $N\geq 1$ the Borel function $f_ N(\zeta )=-b\max \{ \log |z-\zeta |,-N\} $ is bounded on $D(0,9/10)$, so Jensen's inequality (lemma 2.2.4 ), applied to the convex function $\exp $ on $\mathbb R$ and the probability measure $
u /M$, gives \[  \exp \Bigl (\int f_ N\,  rac{\mathrm d

u /M$ increases to $\int -b\log |z-\zeta |\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta )/M=- eta P(z)$, and therefore \[  \mathrm e^{- eta P(z)}\leq  rac1M\int |z-\zeta |^{-b}\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta )  \] for every $z\in D(0,1/2)$, with the convention $\mathrm e^{\infty }=\infty $. For every $\zeta \in D(0,9/10)$ the translated disc $D(0,1/2)-\zeta $ lies in $D(0,2)$, and $r^{-b}\leq 1+r^{-1}$ for $r>0$ because $0<b\leq 1$; hence \[  \int _{D(0,1/2)}|z-\zeta |^{-b}\, \mathrm dV(z) \leq \int _{D(0,2)}(1+|z|^{-1})\, \mathrm dV(z)=8\pi .  \] Integrating the bound for $\mathrm e^{- eta P(z)}$ over $z\in D(0,1/2)$ with Tonelli's theorem, we obtain $\int _{D(0,1/2)}\mathrm e^{- eta P}\, \mathrm dV\leq 8\pi $. Finally, since $\mathrm e^{- eta v}=\mathrm e^{- eta P}\mathrm e^{- eta h}\leq \mathrm e^{ eta C_0}\mathrm e^{- eta P}$ on $D(0,1/2)$, the lemma follows with $C=8\pi \mathrm e^{C_0}$. $\square$ Proposition 5.10.12 . 219E06AF4230 Let $n\geq 1$, and let $B$ be the unit ball of $\mathbb C^ n$. There are constants $\alpha _ n,C_ n>0$ such that every plurisubharmonic function $v\leq 0$ on $B$ with $\| v\| _{L^1(B)}\leq 1$ satisfies DE8035B23862 5.10.13  egin{equation}  \int _{ rac14B}\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ n v}\, \mathrm dV\leq C_ n. \end{equation} More generally, if $\| v\| _{L^1(B)}\leq M$ for some $M>0$, the same bound holds with the exponent $\alpha _ n/M$ in place of $\alpha _ n$. Proof. Put $A_ n=\max \{ 1,2/| rac18B|\} $. The mean of $|v|$ over $ rac18B$ is at most $1/| rac18B|<A_ n$. Hence the set of points of $ rac18B$ with $|v|\leq A_ n$ has positive measure, since otherwise $|v|>A_ n$ almost everywhere on $ rac18B$ and the mean would be at least $A_ n$; so there is a point $a\in  rac18B$ with $|v(a)|\leq A_ n$. For each unit vector $e\in \mathbb C^ n$, the disc $\{ a+	frac 34\zeta e:|\zeta |<1\} $ lies in $B$, so the function \[  \zeta \longmapsto A_ n^{-1}v(a+	frac 34\zeta e)  \] is subharmonic and nonpositive on $D$, with value at least $-1$ at $0$. Set $\alpha _ n= eta /A_ n$, with $ eta $ as in lemma 5.10.11 . That lemma and the change of variables $\zeta \mapsto  rac34\zeta $ give a bound, independent of $e$ and $v$, for \[  \int _{|\zeta |<3/8}\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ n v(a+\zeta e)}\, \mathrm dV(\zeta ).  \] It remains to pass from these integrals over discs in complex lines to an integral over a ball. Let $	au $ and $s_{2n-1}$ be as in ( 5.8.3 ). By that identity, applied with center $a$, and since $|\zeta |^{2n-2}\leq r^{2n-2}$ for $|\zeta |<r$, every Borel function $F\geq 0$, possibly taking the value $+\infty $, satisfies \[  \int _{|z-a|<r}F(z)\, \mathrm dV(z) \leq  rac{s_{2n-1}r^{2n-2}}{2\pi } \int _{S^{2n-1}}\int _{|\zeta |<r}F(a+\zeta e)\, \mathrm dV(\zeta )\, \mathrm d	au (e)  \] for every $r>0$. We apply this with $F=\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ n v}$ and $r=3/8$. Since $ rac14B\subset B(a,3/8)$, the uniform bound for the line integrals proves ( 5.10.13 ). Finally, if $\| v\| _{L^1(B)}\leq M$ with $M>0$, then $v/M$ is a nonpositive plurisubharmonic function with $\| v/M\| _{L^1(B)}\leq 1$, and ( 5.10.13 ) for $v/M$ is the last assertion. $\square$ Consequently, every plurisubharmonic function $u$ on a complex manifold $X$ is locally exponentially integrable: every point $x\in X$ has a neighborhood $W$ for which there is $\alpha _0>0$ such that $\mathrm e^{-\alpha u}$ is integrable on $W$ for $0<\alpha \leq \alpha _0$, the integrals being computed in local coordinates. In dimension zero we may take $W=\{ x\} $. In dimension $n\geq 1$, choose a chart in which $x=0$ and the closed ball $\overline{B(0,R)}$ lies in the chart domain, for some $R>0$, and let $c$ be an upper bound for $u$ on this ball. The function $v(\zeta )=u(R\zeta )-c$ is plurisubharmonic and nonpositive on the unit ball $B$, and since $u$ is locally integrable there is $A>0$ with $\| v\| _{L^1(B)}\leq A$. Put $\alpha _0=\alpha _ n/A$ and $W=B(0,R/4)$. For $0<\alpha \leq \alpha _0$ we have $\mathrm e^{-\alpha v}\leq \mathrm e^{-\alpha _0v}$, because $v\leq 0$, so the change of variables $z=R\zeta $ and the last assertion of proposition 5.10.12 give \[  \int _ W\mathrm e^{-\alpha u}\, \mathrm dV=R^{2n}\mathrm e^{-\alpha c}\int _{ rac14B}\mathrm e^{-\alpha v}\, \mathrm dV\leq R^{2n}\mathrm e^{-\alpha c}C_ n<\infty .  \]

title: Theorem 5.10.1
text: Theorem 5.10.1 . FE144A69076E Let $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a decreasing net in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$, that is, $u_ j\leq u_ i$ whenever $i\leq j$, and let $u=\lim _ iu_ i=\inf _ iu_ i$ be its pointwise limit. Then on each connected component $X_0$ of $X$, exactly one of the following holds: either $u$ is plurisubharmonic on $X_0$ and $u_ i\to u$ in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X_0)$, or $u\equiv -\infty $ on $X_0$ and $u_ i\to -\infty $ locally uniformly on $X_0$. Proof. The limit $u$ is upper semicontinuous, since $\{ u<c\} =\bigcup _ i\{ u_ i<c\} $ is open for every real $c$. Fix a connected component $X_0$ of $X$; it has a countable basis. Step 1: a decreasing sequence with the same limit. Let $i_0\in I$. We show that there are indices $i_0\leq i_1\leq i_2\leq \cdots $ such that $u_{i_ l}\downarrow u$ pointwise on $X_0$. Replacing $I$ by the cofinal directed set $\{ i\in I:i\geq i_0\} $, which does not change the limit, we only have to find indices $i_1\leq i_2\leq \cdots $. For each rational $c$, the open sets $\{ u_ i<c\} \cap X_0$ cover $\{ u<c\} \cap X_0$, and countably many of them suffice: for each basis element of $X_0$ contained in some set $\{ u_ i<c\} $, choose one such index $i$; every point of $\{ u<c\} \cap X_0$ lies in such a basis element. Let $k_1,k_2,\ldots $ be an enumeration, with repetitions allowed, of the indices chosen for all rational $c$. Since $I$ is directed, we can choose inductively $i_1\geq k_1$ and $i_{l+1}\geq i_ l,k_{l+1}$. The sequence $(u_{i_ l})$ is decreasing and bounded below by $u$. If $u(x)<c$ with $c$ rational and $x\in X_0$, then $u_{k_ l}(x)<c$ for some $l$, hence $u_{i_ l}(x)\leq u_{k_ l}(x)<c$. Therefore $u_{i_ l}\downarrow u$ on $X_0$. Step 2: the limit. Let $V\subset X_0$ be a connected coordinate neighborhood, identified with a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. On each connected component of each affine complex-line section of $V$, the restrictions of the $u_{i_ l}$ form a decreasing sequence of subharmonic functions, whose limit is subharmonic by theorem 3.4.9 . Since $u$ is upper semicontinuous, it is either plurisubharmonic on $V$ or identically $-\infty $ on $V$, by definition 5.8.1 . As $X_0$ is connected, lemma 5.9.4 shows that either $u$ is plurisubharmonic on $X_0$ or $u\equiv -\infty $ on $X_0$. Step 3: convergence. Suppose first that $u$ is plurisubharmonic on $X_0$. Fix $i_0\in I$, take the sequence of Step 1, and let $K$ be a compact subset of a coordinate neighborhood in $X_0$. Then $0\leq u_{i_ l}-u\leq u_{i_0}-u$ almost everywhere, namely wherever $u$ is finite, and $u_{i_0}-u$ is integrable on $K$. By dominated convergence, $\| u_{i_ l}-u\| _{L^1(K)}\to 0$. Given $\varepsilon >0$, choose $l$ with $\| u_{i_ l}-u\| _{L^1(K)}<\varepsilon $; for every $i\geq i_ l$ we have $0\leq u_ i-u\leq u_{i_ l}-u$ almost everywhere, hence $\| u_ i-u\| _{L^1(K)}<\varepsilon $. Thus the net converges to $u$ in $L^1(K)$, and covering an arbitrary compact subset of $X_0$ by finitely many such sets $K$ gives convergence in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X_0)$. Suppose now that $u\equiv -\infty $ on $X_0$, and let $K\subset X_0$ be compact and $A>0$. The open sets $\{ u_ i<-A\} $ cover $K$, so finitely many of them, say those with indices $j_1,\ldots ,j_ p$, already cover $K$. If $i\geq j_1,\ldots ,j_ p$, then $u_ i\leq u_{j_ q}$ for each $q$, and hence $u_ i<-A$ on $K$. This is locally uniform convergence to $-\infty $. $\square$

title: Theorem 5.10.2
text: Theorem 5.10.2 . D32A2FB94F6B Let $(u_ i)_{i\in I}$ be a nonempty family in $\mathrm{PSH}(X)$ that is locally uniformly bounded above, and let $F=\sup _ iu_ i$ be its upper envelope. Then the upper semicontinuous regularization $F^*$ is plurisubharmonic, and $F=F^*$ almost everywhere; more precisely, in every coordinate chart the set $\{ F<F^*\} $ is real polar. If $X$ has a countable basis, there is a countable subset $J\subset I$ such that $(\sup _{i\in J}u_ i)^*=F^*$. Proof. Since $F^*$ is defined by a local formula and plurisubharmonicity is a local property, it suffices to prove that $F^*$ is plurisubharmonic on every connected coordinate neighborhood $V$, which we identify with a domain in $\mathbb {C}^ n$. By theorem 3.4.23 , $F^*$ is subharmonic on $V$, and $F$ is Lebesgue measurable and equal to $F^*$ almost everywhere on $V$. By Choquet's lemma, lemma 3.4.22 , there is a countable set $J_ V\subset I$ with $(\sup _{i\in J_ V}u_ i)^*=F^*$ on $V$. We next show that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F^*\geq 0$ on $V$. Fix $i_0\in I$, enumerate $J_ V\cup \{ i_0\} $ as $i_0,i_1,i_2,\ldots $, with repetitions if this set is finite, and put $v_ j=\max \{ u_{i_0},\ldots ,u_{i_ j}\} $. The functions $v_ j$ are plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.5 , increase with $j$, are locally uniformly bounded above, and dominate the locally integrable function $u_{i_0}$. Their limit $G=\sup _ jv_ j$ lies between $\sup _{i\in J_ V}u_ i$ and $F$, so $G^*=F^*$, and hence $G=F^*$ almost everywhere by theorem 3.4.23 applied to the countable family. On a compact set $K\subset V$ on which every $u_ i$ is bounded above by $M$, we have $0\leq v_ j-u_{i_0}\leq M-u_{i_0}$, so dominated convergence gives $v_ j\to F^*$ in $L^1(K)$. Therefore $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F^*\geq 0$, as a limit of positive currents. Since $F^*$ is subharmonic and dominates the locally integrable function $u_{i_0}$, it is locally integrable and hence the canonical representative of its class, and theorem 5.9.1 shows that $F^*$ is plurisubharmonic on $V$. If $X$ has a countable basis, cover $X$ by countably many connected coordinate neighborhoods $V_1,V_2,\ldots $ and put $J=\bigcup _ mJ_{V_ m}$. On each $V_ m$ we have $F^*=(\sup _{i\in J_{V_ m}}u_ i)^*\leq (\sup _{i\in J}u_ i)^*\leq F^*$, and since the regularization is local, $(\sup _{i\in J}u_ i)^*=F^*$ on $X$. Finally, in each chart the functions $u_ i$ are subharmonic, so the second assertion of theorem 4.1.26 shows that $\{ F<F^*\} $ is polar in the corresponding open subset of $\mathbb R^{2n}$, that is, real polar. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.10.3
text: Proposition 5.10.3 . 1A6F10A07BA5 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, $n\geq 1$, and let $g=(g_1,\ldots ,g_ r)$, $r\geq 1$, be a tuple of holomorphic functions on $\Omega $, not all identically zero. Then the function $\log \sum _ j|g_ j|^2$, with the value $-\infty $ at the common zeros of the $g_ j$, is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $. In particular, for every $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ the function $\log |z-a|^2$ is plurisubharmonic on $\mathbb {C}^ n$. Proof. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, with equality for $\lambda $ proportional to $(\overline{g_1(z)},\ldots ,\overline{g_ r(z)})$, we have \[  \log \sum _ j|g_ j(z)|^2 =\sup _{\sum _ j|\lambda _ j|^2=1}\log \left|\sum _ j\lambda _ jg_ j(z)\right|^2  \] for every $z\in \Omega $, both sides being $-\infty $ at a common zero. The supremum does not change if we omit the $\lambda $ for which $\sum _ j\lambda _ jg_ j$ vanishes identically: at a point $z$ that is not a common zero, the maximizing $\lambda $ gives $\sum _ j\lambda _ jg_ j(z)\neq 0$, and at a common zero all terms equal $-\infty $. Some $g_ j$ is not identically zero, so the remaining family is nonempty. Its members are plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.5.3 , theorem 5.9.1 , and they are locally uniformly bounded above by the left-hand side. Their supremum $\log \sum _ j|g_ j|^2$ is already upper semicontinuous: it is continuous as a map to $[-\infty ,\infty )$, because $\sum _ j|g_ j|^2$ is continuous and its logarithm tends to $-\infty $ at a common zero. Hence it equals its regularization, which is plurisubharmonic by theorem 5.10.2 . The particular case is the tuple $(z_1-a_1,\ldots ,z_ n-a_ n)$. $\square$

title: Theorem 5.10.4
text: Theorem 5.10.4 . C2DB8DFE9E2C Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a domain, $n\geq 1$. Every sequence in $\mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ that is locally uniformly bounded above has a subsequence that either converges locally uniformly to $-\infty $ or converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ to a plurisubharmonic function. If a sequence $(u_ j)$ in $\mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, then its limit has a plurisubharmonic representative $u$, and the following holds: for every compact set $K\subset \Omega $ and every lower semicontinuous function $f\colon K\to \mathbb R$ with $u<f$ on $K$, for instance every real continuous function on $K$, one has $u_ j<f$ on $K$ for all sufficiently large $j$. In particular $\varlimsup _ j u_ j(x)\le u(x)$ for every $x\in \Omega $. Proof. Plurisubharmonic functions are subharmonic by theorem 5.9.1 . Hence, by the compactness theorem (theorem 3.4.19 ), a sequence as in the first assertion either tends to $-\infty $ locally uniformly, or has a subsequence converging in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ to a locally integrable subharmonic function $v$. In the second case $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v\geq 0$, as a distributional limit of positive currents, and $v$ is the canonical representative of its class; so $v$ is plurisubharmonic by theorem 5.9.1 . Now let $(u_ j)$ converge in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$ to $T$. As above, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}T\geq 0$, so $T$ has a plurisubharmonic representative $u$, namely its canonical subharmonic representative. The $u_ j$ are locally integrable subharmonic functions converging in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega )$, and $u$ is the canonical representative of their limit, so the remaining assertions are Hartogs' lemma for subharmonic functions, theorem 3.4.20 , which requires no upper bound on the sequence; the last one is its first assertion with the constant sequence $x_ j=x$. $\square$

title: Lemma 5.10.5
text:
Lemma 5.10.5 . 69CE23EA1637 There is a constant $C_0\geq 1$ with the following property. Let $v\leq 0$ be a subharmonic function on $D$ with $v(0)>-\infty $. Then there are a finite positive Borel measure $
u $ with support in $D(0,9/10)$ and a harmonic function $h$ on $D(0,4/5)$ such that 6A92D19CE668 5.10.6  egin{equation}   egin{gathered} v(z)=P(z)+h(z)\quad (z\in D(0,4/5)),\qquad P(z)= rac1{2\pi }\int \log |z-\zeta |\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta ),\ 
u (D)\leq C_0|v(0)|,\qquad \sup _{\overline{D(0,1/2)}}|h|\leq C_0|v(0)|. \end{gathered} \end{equation} Moreover, for every $1\leq p<\infty $ there is a constant $C_ p>0$ such that every such $v$ satisfies \[  \| v\| _{L^ p(D(0,1/2))}\leq C_ p|v(0)|.  \] Proof. In this proof $C$ denotes constants that depend only on two cutoff functions $\chi $ and $\eta $ fixed below, and $C'$ constants that depend in addition on $p$. Since $v(0)>-\infty $, the function $v$ is not identically $-\infty $, and hence it is locally integrable by proposition 3.4.8 . For $0<r<1$, the ball submean inequality (theorem 3.4.5 ) and $v\leq 0$ give C493F766D641 5.10.7  egin{equation}  \| v\| _{L^1(D(0,r))}=-\int _{D(0,r)}v\, \mathrm dV\leq \pi r^2|v(0)|. \end{equation} Let $\mu =\Delta v$ be the Riesz measure of $v$, and choose a smooth cutoff $\chi \geq 0$ supported in $D(0,19/20)$ and equal to one on $D(0,9/10)$. By the definition of the distributional Laplacian and ( 5.10.7 ), \[  \mu (D(0,9/10))\leq \int \chi \, \mathrm d\mu =\int v\Delta \chi \, \mathrm dV\leq \sup |\Delta \chi |\, \| v\| _{L^1(D(0,19/20))}\leq C|v(0)|.  \] Next choose a smooth cutoff $0\leq \eta \leq 1$ supported in $D(0,9/10)$ and equal to one on a neighborhood of $\overline{D(0,4/5)}$. The fundamental solution in the plane is $(2\pi )^{-1}\log |z|$, so theorem 3.4.14 , applied with the measure $
u =\eta \mu $, which is finite and supported in $\operatorname{Supp}\eta \subset D(0,9/10)$, gives \[  v(z)=P(z)+h(z),\qquad P(z)= rac1{2\pi }\int \log |z-\zeta |\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta ),  \] for every $z\in D(0,4/5)$, with $h$ harmonic on $D(0,4/5)$. We estimate $P$. For $|\zeta |\leq 9/10$, the translated disc $D(0,4/5)-\zeta $ lies in $D(0,2)$, so \[  \int _{D(0,4/5)}|\log |z-\zeta ||^ p\, \mathrm dV(z) \leq L_ p=\int _{D(0,2)}|\log |z||^ p\, \mathrm dV(z)<\infty ;  \] the integral $L_ p$ is finite because its part over $D$ equals $2\pi \int _0^1r|\log r|^ p\, \mathrm dr$, whose integrand is bounded on $(0,1]$, while $|\log |z||\leq \log 2$ on the rest of $D(0,2)$. Let $m=
u (D)=\int \eta \, \mathrm d\mu $, so that $m\leq \mu (D(0,9/10))\leq C|v(0)|$. If $m=0$, then $P=0$. Otherwise, $|P(z)|\leq  rac m{2\pi }\int |\log |z-\zeta ||\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta )/m$, and Hölder's inequality for the probability measure $
u /m$ gives \[  |P(z)|^ p\leq \Bigl ( rac m{2\pi }\Bigr )^ p\int |\log |z-\zeta ||^ p\,  rac{\mathrm d
u (\zeta )}m,  \] and integrating over $z\in D(0,4/5)$ with Tonelli's theorem yields $\| P\| _{L^ p(D(0,4/5))}\leq L_ p^{1/p}m/(2\pi )\leq C'|v(0)|$. We now estimate $h$. The case $p=1$ of the bound for $P$, in which $L_1$ is an absolute constant, and ( 5.10.7 ) give $\| h\| _{L^1(D(0,4/5))}\leq C|v(0)|$. For $|z|\leq 1/2$, the closed disc $\overline{D(z,1/4)}$ lies in $D(0,4/5)$, and the ball mean-value property of the harmonic function $h$ (proposition 3.1.5 ) gives $|h(z)|\leq (16/\pi )\| h\| _{L^1(D(0,4/5))}$. We have thus found a constant $C_0\geq 1$, depending only on the cutoff functions $\chi $ and $\eta $, such that $
u (D)=m\leq C_0|v(0)|$ and $\sup _{\overline{D(0,1/2)}}|h|\leq C_0|v(0)|$; this proves ( 5.10.6 ). Adding the estimates for $P$ and $h$ on $D(0,1/2)$, we obtain \[  \| v\| _{L^ p(D(0,1/2))}\leq \| P\| _{L^ p(D(0,4/5))}+(\pi /4)^{1/p}C_0|v(0)|\leq C'|v(0)|,  \] which proves the last assertion. $\square$
