title: Proposition 5.10.8
text: Proposition 5.10.8 . B979DF329B28 Let $n\geq 1$ and $1\leq p<\infty $. There are constants $C_{n,p},A_{n,p}>0$ such that every plurisubharmonic function $v\leq 0$ on the unit polydisc $D^ n$ satisfies \[  \| v\| _{L^ p((\tfrac 12D)^ n)}\leq C_{n,p}|v(0)| \quad \text{if }v(0)>-\infty ,  \] and 8326366018BB 5.10.9 \begin{equation}  \| v\| _{L^ p((\tfrac 14D)^ n)}\leq A_{n,p}\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}. \end{equation} Here $\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}$ may be infinite, in which case there is nothing to prove. Proof. We prove the first estimate by induction on $n$. For $n=1$ it is lemma 5.10.5 . Let $n\geq 2$, write $z=(z_1,z')$ with $z'\in \mathbb C^{n-1}$, and let $v$ be as in the statement with $v(0)>-\infty $. The function $w(z')=v(0,z')$ is the composition of $v$ with the holomorphic map $z'\mapsto (0,z')$, so by proposition 5.9.3 it is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $D^{n-1}$. Since $w(0)=v(0)>-\infty $, it is plurisubharmonic, hence locally integrable and finite outside a Lebesgue null set $E\subset D^{n-1}$. For $z'\in D^{n-1}\setminus E$, the function $z_1\mapsto v(z_1,z')$ is subharmonic and nonpositive on $D$, with the finite value $w(z')$ at the center, so lemma 5.10.5 gives \[  \int _{\frac12D}|v(z_1,z')|^ p\, \mathrm dV(z_1) \leq C_ p^ p|w(z')|^ p.  \] We integrate over $z'\in (\tfrac 12D)^{n-1}$ using Tonelli's theorem; the null set $E$, on which the inner integral may be infinite, does not contribute. The induction hypothesis applied to $w$ then gives \[  \| v\| _{L^ p((\frac12D)^ n)}^ p\leq C_ p^ p\| w\| _{L^ p((\frac12D)^{n-1})}^ p\leq C_ p^ pC_{n-1,p}^ p|v(0)|^ p,  \] which is the first estimate with $C_{n,p}=C_ pC_{n-1,p}$. For the second estimate, let $Q=(\tfrac 1{10}D)^ n$ and $|Q|$ its volume. If $\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}=0$, then $v=0$ almost everywhere, hence $v\equiv 0$ by theorem 5.9.1 , and there is nothing to prove; we may also assume that $\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}<\infty $. Put $\lambda =2|Q|^{-1}\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}>0$. By Chebyshev's inequality, the set of points of $Q$ with $|v|>\lambda $ has measure at most $\lambda ^{-1}\int _ Q|v|\, \mathrm dV\leq |Q|/2$, so its complement in $Q$ has positive measure. Since $v$ is finite almost everywhere, there is a point $a\in Q$ with $v(a)>-\infty $ and \[  |v(a)|\leq 2|Q|^{-1}\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}.  \] The polydisc of radius $4/5$ centered at $a$ lies in $D^ n$, and the polydisc of radius $2/5$ centered at $a$ contains $(\tfrac 14D)^ n$, since $\tfrac 14+\tfrac 1{10}<\tfrac 25$. We apply the first estimate to the plurisubharmonic function $\zeta \mapsto v(a+\tfrac 45\zeta )\leq 0$ on $D^ n$ and change variables: \[  \| v\| _{L^ p((\frac14D)^ n)}\leq \bigl (\tfrac 45\bigr )^{2n/p}C_{n,p}|v(a)|\leq 2\bigl (\tfrac 45\bigr )^{2n/p}C_{n,p}|Q|^{-1}\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}.  \] This is ( 5.10.9 ). $\square$

title: Equation 5.10.9
text: 8326366018BB 5.10.9 \begin{equation}  \| v\| _{L^ p((\tfrac 14D)^ n)}\leq A_{n,p}\| v\| _{L^1(D^ n)}. \end{equation}

title: Theorem 5.10.10
text: Theorem 5.10.10 . F2A3CA649325 Let $X$ be a complex manifold and $1\leq p<\infty $. Every plurisubharmonic function on $X$ belongs to $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$. If a sequence of plurisubharmonic functions on $X$ converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$, then it converges in $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$ to the same limit. Proof. If $X$ has dimension zero, every compact subset of $X$ is finite, plurisubharmonic functions are real-valued, and convergence in $L^ p_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is pointwise convergence; so both assertions hold. Let $X$ have dimension $n\geq 1$. Every compact subset of $X$ is covered by finitely many coordinate polydiscs, so it suffices to work near a point $x\in X$ in a chart in which $x=0$ and the closed polydisc $\overline{(RD)^ n}$ lies in the chart, for some $R>0$. Let $v$ be plurisubharmonic. Being upper semicontinuous, $v$ is bounded above on $\overline{(RD)^ n}$ by some constant $A$. The function $\zeta \mapsto v(R\zeta )-A$ is plurisubharmonic and nonpositive on $D^ n$, and its $L^1$ norm on $D^ n$ is finite because $v$ is locally integrable. By ( 5.10.9 ), $v$ belongs to $L^ p$ on the polydisc $(\tfrac R4D)^ n$. This proves the first assertion. Now let $(u_ j)$ be a sequence of plurisubharmonic functions converging in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(X)$. For $p=1$ there is nothing to prove, so let $p>1$. By theorem 5.10.4 applied in charts, together with the uniqueness in theorem 5.9.1 , the limit is represented by a plurisubharmonic function $u$. The norms $\| u_ j\| _{L^1((RD)^ n)}$ are bounded because the sequence converges. If $y\in (\tfrac R2D)^ n$, the ball $B(y,R/2)$ lies in $(RD)^ n$, so the ball submean inequality gives $u_ j(y)\leq |B(y,R/2)|^{-1}\| u_ j\| _{L^1((RD)^ n)}$. Hence there is a constant $M$, independent of $j$, with $u_ j\leq M$ and $u\leq M$ on $(\tfrac R2D)^ n$. Applying ( 5.10.9 ) to $\zeta \mapsto u_ j(\tfrac R2\zeta )-M$ and to $\zeta \mapsto u(\tfrac R2\zeta )-M$, whose $L^1$ norms on $D^ n$ are bounded independently of $j$, we obtain a bound for the $L^{2p}$ norms of $u_ j$ and $u$ on $(\tfrac R8D)^ n$ that is uniform in $j$. By a finite covering, for every compact set $K\subset X$ the norms $\| u_ j\| _{L^{2p}(K)}$ and $\| u\| _{L^{2p}(K)}$ are bounded independently of $j$. We interpolate between $L^1$ and $L^{2p}$. For a function $f$ on $K$, write $|f|^ p=|f|^{p/(2p-1)}\cdot |f|^{p(2p-2)/(2p-1)}$ and apply Hölder's inequality with the conjugate exponents $(2p-1)/p$ and $(2p-1)/(p-1)$; since $\frac{p(2p-2)}{2p-1}\cdot \frac{2p-1}{p-1}=2p$, this gives \[  \int _ K|f|^ p\, \mathrm dV\leq \Bigl (\int _ K|f|\, \mathrm dV\Bigr )^{p/(2p-1)}\Bigl (\int _ K|f|^{2p}\, \mathrm dV\Bigr )^{(p-1)/(2p-1)},  \] that is, $\| f\| _{L^ p(K)}\leq \| f\| _{L^1(K)}^{1/(2p-1)}\| f\| _{L^{2p}(K)}^{(2p-2)/(2p-1)}$. With $f=u_ j-u$, whose $L^{2p}(K)$ norms are bounded independently of $j$, we obtain \[  \| u_ j-u\| _{L^ p(K)} \leq \| u_ j-u\| _{L^1(K)}^{1/(2p-1)} \| u_ j-u\| _{L^{2p}(K)}^{(2p-2)/(2p-1)}\longrightarrow 0.  \] $\square$

title: Lemma 5.10.11
text:
Lemma 5.10.11 . 03676DBFBA61 There are constants $ eta ,C>0$ such that every subharmonic function $v\leq 0$ on $D$ with $v(0)\geq -1$ satisfies \[  \int _{D(0,1/2)}\mathrm e^{- eta v}\, \mathrm dV\leq C.  \] Proof. Since $v(0)\geq -1>-\infty $, lemma 5.10.5 gives a finite positive measure $
u $ with support in $D(0,9/10)$ and a harmonic function $h$ on $D(0,4/5)$ such that \[  v=P+h,\qquad P(z)= rac1{2\pi }\int \log |z-\zeta |\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta )  \] at every point of $D(0,4/5)$. Since $|v(0)|\leq 1$, the bounds ( 5.10.6 ) give $M=
u (D)\leq C_0$ and $\sup _{D(0,1/2)}|h|\leq C_0$, where $C_0\geq 1$ is the universal constant of that lemma. Fix $ eta \in (0,1]$ with $ eta C_0\leq 2\pi $. We show that $\int _{D(0,1/2)}\mathrm e^{- eta P}\, \mathrm dV\leq 8\pi $. If $M=0$, then $P=0$, and this integral is $\pi /4$. Assume $M>0$ and put $b= eta M/(2\pi )\in (0,1]$. Fix $z\in D(0,1/2)$. For $N\geq 1$ the Borel function $f_ N(\zeta )=-b\max \{ \log |z-\zeta |,-N\} $ is bounded on $D(0,9/10)$, so Jensen's inequality (lemma 2.2.4 ), applied to the convex function $\exp $ on $\mathbb R$ and the probability measure $
u /M$, gives \[  \exp \Bigl (\int f_ N\,  rac{\mathrm d
u }M\Bigr )\leq \int \mathrm e^{f_ N}\,  rac{\mathrm d
u }M\leq  rac1M\int |z-\zeta |^{-b}\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta ).  \] As $N	o \infty $, the functions $f_ N$ increase to $-b\log |z-\zeta |$, which may take the value $+\infty $, and they are bounded below by the bounded function $f_1$. By monotone convergence, $\int f_ N\, \mathrm d
u /M$ increases to $\int -b\log |z-\zeta |\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta )/M=- eta P(z)$, and therefore \[  \mathrm e^{- eta P(z)}\leq  rac1M\int |z-\zeta |^{-b}\, \mathrm d
u (\zeta )  \] for every $z\in D(0,1/2)$, with the convention $\mathrm e^{\infty }=\infty $. For every $\zeta \in D(0,9/10)$ the translated disc $D(0,1/2)-\zeta $ lies in $D(0,2)$, and $r^{-b}\leq 1+r^{-1}$ for $r>0$ because $0<b\leq 1$; hence \[  \int _{D(0,1/2)}|z-\zeta |^{-b}\, \mathrm dV(z) \leq \int _{D(0,2)}(1+|z|^{-1})\, \mathrm dV(z)=8\pi .  \] Integrating the bound for $\mathrm e^{- eta P(z)}$ over $z\in D(0,1/2)$ with Tonelli's theorem, we obtain $\int _{D(0,1/2)}\mathrm e^{- eta P}\, \mathrm dV\leq 8\pi $. Finally, since $\mathrm e^{- eta v}=\mathrm e^{- eta P}\mathrm e^{- eta h}\leq \mathrm e^{ eta C_0}\mathrm e^{- eta P}$ on $D(0,1/2)$, the lemma follows with $C=8\pi \mathrm e^{C_0}$. $\square$

title: Proposition 5.10.12
text: Proposition 5.10.12 . 219E06AF4230 Let $n\geq 1$, and let $B$ be the unit ball of $\mathbb C^ n$. There are constants $\alpha _ n,C_ n>0$ such that every plurisubharmonic function $v\leq 0$ on $B$ with $\| v\| _{L^1(B)}\leq 1$ satisfies DE8035B23862 5.10.13 \begin{equation}  \int _{\frac14B}\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ n v}\, \mathrm dV\leq C_ n. \end{equation} More generally, if $\| v\| _{L^1(B)}\leq M$ for some $M>0$, the same bound holds with the exponent $\alpha _ n/M$ in place of $\alpha _ n$. Proof. Put $A_ n=\max \{ 1,2/|\frac18B|\} $. The mean of $|v|$ over $\frac18B$ is at most $1/|\frac18B|<A_ n$. Hence the set of points of $\frac18B$ with $|v|\leq A_ n$ has positive measure, since otherwise $|v|>A_ n$ almost everywhere on $\frac18B$ and the mean would be at least $A_ n$; so there is a point $a\in \frac18B$ with $|v(a)|\leq A_ n$. For each unit vector $e\in \mathbb C^ n$, the disc $\{ a+\tfrac 34\zeta e:|\zeta |<1\} $ lies in $B$, so the function \[  \zeta \longmapsto A_ n^{-1}v(a+\tfrac 34\zeta e)  \] is subharmonic and nonpositive on $D$, with value at least $-1$ at $0$. Set $\alpha _ n=\beta /A_ n$, with $\beta $ as in lemma 5.10.11 . That lemma and the change of variables $\zeta \mapsto \frac34\zeta $ give a bound, independent of $e$ and $v$, for \[  \int _{|\zeta |<3/8}\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ n v(a+\zeta e)}\, \mathrm dV(\zeta ).  \] It remains to pass from these integrals over discs in complex lines to an integral over a ball. Let $\tau $ and $s_{2n-1}$ be as in ( 5.8.3 ). By that identity, applied with center $a$, and since $|\zeta |^{2n-2}\leq r^{2n-2}$ for $|\zeta |<r$, every Borel function $F\geq 0$, possibly taking the value $+\infty $, satisfies \[  \int _{|z-a|<r}F(z)\, \mathrm dV(z) \leq \frac{s_{2n-1}r^{2n-2}}{2\pi } \int _{S^{2n-1}}\int _{|\zeta |<r}F(a+\zeta e)\, \mathrm dV(\zeta )\, \mathrm d\tau (e)  \] for every $r>0$. We apply this with $F=\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ n v}$ and $r=3/8$. Since $\frac14B\subset B(a,3/8)$, the uniform bound for the line integrals proves ( 5.10.13 ). Finally, if $\| v\| _{L^1(B)}\leq M$ with $M>0$, then $v/M$ is a nonpositive plurisubharmonic function with $\| v/M\| _{L^1(B)}\leq 1$, and ( 5.10.13 ) for $v/M$ is the last assertion. $\square$

title: Equation 5.10.13
text: DE8035B23862 5.10.13 \begin{equation}  \int _{\frac14B}\mathrm e^{-\alpha _ n v}\, \mathrm dV\leq C_ n. \end{equation}

title: 5.11 Extension across closed exceptional sets
text:
Let $S$ be a relatively closed subset of a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$. We give two conditions under which plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega \setminus S$ extend across $S$. In the first, $S$ is locally contained in the zero set of a holomorphic function, and the function is assumed to be locally bounded above near $S$; a logarithmic barrier built from the holomorphic function then gives the extension. In the second, $S$ is small in the sense of Hausdorff measure, and the local upper bound is not assumed but follows from the smallness of $S$ by an argument with complex lines. Theorem 5.11.1 . C910F1109424 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, $n\ge 1$, and let $S\subset \Omega $ be relatively closed. Assume that every point of $S$ has a connected neighborhood $W\subset \Omega $ with a holomorphic function $f
ot\equiv 0$ on $W$ such that $S\cap W\subset \{ f=0\} $. Let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega \setminus S$ that is locally bounded above near $S$, that is, every point of $S$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $u$ is bounded above on $W\setminus S$. Then $u$ has a unique plurisubharmonic extension $\widetilde u$ to $\Omega $, and its value at $x\in S$ is \[  \widetilde u(x)=\varlimsup _{\Omega \setminus S
i y	o x}u(y).  \] Proof. Define $\widetilde u$ by $u$ on $\Omega \setminus S$ and by the displayed formula on $S$. Since plurisubharmonicity is a local property, it suffices to show that every point $x_0\in S$ has a neighborhood on which $\widetilde u$ is plurisubharmonic; uniqueness is proved at the end. By hypothesis there are a connected neighborhood $W_0$ of $x_0$ with a holomorphic function $f
ot\equiv 0$ on $W_0$ such that $S\cap W_0\subset \{ f=0\} $, and a neighborhood $W_1$ of $x_0$ such that $u$ is bounded above on $W_1\setminus S$. Choose a ball $W$ about $x_0$ with $\overline W\subset W_0\cap W_1$. By the identity theorem, $f$ does not vanish identically on $W$, and $u$ is bounded above on $W\setminus S$. Multiplying $f$ by a nonzero constant, we may assume that $|f|\leq 1$, that is, $\log |f|^2\le 0$, on $W$. For $\varepsilon >0$ define $u_\varepsilon $ on $W$ by \[  u_\varepsilon =u+\varepsilon \log |f|^2\quad 	ext{on }W\setminus S,\qquad u_\varepsilon =-\infty \quad 	ext{on }S\cap W.  \] Step 1: $u_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(W)$. At a point $x\in S\cap W$ we have $f(x)=0$, so $\log |f(y)|^2	o -\infty $ as $y	o x$, while $u$ is bounded above near $x$; hence $u_\varepsilon (y)	o -\infty $ as $y	o x$, and $u_\varepsilon $ is upper semicontinuous at $x$. On $W\setminus S$, $u_\varepsilon $ is upper semicontinuous as a sum of upper semicontinuous functions. Now let $\Lambda $ be a connected component of $L\cap W$ for an affine complex line $L$. If $f$ vanishes identically on $\Lambda $, then $u_\varepsilon \equiv -\infty $ on $\Lambda $. Otherwise the zeros of $f$ on the connected set $\Lambda $ are isolated, by the identity theorem in one variable. Since $S$ is relatively closed, $A=S\cap \Lambda $ is therefore a closed discrete subset of $\Lambda $, hence countable, because each of the countably many compact sets exhausting $\Lambda $ contains only finitely many of its points. It is polar, because points are polar in the plane and countable unions of polar sets are polar by proposition 4.1.11 . Each connected component of $\Lambda \setminus A$ is a connected subset of $L\cap (\Omega \setminus S)$ and therefore lies in a connected component of this line section, on which the restriction of $u$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Hence the restriction of $u$ to $\Lambda \setminus A$ is subharmonic, the constant $-\infty $ being subharmonic. The function $\log |f|^2$ is subharmonic on $\Lambda $ by example 3.4.15 . Thus $u_\varepsilon $ is subharmonic on $\Lambda \setminus A$, and it is bounded above there by $\sup _{W\setminus S}u$, because $\log |f|^2\leq 0$. By theorem 3.4.27 , it has a subharmonic extension to $\Lambda $ whose value at $x\in A$ is $\varlimsup _{\Lambda \setminus A
i y	o x}u_\varepsilon (y)=-\infty $, which is the value of $u_\varepsilon $ at $x$. Hence the restriction of $u_\varepsilon $ to $\Lambda $ is subharmonic. Finally, $u_\varepsilon $ is not identically $-\infty $, because $u$ is finite almost everywhere on $W\setminus S$ and $\{ f=0\} $ is Lebesgue null by lemma 5.5.1 . Thus $u_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(W)$. Step 2: the extension. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ the functions $u_\varepsilon $ increase, because $\log |f|^2\leq 0$, and they are bounded above on $W$ by $\sup _{W\setminus S}u$. Let $F=\sup _{\varepsilon >0}u_\varepsilon $. By theorem 5.10.2 , $F^*\in \mathrm{PSH}(W)$ and $F^*=F$ almost everywhere. Since $F=u$ outside the null set $\{ f=0\} $, we get $F^*=u$ almost everywhere on $W\setminus S$; both functions are locally integrable and subharmonic there, so $F^*=u$ everywhere on $W\setminus S$ by theorem 3.4.12 . It remains to show that $F^*=\widetilde u$ on $S\cap W$, which is Lebesgue null as a subset of $\{ f=0\} $. Let $x\in S\cap W$. Since $F^*=u$ on $W\setminus S$, the upper semicontinuity of $F^*$ gives $\widetilde u(x)=\varlimsup _{W\setminus S
i y	o x}u(y)\leq F^*(x)$. Conversely, for small $r>0$ the ball submean inequality for $F^*$ gives $F^*(x)\leq |B(x,r)|^{-1}\int _{B(x,r)\setminus S}F^*\, \mathrm dV\leq \sup _{B(x,r)\setminus S}u$, because removing the null set $S$ does not change the integral, and letting $r	o 0$ gives $F^*(x)\leq \widetilde u(x)$. Hence $\widetilde u=F^*$ on $W$, and $\widetilde u$ is plurisubharmonic on $W$. Uniqueness. The set $S$ is Lebesgue null, since it is covered by countably many neighborhoods $W$ as in the hypothesis and $S\cap W\subset \{ f=0\} $ is null. Two plurisubharmonic extensions of $u$ therefore agree almost everywhere, and hence everywhere by theorem 5.9.1 . $\square$ For the second criterion we measure the size of $S$ by Hausdorff measure. Let $q>0$. A subset $E$ of a metric space is $\mathcal H^ q$-null if for all $\delta ,\eta >0$ it can be covered by countably many balls of radii $r_ l<\delta $ with $\sum _ l r_ l^ q<\eta $. This means that the $q$-dimensional Hausdorff measure of $E$, which is defined by coverings with sets of small diameter, vanishes, whatever its normalization: a set of diameter $\ell $ lies in the ball of radius $\ell '$ about any of its points for every $\ell '>\ell $, and a ball of radius $r$ has diameter at most $2r$. Every subset of an $\mathcal H^ q$-null set is $\mathcal H^ q$-null, and so is every countable union of $\mathcal H^ q$-null sets $E_1,E_2,\ldots $: cover $E_ l$ by balls of radii less than $\delta $ with sum of the $q$-th powers of the radii less than $2^{-l}\eta $. We use two further elementary properties. First, if $E$ is $\mathcal H^ q$-null and $\Phi $ is a Lipschitz map with constant $L>0$ from $E$ to a metric space, then $\Phi (E)$ is $\mathcal H^ q$-null. To see this, discard the covering balls that do not meet $E$, and replace each remaining ball $B(c,r)$ by $B(c',2r)$ with $c'\in E\cap B(c,r)$; then $\Phi (E\cap B(c',2r))\subset B(\Phi (c'),2Lr)$, so $\Phi (E)$ is covered by balls of radii $2Lr_ l<2L\delta $ with $\sum _ l(2Lr_ l)^ q<(2L)^ q\eta $. Second, if $q\leq b$, every $\mathcal H^ q$-null subset of $\mathbb R^ b$ is Lebesgue null, because the total volume of the covering balls is at most a constant times $\sum _ lr_ l^ b\leq \delta ^{b-q}\sum _ l r_ l^ q$. For $n\geq 2$, let $\sigma $ be the unitarily invariant probability measure on $\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ and $d$ the metric on $\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ introduced in subsection 2.9.17 . For $v\in \mathbb {C}^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $ we write $[v]\in \mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ for the complex line spanned by $v$; thus the restriction of $v\mapsto [v]$ to the unit sphere is the Hopf map of subsection 2.9.17 . For $y
eq x$ in $\mathbb {C}^ n$, the point $[y-x]$ is the direction of $y$ from $x$. Lemma 5.11.2 . B88B826B1EDC Let $n\ge 2$ and let $K\subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a compact $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null set. Then: $K$ is real polar; for every $x\in \mathbb {C}^ n$, the set of directions from $x$ of the points of $K\setminus \{ x\} $ has $\sigma $-measure zero; the orthogonal projection of $K$ onto any complex hyperplane is Lebesgue null. Proof. (1) Suppose that $K$ is not polar. By theorem 4.1.17 , $K$ carries a nonzero positive measure of finite energy; dividing it by its mass, we obtain a probability measure $\mu $ on $K$ of finite energy $I(\mu )$ for the Newtonian kernel $k(x,y)=|x-y|^{2-2n}/((2n-2)s_{2n-1})$ of subsection 4.1.1 in $\mathbb R^{2n}$. Its potential $U^\mu $ is lower semicontinuous, and it is finite $\mu $-almost everywhere because $\int U^\mu \, \mathrm d\mu =I(\mu )<\infty $. The sets $E_ M=K\cap \{ U^\mu \le M\} $, $M\in \mathbb N$, are compact, because $U^\mu $ is lower semicontinuous, and they increase to a set of full $\mu $-measure; hence $\mu (E_ M)>0$ for $M$ large enough. Let $
u $ be the restriction of $\mu $ to $E_ M$. For $a\in E_ M$ and $r>0$, \[   rac{r^{2-2n}\, 
u (B(a,r))}{(2n-2)s_{2n-1}}\leq \int _{B(a,r)}k(a,y)\, \mathrm d
u (y)\leq U^\mu (a)\leq M,  \] so $
u (B(a,r))\le C_ nMr^{2n-2}$ with $C_ n=(2n-2)s_{2n-1}$. Now cover $E_ M$ by balls $B(c_ l,r_ l)$ with $r_ l<1$ and $\sum _ lr_ l^{2n-3}<\eta $, and discard those not meeting $E_ M$. Each remaining ball lies in $B(a_ l,2r_ l)$ for some $a_ l\in E_ M$, so \[  
u (E_ M)\leq \sum _ l
u (B(a_ l,2r_ l))\leq 2^{2n-2}C_ nM\sum _ lr_ l^{2n-2}\leq 2^{2n-2}C_ nM\eta ,  \] where we used $r_ l<1$. Since $\eta >0$ is arbitrary, $
u (E_ M)=0$, a contradiction. Hence $K$ is polar. (2) Fix $x$. For $m\geq 1$ the set $K_ m=K\cap \{ |y-x|\geq 1/m\} $ is compact and $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null, and $K\setminus \{ x\} = igcup _ mK_ m$. The direction map $\Phi (y)=[y-x]$ is Lipschitz on $K_ m$. Indeed, $\Phi (y)=[(y-x)/|y-x|]$. The normalization $y\mapsto (y-x)/|y-x|$ has Lipschitz constant at most $2m$ on $\{ |y-x|\geq 1/m\} $: for nonzero vectors $a,b$, \[  \Bigl | rac a{|a|}- rac b{|b|}\Bigr |\leq  rac{|a-b|}{|a|}+|b|\, \Bigl | rac1{|a|}- rac1{|b|}\Bigr |= rac{|a-b|+ igl ||b|-|a| igr |}{|a|}\leq  rac{2|a-b|}{|a|},  \] and we apply this with $a=y-x$, $b=y'-x$ and $|a|\geq 1/m$. The Hopf map is Lipschitz with constant $\pi /2$ for the metric $d$. Indeed, let $e,e'$ be unit vectors and $\delta =\arccos \operatorname{Re}\langle e,e'angle \in [0,\pi ]$ their spherical distance. Since $d$ is the minimum of the spherical distance over the unit representatives (subsection 2.9.17 ), we have $d([e],[e'])\leq \delta $. Moreover $|e-e'|^2=2-2\cos \delta =4\sin ^2(\delta /2)$, and $\sin s\geq 2s/\pi $ for $0\leq s\leq \pi /2$, so $|e-e'|\geq 2\delta /\pi $. Hence \[  d([e],[e'])\leq \delta \leq 	frac \pi 2|e-e'|.  \] Since Lipschitz images of $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null sets are $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null, the compact set $\Phi (K_ m)$ is $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null in $(\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C),d)$. Cover it by balls of radii $r_ l<1$ with $\sum _ lr_ l^{2n-3}<\eta $. By lemma 2.9.19 , and since $r_ l<1$, we have $\sigma (\Phi (K_ m))\leq \sum _ lr_ l^{2n-2}<\eta $, so $\sigma (\Phi (K_ m))=0$. Hence the set of directions $\Phi (K\setminus \{ x\} )= igcup _ m\Phi (K_ m)$ is a Borel set of $\sigma $-measure zero. (3) An orthogonal projection onto a complex hyperplane $H\cong \mathbb R^{2n-2}$ is $1$-Lipschitz. Hence the projection of $K$ is $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null in $H$, and therefore Lebesgue null because $2n-3<2n-2$. $\square$ Theorem 5.11.3 . 76D63A606619 Let $n\ge 2$, let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, and let $S\subset \Omega $ be relatively closed and locally $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null, that is, every point of $S$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $S\cap W$ is $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null. Then every plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega \setminus S$ extends uniquely to a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $, given on $S$ by the same upper-limit formula as in theorem 5.11.1 . Proof. Let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega \setminus S$. For every closed ball $\overline B\subset \Omega $, the compact set $S\cap \overline B$ is covered by finitely many neighborhoods $W$ as in the hypothesis, and is therefore $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null. Step 1: $u$ is locally bounded above near $S$. Fix $p\in S$ and $r>0$ with $\overline B=\overline{B(p,r)}\subset \Omega $, and write $B=B(p,r)$. By lemma 5.11.2 (2) applied with $x=p$, almost every complex line through $p$ meets $S\cap \overline B$ only at $p$; fix such a line $L=\{ p+te:t\in \mathbb {C}\} $, with $|e|=1$. The circle $\Gamma =L\cap \partial B$ is a compact subset of $\Omega \setminus S$, so the upper semicontinuous function $u$ is bounded above on $\Gamma $ by a finite constant $C$, and the open set $O=\{ y\in \Omega \setminus S:u(y)<C+1\} $ contains $\Gamma $. Suppose that $u$ is not bounded above near $p$. Then there are points $x_ j\in B\setminus S$ with $x_ j	o p$ and $u(x_ j)	o +\infty $. For each $j$, lemma 5.11.2 (2) applied with $x=x_ j$ shows that the directions of the lines through $x_ j$ meeting $S\cap \overline B$ form a $\sigma $-null set. Every nonempty open ball in $\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ has positive $\sigma $-measure by lemma 2.9.19 , so the complement of this null set is dense. We can therefore choose directions $\xi _ j$ outside this null set with $d(\xi _ j,[e])<1/j$. Since $d$ is the minimum of the spherical distance over the unit representatives, $\xi _ j$ has a unit representative $e_ j$ whose spherical distance to $e$ is less than $1/j$, and then $|e_ j-e|<1/j$, because a chord is shorter than the arc. Thus $e_ j	o e$, and the lines $L_ j=\{ x_ j+te_ j:t\in \mathbb {C}\} $ do not meet $S\cap \overline B$. We claim that $L_ j\cap \partial B\subset O$ for all large $j$. Let $c_ j$ be the point of $L_ j$ closest to $p$, that is, the orthogonal projection of $p$ to $L_ j$; then $|c_ j-p|\leq |x_ j-p|	o 0$. Since $L_ j$ is a complex line, $c_ j=x_ j+\langle p-x_ j,e_ jangle e_ j$ and $\langle c_ j-p,e_ jangle =0$ for the Hermitian inner product, so $\operatorname{Re}\langle c_ j-p,se_ jangle =0$ and $|c_ j+se_ j-p|^2=|c_ j-p|^2+|s|^2$ for $s\in \mathbb {C}$. Hence $L_ j\cap \partial B$ is the circle $\{ c_ j+ho _ j\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta }e_ j\} $ with $ho _ j=(r^2-|c_ j-p|^2)^{1/2}	o r$. Since $|c_ j+ho _ j\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta }e_ j-p-r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta }e|\leq |c_ j-p|+|ho _ j-r|+r|e_ j-e|$, these circles converge uniformly in $	heta $ to $\Gamma =\{ p+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}	heta }e\} $. The distance from the compact set $\Gamma $ to the closed complement of the open set $O$ is positive, so the circles lie in $O$ for large $j$. For such $j$, the closed disc $\Delta _ j=L_ j\cap \overline B$ lies in $\Omega \setminus S$, and the restriction of $u$ to the connected component of $L_ j\cap (\Omega \setminus S)$ containing $\Delta _ j$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Its values on the boundary circle of $\Delta _ j$ are less than $C+1$, so the maximum principle, that is, theorem 3.4.5 with the constant harmonic function $C+1$, gives $u\leq C+1$ on $\Delta _ j$. Since $x_ j\in B\cap L_ j\subset \Delta _ j$, this gives $u(x_ j)\leq C+1$, contradicting $u(x_ j)	o +\infty $. Hence $u$ is bounded above near every point of $S$. Step 2: the subharmonic extension. By lemma 5.11.2 (1), every compact set $S\cap \overline B$ as above is real polar. Countably many such sets cover $S$, so $S$ is real polar by proposition 4.1.11 . By Step 1 and the upper semicontinuity of $u$ on $\Omega \setminus S$, the function $u$ is bounded above on $K\setminus S$ for every compact $K\subset \Omega $. Moreover $u$ is subharmonic on $\Omega \setminus S$ by theorem 5.9.1 . By theorem 3.4.27 , $u$ has a subharmonic extension $\widetilde u$ to $\Omega $, given on $S$ by the upper-limit formula. Since $S$ is Lebesgue null and $u$ is finite almost everywhere on $\Omega \setminus S$, the function $\widetilde u$ is not identically $-\infty $ on the domain $\Omega $, so it is locally integrable. Step 3: $\widetilde u$ is plurisubharmonic. We verify the hypothesis of lemma 5.8.2 for the locally integrable function $\widetilde u$. Fix a unit vector $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ and a nonnegative $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$, and write $z=v+ta$ with $v\in (\mathbb {C}a)^\perp $ and $t\in \mathbb {C}$, as in that lemma. The compact set $S\cap \operatorname{Supp}\chi $ is $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null, since it is covered by finitely many of the sets $S\cap \overline B$ of the first paragraph, so by lemma 5.11.2 (3) its orthogonal projection onto $(\mathbb {C}a)^\perp $ is Lebesgue null. For $v$ outside this projection, the line $\{ v+ta:t\in \mathbb {C}\} $ meets $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ only in $\Omega \setminus S$. Thus the open set $G_ v=\{ t:v+ta\in \Omega \setminus S\} $ contains $K_ v=\{ t:v+ta\in \operatorname{Supp}\chi \} $, and its connected components are the connected components of an affine complex-line section of $\Omega \setminus S$, on each of which the restriction of $\widetilde u=u$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. As $a$ and $\chi $ are arbitrary, lemma 5.8.2 gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u\geq 0$. Since $\widetilde u$ is a locally integrable subharmonic function, it is the canonical representative of its class, and it is plurisubharmonic by theorem 5.9.1 . Uniqueness follows from the same theorem, since two plurisubharmonic extensions agree outside the Lebesgue null set $S$. $\square$

title: Theorem 5.11.1
text:
Theorem 5.11.1 . C910F1109424 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, $n\ge 1$, and let $S\subset \Omega $ be relatively closed. Assume that every point of $S$ has a connected neighborhood $W\subset \Omega $ with a holomorphic function $f
ot\equiv 0$ on $W$ such that $S\cap W\subset \{ f=0\} $. Let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega \setminus S$ that is locally bounded above near $S$, that is, every point of $S$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $u$ is bounded above on $W\setminus S$. Then $u$ has a unique plurisubharmonic extension $\widetilde u$ to $\Omega $, and its value at $x\in S$ is \[  \widetilde u(x)=\varlimsup _{\Omega \setminus S
i y	o x}u(y).  \] Proof. Define $\widetilde u$ by $u$ on $\Omega \setminus S$ and by the displayed formula on $S$. Since plurisubharmonicity is a local property, it suffices to show that every point $x_0\in S$ has a neighborhood on which $\widetilde u$ is plurisubharmonic; uniqueness is proved at the end. By hypothesis there are a connected neighborhood $W_0$ of $x_0$ with a holomorphic function $f
ot\equiv 0$ on $W_0$ such that $S\cap W_0\subset \{ f=0\} $, and a neighborhood $W_1$ of $x_0$ such that $u$ is bounded above on $W_1\setminus S$. Choose a ball $W$ about $x_0$ with $\overline W\subset W_0\cap W_1$. By the identity theorem, $f$ does not vanish identically on $W$, and $u$ is bounded above on $W\setminus S$. Multiplying $f$ by a nonzero constant, we may assume that $|f|\leq 1$, that is, $\log |f|^2\le 0$, on $W$. For $\varepsilon >0$ define $u_\varepsilon $ on $W$ by \[  u_\varepsilon =u+\varepsilon \log |f|^2\quad 	ext{on }W\setminus S,\qquad u_\varepsilon =-\infty \quad 	ext{on }S\cap W.  \] Step 1: $u_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(W)$. At a point $x\in S\cap W$ we have $f(x)=0$, so $\log |f(y)|^2	o -\infty $ as $y	o x$, while $u$ is bounded above near $x$; hence $u_\varepsilon (y)	o -\infty $ as $y	o x$, and $u_\varepsilon $ is upper semicontinuous at $x$. On $W\setminus S$, $u_\varepsilon $ is upper semicontinuous as a sum of upper semicontinuous functions. Now let $\Lambda $ be a connected component of $L\cap W$ for an affine complex line $L$. If $f$ vanishes identically on $\Lambda $, then $u_\varepsilon \equiv -\infty $ on $\Lambda $. Otherwise the zeros of $f$ on the connected set $\Lambda $ are isolated, by the identity theorem in one variable. Since $S$ is relatively closed, $A=S\cap \Lambda $ is therefore a closed discrete subset of $\Lambda $, hence countable, because each of the countably many compact sets exhausting $\Lambda $ contains only finitely many of its points. It is polar, because points are polar in the plane and countable unions of polar sets are polar by proposition 4.1.11 . Each connected component of $\Lambda \setminus A$ is a connected subset of $L\cap (\Omega \setminus S)$ and therefore lies in a connected component of this line section, on which the restriction of $u$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Hence the restriction of $u$ to $\Lambda \setminus A$ is subharmonic, the constant $-\infty $ being subharmonic. The function $\log |f|^2$ is subharmonic on $\Lambda $ by example 3.4.15 . Thus $u_\varepsilon $ is subharmonic on $\Lambda \setminus A$, and it is bounded above there by $\sup _{W\setminus S}u$, because $\log |f|^2\leq 0$. By theorem 3.4.27 , it has a subharmonic extension to $\Lambda $ whose value at $x\in A$ is $\varlimsup _{\Lambda \setminus A
i y	o x}u_\varepsilon (y)=-\infty $, which is the value of $u_\varepsilon $ at $x$. Hence the restriction of $u_\varepsilon $ to $\Lambda $ is subharmonic. Finally, $u_\varepsilon $ is not identically $-\infty $, because $u$ is finite almost everywhere on $W\setminus S$ and $\{ f=0\} $ is Lebesgue null by lemma 5.5.1 . Thus $u_\varepsilon \in \mathrm{PSH}(W)$. Step 2: the extension. As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ the functions $u_\varepsilon $ increase, because $\log |f|^2\leq 0$, and they are bounded above on $W$ by $\sup _{W\setminus S}u$. Let $F=\sup _{\varepsilon >0}u_\varepsilon $. By theorem 5.10.2 , $F^*\in \mathrm{PSH}(W)$ and $F^*=F$ almost everywhere. Since $F=u$ outside the null set $\{ f=0\} $, we get $F^*=u$ almost everywhere on $W\setminus S$; both functions are locally integrable and subharmonic there, so $F^*=u$ everywhere on $W\setminus S$ by theorem 3.4.12 . It remains to show that $F^*=\widetilde u$ on $S\cap W$, which is Lebesgue null as a subset of $\{ f=0\} $. Let $x\in S\cap W$. Since $F^*=u$ on $W\setminus S$, the upper semicontinuity of $F^*$ gives $\widetilde u(x)=\varlimsup _{W\setminus S
i y	o x}u(y)\leq F^*(x)$. Conversely, for small $r>0$ the ball submean inequality for $F^*$ gives $F^*(x)\leq |B(x,r)|^{-1}\int _{B(x,r)\setminus S}F^*\, \mathrm dV\leq \sup _{B(x,r)\setminus S}u$, because removing the null set $S$ does not change the integral, and letting $r	o 0$ gives $F^*(x)\leq \widetilde u(x)$. Hence $\widetilde u=F^*$ on $W$, and $\widetilde u$ is plurisubharmonic on $W$. Uniqueness. The set $S$ is Lebesgue null, since it is covered by countably many neighborhoods $W$ as in the hypothesis and $S\cap W\subset \{ f=0\} $ is null. Two plurisubharmonic extensions of $u$ therefore agree almost everywhere, and hence everywhere by theorem 5.9.1 . $\square$

title: Theorem 5.11.3
text: Theorem 5.11.3 . 76D63A606619 Let $n\ge 2$, let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a domain, and let $S\subset \Omega $ be relatively closed and locally $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null, that is, every point of $S$ has a neighborhood $W$ such that $S\cap W$ is $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null. Then every plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega \setminus S$ extends uniquely to a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $, given on $S$ by the same upper-limit formula as in theorem 5.11.1 . Proof. Let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega \setminus S$. For every closed ball $\overline B\subset \Omega $, the compact set $S\cap \overline B$ is covered by finitely many neighborhoods $W$ as in the hypothesis, and is therefore $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null. Step 1: $u$ is locally bounded above near $S$. Fix $p\in S$ and $r>0$ with $\overline B=\overline{B(p,r)}\subset \Omega $, and write $B=B(p,r)$. By lemma 5.11.2 (2) applied with $x=p$, almost every complex line through $p$ meets $S\cap \overline B$ only at $p$; fix such a line $L=\{ p+te:t\in \mathbb {C}\} $, with $|e|=1$. The circle $\Gamma =L\cap \partial B$ is a compact subset of $\Omega \setminus S$, so the upper semicontinuous function $u$ is bounded above on $\Gamma $ by a finite constant $C$, and the open set $O=\{ y\in \Omega \setminus S:u(y)<C+1\} $ contains $\Gamma $. Suppose that $u$ is not bounded above near $p$. Then there are points $x_ j\in B\setminus S$ with $x_ j\to p$ and $u(x_ j)\to +\infty $. For each $j$, lemma 5.11.2 (2) applied with $x=x_ j$ shows that the directions of the lines through $x_ j$ meeting $S\cap \overline B$ form a $\sigma $-null set. Every nonempty open ball in $\mathbb P^{n-1}(\mathbb C)$ has positive $\sigma $-measure by lemma 2.9.19 , so the complement of this null set is dense. We can therefore choose directions $\xi _ j$ outside this null set with $d(\xi _ j,[e])<1/j$. Since $d$ is the minimum of the spherical distance over the unit representatives, $\xi _ j$ has a unit representative $e_ j$ whose spherical distance to $e$ is less than $1/j$, and then $|e_ j-e|<1/j$, because a chord is shorter than the arc. Thus $e_ j\to e$, and the lines $L_ j=\{ x_ j+te_ j:t\in \mathbb {C}\} $ do not meet $S\cap \overline B$. We claim that $L_ j\cap \partial B\subset O$ for all large $j$. Let $c_ j$ be the point of $L_ j$ closest to $p$, that is, the orthogonal projection of $p$ to $L_ j$; then $|c_ j-p|\leq |x_ j-p|\to 0$. Since $L_ j$ is a complex line, $c_ j=x_ j+\langle p-x_ j,e_ j\rangle e_ j$ and $\langle c_ j-p,e_ j\rangle =0$ for the Hermitian inner product, so $\operatorname{Re}\langle c_ j-p,se_ j\rangle =0$ and $|c_ j+se_ j-p|^2=|c_ j-p|^2+|s|^2$ for $s\in \mathbb {C}$. Hence $L_ j\cap \partial B$ is the circle $\{ c_ j+\rho _ j\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }e_ j\} $ with $\rho _ j=(r^2-|c_ j-p|^2)^{1/2}\to r$. Since $|c_ j+\rho _ j\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }e_ j-p-r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }e|\leq |c_ j-p|+|\rho _ j-r|+r|e_ j-e|$, these circles converge uniformly in $\theta $ to $\Gamma =\{ p+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }e\} $. The distance from the compact set $\Gamma $ to the closed complement of the open set $O$ is positive, so the circles lie in $O$ for large $j$. For such $j$, the closed disc $\Delta _ j=L_ j\cap \overline B$ lies in $\Omega \setminus S$, and the restriction of $u$ to the connected component of $L_ j\cap (\Omega \setminus S)$ containing $\Delta _ j$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. Its values on the boundary circle of $\Delta _ j$ are less than $C+1$, so the maximum principle, that is, theorem 3.4.5 with the constant harmonic function $C+1$, gives $u\leq C+1$ on $\Delta _ j$. Since $x_ j\in B\cap L_ j\subset \Delta _ j$, this gives $u(x_ j)\leq C+1$, contradicting $u(x_ j)\to +\infty $. Hence $u$ is bounded above near every point of $S$. Step 2: the subharmonic extension. By lemma 5.11.2 (1), every compact set $S\cap \overline B$ as above is real polar. Countably many such sets cover $S$, so $S$ is real polar by proposition 4.1.11 . By Step 1 and the upper semicontinuity of $u$ on $\Omega \setminus S$, the function $u$ is bounded above on $K\setminus S$ for every compact $K\subset \Omega $. Moreover $u$ is subharmonic on $\Omega \setminus S$ by theorem 5.9.1 . By theorem 3.4.27 , $u$ has a subharmonic extension $\widetilde u$ to $\Omega $, given on $S$ by the upper-limit formula. Since $S$ is Lebesgue null and $u$ is finite almost everywhere on $\Omega \setminus S$, the function $\widetilde u$ is not identically $-\infty $ on the domain $\Omega $, so it is locally integrable. Step 3: $\widetilde u$ is plurisubharmonic. We verify the hypothesis of lemma 5.8.2 for the locally integrable function $\widetilde u$. Fix a unit vector $a\in \mathbb {C}^ n$ and a nonnegative $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$, and write $z=v+ta$ with $v\in (\mathbb {C}a)^\perp $ and $t\in \mathbb {C}$, as in that lemma. The compact set $S\cap \operatorname{Supp}\chi $ is $\mathcal H^{2n-3}$-null, since it is covered by finitely many of the sets $S\cap \overline B$ of the first paragraph, so by lemma 5.11.2 (3) its orthogonal projection onto $(\mathbb {C}a)^\perp $ is Lebesgue null. For $v$ outside this projection, the line $\{ v+ta:t\in \mathbb {C}\} $ meets $\operatorname{Supp}\chi $ only in $\Omega \setminus S$. Thus the open set $G_ v=\{ t:v+ta\in \Omega \setminus S\} $ contains $K_ v=\{ t:v+ta\in \operatorname{Supp}\chi \} $, and its connected components are the connected components of an affine complex-line section of $\Omega \setminus S$, on each of which the restriction of $\widetilde u=u$ is subharmonic or identically $-\infty $. As $a$ and $\chi $ are arbitrary, lemma 5.8.2 gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widetilde u\geq 0$. Since $\widetilde u$ is a locally integrable subharmonic function, it is the canonical representative of its class, and it is plurisubharmonic by theorem 5.9.1 . Uniqueness follows from the same theorem, since two plurisubharmonic extensions agree outside the Lebesgue null set $S$. $\square$

title: 5.12 Kiselman's minimum principle
text:
An infimum of plurisubharmonic functions need not be plurisubharmonic. For instance, the function $v(z,w)=|w|^2+2\operatorname{Re}(zw)=|w+\bar z|^2-|z|^2$ is plurisubharmonic on $\mathbb {C}^2$, since $2\operatorname{Re}(zw)$ is pluriharmonic, but $\inf _{w\in \mathbb {C}}v(z,w)=-|z|^2$ is not. Kiselman's minimum principle shows that, under convexity assumptions on the domain, the infimum is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ if it is taken only over the real parts of some variables and the function does not depend on their imaginary parts. The reason is visible for a smooth function $u(z,w)$ that depends only on $z$ and $\operatorname{Re}w$. Its complex Hessian in $w$ is a quarter of its real Hessian in $\operatorname{Re}w$, and at a nondegenerate minimum over $\operatorname{Re}w$, the complex Hessian of the infimum is the Schur complement of the $w$-block in the complex Hessian of $u$, which is positive semidefinite. Throughout this section, points of $\mathbb {C}^ m\times \mathbb {C}^ k$ are written $(z,w)$, and $w=t+\mathrm{i}s$ with $t=\operatorname{Re}w$ and $s=\operatorname{Im}w$ in $\mathbb R^ k$. A set $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ m\times \mathbb {C}^ k$ is invariant under imaginary translations if $(z,w+\mathrm{i}s')\in \Omega $ for all $(z,w)\in \Omega $ and $s'\in \mathbb R^ k$. A function $u$ on such a set is invariant under imaginary translations if $u(z,w+\mathrm{i}s')=u(z,w)$ for all such $(z,w)$ and $s'$, that is, if $u(z,w)$ depends only on $z$ and $\operatorname{Re}w$. For such $\Omega $ and $u$, we identify $t\in \mathbb R^ k$ with $t+\mathrm{i}0\in \mathbb {C}^ k$, so that $u(z,t)$ is defined. We write \[  V_ z=\{ t\in \mathbb R^ k:(z,t)\in \Omega \} ,\qquad \Omega _{\mathbb R}=\{ (z,t)\in \mathbb {C}^ m\times \mathbb R^ k:t\in V_ z\}   \] for the real fiber of $\Omega $ over $z\in \mathbb {C}^ m$ and the real slice of $\Omega $, and $p(\Omega )=\{ z:V_ z\neq \varnothing \} $ for the projection of $\Omega $ to $\mathbb {C}^ m$; it is the image of $\Omega $ under $(z,w)\mapsto z$, because $(z,\operatorname{Re}w)\in \Omega $ for every $(z,w)\in \Omega $ by invariance. Since this projection is continuous and open, $p(\Omega )$ is open if $\Omega $ is open, and connected if $\Omega $ is connected. Theorem 5.12.1 (Kiselman's minimum principle) . 1F87EF4FCF69 Let $m,k\ge 1$, and let $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ m\times \mathbb {C}^ k$ be a domain invariant under imaginary translations whose nonempty real fibers $V_ z$ are convex. Assume that there is a plurisubharmonic function $\psi $ on $\Omega $, invariant under imaginary translations, such that for every $c\in \mathbb R$ the set \[  \{ (z,t)\in \Omega _{\mathbb R}:\psi (z,t)\le c\}   \] is compact. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ is invariant under imaginary translations, then the function \[  v(z)=\inf _{t\in V_ z}u(z,t)  \] is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $p(\Omega )$. Proof. We first treat smooth functions with positive definite real Hessian in $t$ that tend to $+\infty $ at the boundary of the real fibers (Step 1). We then approximate $u$ by such functions on subdomains exhausting $\Omega $ (Step 2) and pass to the limit (Step 3). Step 1: a smooth case. In this step, $\Omega $ may be any open set invariant under imaginary translations whose real fibers are convex. Suppose that $u$ is smooth and plurisubharmonic, invariant under imaginary translations, and that for every $z\in p(\Omega )$ the function $t\mapsto u(z,t)$ has positive definite real Hessian on $V_ z$ and tends to $+\infty $ at the boundary of $V_ z$ and, if $V_ z$ is unbounded, as $|t|\to \infty $. We show that $v$ is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $p(\Omega )$. Fix $z\in p(\Omega )$ and put $f(t)=u(z,t)$ for $t\in V_ z$. Since its Hessian is positive definite, $f$ is strictly convex on every segment in the open convex set $V_ z$, hence on $V_ z$. Its sublevel sets $\{ t\in V_ z:f(t)\leq c\} $ are compact: they are bounded, because $f\to +\infty $ as $|t|\to \infty $ when $V_ z$ is unbounded, and the limit in $\mathbb R^ k$ of a convergent sequence in such a set cannot lie on the boundary of $V_ z$, because $f\to +\infty $ there, so it lies in $V_ z$ and, since $f$ is continuous on $V_ z$, in the sublevel set. Hence $f$ attains its minimum on the nonempty set $V_ z$, and by strict convexity at a unique point $g(z)$. This point is the only critical point of $f$: if $\nabla f(t_1)=0$, then the convex function $s\mapsto f(t_1+s(t_2-t_1))$ has derivative zero at $s=0$, hence $f(t_2)\geq f(t_1)$ for every $t_2\in V_ z$, and $t_1=g(z)$. Fix $z_0\in p(\Omega )$. Since the $t$-Hessian is invertible, the implicit function theorem gives a smooth solution $t=G(z)$ of $\partial _ tu(z,t)=0$ near $z_0$ with $G(z_0)=g(z_0)$, and $G=g$ near $z_0$ because $g(z)$ is the only critical point. Hence $g$ and $v(z)=u(z,g(z))$ are smooth on $p(\Omega )$. At the point $(z,g(z))$, let $H=(\partial ^2u/\partial t_ a\partial t_ b)$, $B=(\partial ^2u/\partial z_ j\partial t_ a)$ and $C=(\partial ^2u/\partial z_ j\partial \bar z_ l)$. Thus $H$ is a real symmetric positive definite $k\times k$ matrix and $B$ is a complex $m\times k$ matrix; since $u$ is real, $(\partial ^2u/\partial t_ a\partial \bar z_ j)=B^*$, the conjugate transpose of $B$. Differentiating the identity $\partial _ tu(z,g(z))=0$ with respect to $\bar z$ gives $B^*+Hg_{\bar z}=0$, where $g_{\bar z}=(\partial g_ a/\partial \bar z_ j)$; hence $g_{\bar z}=-H^{-1}B^*$. By the chain rule and the same identity, $v_{z_ j}(z)=u_{z_ j}(z,g(z))$, and differentiating once more with respect to $\bar z$ gives \[  v_{z\bar z}=C+Bg_{\bar z}=C-BH^{-1}B^*.  \] On the other hand, for functions of $z$ and $\operatorname{Re}w$ we have $\partial _{w_ a}=\partial _{\bar w_ a}=\frac12\partial _{t_ a}$. Hence the complex Hessian of $u$ with respect to $(z,w)$, which is positive semidefinite by proposition 5.9.2 (1), is \[  \begin{pmatrix}  C

& B/2

\\  B^*/2

& H/4

\end{pmatrix}\ge 0.  \] Evaluating the associated Hermitian quadratic form at $(\xi ,-2H^{-1}B^*\xi )$, $\xi \in \mathbb {C}^ m$, gives $\xi ^*(C-BH^{-1}B^*)\xi \geq 0$. Thus $v_{z\bar z}\geq 0$, and the smooth function $v$ is plurisubharmonic on each component of $p(\Omega )$ by proposition 5.9.2 (1). Step 2: regularization. Now let $u$ be as in the theorem. For $\varepsilon >0$ let $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $ and $\psi _\varepsilon =\psi *\rho _\varepsilon $ on $\Omega _\varepsilon =\{ x\in \Omega :\operatorname {dist}(x,\mathbb {C}^{m+k}\setminus \Omega )>\varepsilon \} $, where $\rho _\varepsilon $ is the radial mollifier of section 2.5 . Imaginary translations are isometries preserving $\Omega $, and convolution commutes with translations, so $\Omega _\varepsilon $, $u_\varepsilon $ and $\psi _\varepsilon $ are invariant under imaginary translations. By proposition 5.9.2 , the functions $u_\varepsilon $ and $\psi _\varepsilon $ are smooth and plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $\Omega _\varepsilon $, so their complex Hessians are positive semidefinite at every point, and they decrease to $u$ and $\psi $ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; in particular $u_\varepsilon \geq u$ and $\psi _\varepsilon \geq \psi $. The real fibers of $\Omega _\varepsilon $ are convex. Indeed, $(z,t)\in \Omega _\varepsilon $ if and only if the closed ball of radius $\varepsilon $ about $(z,t)$ lies in $\Omega $ (if it does, its distance to the closed complement of $\Omega $ is positive, because it is compact); by invariance this means that $(z+y,t+y')\in \Omega _{\mathbb R}$ for all $(y,y')\in \mathbb {C}^ m\times \mathbb R^ k$ with $|y|^2+|y'|^2\leq \varepsilon ^2$. Hence the real fiber of $\Omega _\varepsilon $ over $z$ is the intersection of the convex sets $V_{z+y}-y'$ over these $(y,y')$. Moreover, on each real fiber of $\Omega _\varepsilon $ the function $t\mapsto \psi _\varepsilon (z,t)$ is convex, since by invariance its real Hessian is four times the complex Hessian of $\psi _\varepsilon $ in $w$, which is positive semidefinite, and a smooth function with positive semidefinite Hessian on an open convex set is convex along every segment. For $c\in \mathbb R$ let $K_ c=\{ (z,t)\in \Omega _{\mathbb R}:\psi (z,t)\le c\} $; it is a compact subset of $\Omega $. Choose $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, $j\geq 1$, such that $\operatorname {dist}(K_{j+1},\mathbb {C}^{m+k}\setminus \Omega )>4\varepsilon _ j$ whenever $K_{j+1}\neq \varnothing $. Since $\psi $ and the distance to the complement of $\Omega $ are invariant under imaginary translations, the same bound holds for the set $\{ x\in \Omega :\psi (x)\leq j+1\} =K_{j+1}+\mathrm{i}\mathbb R^ k$. Define \[  G_ j=\{ (z,w)\in \Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}:\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}(z,w)<j\} ,\qquad U_ j=u_{\varepsilon _ j}+\frac{|\operatorname{Re}w|^2}{j} +\frac{1}{j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}}\quad \text{on }G_ j.  \] The open set $G_ j$ is invariant under imaginary translations, and its real fiber over $z$ is a sublevel set of the convex function $\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}(z,\, \cdot \, )$ on the convex real fiber of $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}$, hence convex. Since $\psi \leq \psi _{\varepsilon _ j}$, the real slice of $G_ j$ is contained in the compact set $K_ j\subset K_{j+1}$, which lies in $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}$ at positive distance from its complement. Consequently, for each $z$, the closure of the real fiber of $G_ j$ over $z$ is a compact subset of the real fiber of $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}$, and $\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}(z,\, \cdot \, )=j$ on its boundary. The function $U_ j$ is smooth, plurisubharmonic and invariant under imaginary translations. Indeed, by the chain rule the complex Hessian of $1/(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})$ has the entries \[  \frac{(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_{a\bar b}}{(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})^2} +\frac{2(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_ a(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_{\bar b}}{(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})^3},  \] where the subscripts denote derivatives with respect to the coordinates of $(z,w)$. Since $j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}>0$ on $G_ j$ and $(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_{\bar b}=\overline{(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_ b}$, this matrix is the sum of positive multiples of the complex Hessian of $\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}$ and of a positive semidefinite matrix of rank at most one, hence positive semidefinite. Moreover, $|\operatorname{Re}w|^2$ has the positive semidefinite complex Hessian in $(z,w)$ given by the diagonal matrix with entries $0$ in the $z$-directions and $\frac12$ in the $w$-directions. Hence $U_ j$ is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $G_ j$, by proposition 5.9.2 (1). The real $t$-Hessian of $U_ j$ is positive definite: the $t$-Hessians of $u_{\varepsilon _ j}$ and $1/(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})$ are positive semidefinite, as for $\psi _\varepsilon $ above, and that of $|t|^2/j$ is $(2/j)I$. On each real fiber of $G_ j$, which is bounded, $U_ j(z,t)\to +\infty $ at the boundary, because $1/(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})\to +\infty $ there while the other two terms are bounded below on the compact closure of the fiber. Hence Step 1 applies to $U_ j$ on $G_ j$, and \[  v_ j(z)=\inf \{ U_ j(z,t):(z,t)\in G_ j\}   \] is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $p(G_ j)$. Step 3: passage to the limit. The sets $G_ j$ increase to $\Omega $. Indeed, $\varepsilon _{j+1}\leq \varepsilon _ j$ gives $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}\subset \Omega _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}$ and $\psi _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}\leq \psi _{\varepsilon _ j}<j<j+1$ on $G_ j$. Every point $x\in \Omega $ lies in $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}$ for large $j$, and $\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}(x)\to \psi (x)<\infty $, so $x\in G_ j$ for large $j$. On $G_ j$ we have $U_{j+1}\leq U_ j$, since $u_{\varepsilon _{j+1}}\leq u_{\varepsilon _ j}$, $|\operatorname{Re}w|^2/(j+1)\leq |\operatorname{Re}w|^2/j$ and $0<j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}\leq j+1-\psi _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}$. Hence the functions $v_ j$ decrease on the increasing open sets $p(G_ j)$. They satisfy $v_ j\geq v$, since $U_ j\geq u_{\varepsilon _ j}\geq u$. Conversely, let $z\in p(\Omega )$ and $t\in V_ z$. Then $(z,t)\in G_ j$ for large $j$, and $U_ j(z,t)\to u(z,t)$, also when $u(z,t)=-\infty $, because $u_{\varepsilon _ j}(z,t)\to u(z,t)$ and the other two terms tend to zero. Hence $\lim _ jv_ j(z)\leq u(z,t)$ for every $t\in V_ z$, and therefore $v_ j\downarrow v$ on $p(\Omega )$. Let $B'\Subset p(\Omega )$ be a ball. Since $\overline{B'}$ is compact and covered by the increasing open sets $p(G_ j)$, we have $B'\subset p(G_ j)$ for large $j$, and the $v_ j$ with such $j$ form a decreasing sequence of plurisubharmonic functions on $B'$. By theorem 5.10.1 , $v$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $B'$. Since every point of the connected open set $p(\Omega )$ lies in such a ball, lemma 5.9.4 shows that $v$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $p(\Omega )$; this proves the theorem. $\square$ Corollary 5.12.2 . 2C1A82803889 Let $m,k\geq 1$, let $D\subset \mathbb {C}^ m$ be a domain and let $V\subset \mathbb {R}^ k$ be a nonempty open convex set. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(D\times (V+\mathrm{i}\mathbb {R}^ k))$ is invariant under imaginary translations, then the function $z\mapsto \inf _{t\in V}u(z,t)$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $D$. The same holds for $z\mapsto \inf _{t\in V}(u(z,t)-\ell (t))$, for every real affine function $\ell $ on $\mathbb R^ k$. Proof. It suffices to prove the assertion on every ball $B(z_0,r)\Subset D$: since $D$ is connected, lemma 5.9.4 then gives it on $D$. We construct a function $\psi $ as in theorem 5.12.1 for the domain $B(z_0,r)\times (V+\mathrm{i}\mathbb R^ k)$, which is invariant under imaginary translations and has real fibers $V$. We first need a continuous convex function $b\geq 0$ on $V$ with compact sublevel sets. If $V=\mathbb R^ k$, take $b(t)=|t|^2$. Otherwise let $\delta (t)=\operatorname {dist}(t,\mathbb {R}^ k\setminus V)$, which is continuous and positive on $V$. It is concave on $V$: if the balls $B(t_1,r_1)$ and $B(t_2,r_2)$ lie in $V$ and $0\leq \lambda \leq 1$, then by convexity $V$ contains $\lambda B(t_1,r_1)+(1-\lambda )B(t_2,r_2)=B(\lambda t_1+(1-\lambda )t_2,\lambda r_1+(1-\lambda )r_2)$, so $\delta (\lambda t_1+(1-\lambda )t_2)\geq \lambda r_1+(1-\lambda )r_2$, and letting $r_ i\uparrow \delta (t_ i)$ gives concavity. Consequently $1/\delta $ is convex: since $x\mapsto 1/x$ is decreasing and convex on $(0,\infty )$, \[  \frac1{\delta (\lambda t_1+(1-\lambda )t_2)}\leq \frac1{\lambda \delta (t_1)+(1-\lambda )\delta (t_2)}\leq \frac\lambda {\delta (t_1)}+\frac{1-\lambda }{\delta (t_2)}.  \] Put $b(t)=|t|^2+1/\delta (t)$. For $c>0$ the set $\{ b\leq c\} $ is closed in $V$ and contained in the compact set $\{ t:|t|^2\leq c,\  \delta (t)\geq 1/c\} \subset V$, hence compact. A continuous convex function $f$ on $V$ defines a plurisubharmonic function $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ on every domain of the form $D'\times (V+\mathrm{i}\mathbb R^ k)$. Indeed, $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ is continuous, and its restriction to an affine complex line is $f\circ A$ for a real affine map $A$ from an open subset of $\mathbb {C}$ to $V$. If the closed disc of radius $r$ about $\zeta _0$ lies in the domain of $A$, then, since $A$ is affine, $A(\zeta _0)$ is the midpoint of $A(\zeta _0+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta })$ and $A(\zeta _0-r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta })$ for every $\theta $, and the convexity of $f$ gives \[  f(A(\zeta _0))\leq \tfrac 12\bigl (f(A(\zeta _0+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }))+f(A(\zeta _0-r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }))\bigr ).  \] Averaging over $\theta \in [0,2\pi ]$, we obtain the submean inequality for the continuous function $f\circ A$ on this circle. Now put $\psi (z,w)=(r^2-|z-z_0|^2)^{-1}+b(\operatorname{Re}w)$. This function is continuous, positive and invariant under imaginary translations. It is plurisubharmonic as a sum of two plurisubharmonic functions (proposition 5.9.5 ). The second term is plurisubharmonic by the preceding paragraph. For the first, $x\mapsto (r^2-x)^{-1}$ is convex and increasing on $(-\infty ,r^2)$ and $|z-z_0|^2$ has the complex Hessian $I$, so by the chain rule the complex Hessian of $(r^2-|z-z_0|^2)^{-1}$ is positive semidefinite, and proposition 5.9.2 (1) applies. For $c>0$, the set $\{ (z,t)\in B(z_0,r)\times V:\psi (z,t)\leq c\} $ is closed in $B(z_0,r)\times V$ and, since both terms of $\psi $ are nonnegative, contained in the compact set $\{ |z-z_0|^2\leq r^2-1/c\} \times \{ b\leq c\} $; it is therefore compact, and for $c\leq 0$ it is empty. Hence theorem 5.12.1 applies on $B(z_0,r)\times (V+\mathrm{i}\mathbb R^ k)$, and shows that $\inf _{t\in V}u(z,t)$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $B(z_0,r)$. Finally, if $\ell $ is real affine, then $\ell (\operatorname{Re}w)$ is the real part of a complex affine function of $w$. Hence $-\ell (\operatorname{Re}w)$ is smooth with vanishing complex Hessian, so it is plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.2 (1), and $u-\ell (\operatorname{Re}w)$ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.5 . It is invariant under imaginary translations, and the first part applies to it. $\square$

text:

& B/2

\\  B^*/2

& H/4

\end{pmatrix}\ge 0.  \] Evaluating the associated Hermitian quadratic form at $(\xi ,-2H^{-1}B^*\xi )$, $\xi \in \mathbb {C}^ m$, gives $\xi ^*(C-BH^{-1}B^*)\xi \geq 0$.
