The real fibers of $\Omega _\varepsilon $ are convex. Indeed, $(z,t)\in \Omega _\varepsilon $ if and only if the closed ball of radius $\varepsilon $ about $(z,t)$ lies in $\Omega $ (if it does, its distance to the closed complement of $\Omega $ is positive, because it is compact); by invariance this means that $(z+y,t+y')\in \Omega _{\mathbb R}$ for all $(y,y')\in \mathbb {C}^ m\times \mathbb R^ k$ with $|y|^2+|y'|^2\leq \varepsilon ^2$. Hence the real fiber of $\Omega _\varepsilon $ over $z$ is the intersection of the convex sets $V_{z+y}-y'$ over these $(y,y')$. Moreover, on each real fiber of $\Omega _\varepsilon $ the function $t\mapsto \psi _\varepsilon (z,t)$ is convex, since by invariance its real Hessian is four times the complex Hessian of $\psi _\varepsilon $ in $w$, which is positive semidefinite, and a smooth function with positive semidefinite Hessian on an open convex set is convex along every segment. For $c\in \mathbb R$ let $K_ c=\{ (z,t)\in \Omega _{\mathbb R}:\psi (z,t)\le c\} $; it is a compact subset of $\Omega $. Choose $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, $j\geq 1$, such that $\operatorname {dist}(K_{j+1},\mathbb {C}^{m+k}\setminus \Omega )>4\varepsilon _ j$ whenever $K_{j+1}\neq \varnothing $. Since $\psi $ and the distance to the complement of $\Omega $ are invariant under imaginary translations, the same bound holds for the set $\{ x\in \Omega :\psi (x)\leq j+1\} =K_{j+1}+\mathrm{i}\mathbb R^ k$. Define \[  G_ j=\{ (z,w)\in \Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}:\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}(z,w)<j\} ,\qquad U_ j=u_{\varepsilon _ j}+\frac{|\operatorname{Re}w|^2}{j} +\frac{1}{j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}}\quad \text{on }G_ j.  \] The open set $G_ j$ is invariant under imaginary translations, and its real fiber over $z$ is a sublevel set of the convex function $\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}(z,\, \cdot \, )$ on the convex real fiber of $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}$, hence convex. Since $\psi \leq \psi _{\varepsilon _ j}$, the real slice of $G_ j$ is contained in the compact set $K_ j\subset K_{j+1}$, which lies in $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}$ at positive distance from its complement. Consequently, for each $z$, the closure of the real fiber of $G_ j$ over $z$ is a compact subset of the real fiber of $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}$, and $\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}(z,\, \cdot \, )=j$ on its boundary. The function $U_ j$ is smooth, plurisubharmonic and invariant under imaginary translations. Indeed, by the chain rule the complex Hessian of $1/(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})$ has the entries \[  \frac{(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_{a\bar b}}{(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})^2} +\frac{2(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_ a(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_{\bar b}}{(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})^3},  \] where the subscripts denote derivatives with respect to the coordinates of $(z,w)$. Since $j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}>0$ on $G_ j$ and $(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_{\bar b}=\overline{(\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})_ b}$, this matrix is the sum of positive multiples of the complex Hessian of $\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}$ and of a positive semidefinite matrix of rank at most one, hence positive semidefinite. Moreover, $|\operatorname{Re}w|^2$ has the positive semidefinite complex Hessian in $(z,w)$ given by the diagonal matrix with entries $0$ in the $z$-directions and $\frac12$ in the $w$-directions. Hence $U_ j$ is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $G_ j$, by proposition 5.9.2 (1). The real $t$-Hessian of $U_ j$ is positive definite: the $t$-Hessians of $u_{\varepsilon _ j}$ and $1/(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})$ are positive semidefinite, as for $\psi _\varepsilon $ above, and that of $|t|^2/j$ is $(2/j)I$. On each real fiber of $G_ j$, which is bounded, $U_ j(z,t)\to +\infty $ at the boundary, because $1/(j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j})\to +\infty $ there while the other two terms are bounded below on the compact closure of the fiber. Hence Step 1 applies to $U_ j$ on $G_ j$, and \[  v_ j(z)=\inf \{ U_ j(z,t):(z,t)\in G_ j\}   \] is plurisubharmonic on each connected component of $p(G_ j)$. Step 3: passage to the limit. The sets $G_ j$ increase to $\Omega $. Indeed, $\varepsilon _{j+1}\leq \varepsilon _ j$ gives $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}\subset \Omega _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}$ and $\psi _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}\leq \psi _{\varepsilon _ j}<j<j+1$ on $G_ j$. Every point $x\in \Omega $ lies in $\Omega _{\varepsilon _ j}$ for large $j$, and $\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}(x)\to \psi (x)<\infty $, so $x\in G_ j$ for large $j$. On $G_ j$ we have $U_{j+1}\leq U_ j$, since $u_{\varepsilon _{j+1}}\leq u_{\varepsilon _ j}$, $|\operatorname{Re}w|^2/(j+1)\leq |\operatorname{Re}w|^2/j$ and $0<j-\psi _{\varepsilon _ j}\leq j+1-\psi _{\varepsilon _{j+1}}$. Hence the functions $v_ j$ decrease on the increasing open sets $p(G_ j)$. They satisfy $v_ j\geq v$, since $U_ j\geq u_{\varepsilon _ j}\geq u$. Conversely, let $z\in p(\Omega )$ and $t\in V_ z$. Then $(z,t)\in G_ j$ for large $j$, and $U_ j(z,t)\to u(z,t)$, also when $u(z,t)=-\infty $, because $u_{\varepsilon _ j}(z,t)\to u(z,t)$ and the other two terms tend to zero. Hence $\lim _ jv_ j(z)\leq u(z,t)$ for every $t\in V_ z$, and therefore $v_ j\downarrow v$ on $p(\Omega )$. Let $B'\Subset p(\Omega )$ be a ball. Since $\overline{B'}$ is compact and covered by the increasing open sets $p(G_ j)$, we have $B'\subset p(G_ j)$ for large $j$, and the $v_ j$ with such $j$ form a decreasing sequence of plurisubharmonic functions on $B'$. By theorem 5.10.1 , $v$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $B'$. Since every point of the connected open set $p(\Omega )$ lies in such a ball, lemma 5.9.4 shows that $v$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $p(\Omega )$; this proves the theorem. $\square$

title: Corollary 5.12.2
text: Corollary 5.12.2 . 2C1A82803889 Let $m,k\geq 1$, let $D\subset \mathbb {C}^ m$ be a domain and let $V\subset \mathbb {R}^ k$ be a nonempty open convex set. If $u\in \mathrm{PSH}(D\times (V+\mathrm{i}\mathbb {R}^ k))$ is invariant under imaginary translations, then the function $z\mapsto \inf _{t\in V}u(z,t)$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $D$. The same holds for $z\mapsto \inf _{t\in V}(u(z,t)-\ell (t))$, for every real affine function $\ell $ on $\mathbb R^ k$. Proof. It suffices to prove the assertion on every ball $B(z_0,r)\Subset D$: since $D$ is connected, lemma 5.9.4 then gives it on $D$. We construct a function $\psi $ as in theorem 5.12.1 for the domain $B(z_0,r)\times (V+\mathrm{i}\mathbb R^ k)$, which is invariant under imaginary translations and has real fibers $V$. We first need a continuous convex function $b\geq 0$ on $V$ with compact sublevel sets. If $V=\mathbb R^ k$, take $b(t)=|t|^2$. Otherwise let $\delta (t)=\operatorname {dist}(t,\mathbb {R}^ k\setminus V)$, which is continuous and positive on $V$. It is concave on $V$: if the balls $B(t_1,r_1)$ and $B(t_2,r_2)$ lie in $V$ and $0\leq \lambda \leq 1$, then by convexity $V$ contains $\lambda B(t_1,r_1)+(1-\lambda )B(t_2,r_2)=B(\lambda t_1+(1-\lambda )t_2,\lambda r_1+(1-\lambda )r_2)$, so $\delta (\lambda t_1+(1-\lambda )t_2)\geq \lambda r_1+(1-\lambda )r_2$, and letting $r_ i\uparrow \delta (t_ i)$ gives concavity. Consequently $1/\delta $ is convex: since $x\mapsto 1/x$ is decreasing and convex on $(0,\infty )$, \[  \frac1{\delta (\lambda t_1+(1-\lambda )t_2)}\leq \frac1{\lambda \delta (t_1)+(1-\lambda )\delta (t_2)}\leq \frac\lambda {\delta (t_1)}+\frac{1-\lambda }{\delta (t_2)}.  \] Put $b(t)=|t|^2+1/\delta (t)$. For $c>0$ the set $\{ b\leq c\} $ is closed in $V$ and contained in the compact set $\{ t:|t|^2\leq c,\  \delta (t)\geq 1/c\} \subset V$, hence compact. A continuous convex function $f$ on $V$ defines a plurisubharmonic function $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ on every domain of the form $D'\times (V+\mathrm{i}\mathbb R^ k)$. Indeed, $f(\operatorname{Re}w)$ is continuous, and its restriction to an affine complex line is $f\circ A$ for a real affine map $A$ from an open subset of $\mathbb {C}$ to $V$. If the closed disc of radius $r$ about $\zeta _0$ lies in the domain of $A$, then, since $A$ is affine, $A(\zeta _0)$ is the midpoint of $A(\zeta _0+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta })$ and $A(\zeta _0-r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta })$ for every $\theta $, and the convexity of $f$ gives \[  f(A(\zeta _0))\leq \tfrac 12\bigl (f(A(\zeta _0+r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }))+f(A(\zeta _0-r\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i}\theta }))\bigr ).  \] Averaging over $\theta \in [0,2\pi ]$, we obtain the submean inequality for the continuous function $f\circ A$ on this circle. Now put $\psi (z,w)=(r^2-|z-z_0|^2)^{-1}+b(\operatorname{Re}w)$. This function is continuous, positive and invariant under imaginary translations. It is plurisubharmonic as a sum of two plurisubharmonic functions (proposition 5.9.5 ). The second term is plurisubharmonic by the preceding paragraph. For the first, $x\mapsto (r^2-x)^{-1}$ is convex and increasing on $(-\infty ,r^2)$ and $|z-z_0|^2$ has the complex Hessian $I$, so by the chain rule the complex Hessian of $(r^2-|z-z_0|^2)^{-1}$ is positive semidefinite, and proposition 5.9.2 (1) applies. For $c>0$, the set $\{ (z,t)\in B(z_0,r)\times V:\psi (z,t)\leq c\} $ is closed in $B(z_0,r)\times V$ and, since both terms of $\psi $ are nonnegative, contained in the compact set $\{ |z-z_0|^2\leq r^2-1/c\} \times \{ b\leq c\} $; it is therefore compact, and for $c\leq 0$ it is empty. Hence theorem 5.12.1 applies on $B(z_0,r)\times (V+\mathrm{i}\mathbb R^ k)$, and shows that $\inf _{t\in V}u(z,t)$ is plurisubharmonic or identically $-\infty $ on $B(z_0,r)$. Finally, if $\ell $ is real affine, then $\ell (\operatorname{Re}w)$ is the real part of a complex affine function of $w$. Hence $-\ell (\operatorname{Re}w)$ is smooth with vanishing complex Hessian, so it is plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.2 (1), and $u-\ell (\operatorname{Re}w)$ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.5 . It is invariant under imaginary translations, and the first part applies to it. $\square$

title: 7.1 Bedford–Taylor products and local capacity
text: Let $u$ be a plurisubharmonic function on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$. By theorem 5.9.1 , $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ is a closed positive $(1,1)$-current, but in general its coefficients are only measures. Since products of measures have no general meaning, the exterior powers of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$ cannot be formed by multiplying coefficients. For $u\in C^2(\Omega )$ the top power is the Monge–Ampère measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=n!\, \pi ^{-n}\det (u_{j\bar k})\, \mathrm{d}V_{2n}$. This fully nonlinear expression in the second derivatives of $u$ plays in pluripotential theory the role that the Laplacian plays in classical potential theory. Bedford and Taylor showed that for locally bounded $u$ these powers can be defined by induction, and so can the mixed products $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$ with a closed positive current $T$. Indeed, since $T$ has measure coefficients and $u$ is a locally bounded Borel function, the product $uT$ makes sense, and one puts $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uT)$. This chapter develops the local theory of these products, whose factors are always locally bounded; products of unbounded potentials are treated in section 13.1 . The first two sections establish the basic properties of the products: positivity, the Chern–Levine–Nirenberg mass bounds, continuity along decreasing sequences and symmetry (theorem 7.3.7 ), and the comparison principle. The products then define the Monge–Ampère capacity, a complex analogue of the relative capacity of section 4.1 . Locally, pole sets of plurisubharmonic functions have outer capacity zero; plurisubharmonic functions are quasi-continuous with respect to this capacity, and the products are continuous under convergence in capacity and along increasing sequences. Solving the homogeneous Monge–Ampère equation on a ball, we show that a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function is maximal if and only if its Monge–Ampère measure vanishes. These are the tools with which section 5.47 characterizes pluripolar sets. The remaining sections, needed for non-pluripolar products and envelopes on compact manifolds in section 13.1 , section 16.10 , solve the equation $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mu $ on a ball for increasingly singular measures $\mu $: continuous densities, bounded densities, and finally compactly supported measures dominated by the Monge–Ampère measure of a bounded plurisubharmonic function. The main application is a lower bound for mixed products: if $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ i)^ n\geq f_ i\mu $ for $1\le i\le n$, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ n\geq (f_1\cdots f_ n)^{1/n}\mu $ (theorem 7.12.1 ). The chapter closes with the locality of complex Hessians on contact sets and a chain rule for gradients against positive currents. Historical remarks and references for this chapter are collected in subsection 25.1.9 .

title: 7.2 Bounded potentials and recursive products
text: Throughout this section and the next, $\Omega \subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ is open, $n\ge 1$, and $T$ is a closed positive current on $\Omega $ of bidimension $(r,r)$, where $0\le r\le n$ is an integer; thus $T$ has bidegree $(n-r,n-r)$. Let $\beta =(\mathrm{i}/2)\sum _ j\mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ j$ be the form of ( 5.2.8 ). For a positive current $S$ of bidimension $(s,s)$ on $\Omega $ and a compact set $K\subset \Omega $ we write \[  \| S\| _ K=\int _ KS\wedge \frac{\beta ^ s}{s!}  \] for the mass of $S$ on $K$; it is $1/s!$ times the value on $K$ of the trace measure of $S$ (definition 5.3.5 ). By theorem 5.3.7 , $S$ is a current of order zero, and the total variations of its coefficient measures are bounded by a constant multiple, depending only on $n$ and $s$, of its trace measure. Since plurisubharmonic functions are upper semicontinuous, they are bounded above on compact sets; hence a plurisubharmonic function is locally bounded if and only if it is bounded below on compact sets. Definition 7.2.1 . 254CDCCCAB5E Suppose that $r\ge 1$, and let $u$ be a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $. Let $uT$ be the current of order zero obtained by multiplying the coefficient measures of $T$ by the locally bounded Borel function $u$ (section 5.3 ), and define \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uT).  \] For an integer $1\le q\le r$ and locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ on $\Omega $, define recursively \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl (u_1\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T\bigr ).  \] Here $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$ is a closed positive current, hence of order zero, by proposition 7.2.2 below applied to $q-1$ factors; so its product with $u_1$ is defined as before. The product with no factors is $T$. When $T=1$ (so that $r=n$), $q=n$ and $u_1=\cdots =u_ n=u$, the resulting positive current of bidegree $(n,n)$ is a positive measure, the Monge–Ampère measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ of $u$. Proposition 7.2.2 . D9911E035563 Every product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$ of definition 7.2.1 is a closed positive current, and it has the following properties. If $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ are smooth, it coincides with the exterior product of the smooth forms $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$ with $T$. The construction is local: if $u_ j=v_ j$ for every $j$ and $T=T'$ on an open set $U\subset \Omega $, then the two products agree on $U$. It is additive and positively homogeneous in each $u_ j$ and in $T$, whenever the summands are locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions, respectively closed positive currents of bidimension $(r,r)$, and it does not change if a real constant is added to some $u_ j$. If $\gamma $ is a smooth closed form of bidegree $(s,s)$, $q\le r-s$, such that $T\wedge \gamma $ is positive (for instance, $\gamma $ strongly positive), then \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge (T\wedge \gamma )=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T)\wedge \gamma .  \] It is invariant under biholomorphic maps: if $F\colon \Omega '\to \Omega $ is biholomorphic and $F^*$ denotes the pullback of currents of proposition 5.6.2 , then \[  F^*\bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T\bigr )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_1\circ F)\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ q\circ F)\wedge F^*T.  \] Proof. We first record two consequences of the Leibniz rule of section 5.3 . Let $R$ be a current of even degree on an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$ such that $\partial R=\bar\partial R=0$; this holds if $R$ is closed and of pure bidegree. If $f$ is a smooth function, then $\mathrm d(fR)=\mathrm df\wedge R$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(fR)=\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge R$, and applying $\mathrm d$ to the latter gives EDF346A35F76 7.2.3 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(fR)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge R. \end{equation} If $\gamma $ is a smooth closed form of pure bidegree, then $\partial \gamma $ and $\bar\partial \gamma $ are the components of $\mathrm d\gamma =0$ of two different bidegrees, so they vanish, and the Leibniz rule gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(R'\wedge \gamma )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R'\wedge \gamma $ for every current $R'$. We now prove positivity and closedness, first for a single factor $u$. By proposition 5.9.2 , the regularizations $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $ by the radial mollifiers of section 2.5 are smooth plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ with positive semidefinite complex Hessians, and they decrease to $u$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. On each compact set the $u_\varepsilon $ are bounded uniformly in $\varepsilon $, because $u\le u_\varepsilon \le u_{\varepsilon _0}$ for $\varepsilon \le \varepsilon _0$ and $u$ is locally bounded. Dominated convergence with respect to the total variations of the coefficient measures of $T$ therefore gives $u_\varepsilon T\to uT$ weakly. By ( 7.2.3 ), $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_\varepsilon T)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon \wedge T$. Since weak and strong positivity agree in bidegree $(1,1)$ (section 5.3 ), the positive smooth form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon $ is strongly positive, so its product with the positive current $T$ is positive; it is also closed. As $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ is continuous for weak convergence, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon \wedge T\to \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uT)$ weakly, and positivity and closedness pass to the limit. Thus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T$ is positive and closed. Applying this with $T$ replaced by the closed positive current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$, we obtain the first assertion by induction on $q$. (1) If the $u_ j$ are smooth, ( 7.2.3 ) shows at each step of the recursion that the product is the exterior product of smooth forms with $T$. (2), (3) The definition uses only multiplication of coefficient measures by functions and the operator $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$; both operations are local and linear, and no product of two measures occurs. This gives locality, and additivity and positive homogeneity in $u_1$ and in $T$; for the other factors they follow by induction on $q$, since multiplication by $u_1$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ are linear. If $c$ is a constant and $R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((u_1+c)R)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_1R)+c\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_1R)$, since $R$ is closed; for the other factors the invariance under constants follows again by induction. (4) The product $T\wedge \gamma $ is closed, and multiplication of coefficient measures by $u_1$ commutes with the exterior product by $\gamma $. By the identity $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(R'\wedge \gamma )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R'\wedge \gamma $ and induction on $q$, every step of the recursion commutes with $\wedge \gamma $. (5) The pullback $F^*T$ is closed and positive and commutes with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, hence with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ (proposition 5.6.2 ), and the functions $u_ j\circ F$ are locally bounded and plurisubharmonic (proposition 5.9.3 ). We claim that $F^*(uT)=(u\circ F)F^*T$ for a locally bounded plurisubharmonic $u$. For a smooth function $f$ we have $F^*(fT)=(f\circ F)F^*T$: both sides are weakly continuous in $T$, they agree when $T$ is smooth, and on every relatively compact open subset of $\Omega $ the current $T$ is the weak limit of its smooth regularizations (discussion following theorem 5.3.7 ). Applying this to the regularizations $u_\varepsilon $ on relatively compact open subsets, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we obtain the claim: $u_\varepsilon T\to uT$ as shown above, so $F^*(u_\varepsilon T)\to F^*(uT)$, while $(u_\varepsilon \circ F)F^*T\to (u\circ F)F^*T$ by dominated convergence with respect to the coefficient measures of the positive current $F^*T$. Consequently every step of the recursion commutes with $F^*$, which proves (5). In particular, by (2) and (5), products of locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions with closed positive currents on a complex manifold can be computed in holomorphic charts: the products defined in two charts agree on their overlap. $\square$ Let $u\in C^2(\Omega )$ be real, and write $a_{jk}=u_{j\bar k}$, so that $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\sum _{j,k}a_{jk}\, \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ k$ by ( 5.2.9 ). The $2$-forms $\alpha _{jk}=\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ k$ commute with each other, and $\alpha _{j_1k_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \alpha _{j_ nk_ n}=0$ unless $(j_1,\ldots ,j_ n)$ and $(k_1,\ldots ,k_ n)$ are permutations of $(1,\ldots ,n)$. If $j_ i=\sigma (i)$ and $k_ i=\tau (i)$ for permutations $\sigma ,\tau $, we may reorder the commuting factors so that the first indices increase; with $\kappa =\tau \circ \sigma ^{-1}$ we get $\mathrm dz_1\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_{\kappa (1)}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_{\kappa (n)}$, and permuting the $1$-forms $\mathrm d\bar z_{\kappa (i)}$ among themselves gives the sign $\operatorname {sgn}\kappa $. Hence \[  \Bigl (\sum _{j,k}a_{jk}\alpha _{jk}\Bigr )^ n =\sum _{\sigma ,\tau }\prod _{i=1}^ na_{\sigma (i)\tau (i)}\, \operatorname {sgn}(\tau \sigma ^{-1})\, \bigwedge _{j=1}^ n\alpha _{jj} =n!\det (a_{jk})\bigwedge _{j=1}^ n\alpha _{jj},  \] because for each of the $n!$ permutations $\sigma $ the sum over $\tau $ is $\sum _\kappa \operatorname {sgn}\kappa \prod _ ja_{j\kappa (j)}=\det (a_{jk})$. Since $\mathrm{i}\, \mathrm{d}z_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}\bar z_ j=2\, \mathrm{d}x_ j\wedge \mathrm{d}y_ j$, we have $\bigwedge _ j(\mathrm i\alpha _{jj})=2^ n\mathrm dV_{2n}$, and therefore 706A589A680C 7.2.4 \begin{equation}  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\Bigl (\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\Bigr )^ nn!\det (u_{j\bar k})\bigwedge _{j=1}^ n\alpha _{jj}=\frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\det (u_{j\bar k})\, \mathrm{d}V_{2n}. \end{equation} Here $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ is the exterior power of the continuous form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u$; when $u$ is smooth and plurisubharmonic, it is the Monge–Ampère measure of $u$, by proposition 7.2.2 (1), and the same holds for plurisubharmonic $u\in C^2(\Omega )$ (see the remark after proposition 7.2.6 ). In particular $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\sum _ j\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j=\beta /\pi $ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2)^ n=n!\pi ^{-n}\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$. (The formula also holds for $n=0$: the empty product is the constant $1$, and both sides are the unit mass $\mathrm{d}V_0$ on the point $\mathbb C^0$.) Theorem 7.2.5 (Chern–Levine–Nirenberg) . 2A84C325AB58 Let $K,L\subset \Omega $ be compact sets with $K\subset \operatorname{Int}L$, and let $0\le q\le r$ be an integer. There is a constant $C_{K,L,q}$, depending only on $K$, $L$, $n$ and $q$, such that \[  \| \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T\| _ K \le C_{K,L,q}\| T\| _ L\prod _{j=1}^ q\| u_ j\| _{L^\infty (L)}  \] for every closed positive current $T$ of bidimension $(r,r)$ on $\Omega $ and all locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ on $\Omega $. Here $\| u_ j\| _{L^\infty (L)}=\sup _ L|u_ j|$ is the pointwise supremum. Proof. For $q=0$ the estimate holds with constant $1$, since $K\subset L$. Let $q=1$ and write $u=u_1$. By lemma 2.5.1 there is a smooth function $0\le \chi \le 1$ with compact support in $\operatorname{Int}L$ which equals $1$ on a neighborhood of $K$; it depends only on $K$ and $L$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1}$ is a positive measure, $\beta $ is closed, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S)(\chi )=S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi )$ for currents $S$ of bidimension $(1,1)$, we have \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _ K\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1} & \le \int \chi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uT)\wedge \beta ^{r-1} =\bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uT\wedge \beta ^{r-1})\bigr )(\chi )\\ & =\int uT\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \wedge \beta ^{r-1} \le C\| u\| _{L^\infty (L)}\| T\| _ L. \end{aligned}  \] The form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \wedge \beta ^{r-1}$ is smooth with support in $L$, though in general not positive; its coefficients are bounded by a constant depending only on $\chi $ and $n$. The last inequality therefore holds because the total variations of the coefficient measures of $T$ on $L$ are bounded by a constant multiple of $\| T\| _ L$, the multiple depending only on $n$ and $r$ (theorem 5.3.7 ). Dividing by $(r-1)!$ and taking the largest of the constants obtained for $r=1,\ldots ,n$, we obtain the case $q=1$ with a constant depending only on $K$, $L$ and $n$. For $q>1$, let $\delta >0$ be the distance from $K$ to $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \operatorname{Int}L$ (if $K=\varnothing $ there is nothing to prove), and put $L_ j=\{ z:\operatorname {dist}(z,K)\le j\delta /(q+1)\} $ for $0\le j<q$ and $L_ q=L$. These are compact sets, depending only on $K$, $L$ and $q$, with $K=L_0$ and $L_{j-1}\subset \operatorname{Int}L_ j$ for $1\le j\le q$. By proposition 7.2.2 , the currents $S_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{j+1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$, $0\le j\le q$, are positive and closed, and $S_{j-1}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\wedge S_ j$. The case $q=1$, applied to $S_ j$ and the pair $L_{j-1}\subset \operatorname{Int}L_ j$, gives $\| S_{j-1}\| _{L_{j-1}}\le C_ j\| u_ j\| _{L^\infty (L)}\| S_ j\| _{L_ j}$ for $j=1,\ldots ,q$, since $\| u_ j\| _{L^\infty (L_ j)}\le \| u_ j\| _{L^\infty (L)}$. Combining these $q$ inequalities, we obtain the estimate with $C_{K,L,q}=C_1\cdots C_ q$. $\square$ For continuous potentials, uniform convergence is enough to pass to the limit in the products. Proposition 7.2.6 . 2F39A3F97E8E Let $T_ k\to T$ weakly, where $T_ k$ and $T$ are closed positive currents on $\Omega $ of bidimension $(r,r)$, and let $0\le q\le r$. For $1\le j\le q$, let $(u_{j,k})_{k\ge 1}$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $ converging locally uniformly, as $k\to \infty $, to a continuous function $u_ j$, and let $(u_{0,k})_{k\ge 1}$ be locally bounded Borel functions on $\Omega $ converging locally uniformly to a continuous function $u_0$. Then $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ are plurisubharmonic, and \[  \begin{aligned}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q,k}\wedge T_ k & \longrightarrow \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T,\\  u_{0,k}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q,k}\wedge T_ k & \longrightarrow u_0\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T \end{aligned}  \] weakly as $k\to \infty $. Proof. We first show that $u_ j$ is plurisubharmonic for $1\le j\le q$. Since plurisubharmonicity is a local property, it suffices to prove this on every ball $W\Subset \Omega $. Choose $k_1<k_2<\cdots $ such that $|u_{j,k_ m}-u_ j|\le 2^{-m}$ on $W$, and put $w_ m=u_{j,k_ m}+3\cdot 2^{-m}$. These functions are plurisubharmonic on $W$, and they decrease, because \[  w_{m+1}\le u_ j+2^{-m-1}+3\cdot 2^{-m-1}=u_ j+2^{1-m}\le u_{j,k_ m}+2^{-m}+2^{1-m}=w_ m.  \] Their limit $u_ j$ is finite, so it is plurisubharmonic on $W$ by theorem 5.10.1 . Since the $u_{j,k}$ converge locally uniformly to continuous functions, they are bounded on each compact set uniformly in $k$. Since $T_ k\to T$ weakly, the masses $\| T_ k\| _ L$ are bounded for each compact set $L$: if $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(\Omega )$ satisfies $0\le \chi \le 1$ and $\chi =1$ on $L$, then $\| T_ k\| _ L\le T_ k(\chi \beta ^ r)/r!$, and the right-hand side converges. By theorem 7.2.5 , the masses of all the products considered below are therefore bounded on compact sets uniformly in $k$, and so are the total variations of their coefficient measures (theorem 5.3.7 ). We claim: if $S_ k\to S$ weakly, where $S_ k$ and $S$ are closed positive currents whose masses are bounded on compact sets uniformly in $k$, and if locally bounded Borel functions $v_ k$ converge locally uniformly to a continuous function $v$, then $v_ kS_ k\to vS$ weakly. Applying this to $S_ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{2,k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q,k}\wedge T_ k$ and $v_ k=u_{1,k}$, and then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, which is weakly continuous, proves the first assertion by induction on $q$; the case $q=0$ is the hypothesis. The second assertion is the claim with $v_ k=u_{0,k}$. To prove the claim, fix a test form $\varphi $ with compact support $K$ and $\varepsilon >0$. By lemma 2.5.1 (1), applied to $v$ on a relatively compact open neighborhood of $K$, there is a smooth function $v_\varepsilon $ on a neighborhood of $K$ with $|v-v_\varepsilon |\le \varepsilon $ on $K$. Write \[  v_ kS_ k-vS=(v_ k-v)S_ k+(v-v_\varepsilon )S_ k +v_\varepsilon (S_ k-S)+(v_\varepsilon -v)S.  \] Evaluated on $\varphi $, a term $fS_ k$ with a bounded Borel function $f$ is at most $C_\varphi \sup _ K|f|$ times the total variation on $K$ of the coefficient measures of $S_ k$, where $C_\varphi $ bounds the coefficients of $\varphi $; the same holds for $S$. Hence the first term tends to zero, since $v_ k\to v$ uniformly on $K$; the second and fourth terms are bounded by a constant times $\varepsilon $, uniformly in $k$; and the third tends to zero as $k\to \infty $, since $v_\varepsilon \varphi $ is a test form. Letting first $k\to \infty $ and then $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ proves the claim. $\square$ If $u\in C^2(\Omega )$ is plurisubharmonic, its Monge–Ampère measure is given by ( 7.2.4 ). Indeed, the regularizations $u_\varepsilon $ are smooth and plurisubharmonic on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ (proposition 5.9.2 ) and converge to $u$ locally uniformly (lemma 2.5.1 (1)), and their second derivatives are the regularizations of the continuous second derivatives of $u$ (proposition 2.5.3 ), so they also converge locally uniformly. Hence $\det ((u_\varepsilon )_{j\bar k})\to \det (u_{j\bar k})$ locally uniformly. Applying ( 7.2.4 ) to $u_\varepsilon $ and proposition 7.2.6 on each $\Omega _{\varepsilon _0}$, along a sequence $\varepsilon _ k\downarrow 0$ with $\varepsilon _ k<\varepsilon _0$, we obtain the formula for $u$ on every $\Omega _{\varepsilon _0}$, hence on $\Omega $.

title: Definition 7.2.1
text: Definition 7.2.1 . 254CDCCCAB5E Suppose that $r\ge 1$, and let $u$ be a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $. Let $uT$ be the current of order zero obtained by multiplying the coefficient measures of $T$ by the locally bounded Borel function $u$ (section 5.3 ), and define \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uT).  \] For an integer $1\le q\le r$ and locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ on $\Omega $, define recursively \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl (u_1\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T\bigr ).  \] Here $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$ is a closed positive current, hence of order zero, by proposition 7.2.2 below applied to $q-1$ factors; so its product with $u_1$ is defined as before. The product with no factors is $T$. When $T=1$ (so that $r=n$), $q=n$ and $u_1=\cdots =u_ n=u$, the resulting positive current of bidegree $(n,n)$ is a positive measure, the Monge–Ampère measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ of $u$.

title: Proposition 7.2.2
text: Proposition 7.2.2 . D9911E035563 Every product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$ of definition 7.2.1 is a closed positive current, and it has the following properties. If $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ are smooth, it coincides with the exterior product of the smooth forms $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j$ with $T$. The construction is local: if $u_ j=v_ j$ for every $j$ and $T=T'$ on an open set $U\subset \Omega $, then the two products agree on $U$. It is additive and positively homogeneous in each $u_ j$ and in $T$, whenever the summands are locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions, respectively closed positive currents of bidimension $(r,r)$, and it does not change if a real constant is added to some $u_ j$. If $\gamma $ is a smooth closed form of bidegree $(s,s)$, $q\le r-s$, such that $T\wedge \gamma $ is positive (for instance, $\gamma $ strongly positive), then \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge (T\wedge \gamma )=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T)\wedge \gamma .  \] It is invariant under biholomorphic maps: if $F\colon \Omega '\to \Omega $ is biholomorphic and $F^*$ denotes the pullback of currents of proposition 5.6.2 , then \[  F^*\bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T\bigr )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_1\circ F)\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_ q\circ F)\wedge F^*T.  \] Proof. We first record two consequences of the Leibniz rule of section 5.3 . Let $R$ be a current of even degree on an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$ such that $\partial R=\bar\partial R=0$; this holds if $R$ is closed and of pure bidegree. If $f$ is a smooth function, then $\mathrm d(fR)=\mathrm df\wedge R$ and $\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}(fR)=\mathrm d^{\mathrm c}f\wedge R$, and applying $\mathrm d$ to the latter gives EDF346A35F76 7.2.3 \begin{equation}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(fR)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}f\wedge R. \end{equation} If $\gamma $ is a smooth closed form of pure bidegree, then $\partial \gamma $ and $\bar\partial \gamma $ are the components of $\mathrm d\gamma =0$ of two different bidegrees, so they vanish, and the Leibniz rule gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(R'\wedge \gamma )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R'\wedge \gamma $ for every current $R'$. We now prove positivity and closedness, first for a single factor $u$. By proposition 5.9.2 , the regularizations $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $ by the radial mollifiers of section 2.5 are smooth plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ with positive semidefinite complex Hessians, and they decrease to $u$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. On each compact set the $u_\varepsilon $ are bounded uniformly in $\varepsilon $, because $u\le u_\varepsilon \le u_{\varepsilon _0}$ for $\varepsilon \le \varepsilon _0$ and $u$ is locally bounded. Dominated convergence with respect to the total variations of the coefficient measures of $T$ therefore gives $u_\varepsilon T\to uT$ weakly. By ( 7.2.3 ), $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_\varepsilon T)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon \wedge T$. Since weak and strong positivity agree in bidegree $(1,1)$ (section 5.3 ), the positive smooth form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon $ is strongly positive, so its product with the positive current $T$ is positive; it is also closed. As $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ is continuous for weak convergence, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon \wedge T\to \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uT)$ weakly, and positivity and closedness pass to the limit. Thus $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T$ is positive and closed. Applying this with $T$ replaced by the closed positive current $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$, we obtain the first assertion by induction on $q$. (1) If the $u_ j$ are smooth, ( 7.2.3 ) shows at each step of the recursion that the product is the exterior product of smooth forms with $T$. (2), (3) The definition uses only multiplication of coefficient measures by functions and the operator $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$; both operations are local and linear, and no product of two measures occurs. This gives locality, and additivity and positive homogeneity in $u_1$ and in $T$; for the other factors they follow by induction on $q$, since multiplication by $u_1$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ are linear. If $c$ is a constant and $R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$, then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}((u_1+c)R)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_1R)+c\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(u_1R)$, since $R$ is closed; for the other factors the invariance under constants follows again by induction. (4) The product $T\wedge \gamma $ is closed, and multiplication of coefficient measures by $u_1$ commutes with the exterior product by $\gamma $. By the identity $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(R'\wedge \gamma )=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}R'\wedge \gamma $ and induction on $q$, every step of the recursion commutes with $\wedge \gamma $. (5) The pullback $F^*T$ is closed and positive and commutes with $\partial $ and $\bar\partial $, hence with $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ (proposition 5.6.2 ), and the functions $u_ j\circ F$ are locally bounded and plurisubharmonic (proposition 5.9.3 ). We claim that $F^*(uT)=(u\circ F)F^*T$ for a locally bounded plurisubharmonic $u$. For a smooth function $f$ we have $F^*(fT)=(f\circ F)F^*T$: both sides are weakly continuous in $T$, they agree when $T$ is smooth, and on every relatively compact open subset of $\Omega $ the current $T$ is the weak limit of its smooth regularizations (discussion following theorem 5.3.7 ). Applying this to the regularizations $u_\varepsilon $ on relatively compact open subsets, and letting $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, we obtain the claim: $u_\varepsilon T\to uT$ as shown above, so $F^*(u_\varepsilon T)\to F^*(uT)$, while $(u_\varepsilon \circ F)F^*T\to (u\circ F)F^*T$ by dominated convergence with respect to the coefficient measures of the positive current $F^*T$. Consequently every step of the recursion commutes with $F^*$, which proves (5). In particular, by (2) and (5), products of locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions with closed positive currents on a complex manifold can be computed in holomorphic charts: the products defined in two charts agree on their overlap. $\square$

title: Theorem 7.2.5 (Chern–Levine–Nirenberg)
text: Theorem 7.2.5 (Chern–Levine–Nirenberg) . 2A84C325AB58 Let $K,L\subset \Omega $ be compact sets with $K\subset \operatorname{Int}L$, and let $0\le q\le r$ be an integer. There is a constant $C_{K,L,q}$, depending only on $K$, $L$, $n$ and $q$, such that \[  \| \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T\| _ K \le C_{K,L,q}\| T\| _ L\prod _{j=1}^ q\| u_ j\| _{L^\infty (L)}  \] for every closed positive current $T$ of bidimension $(r,r)$ on $\Omega $ and all locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ on $\Omega $. Here $\| u_ j\| _{L^\infty (L)}=\sup _ L|u_ j|$ is the pointwise supremum. Proof. For $q=0$ the estimate holds with constant $1$, since $K\subset L$. Let $q=1$ and write $u=u_1$. By lemma 2.5.1 there is a smooth function $0\le \chi \le 1$ with compact support in $\operatorname{Int}L$ which equals $1$ on a neighborhood of $K$; it depends only on $K$ and $L$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1}$ is a positive measure, $\beta $ is closed, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}S)(\chi )=S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi )$ for currents $S$ of bidimension $(1,1)$, we have \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _ K\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge T\wedge \beta ^{r-1} & \le \int \chi \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uT)\wedge \beta ^{r-1} =\bigl (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(uT\wedge \beta ^{r-1})\bigr )(\chi )\\ & =\int uT\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \wedge \beta ^{r-1} \le C\| u\| _{L^\infty (L)}\| T\| _ L. \end{aligned}  \] The form $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi \wedge \beta ^{r-1}$ is smooth with support in $L$, though in general not positive; its coefficients are bounded by a constant depending only on $\chi $ and $n$. The last inequality therefore holds because the total variations of the coefficient measures of $T$ on $L$ are bounded by a constant multiple of $\| T\| _ L$, the multiple depending only on $n$ and $r$ (theorem 5.3.7 ). Dividing by $(r-1)!$ and taking the largest of the constants obtained for $r=1,\ldots ,n$, we obtain the case $q=1$ with a constant depending only on $K$, $L$ and $n$. For $q>1$, let $\delta >0$ be the distance from $K$ to $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \operatorname{Int}L$ (if $K=\varnothing $ there is nothing to prove), and put $L_ j=\{ z:\operatorname {dist}(z,K)\le j\delta /(q+1)\} $ for $0\le j<q$ and $L_ q=L$. These are compact sets, depending only on $K$, $L$ and $q$, with $K=L_0$ and $L_{j-1}\subset \operatorname{Int}L_ j$ for $1\le j\le q$. By proposition 7.2.2 , the currents $S_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{j+1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$, $0\le j\le q$, are positive and closed, and $S_{j-1}=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j\wedge S_ j$. The case $q=1$, applied to $S_ j$ and the pair $L_{j-1}\subset \operatorname{Int}L_ j$, gives $\| S_{j-1}\| _{L_{j-1}}\le C_ j\| u_ j\| _{L^\infty (L)}\| S_ j\| _{L_ j}$ for $j=1,\ldots ,q$, since $\| u_ j\| _{L^\infty (L_ j)}\le \| u_ j\| _{L^\infty (L)}$. Combining these $q$ inequalities, we obtain the estimate with $C_{K,L,q}=C_1\cdots C_ q$. $\square$

title: Proposition 7.2.6
text: Proposition 7.2.6 . 2F39A3F97E8E Let $T_ k\to T$ weakly, where $T_ k$ and $T$ are closed positive currents on $\Omega $ of bidimension $(r,r)$, and let $0\le q\le r$. We claim: if $S_ k\to S$ weakly, where $S_ k$ and $S$ are closed positive currents whose masses are bounded on compact sets uniformly in $k$, and if locally bounded Borel functions $v_ k$ converge locally uniformly to a continuous function $v$, then $v_ kS_ k\to vS$ weakly. Applying this to $S_ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{2,k}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q,k}\wedge T_ k$ and $v_ k=u_{1,k}$, and then $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, which is weakly continuous, proves the first assertion by induction on $q$; the case $q=0$ is the hypothesis. The second assertion is the claim with $v_ k=u_{0,k}$. To prove the claim, fix a test form $\varphi $ with compact support $K$ and $\varepsilon >0$. By lemma 2.5.1 (1), applied to $v$ on a relatively compact open neighborhood of $K$, there is a smooth function $v_\varepsilon $ on a neighborhood of $K$ with $|v-v_\varepsilon |\le \varepsilon $ on $K$. Write \[  v_ kS_ k-vS=(v_ k-v)S_ k+(v-v_\varepsilon )S_ k +v_\varepsilon (S_ k-S)+(v_\varepsilon -v)S.  \] Evaluated on $\varphi $, a term $fS_ k$ with a bounded Borel function $f$ is at most $C_\varphi \sup _ K|f|$ times the total variation on $K$ of the coefficient measures of $S_ k$, where $C_\varphi $ bounds the coefficients of $\varphi $; the same holds for $S$. Hence the first term tends to zero, since $v_ k\to v$ uniformly on $K$; the second and fourth terms are bounded by a constant times $\varepsilon $, uniformly in $k$; and the third tends to zero as $k\to \infty $, since $v_\varepsilon \varphi $ is a test form. title: Lemma 7.3.3
text: Lemma 7.3.3 . 9C6450BF0E32 Let $B$ be a ball and $R$ a closed positive current of bidimension $(1,1)$ on a neighborhood of $\overline B$. Let $a$ be a smooth function and $b$ a bounded plurisubharmonic function on a neighborhood of $\overline B$, and suppose that $a=b$ on a collar of $\partial B$. Then \[  \int _ B a\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge R=\int _ B b\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R.  \] In particular one may take $R=S\wedge \gamma $, where $S$ is a closed positive current, $\gamma $ is a smooth closed form of pure bidegree, and $S\wedge \gamma $ is positive of bidimension $(1,1)$. Proof. Both integrals are finite, since $a$ and $b$ are bounded on $B$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge R$ are measures of finite total variation near $\overline B$. The function $h=b-a$ is bounded and Borel, and it vanishes on a collar $V$ of $\partial B$; hence its restriction to $B$ vanishes outside the compact set $K_0=\overline B\setminus V\subset B$. On $B$ we have $bR=aR+hR$, and since $R$ is closed, $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(aR)=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R$ by ( 7.2.3 ); thus \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R+\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(hR)\quad \text{on }B,  \] where $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(hR)$ is a signed measure with support in $K_0$. Choose $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(B)$ equal to $1$ on a neighborhood of $K_0$. By the definition of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ on currents, \[  \int _ Ba\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(hR)=\int \chi a\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(hR)=\int h\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(\chi a)\wedge R=\int _ Bh\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R.  \] Consequently \[  \int _ Ba\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge R=\int _ Ba\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R+\int _ Bh\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R=\int _ Bb\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R.  \] The last assertion holds because $S\wedge \gamma $ is then closed, by the Leibniz rule, and positive of bidimension $(1,1)$; moreover $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge (S\wedge \gamma )=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge S)\wedge \gamma $ by proposition 7.2.2 (4). $\square$

title: Lemma 7.3.4
Lemma 7.3.5
text: Lemma 7.3.5 . C04BF828EE91 There are smooth convex functions $M_\varepsilon \colon \mathbb {R}^2\to \mathbb {R}$, $\varepsilon >0$, increasing in each variable, such that $M_\varepsilon \downarrow \max $ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, $\max \le M_\varepsilon \le \max +\varepsilon $, and $M_\varepsilon (s,t)=\max \{ s,t\} $ when $|s-t|>2\varepsilon $. If $a$ and $b$ are smooth plurisubharmonic functions, so is $M_\varepsilon (a,b)$. Proof. Let $\rho _\varepsilon $ be the mollifier of section 2.5 on $\mathbb {R}^2$; it is a nonnegative even radial probability density supported in the disc of radius $\varepsilon $. Put $M_\varepsilon =\max *\rho _\varepsilon $, that is, $M_\varepsilon (x)=\int \max (x-y)\rho _\varepsilon (y)\, \mathrm dy$, where $\max (s,t)=\max \{ s,t\} $; it is smooth, since $\rho _\varepsilon $ is (section 2.5 ). Since $\rho _\varepsilon \ge 0$ has integral $1$, and $x\mapsto \max (x-y)$ is convex and increasing in each variable for each $y$, the function $M_\varepsilon $ is convex and increasing in each variable. Since $\rho _\varepsilon $ is even, $\int y_ i\rho _\varepsilon (y)\, \mathrm dy=0$ for $i=1,2$; integrating $\max (s-y_1,t-y_2)\ge s-y_1$ and $\max (s-y_1,t-y_2)\ge t-y_2$ against $\rho _\varepsilon $ therefore gives $M_\varepsilon (s,t)\ge s$ and $M_\varepsilon (s,t)\ge t$, that is, $M_\varepsilon \ge \max $. Since $|\max (x-y)-\max (x)|\le |y|\le \varepsilon $ on the support of $\rho _\varepsilon $, we have $M_\varepsilon \le \max +\varepsilon $. If $s-t>2\varepsilon $ and $|y|\le \varepsilon $, then $(s-y_1)-(t-y_2)\ge s-t-2\varepsilon >0$, so $M_\varepsilon (s,t)=\int (s-y_1)\rho _\varepsilon (y)\, \mathrm dy=s$; similarly $M_\varepsilon (s,t)=t$ if $t-s>2\varepsilon $. It remains to show that $M_\varepsilon $ increases with $\varepsilon $. For fixed $x\in \mathbb R^2$, the function $g(\varepsilon )=\int \max (x-\varepsilon y)\rho _1(y)\, \mathrm{d}y$, defined for all real $\varepsilon $, equals $M_\varepsilon (x)$ for $\varepsilon >0$ and $\max (x)$ for $\varepsilon =0$; it is convex, since $\varepsilon \mapsto \max (x-\varepsilon y)$ is convex, and even, since $\rho _1$ is even. For $0\le \varepsilon _1<\varepsilon _2$, writing $\varepsilon _1=\lambda (-\varepsilon _2)+(1-\lambda )\varepsilon _2$ with $\lambda \in (0,1]$, we get $g(\varepsilon _1)\le \lambda g(-\varepsilon _2)+(1-\lambda )g(\varepsilon _2)=g(\varepsilon _2)$. This proves the monotonicity, and together with $\max \le M_\varepsilon \le \max +\varepsilon $ this gives $M_\varepsilon \downarrow \max $ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Finally, let $a$ and $b$ be smooth and plurisubharmonic, and write $(a_1,a_2)=(a,b)$. Denoting by $\partial _ kM_\varepsilon $ and $\partial _ k\partial _ lM_\varepsilon $ the partial derivatives evaluated at $(a,b)$, the chain rule gives \[  \mathrm{i}\partial \bar\partial M_\varepsilon (a,b) =\sum _{k=1}^2\partial _ kM_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{i}\partial \bar\partial a_ k +\mathrm{i}\sum _{k,l=1}^2\partial _ k\partial _ lM_\varepsilon \, \partial a_ k\wedge \bar\partial a_ l.  \] The first sum is positive because $\partial _ kM_\varepsilon \ge 0$, $M_\varepsilon $ being increasing in each variable, and the forms $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial a_ k$ are positive, since the smooth plurisubharmonic functions $a_ k$ have positive semidefinite complex Hessians (proposition 5.9.2 ). For the second, note that the real Hessian $H=(\partial _ k\partial _ lM_\varepsilon )$ is positive semidefinite: for $v\in \mathbb R^2$, the function $t\mapsto M_\varepsilon (x+tv)$ is convex, so its second derivative $v^ tHv$ is nonnegative. Writing $H=\sum _ m\lambda _ mv_ mv_ m^ t$ with $\lambda _ m\ge 0$ and real orthonormal vectors $v_ m$, and putting $\theta _ m=\sum _ k(v_ m)_ k\partial a_ k$, we get $\mathrm i\sum _{k,l}\partial _ k\partial _ lM_\varepsilon \, \partial a_ k\wedge \bar\partial a_ l=\sum _ m\lambda _ m\mathrm i\theta _ m\wedge \bar\theta _ m$, because $\bar\partial a_ l=\overline{\partial a_ l}$ for real $a_ l$; this is a positive $(1,1)$-form. Hence the complex Hessian of $M_\varepsilon (a,b)$ is positive semidefinite, and $M_\varepsilon (a,b)$ is plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.2 . $\square$

title: Lemma 7.3.6
text: Lemma 7.3.6 . 4286535DCE99 Let $S_ j$, $j\ge 1$, and $S$ be currents of the same degree on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$. If every point of $\Omega $ has an open neighborhood $U\subset \Omega $ such that $S_ j\to S$ weakly on $U$, then $S_ j\to S$ weakly on $\Omega $. Proof. Let $\varphi $ be a test form on $\Omega $ of complementary degree. Its support is compact, so it is covered by finitely many open sets $U_1,\ldots ,U_ m$ as in the hypothesis. By lemma 2.5.2 , there are smooth functions $\eta _1,\ldots ,\eta _ m$ with compact supports in $U_1,\ldots ,U_ m$, respectively, such that $\sum _ i\eta _ i=1$ on a neighborhood of $\operatorname{Supp}\varphi $. Then $\varphi =\sum _ i\eta _ i\varphi $, where $\eta _ i\varphi $ is a test form supported in $U_ i$, and therefore $S_ j(\varphi )=\sum _ iS_ j(\eta _ i\varphi )\to \sum _ iS(\eta _ i\varphi )=S(\varphi )$. $\square$

title: Theorem 7.3.7 (Bedford–Taylor)
text: Theorem 7.3.7 (Bedford–Taylor) . D87C13B3250A Let $T$ be a closed positive current on $\Omega $ of bidimension $(r,r)$, and let $0\le q\le r$ be an integer. For $0\le l\le q$, let $(u_{l,j})_{j\ge 1}$ be a decreasing sequence of locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $ whose limit $u_ l$ is locally bounded (and therefore plurisubharmonic, by theorem 5.10.1 ). Then \[  \begin{aligned}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q,j}\wedge T & \longrightarrow \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T,\\  u_{0,j}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q,j}\wedge T & \longrightarrow u_0\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T \end{aligned}  \] weakly as $j\to \infty $. Moreover, the product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$ of locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions is symmetric in $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$. Proof. We argue by induction on $q$. Step 1 derives the unweighted assertion and the symmetry from the weighted assertion for fewer factors. The other steps prove the weighted assertion on a ball, after a modification near its boundary: every weak limit of the weighted products is at most the expected limit (Step 4), and repeated integration by parts gives the reverse inequality for the total masses (Step 5). Step 1: the induction. We prove the second (weighted) assertion by induction on $q$, simultaneously for all open sets $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, all $r\ge q$, all closed positive currents $T$ of bidimension $(r,r)$ on $\Omega $ and all decreasing sequences as in the statement. For $q=0$ it states that $u_{0,j}T\to u_0T$; this follows from dominated convergence with respect to the total variations of the coefficient measures of $T$, since $u_0\le u_{0,j}\le u_{0,1}$. Let $q\ge 1$ and assume the weighted assertion for fewer than $q$ factors. Applying it to the $q-1$ factors $u_{2,j},\ldots ,u_{q,j}$ with the weight $u_{1,j}$, and then applying the weakly continuous operator $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$, we obtain the unweighted assertion for $q$ factors. Next we prove symmetry for $q$ factors. Let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ be locally bounded and plurisubharmonic, let $\varepsilon >0$, and choose $\varepsilon _ k\downarrow 0$ with $\varepsilon _ k<\varepsilon $. The regularizations $u_ l*\rho _{\varepsilon _ k}$ are smooth plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ decreasing to $u_ l$ (proposition 5.9.2 ). By the unweighted assertion, the product $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T$ on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ is therefore the weak limit of exterior products of smooth forms with $T$ (proposition 7.2.2 (1)), and these are symmetric in the factors because $2$-forms commute. Since the sets $\Omega _\varepsilon $ exhaust $\Omega $, products with $q$ factors are symmetric. It remains to prove the weighted assertion for $q$ factors; in doing so we may use the unweighted assertion and the symmetry for $q$ factors. Step 2: reduction to a common collar. By lemma 7.3.6 , it suffices to prove the convergence near every point. Fix a ball $B=B(a,R)$, a larger ball $B_1$ with $\overline B\subset B_1\Subset \Omega $, and a compact set $K\subset B$; we prove the convergence on a neighborhood of $K$. Since $u_ l\le u_{l,j}\le u_{l,1}$, all the functions $u_{l,j}$ and $u_ l$ are bounded on $B_1$ uniformly in $j$. Subtracting a constant from $u_{l,j}$ and $u_ l$ changes neither the Hessians nor, since the unweighted assertion is already known, the validity of the weighted assertion. We may therefore assume that $-N\le u_{l,j},u_ l\le -1$ on $B_1$ for all $l$ and $j$, where $N\ge 1$. Put $\psi =|z-a|^2-R^2$, choose $\delta >0$ with $K\subset \{ \psi <-\delta \} $, and replace every function $v$ among the $u_{l,j}$ and $u_ l$ by the function $\max \{ v,A\psi \} $ of ( 7.3.2 ), with $U=B_1$ and $A=N/\delta $. The new functions are plurisubharmonic on $B_1$, and the new sequences still decrease to the new limits. The functions are unchanged on the neighborhood $\{ \psi <-\delta \} $ of $K$, and by locality so are their products. From now on, $u_{l,j}$ and $u_ l$ denote the new functions; they take values in $[-N,0)$ on $B$ and coincide with $A\psi $ on the collar $V=\{ z\in B_1:\psi (z)>-1/A\} $ of $\partial B$. Step 3: smooth approximation with the same collar. Fix $\eta >0$ such that $\{ \psi \le \eta \} \subset B_1$, and let $V'=\{ z:-1/(2A)<\psi (z)<\eta \} $; it is a collar of $\partial B$ contained in $V$. Fix $l$ and $j$, and let $\tilde u$ be the function $u_{l,j}$ before the modification of Step 2, so that $\tilde u\le -1$ on $B_1$ and $u_{l,j}=\max \{ \tilde u,A\psi \} $. For $0<\varepsilon <1/4$ smaller than the distance from $\{ \psi \le \eta \} $ to $\partial B_1$, put \[  u^\varepsilon _{l,j}=M_\varepsilon (\tilde u*\rho _\varepsilon ,A\psi ),  \] with $M_\varepsilon $ as in lemma 7.3.5 . The functions $\tilde u*\rho _\varepsilon $ are smooth and plurisubharmonic on $\{ \psi <\eta \} $ and decrease to $\tilde u$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ (proposition 5.9.2 ), so the $u^\varepsilon _{l,j}$ are smooth and plurisubharmonic on $\{ \psi <\eta \} $ by lemma 7.3.5 . Since $\tilde u*\rho _\varepsilon \le -1$, on $V'$ we have $A\psi -\tilde u*\rho _\varepsilon >1/2>2\varepsilon $, and therefore $u^\varepsilon _{l,j}=A\psi $. Since $M_\varepsilon $ decreases to $\max $, is increasing in each variable and satisfies $\max \le M_\varepsilon \le \max +\varepsilon $, the functions $u^\varepsilon _{l,j}$ decrease to $\max \{ \tilde u,A\psi \} =u_{l,j}$. In particular $u^\varepsilon _{l,j}\ge u_{l,j}\ge u_ l$, and all the functions $u_{l,j}$, $u_ l$ and $u^\varepsilon _{l,j}$ coincide with $A\psi $ on $V'$. Step 4: an upper bound for weak limits. Put \[  S_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q,j}\wedge T,\qquad S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T.  \] By Step 1, $S_ j\to S$ weakly. On $B$ the weights $u_{0,j}$ take values in $[-N,0)$, so the currents $-u_{0,j}S_ j$ are positive there, and by theorem 7.2.5 , since $|u_{l,j}|\le N$ on $B$, their masses on compact subsets of $B$ are bounded uniformly in $j$. By the compactness part of theorem 5.3.7 , every subsequence of $(u_{0,j}S_ j)$ has a further subsequence converging weakly on $B$. Let $\Theta $ be the limit of such a subsequence. Let $\varphi $ be a strongly positive test form on $B$ of complementary bidegree. The measures $\mu _ j=S_ j\wedge \varphi $ are positive and converge weakly to $S\wedge \varphi $, and along the chosen subsequence $u_{0,j}\mu _ j\to \Theta \wedge \varphi $. Hence lemma 7.3.4 , applied on $B$ with the real-valued upper semicontinuous functions $f_ j=u_{0,j}$, gives $\Theta \wedge \varphi \le u_0S\wedge \varphi $. Evaluating this inequality of measures on a nonnegative test function equal to $1$ on $\operatorname{Supp}\varphi $, we get $(u_0S-\Theta )(\varphi )\ge 0$; thus $u_0S-\Theta $ is a positive current on $B$. By locality (proposition 7.2.2 ), all the currents $u_{0,j}S_ j$, and also $u_0S$, coincide on $V'$ with the fixed current $A\psi \, (A\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ q\wedge T$; hence so does $\Theta $, and $u_0S-\Theta $ has compact support in $B$. Step 5: comparison of masses. Set $\gamma =\beta ^{r-q}$ and \[  I=\int _ Bu_0S\wedge \gamma , \qquad I_ j=\int _ Bu_{0,j}S_ j\wedge \gamma .  \] We claim that $I\le I_ j$ for every $j$. Fix $j$ and parameters $\varepsilon _0,\ldots ,\varepsilon _ q$, and abbreviate $w_ l=u^{\varepsilon _ l}_{l,j}$. For $0\le k\le q$ put \[  J_ k=\int _ Bu_ k\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_0\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_{k-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{k+1}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T\wedge \gamma ,  \] so that $J_0=I$. The measure in $J_ k$ is positive and $u_ k\le w_ k$, so $J_ k$ does not decrease if $u_ k$ is replaced by $w_ k$. If $k<q$, symmetry of products with $q$ factors and proposition 7.2.2 (4) let us write that measure as $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{k+1}\wedge R_ k$, where \[  R_ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_0\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_{k-1}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{k+2}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T\wedge \gamma  \] is a closed positive current of bidimension $(1,1)$ on $\{ \psi <\eta \} $; then lemma 7.3.3 , with $a=w_ k$ and $b=u_{k+1}$, which both equal $A\psi $ on the collar $V'$, gives \[  J_ k\le \int _ Bw_ k\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{k+1}\wedge R_ k=\int _ Bu_{k+1}\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ k\wedge R_ k=J_{k+1}.  \] Hence \[  I=J_0\le J_1\le \cdots \le J_ q\le \int _ Bw_ q\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_0\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_{q-1}\wedge T\wedge \gamma .  \] Now let $\varepsilon _ q\downarrow 0$, then $\varepsilon _{q-1}\downarrow 0$, and so on down to $\varepsilon _1\downarrow 0$, keeping $\varepsilon _0$ fixed. We claim that the right-hand side of the last inequality then tends to \[  \int _ Bu_{q,j}\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_0\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q-1,j}\wedge T\wedge \gamma .  \] When $\varepsilon _ q\downarrow 0$, the measure is fixed and the bounded weights $w_ q$ decrease to $u_{q,j}$, so dominated convergence applies. When $\varepsilon _ k\downarrow 0$ for some $1\le k\le q-1$, the integrand is, after moving the smooth factors next to $T$ by symmetry, \[  u_{q,j}\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u^{\varepsilon _ k}_{k,j}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{k+1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q-1,j}\wedge T_ k\wedge \gamma ,  \] where $T_ k=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_0\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_{k-1}\wedge T$ is a fixed closed positive current on $\{ \psi <\eta \} $ of bidimension $(r-k,r-k)$. There are $q-k\le q-1$ Hessian factors and the fixed weight $u_{q,j}$. Along any sequence $\varepsilon _ k\downarrow 0$, the functions $u^{\varepsilon _ k}_{k,j}$ decrease to $u_{k,j}$ (Step 3), so the induction hypothesis, applied on $\{ \psi <\eta \} $ with the base current $T_ k$, constant sequences for the other factors and the constant weight $u_{q,j}$, shows that these currents converge weakly; so do their exterior products with $\gamma $. In each case the convergence holds for the integrals over $B$, and not only against compactly supported test forms, because all the currents involved coincide on the collar $V'$ with the same fixed current: if $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(B)$ equals $1$ on $B\setminus V'$, the integrals against $\chi $ converge, and the integrals against $1-\chi $ do not depend on the parameters. By lemma 7.3.3 , with $a=w_0$ and $b=u_{q,j}$, and by symmetry of products with $q$ factors, the limit integral equals \[  \int _ Bw_0\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q,j}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q-1,j}\wedge T\wedge \gamma =\int _ Bu^{\varepsilon _0}_{0,j}\, S_ j\wedge \gamma .  \] Hence $I\le \int _ Bu^{\varepsilon _0}_{0,j}S_ j\wedge \gamma $ for every $\varepsilon _0$, and dominated convergence with respect to the finite measure $S_ j\wedge \gamma $ on $B$ gives $I\le I_ j$ as $\varepsilon _0\downarrow 0$. Step 6: conclusion. Along the subsequence defining $\Theta $, splitting the integrals with a cutoff as in Step 5 shows that $I_ j\to \int _ B\Theta \wedge \gamma $. Therefore \[  \int _ B(u_0S-\Theta )\wedge \gamma =I-\lim _ jI_ j\le 0.  \] Since $u_0S-\Theta $ is positive with compact support in $B$, its trace measure $(u_0S-\Theta )\wedge \gamma $ is a positive measure of total mass at most zero, hence zero; by the coefficient bounds of theorem 5.3.7 , $u_0S-\Theta =0$ on $B$. Thus every subsequence of $(u_{0,j}S_ j)$ has a further subsequence converging weakly to $u_0S$ on $B$. Hence the whole sequence converges to $u_0S$ on $B$: otherwise there would be a test form $\varphi $ on $B$ and a subsequence along which $|(u_{0,j}S_ j-u_0S)(\varphi )|$ stays bounded away from zero, and no further subsequence of it could converge to $u_0S$. The replacement by maxima in Step 2 changes neither the functions nor, by locality, the weighted products on the neighborhood $\{ \psi <-\delta \} $ of $K$, and the subtraction of constants does not affect the convergence; hence the original weighted products converge on this neighborhood. As $K$ and $B$ were arbitrary, this proves the weighted assertion for $q$ factors on $\Omega $ and completes the induction. $\square$

title: Corollary 7.3.8
text: Corollary 7.3.8 . 8BD7803A393B Let $P$ be a real polynomial in $m$ variables and, for $1\le i\le m$, let $(v_{i,j})_{j\ge 1}$ be a decreasing sequence of locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $ with locally bounded limit $v_ i$. Then in theorem 7.3.7 the weight $u_{0,j}$ may be replaced by $P(v_{1,j},\ldots ,v_{m,j})$, and the limit is then \[  P(v_1,\ldots ,v_ m)\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge T.  \] Moreover, the identity of lemma 7.3.3 also holds when $a$ and $b$ are both bounded plurisubharmonic functions on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ which coincide on a collar of $\partial B$. Proof. Since weak convergence is a local property (lemma 7.3.6 ), it suffices to prove the convergence on every relatively compact open set $W\Subset \Omega $. On $W$ all the functions $v_{i,j}$ and $v_ i$ are bounded, because $v_ i\le v_{i,j}\le v_{i,1}$. Adding a constant $c_ i$ to each $v_{i,j}$ and to $v_ i$ replaces $P$ by the polynomial $P(x_1-c_1,\ldots ,x_ m-c_ m)$; so we may assume that all these functions are nonnegative on $W$. Since the weighted products depend linearly on the weight, it suffices to treat a monomial. A constant weight is covered by the unweighted assertion of the theorem. A monomial of degree $N\ge 1$ is a product $a_1\cdots a_ N$, where each $a_ l$ is one of the $v_ i$, repetitions being allowed; we write $a_{l,j}$ for the corresponding function $v_{i,j}$. For real numbers $x_1,\ldots ,x_ N$ we have the polarization identity 8BEFFD328D36 7.3.9 \begin{equation}  N!\, x_1\cdots x_ N=\sum _{I\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,N\} }(-1)^{N-|I|}\Bigl (\sum _{l\in I}x_ l\Bigr )^ N. \end{equation} To prove it, expand $(\sum _{l\in I}x_ l)^ N=\sum _\alpha \frac{N!}{\alpha !}x^\alpha $, the sum running over the multi-indices $\alpha \in \mathbb N^ N$ with $|\alpha |=N$ and $\alpha _ l=0$ for $l\notin I$. Fix such an $\alpha $, and let $J=\{ l:\alpha _ l>0\} $ have $k$ elements. The monomial $x^\alpha $ occurs exactly in the terms with $I\supset J$, so its total coefficient on the right-hand side is \[  \frac{N!}{\alpha !}\sum _{I\supset J}(-1)^{N-|I|}=\frac{N!}{\alpha !}\sum _{i=0}^{N-k}\binom {N-k}{i}(-1)^{N-k-i}=\frac{N!}{\alpha !}(1-1)^{N-k}.  \] This vanishes unless $k=N$, in which case $\alpha =(1,\ldots ,1)$ and the coefficient is $N!$. Each sum $s=\sum _{l\in I}a_ l$ is a bounded nonnegative plurisubharmonic function on $W$, and so is $s^ N$. For $N=1$ there is nothing to prove; for $N\ge 2$ and smooth $s$ this follows from \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}(s^ N)=Ns^{N-1}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}s+N(N-1)s^{N-2}\, \mathrm{d}s\wedge \mathrm{d}^{\mathrm c}s,  \] in which both terms are positive $(1,1)$-forms, the first because $s\ge 0$ and $s$ has a positive semidefinite complex Hessian, and the second by ( 7.3.1 ); hence $s^ N$ is plurisubharmonic, by both directions of proposition 5.9.2 . In general, the regularizations $s*\rho _\varepsilon $ are smooth, plurisubharmonic and nonnegative, and they decrease to $s$ (proposition 5.9.2 ); since $t\mapsto t^ N$ is increasing on $[0,\infty )$, the plurisubharmonic functions $(s*\rho _\varepsilon )^ N$ decrease to $s^ N$, which is therefore plurisubharmonic by theorem 5.10.1 . Likewise the sums $s_ j=\sum _{l\in I}a_{l,j}$ are nonnegative and decrease to $s$, so the $s_ j^ N$ are bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $W$ decreasing to $s^ N$. The weighted assertion of the theorem therefore applies with the weights $s_ j^ N$, and by ( 7.3.9 ), with $x_ l=a_{l,j}$, it applies to the monomial weights $a_{1,j}\cdots a_{N,j}$. For the second assertion, let $a$ and $b$ be bounded plurisubharmonic functions on a neighborhood $U$ of $\overline B$ which are equal on a collar $V$ of $\partial B$. Let $d>0$ be smaller than the distances from $\partial B$ to $\mathbb C^ n\setminus V$ and from $\overline B$ to $\mathbb C^ n\setminus U$, and put $V'=\{ z:\operatorname {dist}(z,\partial B)<d/2\} $. For $\varepsilon =\varepsilon _ k\downarrow 0$ with $\varepsilon _ k<d/2$, the regularizations $a_\varepsilon =a*\rho _\varepsilon $ and $b_\varepsilon =b*\rho _\varepsilon $ are smooth and plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ and decrease to $a$ and $b$ (proposition 5.9.2 ); moreover $a_\varepsilon =b_\varepsilon $ on the collar $V'$, because $a=b$ on the ball $B(z,\varepsilon )\subset V$ for $z\in V'$. By lemma 7.3.3 , applied to the smooth function $a_\varepsilon $ and the bounded plurisubharmonic function $b_\varepsilon $, \[  \int _ Ba_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_\varepsilon \wedge R=\int _ Bb_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_\varepsilon \wedge R.  \] Choose $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(B)$ equal to $1$ on $B\setminus V'$. On $V'$ the measures $a_\varepsilon \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_\varepsilon \wedge R$ and $b_\varepsilon \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_\varepsilon \wedge R$ coincide, by locality, so the identity is equivalent to $\int \chi a_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b_\varepsilon \wedge R=\int \chi b_\varepsilon \, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a_\varepsilon \wedge R$. By the weighted assertion of the theorem with one factor and the fixed base current $R$, this passes to the limit: $\int \chi a\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge R=\int \chi b\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R$. Since $a=b$ on $V$, the measures $a\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b\wedge R$ and $b\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}a\wedge R$ also coincide on $V'$, and adding the integrals against $1-\chi $ over $B$ gives the identity for $a$ and $b$. $\square$

title: Equation 7.3.9
text: 8BEFFD328D36 7.3.9 \begin{equation}  N!\, x_1\cdots x_ N=\sum _{I\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,N\} }(-1)^{N-|I|}\Bigl (\sum _{l\in I}x_ l\Bigr )^ N. \end{equation}

title: Proposition 7.3.10
text: Proposition 7.3.10 . 0453AAB39932 Let $T$ be a closed positive current on $\Omega $ of bidimension $(r,r)$, let $u$ and $v$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $, and let $0\le p\le r$ be an integer. Then \[  \mathbf1_{\{ u>v\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\max \{ u,v\} )^ p\wedge T =\mathbf1_{\{ u>v\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ p\wedge T.  \] Here the indicator function multiplies the coefficient measures of these currents of order zero, as in section 5.3 ; the set $\{ u>v\} $ is Borel, but in general not open (see the example following the proof). Proof. The assertion is local, so it suffices to prove it on each $\Omega _{\varepsilon _0}$, $\varepsilon _0>0$. Let $u_ j=u*\rho _{\varepsilon _ j}$ with $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$, $\varepsilon _ j<\varepsilon _0$; these are smooth plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega _{\varepsilon _0}$ decreasing to $u$ (proposition 5.9.2 ). Since $u_ j$ is continuous and $v$ is upper semicontinuous, the set $\{ u_ j>v\} $ is open, and on it $w_ j=\max \{ u_ j,v\} $ equals $u_ j$; by locality, $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)^ p\wedge T=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ p\wedge T$ there. The nonnegative Borel function $f_ j=w_ j-v$ vanishes outside $\{ u_ j>v\} $, so \[  f_ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)^ p\wedge T=f_ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ j)^ p\wedge T.  \] The functions $w_ j$ decrease to $w=\max \{ u,v\} $. Both sides of the last identity are differences of weighted products, for instance $f_ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)^ p\wedge T=w_ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)^ p\wedge T-v(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w_ j)^ p\wedge T$. Applying theorem 7.3.7 to them, with the weights $w_ j$ and the constant weight $v$, and with the factors $w_ j$ on the left and $u_ j$ on the right, we obtain $f(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ p\wedge T=f(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ p\wedge T$, where $f=w-v\ge 0$. Multiply the coefficient measures of both sides by $1/(f+\varepsilon )$ and let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. Since $f/(f+\varepsilon )$ increases to the indicator of $\{ f>0\} =\{ u>v\} $, dominated convergence with respect to the locally finite total variations of the coefficient measures gives the assertion. $\square$

title: Theorem 7.3.11
text: Theorem 7.3.11 . D0AF90DDC7A5 Let $D\subset \mathbb {C}^ n$ be a bounded open set, and let $u$ and $v$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $D$ such that $\varliminf _{D\ni z\to x}(u(z)-v(z))\ge 0$ for every $x\in \partial D$. Then \[  \int _{\{ u<v\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\le \int _{\{ u<v\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n,  \] where both sides may be infinite. If $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$, then $u\ge v$ on $D$. Proof. Let $\varepsilon >0$ and $w=\max \{ u,v-\varepsilon \} $. We show that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ have the same mass near a compact set outside which $w=u$, and then identify $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$ by proposition 7.3.10 . Every $x\in \partial D$ has an open neighborhood $U_ x$ with $u>v-\varepsilon $ on $U_ x\cap D$, and finitely many of them cover the compact set $\partial D$; let $U$ be their union. Then $F=D\setminus U=\overline D\setminus U$ is a compact subset of $D$, it contains $\{ u\le v-\varepsilon \} $, and $w=u$ on $D\setminus F$. For $0\le l\le n-1$ put $R_ l=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ l\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{n-1-l}$. By additivity and symmetry of the products (proposition 7.2.2 , theorem 7.3.7 ), \[  \begin{aligned}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\bigl ((w-u)R_ l\bigr )& =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w\wedge R_ l-\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u\wedge R_ l\\ & =(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^{l+1}\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{n-1-l}-(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ l\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{n-l}, \end{aligned}  \] and summing over $l$, the right-hand sides telescope: \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n-(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\Bigl ((w-u)\sum _{l=0}^{n-1}R_ l\Bigr ).  \] The current in parentheses vanishes outside $F$, since $w-u$ does. Hence the signed measure $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n-(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ is supported in $F$, and if $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(D)$ equals $1$ on a neighborhood of $F$, then its total mass is \[  \int \chi \, \mathrm d\bigl ((\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n-(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\bigr )=\Bigl ((w-u)\sum _ lR_ l\Bigr )(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi )=0,  \] because $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\chi =0$ on a neighborhood of $F$. Choose a relatively compact open set $D'\subset D$ containing $F$. Both measures are finite on $D'$, and $\int _{D'}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n=\int _{D'}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$. By proposition 7.3.10 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n$ coincides with $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ on $\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} $ and with $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ on $\{ u>v-\varepsilon \} $; here we use that adding the constant $-\varepsilon $ does not change $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$. Since $\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} $ and $D'\cap \{ u>v-\varepsilon \} $ are disjoint Borel subsets of $D'$, and $\{ u\le v-\varepsilon \} \subset F\subset D'$, \[  \begin{aligned}  \int _{\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n & \le \int _{D'}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}w)^ n -\int _{D'\cap \{ u>v-\varepsilon \} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\\ & =\int _{\{ u\le v-\varepsilon \} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n \le \int _{\{ u<v\} }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n. \end{aligned}  \] As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the sets $\{ u<v-\varepsilon \} $ increase to $\{ u<v\} $, and monotone convergence proves the comparison inequality. The last assertion is the case of corollary 7.3.12 below in which the roles of $u$ and $v$ are interchanged: if $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$, then $v\le u$ holds almost everywhere for $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$. The proof of that corollary uses only the comparison inequality. $\square$

title: Corollary 7.3.12
text: Corollary 7.3.12 . F2BBEF3BF09B Let $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a bounded open set, $n\geq 1$, and let $u$ and $v$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $D$. Suppose that \[  \varliminf _{D\ni z\to x}(v(z)-u(z))\geq 0 \quad (x\in \partial D),\qquad u\leq v\quad \text{almost everywhere for }(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n.  \] Then $u\leq v$ everywhere on $D$. Proof. Choose $R$ with $D\subset B(0,R)$, and for $\delta >0$ put $u_\delta =u+\delta (|z|^2-R^2)$, a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function. Since $u_\delta \le u$ on $D$, the boundary condition still holds for $v$ and $u_\delta $, and the set $A=\{ v<u_\delta \} $ is contained in $\{ v<u\} $. By additivity, positive homogeneity and symmetry of the products (proposition 7.2.2 , theorem 7.3.7 ), $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\delta )^ n=\sum _{k=0}^ n\binom nk\delta ^ k(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^{n-k}\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2)^ k$ is a sum of positive measures, and its term with $k=n$ is $\delta ^ nn!\, \pi ^{-n}\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$, by ( 7.2.4 ). The comparison inequality of theorem 7.3.11 , applied to $v$ and $u_\delta $, therefore gives \[  \delta ^ n\frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}|A|\leq \int _ A(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\delta )^ n\leq \int _ A(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n=0,  \] where the last equality holds because $A\subset \{ v<u\} $ and $u\le v$ almost everywhere for $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$. Thus $A$ is a Lebesgue null set, and $\max \{ u_\delta ,v\} =v$ almost everywhere. Both functions are plurisubharmonic, so the uniqueness of plurisubharmonic representatives in theorem 5.9.1 , applied on each connected component of $D$, gives $\max \{ u_\delta ,v\} =v$ everywhere, that is, $u_\delta \leq v$. Letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ gives $u\le v$. $\square$

title: 7.4 Weighted estimates and Monge–Ampère capacity
text: We now use the products to define a capacity adapted to plurisubharmonic functions. The Monge–Ampère capacity of a set $E$ is the supremum of the masses that the measures $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n$ give to $E$ when $v$ ranges over the plurisubharmonic functions with values in $[0,1]$. To control exceptional sets with it, we need integral estimates that are uniform over this whole class. The first one is a version of the Chern–Levine–Nirenberg inequality with an unbounded plurisubharmonic weight. Theorem 7.4.1 . 7C68264563C0 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, $n\ge 1$, let $K,L\subset \Omega $ be compact sets with $K\subset \operatorname{Int}L$, and let $0\le q\le n$ be an integer. There is a constant $C_{K,L,q}$, depending only on $K$, $L$, $n$ and $q$, such that for every $V\in \mathrm{PSH}(\Omega )$ and all locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ on $\Omega $, \[  \int _ K |V|\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge \beta ^{n-q} \le C_{K,L,q}\| V\| _{L^1(L)} \prod _{l=1}^ q\| u_ l\| _{L^\infty (L)}.  \] In particular, the function $V$, with its values $-\infty $ on the pole set $\{ V=-\infty \} $, is locally integrable with respect to the trace measure $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge \beta ^{n-q}$. Proof. For $q\le n-1$ we integrate $V$ by parts against a cutoff function on a ball, after making the factors coincide near its boundary (Steps 1–4); the case $q=n$ follows by adding one variable (Step 5). Step 1: reductions. By theorem 5.9.1 , $V$ is locally integrable, so $\| V\| _{L^1(L)}<\infty $. For $q=0$ the left-hand side equals $n!\int _ K|V|\, \mathrm{d}V_{2n}\le n!\| V\| _{L^1(L)}$, by ( 5.2.8 ). Let $q\ge 1$. If $\| u_ l\| _{L^\infty (L)}=0$ for some $l$, then $u_ l=0$ on $\operatorname{Int}L$, so the product vanishes on $\operatorname{Int}L\supset K$ by locality.
