Then $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G)<\varepsilon $, and on $B\setminus G$ we have $0\le g_{j_ l}-g\le 2^{-l}$ for every $l$. Thus $g$ is a uniform limit of continuous functions on $B\setminus G$, hence continuous there; in particular $u=g$ is continuous on $\overline{B'}\setminus G$. Step 2: arbitrary $u$. Let $K\subset D$ be compact and $\varepsilon >0$. By proposition 7.4.4 , applied to $K$ and a compact neighborhood $L$ of $K$ in $D$, there is $s>0$ with $\operatorname {Cap}^*_ D(K\cap \{ u<-s\} )<\varepsilon /2$, and hence an open set $G_1\supset K\cap \{ u<-s\} $ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G_1)<\varepsilon /2$. By Step 1, applied to the locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $\max \{ u,-s\} $, there is an open set $G_2$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G_2)<\varepsilon /2$ such that $\max \{ u,-s\} $ is continuous on $K\setminus G_2$. On $K\setminus (G_1\cup G_2)$ we have $u\ge -s$, hence $u=\max \{ u,-s\} $. Thus $G=G_1\cup G_2$ contains $K\cap \{ u=-\infty \} $, $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G)<\varepsilon $, and $u$ is finite and continuous on $K\setminus G$. Step 3: a single exceptional set. Choose compact sets $K_ l$ with $K_ l\subset \operatorname{Int}K_{l+1}$ and $\bigcup _ lK_ l=D$. By Step 2 there are open sets $G^{(l)}\supset K_ l\cap \{ u=-\infty \} $ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G^{(l)})<\varepsilon 2^{-l}$ such that $u$ is finite and continuous on $K_ l\setminus G^{(l)}$. Put $G=\bigcup _ lG^{(l)}$. Then $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G)<\varepsilon $, and $G$ contains the pole set of $u$. Every $x\in D\setminus G$ lies in some $\operatorname{Int}K_ l$, and on the neighborhood $\operatorname{Int}K_ l\setminus G$ of $x$ in $D\setminus G$ the function $u$ is a restriction of the continuous function $u|_{K_ l\setminus G^{(l)}}$. Hence $u|_{D\setminus G}$ is finite and continuous. $\square$

title: Lemma 7.5.3
text: Lemma 7.5.3 . D127F8356D96 Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space, let $F\subset X$ be compact, and let $f\colon F\to \mathbb R$ be continuous with $|f|\le a$. Then $f$ has a continuous extension $g\colon X\to \mathbb R$ with $|g|\le a$. Proof. If $F=\varnothing $ or $a=0$, take $g=0$. Otherwise, for $L>0$ put \[  f_ L(x)=\max \Bigl \{ -a,\min \bigl \{ a,\inf _{y\in F}(f(y)+L\, d(x,y))\bigr \} \Bigr \} ,\qquad x\in X.  \] The infimum is finite, since $f\ge -a$, and as an infimum of functions that are Lipschitz with constant $L$ it is Lipschitz with constant $L$; hence $f_ L$ is continuous and $|f_ L|\le a$. We claim that $f_ L\to f$ uniformly on $F$ as $L\to \infty $. Taking $y=x$ shows $f_ L\le f$ on $F$. Given $\eta >0$, uniform continuity of $f$ on the compact set $F$ gives $r>0$ with $|f(y)-f(x)|<\eta $ for $x,y\in F$ with $d(x,y)<r$. Let $Lr>2a$ and $x\in F$. Points $y\in F$ with $d(x,y)\ge r$ give $f(y)+L\, d(x,y)\ge -a+Lr>a\ge f(x)$, and the other points give $f(y)+L\, d(x,y)>f(x)-\eta $. Hence the infimum is at least $f(x)-\eta $, and so is $f_ L(x)$, because $a\ge f(x)>f(x)-\eta $ and $-a\le f(x)$. This proves the claim. Consequently there is a continuous $g_1$ on $X$ with $|g_1|\le a$ and $|f-g_1|\le a/2$ on $F$. Applying the same construction to $f-g_1$ on $F$, we find a continuous $g_2$ with $|g_2|\le a/2$ and $|f-g_1-g_2|\le a/4$ on $F$, and inductively continuous $g_ k$ with $|g_ k|\le 2^{1-k}a$ and $|f-g_1-\cdots -g_ k|\le 2^{-k}a$ on $F$. The series $\sum _ kg_ k$ converges uniformly on $X$; its sum is continuous and equals $f$ on $F$, and clamping it to $[-a,a]$, that is, replacing it by $\max \{ -a,\min \{ a,\sum _ kg_ k\} \} $, does not change its values on $F$. $\square$

title: Lemma 7.5.4
text: Lemma 7.5.4 . 56B45ADBA326 Let $K,L\subset D$ be compact sets with $K\subset \operatorname{Int}L$, and let $f$ be a real Borel function which is defined and quasi-continuous on a neighborhood of $L$. Then, for every $\delta >0$, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(K\cap \{ |f|>\delta \} ) \le \operatorname {Cap}_ D(L\cap \{ |f|>\delta /2\} ).  \] Proof. Let $\eta >0$. By quasi-continuity, applied to the compact set $L$, there is an open set $G\subset D$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G)<\eta $ such that $f$ is continuous on $L\setminus G$; let $g$ be a continuous extension of $f|_{L\setminus G}$ to $\mathbb {C}^ n$ (lemma 7.5.3 ); here $f|_{L\setminus G}$ is bounded, being continuous on a compact set. The open set $G\cup (\operatorname{Int}L\cap \{ |g|>\delta /2\} )$ contains $K\cap \{ |f|>\delta \} $, since $K\subset \operatorname{Int}L$ and $g=f$ on $K\setminus G$. Its part outside $G$ is a Borel set contained in $L\cap \{ |f|>\delta /2\} $, because $g=f$ on $L\setminus G$. By monotonicity and subadditivity, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(K\cap \{ |f|>\delta \} )\le \eta +\operatorname {Cap}_ D(L\cap \{ |f|>\delta /2\} ).  \] Let $\eta \downarrow 0$. $\square$

title: Definition 7.5.5
text: Definition 7.5.5 . DAD5D0809372 A net $(f_ a)$ of Borel functions $f_ a\colon D\to [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ converges locally in capacity to a Borel function $f\colon D\to [-\infty ,+\infty ]$ if, for every compact set $K\subset D$ and every $\delta >0$, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(K\cap \{ f_ a>f+\delta \} )\longrightarrow 0, \qquad \operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(K\cap \{ f_ a<f-\delta \} )\longrightarrow 0.  \] Here $\pm \infty +\delta =\pm \infty $ and $\pm \infty -\delta =\pm \infty $.

title: Proposition 7.5.6
text: Proposition 7.5.6 . 9542ED69E1C1 Let $u_ j$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $D$ decreasing to a locally bounded function $u$. Then $u_ j\to u$ locally in capacity. Moreover, a net of real Borel functions on $D$ which is uniformly bounded on each compact subset of $D$ and converges locally in capacity to a locally bounded real Borel function also converges in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(D)$. Proof. Let $K\subset D$ be compact and $\delta >0$. Since $u_ j\ge u$, the sets $\{ u_ j<u-\delta \} $ are empty, and we must show that $\operatorname {Cap}^*_ D(K\cap \{ u_ j-u>\delta \} )\to 0$. By theorem 5.10.1 , $u$ is plurisubharmonic. Covering $K$ by finitely many balls $B(x,r)$ with $\overline{B(x,4r)}\subset D$ and using subadditivity of outer capacity, we may assume that $K\subset \overline{B(x,r)}$ for such a ball; put $L=\overline{B(x,3r/2)}$, $B=B(x,3r)$ and $B_1=B(x,4r)$. We first make the functions coincide near $\partial B$. Since $u\le u_ j\le u_1$, all these functions are bounded on $B_1$ uniformly in $j$, so there are constants $c$ and $N\ge 1$ with $-N\le u_ j-c,\, u-c\le -1$ on $B_1$. Put $\psi =|z-x|^2-9r^2$, choose $\delta _0>0$ with $L\subset \{ \psi <-\delta _0\} $, and let $\hat u_ j=\max \{ u_ j-c,A\psi \} $ and $\hat u=\max \{ u-c,A\psi \} $, with $A=N/\delta _0$, be the functions ( 7.3.2 ) on $B_1$, with $\delta _0$ in place of $\delta $. They are bounded and plurisubharmonic on $B_1$, $\hat u_ j\downarrow \hat u$, $\hat u_ j-\hat u=u_ j-u$ on $L$, and $\hat u_ j=\hat u$ on a collar of $\partial B$. By ( 7.4.6 ), applied with $u=\hat u$ and $h=\hat u_ j$, \[  \operatorname {Cap}_ D\bigl (B\cap \{ \hat u_ j-\hat u>\delta /2\} \bigr ) \le (n+1)!\, (2/\delta )^{n+1}\int _ B(\hat u_ j-\hat u)(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\hat u)^ n,  \] and the right-hand side tends to zero by dominated convergence, since $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\hat u)^ n$ has finite mass on $B$ and $0\le \hat u_ j-\hat u\le \hat u_1-\hat u$ decreases to zero. The real function $w_ j=u_ j-u$ is quasi-continuous on $D$, as a difference of two real quasi-continuous functions (theorem 7.5.2 and the remark following definition 7.5.1 ), and $w_ j=\hat u_ j-\hat u$ on $L$. Hence lemma 7.5.4 gives \[  \operatorname {Cap}^*_ D(K\cap \{ w_ j>\delta \} )\le \operatorname {Cap}_ D(L\cap \{ w_ j>\delta /2\} )\le \operatorname {Cap}_ D\bigl (B\cap \{ \hat u_ j-\hat u>\delta /2\} \bigr )\longrightarrow 0.  \] For the second assertion, let $f_ a\to f$ be as in the statement, let $K\subset D$ be compact, and let $M$ bound $|f_ a|$ and $|f|$ on $K$. Splitting $K$ into the Borel set where $|f_ a-f|>\delta $ and its complement, and using proposition 7.4.3 (3) together with $\operatorname {Cap}_ D\le \operatorname {Cap}^*_ D$ on Borel sets, we get \[  \int _ K|f_ a-f|\, \mathrm{d}V_{2n} \le 2MC_ D\operatorname {Cap}_ D^*(K\cap \{ |f_ a-f|>\delta \} ) +\delta |K|.  \] Taking the limit along the net and then letting $\delta \downarrow 0$ proves $L^1$ convergence on $K$. $\square$

title: Lemma 7.5.7
text: Lemma 7.5.7 . 880C30054932 Let $B\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a ball, and let $\mathcal U$ be a family of plurisubharmonic functions on $B$ which is uniformly bounded on each compact subset of $B$. For every compact set $K\subset B$ there is a constant $C$ such that, for all integers $0\le q\le n$, all $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q\in \mathcal U$ and all Borel sets $E\subset K$, the trace measure $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge \beta ^{n-q}$, and the total variation of every coefficient measure of $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q$, give $E$ mass at most $C\operatorname {Cap}_ B(E)$. Let $S_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q,j}$ with $u_{l,j}\in \mathcal U$, and suppose that $S_ j\to S$ weakly. Let $f_ j$ be real Borel functions on $B$, uniformly bounded on each compact subset of $B$, which converge locally in capacity (for $\operatorname {Cap}_ B$) to a real Borel function $f$ that is locally bounded and quasi-continuous. Then $f_ jS_ j\to fS$ weakly, and the same holds for the trace measures of $S_ j$ and $S$. This applies in particular to a fixed weight $f_ j=f$. Proof. (1) Let $B=B(a,R)$, fix $K$, and choose $R'<R$ with $K\subset B'=B(a,R')$. Let $M\ge 1$ be a common bound for $|u|$ on $B'$, $u\in \mathcal U$. For $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q\in \mathcal U$ put $v_ l=(u_ l+M)/(2M)$ and $\phi =|z-a|^2/R'^2$; these functions take values in $[0,1]$ on $B'$, and so does \[  F=\frac1n\bigl (v_1+\cdots +v_ q+(n-q)\phi \bigr ),  \] which is therefore a competitor for $\operatorname {Cap}_{B'}$. Expand $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^ n$ by additivity, positive homogeneity and symmetry (proposition 7.2.2 , theorem 7.3.7 ). All terms are positive measures, and those in which each $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ l$ occurs once and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi $ occurs $n-q$ times add up to $c_{n,q}\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ q\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi )^{n-q}$, where $c_{n,q}=n^{-n}\, n!\, (n-q)^{n-q}/(n-q)!>0$ (with $0^0=1$) is the corresponding multinomial coefficient. Hence $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ q\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi )^{n-q}\le c_{n,q}^{-1}(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}F)^ n$. Since $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\phi =\beta /(\pi R'^2)$ and $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ l=2M\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_ l$, it follows that $\int _ E\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge \beta ^{n-q}\le C\operatorname {Cap}_{B'}(E)$ for Borel $E\subset B'$. The bound for the coefficient measures follows from theorem 5.3.7 , and proposition 7.4.3 (4), applied to $B'\Subset B$ and $K$, replaces $\operatorname {Cap}_{B'}$ by $\operatorname {Cap}_ B$ on subsets of $K$. (2) The weak limit $S$ is a positive current (theorem 5.3.7 ). Let $\sigma _ j$ be either the trace measure or a coefficient measure of $S_ j$, and $\sigma $ the corresponding measure of $S$; then $\int \psi \, \mathrm d\sigma _ j\to \int \psi \, \mathrm d\sigma $ for every test function $\psi $, since this integral is the value of $S_ j$ on a test form. Fix a continuous function $\chi $ with compact support in $B$ and a compact set $K\subset B$ with $\operatorname{Supp}\chi \subset \operatorname{Int}K$, and let $C$ be the constant of (1) for $K$; in particular $|\sigma _ j|(K)\le C\operatorname {Cap}_ B(K)$, which is finite by proposition 7.4.3 (1). A similar bound holds for $\sigma $ on open subsets $U\subset \operatorname{Int}K$: for the trace measure, which is the vague limit of the trace measures of $S_ j$ (section 5.3 ), proposition 2.6.2 gives $\sigma (U)\le \varliminf _ j\sigma _ j(U)\le C\operatorname {Cap}_ B(U)$, and the total variations of the coefficient measures of the positive current $S$ are bounded by a constant multiple of its trace measure. Since the total variations $|\sigma _ j|(K)$ are bounded, the convergence $\int \psi \, \mathrm d\sigma _ j\to \int \psi \, \mathrm d\sigma $ extends to continuous functions $\psi $ with support in $\operatorname{Int}K$: approximating $\psi $ uniformly by test functions supported in a fixed compact subset of $\operatorname{Int}K$ (lemma 2.5.1 (5)) changes the integrals by at most $\sup |\psi -\psi _\varepsilon |$ times a bound for $|\sigma _ j|(K)$ and $|\sigma |(K)$. Consider first the fixed weight $f$, and let $\eta >0$. Since $f$ is quasi-continuous, there is an open set $G\subset B$ with $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(G)<\eta $ such that $f$ is continuous on $K\setminus G$; let $g$ be a continuous extension of $f|_{K\setminus G}$ to $\mathbb C^ n$ with $\sup |g|\le \sup _ K|f|$ (lemma 7.5.3 ). Then \[  \Bigl |\int \chi f\, \mathrm{d}\sigma _ j-\int \chi g\, \mathrm{d}\sigma _ j\Bigr |\le 2\sup _ K|f|\sup |\chi |\, |\sigma _ j|(G\cap \operatorname{Supp}\chi )\le C'\eta ,  \] and similarly for $\sigma $, using the open set $G\cap \operatorname{Int}K$. Since $\chi g$ is continuous with support in $\operatorname{Int}K$, we have $\int \chi g\, \mathrm{d}\sigma _ j\to \int \chi g\, \mathrm{d}\sigma $. Hence $\varlimsup _ j|\int \chi f\, \mathrm{d}\sigma _ j-\int \chi f\, \mathrm{d}\sigma |\le 2C'\eta $ for every $\eta >0$, which proves $f\sigma _ j\to f\sigma $. For varying weights, let $M_ K$ bound $|f_ j|$ and $|f|$ on $K$, and let $\delta >0$. By (1), \[  \Bigl |\int \chi (f_ j-f)\, \mathrm{d}\sigma _ j\Bigr | \le \sup |\chi |\Bigl (\delta \, C\operatorname {Cap}_ B(K)+2M_ KC\operatorname {Cap}^*_ B\bigl (K\cap \{ |f_ j-f|>\delta \} \bigr )\Bigr ).  \] As $j\to \infty $, the second term tends to zero by convergence in capacity; then we let $\delta \downarrow 0$. Together with the fixed-weight case, this proves $f_ j\sigma _ j\to f\sigma $, and hence $f_ jS_ j\to fS$. $\square$

title: Theorem 7.5.8
text: Theorem 7.5.8 . 42828E3BDDFA Let $0\le q\le n$ be an integer. For $1\le l\le q$, let $(u_{l,j})_{j\ge 1}$ be a sequence of plurisubharmonic functions on $D$, uniformly bounded on each compact subset of $D$, which converges locally in capacity to a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $u_ l$. Then \[  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q,j} \longrightarrow \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q  \] weakly. More generally, if $f_ j$ are real Borel functions on $D$, uniformly bounded on each compact subset of $D$, which converge locally in capacity to a locally bounded, quasi-continuous real Borel function $f$, then $f_ j\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q,j}\to f\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q$ weakly. Proof. Weak convergence is local (lemma 7.3.6 ), so it suffices to prove the convergence on every ball $B\Subset D$. By the remark following definition 7.5.5 , the convergence in capacity holds with $\operatorname {Cap}_ B$ in place of $\operatorname {Cap}_ D$ on every ball $B\Subset D$. The limit $f$ is quasi-continuous for $\operatorname {Cap}_ B$ as well: if $K\subset B$ is compact, $K'$ is a compact neighborhood of $K$ in $B$, and $G\subset D$ is open with $f$ continuous on $K'\setminus G$, then $G\cap \operatorname{Int}K'$ is open in $B$, $f$ is continuous on $K\setminus (G\cap \operatorname{Int}K')=K\setminus G$, and $\operatorname {Cap}_ B(G\cap \operatorname{Int}K')\le C\operatorname {Cap}_ D(G)$ by proposition 7.4.3 (4) applied to $K'$. Finally, the functions $u_{l,j}$ and $u_ l$, restricted to $B$, form a family which is uniformly bounded on compact subsets of $B$. We may therefore work on such a ball and use lemma 7.5.7 . We argue by induction on $q$. For $q=0$ the product is $1$, and the weighted assertion is the second part of the lemma with $S_ j=1$. Let $q\ge 1$, and assume that $S_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{2,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q,j}$ converges weakly to $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q$. The functions $u_{1,j}$ converge in capacity to $u_1$, which is quasi-continuous by theorem 7.5.2 ; hence the second part of the lemma gives $u_{1,j}S_ j\to u_1S$, and applying $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ proves the unweighted assertion for $q$ factors. The weighted assertion then follows from the second part of the lemma once more. $\square$

title: 7.6 Increasing limits and exceptional envelopes
text:
The supremum of an increasing sequence of plurisubharmonic functions need not be upper semicontinuous, and it may differ from its upper semicontinuous regularization on an exceptional set. For instance, on the unit ball of $\mathbb C^ n$ the functions $\max \{ j^{-1}\log |z_1|,-1\} $ are plurisubharmonic (proposition 5.10.3 , proposition 5.9.5 ) and increase with $j$, since $\log |z_1|<0$ there; their supremum equals $0$ where $z_1
e 0$ and $-1$ on the hyperplane $\{ z_1=0\} $, while its upper semicontinuous regularization is $0$. We show that the products are nevertheless continuous along increasing sequences. The proof follows the pattern of the decreasing case: the inequality $u_{0,j}\le u_0$ bounds weak limits from above, while the quasi-continuity of the fixed weights, through lemma 7.5.7 , supplies the lower bound for the masses. As a consequence, the exceptional set of an upper envelope has outer capacity zero. Theorem 7.6.1 . A4C45B704647 Let $0\le q\le n$ be an integer. For $0\le l\le q$, let $(u_{l,j})_{j\ge 1}$ be an increasing sequence of locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $D$ which converges almost everywhere to a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $u_ l$. Then \[   egin{aligned}  \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q,j} & \longrightarrow \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q,\  u_{0,j}\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q,j} & \longrightarrow u_0\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q \end{aligned}  \] weakly. Moreover $u_{l,j}	o u_ l$ locally in capacity for every $l$. Proof. We first note that $u_{l,j}\le u_ l$ everywhere. Indeed, $u_{l,j}\le u_ l$ almost everywhere, so the plurisubharmonic functions $\max \{ u_{l,j},u_ l\} $ and $u_ l$ agree almost everywhere, and hence everywhere, by the uniqueness of plurisubharmonic representatives in theorem 5.9.1 , applied on each connected component of $D$. Consequently $u_{l,1}\le u_{l,j}\le u_ l$, and the sequences are uniformly bounded on each compact subset of $D$. As in the proof of theorem 7.3.7 , we prove the weighted assertion by induction on $q$, for all bounded open sets $D$ and all sequences as in the statement; convergence in capacity is proved at the end. For $q=0$ it follows from dominated convergence with respect to Lebesgue measure. Let $q\ge 1$ and assume the weighted assertion for $q-1$ factors; applying $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}$ to it, with the weight $u_{1,j}$, gives the unweighted assertion for $q$ factors. Put $S_ j=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{q,j}$ and $S=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q$, so that $S_ j	o S$ weakly. Weak convergence is a local property (lemma 7.3.6 ). Fix $x\in D$ and $r>0$ with $\overline{B(x,4r)}\subset D$, and put $B=B(x,3r)$ and $B_1=B(x,4r)$; we prove the convergence on $B(x,2r)$. Subtracting constants does not affect the assertions, since the unweighted assertion for $q$ factors is known, so we may assume that $-N\le u_{l,j},u_ l\le -1$ on $B_1$ for all $l$ and $j$, where $N\ge 1$. Put $\psi =|z-x|^2-9r^2$, choose $\delta _0>0$ such that $\overline{B(x,2r)}\subset \{ \psi <-\delta _0\} $, and replace each function $v$ among the $u_{l,j}$ and $u_ l$ by the function $\max \{ v,A\psi \} $ of ( 7.3.2 ), with $U=B_1$, $\delta _0$ in place of $\delta $ and $A=N/\delta _0$. The new functions are plurisubharmonic on $B_1$ and take values in $[-N,0)$ on $B$; the new sequences still increase, satisfy $u_{l,j}\le u_ l$ and converge almost everywhere. The functions do not change on $B(x,2r)$, and by locality neither do the products. On the collar $V=\{ z\in B_1:\psi (z)>-1/A\} $ of $\partial B$ the new functions coincide with $A\psi $. By locality, on $V$ all the currents considered below coincide with fixed currents, independent of $j$ and $k$. Hence, if $\chi \in C^\infty _ c(B)$ equals $1$ on $B\setminus V$, the integral over $B$ of each of these currents splits into its integral against $\chi $, to which weak convergence applies, and its integral against $(1-\chi )\mathbf1_ B$, which only involves values on $V$ and therefore does not change; we use this without further comment. The currents $-u_{0,j}S_ j$ are positive on $B$, and their masses on compact subsets of $B$ are bounded uniformly in $j$ by theorem 7.2.5 ; by the compactness part of theorem 5.3.7 , every subsequence of $(u_{0,j}S_ j)$ has a further subsequence converging weakly on $B$. Let $\Theta $ be the limit of such a subsequence. Since $u_{0,j}\le u_0$, the currents $(u_0-u_{0,j})S_ j$ are positive. Let $\varphi $ be a strongly positive test form on $B$ of complementary bidegree. The positive measures $-u_0S_ j\wedge \varphi $ have bounded masses on compact sets, so by theorem 2.6.5 a further subsequence of $u_0S_ j\wedge \varphi $ converges weakly to some $
u $, and lemma 7.3.4 , applied to the constant sequence $f_ j=u_0$ and the measures $S_ j\wedge \varphi 	o S\wedge \varphi $, gives $
u \le u_0S\wedge \varphi $. The measures $(u_0-u_{0,j})S_ j\wedge \varphi $ are positive and converge along this subsequence to $
u -\Theta \wedge \varphi $, which is therefore positive. Hence $\Theta \wedge \varphi \le u_0S\wedge \varphi $. Evaluating this inequality of measures on a nonnegative test function equal to $1$ on $\operatorname{Supp}\varphi $, we get $(u_0S-\Theta )(\varphi )\ge 0$. Thus $u_0S-\Theta $ is a positive current on $B$, and it vanishes on $V$, since all the currents $u_{0,j}S_ j$ and $u_0S$ coincide there with $A\psi (A\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\psi )^ q$. Write $\gamma = eta ^{n-q}$. For fixed $k$ and all $j\ge k$, positivity of $S_ j\wedge \gamma $ and $u_{0,j}\ge u_{0,k}$ give \[  \int _ Bu_{0,j}S_ j\wedge \gamma \ge \int _ Bu_{0,k}S_ j\wedge \gamma .  \] Let $j	o \infty $ along the subsequence defining $\Theta $. The left-hand side tends to $\int _ B\Theta \wedge \gamma $. The fixed weight $u_{0,k}$ is quasi-continuous for $\operatorname {Cap}_ B$ by theorem 7.5.2 , and the functions $u_{l,j}$, $u_ l$ form a family which is uniformly bounded on $B$; so by lemma 7.5.7 (2) the right-hand side tends to $\int _ Bu_{0,k}S\wedge \gamma $. By the second assertion of corollary 7.3.8 , applied with $a=u_{0,k}$, $b=u_1$ and $R=\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge \gamma $, and by symmetry, \[  \int _ Bu_{0,k}S\wedge \gamma =\int _ Bu_1\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{0,k}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge \gamma .  \] As $k	o \infty $, the unweighted assertion for $q$ factors, already established, gives $\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_{0,k}\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q	o \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_0\wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_2\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q$ weakly, and lemma 7.5.7 , with the fixed quasi-continuous weight $u_1$, passes the integral to the limit. A second application of corollary 7.3.8 identifies the limit with $\int _ Bu_0\, \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_ q\wedge \gamma =\int _ Bu_0S\wedge \gamma $. We have shown that $\int _ B\Theta \wedge \gamma \ge \int _ Bu_0S\wedge \gamma $. Since $u_0S-\Theta $ is positive with compact support in $B$, its trace measure has total mass $\int _ B(u_0S-\Theta )\wedge \gamma \le 0$ and therefore vanishes, and $\Theta =u_0S$ by theorem 5.3.7 . Thus every subsequence of $(u_{0,j}S_ j)$ has a further subsequence converging weakly to $u_0S$ on $B$. Hence the whole sequence converges to $u_0S$ on $B$: otherwise there would be a test form $\varphi $ on $B$ and a subsequence along which $|(u_{0,j}S_ j-u_0S)(\varphi )|$ stays bounded away from zero, and no further subsequence of it could converge to $u_0S$. section: 7.7 The homogeneous Dirichlet problem and balayage
text:
A plurisubharmonic function is maximal if it cannot be increased on a compact set without losing plurisubharmonicity (definition 7.7.6 ). We show in theorem 7.7.7 that, for locally bounded functions, maximality is equivalent to $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$. The proof replaces $u$ on a ball by a solution $H$ of the homogeneous equation $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=0$ with the same boundary values (corollary 7.7.5 ); in section 5.47 the same replacement shows that relative extremal functions have vanishing Monge–Ampère measure away from the sets on which they are constrained. We construct $H$ as an upper envelope. To show that it solves the equation, we bound its second differences by composing with automorphisms of the ball (lemma 7.7.1 ), which makes it twice differentiable almost everywhere (lemma 7.7.2 ). Lemma 7.7.1 . 4521AF3E3E5C Let $B\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be the unit ball. For $a\in B$ and $h\in \mathbb C^ n$ with $|h|$ small, depending on $a$, there are biholomorphic automorphisms $S_{a,h}$ of $B$ such that $S_{a,0}$ is the identity and $S_{a,h}(a)=a+h$. Each $S_{a,h}$ extends to a holomorphic map on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ which maps $\partial B$ onto $\partial B$. For every compact set $K\subset B$ there is $h_0>0$ such that the map $(a,h,z)\mapsto S_{a,h}(z)$ is defined and smooth on an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n	imes \mathbb C^ n	imes \mathbb C^ n$ containing $K	imes \overline{B(0,h_0)}	imes \overline B$, and holomorphic in $z$ there. In particular, there is a constant $C$ such that, for $a\in K$, $|h|\le h_0$ and $z\in \overline B$, the first and second derivatives of $S_{a,h}(z)$ with respect to the real variable $h\in \mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ are bounded by $C$. Proof. Use the Hermitian product $\langle z,aangle =\sum z_ j ar a_ j$, put $s_ a=\sqrt{1-|a|^2}$, and define \[  T_ a(z)= rac{s_ a z+\langle z,aangle a/(1+s_ a)-a}{1-\langle z,aangle }.  \] This expression depends smoothly on $(a,z)$ in the open set $\{ (a,z):|a|<1,\  |a||z|<1\} $, where the denominator does not vanish, and it is holomorphic in $z$; moreover $T_0$ is the identity. If $U$ is a unitary matrix, then $\langle Uz,Uaangle =\langle z,aangle $ and $s_{Ua}=s_ a$, so $T_{Ua}(Uz)=UT_ a(z)$. Given $a
e 0$, choose $U$ with $Ua=(t,0,\ldots ,0)$, $t=|a|$; it therefore suffices to verify the following identities for $a=(t,0,\ldots ,0)$ with $0\le t<1$, and also for $-a=(-t,0,\ldots ,0)$. Put $s=s_ a=\sqrt{1-t^2}$. Then $\langle z,aangle =tz_1$, and the first component of the numerator of $T_ a(z)$ is $sz_1+t^2z_1/(1+s)-t=z_1-t$, because $s(1+s)+t^2=s+s^2+t^2=1+s$. Hence \[   egin{aligned}  T_ a(z)& =\left( rac{z_1-t}{1-tz_1},  rac{s\, z_2}{1-tz_1},\ldots ,  rac{s\, z_ n}{1-tz_1}ight),\  T_{-a}(w)& =\left( rac{w_1+t}{1+tw_1},  rac{s\, w_2}{1+tw_1},\ldots ,  rac{s\, w_ n}{1+tw_1}ight), \end{aligned}  \] the second formula by the same computation with $t$ replaced by $-t$. In particular $T_ a(a)=0$ and $T_{-a}(0)=a$. If $w=T_ a(z)$, then \[  w_1+t= rac{(1-t^2)z_1}{1-tz_1},\qquad 1+tw_1= rac{1-t^2}{1-tz_1},  \] so the first component of $T_{-a}(w)$ is $z_1$ and the others are $s\cdot sz_ k/(1-tz_1)\cdot (1-tz_1)/(1-t^2)=z_ k$; thus $T_{-a}\circ T_ a=\mathrm{id}$, and by symmetry $T_ a\circ T_{-a}=\mathrm{id}$. Set $S_{a,h}=T_{-(a+h)}\circ T_ a$ for $|a+h|<1$. It maps $a$ to $T_{-(a+h)}(0)=a+h$ and is the identity for $h=0$. The map $T_ a$ is holomorphic on the neighborhood $\{ z:|a||z|<1\} $ of $\overline B$, and, as we have just seen, it maps $\overline B$ into $\overline B$ and $\partial B$ onto $\partial B$; the same holds for $T_{-(a+h)}$. Hence $S_{a,h}$ is holomorphic on the neighborhood $\{ z:|a||z|<1,\  |a+h||T_ a(z)|<1\} $ of $\overline B$, and it maps $\partial B$ onto $\partial B$. Let $K\subset B$ be compact (we may assume $K
eq \varnothing $), put $t_ K=\max _ K|a|<1$, and choose $h_0>0$ with $t_ K+3h_0<1$. On the open set $O$ of all $(a,h,z)$ with $|a|<t_ K+h_0$, $|h|<2h_0$, $|a||z|<1$ and $(t_ K+3h_0)|T_ a(z)|<1$, we have $|a+h|<1$ and $|a+h||T_ a(z)|<1$, so $(a,h,z)\mapsto S_{a,h}(z)$ is defined and smooth on $O$, and holomorphic in $z$. Since $|T_ a(z)|\le 1$ for $|z|\le 1$, the set $O$ contains the compact set $K	imes \overline{B(0,h_0)}	imes \overline B$, on which the continuous first and second derivatives of $S_{a,h}(z)$ with respect to $h$ are therefore bounded by a constant $C$. $\square$ A plurisubharmonic function whose second differences are bounded above is locally of class $C^{1,1}$, and its Monge–Ampère measure is then given by the determinant of its complex Hessian. Lemma 7.7.2 . 0E5A3E632224 Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, $n\ge 1$, and let $H$ be a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $U$. Suppose that for every compact set $K\subset U$ there are constants $C_ K\ge 0$ and $h_ K>0$ such that, for all $a\in K$ and all $h\in \mathbb C^ n$ with $|h|\le h_ K$, the points $a\pm h$ lie in $U$ and 332CD5FE501E 7.7.3  egin{equation}  H(a+h)+H(a-h)-2H(a)\le 2C_ K|h|^2\qquad (a\in K,\  |h|\le h_ K). \end{equation} Then $H$ is continuous, $H\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, and the distributional real Hessian of $H$ is a matrix $A=(A_{ab})$ of measurable functions which are bounded on compact subsets of $U$. Almost every $x\in U$ satisfies \[  H(x+h)=H(x)+
abla H(x)\cdot h+	frac 12h^ tA(x)h+o(|h|^2)\qquad (h	o 0).  \] Moreover, let $H_{j ar k}$ be the coefficients of the distributional complex Hessian of $H$, which are fixed complex linear combinations of the $A_{ab}$. Then the matrix $(H_{j ar k})$ is positive semidefinite almost everywhere, and \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n= rac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\det (H_{j ar k})\, \mathrm dV_{2n}.  \] Proof. Let $H_\varepsilon =H*ho _\varepsilon $. Fix $a_0\in U$ and $r>0$ with $\overline{B(a_0,4r)}\subset U$, put $K=\overline{B(a_0,3r)}$, and let $M_0=\sup _ K|H|$, which is finite because $H$ is locally bounded. text: Lemma 7.7.1 . 4521AF3E3E5C Let $B\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be the unit ball. For $a\in B$ and $h\in \mathbb C^ n$ with $|h|$ small, depending on $a$, there are biholomorphic automorphisms $S_{a,h}$ of $B$ such that $S_{a,0}$ is the identity and $S_{a,h}(a)=a+h$. Each $S_{a,h}$ extends to a holomorphic map on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ which maps $\partial B$ onto $\partial B$. For every compact set $K\subset B$ there is $h_0>0$ such that the map $(a,h,z)\mapsto S_{a,h}(z)$ is defined and smooth on an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n\times \mathbb C^ n\times \mathbb C^ n$ containing $K\times \overline{B(0,h_0)}\times \overline B$, and holomorphic in $z$ there. In particular, there is a constant $C$ such that, for $a\in K$, $|h|\le h_0$ and $z\in \overline B$, the first and second derivatives of $S_{a,h}(z)$ with respect to the real variable $h\in \mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$ are bounded by $C$. Proof. Use the Hermitian product $\langle z,a\rangle =\sum z_ j\bar a_ j$, put $s_ a=\sqrt{1-|a|^2}$, and define \[  T_ a(z)=\frac{s_ a z+\langle z,a\rangle a/(1+s_ a)-a}{1-\langle z,a\rangle }.  \] This expression depends smoothly on $(a,z)$ in the open set $\{ (a,z):|a|<1,\  |a||z|<1\} $, where the denominator does not vanish, and it is holomorphic in $z$; moreover $T_0$ is the identity. If $U$ is a unitary matrix, then $\langle Uz,Ua\rangle =\langle z,a\rangle $ and $s_{Ua}=s_ a$, so $T_{Ua}(Uz)=UT_ a(z)$. Given $a\ne 0$, choose $U$ with $Ua=(t,0,\ldots ,0)$, $t=|a|$; it therefore suffices to verify the following identities for $a=(t,0,\ldots ,0)$ with $0\le t<1$, and also for $-a=(-t,0,\ldots ,0)$. Put $s=s_ a=\sqrt{1-t^2}$. Then $\langle z,a\rangle =tz_1$, and the first component of the numerator of $T_ a(z)$ is $sz_1+t^2z_1/(1+s)-t=z_1-t$, because $s(1+s)+t^2=s+s^2+t^2=1+s$. Hence \[  \begin{aligned}  T_ a(z)& =\left(\frac{z_1-t}{1-tz_1}, \frac{s\, z_2}{1-tz_1},\ldots , \frac{s\, z_ n}{1-tz_1}\right),\\  T_{-a}(w)& =\left(\frac{w_1+t}{1+tw_1}, \frac{s\, w_2}{1+tw_1},\ldots , \frac{s\, w_ n}{1+tw_1}\right), \end{aligned}  \] the second formula by the same computation with $t$ replaced by $-t$. In particular $T_ a(a)=0$ and $T_{-a}(0)=a$. If $w=T_ a(z)$, then \[  w_1+t=\frac{(1-t^2)z_1}{1-tz_1},\qquad 1+tw_1=\frac{1-t^2}{1-tz_1},  \] so the first component of $T_{-a}(w)$ is $z_1$ and the others are $s\cdot sz_ k/(1-tz_1)\cdot (1-tz_1)/(1-t^2)=z_ k$; thus $T_{-a}\circ T_ a=\mathrm{id}$, and by symmetry $T_ a\circ T_{-a}=\mathrm{id}$. Finally, \[  |1-tz_1|^2-|z_1-t|^2-(1-t^2)\sum _{k\ge 2}|z_ k|^2=(1-t^2)(1-|z_1|^2)-(1-t^2)\sum _{k\ge 2}|z_ k|^2,  \] because the terms $\mp 2t\operatorname{Re}z_1$ cancel; dividing by $|1-tz_1|^2$ gives \[  1-|T_ a(z)|^2=\frac{(1-|a|^2)(1-|z|^2)}{|1-\langle z,a\rangle |^2}.  \] Hence $T_ a$ maps $B$ into $B$ and the sphere $\partial B$ into itself, and the same holds for $T_{-a}$; since $T_{-a}$ is inverse to $T_ a$, the map $T_ a$ is a biholomorphic automorphism of $B$ which maps $\partial B$ onto itself. Set $S_{a,h}=T_{-(a+h)}\circ T_ a$ for $|a+h|<1$. It maps $a$ to $T_{-(a+h)}(0)=a+h$ and is the identity for $h=0$. The map $T_ a$ is holomorphic on the neighborhood $\{ z:|a||z|<1\} $ of $\overline B$, and, as we have just seen, it maps $\overline B$ into $\overline B$ and $\partial B$ onto $\partial B$; the same holds for $T_{-(a+h)}$. Hence $S_{a,h}$ is holomorphic on the neighborhood $\{ z:|a||z|<1,\  |a+h||T_ a(z)|<1\} $ of $\overline B$, and it maps $\partial B$ onto $\partial B$. Let $K\subset B$ be compact (we may assume $K\neq \varnothing $), put $t_ K=\max _ K|a|<1$, and choose $h_0>0$ with $t_ K+3h_0<1$. On the open set $O$ of all $(a,h,z)$ with $|a|<t_ K+h_0$, $|h|<2h_0$, $|a||z|<1$ and $(t_ K+3h_0)|T_ a(z)|<1$, we have $|a+h|<1$ and $|a+h||T_ a(z)|<1$, so $(a,h,z)\mapsto S_{a,h}(z)$ is defined and smooth on $O$, and holomorphic in $z$. Since $|T_ a(z)|\le 1$ for $|z|\le 1$, the set $O$ contains the compact set $K\times \overline{B(0,h_0)}\times \overline B$, on which the continuous first and second derivatives of $S_{a,h}(z)$ with respect to $h$ are therefore bounded by a constant $C$. $\square$

text: Lemma 7.7.2 . 0E5A3E632224 Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, $n\ge 1$, and let $H$ be a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $U$. Suppose that for every compact set $K\subset U$ there are constants $C_ K\ge 0$ and $h_ K>0$ such that, for all $a\in K$ and all $h\in \mathbb C^ n$ with $|h|\le h_ K$, the points $a\pm h$ lie in $U$ and 332CD5FE501E 7.7.3 \begin{equation}  H(a+h)+H(a-h)-2H(a)\le 2C_ K|h|^2\qquad (a\in K,\  |h|\le h_ K). \end{equation} Then $H$ is continuous, $H\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, and the distributional real Hessian of $H$ is a matrix $A=(A_{ab})$ of measurable functions which are bounded on compact subsets of $U$. Then the matrix $(H_{j\bar k})$ is positive semidefinite almost everywhere, and \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=\frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\det (H_{j\bar k})\, \mathrm dV_{2n}.  \] Proof. Let $H_\varepsilon =H*\rho _\varepsilon $. Fix $a_0\in U$ and $r>0$ with $\overline{B(a_0,4r)}\subset U$, put $K=\overline{B(a_0,3r)}$, and let $M_0=\sup _ K|H|$, which is finite because $H$ is locally bounded. For $0<\varepsilon <r$, the regularization $H_\varepsilon $ is smooth and plurisubharmonic on a neighborhood of $\overline{B(a_0,2r)}$ (proposition 5.9.2 ), and $|H_\varepsilon |\le M_0$ on $\overline{B(a_0,2r)}$, since its values there are averages of values of $H$ on $K$. For $x\in \overline{B(a_0,2r)}$ and $|h|\le h_ K$, \[  \begin{aligned} & H_\varepsilon (x+h)+H_\varepsilon (x-h)-2H_\varepsilon (x)\\ & \qquad =\int \bigl (H(x-y+h)+H(x-y-h)-2H(x-y)\bigr )\rho _\varepsilon (y)\, \mathrm dy\le 2C_ K|h|^2, \end{aligned}  \] by ( 7.7.3 ), because $x-y\in K$ for $|y|\le \varepsilon $. Replacing $h$ by $th$ with $0<t\le 1$, dividing by $t^2$ and letting $t\to 0$, we get $D^2H_\varepsilon (x)[h,h]\le 2C_ K|h|^2$ for $|h|\le h_ K$, and hence, by homogeneity, for all $h\in \mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$. On the other hand, the complex Hessian of the smooth plurisubharmonic function $H_\varepsilon $ is positive semidefinite (proposition 5.9.2 ), and $D^2H_\varepsilon [h,h]+D^2H_\varepsilon [\mathrm ih,\mathrm ih]=4\sum _{j,k}(H_\varepsilon )_{j\bar k}h_ j\bar h_ k\ge 0$; hence $D^2H_\varepsilon (x)[h,h]\ge -2C_ K|h|^2$ as well. Thus the second derivatives of the $H_\varepsilon $ are bounded on $\overline{B(a_0,2r)}$ by a constant $\Lambda _0$ independent of $\varepsilon $. For $x\in \overline{B(a_0,r)}$ and a unit vector $e$, Taylor's formula \[  H_\varepsilon (x+re)=H_\varepsilon (x)+r\, \partial _ eH_\varepsilon (x)+\int _0^ r(r-t)D^2H_\varepsilon (x+te)[e,e]\, \mathrm dt  \] gives $|\partial _ eH_\varepsilon (x)|\le 2M_0/r+\Lambda _0r=\Lambda $. By the mean value theorem on the convex set $B(a_0,r)$, $|H_\varepsilon (x)-H_\varepsilon (y)|\le \Lambda |x-y|$ for $x,y\in B(a_0,r)$. Since $H_\varepsilon \to H$ pointwise as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, by ( 3.4.13 ), the same inequality holds for $H$. Hence $H$ is continuous on $B(a_0,r)$, and, as $a_0$ was arbitrary, on $U$. Moreover, $H_\varepsilon \to H$ in $L^1$ on compact subsets of $U$, by dominated convergence, and hence in the sense of distributions; and every ball $B_0\Subset U$ is covered by finitely many balls $B(a_0,2r)$ as above, so the second derivatives of the $H_\varepsilon $ are bounded on $B_0$ uniformly in small $\varepsilon $. By the converse part of proposition 2.8.5 , the distributional real Hessian of $H$ has locally bounded measurable coefficients $A_{ab}$; hence $H\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$, and almost every $x\in U$ satisfies the second-order expansion of the statement. The functions $H_{j\bar k}$ are bounded measurable functions on compact subsets of $U$. By proposition 2.5.3 , the complex Hessian of $H_\varepsilon $ has the coefficients $(H_{j\bar k})_\varepsilon $; these are bounded on compact sets uniformly in small $\varepsilon $, and they converge to $H_{j\bar k}$ at every Lebesgue point of $H_{j\bar k}$, hence almost everywhere (theorem 2.8.3 ). In particular, the matrix $(H_{j\bar k})$ is positive semidefinite almost everywhere, as an almost everywhere limit of the positive semidefinite complex Hessians of the smooth plurisubharmonic functions $H_\varepsilon $. Since $H$ is continuous, $H_\varepsilon \to H$ locally uniformly (lemma 2.5.1 (1)), so $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_\varepsilon )^ n\to (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n$ weakly on every ball $B_0\Subset U$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ along a sequence, by proposition 7.2.6 applied on $B_0$. By ( 7.2.4 ), $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_\varepsilon )^ n=n!\pi ^{-n}\det ((H_{j\bar k})_\varepsilon )\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$, and the determinants converge almost everywhere and are bounded on compact sets uniformly in small $\varepsilon $. Hence, for every test function $\chi $ supported in such a ball $B_0$, dominated convergence gives \[  \int \chi \, (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=\frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\int \chi \det (H_{j\bar k})\, \mathrm dV_{2n}.  \] By lemma 2.5.2 , every test function on $U$ is a finite sum of test functions supported in balls $B_0\Subset U$, so this identity holds for all test functions on $U$, and the two Radon measures coincide by proposition 2.5.3 (4). $\square$

title: Theorem 7.7.4
section: 7.7 The homogeneous Dirichlet problem and balayage
text: Theorem 7.7.4 . 9181532558D7 Let $B\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a ball and $\varphi $ a real continuous function on $\partial B$. There is a unique $H\in \mathrm{PSH}(B)\cap C(\overline B)$ such that \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=0\quad \text{on }B,\qquad H|_{\partial B}=\varphi .  \] It is the upper envelope of the class of all $v\in \mathrm{PSH}(B)$ with $\varlimsup _{B\ni z\to x}v(z)\le \varphi (x)$ for every $x\in \partial B$. If $\varphi $ is the restriction of a $C^2$ function on a neighborhood of $\partial B$, then $H\in C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$. Proof. After an affine change of coordinates $z\mapsto z_0+Rz$ with $R>0$, we may assume that $B$ is the unit ball; plurisubharmonicity, the boundary conditions, $C^2$ data and the vanishing of the Monge–Ampère measure are preserved by such a change, by proposition 5.9.3 and proposition 7.2.2 (5). We call the functions $v$ in the statement the subsolutions for $\varphi $ of the homogeneous equation. If $v$ is a subsolution for $\varphi $ and $\varphi \le \varphi '+c$ on $\partial B$ with a constant $c$, then $v-c$ is a subsolution for $\varphi '$. Every subsolution is subharmonic on $B$ (theorem 5.9.1 ), so the comparison principle (theorem 3.4.5 and the remark following it), applied with the harmonic function $P\varphi $, the Poisson integral of $\varphi $ given by theorem 3.1.18 , gives $v\le P\varphi $, and $P\varphi \le \max _{\partial B}\varphi $ because the Poisson kernel is positive with integral $1$. Hence, as soon as the class of subsolutions is nonempty, its upper envelope $H$ is defined, and $H\le P\varphi $. Step 1: the envelope for $C^2$ data. Suppose that $\varphi $ is the restriction of a $C^2$ function on a neighborhood of $\partial B$. Multiplying this function by a cutoff equal to $1$ near $\partial B$, we obtain a $C^2$ function $\tilde\varphi $ with compact support in $\mathbb {C}^ n$ and $\tilde\varphi =\varphi $ on $\partial B$. Its complex Hessian is continuous with compact support, so there is $\lambda >0$ with $\sum _{j,k}\tilde\varphi _{j\bar k}\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k\ge -\lambda |\xi |^2$ everywhere. The function $s=\tilde\varphi +\lambda (|z|^2-1)$ is then of class $C^2$ with positive semidefinite complex Hessian, so it is plurisubharmonic by proposition 5.9.2 . As $s=\varphi $ on $\partial B$, it is a subsolution. Hence $s\le H\le P\varphi $. By theorem 5.10.2 , the upper semicontinuous regularization $H^*$ is plurisubharmonic, and $s\le H^*\le P\varphi $ since $P\varphi $ is continuous. As $s$ and $P\varphi $ are continuous on $\overline B$ with boundary values $\varphi $, we have $H^*(z)\to \varphi (x)$ as $z\to x\in \partial B$; so $H^*$ is a subsolution, $H^*\le H$, and $H=H^*$ is plurisubharmonic. Moreover $H(z)\to \varphi (x)$ as $z\to x\in \partial B$, and $H$ is bounded. Step 2: second differences. Let $K\subset B$ be compact, and let $S_{a,h}$, $h_0$ and $C$ be as in lemma 7.7.1 . For $x\in \partial B$ and $a\in K$, the function $g(h)=\tilde\varphi (S_{a,h}(x))$, $|h|\le h_0$, is of class $C^2$, and by the chain rule its second derivatives are bounded by a constant $2C_ K$ independent of $a$ and $x$, since the first and second derivatives of $\tilde\varphi $ are bounded and those of $S_{a,h}(x)$ with respect to $h$ are bounded by $C$. Since $g(0)=\varphi (x)$, Taylor's formula with integral remainder gives $g(h)+g(-h)-2g(0)=\int _0^1(1-t)\bigl (D^2g(th)[h,h]+D^2g(-th)[h,h]\bigr )\, \mathrm dt\le 2C_ K|h|^2$. As $S_{a,\pm h}$ maps $\partial B$ to $\partial B$, where $\tilde\varphi =\varphi $, this reads \[  \tfrac 12\bigl (\varphi \circ S_{a,h}+\varphi \circ S_{a,-h}\bigr ) \le \varphi +C_ K|h|^2\quad \text{on }\partial B\qquad (a\in K,\  |h|\le h_0).  \] The function $w=\frac12(H\circ S_{a,h}+H\circ S_{a,-h})-C_ K|h|^2$ is plurisubharmonic on $B$, by proposition 5.9.3 , proposition 5.9.5 , since $S_{a,\pm h}$ are automorphisms of $B$ and $H$ is bounded. If $y\in \partial B$ and $z\to y$ in $B$, then $S_{a,\pm h}(z)\to S_{a,\pm h}(y)\in \partial B$, so $H(S_{a,\pm h}(z))\to \varphi (S_{a,\pm h}(y))$ by Step 1, and the preceding inequality gives $\varlimsup _{z\to y}w(z)\le \varphi (y)$. Thus $w$ is a subsolution, so $w\le H$. Evaluating at $z=a$, where $S_{a,\pm h}(a)=a\pm h$, we obtain \[  H(a+h)+H(a-h)-2H(a)\le 2C_ K|h|^2\qquad (a\in K,\  |h|\le h_0).  \] Since $K$ was arbitrary and the points $a\pm h=S_{a,\pm h}(a)$ lie in $B$, lemma 7.7.2 applies on $U=B$. Thus $H$ is continuous on $B$ and belongs to $C^{1,1}_{\mathrm{loc}}(B)$, and its distributional real Hessian $A$ and complex Hessian $(H_{j\bar k})$ have the properties stated there: the second-order expansion holds almost everywhere, $(H_{j\bar k})$ is positive semidefinite almost everywhere, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=n!\, \pi ^{-n}\det (H_{j\bar k})\, \mathrm dV_{2n}$. Step 3: the equation. Suppose that $\det (H_{j\bar k})>0$ on a set of positive measure, and choose a point $a$ of this set at which $(H_{j\bar k}(a))$ is positive semidefinite and the second-order expansion holds. The Taylor polynomial $Q(z)=H(a)+\nabla H(a)\cdot (z-a)+\frac12(z-a)^ tA(a)(z-a)$ is a real quadratic polynomial with real Hessian $A(a)$, so its complex Hessian is the constant matrix $(H_{j\bar k}(a))$; this matrix is positive semidefinite with positive determinant, hence positive definite. Let $\eta >0$ be smaller than its smallest eigenvalue; then $Q-\eta |z-a|^2$ has positive semidefinite complex Hessian and is plurisubharmonic (proposition 5.9.2 ). For sufficiently small $r>0$ we have $\overline{B(a,r)}\subset B$ and, by the expansion, $|H-Q|<\eta r^2/2$ on the sphere $|z-a|=r$. The polynomial $\tilde Q=Q-\eta |z-a|^2+\eta r^2/4$ is then strictly smaller than $H$ on that sphere, since there $\tilde Q<H+\eta r^2/2-3\eta r^2/4$, and $\tilde Q(a)=H(a)+\eta r^2/4>H(a)$. By proposition 5.9.5 , applied with $D=B(a,r)$ and $v=\tilde Q$, whose boundary inequality holds because $\tilde Q$ and $H$ are continuous, the function equal to $\max \{ H,\tilde Q\} $ on $B(a,r)$ and to $H$ elsewhere is plurisubharmonic on $B$. It coincides with $H$ near $\partial B$, so it is a subsolution, and it exceeds $H$ at $a$, a contradiction. Hence $\det (H_{j\bar k})=0$ almost everywhere, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=0$. This proves the theorem for $C^2$ data, including the $C^{1,1}$ regularity, except for uniqueness. Step 4: continuous data and uniqueness. For continuous $\varphi $, the function $z\mapsto \varphi (z/|z|)$ is continuous on the annulus $\{ 1/2<|z|<2\} $, and its mollifications $\varphi _ j$, $j\ge 4$, are smooth on the neighborhood $\{ 3/4<|z|<3/2\} $ of $\partial B$ and converge to $\varphi $ uniformly on $\partial B$ (lemma 2.5.1 (1)). Let $H_ j$ be the envelope for $\varphi _ j|_{\partial B}$; by Steps 1–3 it is continuous on $\overline B$ with boundary values $\varphi _ j$, plurisubharmonic, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ j)^ n=0$. Put $c_ j=\max _{\partial B}|\varphi _ j-\varphi |$. Since $H_ j-c_ j$ is a subsolution for $\varphi $, the class of subsolutions for $\varphi $ is nonempty, and its envelope $H$ satisfies $H_ j-c_ j\le H$; symmetrically, $H-c_ j\le H_ j$. Therefore $\sup _ B|H_ j-H|\le c_ j\to 0$, so $H$ is a uniform limit of continuous functions on $B$; it is continuous, extends continuously to $\overline B$ with the boundary values $\varphi $, and is plurisubharmonic, being equal to its regularization $H^*$, which is plurisubharmonic by theorem 5.10.2 . By proposition 7.2.6 , $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=\lim _ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ j)^ n=0$. Finally, if $H'$ and $H''$ are two solutions, then $H'-H''\to 0$ at $\partial B$, and the last assertion of theorem 7.3.11 , applied in both directions, gives $H'=H''$. $\square$

Corollary 7.7.5 . 2E8B947536C1 Let $u$ be a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, and let $B\Subset \Omega $ be a ball. There is a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $\widehat u$ on $\Omega $ which equals $u$ outside $B$, satisfies $\widehat u\ge u$ on $B$, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widehat u)^ n=0$ on $B$. The function $\widehat u$ is increasing in $u$, and its restriction to $B$ is the largest plurisubharmonic function $v$ on $B$ with $\varlimsup _{B
i z	o x}v(z)\le u(x)$ for every $x\in \partial B$. Proof. Let $u_ j=u*ho _{\varepsilon _ j}$, with $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$ smaller than the distance from $\overline B$ to $\mathbb C^ n\setminus \Omega $, be radial regularizations of $u$; they are smooth plurisubharmonic functions on a neighborhood of $\overline B$ decreasing to $u$ (proposition 5.9.2 ). Let $H_ j$ be the solution of theorem 7.7.4 with boundary values $u_ j|_{\partial B}$, that is, the upper envelope of the subsolutions for $u_ j|_{\partial B}$. Since $u_ j$ is such a subsolution, $u\le u_ j\le H_ j$ on $B$. Since $u_{j+1}\le u_ j$ on $\partial B$, every subsolution for $u_{j+1}|_{\partial B}$ is one for $u_ j|_{\partial B}$, so the envelopes decrease: $H_{j+1}\le H_ j$. Let $H=\lim _ jH_ j$. The function $H_1$ is subharmonic on $B$ and continuous on $\overline B$ with boundary values $u_1$, so $H_1\le \max _{\partial B}u_1$ by the comparison principle (theorem 3.4.5 ). Hence $\inf _{\overline B}u\le H\le \max _{\partial B}u_1$, so $H$ is bounded; it is plurisubharmonic by theorem 5.10.1 , and theorem 7.3.7 gives $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=\lim _ j(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H_ j)^ n=0$. For $x\in \partial B$, since $H\le H_ j$ and $H_ j$ is continuous on $\overline B$ with $H_ j=u_ j$ on $\partial B$, \[  \varlimsup _{B
i z	o x}H(z)\le u_ j(x)\quad 	ext{for every }j, \qquad 	ext{hence}\quad \varlimsup _{B
i z	o x}H(z)\le u(x).  \] By proposition 5.9.5 , the function $\widehat u$ equal to $\max \{ u,H\} =H$ on $B$ and to $u$ outside $B$ is plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $. It is locally bounded, since $H$ is bounded and $u$ is locally bounded; it equals $u$ outside $B$, satisfies $\widehat u\ge u$ on $B$, and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widehat u)^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}H)^ n=0$ on $B$ by locality. Let $v$ be plurisubharmonic on $B$ with $\varlimsup _{B
i z	o x}v(z)\le u(x)$ for $x\in \partial B$. Since $u\le u_ j$, the function $v$ is a subsolution for the boundary values $u_ j|_{\partial B}$, so $v\le H_ j$ by theorem 7.7.4 . Letting $j	o \infty $ gives $v\le H$. Conversely, $H$ belongs to this class by the displayed estimate, so $H$ is its largest member. If $u\le u'$, the class for $u$ is contained in the class for $u'$, which proves that $\widehat u\le \widehat{u'}$. $\square$

text: Definition 7.7.6 . FD8547B922C9 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open. A plurisubharmonic function $u$ on $\Omega $ is maximal if every plurisubharmonic function $v$ on $\Omega $ with $v\le u$ outside a compact subset of $\Omega $ satisfies $v\le u$ everywhere.

title: Theorem 7.7.7
section: 7.7 The homogeneous Dirichlet problem and balayage
text: Theorem 7.7.7 . BCFDDA1FCB7A A locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $u$ on an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ is maximal if and only if $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$. In particular, maximality is a local property for locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions. Proof. Suppose that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$, and let $v$ be plurisubharmonic on $\Omega $ with $v\le u$ outside a compact set $K$. Choose a bounded open set $D$ with $K\subset D\Subset \Omega $. By upper semicontinuity, $v$ is bounded above on $\overline D$; since $u$ is bounded on $\overline D$, we may choose $M$ with $-M<\inf _ Du$. The function $\max \{ v,-M\} $ is bounded and plurisubharmonic on $D$, and it is at most $u$ on $D\setminus K$; since every point of $D$ near $\partial D$ lies in $D\setminus K$, we get $\varliminf _{D\ni z\to x}(u(z)-\max \{ v(z),-M\} )\ge 0$ for $x\in \partial D$. The last assertion of theorem 7.3.11 therefore gives $\max \{ v,-M\} \le u$ on $D$. Hence $v\le u$ everywhere, and $u$ is maximal. Conversely, suppose that $u$ is maximal, and let $B\Subset \Omega $ be a ball. The function $\widehat u$ of corollary 7.7.5 is plurisubharmonic, satisfies $\widehat u\ge u$, and equals $u$ outside the compact set $\overline B$. Maximality gives $\widehat u\le u$, so $\widehat u=u$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}\widehat u)^ n=0$ on $B$. Since the balls $B\Subset \Omega $ cover $\Omega $, and a distribution vanishing on each member of a family of open sets vanishes on their union (lemma 2.5.2 ), $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$ on $\Omega $. For the last assertion, let every point of $\Omega $ have an open neighborhood $U$ such that $u|_ U$ is maximal on $U$. By the first part applied on $U$, and by locality of the products (proposition 7.2.2 ), $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ vanishes on each such $U$, hence on $\Omega $, and $u$ is maximal on $\Omega $. Conversely, if $u$ is maximal on $\Omega $, then $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=0$ on every open set $U\subset \Omega $, so $u|_ U$ is maximal on $U$. $\square$

title: 7.8 Density lower bounds and mixed products
search_title: Density lower bounds and mixed products
section: 7.8 Density lower bounds and mixed products
text: We now turn to the equation $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\mu $ with a prescribed measure $\mu $ on a ball, and to the lower bounds that mixed products inherit from lower bounds of the pure Monge–Ampère measures. From here to the end of section 7.12 , $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ is open, $n\ge 1$, and \[  \eta =\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}|z|^2=\beta /\pi ,\qquad \text{so that}\qquad \eta ^ n=\frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}\, \mathrm dV_{2n}  \] by ( 7.2.4 ). Densities of Monge–Ampère measures are taken with respect to $\eta ^ n$; thus, by ( 7.2.4 ) and the remark following proposition 7.2.6 , a plurisubharmonic function $u\in C^2(\Omega )$ satisfies $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n=\det (u_{j\bar k})\, \eta ^ n$. A lower bound $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ is a nonlinear condition on $u$, and it is not evident that it is preserved by convolution. We show that, for a continuous density $f$, it can be tested pointwise with $C^2$ functions touching $u$ from above, and that it is equivalent to a family of linear elliptic inequalities, one for each positive definite Hermitian matrix of determinant one (proposition 7.8.3 ). Two lemmas prepare it: an expression of $(\det A)^{1/n}$ as an infimum of traces, and a passage from test functions to distributions. Since linear inequalities are preserved by convolution, the determinant inequalities for mixed products of smooth functions then pass to locally bounded potentials (corollary 7.8.4 , corollary 7.8.8 ). The same characterization will make subsolutions of the Dirichlet problem stable under the operations used in section 7.9 . Let $u$ be a real function on an open subset of $\mathbb R^ d$. A real $C^2$ function $q$ defined near a point $x$ touches $u$ from above at $x$ if $q(x)=u(x)$ and $q\ge u$ on a neighborhood of $x$; we then call $q$ an upper test function for $u$ at $x$. Lemma 7.8.1 . BB19C89586B1 Let $A$ be a positive semidefinite Hermitian $n\times n$ matrix. Then \[  (\det A)^{1/n}=\inf \left\{ \frac{\operatorname {tr}(BA)}n:\  B\text{ positive definite Hermitian},\  \det B=1\right\} .  \] If $C$ is another positive semidefinite Hermitian $n\times n$ matrix, define the numbers $M_ k(A,C)$, $0\le k\le n$, by \[  \det (tA+sC)=\sum _{k=0}^ n\binom nk M_ k(A,C)\, t^ ks^{n-k}\qquad (t,s\in \mathbb R).  \] Then $M_ n(A,C)=\det A$, $M_0(A,C)=\det C$, and for each integer $1\le k\le n-1$, \[  M_ k(A,C)\ge (\det A)^{k/n}(\det C)^{(n-k)/n}.  \] Proof. Let $B$ be positive definite with $\det B=1$. The positive semidefinite matrix $B^{1/2}AB^{1/2}$ has trace $\operatorname {tr}(BA)$ and determinant $\det A$, so the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality for its eigenvalues gives $\operatorname {tr}(BA)/n\ge (\det A)^{1/n}$. If $A$ is positive definite, equality holds for $B=(\det A)^{1/n}A^{-1}$. If $A$ is singular, the matrices $B_\varepsilon =\det (A+\varepsilon I)^{1/n}(A+\varepsilon I)^{-1}$, $\varepsilon >0$, are admissible and \[  0\le \operatorname {tr}(B_\varepsilon A)\le \operatorname {tr}\bigl (B_\varepsilon (A+\varepsilon I)\bigr )=n\det (A+\varepsilon I)^{1/n}\longrightarrow 0  \] as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. The formulas for $M_ n$ and $M_0$ follow from $\det (tA)=t^ n\det A$ and $\det (sC)=s^ n\det C$. Suppose first that $A$ and $C$ are positive definite, and let $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ n>0$ be the eigenvalues of $A^{-1/2}CA^{-1/2}$. Since $\det (tA+sC)=\det A\prod _{i=1}^ n(t+s\lambda _ i)$, comparison of coefficients gives \[  M_ k(A,C)=\frac{\det A}{\binom nk}\sum _{|J|=n-k}\prod _{j\in J}\lambda _ j,  \] the sum being over the subsets $J\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} $ with $n-k$ elements. Each eigenvalue occurs in exactly $\binom {n-1}{n-k-1}$ of these $\binom n{n-k}$ products, so the geometric mean of the products is $(\lambda _1\cdots \lambda _ n)^{(n-k)/n}$. Since $\lambda _1\cdots \lambda _ n=\det C/\det A$, the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives \[  M_ k(A,C)\ge \det A\left(\frac{\det C}{\det A}\right)^{(n-k)/n}=(\det A)^{k/n}(\det C)^{(n-k)/n}.  \] For semidefinite $A$ and $C$, apply this to $A+\varepsilon I$ and $C+\varepsilon I$ and let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; both sides depend continuously on the matrices. $\square$ Lemma 7.8.2 . 1BE242B641AA Let $d\ge 1$, let $(c_{kl})$ be a real symmetric positive definite $d\times d$ matrix, and put $L=\sum _{k,l=1}^ dc_{kl}\partial _ k\partial _ l$. Let $U\subset \mathbb R^ d$ be open, let $w\colon U\to \mathbb R$ be upper semicontinuous, and let $F\colon U\to \mathbb R$ be continuous. Suppose that, for every $x\in U$, every upper test function $q$ for $w$ at $x$ satisfies $Lq(x)\ge F(x)$. Then $w$ is locally integrable, and $Lw\ge F$ in the sense of distributions on $U$. Proof. We reduce to the Laplacian, treat the case $F=0$ by a maximum principle argument, and reduce the general case to it. Step 1. Reduction to $L=\Delta $. Let $C=(c_{kl})$, let $P$ be the positive definite square root of $C^{-1}$, so that $PCP=I$, and put $\tilde U=P(U)$, $\tilde w=w\circ P^{-1}$ and $\tilde F=F\circ P^{-1}$. If $q$ is a $C^2$ function near $x\in U$ and $\tilde q=q\circ P^{-1}$, then $\partial _ k\partial _ lq(x)=\sum _{a,b}P_{ak}P_{bl}(\partial _ a\partial _ b\tilde q)(Px)$ by the chain rule, and hence \[  (Lq)(x)=\sum _{a,b}(PCP)_{ab}(\partial _ a\partial _ b\tilde q)(Px)=(\Delta \tilde q)(Px).  \] The map $q\mapsto \tilde q$ is a bijection from the upper test functions for $w$ at $x$ onto those for $\tilde w$ at $Px$, so $\tilde w$, $\Delta $ and $\tilde F$ satisfy the hypothesis of the lemma on $\tilde U$. Suppose that the lemma holds for them. Then $w=\tilde w\circ P$ is locally integrable, and for every nonnegative test function $\chi $ on $U$ the change of variables $y=Px$, with $\tilde\chi =\chi \circ P^{-1}$ and $L\chi =(\Delta \tilde\chi )\circ P$, gives \[  \langle Lw,\chi \rangle =\int _ Uw\, L\chi \, \mathrm dx =\frac1{|\det P|}\int _{\tilde U}\tilde w\, \Delta \tilde\chi \, \mathrm dy \ge \frac1{|\det P|}\int _{\tilde U}\tilde F\tilde\chi \, \mathrm dy=\int _ UF\chi \, \mathrm dx;  \] the first equality is the definition of distributional derivatives. We may therefore assume that $L=\Delta $. Step 2. The case $F=0$. We show that $w$ satisfies assertion (1) of theorem 3.4.5 for every ball $D=B(y,r)$ with $\overline{B(y,r)}\subset U$; by the converse part of that theorem, $w$ is then subharmonic on $U$. Let $h$ be a real function which is harmonic on $B(y,r)$ and continuous on $\overline{B(y,r)}$, with $\varlimsup _{B(y,r)\ni x\to \zeta }w(x)\le h(\zeta )$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B(y,r)$, and suppose that $w(x_1)>h(x_1)$ for some $x_1\in B(y,r)$. Choose $\varepsilon >0$ so small that the upper semicontinuous function $g(x)=w(x)-h(x)-\varepsilon (r^2-|x-y|^2)$ on $B(y,r)$ satisfies $g(x_1)>0$. Since $h$ is continuous on the closed ball, $\varlimsup _{B(y,r)\ni x\to \zeta }g(x)\le 0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B(y,r)$. Hence every $\zeta \in \partial B(y,r)$ has an open neighborhood $N_\zeta $ with $g<g(x_1)/2$ on $N_\zeta \cap B(y,r)$; finitely many of these neighborhoods cover the sphere, and the complement $K$ of their union in $\overline{B(y,r)}$ is a compact subset of $B(y,r)$ containing $x_1$. The upper semicontinuous function $g$ attains its maximum over $K$ at a point $x_0$, and $c=g(x_0)\ge g(x_1)>0$; since $g<g(x_1)/2$ outside $K$, we have $g\le c$ on $B(y,r)$. The function $q=h+\varepsilon (r^2-|x-y|^2)+c$ is smooth on $B(y,r)$, satisfies $q-w=c-g\ge 0$ there and $q(x_0)=w(x_0)$, so it is an upper test function for $w$ at $x_0$. But $\Delta q=-2d\varepsilon <0$, which contradicts the hypothesis. Hence $w\le h$ on $B(y,r)$, and $w$ is subharmonic on $U$. Being real-valued, it is not identically $-\infty $ on any connected component of $U$, so theorem 3.4.12 (1) shows that $w$ is locally integrable and $\Delta w\ge 0$. Step 3. The general case. Let $V\Subset U$ be open. Every compact subset of $U$ lies in such a set $V$, so it suffices to show that $w$ is locally integrable on $V$ and that $\Delta w\ge F$ on $V$. Choose an open set $V'$ with $\overline V\subset V'\Subset U$. By lemma 2.5.1 (1), the mollifications of $F$ converge to $F$ uniformly on $\overline{V'}$; subtracting from each of them its maximal deviation from $F$ on $\overline{V'}$, we obtain smooth functions $F_ j$ on a neighborhood of $\overline{V'}$ such that $F_ j\le F$ on $\overline{V'}$ and $F_ j\to F$ uniformly there. Let $\vartheta \in C^\infty _ c(V')$ be equal to one on an open set $W\supset \overline V$ (lemma 2.5.1 (4)). By proposition 3.1.13 , the convolution $h_ j=E_ d*(\vartheta F_ j)$, where $\vartheta F_ j$ is extended by zero, is a smooth function on $\mathbb R^ d$ with $\Delta h_ j=\vartheta F_ j$; in particular $\Delta h_ j=F_ j$ on $W$. If $q$ is an upper test function for $w-h_ j$ at $x\in V$, then $q+h_ j$ is an upper test function for $w$ at $x$, so that $\Delta q(x)+F_ j(x)\ge F(x)$, that is, $\Delta q(x)\ge F(x)-F_ j(x)\ge 0$. Step 2, applied to the real upper semicontinuous function $w-h_ j$ on $V$, shows that $w-h_ j$ is locally integrable on $V$ and $\Delta (w-h_ j)\ge 0$ there. Hence $w$ is locally integrable on $V$ and $\Delta w\ge F_ j$ on $V$. Testing against a nonnegative test function on $V$ and letting $j\to \infty $, we obtain $\Delta w\ge F$ on $V$. $\square$ For a real $C^2$ function $q$ on an open subset of $\mathbb C^ n$, we write $\mathcal H(q)=(q_{j\bar k})$ for its complex Hessian matrix, normalized as in ( 5.2.9 ). For a positive definite Hermitian matrix $B$ with $\det B=1$, put \[  L_ Bq=\operatorname {tr}\bigl (B\mathcal H(q)\bigr ).  \] This is a real operator with constant coefficients, since $B$ and $\mathcal H(q)$ are Hermitian, and it is elliptic. Indeed, write $B=V\operatorname {diag}(b_1,\ldots ,b_ n)V^*$ with $V$ unitary and $b_1,\ldots ,b_ n>0$, and introduce coordinates $\zeta $ by $z=\bar V\zeta $. By the chain rule, the complex Hessian of $\tilde q(\zeta )=q(\bar V\zeta )$ is $V^*\mathcal H(q)V$, so that \[  L_ Bq=\operatorname {tr}\bigl (\operatorname {diag}(b_1,\ldots ,b_ n)\, V^*\mathcal H(q)V\bigr )=\sum _{j=1}^ nb_ j\tilde q_{j\bar j}=\frac14\sum _{j=1}^ nb_ j\Delta _ j\tilde q  \] by ( 5.2.9 ), where $\Delta _ j$ is the Laplacian in the variable $\zeta _ j$. The real-linear map $z\mapsto \zeta $ is orthogonal on $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$; let $O$ be its matrix. By the chain rule, in the real coordinates of $\mathbb C^ n$ the operator $L_ B$ takes the form $\sum _{k,l}c_{kl}\partial _ k\partial _ l$ with $(c_{kl})=O^ t\Lambda O$, where $\Lambda $ is the diagonal matrix with entries $b_1/4,b_1/4,\ldots ,b_ n/4,b_ n/4$. This matrix is symmetric and positive definite, so lemma 7.8.2 applies to $L_ B$. Proposition 7.8.3 . EB2AFC8FB17C Let $u$ be a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function on $\Omega $, and let $f\ge 0$ be a continuous function on $\Omega $. The following conditions are equivalent: $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ as measures on $\Omega $; $\det \mathcal H(q)(x)\ge f(x)$ for every $x\in \Omega $ and every upper test function $q$ for $u$ at $x$; $L_ Bu\ge nf^{1/n}$ in the sense of distributions on $\Omega $, for every positive definite Hermitian matrix $B$ with $\det B=1$. If these conditions hold, then for every $\varepsilon >0$ the mollification $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $ satisfies $\det \mathcal H(u_\varepsilon )\ge (f^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )^ n$ on $\Omega _\varepsilon $. Proof. We first observe that the complex Hessian $\mathcal H(q)(x)$ of an upper test function $q$ for $u$ at $x$ is positive semidefinite. Indeed, let $\xi \in \mathbb C^ n\setminus \{ 0\} $, and let $r>0$ be so small that the closed disc $\{ x+\zeta \xi :|\zeta |\le r\} $ lies in the neighborhood of $x$ on which $q\ge u$. The function $\zeta \mapsto u(x+\zeta \xi )$ is subharmonic near this disc and finite at $\zeta =0$, so theorem 3.4.5 (2) gives \[  q(x)=u(x)\le \frac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }u(x+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }\xi )\, \mathrm d\theta \le \frac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }q(x+r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }\xi )\, \mathrm d\theta .  \] Write $q_ j=\partial _{z_ j}q$ and $q_{jk}=\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{z_ k}q$. Since $q$ is real and of class $C^2$, Taylor's formula gives \[  q(x+h)=q(x)+2\operatorname{Re}\sum _ jq_ j(x)h_ j+\operatorname{Re}\sum _{j,k}q_{jk}(x)h_ jh_ k+\sum _{j,k}q_{j\bar k}(x)h_ j\bar h_ k+o(|h|^2).  \] For $h=r\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }\xi $ the terms containing $\mathrm e^{\mathrm i\theta }$ and $\mathrm e^{2\mathrm i\theta }$ have mean zero over $\theta \in [0,2\pi ]$, so the right-hand side of the preceding display equals $q(x)+r^2\sum _{j,k}q_{j\bar k}(x)\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k+o(r^2)$. Dividing by $r^2$ and letting $r\downarrow 0$, we obtain $\sum _{j,k}q_{j\bar k}(x)\xi _ j\bar\xi _ k\ge 0$. (1) implies (2). Assume (1), let $q$ be an upper test function for $u$ at $x$, and suppose that $\det \mathcal H(q)(x)<f(x)$. Since $\mathcal H(q)(x)$ is positive semidefinite, we can choose $\delta >0$ so small that $q_\delta =q+\delta |z-x|^2$ satisfies $\mathcal H(q_\delta )(x)=\mathcal H(q)(x)+\delta I>0$ and still $\det \mathcal H(q_\delta )(x)<f(x)$. Since $q$ is of class $C^2$ and $f$ is continuous, there is $r>0$ such that $\overline{B(x,r)}\subset \Omega $, $q\ge u$ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$, the complex Hessian $\mathcal H(q_\delta )$ is positive definite on $\overline{B(x,r)}$, and $\det \mathcal H(q_\delta )<f$ on $\overline{B(x,r)}$; in particular, $q_\delta $ is plurisubharmonic on $B(x,r)$ by proposition 5.9.2 . Put $b=q_\delta -\delta r^2/2$. Then $b=q+\delta r^2/2>u$ on the sphere $\partial B(x,r)$, while $b(x)=u(x)-\delta r^2/2<u(x)$. The Borel set $S=\{ z\in B(x,r):b(z)<u(z)\} $ has positive Lebesgue measure. Otherwise $\max \{ u,b\} =b$ almost everywhere on $B(x,r)$; since both functions are plurisubharmonic, the uniqueness assertion of theorem 5.9.1 gives $\max \{ u,b\} =b$ everywhere, contradicting $b(x)<u(x)$. The function $b-u$ is lower semicontinuous and positive on $\partial B(x,r)$, so $\varliminf _{z\to \zeta }(b(z)-u(z))>0$ for every $\zeta \in \partial B(x,r)$. The comparison principle theorem 7.3.11 , applied on $B(x,r)$ with the bounded plurisubharmonic functions $b$ and $u$ in place of $u$ and $v$, therefore gives \[  \int _ S f\eta ^ n\le \int _ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\le \int _ S(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b)^ n=\int _ S\det \mathcal H(q_\delta )\, \eta ^ n.  \] Here $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}b)^ n=\det \mathcal H(q_\delta )\, \eta ^ n$ on $B(x,r)$ because $b$ is a plurisubharmonic $C^2$ function there (see the beginning of this section), and the integrals are finite because $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ is a Radon measure on $\Omega $ and $\overline{B(x,r)}$ is a compact subset of $\Omega $. Since $\det \mathcal H(q_\delta )<f$ on $S$ and $S$ has positive measure, the right side is strictly smaller than the left side, a contradiction. Thus (2) holds. (2) implies (3). Let $q$ be an upper test function for $u$ at $x$, and let $B$ be positive definite with $\det B=1$. Since $\mathcal H(q)(x)$ is positive semidefinite, the infimum formula of lemma 7.8.1 and (2) give \[  L_ Bq(x)=\operatorname {tr}\bigl (B\mathcal H(q)(x)\bigr )\ge n\bigl (\det \mathcal H(q)(x)\bigr )^{1/n}\ge nf(x)^{1/n}.  \] Since $u$ is real-valued and upper semicontinuous, lemma 7.8.2 , applied to $L_ B$ and the continuous function $nf^{1/n}$, gives (3). (3) implies (1). The mollifications $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $ of section 2.5 are smooth plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ which decrease to $u$ as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ (proposition 5.9.2 ). Fix $B$ as in (3). The distribution $L_ Bu-nf^{1/n}$ is positive, so its mollification is a nonnegative function on $\Omega _\varepsilon $ (proposition 2.5.3 (3)). Since $L_ B$ has constant coefficients, proposition 2.5.3 (1) identifies the mollification of $L_ Bu$ with $L_ Bu_\varepsilon $, and we obtain the pointwise inequality \[  \operatorname {tr}\bigl (B\mathcal H(u_\varepsilon )\bigr )\ge n\, (f^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )\quad \text{on }\Omega _\varepsilon \qquad (B>0,\  \det B=1).  \] Since $\mathcal H(u_\varepsilon )$ is positive semidefinite (proposition 5.9.2 ), taking the infimum over $B$ and using lemma 7.8.1 , we obtain $\det \mathcal H(u_\varepsilon )\ge (f^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )^ n$, which is the last assertion of the proposition. By the formula recalled at the beginning of this section, it reads \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon )^ n\ge (f^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )^ n\eta ^ n\quad \text{on }\Omega _\varepsilon .  \] As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the density on the right converges locally uniformly to $f$ by lemma 2.5.1 (1), and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon )^ n\to (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n$ weakly by theorem 7.3.7 , applied along any sequence $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$. Testing against nonnegative functions in $C_ c(\Omega )$ gives (1). $\square$ Corollary 7.8.4 . EADDEAF9FAD9 Let $u,v$ be locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions on $\Omega $, and let $f,g\ge 0$ be continuous functions on $\Omega $ such that $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ n\ge f\eta ^ n$ and $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^ n\ge g\eta ^ n$. Then, for each integer $1\le k\le n-1$, \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-k}\ge f^{k/n}g^{(n-k)/n}\eta ^ n.  \] For $k=0$ and $k=n$ the same inequality is the hypothesis. Proof. Let $u_\varepsilon =u*\rho _\varepsilon $ and $v_\varepsilon =v*\rho _\varepsilon $, with the same mollifiers for both functions. By the last assertion of proposition 7.8.3 , applied to $u$ with the density $f$ and to $v$ with the density $g$, \[  \det \mathcal H(u_\varepsilon )\ge (f^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )^ n, \qquad \det \mathcal H(v_\varepsilon )\ge (g^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )^ n.  \] For real $t$ and $s$, ( 7.2.4 ), applied to the smooth function $tu_\varepsilon +sv_\varepsilon $, gives $(t\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon +s\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^ n=\det \bigl (t\mathcal H(u_\varepsilon )+s\mathcal H(v_\varepsilon )\bigr )\eta ^ n$ for the exterior powers of smooth forms. Since $2$-forms commute, the left side can be expanded by the binomial formula. Comparing the coefficients of $\binom nkt^ ks^{n-k}$, and recalling that Bedford–Taylor products of smooth functions are exterior products of smooth forms (proposition 7.2.2 (1)), we find \[  (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u_\varepsilon )^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v_\varepsilon )^{n-k}=M_ k\bigl (\mathcal H(u_\varepsilon ),\mathcal H(v_\varepsilon )\bigr )\eta ^ n\ge (f^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )^ k(g^{1/n}*\rho _\varepsilon )^{n-k}\eta ^ n,  \] where the inequality is the second assertion of lemma 7.8.1 , applied to the matrices $\mathcal H(u_\varepsilon )$ and $\mathcal H(v_\varepsilon )$, which are positive semidefinite by proposition 5.9.2 . As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, the density on the right converges locally uniformly to $f^{k/n}g^{(n-k)/n}$, while the left side converges weakly to $(\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}u)^ k\wedge (\mathrm{dd}^{\mathrm{c}}v)^{n-k}$ by theorem 7.3.7 , since $u_\varepsilon $ and $v_\varepsilon $ are smooth plurisubharmonic functions decreasing to $u$ and $v$ (proposition 5.9.2 ). $\square$

title: Lemma 7.8.1
section: 7.8 Density lower bounds and mixed products
text: Lemma 7.8.1 . BB19C89586B1 Let $A$ be a positive semidefinite Hermitian $n\times n$ matrix. Then \[  (\det A)^{1/n}=\inf \left\{ \frac{\operatorname {tr}(BA)}n:\  B\text{ positive definite Hermitian},\  \det B=1\right\} .  \] If $C$ is another positive semidefinite Hermitian $n\times n$ matrix, define the numbers $M_ k(A,C)$, $0\le k\le n$, by \[  \det (tA+sC)=\sum _{k=0}^ n\binom nk M_ k(A,C)\, t^ ks^{n-k}\qquad (t,s\in \mathbb R).  \] Then $M_ n(A,C)=\det A$, $M_0(A,C)=\det C$, and for each integer $1\le k\le n-1$, \[  M_ k(A,C)\ge (\det A)^{k/n}(\det C)^{(n-k)/n}.  \] Proof. Let $B$ be positive definite with $\det B=1$. The positive semidefinite matrix $B^{1/2}AB^{1/2}$ has trace $\operatorname {tr}(BA)$ and determinant $\det A$, so the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality for its eigenvalues gives $\operatorname {tr}(BA)/n\ge (\det A)^{1/n}$. If $A$ is positive definite, equality holds for $B=(\det A)^{1/n}A^{-1}$. If $A$ is singular, the matrices $B_\varepsilon =\det (A+\varepsilon I)^{1/n}(A+\varepsilon I)^{-1}$, $\varepsilon >0$, are admissible and \[  0\le \operatorname {tr}(B_\varepsilon A)\le \operatorname {tr}\bigl (B_\varepsilon (A+\varepsilon I)\bigr )=n\det (A+\varepsilon I)^{1/n}\longrightarrow 0  \] as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$. The formulas for $M_ n$ and $M_0$ follow from $\det (tA)=t^ n\det A$ and $\det (sC)=s^ n\det C$. Suppose first that $A$ and $C$ are positive definite, and let $\lambda _1,\ldots ,\lambda _ n>0$ be the eigenvalues of $A^{-1/2}CA^{-1/2}$. Since $\det (tA+sC)=\det A\prod _{i=1}^ n(t+s\lambda _ i)$, comparison of coefficients gives \[  M_ k(A,C)=\frac{\det A}{\binom nk}\sum _{|J|=n-k}\prod _{j\in J}\lambda _ j,  \] the sum being over the subsets $J\subset \{ 1,\ldots ,n\} $ with $n-k$ elements. Each eigenvalue occurs in exactly $\binom {n-1}{n-k-1}$ of these $\binom n{n-k}$ products, so the geometric mean of the products is $(\lambda _1\cdots \lambda _ n)^{(n-k)/n}$. Since $\lambda _1\cdots \lambda _ n=\det C/\det A$, the arithmetic–geometric mean inequality gives \[  M_ k(A,C)\ge \det A\left(\frac{\det C}{\det A}\right)^{(n-k)/n}=(\det A)^{k/n}(\det C)^{(n-k)/n}.  \] For semidefinite $A$ and $C$, apply this to $A+\varepsilon I$ and $C+\varepsilon I$ and let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$; both sides depend continuously on the matrices. $\square$
